artigo.texto: Data center é o espaço físico que armazena toda a estrutura de computação necessária para o processamento, armazenamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais. Eles são importantes para a manutenção de serviços de internet e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial, o que explica o rápido crescimento no número de data centers em todo o mundo. Dentro de um data center, é possível encontrar racks com elementos como switches, firewalls e servidores, bem como bancos de baterias, painéis elétricos e sistemas de refrigeração. Atualmente mais de 180 data centers estão em atividade no Brasil. Devido ao crescente uso da inteligência artificial, o país busca dar continuidade ao seu processo de desenvolvimento tecnológico por meio da atração de novos data centers. Para isso, criou uma medida conhecida como Redata, que foca na oferta de incentivos fiscais com contrapartidas. Contudo, há muitas críticas com relação a essa política por conta dos impactos ambientais dos data centers. Leia também: Por que tem se falado em uma bolha econômica em torno da IA? Data center é o espaço físico onde ficam as máquinas e equipamentos de computação que realizam o armazenamento, o processamento e a transmissão segura de dados digitais. São importantes porque mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet e as ferramentas de inteligência artificial, cuja demanda cresceu de forma acelerada nos últimos anos. A capacidade instalada de data centers cresceu cinco vezes entre 2005 e 2025. O atual número de data centers no mundo passa de 13 mil, maioria dos quais está nos EUA. Dentro de um data center tem, entre outros: racks, onde ficam itens como painéis de conexão, servidores, firewalls e switches; banco de baterias e painéis de energia elétrica; sistemas de ventilação e de refrigeração; equipamentos para o controle de umidade. Três dos principais tipos de data centers são: data centers corporativos, que ficam no interior das próprias empresas; data centers de colocação, que são espaços compartilhados por várias companhias; data centers hiperescala, que são espaços de grande dimensão construídos exclusivamente para as operações de uma única empresa. A rápida difusão dos data centers tem gerado debates e críticas sobre sustentabilidade desse modelo de estabelecimento por conta do elevado consumo de energia e de água. Os data centers também geram poluição sonora e produzem ilhas de calor por conta da elevação da temperatura média do ar, causando alterações no microclima. O Brasil tem mais de 180 data centers, mas aprovou uma medida que promete isenções fiscais para a instalação de novas unidades no território nacional. Data center é um espaço físico onde ficam instaladas todas as máquinas e os equipamentos de computação responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais de serviços em nuvem e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial (IA). Em função da rápida modernização dos sistemas de propagação de informações e de comunicação que aconteceu nas últimas décadas, cresceu, na mesma proporção, a demanda por softwares e serviços de armazenamento em nuvem. Não obstante essas sejam redes que existem e se multiplicam no ciberespaço, elas demandam um outro tipo de rede, dessa vez, física, para se manter. Essa rede física é mantida em data centers. Os data centers são importantes porque eles mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet que nós utilizamos todos os dias. Uma boa parte do nosso sistema moderno de comunicação depende diretamente de aplicações que são mantidas e aperfeiçoadas por meio desse tipo de infraestrutura. Segundo informações da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, em inglês) trazidas pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE)|1|, o número de usuários da internet aumentou em 78% somente entre 2015 e 2022, quando o tráfego global se expandiu aproximadamente seis vezes. Dentro do atual período técnico em que estamos inseridos, empresas, sistemas financeiros e mesmo governos desenvolveram uma alta dependência de ferramentas de TI para a sua gestão. Então, além de serem parte indissociável desse ecossistema de gerenciamento, os data centers são fundamentais para a garantia da eficácia e, sobretudo, da segurança no processamento e armazenamento de informações que, na maioria das vezes, são sensíveis e/ou confidenciais. Esses espaços físicos também são necessários para o funcionamento da inteligência artificial. As ferramentas de IA, entretanto, são bastante complexas e resultam em um trabalho mais intenso do que aquele desempenhado pelas máquinas que compõem os data centers convencionais. Dada a difusão acelerada das ferramentas de IA, que tem sido empregada tanto para atividades corriqueiras quanto para o gerenciamento de empresas e em setores estratégicos, como o energético, os data centers têm se multiplicado em um ritmo semelhante. Para evidenciar a importância dos data centers dentro do presente contexto tecnológico e informacional, basta analisarmos os dados que mostram a evolução da capacidade energética instalada nos data centers. No ano de 2005, essa capacidade ficava em torno de 20 GW, enquanto 20 anos mais tarde, em 2025, ela cresceu para 114,3 GW, segundo dados da IEA|2|. Essa capacidade corresponde a cerca de 13 mil data centers, a maioria dos quais fica nos Estados Unidos (5 mil), na Índia (348) e no Canadá (299)|3|. As seguintes estruturas e equipamentos são encontrados dentro de um data center: Racks, que é onde ficam todos os equipamentos utilizados para o processamento e armazenamento de dados, como patch panels (painel de conexões), switches, acesso remoto, firewalls, servidores, roteadores, fonte de alimentação de energia (UPS ou nobreak), unidades de distribuição de energia e sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração. Sistemas de ventilação e de refrigeração, como as unidades de ar-condicionado de precisão, que são próprias para data centers. Banco de baterias, painéis de energia elétrica, geradores e transformadores, que mantêm o data center opera

artigo.texto: Fears over plans for battery site near school A group of parents whose children attend a rural primary school have said they are concerned by proposals to build a battery storage plant nearby. These sites, also known as battery energy storage systems (BESS), hold energy generated from wind or solar and release it when needed, but there are concerns about fire safety due to the lithium used in the batteries. Elgin Energy's plans for the site would put it less than one kilometre from St Lucia's Primary School and Nursery in Upton Magna, Shropshire. The firm has said it has "taken on board guidance from Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service and the National Fire Chiefs Council" when designing the site. Planning documents state that the school is 811 metres from a "potential fire source", although local residents have claimed 610 metres is a more accurate figure. Kryssy Sochacki's daughter is a student at the primary school, and feels "terrified" by the prospect. "My main focus has been around the safety of the school," she said. "We fully recognise the importance of renewable energy," Sochacki added, but said "the pursuit of renewable energy shouldn't come at the expense of children's safety". "This is just far too close to the school." The excess electricity is stored in BESS, usually inside lithium-ion batteries, so when conditions are calm and overcast it can be sent back into the power grid. Concerns around fire safety stems from the lithium within the batteries, which can cause an explosion when it overheats. A fire at a battery storage unit in Nottinghamshire in May 2026 saw residents advised to keep doors and windows closed. In planning documents, the school is noted to be one of the locations "at greatest risk" of being affected by smoke in the event of a fire. The smoke plume assessment suggests that "winds from the southwest" could carry smoke towards the school "approximately 18% of the time during a fire event". 'Safety a priority' In its planning application, submitted by agents Berry's, Elgin Energy said it had consulted both Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service and the National Fire Chiefs Council". It also said the plans for the 10-acre site had been drawn up with "safety as a priority". It said that included measures including "fire detection in each container, over-temperature protection, ventilation systems, and aerosol fire extinguishing system". Of the 87 public comments on Shropshire Council's planning portal, 85 are objections and just two are in support. According to the National Fire Chiefs Council, "BESS fires are challenging to extinguish and can continue to burn from several hours to several days." Its guidance adds that "smoke plumes from fires can also harm air quality" and that attempting to extinguish a BESS fire using water could "result in large volumes of contaminated fire-water runoff which can have a long-term impact on the environment". As such, the NFCC said the "prevailing view" was to adopt a "controlled burn to minimise runoff." Stef Thomas has two children at the primary school, and said the close proximity of the battery site was her main concern. "If there was a fire, the wind blows in [the direction of the school] more often than not," she said. "It's frightening, honestly, it's a massive worry. "Why would we want any sort of chance, any sort of risk to our children, even with like a 1% chance?" Laura Potts, another parent, said: "It's really concerning, and it's frightening." She added that she wanted to see more communication "on what would happen in an emergency". "The safety of the children is of the utmost importance," Potts said. "I think the safety of our children in the schools should be considered more important than even the education itself." The area is represented on Shropshire Council by Reform UK's Brendan Mallon, who said he had "many concerns" about the BESS plans. Mallon said he feared that a fire at the site could "shut down" the adjacent A5, which in turn could, he said, affect the ability of the emergency services to respond. He added that he believed battery storage plants should instead be built on "remote sites, preferably industrial sites". Mallon said that should the BESS be approved, he would feel "extremely let down," adding that the potential impact on the school "should have been applied at the start and rejected". A spokesperson for Shropshire Council said that "all planning applications are considered on their merits," with comments raised as part of the consultation taken into account. Elgin Energy, planning agent Berry's, and St Lucia's CofE Primary School and Nursery have all been contacted for comment.

artigo.texto: Elecom will launch a new cable-integrated 10,000mAh power bank in mid-November, featuring a semi-solid-state lithium-ion battery. It boasts high safety, a long lifespan, and wide temperature resistance for extreme cold and intense heat. The price is 7,480 yen. It will be available in three colors: Black, Shiro-chan (White x Black), and White. With a capacity of 10,000mAh, it features a lightweight design, weighing approximately 190g. A key feature is its integrated USB Type-C cable, allowing users to simply take it out of their bag and start charging immediately. Semi-solid-state lithium-ion batteries suppress electrolyte leakage by gelling the electrolyte, thereby enhancing chemical stability. Compared to the approximately 500 charge/discharge cycles of products using conventional lithium-ion batteries, this new battery boasts a cycle life of approximately 2,000 times, achieving about four times the lifespan of conventional models. Furthermore, it supports an operating temperature range of -15°C to 45°C during power supply, making it easy to use in cold regions or outdoors during summer. It also includes a "Health Monitor" that indicates battery status via LEDs, "Thermal Protection" for monitoring and controlling temperature, and multiple other protection functions. For charging, in addition to the integrated USB Type-C cable, it features one USB Type-C port and one USB-A port, allowing up to three devices to be charged simultaneously. It supports USB Power Delivery and PPS, supplying optimal power according to the connected device, thus enabling efficient charging of smartphones and tablets. When used alone, it supports a maximum output of 22.5W, while for multiple devices simultaneously, it distributes a total maximum of 21W. Furthermore, it supports pass-through charging, low-current mode, and "Omakase Charging" (auto-optimized charging), and is compatible with charging the Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch, and Nintendo Switch Lite.

artigo.texto: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. Kazakhstan's Kurultai has approved, in the first reading, amendments aimed at developing alternative energy sources and strengthening the resilience of the country's power system, the Kurultai press service announced. The bill was presented by Minister of Energy Yerlan Akkenzhenov and was drafted in line with President Kassym Jomart Tokayev's Nation Address on October 28 on strengthening the stability of the energy system. The proposed amendments introduce new mechanisms for developing the energy sector, aimed at improving power system reliability, attracting investment and expanding the use of alternative energy sources. One of the key provisions is the introduction of competitive auctions to select electricity storage system projects. To make these projects more attractive to investors, the bill proposes long-term payments for maintaining available capacity for up to 15 years. "Currently, the power system's need for flexible capacity is estimated at approximately 3 GW: around 2 GW is planned to be provided through renewable energy projects, while additional mechanisms are being developed to attract investment for the remaining 1 GW. To this end, competitive auctions for selecting energy storage system projects are proposed," Akkenzhenov said. The bill also proposes improving the mechanism for selling electricity under bilateral contracts. Power facilities that have supplied electricity under such contracts for at least 36 months will be eligible to switch to selling electricity to the Single Purchaser. This measure is expected to reduce the risk of losing sales outlets and improve the sustainability of investment projects. Another section of the amendments focuses on more efficient use of energy resources in heating and industry. In particular, the proposals envisage wider use of secondary energy resources, low-grade and waste heat, heat pumps, biomass, biogas and hydrogen. The bill also establishes a legal framework for developing hydrogen technologies, using energy generated by industrial processes and recovering energy through waste utilization. Overall, the proposed amendments are expected to introduce competitive mechanisms for developing energy storage systems, improve the investment appeal of projects, reduce electricity sales risks under bilateral contracts, and promote the wider use of modern energy technologies.

artigo.texto: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 9. Uzbekistan plans to increase its energy storage capacity to 4.5 gigawatts by 2030 and expand domestic production of electrical equipment, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said during a visit to NURA Electric in Tashkent Region on Monday. The announcement was published on the official channel of Sherzod Asadov, the president's press secretary. Mirziyoyev said the next priority for the electrical engineering industry should be achieving a major technological leap rather than simply expanding production capacity. Foreign partners are ready to use locally manufactured products in energy storage projects, but some of the required equipment is not yet produced domestically, he said. Moreover, the president highlighted growing demand for video surveillance equipment in shopping centers, businesses, residential buildings and public spaces. Annual demand for such equipment in Uzbekistan is estimated at $200 million, while the market exceeds $600 million when neighboring countries are included. Companies such as Digital Security in Bukhara and Samvision in Samarkand currently produce around 2,000 cameras annually using their own software. Mirziyoyev emphasized the need to expand such projects to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and capture a larger share of regional demand. Uzbekistan has been pursuing an energy sector transformation aimed at expanding generation capacity, diversifying its energy mix and improving energy efficiency. The country is investing in large-scale solar and wind power projects, modernizing electricity infrastructure and developing energy storage systems to integrate a growing share of renewable energy into the national grid. These efforts are part of its broader strategy to meet rising electricity demand while strengthening energy security and supporting industrial growth.

artigo.texto: U.S. utility-scale solar, wind, and battery storage hit new capacity records in Q2 2026, S&P Global finds The U.S. clean energy buildout hit a notable milestone in the second quarter of 2026. According to new analysis from S&P Global Market Intelligence, developers added nearly 7.5 GW of utility-scale solar — a 21% jump year-over-year — while battery storage set a quarterly record at 5.6 GW and wind posted its strongest quarter since 2021 with 5.1 GW of new capacity. All three sectors hit significant milestones in the same quarter. That’s not a coincidence — it points to something broader shifting in U.S. energy infrastructure. Q2 2026 capacity additions by the numbers The headline figures from S&P Global Market Intelligence are striking on their own. They carry even more weight when you look at them side by side. Cost trends helped too — solar panel prices and battery system costs have declined over time, making large-scale projects more financially viable at a faster pace. Solar led the way with nearly 7.5 GW of utility-scale capacity added during Q2 2026 — a 21% increase compared to the same quarter a year earlier. That’s a meaningful jump for a sector that was already growing steadily. Battery storage grabbed attention in a different way. The 5.6 GW added during the quarter set an all-time quarterly record for the technology in the U.S., reflecting how quickly storage has moved from a niche grid tool to a mainstream infrastructure component. Wind rounded out the picture. At 5.1 GW, Q2 2026 marked the technology’s strongest quarterly performance since 2021 — a real rebound for a sector that had faced supply chain disruptions and siting challenges in recent years. What makes this quarter stand out isn’t any single number — it’s that all three sectors hit significant milestones simultaneously, according to S&P Global’s data. Drivers behind the surge in renewable and storage deployment Several forces converged to produce these results. None of them is entirely new, but their combined effect appears to have pushed deployment into a higher gear. Investment momentum in utility-scale clean energy has stayed strong. Grid operators and corporate buyers have kept seeking reliable renewable capacity, and developers have responded by accelerating project timelines to meet that demand. Cost trends helped too — solar panel prices and battery system costs have declined over time, making large-scale projects more financially viable at a faster pace. Lower costs mean more projects can clear the financial hurdles required to reach construction. Federal tax credits have also played a meaningful role in pushing projects forward. Incentives tied to clean energy development motivated developers to move quickly, especially given uncertainty about whether those credits will stick around long-term. When expiration looms, activity tends to concentrate in the near term — developers race to qualify projects under current rules before anything changes. What the record additions mean for the U.S. grid These aren’t just impressive stats. They have real implications for how the U.S. power grid actually operates. Battery storage is the most consequential piece of the Q2 story from a grid reliability standpoint. Variable renewable sources like solar and wind produce power when the sun shines and the wind blows — not necessarily when demand peaks. Storage helps bridge that gap by capturing excess generation and dispatching it when it’s needed most. The combination of record solar and record storage additions in the same quarter suggests the industry is increasingly building the two together, producing something closer to dispatchable clean energy rather than purely intermittent generation. Wind’s strong quarter adds a different dimension. Wind resources are geographically distributed differently than solar — stronger in the Great Plains and parts of the Midwest, for example — so more wind capacity means more regional diversification in the renewable mix, which can strengthen grid resilience. Taken together, these additions suggest the U.S. energy transition may actually be picking up speed. Development pipeline and industry headwinds through 2031 If Q2 2026 shows where the industry is now, the development pipeline offers a glimpse of where it’s headed. S&P Global’s analysis identified nearly 300 GW of solar and more than 212 GW of storage targeted for completion between 2026 and 2031. Those are large numbers, and they suggest developers are planning for continued aggressive buildout over the next several years. The pipeline doesn’t guarantee delivery, though. Trade tariffs on imported components — including solar panels and battery materials — continue to pressure project costs. When input costs rise, projects that looked financially viable on paper become harder to finance and build. Expiring federal tax credits create a separate layer of uncertainty, complicating long-term financing and sometimes delaying final investment decisions altogether. Permitting constraints remain a structural bottleneck that hasn’t meaningfully improved despite the scale of the buildout. Even projects with financing in place can face years of delays navigating federal, state, and local approval processes — a problem that shows no signs of resolving quickly. What to take away from Q2 2026’s clean energy milestone Q2 2026 was a standout quarter for U.S. clean energy deployment. Solar hit a new year-over-year growth benchmark, battery storage set an all-time quarterly record, and wind posted its best performance in five years — all at once, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Sustained investment, declining costs, and policy incentives motivating near-term action all contributed. The grid implications are real, particularly as storage and solar grow together into a more dispatchable pairing. artigo.texto: A crescente onda de protestos contra a instalação de data centers nos Estados Unidos, impulsionada pelo temor de aumento nas contas de energia, consumo excessivo de água e impactos ambientais, ganhou força nas disputas eleitorais e ampliou a pressão sobre candidatos republicanos e democratas. A reação dos moradores norte-americanos desperta questionamentos sobre os reflexos desse movimento na expansão dos centros de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial no Brasil, especialmente no Ceará, onde um empreendimento anunciado para Caucaia, na Região Metropolitana de Fortaleza, também foi alvo de manifestações de comunidades locais. Nos Estados Unidos, a resistência aos grandes centros tecnológicos deixou de ser uma discussão restrita ao meio ambiente e passou a integrar o debate político. O assunto ganhou espaço nas eleições de meio de mandato, realizadas no dia 3 de novembro, com candidatos pressionados a apresentar propostas para controlar os custos de energia, proteger os recursos hídricos e estabelecer limites à instalação dessas estruturas. A insatisfação popular se tornou um desafio para políticos dos dois principais partidos norte-americanos, especialmente em regiões onde moradores reclamam dos efeitos da chegada de grandes empresas de tecnologia. O movimento também provocou questionamentos sobre incentivos fiscais e benefícios concedidos pelos governos a empreendimentos que demandam enormes quantidades de eletricidade e água. QUESTIONAMENTOS SOBRE O CEARÁ O avanço dos protestos nos Estados Unidos chama a atenção para o Brasil, que busca ampliar sua participação no mercado internacional de inteligência artificial e processamento de dados. No Ceará, um dos principais exemplos dessa expansão é o projeto de instalação de um data center em Caucaia. O empreendimento recebeu apoio do prefeito Naumi Amorim, que defende a iniciativa como uma oportunidade de desenvolvimento tecnológico, atração de investimentos, geração de empregos, renda e arrecadação tributária para o município. A proposta, entretanto, também despertou resistência de comunidades locais, preocupadas com os possíveis impactos ambientais e com a utilização de recursos naturais, especialmente água e energia elétrica. EFEITOS NAS COMUNIDADES A experiência norte-americana coloca novas questões no debate cearense: quais serão os efeitos desses empreendimentos sobre o abastecimento de água? Quem arcará com os custos da infraestrutura energética necessária? Quantos empregos permanentes serão efetivamente criados? E quais contrapartidas ambientais e econômicas serão asseguradas às comunidades? São questionamentos que ganham importância diante da perspectiva de crescimento do setor no Estado. BRASIL TEM 169 DATA CENTERS MAPEADOS O Brasil já conta com 169 data centers mapeados, dos quais 132 estão em operação. Segundo levantamento do Maravalley, polo de inovação e tecnologia do Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo concentra 76 unidades, liderando a distribuição dessas estruturas no território nacional. A expansão é impulsionada principalmente pelo crescimento da inteligência artificial, dos serviços em nuvem, das redes sociais e de outras atividades digitais que exigem grande capacidade de armazenamento e processamento de informações. O Governo Federal também colocou o setor entre suas prioridades de desenvolvimento tecnológico. Durante a campanha presidencial de 2026, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defendeu estímulos à instalação de data centers, associados a exigências ambientais, utilização de energia renovável e contrapartidas para o mercado brasileiro, como a reserva de capacidade computacional. CONSUMO DE ÁGUA E ENERGIA ESTÁ NO CENTRO DOS PROTESTOS A resistência à construção de data centers, registrada durante a campanha eleitoral nos Estados Unidos, se concentrou, principalmente, nos impactos sobre as contas de eletricidade e o meio ambiente. As instalações abrigam milhares de servidores que precisam funcionar continuamente. Dependendo do porte e da tecnologia utilizada, podem consumir volumes de energia comparáveis aos de cidades inteiras. Sistemas de resfriamento também podem exigir grandes quantidades de água, embora esse consumo varie conforme as tecnologias adotadas. Além da demanda energética e hídrica, moradores questionam a ocupação de áreas rurais, a perda de terrenos agrícolas, o barulho das instalações e a poluição provocada por geradores utilizados em situações de emergência. RESTRIÇÃO Segundo levantamento divulgado pela agência Reuters, pelo menos 41 propostas de restrição à construção de data centers foram apresentadas em 38 localidades de dez estados norte-americanos no contexto das eleições. Ohio aparece entre os estados com maior mobilização. Na cidade de Sunbury, uma proposta de limitação da potência dos empreendimentos pode comprometer um projeto da Amazon avaliado em US$ 2 bilhões. PRESSÃO POPULAR ATINGE GOVERNADORES E CANDIDATOS A resistência também alcançou as disputas pelos governos estaduais norte-americanos. Na Pensilvânia, o governador democrata Josh Shapiro passou a defender exigências mais rigorosas para novos empreendimentos, incluindo medidas relacionadas ao consumo de água, aos custos de energia e à aprovação dos projetos pelas administrações municipais. No Texas, o republicano Greg Abbott também passou a enfrentar questionamentos sobre os benefícios fiscais concedidos ao setor e os custos que podem ser transferidos aos consumidores. A pressão mostra que a instalação de data centers, antes apresentada principalmente como oportunidade de investimentos e desenvolvimento econômico, passou a exigir respostas mais amplas sobre seus impactos sociais e ambientais. Apesar da resistência, o setor continua em expansão. De acordo com a consultoria Cushman & Wakefield, a capacidade dos data centers em construção nos Estados Unidos cresceu 48% entre dezembro de 2025 e junho de 2026

artigo.texto: CATL Builds an Ecosystem Around the Battery: Transit Deals, European Storage and an Aviation Niche Published on 11/11/2026 at 01:31 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is pushing past the simple sale of battery cells. In a burst of announcements spanning public transport, home energy storage and electric aviation, the Chinese battery giant has sketched out a strategy in which the battery becomes the starting point for a wider set of services — swapping, servicing, recycling and grid interaction — rather than the end product itself. The most concrete piece of that puzzle arrived in the form of strategic cooperation agreements with four Chinese transit operators: Benxi Passenger Transport Group, Changzhou Transit Group, Guiyang Public Transport Group and Lanzhou Public Transport Group. According to media reports, the arrangements cover battery supply and exchange, customer service, citywide battery-swap networks, recycling, and vehicle-to-grid interaction. The breadth is the point. Rather than a one-off delivery notice, the deals tie a battery's deployment to its upkeep and its eventual disposal — a linked chain that only pays off if CATL can actually coordinate the various tasks in day-to-day operations. From the vehicle to the grid The larger idea running through the transit pacts is the coupling of mobility with energy supply. A swap network touches fleet operations; vehicle-to-grid interaction pulls the power system into the frame. That logic gains weight if the operators adopt these building blocks together and extract practical value from them. For investors, the question shifts accordingly: how much value can CATL create around a battery once it has been delivered? The answer hinges on the role the company genuinely takes on in swapping, servicing and recycling. The tighter those tasks can be woven together, the more convincing the strategic case for the package. The citywide approach matters in particular because it places the individual battery in a broader operational context. The test, ultimately, is execution at each transit operator. A related thread runs through CATL's home-storage ambitions. On 4 November, CATL, Ampace and Octopus Energy signed a memorandum of understanding to explore smart storage solutions for Europe, with the UK, France and Spain as the initial focus. Octopus Energy describes the plan as linking its software platform and electricity tariffs with the battery technology and hardware from CATL and Ampace. Here too the approach reaches beyond a single technical product: the collaboration would carry strategic weight for CATL if hardware, controls and household tariff design mesh sensibly. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Storage at scale and a foothold in aviation The same theme recurs at utility scale. On 29 October, CATL gave the TENER+ energy storage system its global debut at All Energy Australia, signing memoranda with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney to implement large battery storage projects and their grid connections. Grid integration is thus a recurring concern across very different applications — a sign of a coherent strategic direction, provided CATL can successfully interlock its battery technology with its partners' contributions. Aviation is the newest frontier. On 3 November, CATL agreed to work with Blue Vector Intelligent Technology on a custom-built aviation battery for the latter's SKYLA V30 electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Blue Vector selected CATL as the exclusive battery partner for the model, so the arrangement covers both development of the specially adapted battery and CATL's sole-supplier role for that aircraft's battery needs. Buyback progress Alongside the deal flow, CATL disclosed the state of its share repurchase programme on 3 November. As of 31 October, the company had bought back a total of 19.6 million A-shares at a cost of RMB 5.36 billion, according to its own figures. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. What unites the transit agreements, the European storage memorandum and the Australian grid projects is the embedding of the battery in its surroundings — software and tariffs in the home, swapping, service and grid links in transport. That points to a plausible direction for CATL, so long as partners combine their respective contributions into offerings that work in practice. The yardstick for the stock is delivery on those connections: supply, operation and recycling coming together, and the agreed cooperation holding up in the everyday business of each partner. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no SoftBank registra prejuízo de US$ 7 bilhões após perdas com data centers nos EUA e queda das ações da Intel Publicado 10/11/2026 • 11:24 | Atualizado há 20 horas Nos bastidores da Nvidia: o primeiro dia de Jensen Huang de volta ao escritório após a revelação do caso extraconjugal Senador acusa Trump de defender o CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, em detrimento da segurança nacional Caso envolvendo Jensen Huang amplia pressão sobre negócios da Nvidia na China Nvidia contrata escritório de advocacia Wachtell Lipton para liderar a investigação do caso Jensen Huang Laços da Nvidia com Trump entram na mira após relatos de que Jensen Huang foi alvo da inteligência chinesa KEY POINTS Foto: Divulgação O SoftBank registrou prejuízo líquido de 1,12 trilhão de ienes (US$ 7 bilhões) no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal, divulgado nesta terça-feira (10). O resultado foi pressionado por perdas relacionadas à aquisição de equipamentos para data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos e pela desvalorização das ações da Intel. O conglomerado japonês também registrou uma perda de 597,2 bilhões de ienes (US$ 3,7 bilhões) nos seis meses encerrados em 30 de setembro, devido a mudanças nos planos de aquisição de equipamentos de geração de energia para projetos de data centers de IA nos EUA. O SoftBank afirmou que realizou investimentos antecipados para garantir o fornecimento de equipamentos de geração de energia para seus projetos de data centers de IA nos Estados Unidos, diante de preocupações com possíveis escassez e longos prazos de aquisição. Leia também: Por que a China barrou o negócio de US$ 5,4 bilhões do SoftBank? A disponibilidade de energia está se tornando uma das principais limitações para a expansão dos data centers de IA, à medida que as redes elétricas ficam sobrecarregadas com pedidos de grandes consumidores de energia, como essas instalações. Os pagamentos acumulados por equipamentos de geração de energia destinados aos projetos de data centers de IA nos EUA, incluindo o PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, no condado de Pike, em Ohio, totalizavam US$ 9,48 bilhões no fim de setembro. “Fizemos investimentos-ponte antecipadamente para garantir equipamentos de geração de energia, diante da expectativa de escassez”, afirmou um executivo do SoftBank durante a teleconferência de resultados da companhia. Veja o desempenho do SoftBank no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal: A receita avançou 13,3% no semestre encerrado em 30 de setembro, impulsionada pelo crescimento dos negócios de telecomunicações e computação em inteligência artificial. A empresa informou que o segmento SoftBank registrou aumento nas vendas em todas as suas operações, enquanto a receita da divisão de computação em IA também cresceu. O segmento Vision Fund passou a registrar prejuízo de 81,58 bilhões de ienes no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal, ante lucro de 2,38 trilhões de ienes no mesmo período do ano anterior. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O Vision Fund 1 registrou perda de US$ 20 milhões em investimentos no trimestre, apesar de um ganho de US$ 1,3 bilhão com a ByteDance. O resultado foi influenciado pela queda das ações de empresas de capital aberto que integram seu portfólio, incluindo Coupang e Grab. Os fundos Vision Funds registraram ganhos de investimento de 85,45 bilhões de ienes, uma queda acentuada em relação aos 2,81 trilhões de ienes do mesmo período do ano anterior. O Vision Fund 2 apresentou ganhos de investimento de 89,26 bilhões de ienes, enquanto o Vision Fund 1 registrou perdas de 3,86 bilhões de ienes em seus investimentos. Até o fim de setembro, o investimento acumulado do SoftBank na OpenAI somava US$ 54,6 bilhões. O valor justo da participação era de US$ 99,6 bilhões, com ganho acumulado de US$ 45 bilhões, segundo a companhia. O SoftBank afirmou que uma possível elevação da avaliação da OpenAI após uma nova rodada de financiamento ainda não havia sido incorporada aos resultados, pois dependia de um anúncio oficial. A nova avaliação poderá ser refletida no terceiro trimestre do ano fiscal, com potencial para elevar o valor líquido dos ativos da companhia e melhorar sua relação entre dívida e valor dos ativos (loan-to-value, ou LTV). “ O ChatGPT tem sido continuamente uma arma da OpenAI, especialmente para os consumidores”, afirmou o executivo do SoftBank durante a teleconferência de resultados, ao destacar o crescimento da base de usuários do chatbot. Leia também: SoftBank registra lucro acima do esperado após ganho de US$ 8,2 bilhões com Intel As ações do conglomerado japonês fecharam em alta de 13,9% nesta terça-feira. O avanço ocorreu em meio à valorização de empresas asiáticas de tecnologia, incluindo Samsung Electronics e SK Hynix, após uma recuperação das ações do setor em Wall Street na noite anterior. Em relação aos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA, o SoftBank destacou um contrato de arrendamento de 20 anos com a OpenAI para oito gigawatts de capacidade de tecnologia da informação (TI) em um projeto de data center em Ohio. Sobre as preocupações com o consumo de água no data center planejado no Texas, o SoftBank afirmou que está adotando medidas para reduzir o uso do recurso por meio de um sistema de circuito fechado com resfriamento a ar. A companhia também mencionou planos de contratar trabalhadores e adquirir insumos localmente. Antes da divulgação dos resultados, o SoftBank Group anunciou, na segunda-feira (9), planos com a Grab e a empresa malaia PETROS para investir, em conjunto, US$ 1,85 bilhão em capital inicial no desenvolvimento de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial na Malásia. artigo.texto: Data center é o espaço físico que armazena toda a estrutura de computação necessária para o processamento, armazenamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais. Eles são importantes para a manutenção de serviços de internet e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial, o que explica o rápido crescimento no número de data centers em todo o mundo. Dentro de um data center, é possível encontrar racks com elementos como switches, firewalls e servidores, bem como bancos de baterias, painéis elétricos e sistemas de refrigeração. Atualmente mais de 180 data centers estão em atividade no Brasil. Devido ao crescente uso da inteligência artificial, o país busca dar continuidade ao seu processo de desenvolvimento tecnológico por meio da atração de novos data centers. Para isso, criou uma medida conhecida como Redata, que foca na oferta de incentivos fiscais com contrapartidas. Contudo, há muitas críticas com relação a essa política por conta dos impactos ambientais dos data centers. Leia também: Por que tem se falado em uma bolha econômica em torno da IA? Tópicos deste artigo Resumo sobre datas centers - Data center é o espaço físico onde ficam as máquinas e equipamentos de computação que realizam o armazenamento, o processamento e a transmissão segura de dados digitais. - São importantes porque mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet e as ferramentas de inteligência artificial, cuja demanda cresceu de forma acelerada nos últimos anos. - A capacidade instalada de data centers cresceu cinco vezes entre 2005 e 2025. O atual número de data centers no mundo passa de 13 mil, maioria dos quais está nos EUA. - Dentro de um data center tem, entre outros: - racks, onde ficam itens como painéis de conexão, servidores, firewalls e switches; - banco de baterias e painéis de energia elétrica; - sistemas de ventilação e de refrigeração; Anuncie aqui - equipamentos para o controle de umidade. - Três dos principais tipos de data centers são: - data centers corporativos, que ficam no interior das próprias empresas; - data centers de colocação, que são espaços compartilhados por várias companhias; - data centers hiperescala, que são espaços de grande dimensão construídos exclusivamente para as operações de uma única empresa. - A rápida difusão dos data centers tem gerado debates e críticas sobre sustentabilidade desse modelo de estabelecimento por conta do elevado consumo de energia e de água. - Os data centers também geram poluição sonora e produzem ilhas de calor por conta da elevação da temperatura média do ar, causando alterações no microclima. - O Brasil tem mais de 180 data centers, mas aprovou uma medida que promete isenções fiscais para a instalação de novas unidades no território nacional. Anuncie aqui O que é um data center? Data center é um espaço físico onde ficam instaladas todas as máquinas e os equipamentos de computação responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais de serviços em nuvem e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial (IA). Em função da rápida modernização dos sistemas de propagação de informações e de comunicação que aconteceu nas últimas décadas, cresceu, na mesma proporção, a demanda por softwares e serviços de armazenamento em nuvem. Não obstante essas sejam redes que existem e se multiplicam no ciberespaço, elas demandam um outro tipo de rede, dessa vez, física, para se manter. Essa rede física é mantida em data centers. Por que data centers são importantes? Os data centers são importantes porque eles mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet que nós utilizamos todos os dias. Uma boa parte do nosso sistema moderno de comunicação depende diretamente de aplicações que são mantidas e aperfeiçoadas por meio desse tipo de infraestrutura. Segundo informações da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, em inglês) trazidas pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE)|1|, o número de usuários da internet aumentou em 78% somente entre 2015 e 2022, quando o tráfego global se expandiu aproximadamente seis vezes. Dentro do atual período técnico em que estamos inseridos, empresas, sistemas financeiros e mesmo governos desenvolveram uma alta dependência de ferramentas de TI para a sua gestão. Então, além de serem parte indissociável desse ecossistema de gerenciamento, os data centers são fundamentais para a garantia da eficácia e, sobretudo, da segurança no processamento e armazenamento de informações que, na maioria das vezes, são sensíveis e/ou confidenciais. Esses espaços físicos também são necessários para o funcionamento da inteligência artificial. As ferramentas de IA, entretanto, são bastante complexas e resultam em um trabalho mais intenso do que aquele desempenhado pelas máquinas que compõem os data centers convencionais. Dada a difusão acelerada das ferramentas de IA, que tem sido empregada tanto para atividades corriqueiras quanto para o gerenciamento de empresas e em setores estratégicos, como o energético, os data centers têm se multiplicado em um ritmo semelhante. Para evidenciar a importância dos data centers dentro do presente contexto tecnológico e informacional, basta analisarmos os dados que mostram a evolução da capacidade energética instalada nos data centers. No ano de 2005, essa capacidade ficava em torno de 20 GW, enquanto 20 anos mais tarde, em 2025, ela cresceu para 114,3 GW, segundo dados da IEA|2|. Essa capacidade corresponde a cerca de 13 mil data centers, a maioria dos quais fica nos Estados Unidos (5 mil), na Índia (348) e no Canadá (299)|3|. O que tem dentro de um data center? As seguintes estruturas e equipamentos são encontrados dentro de um data center: - Racks, que é onde ficam todos os equipamentos utilizados para o processamento e armazenamento de dados, como patch panels (painel de conexões), switches, acesso remoto, firewalls, servidores, roteadores, fonte de alimentação de energia (UPS ou nobreak), unidades de distribuição de energia e sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração. artigo.texto: A transitioning Congress finds itself in a pickle on AI data centers Table of Contents As Congress returns to Washington this week, the massive power demands of the AI boom have forced a reckoning over data center infrastructure. The Senate is preparing for a pivotal procedural vote on legislation that would speed approvals for energy projects while requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs they impose on the power grid. The bipartisan bill would add much-needed regulations on data centers, but, as some politicians believe, may also encourage more data center construction. Silicon Valley vs. a changed D.C. In the sweeping and history-making midterm elections last week, voters didn't just elect a new generation of Democratic lawmakers. They also sent a pretty unmistakable message to Big Tech, particularly the artificial intelligence industry: Enough with the data centers already. Or, more bluntly, "get out of town." Across the country, local communities are pushing to stop, restrict, or impose conditions on data center development. The election results reinforced that message, making clear that the AI gold rush is facing growing resistance. For the last two years, Silicon Valley has busied itself building more, building bigger and doing it ASAP. If a tech giant wanted to drop a warehouse-sized data center into a community, local governments often offered tax breaks and other incentives, then told residents it was harmless and would mean more jobs. Voters increasingly aren't buying it. Democrats now find themselves in a pickle. Many campaigned on restricting data center development, responding to voters concerned about electricity costs, water consumption, and the impact these enormous facilities have on their communities. Now, the aforementioned pending legislation forces a stark about-face — since, as Reuters reports, some Democrats believe provisions in the proposed bill could encourage the creation of more data centers. If that comes to pass, incoming lawmakers would need to explain why those campaign promises to halt data center construction no longer apply. Can data centers be built responsibly? There's a risk, too, in the new Democratic Congress pushing too forcefully for restrictions on AI, specifically on data centers. My well-seasoned brain believes AI companies will respond to restrictions not simply by complaining about the cost of doing business, but by slowing down the rollout of new technology. Some of that slowdown will be unavoidable. Without enough data centers, electricity, and computing capacity, companies cannot expand indefinitely. But some of it could be strategic. I suspect the message from Silicon Valley will be slightly PR-ish: If you don't want us building data centers, don't expect your ChatGPT, Claude, or Siri to keep getting faster, smarter, and more capable. That "hurry up and now" diagnosis for your sore knee might take a little longer. Picture AI as something other than a magical cloud floating above our heads. Every time you ask an AI assistant to write an email, generate an image, or summarize a document, powerful chips in actual buildings are cranking away, consuming tremendous amounts of electricity and water and pressuring local power grids. And all that power costs mega cash. Utility rates, grid upgrades, and higher electricity bills have turned an abstract technology debate into something much more personal. I don't blame communities for pushing back. Why should residents subsidize a multibillion-dollar technology company's expansion while wondering whether their electric bills will keep climbing? They're already fed up with rising gas and grocery prices and the cost of a new home. But there's another side to this costly coin that Democrats shouldn't ignore. Data centers can bring economic benefits, too, provided technology companies invest in the communities that host them. While data centers rarely employ local, low-skill workers directly, AI companies can bridge this gap by funding local infrastructure projects that immediately put the existing workforce to work. Furthermore, the resulting influx of permanent, high-salaried technicians injects new tax revenue into the community, triggering a powerful economic ripple effect for local restaurants and shops. Communities shouldn't have to choose between protecting residents and benefiting from technological investment. Companies that want to build in these towns should contribute meaningfully to their economic well-being. The risks of slowing down the AI gold rush Government intervention, even when well-intentioned, can also produce unintended consequences that ultimately hurt consumers. Just look at Europe. In 2024, Apple said it would hold back Apple Intelligence and other new features from EU customers, citing "regulatory uncertainties" tied to the Digital Markets Act. Regulators were trying to rein in Big Tech and protect competition. Whether you buy Apple's explanation or see it as a pressure tactic, European customers were left waiting while others got the shiny new toys. This doesn't mean all regulation is bad. It's a reminder that lawmakers cannot promise to put a tight leash on an industry without potentially creating bottlenecks in the products and services it provides. That's precisely the dilemma Democrats now face. If they make it too difficult or expensive to build data centers, AI companies will have fewer places to house the computing power necessary to expand their products. New features could take longer to arrive. More sophisticated applications could cost more. And I wouldn't be surprised if the industry makes sure consumers understand exactly who's responsible. artigo.texto: O Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) aprovou a destinação de R$ 46,3 milhões para o desenvolvimento de uma plataforma inteligente de gerenciamento de data centers. O projeto batizado de Prisma terá duração de 36 meses e será executado pelo CPQD A iniciativa terá como base um convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação com a Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), entidade responsável pela administração dos recursos. Em linhas gerais, a intenção do projeto é usar Inteligência Artificial (IA) para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados em operações com diferentes infraestruturas computacionais, de modo a tornar os data centers mais eficientes, seguros e sustentáveis. Segundo o Ministério das Comunicações (MCom), a expectativa é de que a tecnologia também reduza o consumo de energia e a pegada de carbono, aumente a resiliência contra falhas no fornecimento de energia, eleve a proteção contra ataques cibernéticos, diminua os custos operacionais, acelere o acesso à informação e aumente a proteção de dados estratégicos. "Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior", afirmou o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, em nota. Data centers de borda O Prisma também deve estimular a expansão de data centers de borda (também chamados de minidata centers) pelo território nacional, com o objetivo de levar o processamento de dados para mais perto de onde são gerados e utilizados, o que reduz o tempo de resposta dos sistemas e melhora o desempenho de serviços digitais. A tecnologia deve beneficiar, sobretudo, setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. "Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda", destaca o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima.

artigo.texto: On Monday, the Senate voted to advance a bipartisan bill aimed at easing the construction of new energy infrastructure. The bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), has a broad base of support, including from labor leaders who contend it will produce thousands of jobs and clean energy proponents who believe it could unlock wind and solar. Its sponsors are hoping to pass the bill before the current Congress ends in January. But the bill has also received vehement blowback from a growing coalition of anti-data center critics, who argue that it would accelerate the buildout of an industry that Americans resoundingly voted against in the midterm elections. BAAJA does address affordability concerns by forcing data centers to pay the full cost of the upgrades they trigger, and contains transmission reforms designed to modernize the grid. But it also strips back environmental protections and could lead to more data centers powered by gas and built on public lands. Hundreds of local and national organizations have signed letters urging Congress not to pass the bill as written, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council. Conversely, many industry trade groups have been supportive of the bill, despite the fact that it would likely make building more expensive. On Sunday, Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass the bill on Truth Social, writing that “China will take any Data Center that we don’t want.” The bill represents the first major test for Democrats post-election, as they contend with how to deliver on affordability and many other issues in their sprawling coalition at the same time. “Everything about BAAJA goes against the spirit of voters this midterms, in which we saw voters turn out for candidates who directly oppose data centers,” says Allie Rosenbluth, U.S. campaigns manager at the environmental nonprofit Oil Change International. “This bill is a massive giveaway to the data center industry—and creates a backdoor for fossil fuels to enter the grid through data centers.” Read More: How AI Backlash Shaped the 2026 Midterms Gas and Fossil Fuels America’s data center boom has also been a gas boom. In the scramble to bring AI data centers online as fast as possible, many developers have built their own gas power plants instead of waiting to connect to the grid. Global Energy Monitor data reported by Wired show that U.S. gas projects powering data centers increased from roughly 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to 189 gigawatts in development by mid-2026. In some cases, these gas plants have worsened local pollution and exacerbated health issues like asthma, scientific researchers contend. BAAJA incentivizes a wide range of energy sources to come online faster, including solar and wind. Many experts are hopeful that the bill will accelerate the buildout of transmission lines that are essential for bringing clean energy online. But environmentalists worry that the first and foremost beneficiary of the bill won’t be clean energy sources but rather gas-powered data centers, because there is already a massive pipeline of proposed projects waiting for various approvals. Rosenbluth points to several gas-powered data centers that are currently plodding through the permitting process, including the Ports-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio and the STAK Energy Campus in Alaska. If BAAJA were to pass, she says, key environmental permits they are trying to obtain could be fast-tracked, potentially allowing them to come online much more quickly. Holly Bender, chief program officer of the Sierra Club, says that "based on their need for speed to power, the data center industry is driving a historic and alarming investment in gas and fossil fuels. There’s a lot in this bill that will make it easier and faster to build gas pipelines, while making it harder for communities to have a say.” Public and Tribal lands Another major concern from critics is that the bill will lead to many more data centers getting built on federally-owned land. The Trump administration has embraced this idea, and signed an executive order in July 2025 directing the Interior and Energy departments to make federal sites available for data centers and to streamline their environmental reviews. “We’re going to ‘mine, baby, mine’ so we can ‘build, baby, build’ because we’ve got to build AI data centers,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in 2025. There are at least 17 active applications connected to data center campuses on public land, covering thousands of acres in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, and other states, one recent study found. BAAJA’s permitting provisions could make those projects easier to advance and harder to stop, including limiting judges’ ability to halt construction due to environmental review. Additionally, some Tribal organizations and leaders have spoken out forcefully against the bill, with a coalition of Tribal leaders writing on Saturday that the bill would “gut the ability of Tribal Nations and the American public to identify and protect historic and cultural places threatened by federally connected projects—including data centers.” Potential benefits However, the bill’s advocates argue that it addresses several of the public’s most pressing data center concerns. The first is around affordability: The bill contains ratepayer protections which would require developers to pay for the added cost of transmission. One study estimates that data centers would pay approximately $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years—about $35 billion more than under current policy. The bill establishes protections to prevent households and businesses from being left with the bill for failed projects. “The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the bill’s Democratic sponsors, said last week. He added on Monday that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on substantial clean energy policies next year when they control bot

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI have each won an Innovation Award at the world's largest electronics and IT exhibition, "CES 2027." LG Energy Solution was recognized for a software technology that shortens the diagnostic time of used batteries to within 10 minutes, while Samsung SDI was acknowledged for its uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery solution for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. According to the battery industry on the 10th, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI have been named among the companies selected for the "CES 2027 Innovation Award" by the Consumer Technology Association (CTA). LG Energy Solution received the award in the Advanced Mobility category, while Samsung SDI won in the Enterprise Tech category. LG Energy Solution's winning entry is its software-based used battery diagnostic solution, "Re.Pulse." The technology involves applying specific current pulses to a battery to measure voltage changes and analyzing them with an AI-based proprietary model to evaluate the battery's state of health (SoH) and residual performance. Its most notable feature is reducing the battery diagnostic time from over seven hours to within 10 minutes. It also enables precise diagnosis down to the cell level within a battery pack, allowing for the repair or replacement of only the degraded parts. Another characteristic is its ability to link with existing battery charge/discharge testers or electric vehicle chargers without requiring separate dedicated equipment. Because it can perform diagnostics without removing the battery from the vehicle, it can be utilized in used battery energy storage systems (ESS) and electric vehicle maintenance and inspection centers. Based on diagnostic results, it can also contribute to increasing resource utilization and reducing carbon emissions by classifying batteries suitable for reuse, remanufacturing, or recycling. Following its award last year for the battery life enhancement technology "Better.Re," LG Energy Solution has won the CES Innovation Award with pure software technology for two consecutive years. Lee Sang-hoon, an official at LG Energy Solution, stated, "This award is a result of recognition for the distinctiveness of our battery diagnostic technology and software competitiveness." He added, "We will continue to advance our diagnostic and management technologies to enhance the utilization value of used batteries and strive to build a sustainable battery circular ecosystem." Samsung SDI made the Innovation Award list with its prismatic battery solution for UPS, "SDI U8A3-UPS." A UPS is a system that supplies emergency power to critical facilities such as data centers when unexpected power outages occur. Recently, it has gained attention as essential equipment for stable power supply as power demand at AI data centers surges. The SDI U8A3-UPS is a product featuring prismatic battery cells made of lithium manganate (LMO) material. It achieves ultra-high output and high energy density, improving space efficiency by 33% compared to existing products. Stable power supply is possible with fewer batteries. It also has the advantage of supplying auxiliary power when power demand spikes during AI computing processes, preventing server failures or data damage. Recently, it demonstrated fire safety by becoming the first in the world to meet all evaluation criteria in a large-scale indoor fire test conducted by UL Solutions, a global safety certification body. With this, Samsung SDI has set a record of winning awards for three consecutive years since its initial participation in CES 2025. Last year, its ultra-high output cylindrical battery "SDI 25U-Power" won the Best of Innovation Award, and its thermal runaway blocking technology "No TP" received an Innovation Award. A Samsung SDI official said, "This is a result of recognition for the innovativeness of core power solutions in the AI era." He added, "We will continue to lead the market with products that combine the performance and safety required by customers."

artigo.texto: Revolve Renewable Power signs CAD$1.5 million deal to acquire 6 MW battery storage portfolio in Ontario Revolve Renewable Power Corp. signed a definitive agreement on October 30, 2026, to acquire Logan Energy Storage ULC — a battery energy storage portfolio in Ontario — for CAD$1.5 million, paid entirely from cash on hand. The portfolio totals 6 MW / 11.7 MWh of capacity spread across three sites in the province. Revolve signs deal to acquire Logan Energy Storage portfolio The equity purchase agreement, executed October 30, 2026, covers all issued and outstanding shares of Logan Energy Storage ULC. Through it, Revolve — trading on the Canadian Securities Exchange as REVV and on the OTCQB as REVVF — picks up a three-project BESS portfolio across Ontario. The CAD$1.5 million price comes entirely from Revolve’s existing cash. No external financing involved. The seller operates at arm’s length to Revolve, and the deal still needs to clear customary closing conditions and applicable regulatory approvals, though no specific closing date has been set. A successful close on Logan marks a concrete expansion of the company’s contracted asset base and a real-world demonstration of its stated strategy in action. Acquisition builds on earlier Trillium Storage purchase This deal didn’t come out of nowhere. Just two months earlier, in August 2026, Revolve wrapped up the acquisition of the Trillium Storage portfolio — six projects totaling 14.2 MW / 24.3 MWh, also in Ontario, funded from the balance sheet. That earlier transaction set a recognizable pattern: disciplined, bolt-on acquisitions with no outside capital required. CEO Myke Clark framed Logan as a natural next step. “The Logan acquisition is another important step for Revolve as we continue to build our storage platform in Ontario,” he said in the announcement, adding that the deal is expected to increase the company’s battery storage capacity in the province and deepen its presence there. Revolve’s stated strategy pairs targeted acquisitions with a greenfield development pipeline — both tracks running in parallel, buying operating or near-operating assets while building new ones from scratch. Closing expected to lift Ontario storage capacity to 20.2 MW Once Logan closes, Revolve expects its total Ontario battery storage capacity to reach approximately 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh across nine projects. That’s a significant jump from where things stood before the Trillium deal even closed. The company describes the transaction as accretive to revenue. The portfolio is meant to contribute contracted, cash-generating assets that support long-term recurring income — the kind of stable base storage operators rely on when projects are tied to grid service agreements or similar arrangements. No specific timeline has been given beyond the standard reference to closing conditions and regulatory approvals, and projections around capacity additions and revenue accretion carry the usual execution risks. Revolve’s broader role in North American energy storage Revolve Renewable Power Corp. is headquartered in Vancouver, BC, and describes itself as an owner, operator, and developer of power generation and digital infrastructure projects across North America. Its dual listing — CSE: REVV and OTCQB: REVVF — reflects a cross-border investor base. Ontario is an increasingly active market for grid-scale battery storage. The province has been working to balance a growing share of renewable generation with grid reliability needs, and wind and solar output fluctuates in ways that create real operational pressure. Storage assets help manage that variability by absorbing surplus electricity and releasing it when demand peaks. For Revolve, Ontario’s direction makes it a logical place to concentrate its storage platform. What the Logan deal means for Revolve’s Ontario platform Together, the Trillium and Logan acquisitions have moved Revolve from a standing start to a nine-project, 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh storage portfolio in Ontario — in a matter of months. Both deals were funded from cash on hand, both involved arm’s-length sellers, and both fit the acquisition-plus-development strategy the company has laid out publicly. Logan adds 6 MW / 11.7 MWh to that base at a purchase price of CAD$1.5 million. That’s a relatively modest outlay for a company building scale in a capital-intensive sector. Whether it closes on schedule depends on regulatory approvals and customary conditions, but the structure mirrors what Revolve already pulled off with Trillium — same playbook, different site. If you’re tracking Revolve’s growth in Ontario, the number to watch is 20.2 MW. A successful close on Logan marks a concrete expansion of the company’s contracted asset base and a real-world demonstration of its stated strategy in action. artigo.texto: asharkyu/Shutterstock Save for later Print Download Share LinkedIn Twitter The energy storage market is expanding at a speed that would have seemed impossible just a few years ago. Yet, government targets have not kept pace with the market's growth. Storage is no longer a peripheral technology whose deployment can be left until renewable generation is built. It is becoming a central part of how electricity systems will operate, how much value they can extract from renewable power and how reliably they can meet growing demand. With COP31 focused on accelerating electrification, the gap between storage deployment and government ambition raises questions about whether power systems can deliver on those commitments. Ember’s analysis of national 2030 storage targets shows how far countries have come and how far they still have to go. The combined ambition of countries and the EU has reached 822 gigawatts, nearly three times the 284 GW assessed when governments agreed the Global Energy Storage and Grids Pledge at COP29 in 2024. But that total remains 45% below the pledge’s 1,500 GW goal. More revealing still is where the increase has come from. China and the EU account for most of the increase in national storage targets worldwide. The global headline suggests a broad shift in ambition. The underlying picture is much more concentrated. Global Storage Ambition Rests on 2 Markets China has raised its 2030 storage ambition from 130 GW to 460 GW under its 15th Five-Year Plan. The target combines 300 GW of new-type energy storage, mostly lithium-ion batteries, with 160 GW of pumped hydro. The EU, meanwhile, established its first bloc-wide storage target at 200 GW in June 2026. These decisions are significant. China’s target reflects the need to integrate its rapidly expanding renewable capacity, while the EU’s agreement explicitly links storage to reducing gas demand and making better use of renewable electricity. But the concentration of ambition matters. Since COP29, only eight countries and the EU have increased or introduced 2030 storage targets. Many other major markets have made little change to their plans. The result is a global total that looks much stronger than the underlying policy shift. Two major economies have moved decisively, while much of the rest of the world has yet to follow. That matters because the energy transition is not being built in two markets alone. Countries are pursuing different combinations of solar, wind, electrification and grid investment. They will not all need identical storage technologies or deployment pathways. But they do need to understand what their own power systems require and plan accordingly. A global pledge is only as strong as the national plans on how to deliver it. The Market Is Already Moving Faster Than the Plans Annual storage additions reached a record 118 GW in 2025, 108 GW of them batteries, and installed capacity reached 430 GW by the end of the year. The pace of change is remarkable. It took four years for annual battery additions to rise from around 10 GW to 100 GW. Solar took nine years to cross the same threshold, while wind took 15 years. Falling costs have helped drive this expansion. Battery storage costs have declined by roughly 20% per year on average over the past decade, improving the economics of projects and opening up new opportunities for power systems. Current deployment also puts the shortfall in national targets into perspective. If annual additions remained at the 2025 level through to 2030, global installed storage capacity would reach around 1,020 GW. That would exceed the combined national targets by almost one-quarter. Reaching the 1,500 GW global pledge will require further growth. But our analysis suggests that the necessary acceleration is well within reach of recent market performance. Battery additions have grown at almost 80% a year since 2020. To reach the 1,200 GW of battery storage envisaged in the International Energy Agency’s net-zero scenario update, annual additions would need to grow at only about one-fifth of that rate. The market has already demonstrated that it can grow at extraordinary speed. The question is whether governments are planning for the power systems that this growth makes possible. Solar Policy Without Storage Planning Is Incomplete The consequences and benefits are clearest in solar markets. Solar power is generated mostly during the day, but electricity demand continues into the evening and overnight. Batteries can shift some of that daytime generation to periods when it is needed, reducing curtailment, easing pressure on grids and allowing existing renewable capacity to deliver more useful electricity. Storage and solar are therefore not separate policy choices. They are complementary parts of a power system. Building more solar without planning for flexibility risks leaving some of its potential untapped. Of the 20 largest solar markets by capacity in 2025, 12 have a 2030 storage target and eight do not. Some of these markets are already deploying storage at scale. The US has installed roughly 52 GW of utility-scale battery power capacity, while Germany has around 30 GWh of battery storage. Market signals can drive projects where the economics are attractive. But they do not necessarily ensure that the right amount and type of storage will be built in the right locations and on the right timelines. Nor do they guarantee that storage deployment will be coordinated with new generation, transmission infrastructure and changing patterns of demand. Credible targets can provide a direction around which these decisions are made. Storage Belongs at the Center of Energy Planning The stakes will grow as electricity takes on a larger role across transport, buildings and industry. The Global Electrification Pledge proposed by the COP31 presidency aims to raise electricity’s share of final energy demand from around 20% to 35% by 2035. artigo.texto: Elon Musk e data centers: o que muda após eleições nos EUA Eleitores americanos barraram projetos de data centers em diversas localidades. A onda democrata pressiona big techs e pode redesenhar a infraestrutura de IA nos próximos anos. As eleições legislativas de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos trouxeram uma vitória histórica para o Partido Democrata. Mas o resultado das urnas não se limitou a disputas partidárias tradicionais. Em dezenas de votações locais espalhadas pelo país, eleitores rejeitaram projetos de construção de data centers ou aprovaram medidas que impõem restrições e moratórias à expansão dessas instalações. O recado é claro: a infraestrutura que sustenta a corrida por inteligência artificial virou um problema político. E quem mais sente o impacto é justamente quem mais apostou no lado oposto da mesa. O custo político de meio bilhão de dólares Elon Musk destinou cerca de meio bilhão de dólares em doações ao Partido Republicano neste ciclo eleitoral. O retorno, até agora, foi próximo de zero. O empresário, que transferiu a sede de suas principais empresas para o Texas, agora opera em um estado que elegeu a democrata Gina Hinojosa como governadora, derrotando Greg Abbott. Hinojosa fez da restrição a data centers uma bandeira de campanha. Para Musk, que é um dos maiores construtores de infraestrutura de computação do mundo por meio da xAI e de seus projetos ligados à Tesla, o cenário se tornou significativamente mais hostil. A ironia é difícil de ignorar: suas empresas agora respondem a um governo estadual eleito com a promessa de limitar exatamente o tipo de operação que ele pretende expandir. O caso de Musk é emblemático, mas não isolado. Como discutimos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a relação entre big techs e governos locais nos EUA vem se deteriorando há meses. A diferença é que agora essa tensão tem tradução eleitoral concreta. Por que data centers viraram alvo de eleitores A rejeição aos data centers não é um fenômeno exclusivamente partidário. Republicanos, independentes e democratas votaram contra esses projetos por razões que vão além de ideologia. O problema é operacional e ambiental. Grandes empresas de tecnologia adotaram uma postura de sigilo extremo para aprovar projetos. Em muitos casos, exigiram que autoridades eleitas assinassem acordos de confidencialidade (NDAs) antes de conhecer os detalhes das propostas. Informações sobre o tamanho real das instalações e o impacto ambiental foram omitidas, mesmo em regiões do sudoeste americano onde a escassez de água já é crítica. Essa estratégia de opacidade transformou o que poderia ser uma questão técnica em uma causa popular. Movimentos de base, sem coordenação nacional centralizada, se organizaram em diversas comunidades para barrar ou ao menos condicionar a aprovação desses empreendimentos. O sentimento anti-data center se mostrou um motor eleitoral eficiente, especialmente quando canalizado por candidatos democratas. O paralelo com o Brasil é relevante. Como analisamos em matéria sobre o impacto da IA generativa na demanda por infraestrutura, o consumo energético e hídrico dessas instalações é uma preocupação global, não apenas americana. OpenAI já mudou de postura A resposta do mercado foi rápida. A OpenAI divulgou o que chamou de “compute campus policy blueprint”, um conjunto de diretrizes para seus futuros projetos de infraestrutura. Entre as mudanças anunciadas: fim da exigência de NDAs para autoridades públicas, maior transparência sobre a escala dos projetos e compartilhamento antecipado de planos com comunidades locais. A manobra inclui um detalhe revelador. A empresa evitou o termo “data center” em seu documento, preferindo “compute campus”. A tentativa de rebranding é uma admissão de que a expressão “data center” se tornou politicamente tóxica. Se a nova nomenclatura vai pegar, é outra história. Mas o movimento mostra que a pressão regulatória funciona. Esse padrão é conhecido em outros setores. Quando há sinalização clara de que o ambiente regulatório vai endurecer, empresas se antecipam com concessões voluntárias para evitar restrições mais severas. A questão é se essas mudanças são substantivas ou cosméticas. O que vem pela frente para a infraestrutura de IA Os próximos dois anos prometem ser mais difíceis para hyperscalers e construtores de data centers nos Estados Unidos. Com democratas no controle de governos estaduais estratégicos e um sentimento popular contrário à expansão desenfreada, o ritmo de aprovação de novos projetos tende a desacelerar. O impacto não se limita ao ciclo eleitoral atual. A resistência a data centers pode se consolidar como tema permanente, presente também nas eleições de 2028. Para empresas como Microsoft, Google, Amazon e Meta, que planejam investir centenas de bilhões de dólares em infraestrutura de IA nos próximos anos, isso significa custos mais altos, prazos mais longos e maior incerteza jurídica. Para investidores que acompanham o setor, o dado mais relevante é este: a escassez de capacidade computacional, que já era um gargalo técnico, agora é também um gargalo político. Como abordamos em nossa análise sobre IA e investimentos, o preço da computação é cada vez mais determinado por fatores que vão além de silício e energia. A lição para o mercado de tecnologia O caso Musk é instrutivo por várias razões. A primeira é que dinheiro político tem retorno incerto, especialmente quando a causa que você financia entra em conflito com preocupações locais de eleitores. A segunda é que a infraestrutura física da revolução de IA não pode ser tratada como um detalhe logístico. Ela é, cada vez mais, um tema de política pública. Empresas que entenderem isso cedo, como a OpenAI parece estar tentando fazer, terão mais chances de navegar o novo ambiente. As que insistirem na estratégia de sigilo e lobby pesado podem descobrir que o custo político é tão real quanto o custo de capital.
