artigo.texto: In delivering the Benchmark Lifetime Achievement Award 2026 to CATL (HKG:3750) Chairman Robin Zeng, former recipient and long-time colleague Bob Galyen says Zeng has helped transform batteries from a niche technology into a global industry. Gaylen, CATL’s former CTO, credits him with bringing electrification to scale and positioning batteries at the heart of the modern economy. The award was delivered at Benchmark Week 2026 in Shanghai, held on 10–11 November at the Pudong Shangri-La. Zeng founded CATL in 2011, recognising that batteries would become an essential part of the global economy. Over the last 15 years, he has grown the company around that vision. Zeng was also named to the TIME100 Climate 2025 list for his leadership in business climate action. In 2023, he received a Nobel Sustainability Trust award recognising his contributions to transportation electrification and the energy transition. Galyen notes that Zeng recognised early on the need to electrify at scale and has since focused on making battery technology reliable, affordable, and available across income levels. Zeng points to five factors that matter for EVs: safety, performance, lifespan, cost, and environmental impact. That last factor extends to the company’s own operations, not just the impact of EV adoption. CATL says it achieved carbon neutrality across its core manufacturing operations in 2025 and aims to reach full value-chain carbon neutrality by 2035. A rising tide for the battery ecosystem In line with the event’s theme of collaboration across the battery value chain, Zeng says the industry can only achieve long-term success if it grows together. Rather than concentrating profits in one part of the supply chain, he believes value should be shared so that participants can continue investing, innovating, and scaling. Zeng likens the approach to ensuring everyone has enough oxygen to survive. A healthy industry, he says, relies on miners, processors, manufacturers, automakers, and technology providers all benefiting from growth. That philosophy extends beyond CATL. While acknowledging the geopolitical pressures affecting the industry and growing competition for control of battery supply chains, Zeng says no single country or business can dominate the energy transition alone. Achieving carbon neutrality requires nations and industries to work together, share expertise, and share the value created. Galyen agrees, noting the opportunities for communities and economies. He says global expertise is needed and that the West has much to learn from China in this area. CATL has put those principles into practice through partnerships around the world that allow participants to learn from each other. Innovation drives the next chapter For Zeng, the next phase of the battery industry will be driven by innovation. Since the early 2000s, falling prices and more efficient manufacturing have helped bring batteries and EVs into the mainstream. Zeng notes that long-term growth still depends on the industry’s ability to innovate, develop new technologies, and improve upon existing ones. He describes the battery sector as a “teenager”, with much more room to grow. As demand for electrification continues to rise, innovation across the supply chain remains a key challenge for industry leaders. AI can be a major enabler, Zeng notes, helping researchers identify new materials, accelerate laboratory work, and uncover opportunities for new battery technologies. Zeng believes that lithium-ion batteries will continue to play a dominant role, but sees growing opportunities for alternative chemistries such as sodium-ion, particularly in energy storage and urban transport. The end use will ultimately determine the most suitable chemistry, with producers matching batteries to each application and customer. Battery swapping is another innovation Zeng highlights, allowing users to access different batteries depending on their needs. Looking ahead, both Zeng and Galyen see opportunities in new materials, improved surface chemistry, and innovations such as low-cost graphene. As electrification expands, they expect the industry’s next breakthroughs to emerge through materials research and development, AI, and collaboration across industries and borders. Write to Amy Rotman at Mining.com.au Main image: Mining.com.au

artigo.texto: Lexus ES EV Takes Aim at South Korea's approximately $50,000 Segment — With a CATL Battery Again Toyota's premium brand Lexus has introduced electrified versions of its upper-midsize ES sedan in South Korea, rapidly reshaping the competitive landscape of the roughly 70 million won (approximately $52,000) EV market. This price band is the last stretch where automakers can maintain a luxury brand image while still qualifying for government subsidies, making it the segment where imported carmakers are racing to concentrate their new models. The catch: many of the leading EVs in this bracket run on batteries from China's CATL, leaving South Korea's three battery makers with even less room to maneuver. Lexus unveiled the fully redesigned eighth-generation ES in the South Korean market on the 13th of last month. Three powertrains were introduced together: the pure-electric ES350e and ES500e, and the hybrid ES350h. Since its global debut in 1989, the ES had been sold only with combustion and hybrid powertrains; the eighth generation marks the first time it has a pure-electric lineup. Lexus has discontinued combustion-engine models entirely for this generation. The pricing drew market attention. The entry-level Premium trim of the ES350e was set at 71.6 million won (approximately $53,000) — 1.3 million won (approximately $970) below the equivalent hybrid, the ES350h Premium at 72.9 million won (approximately $54,000). EVs typically cost more than combustion or hybrid models of the same class because of their expensive batteries, so this reversal is read as an intent to lift market share through price competitiveness. The ES500e Premium, a dual-motor all-wheel-drive variant, was priced in the 77 million won (approximately $57,000) range. Performance splits the two models' characters. The ES350e is a single-motor front-wheel-drive model with 478 km of range per charge and 227 horsepower. The ES500e is dual-motor all-wheel drive; range drops to 435 km but output rises to 347 horsepower. Note: Prices are for the South Korean market. With a lower-than-expected starting price, orders moved quickly. According to industry sources, cumulative orders for the new ES stand at about 5,000 units, including pre-orders taken over the past month. The electric ES350e and ES500e are said to account for roughly half. There is no shortage of rivals battling in the 70 million won band. Volvo's upper-midsize sedan ES90, Polestar's upper-midsize SUV Polestar 3 and BMW's midsize SUV iX3 all sit in the same range. Tesla's Model Y, which dominates South Korea's EV market, starts at 49.99 million won (approximately $37,000) for the rear-wheel-drive Premium, while the all-wheel-drive Model Y L Premium sells for 72.99 million won (approximately $54,000). Behind the rush of import brands into this price range is a restructuring of the subsidy system. EVs under 85 million won (approximately $63,000) currently qualify for subsidies, but the South Korean government plans to lower the threshold to under 80 million won (approximately $59,000) starting next year. Vehicles priced at 80 million won or more must carry green license plates when purchased as corporate cars. Drop below the 60 million won (approximately $45,000) range and the premium image fades; climb into the 80 million won range and you take on both the loss of subsidies and the license-plate regulation. That is why the 70 million won band — where brand value and practical benefits can be secured together — has emerged as effectively the only safe zone. The problem is that the heart of EVs in this segment is Chinese. The Lexus ES350e and ES500e, Volvo ES90 and Polestar 3 all carry CATL's LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries. The Model Y also uses LG Energy Solution's NCM (nickel cobalt manganese) batteries in its Long Range and Performance trims, but the cheaper rear-wheel-drive trim is fitted with CATL's LFP battery. The BMW iX3 runs on batteries from China's EVE Energy. CATL held the top spot in the global EV battery market with a 39.1% share in the January-September period this year. The reason automakers choose Chinese batteries is simple. The NCM batteries that South Korean companies focus on have high energy density and long range, but contain expensive raw materials such as cobalt and nickel. LFP batteries, by contrast, are based on iron and phosphorus, keeping procurement costs low. For automakers that must hold prices in the 70 million won range while preserving a premium image, cost reduction is a structural necessity. The sense of crisis in South Korea's battery industry goes further. The high-priced premium EV market has limited room to expand, and with Hyundai and Kia's EV sales stagnating, Chinese companies are encroaching on the South Korean market. "To make matters worse, Chinese EV makers such as BYD, followed by Zeekr and Xpeng, are entering South Korea one after another, further narrowing the ground for Hyundai and Kia," a battery industry official said. "The reason South Korean battery makers have recently been putting effort into the energy storage system (ESS) market is also the judgment that it will be difficult to reclaim leadership in the EV segment from Chinese companies for the time being." The implications for South Korea's three battery makers are significant. For LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On — which have been expanding their LFP lineups — the situation now requires head-on competition with Chinese companies in entry-level and mid-priced EVs where price competitiveness is decisive. If the Lexus ES EV proves a hit, the 70 million won market is expected to grow further, and battery makers that fail to secure an LFP supply chain in this segment may fall behind in the race for volume. Conversely, automakers are expected to further strengthen their 70 million won lineups starting next year, when the subsidy threshold drops below 80 million won, setting the stage for an even fiercer battle for battery orders in this price range.

artigo.texto: Data centers viram alvo político nos EUA e ameaçam planos da big tech Resultados das eleições legislativas nos EUA revelam onda antidata center que já obriga empresas como OpenAI a rever políticas de transparência. As eleições legislativas americanas de 2025 entregaram mais do que uma virada política. Entregaram um recado direto para a indústria de tecnologia: a expansão desenfreada de data centers encontrou um limite concreto na resistência popular. Em dezenas de votações locais espalhadas pelo país, eleitores rejeitaram medidas que facilitariam a construção de novos centros de dados. E onde o tema não estava diretamente na cédula, os candidatos eleitos fizeram campanha prometendo restringir essas instalações. O caso mais emblemático é o do Texas, onde a governadora eleita Gina Hinojosa derrotou Greg Abbott com uma plataforma que incluía limitar a expansão de data centers no estado. O movimento não é trivial. O Texas é hoje um dos principais polos de infraestrutura digital dos Estados Unidos e abriga operações centrais de várias empresas de Elon Musk, que agora se vê em uma posição desconfortável. Meio bilhão de dólares e nenhum retorno político Musk doou cerca de meio bilhão de dólares para o Partido Republicano neste ciclo eleitoral. O resultado prático foi próximo de zero. Seus candidatos perderam em disputas-chave, e o Texas, estado onde concentrou suas operações empresariais, virou democrata pela primeira vez em décadas. É um cenário inédito. O maior doador republicano e um dos maiores construtores de infraestrutura de data centers do mundo opera agora sob um governo estadual que promete dificultar exatamente esse tipo de projeto. A ironia não escapou aos analistas do setor. Mas o problema de Musk é apenas a ponta mais visível de uma tendência mais ampla. A rejeição a data centers virou um fenômeno bipartidário, como já abordamos ao analisar os impactos da inteligência artificial na infraestrutura global. Republicanos, democratas e independentes em diversas regiões se uniram contra projetos que consideravam opacos e prejudiciais ao meio ambiente. Por que eleitores estão contra os data centers A resposta passa por três fatores que se acumularam nos últimos anos. Primeiro, o sigilo excessivo. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, as chamadas hyperscalers, frequentemente exigiam acordos de confidencialidade até de autoridades eleitas antes de compartilhar detalhes de seus projetos. Em muitos casos, a escala real das instalações só ficava clara após a aprovação. Segundo, o impacto ambiental. Data centers consomem volumes enormes de água para resfriamento. No sudoeste americano, onde a escassez hídrica já é uma crise, isso se tornou um ponto de atrito real. Uma única instalação de grande porte pode consumir milhões de litros de água por dia, competindo diretamente com o abastecimento residencial e agrícola. Terceiro, o consumo energético. Em um momento em que a demanda por energia dispara por conta da expansão acelerada da inteligência artificial, comunidades locais começaram a perceber que data centers pressionam as redes elétricas e, em alguns casos, elevam o custo da energia para os moradores. Essa combinação transformou o tema em uma questão genuinamente popular. Não foi uma pauta imposta de cima para baixo, mas algo que emergiu de comunidades que sentiram os efeitos no dia a dia. OpenAI já mudou de postura O mais revelador dos desdobramentos veio rápido. A OpenAI, uma das empresas que mais investem em infraestrutura de computação no mundo, publicou o que chamou de “política de campus de computação”. O documento traz mudanças relevantes: fim da exigência de NDAs para autoridades locais, compromisso de compartilhar planos com as comunidades e promessa de operar com mais transparência. O rebranding também chama atenção. A OpenAI evita deliberadamente o termo “data center” e adota “campus de computação”, uma tentativa clara de se distanciar de uma expressão que se tornou tóxica no debate público americano. É difícil imaginar que a troca de nomenclatura, por si só, mude a percepção popular. Mas as mudanças operacionais que a acompanham são concretas. O episódio ilustra uma dinâmica que investidores e analistas de mercado deveriam observar com atenção: quando o ambiente regulatório sinaliza restrições, as empresas se adaptam. Quando não há pressão, elas operam no limite do que é permitido. O que isso significa para o setor de tecnologia Os próximos dois anos serão mais difíceis para a expansão de infraestrutura digital nos Estados Unidos. E o problema pode se estender para 2028 e além, dependendo de como o sentimento popular evoluir. Para as big techs, o impacto é direto. A corrida pela inteligência artificial depende fundamentalmente de capacidade computacional, e capacidade computacional depende de data centers. Se a construção dessas instalações desacelerar, o ritmo de desenvolvimento de modelos de IA também pode ser afetado. Isso não significa que a expansão vai parar. Significa que vai custar mais, demorar mais e exigir negociações mais complexas com comunidades e governos locais. Empresas que anteciparam essa mudança e construíram relações transparentes com as comunidades terão vantagem. As que operaram no sigilo vão pagar o preço político. Para o mercado como um todo, o recado das urnas americanas é um lembrete de que infraestrutura tecnológica não existe no vácuo. Ela ocupa espaço físico, consome recursos naturais e afeta pessoas reais. Ignorar isso deixou de ser apenas uma falha ética. Agora é um risco de negócio mensurável. A questão que fica para os próximos trimestres é se esse movimento americano vai inspirar restrições semelhantes em outros países. Na Europa, onde a regulação de tecnologia já é mais rígida, a tendência pode se acelerar. No Brasil, onde a discussão sobre data centers ainda é incipiente, a experiência americana serve como antecipação do debate que inevitavelmente chegará. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentab

artigo.texto: South Korea's Samsung, Hyundai Motor Join Forces on Solid-State Battery Mass-Production Processes, Filing 9 Joint Patents Battery cooperation between Samsung and Hyundai Motor Group is moving beyond supply contracts into joint design and next-generation technology development. After jointly filing patents that simultaneously raise the safety and energy density of electric-vehicle battery packs, the two sides have entered a phase in which they are jointly securing not just materials research but mass-production process technology for next-generation solid-state batteries. According to the Korea Intellectual Property Rights Information Service (KIPRIS), a patent titled "Battery Pack and Vehicle Including the Same," jointly filed by Hyundai Motor, Kia and Samsung SDI, was published on the 22nd of last month. Its core is a gas vent at the bottom of the battery cells and a separate channel at the lower part of the battery pack. The structure vents high-temperature gas generated in a thermal-runaway situation to the outside while merging the previously separate gas-venting space and impact-protection space into one to raise energy density. The patent was designed around Samsung SDI's flagship prismatic battery. Five Hyundai Motor and Kia researchers and two Samsung SDI researchers are named as inventors. The key point is that the two companies' cooperation has expanded beyond simple cell supply to joint design of battery packs tailored to vehicles. Samsung SDI signed its first EV battery supply contract with Hyundai Motor in 2023. Under the terms, Samsung SDI will supply prismatic batteries made at its Hungarian plant for Hyundai Motor and Kia's Europe-bound EVs for seven years from this year through 2032. The number of models actually using them is also growing. Starting with Kia's EV2, the number of vehicles using Samsung SDI batteries has expanded to three models, including Hyundai's Ioniq 3 and Genesis's top-tier electric SUV, the GV90. The move is seen as a result of Hyundai Motor and Kia — which have mainly used pouch-type cells — rating the prismatic battery's energy density and safety highly. Cooperation is also taking concrete shape in next-generation solid-state batteries. Hyundai Motor, Kia and Samsung SDI jointly filed a total of nine solid-state-related patents, including divisional applications, from 2022 through last year, two of which were registered last year. Initially the focus was on coating technology to protect sulfide-based solid electrolytes that are vulnerable to moisture, but from 2023 the research scope widened to battery life improvement and mass-production processes. A representative example is the joint filing of temperature-measurement technology for the high-temperature warm isostatic pressing (WIP) process needed to manufacture solid-state batteries, along with battery-cell preheating and transfer devices. Solid-state batteries replace liquid electrolytes with solid ones to improve safety and energy density, and their applications could expand beyond EVs to humanoid robots and other uses. Euisun Chung, chairman of Hyundai Motor Group, said in August regarding the group's electrification strategy: "EVs will go their own way as EVs, but we are also researching solid-state batteries, so that part has to come out before we can move to a more efficient direction." Note: Publication and registration dates and contract terms are based on the Korea Intellectual Property Rights Information Service and industry confirmation. Executive-level exchanges underpin the broadening of the two groups' cooperation. On the 9th, Samsung Electronics hosted "HMG Appreciation Day" at its Seocheon Training Center in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, inviting key Hyundai Motor Group executives. Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman Jeon Young-hyun and Hyundai Motor Group Vice Chairman Jang Jae-hoon presided over the event, which was attended by 177 people, including executives, senior managers and spouses from both groups. It was the first time Samsung has held a large-scale invitation event for a specific South Korean group. At the event, Vice Chairman Jang said, "Samsung and Hyundai Motor Group are expanding the possibilities for cooperation beyond vehicle components such as automotive electronics, audio and batteries to future industries such as robots and energy," adding, "I hope we will respect each other's strengths, pool our efforts and take on future challenges together." Vice Chairman Jeon responded, "I hope Samsung's technology, spanning components to finished products, will come together to open up new value and infinite possibilities." The two companies' ties date back to 2020. In May 2020, when Chairman Chung was senior vice chairman, he visited Samsung SDI's Cheonan plant and discussed next-generation EV batteries with Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong, and two months later Lee paid a return visit to Hyundai Motor and Kia's Namyang Research Institute. This exchange is seen as having paved the way for the 2023 supply contract. A relationship that had been kept at arm's length — partly because of Samsung's foray into the auto business in the 1990s — has turned into a cooperative framework under third-generation management. artigo.texto: Revolve Renewable Power agrees to acquire 6 MW Ontario battery storage portfolio for CAD $1.5 million Revolve Renewable Power Corp. (CSE: REVV; OTCQB: REVVF) signed a definitive agreement on October 30, 2026, to acquire Logan Energy Storage ULC and its three-project battery energy storage portfolio in Ontario. The deal is valued at CAD $1.5 million and covers a combined capacity of 6 MW / 11.7 MWh. Deal terms and structure Revolve executed the definitive equity purchase agreements on October 30, 2026, through a subsidiary. The structure is clean: Revolve is buying all issued and outstanding shares of Logan Energy Storage ULC, which holds the three Ontario BESS projects. The total purchase price is CAD $1,500,000, funded entirely from cash already on the balance sheet — no new debt, no equity financing required to close. The seller is at arm’s length to Revolve, so there are no related-party considerations. The transaction still needs to clear customary closing conditions and applicable regulatory approvals before it’s final, and Revolve hasn’t put a target closing date out there publicly. Once the Logan acquisition closes, Revolve expects its Ontario battery storage capacity to reach approximately 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh across nine projects. Why Revolve is acquiring the Logan portfolio The Logan deal isn’t a one-off move. It fits squarely into Revolve’s stated strategy of building a battery storage platform in Ontario while simultaneously advancing a greenfield development pipeline in the province. Ontario’s energy storage market has become a deliberate focus for the company. Revolve completed its first major step in that direction back in August 2026, when it closed the acquisition of the Trillium Storage portfolio — six projects totaling 14.2 MW / 24.3 MWh. Logan is the follow-on, adding three more projects to that growing base. CEO Myke Clark described the transaction as part of the company’s “disciplined acquisition and development strategy.” That language signals Revolve is selecting assets that fit a defined platform-building approach in a market it’s already committed to — not chasing deals opportunistically. Expected impact on Revolve’s Ontario storage capacity Once the Logan acquisition closes, Revolve expects its Ontario battery storage capacity to reach approximately 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh across nine projects. That’s a meaningful jump from where it stood before Trillium, when the company had zero operating storage assets in the province. The math is straightforward. Six Trillium projects contributed 14.2 MW / 24.3 MWh. Logan’s three projects add 6 MW / 11.7 MWh on top of that, bringing the combined total to nine projects across the two acquisitions. Clark emphasized that the Logan deal is expected to further establish Revolve’s presence in Ontario — and beyond the capacity numbers, the company is targeting contracted, cash-generating assets that produce recurring revenue rather than depending on merchant power prices alone. Worth noting: these are forward-looking expectations. Revolve has flagged that actual results could differ depending on regulatory approvals, operational performance, and whether the portfolio performs in line with management’s assumptions. Background: Revolve’s growth in Canadian energy storage Revolve Renewable Power Corp. is headquartered in Vancouver, BC. The company owns, operates, and develops power generation and digital infrastructure projects across North America, trading on the Canadian Securities Exchange under REVV and on the OTCQB under REVVF. Battery energy storage systems — BESS — store electricity and discharge it back to the grid when it’s needed. They play an increasingly important role in supporting grid stability and integrating variable renewable sources like wind and solar. Ontario, with its evolving energy mix and ongoing grid modernization efforts, has become an active market for exactly this kind of infrastructure. Revolve’s entry into Ontario battery storage is relatively recent; the Trillium acquisition in August 2026 was its first major transaction in this space, and management has indicated it expects to keep building through further acquisitions and development activity. What this deal means for Revolve going forward Taken together, the Trillium and Logan acquisitions give Revolve a nine-project, 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh battery storage footprint in Ontario — assembled in roughly three months. For a company that had no Ontario storage assets before mid-2026, that’s a notable pace of portfolio construction. The Logan deal’s modest price tag — CAD $1.5 million funded from existing cash — also reflects a capital-efficient approach. Revolve isn’t stretching its balance sheet to make this happen, which leaves room for continued deal-making if the right opportunities come up. What happens next depends on closing. Once customary conditions and regulatory approvals are satisfied, Revolve will hold a nine-project Ontario storage portfolio that it describes as a foundation for longer-term growth, both through additional acquisitions and through its greenfield development pipeline in the province. artigo.texto: Is this the only U.S. town to vote 'yes' on data centers? On Election Day, voters approved more than 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth. But not all Americans decided against data centers. The majority of voters in Harwood, North Dakota, said "no" to a ballot measure calling for additional steps when the town evaluates, approves, and administers developments like that of data centers, Tech Insider reported. In a town of 845 people, 430 voted, and around 75 percent voted against added restrictions. (As Tech Insider notes, however, that documentation on small towns could be varied — The Washington Post reports that Harwood's population is 845, while other outlets report 940.) The big project in question is a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot data center right outside Harwood, the Washington Post reports. Data center developer Applied Digital is behind the project. You May Also Like The vote caused the Post to claim that Harwood is "the only town in the U.S. that said yes to data centers." While the building of a data center itself wasn't on the ballot, Harwood residents indeed voted against further bureaucracy towards them. Harwood breaks the trend of what happened on Election Day, which Mashable's Rebecca Ruiz said was a clear message: "The AI reckoning is here." Backlash to both AI and data centers had been mounting in 2026, and voters were able to express their discontent last Tuesday. The list of U.S. states that ban data centers could grow in 2027. artigo.texto: A Eletronet anunciou nesta segunda-feira, 9, um investimento de R$ 25 milhões para construção de um novo data center em São Paulo. Com obras já iniciadas, a previsão é de que a unidade entre em operação no primeiro trimestre de 2027. Segundo a empresa especializada em infraestrutura de telecomunicações, o complexo denominado ELET1 terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 megawatt (MW), podendo chegar a 1 MW em uma futura expansão. A Eletronet informou que o novo centro de dados deve fortalecer a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão, além de ampliar a escala ao atendimento de provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecom, provedores de serviços de Internet (ISPs) e hyperscalers. "O ELET1 representa um passo estratégico para fortalecer nossa atuação no segmento de data centers. Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais", afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet, em nota. Região estratégica De acordo com a Eletronet, o complexo será instalado em uma localização com elevada concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo. Desse modo, estará preparado para atender à crescente demanda por serviços de data center para os segmentos de nuvem, streaming e telecom. A unidade também vai abrigar o ponto de interconexão (PIX) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo, um dos maiores pontos de troca de tráfego de Internet do mundo. O PIX da empresa, inclusive, tem se destacado no volume de tráfego de download na infraestrutura paulista. O objetivo desse movimento, segundo a empresa, é aumentar as possibilidades de conexão dos clientes com diferentes redes e provedores de serviços digitais. A Eletronet ainda ressaltou que o ELET1 integra a sua estratégia no segmento de data centers e de expansão da sua rede nacional de fibra óptica. Quando o centro de dados estiver em plena operação, a empresa planeja migrar a infraestrutura do data center atualmente em operação em São Paulo para o novo ambiente. Sustentabilidade Em comunicado, a Eletronet salientou que o ELET1 será construído levando em conta as melhores práticas globais de infraestrutura, incluindo soluções de proteção física e lógica, seguindo as diretrizes da norma ISO 27001. Além disso, o data center terá aplicações modernas de gestão ambiental e energética, com base nos padrões ISO 14001, ISO 50001 e LEED. A unidade ainda deve contar com dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVa, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predical (BMS) atualizado, monitoramento contínuo e um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência.

artigo.texto: Investing.com -- The European Union and Britain are nearing an agreement to reconnect their carbon emissions trading markets, potentially reducing trade costs and improving liquidity, Bloomberg exclusively reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the negotiations. The agreement could be announced at a November 20 summit, nearly six years after Britain established its own emissions trading system following Brexit. Negotiators have settled provisions covering emissions limits, permit supply controls and free allowances. Rules governing financial derivatives remain the final unresolved issue. Linking the markets would allow companies to use permits from either system to meet regulatory obligations, reducing compliance complexity for businesses operating across both jurisdictions. The arrangement could eventually eliminate carbon border charges on qualifying trade, although exemptions would not take effect automatically. Under EU legislation, Britain must establish full market linkage and maintain effective carbon pricing without preferential rebates before receiving an exemption from the bloc's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. The EU's border carbon rules became operational this year, with Britain's equivalent scheduled to begin in January 2027. Carbon prices have already converged as expectations of an agreement strengthened. British December allowances closed Friday at £64.81 per metric ton, compared with €86.55 for benchmark EU permits. ABN Amro expects the price gap to narrow further over the next two years, potentially increasing compliance costs for British companies. The proposed framework would recognize British emissions caps through 2030. From 2031, annual UK permit issuance would be limited to 7.1% of the EU system's allowance supply. Britain would also establish a market stability reserve containing at least 29.5 million allowances when the agreement takes effect. The deal requires approval from British and EU authorities, including the European Parliament and EU member states. Negotiators could provisionally apply the agreement before formal implementation, although its entry into force is linked to separate arrangements covering agricultural trade standards and youth mobility. artigo.texto: BYD may soon have a new electric SUV in its India lineup. The BYD Atto 2 EV has once again been spotted testing on Indian roads, but this time the SUV has been seen without camouflage. This latest spotting has revealed its exterior design, side profile and rear styling more clearly than before. Join Our Youtube Channel to stay updated with daily Indian car & bike news instantly! Earlier, a heavily camouflaged test mule of the Atto 2 was also spotted in India, in which only some details of the front design could be seen. Now the undisguised appearance is another indication that BYD is preparing to expand its electric SUV range in the Indian market. The launch timeline and India-specific specifications have not yet been officially announced. In the international market, the Atto 2 is a relatively accessible model in BYD’s electric SUV range. Upon launch in India, it could be positioned below the Atto 3 and serve as the company’s entry-level electric SUV. Also Read: BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition Costs Rs. 50.60 Lakh, But What Do Buyers Actually Get? BYD Atto 2 EV Spotted: What’s seen in the latest spy shots? The SUV seen in the latest spy shots is the all-electric version, with EV badging on the tailgate. In international markets, the Atto 2 is also available with a plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain, but the test vehicle spotted in India is the electric version. On the side profile, the SUV gets black and silver body cladding that covers the wheel arches and door sills. It features electric-release door handles, sporty dual-tone alloy wheels, and a charging port on the front fender. The overall design is that of a compact midsize SUV, likely targeting urban buyers. The rear section features connected LED tail-lamps, a roof-mounted spoiler, and a dual-tone bumper. The bumper also gets integrated reflectors and subtle silver accents. The latest spotting gives a much clearer picture of the Atto 2’s overall design compared to the earlier camouflaged test vehicle. BYD Atto 2 EV: Battery, Range and Performance International-spec BYD Atto 2 EV is available with two battery pack options – 45.1kWh and 64.8kWh. Both versions get a front-axle-mounted electric motor, but the output battery varies depending on the variant. According to BYD’s international specifications, the BYD Atto 2 EV has a 0-100kph acceleration time of 7.9 seconds, while the claimed top speed is 170kph. The company claims a WLTP-certified range of up to 430km for the larger battery version. For charging, the SUV offers 11kW AC charging support and up to 155kW DC fast-charging capability. Confirmation of which battery pack and charging specification will be offered in India is expected closer to launch. Also Read: BYD Denza Z9 GT Coming to India With 1000hp+ Power: What We Know So Far Cabin Features: 12.8-inch Rotatable Touchscreen and Panoramic Sunroof The cabin of the international-spec BYD Atto 2 EV comes with a minimalist dashboard layout. It features a 12.8-inch rotatable touchscreen infotainment system, which takes center stage, similar to BYD’s larger Atto 3. It also features an 8.8-inch digital driver display. The feature list includes a panoramic sunroof, a 6-speaker audio system, a 50W wireless phone charger, and a 360-degree camera. The SUV also features a Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) function, which allows compatible external devices to be powered by the vehicle’s battery. Front and rear parking sensors are also part of the international model. It is not yet clear which of these features will be standard or available in selected variants in the India-spec model. Local specifications and equipment list should not be taken as confirmed details. Which electric SUVs will it compete with in India? The potential arrival of the BYD Atto 2 EV in India could make the competition in the midsize electric SUV segment more interesting. This category already includes models like the Maruti Suzuki e Vitara, Toyota Urban Cruiser Ebella, MG ZS EV, VinFast VF6, and Hyundai Creta Electric. The upcoming Tata Sierra EV, Mahindra BE 6, and Tata Curvv EV also expand buyers’ options in this competitive space. The Atto 2’s positioning and final pricing will determine how strong an alternative it can be against these models. If BYD introduces a more accessible electric SUV below the Atto 3 in India, it could give the company a chance to reach a wider customer base. But its success will depend on battery options, real-world range, charging performance, and pricing. Auto India Daily Verdict Undisguised spotting has certainly piqued interest in the BYD Atto 2 EV. A 64.8kWh battery, up to 430km claimed WLTP range, 155kW DC charging, and a feature-rich cabin make it a promising electric SUV, as per international specifications. Pricing will be the most important factor in India. If BYD launches it at a noticeably more affordable price point than the Atto 3, the Atto 2 could become an important volume-oriented model for the company. Official confirmation of the India launch date, battery options, and pricing is currently awaited. artigo.texto: Mini data centers – O Governo Federal vai investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma tecnologia nacional para tornar data centers mais eficientes, seguros e sustentáveis. Aprovado pelo Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel), o projeto prevê uma plataforma inteligente para gerenciar e distribuir dados entre diferentes estruturas, incluindo mini data centers em várias regiões do país. Batizada de Prisma, a iniciativa utilizará inteligência artificial (IA) para definir onde as informações devem ser processadas e distribuir os recursos computacionais conforme a demanda. A tecnologia busca reduzir gastos com energia, custos operacionais e tempo de resposta dos sistemas, além de reforçar a proteção de dados estratégicos. LEIA: Inteligência artificial facilita invasões e aumenta alcance de hackers “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirma o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), enquanto o desenvolvimento ficará sob responsabilidade do Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), em Campinas (SP). A expansão dos mini data centers permitirá processar informações mais perto de onde são geradas e utilizadas, beneficiando setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. Eficiência energética e autonomia tecnológica O projeto também pretende diminuir o impacto ambiental dos data centers, que demandam grandes quantidades de energia para processamento e refrigeração. artigo.texto: How We Found Eight Data Center Community Benefit Agreements and Why It Matters These days, data centers are the hot-button topic in policy circles everywhere. Between the explosion of AI and the sheer scale of some of these facilities, it seems like people cannot go a single day without hearing them come up in some capacity. Communities weighing a data center project are considering real opportunities: construction jobs, new tax revenue, and the promise of economic development that comes with a major capital investment landing in town. But they are also considering real costs. Data centers bring elevated noise, especially for homes sitting close to a facility; they also can consume significant amounts of water and energy, affecting rates and the energy grid. And the tax breaks that some of the data centers receive could outweigh any financial benefits the community gets in return. Local governments face a surmounting number of questions, with best practices not readily available. The policy decisions we make today will affect much of the work that comes tomorrow and the decades after that. Beginning in early 2026, FAS began interviewing experts in the field, as well as searching for executed agreements on data center developments that were difficult to find. This included tracking local government ordinances as well as finding Community Benefit Agreements (CBAs). Many times, the negotiations between data center developers and officials from the municipality or county are conducted behind closed doors, protected by non-disclosure agreements (NDAs). As a result, community members have significantly fewer opportunities to influence the terms by which the data center should abide by as a fixture in the community. In the spirit of increased transparency, FAS wants to share our experience of “flipping over rocks” and discovering the hard-to-find contract. This is how we discovered eight community benefit agreements and why it matters. Local Policy Levers: The Ordinance and The Contract Generally, local governments have two enforceable levers to create policies around data centers. First, an ordinance considers issues such as zoning, land use requirements, and other permitting features – ultimately providing a pathway to allowable activities (and specific limitations). The ordinance process includes a public comment period, and it applies to all projects that qualify under the definition of a “data center.” A CBA involves the power of contract law, crafting and entering into binding bilateral (or sometimes multilateral) agreements that dictate the expectations of each party. CBAs are helpful in cases where existing zoning and permitting do not specifically identify “data centers” as a specific type of property to regulate (this is most frequent as the proliferation of data centers is so new). However, CBAs can be negotiated with fewer public comment opportunities, and they are required on a case-by-case basis. CBAs are not a new legal concept, and they have been used for large scale projects before on major development projects, like airports or energy generation infrastructure. They very recently started to be used in the context of data centers, after the explosion in usage of AI. Thus, FAS went searching for every agreement that fit the CBA model. As of the time of this writing, only one fully executed and publicly posted CBA exists that pertains to data centers: The Lancaster AI Hub agreement entered into by the City of Lancaster, Pennsylvania and the developers of two large data center campuses in the city. Lancaster’s CBA contains many terms and conditions that are beneficial to a data center agreement with the host community. It covers community transparency, water use, energy, noise restrictions, funding for public works, decommissioning, and many more. However, this agreement appears to leave much of the substance to be decided later on. Oftentimes, it requires the parties to submit separate plans to the city which detail the specifics of how the developers will conduct themselves. Finding Agreements: Discovering CBAs Finding executed CBAs took expertise, a concentrated effort, and follow-up. To expand beyond the Lancaster CBA, FAS first turned to blog posts that mentioned CBAs from sources like the Brookings Institution and Columbia University to see if there were any stories about localities that are negotiating terms with data center developers, or that have already done so. Initially, that is how FAS found Cedar Rapids, IA, St. Louis, MO, and El Paso, TX. Then, we looked for news articles referencing data center construction in these cities to see if they mentioned anything about an agreement between the city and the developers. If the terms of the agreement, or even discussion about its existence, were covered in these articles, that was where we knew we had to dig deeper. While the majority of agreements found were publicly available, the only way to obtain some of them was through a public records request. Thankfully, most states did not have such broad prohibitions on what can be public record, allowing FAS to uncover more contracts to serve as references. Over the summer of 2026, seven other agreements were uncovered besides the one in Lancaster between cities, counties, and data center developers that mention community benefits: During the search for more agreements, FAS was making note of the trends in each one, and comparing trends among the different agreements. Many of these agreements contain a heavy focus on money and taxes. Tax abatements, exemptions, and Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILOT) schemes served as incentives for the data centers to be built in various communities. artigo.texto: GREENFIELD — Planning Director Ella Wise will have a full plate over the next few months as she leads the Planning Board through changes in permitting for clean energy facilities, as well as carrying out plans to create zoning ordinances regulating battery energy storage systems and data centers in Greenfield. She told the board on Thursday that her work pertaining to changing regulations in technology will start with training city staff on new Massachusetts laws for consolidated permitting for clean energy projects. In 2024, the state Legislature signed a new climate law to speed up permitting for clean energy infrastructure, including solar, wind, anaerobic digestion and battery energy storage facilities. Wise said the law took effect on Oct. 1, allowing developers to opt into a new permitting process in which all departments review projects for approval at the same time, rather than the previous system in which applicants filed with each department individually. “They need to conduct a certain amount of public outreach and meet with city staff, and if all those conditions are met, they have 12 months for us to give them a ‘yes’ or a ‘no’ on their permit,” Wise said. “And that ‘yes’ or ‘no’ has to include the Planning Board and [the Zoning Board of Appeals’] decision, as well as the Conservation Commission’s decision and the Board of Health.” She added that municipalities also have the option of having the state’s Energy Facilities Siting Board assist with or oversee the review. Wise said the city does not need to change any of its zoning codes and regulations because of the state change, but she recommended that the Planning Board review the codes for clean energy facilities. Throughout the rest of the year, Wise said she plans to work with the Franklin Regional Council of Governments on a battery energy storage system ordinance, and come 2027, she will turn her attention to developing data center regulations before City Council’s one-year moratorium expires. The council adopted the moratorium in September. Battery energy storage systems While Greenfield has regulations in place for solar systems and other energy production facilities, Wise told the Planning Board that the city does not have any for battery energy storage systems, and it would be prudent to develop some. “We do have solar zoning. You don’t have any zoning for batteries,” Wise said. “So I think we need to start that process.” Wise said she has drafted an ordinance for battery energy storage systems based on a model state bylaw, and she plans to spend the next few months revising it, with technical assistance from FRCOG. She hopes that by February 2027, the draft will be ready for Planning Board and City Council approval. The draft, which was included in the board’s packet, defines a battery energy storage system as “a system consisting of one or more battery modules for storing electrical energy, any equipment needed to support the safe and proper function or usage of the battery modules, and one or more physical containers providing secondary containment to any of the above. It may be a primary or accessory use to a solar generating facility, power generation facility or other similar uses.” The draft ordinance states that small Tier 1 facilities would be allowed by right in all districts. Larger Tier 2 and 3 facilities would be allowed by right in the General Industrial (GI) and Planned Industry (PI) zoning districts, but would require special permits in the Rural Residential (RC), Suburban Residential (RB), General Commercial (GC) and Office (O) zoning districts. Battery energy storage systems would be prohibited in all other districts. Wise said that while her draft does outline examples of what the different size tiers could be and where they could be allowed, ultimately, the Planning Board would need to make policy decisions on whether battery energy storage systems should be allowed by right or by special permit, what the setback requirements should be and if there should be any required mitigation of environmental impacts. Data centers Wise said she expects a model data center bylaw to be published by the state next month, which would provide the Planning Board with a jumping-off point from which to start drafting its own regulations. “I don’t think I can work on a BESS bylaw while working on a data center one,” Wise said. “It just feels like so much to juggle. … So what I’m proposing is to focus our energy on BESS over the next few months, trying to get it done at the end of winter so that we have spring and summer to really have a robust process around data centers.” She expects that throughout the first few months of 2027, the Planning Board will research best practices and review other municipalities’ regulations. From March to May, the board will deliberate on what Greenfield’s version should look like and conduct public outreach, finalizing the ordinance in June or July. The city’s one-year moratorium on the construction of data centers is set to expire in September 2027. Planning Board member Thomas Bledsoe said he attended some trainings on data centers recently, and that noise was one of the largest concerns among the potential impacts, which the board should look to address with its regulations. “I really do think noise is a key issue here, and since it’s a 24-hour service, when we have to think hard about it, I would love to have some specific noise parameters in our code,” Bledsoe said. As the board moves forward, he said it should plan to work with other departments, particularly the Board of Health, and other communities.

artigo.texto: Swiss battery developer Unbound Potential has begun installing its first external pilot system at Gesundheitspark Thalwil, near Zürich. The stationary battery uses the company’s membrane-free redox flow technology and will store surplus electricity generated by the health and sports centre’s photovoltaic installation. Stored energy will be released when required. The installation follows almost four years of research and development and represents the technology’s first deployment outside Unbound Potential’s own test environment. The company said operating the system under real-world conditions would provide data on its performance and reliability as it works towards commercialisation. Unbound Potential: a simpler cell design by eliminating the membrane The company claims that eliminating the membrane used in conventional redox flow batteries enables a simpler cell design, with the potential to reduce manufacturing costs and resource consumption. The company is targeting stationary, long-duration applications, including renewable-energy integration and grid support. The pilot is being supported by the Municipality of Thalwil through its Climate Funding Programme. Gesundheitspark Thalwil, which operates what Unbound Potential described as the municipality’s largest photovoltaic system, is providing the host site. Dr David Taylor, CEO and co-founder of Unbound Potential, said: “Having our first pilot battery go into operation here in Thalwil, where everything started, means a great deal to us. “After almost four years of development, our technology is being deployed for the first time at an external partner. It is a big moment for our entire team.” The system had arrived at the site and was being installed and prepared for commissioning when the announcement was made. The company did not disclose its rated power, energy capacity, intended storage duration or commissioning date. Unbound Potential was founded in January 2023 and employs 28 people. It said it had raised more than CHF14 million ($17.5 million) in investment and grant funding from backers including the Migros Pioneer Fund, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation, SPRIND, and the Swiss Innovation Agency, Innosuisse. artigo.texto: SoftBank reported a fiscal second-quarter net loss of 1.12 trillion yen ($7 billion) on Tuesday, as losses tied to U.S. AI data center equipment procurement and Intel share declines weighed on earnings. The Japanese investment giant also recorded a 597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) yen loss in the six months ending on Sept. 30 due to changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S. SoftBank said it had made advance investments to secure power generation equipment for its AI data center projects in the U.S. amid concerns over potential shortages and long procurement lead times. Power is increasingly becoming a key constraint for the AI data center buildout as power grids become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers. Cumulative payments for power-generation equipment for U.S. AI data center projects, like the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, totaled $9.48 billion as of the end of September. "We made bridge investments in advance to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortage," a SoftBank executive said during the company's earnings call. Here's how SoftBank fared in the fiscal second quarter: - Net loss of 1.12 trillion yen in the quarter compared with a net profit of 2.5 trillion yen a year earlier. - Revenue stood at 2.22 trillion yen in the quarter, compared with LSEG estimates of 2.02 trillion yen. Revenue rose 13.3% in the six months ended Sept. 30, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing businesses. The company said its SoftBank segment recorded higher sales across all businesses, while revenue at its AI computing segment increased. The company's Vision Fund segment swung to a loss of 81.58 billion yen in the fiscal second quarter, compared with a profit of 2.38 trillion yen a year earlier. Vision Fund 1 recorded an investment loss of $20 million in the quarter, despite a $1.3 billion gain on ByteDance, as shares of publicly traded portfolio companies, including Coupang and Grab, declined. The Vision Funds segment recorded investment gains of 85.45 billion yen, down sharply from 2.81 trillion yen in the year-earlier period. Vision Fund 2 posted investment gains of 89.26 billion yen, while Vision Fund 1 recorded a loss of 3.86 billion yen on its investments. As of the end of September, SoftBank's cumulative investment in OpenAI stood at $54.6 billion, with a fair value of $99.6 billion and a cumulative investment gain of $45 billion, according to the company. SoftBank said a potential increase in OpenAI's valuation following a new funding round had not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement. The updated valuation could be reflected in the fiscal third quarter, potentially boosting its net asset value and improving its loan-to-value ratio, the company said. "ChatGPT has been continuously a weapon of OpenAI, especially for consumers," the SoftBank esecutive said during the company's earnings call, highlighting the chatbot's growing user base. AI worries hit stocks Shares of the Japanese investment giant closed 13.9% higher on Tuesday. The gains came as Asian technology stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, rose following an overnight rebound on Wall Street. On its AI infrastructure investments, SoftBank highlighted a 20-year lease agreement with OpenAI for eight gigawatts of IT capacity at a data center project in Ohio. Addressing concerns of water consumption at its planned data center in Texas, SoftBank said it was taking steps to reduce water use through a closed-loop, air-cooled system. The company also pointed to plans to hire and source locally. Ahead of its earnings release, SoftBank Group announced on Monday plans with Grab and Malaysia's PETROS to commit a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with a long-term target of at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity.

artigo.texto: Anchor Energy launches €75m BESS fund Danish investment platform Anchor Energy Partners has launched a fund with a €75m target that aims to invest in flexibility assets across Europe. Anchor Fund I will acquire and operate derisked, ready-to-build flexibility and storage assets, eventually expanding into renewable colocation and industrial energy. The fund’s initial close was backed by founding investor and co-owner 2degrees, a 50:50 joint venture between Macquarie Asset Management and Aware Super. Financial details were not disclosed. The founding partners are Fabian Siegel, Lasse Helstrup, Alejandra Huerta, Abhi Chirimar and Ludvig Holsteinborg. Their experience spans investing and asset management at Orsted, Danske Commodities, AIP, Icecreek Energy and Boston Consulting Group. The team managed €30bn in funds, including two IPOs, and more than 120MWh of operational BESS in Germany and Finland. Copenhagen-based Anchor said using BESS is the fastest way to add flexibility to Europe’s energy system. The continent has less than 80GWh of BESS capacity against a 1.2GWh requirement by 2050.

artigo.texto: Riverside Council Enshrines Temporary Data Center Ban Language While City Researches AI The Riverside City Council Tuesday voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution barring the city from accepting data center proposals, since the land use is not currently included in city code. Riverside has joined a number of other cities in the county in temporarily banning data centers, though the council took a much different approach than its neighbors. The Riverside City Council Tuesday voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution barring the city from accepting data center proposals, since the land use is not currently included in city code, while a council-led committee researches artificial intelligence (AI) policies, foregoing a second option to impose a 45-day temporary moratorium. “We need to pause the moving forward of development so [we] can figure out, and do that deep dive, and do that research, and set those regulations, and set those parameters,” Councilmember Philip Falcone said at the November 10 council meeting. “To not do them in tandem is disjoint and, I think, not strategic.” Councilmembers Chuck Conder and Sean Mill voted against the resolution — although Mill, in a phone call with The Riverside Record, said he chose to vote against the resolution because he preferred establishing a temporary ban like other cities across the county have done. The council’s decision to move forward with the resolution followed a now-updated agreement between the city of Riverside and a nonprofit organization that previously mentioned a possible data center as part of its proposal. The agreement originally said the nonprofit, and its for-profit counterpart, would “contemplate” the development of a data center after establishing an office in the city. The CEO for both organizations previously told the city’s Economic Development Committee the idea was to create a data center meant for community use — which would have been contained within a typical office server room — to help with training residents on emerging technologies. Falcone, who championed efforts to restrict data centers within city limits, said at the September 14 Land Use Committee meeting that the agreement pushed him to request that staff bring forward a temporary data center ban to the council for discussion. He said he felt a ban would preserve commercial land for sectors he believed would bring more jobs, prevent an electrical grid overload and protect the city’s water supply. The following day, the council voted to create a 13-month AI working group tasked with developing a “forward-looking” strategy to address AI’s rapid growth and outline how the city should utilize the technology in the future. Councilmember Steven Robillard, who is leading the working group, said the group plans to tackle data center policies in the coming months. That decision led city staff to return to the Land Use Committee in October to ask for clarification on how to proceed with the dueling requests. After a discussion, the committee directed staff to bring forward two options: establish an urgency ordinance to impose a temporary 45-day moratorium on the approval of any data center developments that could be extended for up to two years total or adopt language that highlights the city is technically prohibited from accepting data center proposals at this time due to current city code. “There [are] no proposals on the table right now,” Robillard said at the November 10 meeting. “I think the resolution sends the proper message that we currently don’t have a zoning that allows for data centers, we need to discuss the entire conversation in-and-around AI, and its related uses including data centers, and, until we do that, approving the data center doesn’t make any sense.” During public comment, residents and environmental advocates said they supported placing restrictions on data center development due to their concerns with potential long-term negative impacts on the community. However, several union representatives said they were opposed to a ban, citing recently signed California laws placing restrictions on the facilities and concerns that any prohibitions would eliminate job opportunities for union members. “If we utilize the latest technologies like closed loop systems for cooling and a clean energy infrastructure, they could be successful,” Anthony Zambrano, an International Union of Operating Engineers Local 12 representative, said. “In my opinion, no one builds these systems better than union labor.” Conder, throughout his reelection campaign, said he was a proponent of data centers. At a community forum held last month, Conder said he believed the technology has been rapidly improving and could be built to minimize harm to both communities and the environment. “Not all data centers are a million square feet,” Conder said at the November 10 meeting. “They can be as small as a medium-sized box truck that delivers in town here.” He also said, both at the November 10 council meeting and in statements throughout his campaign, that he believed much of the opposition to data centers was funded by foreign governments that prefer to have the facilities built in their countries. An investigation into the claim by NPR found little evidence of a coordinated Chinese campaign to stop data centers in the U.S. The next AI ad hoc committee meeting is scheduled for December 3. The group will continue to meet over the next year to discuss AI-related topics, including data centers, and is set to present a list of policy recommendations for the full council to review later next year. artigo.texto: Riot Platforms Inc (Riot), a digital infrastructure and Bitcoin mining company has signed a 15 year lease with an unnamed Frontier AI Lab for its entire Corsicana data center campus in Texas, covering 910 MW of critical IT capacity and representing approximately US$ 28 billion in contracted revenue with AI safety and research company Antropic as the first tenant. According to a press release, the triple net powered land lease covers a contiguous 332 acre site and is expected to generate approximately US$ 1.8 billion in average annual rent over the initial term. Riot estimates a net operating income (NOI) margin of approximately 99 percent. The contract value could reach US$ 54 billion if the tenant exercises both five year extension options. The project will be delivered in three phases, 400 MW in September 2027, 200 MW in January 2028 and the remaining 310 MW in July 2028. Rent for each phase will begin no later than 60 days after delivery of its powered pads and will be payable on the full contracted capacity regardless of utilization. “Today, we are excited to announce the largest lease in Riot’s history: a 15-year triple-net powered land lease with a leading Frontier AI Lab for the entirety of our Corsicana campus, representing 910 megawatts of critical IT capacity and approximately $28 billion of contracted revenue over the initial term,” said Jason Les, CEO, Riot Platforms. “Together with our AMD contract and the lease signed with the same Frontier AI Lab at Rockdale earlier this year, Riot has contracted 1,151 megawatts and approximately US$ 38 billion of data center revenue, which we expect will generate more than US$ 2 billion of average annual net operating income at full deployment, firmly establishing Riot as a leading developer of large-scale digital infrastructure.” Riot estimates total capital costs of US$ 5.5 billion, or approximately US$ 6 million per IT MW, the company will contribute US$ 2 million per MW toward site work and electrical infrastructure. While the remaining US$ 4 million per MW will be reimbursed by the tenant in stages after each phase is delivered and begins generating rent. The reimbursements are expected to be financed through non-recourse project debt backed by contracted rental income. If financing on comparable market terms is unavailable, the tenant will fund the reimbursements directly and recover the amounts through credits against rent over the remaining lease term. Riot expects to fund its share from existing liquidity and does not currently anticipate issuing equity for the project.

artigo.texto: Expansão em Belo Jardim elevará a capacidade de fornecimento de sistemas de armazenamento de energia para mais de 8 GWh por ano. Empresa atua em parceria com a chinesa CATL e mira o primeiro leilão nacional de baterias. A expansão do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil abriu uma nova oportunidade para a indústria nordestina. O Grupo Moura anunciou um investimento estimado em R$ 200 milhões para ampliar sua estrutura de fabricação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos como BESS, em Belo Jardim, no Agreste de Pernambuco. Com a ampliação, a companhia pretende alcançar uma capacidade de fornecimento superior a 8 GWh por ano. O projeto combina tecnologia da chinesa CATL com montagem, integração e atividades industriais realizadas no Brasil. A princípio, a iniciativa ocorre às vésperas dos primeiros leilões brasileiros destinados à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Belo Jardim entra na disputa por um novo mercado de energia O investimento amplia a atuação de uma empresa que já possui uma trajetória de quase sete décadas na fabricação de baterias. Fundada em 1957, em Belo Jardim, a Moura construiu no município um complexo industrial que atende diferentes segmentos, incluindo os mercados automotivo, industrial e de armazenamento de energia. Segundo informações da companhia, a expansão de aproximadamente R$ 200 milhões reúne investimentos recentes e um novo ciclo de modernização da estrutura produtiva. Além disso, a empresa já possui experiência em mais de 40 projetos de armazenamento instalados no Brasil, com aplicações em setores como indústria, agronegócio, saúde, saneamento e entretenimento. Parceria com empresa chinesa combina tecnologia e produção local A Moura atua ao lado da CATL, fabricante chinesa de baterias e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A parceria entre as empresas começou em 2020, inicialmente com serviços de assistência técnica, manutenção e pós-venda de baterias de lítio. Agora, a cooperação também envolve o fornecimento de sistemas para os projetos que disputarão o leilão brasileiro. Nesse modelo, a CATL participa com sua tecnologia e experiência internacional, enquanto a Moura assume a industrialização e a integração dos equipamentos em Pernambuco. A estratégia busca atender às exigências de conteúdo nacional previstas para uma das modalidades do certame. Conteúdo nacional pode chegar a 60% Um dos diferenciais do projeto é a tentativa de ampliar a participação da indústria brasileira na cadeia de armazenamento de energia. De acordo com o diretor de operações de lítio do Grupo Moura, Spartacus Pedrosa, a empresa trabalha com uma rota de montagem e integração que pode atingir entre 50% e 60% de conteúdo local, conforme os critérios de nacionalização. Entretanto, a estratégia também pode facilitar o acesso dos equipamentos às linhas de financiamento do BNDES, desde que cumpram os requisitos de credenciamento. Primeiro leilão brasileiro de baterias acontece em dezembro A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica aprovou os editais dos dois primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade voltados a sistemas de armazenamento em baterias. O primeiro certame, em 2 de dezembro, será destinado a projetos que atendam às exigências de conteúdo nacional. Já o segundo, previsto para 4 de dezembro, terá regras diferentes de nacionalização. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início do fornecimento previsto para agosto de 2028. Os sistemas deverão disponibilizar potência por até quatro horas em cada ciclo, podendo ser acionados até duas vezes por dia. Dessa forma, as baterias poderão armazenar energia e devolvê-la ao sistema elétrico nos momentos de maior necessidade. Mercado desperta interesse de empresas A dimensão da oportunidade aparece no cadastramento realizado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética. Em agosto de 2026, a instituição informou que recebeu 6.091 projetos para os leilões, somando 296.807 MW de potência. Além disso, o volume demonstra o interesse do mercado por soluções de armazenamento, embora nem todos os projetos inscritos necessariamente participem ou vençam os certames. LEIA TAMBÉM: - Frutas, mel e celulose do Nordeste ganham o mercado da Europa - Estudo revela a situação das rodovias no Nordeste; veja como está por estado - Starbucks anuncia três lojas em Fortaleza e volta expansão no Nordeste - Nordeste ganha loja de gigante com 4 mil lojas pelo mundo; confira onde Investimento amplia importância industrial de Pernambuco Portanto, a ampliação da fábrica reforça a presença de Pernambuco em uma cadeia produtiva relacionada à transição energética. Além da produção de baterias, Belo Jardim concentra atividades de montagem, tecnologia e reciclagem. Em 2025, o Governo de Pernambuco informou que o Grupo Moura contava com 4.114 colaboradores no estado. Afinal, o novo investimento pode ampliar a demanda por profissionais especializados, fornecedores industriais e serviços técnicos. Entretanto, a empresa ainda não divulgou o número de empregos adicionais que pretende gerar com a expansão. Com a entrada em um mercado de maior escala, Belo Jardim passa a disputar espaço em uma atividade estratégica para a modernização do setor elétrico brasileiro. O desafio agora será transformar a capacidade industrial anunciada em contratos efetivos, produção local e novas oportunidades econômicas para o Agreste pernambucano.

artigo.texto: A BYD e a TIM anunciaram duas parcerias no Brasil. A primeira prevê que os veículos leves produzidos pela montadora no país sairão de fábrica com conectividade da operadora embarcada. Ao todo, serão mais de 200 mil veículos com conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. A segunda contempla a implantação de infraestrutura dedicada de redes 4G e 5G no complexo industrial da montadora em Camaçari, na Bahia. Os modelos da empresa chinesa contarão com o eSIM da TIM, o que permitirá a ativação remota de serviços digitais. No complexo industrial da BYD em Camaçari, o projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre galpões e áreas operacionais. A proposta é oferecer uma rede capaz de acompanhar o crescimento da produção e atender às demandas tecnológicas da unidade. As redes 4G e 5G permitirão conectar colaboradores, visitantes, sistemas operacionais e veículos ainda durante o processo de fabricação. Inaugurado em outubro de 2025, o complexo industrial na Bahia possui 4,6 milhões de metros quadrados e é a maior operação industrial da BYD fora da China. A solução de Internet em Veículos (IoV) da TIM conecta, ao todo, mais de 630 mil veículos. Foto: complexo industrial da BYD em Camaçari, na Bahia. Crédito: divulgação.

artigo.texto: A homeowner in the United Kingdom considering spending an extra £2,000 ($2,670) on home battery storage received an unexpected recommendation from their solar installer: buy less capacity. In the installer's view, another battery module would probably cost more than the homeowner would save by avoiding occasional peak-rate electricity purchases. Here's what to know On Reddit, they wrote that they had been considering 15 kWh or 20 kWh as backup capacity given their daily winter consumption of about 14 kWh. However, their solar installer recommended only going with a 10 kWh capacity. "His advice is the cost to buy that little bit extra from grid is probably cheaper than adding another battery," the original poster wrote. "The extra cost might not make sense for ROI/savings." In addition to asking whether Redditors agreed with the solar installer's advice, the OP also wondered how easy it would be to add extra battery capacity down the line. For homeowners considering making the move to battery backup, EnergySage makes it easy to explore battery products and compare competitive installation estimates. EnergySage has partnered with electrification company Qmerit to help homeowners secure the best available battery-storage pricing. What commenters said When it came to the question of capacity, opinions were divided, though some acknowledged that it ultimately came down to what the OP's goals were. For one commenter, 10 kWh was too little capacity for their own goal of powering the entire house during an outage. While a suitably configured battery can keep household essentials running during outages, when paired with solar panels, it can also offer even greater energy independence, including off-grid use with certain systems. For the original poster, however, the priority was not whole-home backup but saving money on their electricity bill. By charging their home battery when rates were cheapest and using that electricity to power their home when rates were high, the OP hoped to limit the impact of soaring energy prices. Not all household electricity use has to be supplied by storage, another commenter explained. Solar generation consumed immediately and grid electricity used during cheap-rate periods both reduce the amount of energy that needs to pass through the battery. For households seeking a smaller backup option, Pila offers a plug-and-play alternative at a substantially lower price point than whole-home backup systems. Other considerations A 10 kWh starting point seemed more reasonable to the homeowner after a commenter raised the panels' potential contribution. Confirming that solar was part of the installation, the OP noted that even 1 to 2 kWh of winter generation could help offset consumption on heavier-use days. For charging and discharging power, commenters advised checking the battery stack's own specifications rather than relying on the inverter's rating. That distinction is particularly important when running several appliances. In one commenter's hypothetical example, an 8 kW inverter would still have only 5 kW available from a pair of battery modules delivering 2.5 kW each. As for the OP's question regarding battery expansion at a later date, one commenter noted that, for their setup, space for new modules had been an issue. Ultimately, that commenter had to have an inverter moved because it blocked the battery additions. The upgrade also required firmware updates, and the commenter recommended checking the manufacturer's commissioning and warranty requirements. Where can I learn more? Other U.K. homeowners have also been comparing the cost of battery storage with the savings it could deliver. • A U.K. homeowner sought retrofit battery storage after an installer said batteries weren't worthwhile. • A U.K. homeowner exploring battery-only storage to avoid peak electricity rates received a G98/G99 warning. • After solar was ruled out, a U.K. homeowner considered battery-only storage for savings. • A U.K. homeowner's 10-kWh battery payback estimate stretched from three years to five. • A U.K. homeowner's £6,999 battery quote drew scrutiny over £3,000 in installation costs.
