artigo.texto: South Korean scientists have just unveiled a new liquid-crystal polymer separator, which, when tested in a lithium-metal battery, retained 94 percent of its capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at a 4C charging rate. The separator was built by the a research team at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST). It could reportedly improve battery stability and charging speed, meaning drivers could charge their EVs in just 15 minutes. The study was led by Dong Ki Yoon, PhD, and Hye Ryung Byon, PhD, professors at KAIST’s Department of Chemistry. “Lithium metal batteries can store more energy than conventional batteries,” they stated. “However, during charging, lithium can accumulate in sharp, branch-like structures known as ‘dendrites.'” For the separator, the researchers used liquid-crystalline polymers to control how the lithium ions move inside lithium-metal batteries. Both Yoon and Byon believe that their find could address slow ion transport and dendrite formation. A highway for lithium ions Lithium-metal batteries can store more energy than conventional ones. However, during charging, lithium can accumulate on the electrode surface and, as a result, form dendrites. These tiny needle-like metallic crystals grow on the anodes, and they can damage the separator between the electrodes, which could cause short circuits and increase the risk of fires. More from Energy See All To address this problem, the team created a porous separator made from liquid-crystalline polymers, which have an ordered structure like solids. They also share some properties with liquids. For the project, the team incorporated polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains into the material to facilitate lithium-ion transport. The scientists then monitored the alignment of the liquid-crystal molecules and arranged them either vertically or horizontally to examine how their orientation affected ion movement. The vertically aligned separator created direct pathways for lithium ions to travel toward the electrodes. In contrast to the horizontally aligned separator, it reduced the tortuosity (winding nature), of the ion transport pathways by about 2.5 times. This allowed the lithium ions to move faster and more uniformly. What’s more, it suppressed the dendrite formation and improved the battery stability. Longer battery life Ultimately, the researchers tested the separator in a working lithium-metal battery to evaluate its performance. To their massive surprise, the cell retained 94 percent of its initial capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at 4C. In simple terms, a 4C charging rate means a battery can fully recharge in 15 minutes. According to the team, controlling how molecules are arranged could potentially make batteries charge faster and last longer without compromising safety. Yoon emphasized the significance of this finding for future battery development. He said that molecular alignment plays a key role in battery performance. “We expect this approach to contribute to the development of high-energy-density next-generation battery technologies, for which long driving ranges and rapid charging are essential,” he concluded in a press release. The scientists believe the approach could contribute to the development of high-energy-density batteries for future EVs, where rapid charging and longer driving ranges are essential. Further tests will, however, show whether it works in larger batteries as well. The study has been published in the journal ACS Nano.

artigo.texto: Mark Trahant Substack There’s a story about Napoleon Bonaparte I have always liked. Something along the lines of “I know he’s a good general, but is he lucky.” Lucky. So often in my career I have been in the exact right place at the right time, being at places where I didn’t plan. Lucky. Last week I was honored with a Rural Power award by Groundswell and its Rural Renaissance Roadshow. Kenrick J. Escalanti, Quechan, nominated me for this honor to “recognize individuals whose leadership, ideas, storytelling, and service are helping shape a stronger and more equitable future for rural communities.” Instead of a mail-order plaque, the group gifted me a unique embroidered jean jacket to wear proclaiming “Rural Power.” Way cool. Here’s the lucky part. I have been thinking a lot about the debate going on in tribal and rural communities about data centers. It’s absolutely fine for tribes to pause or just say no. But could there also be a deeper conversation, what do we need when it comes to data storage, AI, and a digital future? Where is the richer conversation? Turns out that was the theme of the conference: “At the Data Center Crossroads.” The awards’ panel was first evening of the conference; a start of the conversation. And one of the first questions from the audience asked where I stood on data centers. I jumped right into the deep end. Two things. First, we need a better conversation about data centers and where they should be located. And, second, no elected official should ever sign a Non Disclosure Agreement. I think that runs counter to the public good. Transparency is an important value and the lack of it is exactly why we are having a terrible conversation about what’s needed and why. Data Centers at scale “What is a data center and what do people know?” asks Sherry Stout, program manager for the National Laboratory of the Rockies. She works with state and tribal governments. “So first and foremost, 38% of people statistically in this room, you live within five miles of a data center and you just might not know it,” she says. “If you ask what national polls say 35% of people would say that they have heard —quote — a lot about data centers in this past year. And why is that? … there’s 632 local governments have taken up the issue of data centers this year alone. It’s these very conversations that are so twisted. Data centers are pitched as inevitable on private and public land and many of the people involved won’t answer questions because they’ve signed those NDAs. Sherry Stout: “People are encountering news stories. They’re encountering political processes. They’re encountering social media that’s all about data centers. We’re seeing states that have paused large scale data centers and we’re seeing moratorium that are placed to say we need to pause and figure out what are these things? How are they affecting us and how do we need to go forward? There’s also, let’s just talk about the reality. There are a few very visible, very poorly done examples of data centers and those are going to drive conversations like it or not. NDAs are becoming a greater and greater issue. I spent a lot of last week with some of the hyperscalers talking about the issue of NDAs and it used to be in business that NDAs would actually speed things along because you would have some of that non-compete. But now the second a community finds out that their council has an NDA with a hyperscaler, that has changed the conversation and transparency is really changing. How we think about data transparency and what’s going on is really changing. Then there’s also just some of the reality of there’s a huge worldwide debate right now on the future of artificial intelligence or super intelligence if you work in the federal world. Data centers often can be the face, the physical manifestation of that conversation.” Billions, not millions Pearl Eva Walker is a member of the Memphis City Council where a huge generative A-I data center, Colossus, was built by Space X — Elon Musk —for Grok and is now leases computer capacity to Anthropic. Walker said the bill for that lease is $1.5 billion per month. (Soon to be Colossus 2 and Colossus 3.) More than 7,500 construction workers are building the facilities. That number of workers has caused significant impact to the communities in Memphis, including those across the line in Mississippi that don’t get the same benefits. “… God didn’t create data centers and they are not all good,” Walker said. “How do they become better? Hopefully all good. That’s up to us.” When all this started there were not many community rules in place. So the community had to develop legislation as the data centers were under construction while learning about the impacts as (or after) they happened. That leaves few paths forward for to protect the public. “What do municipalities need to know? If you’re thinking that a data center could come to your city or town, you need to check on the legislation that you have first concerning data centers,” she said. That means a comprehensive legislative plan that outlines what companies have to do and how to hold them accountable. Council Member Walker: “We’ve been accused of signing NDAs. I have not signed an NDA. I have not been asked to sign an NDA. Why? Because they didn’t need us for anything. Why not? Because we didn’t have any guardrails and moratoriums or anything that kept them from coming in. And then on the other side, there were entities such as the chamber that helped them come into the city and maneuver certain spaces and circumstances. But you want to start with the zoning because they can’t do anything without a parcel. So keep that in mind. The Paul Laurie location, it’s been zoned for commercial industrial since the 1950s. And we are in the process of doing some rezoning for the entire city already. And it will include zoning specific to data centers. That is very important because that’s going to guide your municipality, your leadership, the business

artigo.texto: - CATL chairman said sodium-ion batteries offer sufficient range for daily urban travel, while more swap stations can ease concerns about longer trips. - The company's swap stations now cover about 200 Chinese cities, with a target of more than 3,000 passenger car stations by year-end. CATL (HKEX: 3750) said its rapidly expanding battery-swapping network in China will help accelerate sodium-ion battery adoption by easing consumer concerns about driving range. The battery maker's chairman Robin Zeng made the remarks at a Benchmark Mineral Intelligence event in Shanghai, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. Sodium-ion batteries offer sufficient range for daily urban travel, while an expanding swap network can ease concerns among drivers looking to make longer trips on weekends, Zeng said. "We are building battery-swapping stations on our own, leasing batteries to the consumers," Zeng said. "We need to build more swapping stations on the highways and in the cities." About 200 Chinese cities already have CATL swap stations, he said. The company aims to have more than 3,000 passenger car swap stations across China by the end of this year. Battery swapping allows drivers to replace depleted packs with fully charged ones within minutes, offering an alternative to conventional charging. CATL is promoting sodium-ion batteries as an alternative to traditional lithium-ion batteries in vehicles. The technology offers advantages in cold weather and is seen as potentially improving safety and reducing costs. However, energy density remains a key concern for sodium-ion battery adoption. CATL previously said it expects 10,000 to 20,000 electric vehicles to use its sodium-ion batteries this year. The company also views the technology as a risk management strategy to reduce its exposure to sharp swings in lithium prices. The company launched its Naxtra sodium-ion battery brand in April 2025 and jointly unveiled a passenger vehicle equipped with the battery with Changan Automobile in February this year. CATL said at the time that the vehicle's cells have an energy density of up to 175 Wh/kg and enable a driving range of more than 400 kilometers (249 miles), demonstrating the technology's ability to meet daily travel needs. Cold-weather performance is another key selling point. According to information CATL released in February, the battery retains more than 90% of its capacity at minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit). The swap network provides supporting infrastructure for broader sodium-ion battery adoption. CATL announced in December 2025 that it had built 1,020 Choco-Swap stations across 45 cities. Its subsidiary Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES) said at the time that it planned to deploy sodium-ion batteries based on Naxtra technology at scale across its swap network starting in 2026.

artigo.texto: The Western Australian Government has awarded $15 million through the Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) New Energies Industries Round 2 to Australian Vanadium Limited (AVL) to establish a high-capacity, relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility in the state. The project will expand AVL’s capacity to produce vanadium electrolyte to support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain. Related article: AVESS wins grant to explore vanadium flow battery manufacturing in Indo-Pacific Vanadium flow batteries use liquid vanadium electrolyte solutions in separate tanks to both store and release electricity. Skilled employment and training opportunities in advanced manufacturing, chemical processing, engineering, construction, commissioning, and plant operations will be created, while its modular and relocatable design enables deployment across regional and industrial centres throughout WA. The IAF funding will also support the development of grid-scale vanadium flow batteries and long-duration energy storage infrastructure in the state. WA State Development and Economic Diversification Minister David Michael said, “The Investment Attraction Fund continues to play a critical role in attracting projects that strengthen Western Australia’s industrial capabilities and support our energy transition. “By supporting AVL’s electrolyte manufacturing capability, we’re creating new opportunities in advanced manufacturing while helping position WA at the forefront of long-duration energy storage technologies. Related article: Western Australia doubles renewable energy target to 75% “The development of a high-capacity vanadium electrolyte facility will support local jobs, strengthen our manufacturing capability, and provide the foundations for future grid-scale battery projects across the state.”

artigo.texto: Nas aldeias da minoria étnica Thai, o conceito de floresta está passando por mudanças positivas. Enquanto no passado as pessoas rezavam aos espíritos da floresta para amenizar a raiva ao colher madeira para a construção de casas, agora suas orações expressam alegria e o desejo de que a floresta floresça ainda mais. As mudanças climáticas deixaram de ser uma ameaça futura e se tornaram uma realidade manifestada por meio de eventos climáticos extremos cada vez mais severos. Sob essa pressão, espera-se que a 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), que começa na Turquia, promova compromissos mais firmes no enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas, especialmente na implementação de soluções de adaptação e na transição energética. Para o Vietname, a COP31 representa uma oportunidade para promover a cooperação internacional e reafirmar os esforços na proteção ambiental e na resposta às alterações climáticas. Em particular, o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal de alta qualidade é uma das direções importantes, contribuindo para reforçar a posição do Vietname no mercado internacional de carbono. Com uma maior conscientização sobre o valor das florestas, as pessoas estão participando cada vez mais ativamente da proteção desse recurso. Além da receita gerada pelos contratos de proteção florestal, os créditos de carbono estão abrindo novas oportunidades para a criação de meios de subsistência e o aumento da renda das comunidades. Contudo, a implementação prática do primeiro acordo de crédito de carbono revelou uma importante lição: a necessidade de uma implementação em larga escala, evitando a fragmentação. Cada projeto precisa abranger pelo menos 100.000 hectares, enquanto as áreas florestais destinadas às famílias são frequentemente dispersas e pequenas. Portanto, a formação de um órgão central de coordenação para conectar e organizar a implementação é um requisito essencial. O Sr. Nguyen Tien An, Diretor do Fundo Provincial de Proteção e Desenvolvimento Florestal de Nghe An , afirmou que o fundo atuará como um ponto focal para apoiar as comunidades participantes. Ao mesmo tempo, o fundo poderá coordenar ou autorizar organizações com plena capacidade jurídica a executar tarefas relacionadas. Além de estabelecer um órgão central de coordenação, também foi dada ênfase à consulta pública e à melhoria da capacidade de medição, relato e avaliação. Muitas localidades, incluindo províncias que se preparam para novos acordos, pesquisaram e prepararam proativamente as condições para participar do mercado interno de carbono e implementar projetos inter-regionais de grande escala. Na província de Lam Dong , as autoridades locais também estão se dedicando a preparar o conhecimento e a capacidade para a implementação de créditos de carbono florestal. O Sr. Le Dinh Viet, vice-chefe do Departamento Provincial de Proteção Florestal de Lam Dong, afirmou que a província organizou uma conferência com a participação de especialistas em carbono do governo central para trocar experiências, disseminar conteúdo e fornecer orientações sobre a implementação de tarefas relacionadas no próximo período. Além dos esforços proativos das autoridades locais, o quadro político para a gestão e o desenvolvimento florestal também está sendo gradualmente aprimorado. Após o decreto sobre o mecanismo piloto de pagamento, o Vietnã emitiu um novo decreto sobre investimento e apoio ao investimento na gestão, proteção, uso e desenvolvimento de florestas. Segundo o Sr. Pham Hong Luong, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal, a nova política é de grande importância para promover os pontos fortes internos dos proprietários florestais, ao mesmo tempo que cria condições para que parceiros e investidores internacionais participem no apoio ao desenvolvimento de projetos de grande escala a nível regional e inter-regional. Desde o compromisso assumido na COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050 até o primeiro acordo de crédito de carbono florestal com o Banco Mundial , nos últimos cinco anos, o Vietnã construiu gradualmente as bases para o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono florestal de alta qualidade. O aprimoramento contínuo das políticas, o fortalecimento da capacidade organizacional e a garantia da participação da comunidade serão fatores cruciais para maximizar o valor dos recursos florestais e contribuir de forma prática para a mitigação das mudanças climáticas.

artigo.texto: Lawmakers in New Jersey will consider a ban on data center non-disclosure agreements after the state Senate passed an identical bill in October. The ban aims to encourage greater transparency around data center developments in New Jersey. At the end of October, the New Jersey Senate passed Bill 4304. The bill stipulates that data center applicants and their agents shall not enter into any agreement, including non-disclosure agreements, with approving authorities, municipal agencies, or property sellers that has the purpose of concealing the details of data center developments. “Transparency is crucial during the data center development process, especially since these projects can have a major impact on our communities,” said Senator Linda Greenstein (D-Mercer/Middlesex) in a press statement in October. “This legislation establishes clear consequences for applicants who attempt to conceal data center development plans and makes clear that these agreements have no place in the approval process.” The bill further states that data center developers applying for approval will have to attest that no party to the property transaction has entered into an agreement with the seller that obfuscates the details of the project or prevents public review of the development plans for the property. “As data center development continues to expand across New Jersey, communities deserve a voice in how these projects affect their neighborhoods,” said Senator Brian Stack (D-Hudson). “This legislation will help ensure residents and local officials have the opportunity to review proposed developments and understand their potential impacts before projects move forward.” Following the passing of Bill 4304 in the Senate, it has now been referred to the Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, which meets on Monday November 16, 2026. The Assembly has its own version of this bill, Bill 2774, which was introduced on January 13, 2026 as a carry-over from December 2025. Once the Senate’s bill was referred to the committee, the two were classified as the same or similar. Save for the sponsors of the bill, the Senate’s version and the Assembly’s version are identical. New Jersey lawmakers join a growing number of states pushing back against data center developments. In August, w.media reported that Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro had signed what he called the strictest guardrails for AI data center developments in the US. The guardrails require developers to pay the full cost of new electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and other infrastructure, and to commit to open, transparent engagement with local residents and leaders. Earlier this year Texas governor Greg Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to conduct a verification audit of all data center projects moving through ERCOT’s interconnection process. The governor also ordered the two bodies to assess the extent to which data centers are paying their own way or depending on state financial incentives. The history of pushback also appears to have elevated fears that incoming Democratic governors and senators, elected during the midterm elections last week, will stall or stop data center developments. These fears reached a breaking point last week when US$ 2.5 trillion in market value evaporated.

artigo.texto: Juntamente com outras certificações obtidas de acordo com as normas UL, IEC e NFPA, a VinEnergo reafirma sua posição como marca líder em segurança e qualidade no campo de baterias para armazenamento de energia em particular e em soluções de energia verde em geral. O sistema BESS desenvolvido pela VinEnergo é fabricado na fábrica de armazenamento de baterias VinES em Ha Tinh , equipado com tecnologia de resfriamento líquido ativo para controlar com precisão a temperatura das células da bateria, reduzir as diferenças de temperatura entre as células e prolongar a vida útil do sistema. Além disso, o sistema incorpora uma solução proativa de prevenção e combate a incêndios, capaz de detecção precoce, alerta, isolamento de incidentes e ativação automática do mecanismo de supressão de incêndio desde o estágio inicial, garantindo a máxima segurança do sistema. Para obter a certificação de segurança UL 9540, o sistema BESS da VinEnergo passou pelo rigoroso teste UL 9540A, que avalia o potencial de fuga térmica, incêndio e liberação de gases dentro do sistema de armazenamento de energia. Os resultados do teste fornecem uma base técnica crucial para avaliar os níveis de segurança e apoiar o processo de certificação UL 9540. Além da certificação UL 9540, o Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (BESS) da VinEnergo obteve outras certificações internacionais de prestígio, como UL 1973, IEC 62619, IEC 63056, e relatórios de testes como IEC 62933-5-2, NFPA 68 e NFPA 69. Em particular, a avaliação e a certificação são realizadas pela UL Solutions (Underwriters Laboratories) - uma organização líder mundial em ciência da segurança de produtos, testes, inspeção e certificação, com mais de 130 anos de experiência global. A certificação UL 9540 é um passo significativo na estratégia da VinEnergo para levar seus produtos BESS aos mercados internacionais, especialmente aqueles com altas exigências de segurança, qualidade e padrões técnicos, como América do Norte, Europa e Ásia. A Sra. Nguyen Huong Giang, Diretora-Geral Adjunta Permanente da VinEnergo, afirmou: “Identificamos as soluções de armazenamento de energia como uma área tecnológica fundamental, que contribui para a modernização da rede elétrica e promove a transição para fontes de energia limpa no Vietnã.” A VinEnergo está a desenvolver as suas capacidades em todo o processo, desde a investigação e desenvolvimento e produção até à integração de sistemas BESS em aplicações e operações práticas, reforçando assim a posição das empresas vietnamitas no mercado internacional de energia.” Atualmente, a VinEnergo fornece e instala mais de 1,6 GWh de baterias de armazenamento de energia para diversos grandes projetos de empresas de energia do Grupo de Eletricidade do Vietnã, bem como para empresas nacionais e internacionais, como Marubeni, MM Mega Market, Usina Termoelétrica Nghi Son 2, etc. Recentemente, a VinEnergo também colocou em operação um sistema de armazenamento de baterias de 45 MWh combinado com energia solar para seu complexo fabril no Parque Industrial de Vung Ang (Ha Tinh).

artigo.texto: The Oakland City Council on Tuesday extended a pause on data centers for almost another year, giving city officials more time to study the impacts of computing facilities and develop rules governing where and how they can operate. The council voted unanimously to extend the existing temporary moratorium for an additional 10 months and 15 days, effective until Oct. 5, 2027. The moratorium is not a permanent ban on data centers; rather, it temporarily suspends new approvals for such facilities. Separately, council members also declared an emergency ordinance prohibiting the city from approving permits, zoning changes, and other land-use agreements for the construction of data centers. “We’re seeing an uprising across the country when it comes to how data centers are operating,” District 3 Councilmember Carroll Fife said during the council meeting. “It was imperative that I take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what we’ve seen in other parts of the country.” The council’s vote comes a little more than a month after it unanimously approved an initial 45-day moratorium on Oct. 6, following hours of public comment from residents concerned about electricity and water consumption, increased air and noise pollution, and other potential impacts of data centers. That moratorium was set to expire on Nov. 20. The extension, introduced by Fife, buys time for the city to research the impacts of data centers on the local energy grid, water supply, air quality, and compliance with local and state laws. It also gives the city a chance to determine whether it should update Oakland’s current zoning and land use regulations to accommodate the facilities. Dozens of community members spoke in support of the moratorium extension and against AI data center development in Oakland. Many residents, including Jamal Khan, a member of the Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment, said Oakland is an easy target for billionaires and developers who prioritize profit over the well-being of vulnerable people. “We’re not talking about proposing a data center over there in Marin County on Skywalker Ranch,” Khan said. “This is part of a design to disenfranchise us again.” Cathy Leonard, a District 1 resident, warned that West Oakland seniors and children, who experience higher rates of asthma and cancer than those in other neighborhoods, would experience more noise and air pollution if data centers come to Oakland. “Let’s bring some productive businesses to Oakland that actually help us, not kill us. These centers are killers,” she said. Not everyone supported the moratorium. Mindy Pechenuk, a District 4 resident who ran unsuccessfully for mayor, argued data centers could create more jobs for young people and boost the local economy. She said developers could build a facility at the former Oakland Army Base. In an agenda report released ahead of Tuesday’s council meeting, Fife argued that the city’s existing infrastructure was not designed to accommodate the “extraordinary” demands of large-scale data centers. The city has yet to determine whether its power grid, water supply, and emergency response systems could support data centers without affecting services for residents, businesses, schools, and hospitals. The city’s planning code also does not specifically define data centers or outline rules about their operations, including requirements for water efficiency, energy use, noise reduction, backup generators, and environmental protections, according to the report. The extension, Fife wrote, is necessary because “data centers have the potential to impose significant negative impacts on local water and electrical resources, air quality, and community livability.” City officials have already received inquiries about establishing data centers in new and existing buildings, according to Fife’s report. Though the document does not provide any names of individuals or companies, one developer, Behring Companies, made headlines in August when it proposed siting a data center inside a downtown Oakland building. Activist group says West Oakland survey shows broad opposition to data centers An hour before the council meeting, Care 4 Community Action, an Oakland-based civic engagement group that grew out of Carroll Fife’s 2020 City Council campaign, held a press conference outside City Hall to go over the findings of a survey they conducted with West Oakland residents about data centers. The group says it knocked on more than 2,400 doors across West Oakland last month. Of the 424 people who spoke with organizers, 73% said they supported a full ban on new artificial intelligence data centers in the city. Other findings from their survey include: - 46% worried about rising electricity and utility bills - 47% were concerned about jobs being replaced by AI - 51% expressed concern about rents going up and residents being displaced because of data center development - 73% wanted the city to establish water and energy use standards before the moratorium expires Forty-five percent of residents who spoke with canvassers said they have lived in West Oakland for at least a decade, according to a news release from Care 4 Community Action. At the press conference, organizers said they supported the moratorium extension because they believe the city needs more time to assess the long-term impacts of data centers. “Forty-five days is not enough to make decisions that can impact West Oakland for generations,” said Bradley Gentry, a Care 4 Community Action organizer who spoke with over 50 residents as part of the effort. Stacy Hogg-Stewart, a District 3 resident whose family has lived in West Oakland for 80 years, said community members deserve transparency when it comes to new development in their neighborhoods. “We’re not against new development, but we deserve to know what the costs of having a data center in West Oakland are,” Hogg-Stewart told The Oaklandside. artigo.texto: Fortunes are diverging lately for Korean and Chinese companies competing in the global battery market. Expectations are rising that domestic manufacturers including LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI will keep improving results on stronger demand in the U.S. energy storage system (ESS) market. Chinese companies, by contrast, face a red light as oversupply worries and U.S. restrictions on Chinese-made products cloud growth. ◇ China's CATL grows in size, but profitability flashes warning signs According to the battery industry on the 9th, China's CATL, the world's largest battery maker, posted third-quarter revenue of 165.221 billion yuan (about 33.3 trillion won), up 58.9% from a year earlier. Net profit rose 14.5% to 21.246 billion yuan (about 4.3 trillion won). Despite double-digit increases in both revenue and net profit from a year earlier, the results fell well short of market expectations. London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) had projected CATL's third-quarter revenue growth rate at 60.2% and net profit growth rate at 41.2%, respectively. The underwhelming results were immediately reflected in the share price. On the 20th of last month, when the third-quarter results were released, CATL's stock on the Hong Kong market fell 6.6% from the previous day. Global investment bank JPMorgan also cut its rating on CATL shares listed in Hong Kong to Neutral from Overweight. Chinese battery makers including CATL continue to expand in scale. In particular, Chinese products have increased their share of the electric-vehicle market this year. Market researcher SNE Research said that from January through September, Chinese companies—seven suppliers including CATL—accounted for a 73% share of batteries installed in electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) and hybrids (HEVs) worldwide, up 3.5 percentage points from a year earlier. Korea's big three—LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On—had a 12.6% share, down 4.1 percentage points. The problem is profitability is slipping relative to topline growth. With domestic competition saturated, China has been pushing large volumes overseas at low prices. Automakers struggling amid cutthroat competition are also diversifying supply chains to smaller battery vendors that sell cheaply to cut costs, a trend seen as squeezing margins at major manufacturers including CATL. According to the South China Morning Post (SCMP), Chinese EV makers Xiaomi and Li Auto said they will team up with battery manufacturers such as CALB and EVE Energy to reduce battery procurement costs. CALB and EVE Energy are classified one tier below giants like CATL and BYD in China. ◇ Korean battery makers spread their wings on rising U.S. ESS demand Korean battery makers, by contrast, are beating market forecasts with improving results. They have struggled in EV batteries against a flood of cheap Chinese products, but demand for ESS batteries has surged in the United States, benefiting domestic suppliers. Samsung SDI posted third-quarter revenue of 4.6856 trillion won and operating profit of 407.8 billion won. Revenue rose 52.6% from a year earlier, and operating profit swung to a surplus from a 591.3 billion won loss. Operating profit, in particular, was twice the previous quarter's 203.8 billion won and the highest in 12 quarters since the third quarter of 2023. Samsung SDI's operating profit far beat the market consensus—an average forecast—of 235.4 billion won, an earnings surprise that stood in contrast to CATL. LG Energy Solution also saw revenue jump 59% in the same period to 9.6434 trillion won, while operating profit rose 25.7% to 756 billion won. Both were record highs on a quarterly basis. Its third-quarter operating profit was more than double the 320 billion won market consensus. Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution said soaring demand for ESS used in U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) data centers drove the improvement. A gradual recovery in Europe's EV market, which lifted EV battery sales, was also a tailwind. ◇ U.S. midterms: Democrats win by a landslide; ESS demand seen rising, China curbs to continue Industry officials expect the U.S. ESS market to grow quickly, likely extending domestic makers' run of stronger results. Many also see the Democrats' landslide in the U.S. midterms held on the 3rd—on a platform of expanding energy infrastructure including ESS—as a boon for Korean companies. Voice of America (VOA) reported on the 9th that although counting was not yet complete, the Democrats had already secured 252 of the 435 House seats, far more than a majority and beating the Republicans' 161. They also won 52 Senate seats to the Republicans' 44. In gubernatorial races, Democrats won in 28 states, ahead of Republicans who won in 20. The Democrats announced in May an energy agenda that included plans to expand investment in the national power grid and energy storage systems (ESS). While they take a dim view of regulating AI data center construction, they intend to keep growing the ESS market as part of grid expansion. Hyundai Motor Securities said in a pre-midterm report, "If Democrats control both chambers, they will push to restore renewable energy tax credits and expand ESS investment," adding, "Both parties have previously toughened tariff policy on Chinese batteries, so the post-election direction will likely remain to block China's supply chain." Some, however, see a chance for a rebound by Chinese battery makers. China is also ramping up ESS investment, and once plants under construction in Europe start up, they could further encroach on Europe's EV battery market. The European Union (EU) is currently imposing high tariffs on Chinese EVs. It is also finalizing details of the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), pursued to counter China and protect domestic industry, ahead of its entry into force. artigo.texto: - Australian Vanadium awarded $15 million from Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) to establish vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility - IAF supporting a diversified economy and unlocking private sector investment - Funds will support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain The Cook Labor Government has awarded $15 million through the Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) New Energies Industries Round 2 to Australian Vanadium Limited (AVL) to establish a high-capacity, relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility in Western Australia. The project will expand AVL's capacity to produce vanadium electrolyte to support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain. Vanadium flow batteries use liquid vanadium electrolyte solutions in separate tanks to both store and release electricity. Skilled employment and training opportunities in advanced manufacturing, chemical processing, engineering, construction, commissioning, and plant operations will be created, while its modular and relocatable design enables deployment across regional and industrial centres throughout the State. The project presents an opportunity for the State to further invest in energy transition initiatives by supporting grid-scale energy storage, strengthening critical minerals supply chains, and help to build local industries required for a low-carbon future. The IAF funding will also support the development of grid-scale vanadium flow batteries and long-duration energy storage infrastructure in the State. The IAF has supported 47 projects since first launching in 2022 with over $215.2 million in funding awarded, generating 290 direct jobs and 1,479 contractors engaged. To date, more than $4 in spending is generated from every $1 distributed through the fund. For more information on the IAF, see: Investment Attraction Fund As stated by State Development and Economic Diversification Minister David Michael: "The Investment Attraction Fund continues to play a critical role in attracting projects that strengthen Western Australia's industrial capabilities and support our energy transition. "By supporting AVL's electrolyte manufacturing capability, we're creating new opportunities in advanced manufacturing while helping position WA at the forefront of long-duration energy storage technologies. "The development of a high-capacity vanadium electrolyte facility will support local jobs, strengthen our manufacturing capability, and provide the foundations for future grid-scale battery projects across the State." As stated by Energy and Decarbonisation and Manufacturing Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson: "The Cook Labor Government wants to see more things made right here in WA. "Our Made in WA plan is working, with new data showing manufacturing jobs have risen 13 per cent over the past year. "This is another great example of the Cook Labor Government backing innovative Western Australian manufacturing projects."

artigo.texto: On November 9, a Dutch new energy delegation led by KURT WU, Founder and General Manager of EverGreen Sustainability, visited Shanghai Metals Market (SMM) for an exchange. The SMM team, including Cherry Li, Key Account Manager, Alissa Peng, Account Manager, and Daniel Huang, Senior Energy Storage Analyst, warmly received the delegation and extended a sincere welcome to the guests from afar. This is a professional and diverse delegation, with members covering the entire industry chain, including project developers, EPCs, system integrators, energy asset owners, EMS technology enterprises, distributors, and industry platforms. The delegation includes: - THEO GROEN, CEO of Groen Energy in the Netherlands; - JAN SCHUT, CEO of Envitron; - ERIK BRINK, CEO of Nettion; - GERARD SCHEPER, Founder and CEO of European Solar & Storage; - RINIE EVERTSE, Founder of Evertse Solar Control; - BEREND PASTOOR, Chairman of Groen Zonenergie; - HENRICO VAN DEN BOOMEN, CEO of Eigenenergie.net B.V.; - PAUL DAANEN, Technical Director, Eigenenergie.net B.V.; - ROBERT MEIJER, CEO of AG Solar; - JOOP POLDERMANS, Senior Energy Project Manager at JOOP POLDERMANS; - WIDJAI JIPAT, CEO of EPTA Energy; - GERBEN DRAGT, CEO of GD Solar; - HASHIM FATMI, COO of EnergyPlanet Global; - REMCO VAN DER HORST, Founder of Greenproc B.V.； - Floriske Deutma, Board Member of Netherlands-China Business Council - KURT WU, Founder and General Manager of EverGreen Sustainability During the exchange, the SMM team first introduced SMM's development history and data service capabilities. Founded in 1999, SMM started with traditional non-ferrous metals business and gradually expanded into the new energy sector. Headquartered in Shanghai, its business covers Asia, Europe, and Africa, and it set up offices in India and Australia this year. The company currently has more than 500 employees, half of whom are analysts, each specializing in specific metals and new energy sub-sectors. Next, the SMM team conducted a special workshop to share market research findings and analytical capabilities across the ESS industry chain: global energy storage demand grew 74% from 2025 to 2026, with growth expected to pull back to 22% in 2027. Regional market divergence is pronounced, with China remaining the world's largest market, North America's share continuing to rise driven by AI data center power demand, Europe constrained by localisation policies, and Australia's residential demand strengthening on the back of subsidies. Daniel Huang also highlighted that the lead time from battery cell shipment to grid connection and commissioning takes only 3–6 months in China, compared with 7–14 months in Europe, where large projects commonly involve 10% advance stockpiling. This difference in delivery cycles profoundly influences the global supply pace. The SMM team further examined price movements in the ESS Stack market, attributing the upward shift in the battery cabinet price center to the combined effects of raw material costs, exchange rate fluctuations, export tax rebate policy adjustments, and the competitive landscape. Scenario analyses were conducted on the transmission path of rebate reductions, margin impacts across different markets, and the trajectory of mid-term FOB prices in Europe amid the iteration toward large-format battery cells. At the battery cell level, the discussion drew on changes in industry operating rates and concentration, as well as the trend of top-tier players tilting production schedules toward large-format cells, to illustrate that growth in shipment volume does not equate to cost breakthroughs. Yield, capacity utilisation rate, and expansion discipline are the true variables for cost reduction. This was further extended to assessments of the medium and long-term share and cost convergence of lithium battery cathode routes and sodium-ion batteries. Finally, returning to upstream lithium carbonate, the meeting reviewed price trends and phase-specific drivers, emphasising that the risk lies not in nominal capacity but in whether supply can be delivered on schedule. Variables such as mine production resumptions, ex-China ore export policies, and midstream settlement terms collectively determine actual available supply and the price pace, thereby providing industry chain clients with a systematic reference for decision-making on pricing, procurement, and project scheduling. After the presentation, the delegation members raised a stream of pertinent questions based on their own businesses, covering the potential impact of EU cybersecurity regulations on the market share of Chinese enterprises, the layout trends of Chinese producers building factories in Indonesia, the selection of lithium price indices in European procurement contracts, the market space for battery recycling, and the independence and release mechanism of SMM data. The SMM analyst team responded one by one and introduced the product system, including databases, built-in AI queries, monthly reports and free spot prices. This visit and exchange has built a bridge for direct dialogue between enterprises in the PV+ESS industry chains of the Netherlands and China. Both sides will take this exchange as a starting point to continuously deepen cooperation in data services and market insights, jointly supporting the energy transition in Europe and globally.

artigo.texto: Resumo - Itaú BBA vê WEG (WEGE3) favorecida pela expansão de data centers no Brasil - Banco mantém recomendação outperform e preço-alvo de R$ 56 para a ação - Projeto Scala AI City, perto de Porto Alegre, já tem aval da ANEEL para 5 GW - Em certos equipamentos elétricos, o tempo de entrega pode chegar a três anos - Servidores de data center sofrem carga tributária de cerca de 70% no país - Programa Redata poderia reduzir essa carga para perto de 20%, estima o BBA A WEG (WEGE3) pode se beneficiar do avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) e da expansão dos data centers pelo mundo. Essa é a avaliação do Itaú BBA, que colocou a companhia entre suas principais apostas nos setores de transportes e bens de capital. O banco reiterou recomendação outperform, equivalente a desempenho acima da média do mercado, e estabeleceu preço-alvo de R$ 56 para a ação. A análise foi divulgada após uma reunião do banco com a Scala, uma das principais desenvolvedoras de data centers de grande porte da América Latina. Segundo o BBA, a procura crescente por equipamentos e a oferta limitada de fornecedores nacionais favorecem a fabricante brasileira. Além disso, os longos prazos de entrega de componentes elétricos ampliam a vantagem competitiva da WEG. Como a companhia já possui estrutura de produção no Brasil, ela está bem posicionada para atender à demanda gerada pelo novo ciclo de investimentos em infraestrutura digital. A Scala também destaca a disponibilidade de energia elétrica no Brasil como um diferencial competitivo. O cenário contrasta com o dos Estados Unidos, onde as restrições de oferta de energia são mais severas. Na cadeia de fornecimento elétrico dos data centers, a WEG já responde por uma parcela expressiva dos equipamentos, posição que poucas empresas nacionais conseguem alcançar. Capacidade de energia favorece expansão dos data centers A administração da Scala informou que o Scala AI City, projeto que pretende construir próximo a Porto Alegre, já recebeu autorização da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) para contar com 5 gigawatts (GW) de energia. Essa capacidade deve permitir a expansão gradual do empreendimento nos próximos anos. Entretanto, a disponibilidade de equipamentos ainda representa um desafio para o setor. Segundo estimativas da Scala, um empreendimento de 1 GW pode esperar cerca de oito meses pela entrega de transformadores. Em contrapartida, o prazo para determinados equipamentos elétricos pode chegar a três anos. Diante desse cenário, a desenvolvedora avalia que fabricantes com operações instaladas no Brasil, como a WEG, levam vantagem sobre concorrentes que ainda precisam estruturar sua produção no país. Os analistas do Itaú BBA também chamam atenção para a valorização das empresas fornecedoras de equipamentos. Fabricantes como a Vertiv, por exemplo, negociam a múltiplos superiores aos das operadoras de data centers. Para o banco, essa diferença indica que o mercado pode atribuir maior valor às companhias responsáveis pelo fornecimento da infraestrutura necessária aos centros de dados do que às próprias operadoras. Redata pode reduzir custos para data centers no Brasil A tributação dos equipamentos também aparece como um fator importante para a expansão do setor no país. Segundo os dados apresentados pela Scala, os servidores de data centers enfrentam atualmente uma carga tributária efetiva próxima de 70%. O impacto é relevante porque esses equipamentos representam cerca de 80% dos investimentos em bens de capital de um centro de dados. Na avaliação da administração da Scala, a carga tributária ajuda a explicar por que aproximadamente 40% das cargas de trabalho brasileiras ainda operam no exterior. Nesse contexto, o Itaú BBA avalia que o Redata, programa voltado ao estímulo de investimentos em data centers no Brasil, pode reduzir a tributação dos servidores para cerca de 20%. Com uma carga menor, os custos de implantação dos centros de dados também diminuiriam. Consequentemente, empresas que hoje mantêm parte de sua infraestrutura fora do país poderiam considerar o mercado brasileiro uma alternativa mais competitiva. artigo.texto: Severn residents express concerns over proposed data center expansion Residents in Anne Arundel County are voicing concerns about a proposed expansion to an existing data center, fearing its impact on Severn and their utility costs. Miguel Ruiz, who has lived in Severn for seven years, said he has seen the area evolve significantly during his time there. "There is definitely a lot of change," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. Ruiz shared his frustration about the addition of the data center, which he passes by daily. "This is a beautiful place, and if they're going to keep on putting that stuff, those monsters here, it's going to destroy the beauty of the place," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. Ruiz also noted changes in his utility costs. "My energy bills have gone up sky-high. (My) water bill, (it's) unbelievable. It's like the service is the same, but the prices are still going up," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. "I don't agree to it. I hope it doesn't happen and we'll do whatever we can for it not to be accomplished." The data center's developer is exploring plans for the expansion. A county representative confirmed the proposal in a statement sent to WBAL-TV 11 News on Tuesday. Shanice Corlette, who lives in an apartment complex next to the site, expressed her concerns about the proposal. "It's not good for the area," Corlette said. Corlette plans to move out of the neighborhood next summer and hopes her next home will not be near a data center. "I'll be out of here by next summer, so hopefully, where I move next, I won't have to deal with that," Corlette told WBAL-TV 11 News. Corlette added that she believes the expansion plans will draw more attention from residents. "I definitely think a lot more will be concerned. It's definitely going to be raising eyebrows," Corlette told WBAL-TV 11 News. The proposal comes after the Anne Arundel County Council approved an extension of its data center moratorium, which prevents new data center developments through January 2028. However, the moratorium does not apply to expansions of existing facilities. A county representative told WBAL-TV 11 News that the proposed expansion will go through the standard review, comment and approval process. Ruiz said he expects the project to face resistance from residents. "We just need more information to make people more aware so we can do something about it." "I think that most of these people would be willing to fight it because the bills are getting too extraordinary," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. Corlette emphasized the need for more information about the project. "We just need more information to make people more aware so we can do something about it," Corlette told WBAL-TV 11 News. The project engineer declined to comment on the expansion plans when reached by email.

artigo.texto: Diferentemente dos sistemas de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS) convencionais, o BESS (Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias) é um sistema de armazenamento de energia em larga escala conectado diretamente à rede elétrica. O sistema pode carregar e armazenar eletricidade em momentos apropriados e devolvê-la à rede quando necessário. O BESS pode ser concebido como uma "instalação de armazenamento de energia" capaz de operar em duas direções: quando o sistema está em estado de flutuação, o BESS recebe eletricidade para armazenamento; quando há necessidade de suporte, o sistema gera eletricidade de volta para a rede. Dessa forma, o BESS pode contribuir para suavizar a curva de demanda, reduzir a pressão durante os horários de pico e aumentar a flexibilidade da operação do sistema elétrico. Com a crescente demanda por eletricidade e as significativas flutuações de carga dependendo do clima e da hora do dia, a melhoria da capacidade operacional do sistema elétrico de Hanói exige não apenas investimentos em fontes de energia e redes, mas também em novas soluções tecnológicas. Antecipando a tendência da tecnologia de armazenamento de energia, a EVNHANOI concluiu a instalação, energização e operação piloto de cinco sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) nas subestações de 110 kV de Bac Thang Long, Quang Minh, Sai Dong 2, Phung Xa e Thanh Oai. Cada sistema possui capacidade de armazenamento de 10 MW/20 MWh, elevando a capacidade total de armazenamento para 50 MW/100 MWh. Esta é a primeira vez que a tecnologia de armazenamento de energia em larga escala é aplicada à rede elétrica de Hanói, representando um novo passo na modernização da infraestrutura de energia e no desenvolvimento de uma rede inteligente. A seleção das subestações para o projeto piloto baseou-se nas características de carga e nos requisitos operacionais da rede elétrica de Hanói. O sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) é uma tecnologia completamente nova na rede elétrica da capital. Desde a instalação, testes e energização até a operação oficial, as unidades da EVNHANOI trabalharam em estreita coordenação para garantir que o sistema atendesse plenamente aos requisitos técnicos e operasse de forma estável e segura. Durante a operação, a equipe técnica monitora continuamente o status das baterias, a capacidade de carga e descarga, a temperatura, os sistemas de proteção e os alertas técnicos. Cada turno de inspeção é realizado de acordo com procedimentos rigorosos, com coordenação entre a equipe de despacho, a unidade de gestão técnica e a equipe diretamente na subestação para garantir que todos os parâmetros permaneçam dentro dos limites de segurança. O processo de operação prática também proporciona à EVNHANOI a oportunidade de acumular dados, aprimorar os procedimentos técnicos, avaliar a confiabilidade dos equipamentos e adquirir experiência em gestão para uma tecnologia ainda muito recente no Vietnã. Segundo o Sr. Pham Huu Manh, Diretor Adjunto do Conselho de Gestão do Projeto de Desenvolvimento de Energia de Hanói, a implementação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) não visa substituir as fontes de energia existentes, mas sim adicionar uma ferramenta técnica que ajude o sistema elétrico a ser mais proativo na resposta às flutuações de carga, além de criar uma base para a pesquisa de modelos modernos de operação da rede no futuro. Quando combinado com sistemas de coleta de dados, monitoramento, controle e gestão de energia, automação da rede e tecnologias digitais , o BESS deixa de ser apenas um sistema de armazenamento de energia e se torna um elo na estrutura de uma rede inteligente. No próximo período, a EVNHANOI continuará monitorando e avaliando a eficiência operacional, aprimorando os procedimentos técnicos e pesquisando soluções de aplicação adequadas. Isso servirá de base para a construção gradual de uma rede elétrica mais inteligente, flexível, segura e moderna na capital, atendendo às necessidades do desenvolvimento socioeconômico e melhorando a qualidade do fornecimento de energia elétrica para a população de Hanói.

artigo.texto: When using electric vehicles or smartphones, users often experience inconvenience from long charging times and gradually shortening battery life. To increase charging speed and extend usage time, next-generation batteries with high energy density are essential. However, fast charging has had limitations because deposits can accumulate inside batteries, degrading performance and even increasing the risk of fire. A Korean research team has developed a new foundational technology to address this problem by creating a "highway" through which lithium ions can move rapidly inside a battery. KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced on November 9 that a joint research team led by Professors Dong Ki Yoon and Hye Ryung Byon from the Department of Chemistry developed a next-generation battery separator technology that precisely controls lithium-ion transport pathways by regulating the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers. Lithium metal batteries can store more energy than conventional batteries. However, during charging, lithium can accumulate in sharp, branch-like structures known as "dendrites." This phenomenon has been a major cause of reduced battery life and can damage the internal separator, potentially leading to explosions. The research team sought to solve this problem using liquid crystal materials, which combine the ordered characteristics of solids with the fluidity of liquids. Because the orientation of liquid crystal molecules can be altered through surface treatment and other methods, the researchers used this property to regularly align the pathways through which lithium ions travel. Based on this liquid-crystal alignment control technology, the team also created a porous liquid-crystalline polymer separator containing nanoscale pores. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, which facilitate lithium-ion transport, were incorporated into the separator. In particular, the researchers freely controlled the alignment direction of the liquid-crystal molecules either vertically or horizontally and compared the resulting lithium-ion transport characteristics. The results showed that the liquid-crystalline polymer separator with vertically aligned molecules formed a kind of "highway" that allowed lithium ions to move directly toward the electrodes. Compared with a horizontally aligned separator, it reduced the tortuosity of the ion transport pathway by approximately 2.5-fold, enabling lithium ions to move much faster and more uniformly. This effectively suppressed dendrite formation and significantly improved stability. The research team applied the newly developed separator to an actual lithium metal battery and verified its fast-charging performance. Even under demanding fast-charging conditions at a high charging rate of 4 C*, the battery retained 94% of its initial capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles. This demonstrates that controlling the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers can be a highly effective strategy for improving both the charging speed and lifespan of next-generation batteries. *4C charging rate: A rate at which a battery can theoretically be fully charged in approximately 15 minutes based on its rated capacity. C is a unit indicating the charging and discharging rate of a battery: 1C corresponds to 1 hour, 2C to 30 minutes, and 4C to 15 minutes. Professor Dong Ki Yoon said, "This study demonstrates that controlling the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers can be used to efficiently design lithium-ion transport pathways and thereby improve battery performance and stability," adding, "We expect this approach to contribute to the development of high-energy-density next-generation battery technologies, for which long driving ranges and rapid charging are essential." Geunjung Lee, a Ph.D. student at KAIST, and Dr. Rak Hyeon Choi participated in the study as co-first authors, while Professors Hye Ryung Byon and Dong Ki Yoon participated as co-corresponding authors. The research was published in the international journal ACS Nano in September 2026. Paper title: Directional Li+ Flux Control via Liquid-Crystalline Polymer Separators for Fast-Charging Lithium Metal Batteries, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.6c09591 Author information: Geunjung Lee†, Rak Hyeon Choi†, Geonhyeong Park, Juri Kim, Younwoo Kim, Hye Ryung Byon*, Dong Ki Yoon*; † co-first authors, * corresponding authors. This research was supported by the Mid-Career Researcher Program of the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Research Foundation of Korea, as well as the GIST InnoCORE Program.

artigo.texto: Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state. McALLEN — SpaceX is planning to build a $24 billion data center and power plant just outside of Brownsville on property that the city had just de-annexed earlier this year at the company’s request, circumventing Brownsville’s data center moratorium that went into effect last week. On Monday, the city of Starbase, which later annexed land where the project will be built into their city limits, notified the public that SpaceX is building a $24 billion “gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility.” The $24 billion investment is expected to cover the initial phases of the project which could include future expansions, according to the Monday notice which stated that the Starbase city commissioners are scheduled to hold a public hearing in December in which they will consider tax breaks for the project. The 444.45 acres of land where the project will be located was the subject of local scrutiny over the summer, when SpaceX asked the city of Brownsville to de-annex that land. In exchange, the company offered to fund $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. A SpaceX representative didn’t provide details as to why the company wanted the land, located near the Port of Brownsville out of Brownsville’s city limits, but the company pressured the city to approve the de-annexation quickly or else the $220 million would be off the table. The city agreed, but the move drew widespread condemnation from residents and environmental activists who believed the city was allowing SpaceX to further take over land in the area. Soon after the city approved the deal, speculation circulated online that SpaceX planned to build a data center on the property and wished to circumvent a data center moratorium that was advancing within Brownsville. That speculation appears to have been correct all along. In response to the news, the South Texas Environmental Justice Network, announced a protest against the project, arguing that the new facilities would pollute the air, use up water and increase energy bills for residents. Other residents responded positively, seeing the project as a source for more jobs. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” said Janie Melendez, a Brownsville resident and school teacher. She previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee but said her politics don’t influence her view on data centers and SpaceX. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. “But I’m one of those [people] that tries to find a balance in everything.” SpaceX did not respond to questions regarding the project. What the future holds for data centers in Texas However, a majority of Texans oppose data center construction, which has received a wave of pushback across the state due to concerns over how much power and water they require to operate at a time when utility bills remain high and water scarcity fears mount. In response to public backlash, several communities have issued temporary moratoriums on data centers. As criticisms of these facilities grew, Gov. Greg Abbott directed operators of the electric grid in August to pause requests for data center connections to the grid until the data centers could be audited. However, not all data centers rely on the state’s power grid and therefore could still move forward by supplying their own electricity. The gas-fired power plant that SpaceX plans to build could provide power to its data center to avoid connecting to the state’s power grid. Abbott also ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing permits for data centers, though critics say that some permits have continued to advance through the permitting process. Data center developers could face stronger headwinds under Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who said she would issue a ban on all data center approvals until state legislators can pass laws “to protect Texans,” she said in a video posted on X. Brownsville approved its own 90-day moratorium which went into effect last week, temporarily hitting pause on data center applications within the city and its extraterritorial jurisdiction. Had the 444.45-acre tract of land remained within Brownsville’s city limits, the SpaceX project likely would have had to find a different location. The city of Brownsville said it stood by its decision to de-annex the property, which was based on “information and circumstances presented at the time,” the city said in a statement. That included the property’s location, municipal service considerations and potential long-term benefits to Brownsville. The city further noted that the land was privately owned and its sale to SpaceX was a transaction between private parties. The $220 million that the city received for the de-annexation will fund critical water infrastructure which the city said would help ensure their water supply keeps up with their future growth. “The City recognizes the concerns raised about data center development and takes those concerns seriously,” the city said. “It remains committed to evaluating those concerns and protecting water resources, evaluating infrastructure impacts and ensuring responsible growth that serves Brownsville’s long-term interests.” Further, the city assured that any future de-annexation requests will be evaluated independently under state law and the city commission will take the circumstances and legal requirements into consideration before taking action. “Residents should have confidence that their concerns about data center development, water resources, energy consumption and responsible growth are being taken seriously,” the city said. “Our responsibility is to ensure that Brownsville’s growth is intentional, that residents’ interests remain a priority, and that decisions involving our c

The company announced that it completed the "Demonstration of High-Safety Energy Storage System Based on Aqueous Zinc Batteries Linked to Solar Power" as the lead organization for the "2025 Climate Change Response Innovative Technology Demonstration Project," which is being promoted by Seoul City and managed by the Seoul Research Institute. For batteries to be installed in living spaces inside and outside buildings, verification is required not only for cell-level performance but also for safety, system control, and operational reliability. TNP Solution plans to utilize the operational experience gained from this demonstration in the product development of future urban-type ESS and building energy storage systems. Kang Seong-gu, CEO of TNP Solution Co., Ltd., stated confidently during a phone interview with this outlet, "The safety of batteries is a value that cannot be compromised in spaces where actual citizens carry out their daily lives." He added, "This demonstration marks a turning point proving that aqueous zinc batteries are high-safety energy solutions immediately applicable in real-life environments, going beyond the laboratory level. We will actively pioneer the urban power market, which absolutely requires safety and reliability, differentiating ourselves from markets focused on high density." Meanwhile, the "aqueous zinc-ion battery" is a secondary battery that has recently attracted attention. As the adoption of solar power and distributed power sources expands, total costs—including energy density, fire safety, installation costs, and maintenance fees—are becoming increasingly important in domestic and international ESS markets. An aqueous zinc-ion battery is a secondary battery that utilizes a water-based electrolyte and a zinc metal anode. By using a non-flammable aqueous electrolyte, it can minimize the risk of ignition from the electrolyte itself. Additionally, by utilizing relatively abundant zinc, it possesses competitiveness in terms of raw material and manufacturing costs. artigo.texto: Following her reelection Tuesday, Nov. 3, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek’s priorities for the next four years include installing a universal statewide preschool program, passing new regulations on data centers and increasing the amount of time Oregon students spend in school. Kotek shared her goals at a Friday, Nov. 6, news conference in Portland following her victory this week over state Sen. Christine Drazan, a Republican from Canby. Drazan late Friday afternoon officially conceded the race and said in a news release she wished Kotek well. “I sincerely hope she recognizes that the challenges facing our state demand a different approach than what we’ve seen over the last four years,” she said in a statement. Going into the election, Kotek was polling as one of the least popular governors in the nation, but her campaign benefitted from nationwide dissatisfaction with Republican President Donald Trump and Republicans in Washington, D.C. Kotek said she’d be engaging with people from across the state differently in her second term to reach voters who were on the fence about her, and she indicated she’d use social media more to communicate her decisions and to have conversations. Kotek during her campaign availed herself to supportive online influencers, inviting them to several events where she eschewed invites to news outlets. She visited every county during her first year in office, though carefully choreographed tour stops meant she met primarily with select elected leaders, nonprofit service agencies and business owners. On Friday, Kotek said she’d also be doing more to assert her power over the Oregon Legislature when the six-month 2027 session begins at the end of January. After presiding over the House for nine years as speaker, she spent her first term as governor largely deferring to lawmakers instead of participating in negotiations, most notably on a large-scale transportation funding package lawmakers failed to pass in 2025. “I am not going to stand back and wait for the Legislature to figure it out. I need to see progress in the first month, the second month, the third month,” she said. “People voted Democrats in because they want stuff to happen, and I need the Legislature to do that. I’m going to be in the building. I’m going to be on top of them every day, saying we got to get stuff done.” Her legislative advocacy for the next session will start with her Dec. 1 recommended budget, which she said will include no additional funding for the Oregon Department of Transportation. Debates over funding for the beleaguered agency with a nine-figure budget deficit consumed the bulk of the last two legislative sessions and culminated in voters resoundingly rejecting a 6-cent gas tax increase and other proposed fee increases in May. “That’s trade-offs, because that means taking money away from highway projects and other things to pay for basic ops and maintenance. But that’s what you’ll see in my budget,” she said. “If legislators want to do something different, we’re going to have to come to the table and talk about it.” Data Canters Kotek said she wants regulations for, and state oversight of, data center development solidified in the first 60 days of the session. She said it should include clear standards and transparency around data center energy and water use, how energy is being obtained, and what agreements data center companies have made with local communities hosting them. Kotek’s data center advisory panel, convened earlier this year, will share with her recommendations that will inform her policy proposal for the Legislature, and she the group would also inform legislation to “take on large corporations who are using artificial intelligence on a regular basis to figure out how they can make more money and charge people more.” Universal preschool Kotek promised universal statewide childcare by the end of her second term. She did an about-face on criticisms of Portland’s Preschool for All program at an event in October, saying she’d find a way to make sure all Oregonians had access to free preschool. She said it’s part of her long-term education goals, which also include increasing the amount of time Oregon kids spend in school (the state has among the shortest school years in the nation) and improving attendance. She said she’d continue to push for funding for her early literacy initiative to improve Oregon kids’ proficiency in reading, which is among the lowest in the nation. “In terms of how to pay for things, I’ve made no commitments,” Kotek said about potential revenue proposals from progressive groups and candidates, including a new wealth tax. State agency reform Kotek said she’d be implementing some of the recommendations from her Prosperity Council’s June report that advocated cutting taxes, climate programs and investing state funds in business infrastructure and development. Among the first will be next week, when Kotek rolls out a fast-track program for statewide permitting, requiring state agencies to approve or deny applications within clear timelines. She said she’d also reorganize Oregon’s economic development agency Business Oregon into a more hands-on Department of Commerce working directly with businesses and industry in the state. And in December, Kotek will also go to the Legislative Emergency Board to ask for $10 million for the Bend-La Pine School District and the city of Bend to help pay for services and support needed in the aftermath of the Oct. 15 school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary that left five people dead including the gunman. artigo.texto: O mercado regulado de carbono brasileiro pode acrescentar 5,8% ao Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) até 2040 e 8,5% até 2050, além de reduzir em 27% as emissões dos setores submetidos ao sistema até meados do século, segundo estimativas do Banco Mundial divulgadas pelo Ministério da Fazenda. Os números foram reportados pelo Monitor do Mercado e apresentados pela Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono (SEMC), vinculada à pasta, durante a COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. A conferência ocorre até 20 de novembro e marca a apresentação dos resultados da primeira etapa de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). O desenho do mercado combina limite de emissões, cotas negociáveis e regras de monitoramento, com o objetivo declarado de criar incentivo econômico para a redução de poluentes e dar previsibilidade a investimentos de baixo carbono. O que o SBCE muda para as empresas Criado pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o SBCE estabelece um teto para as emissões de gases de efeito estufa de empresas de setores regulados. As companhias recebem cotas de emissão, que diminuem gradualmente ao longo dos anos e podem ser comercializadas entre os participantes do mercado. Quem emitir abaixo do limite pode vender o excedente; quem precisar de mais cotas pode comprá-las. Em outubro, o Ministério da Fazenda divulgou o cronograma para que os setores industriais iniciem o monitoramento das emissões e cumpram as exigências de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (MRV). O conjunto de procedimentos define como as empresas devem medir, registrar e comprovar a quantidade de gases de efeito estufa lançada na atmosfera. As regras alcançam operadores com emissões a partir de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente por ano. Segundo o governo, esse grupo representa menos de 1% das empresas brasileiras. A secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis, afirmou que o sistema oferece previsibilidade regulatória para atrair investimentos sustentáveis. A expectativa do governo é que a implementação contribua para a modernização industrial e para a transição a uma economia de baixo carbono. Projeção de PIB e agenda global As projeções do Banco Mundial foram divulgadas pelo Ministério da Fazenda em um momento de implementação gradual do sistema. O ganho estimado de 5,8% do PIB em 2040 e de 8,5% em 2050 é acompanhado pela expectativa de redução de 27% nas emissões dos setores regulados até meados do século. A participação brasileira na COP31 também marca o primeiro ano da Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono (OCCCM), iniciativa apresentada pelo país durante a COP30, em Belém (PA). Presidido pelo Brasil e copresidido pela China e pela União Europeia, o grupo reúne jurisdições responsáveis por 42,2% das emissões globais de gases de efeito estufa e por US$ 49 trilhões do Produto Interno Bruto mundial. O Plano de Trabalho 2026-2027 da coalizão foi aprovado em setembro, em Wuhan, na China. Durante a COP31, a delegação brasileira conduz uma reunião de alto nível e prevê a entrada de novos participantes. Também está prevista a assinatura de um Memorando de Entendimento para a adesão do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB). Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, a instituição será o primeiro banco multilateral de desenvolvimento sediado na Ásia a integrar formalmente a governança da coalizão. Desmatamento recua e ajuda o balanço de emissões Além do mercado de carbono, o Brasil apresentou na conferência dados recentes sobre a redução do desmatamento. Segundo o Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros (BiomasBR), do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), a taxa de desmatamento na Amazônia caiu 41,8% no período 2025/2026, para 3.335 quilômetros quadrados. O resultado é o menor da série histórica, iniciada em 1988. No Cerrado, a redução foi de 23,8%, com área desmatada de 5.516,69 quilômetros quadrados. De acordo com os dados apresentados pelo governo, esse é o menor índice desde 2001. O Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SEEG), iniciativa do Observatório do Clima, atribui à contenção da perda de vegetação uma contribuição para a queda de 6% nas emissões brutas do Brasil em 2025. O conjunto de números apresentado na COP31 reúne a projeção de impacto macroeconômico, o cronograma de adaptação das empresas e os dados de desmatamento. O mercado regulado tem implementação gradual, enquanto a coalizão internacional busca ampliar a coordenação entre jurisdições que respondem por parcela relevante das emissões e do PIB global.
