artigo.texto: Voters just told pollsters, loudly, that they do not want a data center down the road. An NBC News exit poll reported that 76% of voters opposed building a new data center in their community, and the Associated Press reported the same roughly three-quarters share. Yet the AI industry still needs the buildings, the chips and the power that those facilities concentrate in one place. That tension is the political story of November 2026, and it sits at the center of where AI model development goes next. The ballot results backed up the polling. According to The Detroit News, voters in at least 29 jurisdictions passed data-center bans or restrictions on November 3, 2026. The New York Times counted 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives going against the industry. We tracked the early returns in our report on 41 data center votes putting the AI boom on notice, and this piece takes the next step: what the backlash means for the people who build and fund AI models. A caution on the framing first. Headlines this week say voters “hate” data centers, and that phrase is not what the polling shows. The numbers confirm opposition to proposed facilities in voters’ own communities. They do not confirm a blanket rejection of every data center, and they do not confirm that voters understand how much of the AI stack depends on them. The gap between those two readings is where the next two years of policy will be fought. For wider context on the models themselves, see our AI and machine learning coverage. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the NBC Exit Poll Actually Measured The headline number from NBC News is the 76% share of voters who opposed building a new data center in their community. That is a question about a specific, local, physical thing. It asks whether a respondent wants a building, its noise, its traffic and its power draw near their home. Voters answer that kind of question differently from an abstract one about whether AI is good for the country. The same poll then asked how much data centers mattered to the congressional vote. NBC reported that 23% of voters called them “crucial” to their choice, and 33% called them a “major” factor. Add those two groups together and you reach 56%, which matches a separate report summarizing the NBC findings as showing that 56% of voters viewed AI and data centers as a crucial or major factor in their vote. The Associated Press framed the same finding more narrowly, reporting that about one-quarter of voters called AI data centers crucial to their vote for Congress. Those figures deserve a careful read. A voter who ranks an issue as “major” has not necessarily switched parties over it. Nothing in the reported results tells us how many votes actually moved, or in which direction. What the numbers do establish is salience. A topic that barely registered in national polling a few years ago now shows up as a top-tier concern for more than half the electorate, according to the NBC exit poll as summarized in that separate report. We covered the salience angle in more detail in our piece on how midterms put AI on trial. The short version is that the industry can no longer treat local siting fights as isolated zoning disputes. They now function as a national referendum, fought one county at a time. 29 Jurisdictions and 40 of 41 Local Measures Two outlets counted the local results in slightly different ways, and both counts point the same direction. The Detroit News reported that voters in at least 29 jurisdictions passed data-center bans or restrictions on November 3. The New York Times reported that in 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives, voters chose to limit or prevent data-center development. The two figures measure different universes, so they should not be added together or treated as a contradiction. A 40-to-1 split is rare in American politics. Most ballot measures on contested land use come out closer, because developers can usually point to jobs and tax revenue. That the industry lost nearly every contest suggests the usual promises of local economic benefit failed to persuade. The reported results do not tell us why in each case, and we have no verified breakdown of turnout or margins for individual measures, so we will not guess at them. It is also worth separating what a ban or restriction does from what it prevents. A local measure can block a new facility without touching existing ones. It can also set conditions, such as approval requirements, that slow construction without stopping it. The reporting we have confirms that voters chose to limit or prevent development. It does not give a uniform definition of the rules that now apply across those jurisdictions, and readers should treat each measure as its own legal text. Ohio Sits at the Center of the Backlash The New York Times reported that more than half of those 40 successful initiatives were in Ohio. That concentration matters. It means the national count owes a large share of its weight to a single state where organized opposition, local politics and a heavy pipeline of proposed facilities collided at once. The statewide race pointed the same way. According to The Detroit News, Amy Acton was reported as winning election as Ohio’s next governor, and the report said she favored a moratorium and tougher regulations on the industry. We should be precise here. The report describes her policy preference. It does not tell us what legislation she will propose, whether the legislature will go along, or how a state-level moratorium would interact with the local measures already passed. For AI companies planning capacity, Ohio is a warning about concentration risk. A region can look like an ideal site on paper, with land, fiber and power access, and still turn hostile once several projects arrive close together. artigo.texto: The rumors aren't true, Anaconda Chief Executive Bill Everett assured the public Tuesday night: No data centers are coming to town. Nevertheless, Everett said at the city commission meeting that he plans to seek a 12-month moratorium on data centers coming to Anaconda to ensure further examination of the issue. The commission plan to hold a hearing on the proposed moratorium in about three weeks. Data centers have emerged as a flashpoint in communities across Montana. In Butte, a proposal by Sabey Data Center fell apart in April after neighbor REC Silicon exercised a right-of-refusal to buy the 620-acre site where the project was planned. A citizens group had launched a petition requiring public approval of data centers in response to the plan. Last month, the Missoula City Council approved a moratorium on data centers, and a local AI is suing to overturn the measure. In Broadview, developer Quantica broke ground in October on a massive data center on 5,000 acres south of town. The project has been met with protests and angry public comment at Yellowstone County commissioners' meetings.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no COP31 começa nesta segunda (9) na Turquia com Brasil no centro do debate climático e data centers na agenda Publicado 08/11/2026 • 19:44 | Atualizado há 11 horas KEY POINTS A 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31) começa nesta segunda-feira (9), em Antalya, na Turquia, com o Brasil no centro das discussões sobre a continuidade dos compromissos assumidos na COP30, em Belém, e uma nova frente de debates sobre o impacto ambiental dos data centers. Até 20 de novembro, representantes de governos, empresas e organizações internacionais discutirão como ampliar o financiamento climático, acelerar a transição energética e abastecer a expansão da inteligência artificial com eletricidade de fontes renováveis. A COP é o principal fórum multilateral de decisões climáticas vinculado à Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima. As negociações buscam transformar os objetivos do Acordo de Paris em medidas de redução de emissões, adaptação aos eventos extremos e apoio financeiro e tecnológico aos países mais vulneráveis. A conferência será presidida pela Turquia, com o ministro Murat Kurum indicado para comandar a COP31. O australiano Chris Bowen terá a função de presidente das negociações, em um arranjo que divide as responsabilidades políticas e diplomáticas do encontro. Leia também: COP30 termina com aprovação do Pacote de Belém e foco em implementação climática Entre os temas centrais estão a passagem dos compromissos climáticos para a execução, a ampliação dos investimentos em energia limpa e a redução da dependência de combustíveis fósseis. Os governos também discutirão medidas de adaptação, como proteção contra secas, enchentes e ondas de calor. O financiamento climático será outro ponto decisivo: países em desenvolvimento cobram recursos mais acessíveis para reduzir emissões e enfrentar perdas e danos associados a eventos extremos. Também entram no debate mercados de carbono, proteção de florestas e infraestrutura resiliente. A COP31 marca ainda o início do segundo balanço global do Acordo de Paris, processo destinado a avaliar coletivamente o avanço dos países e identificar onde é necessário acelerar a ação climática. Leia também: Presidência da COP30 propõe cronograma global para abandonar combustíveis fósseis até 2033 A expansão dos data centers, instalações que sustentam serviços digitais e sistemas de inteligência artificial, terá espaço específico na programação paralela da conferência. Na terça-feira (10), o Pavilhão da Itália receberá um encontro sobre soluções para abastecer essas estruturas com energia limpa e avaliar seus benefícios climáticos. O evento reunirá especialistas em planejamento energético e infraestrutura digital. Na segunda-feira (16), a Agência Internacional de Energias Renováveis (Irena) e a Global Renewables Alliance organizarão uma discussão sobre data centers verdes, consumo de eletricidade e integração com as redes elétricas. Entre os pontos previstos estão o uso de energia renovável, a transparência das informações de consumo e formas de evitar que a demanda da inteligência artificial amplie a geração baseada em combustíveis fósseis. A programação de Ação Digital Verde também inclui o Compromisso de Antalya sobre Inteligência Artificial, iniciativa da presidência da COP31 para incentivar práticas digitais alinhadas às metas climáticas. No mesmo dia 16, o Pavilhão Brasil receberá o lançamento do AI Climate Institute. Esses eventos integram a agenda de debates e iniciativas da conferência, sem representar, por si só, um acordo obrigatório entre os países. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A Cúpula de Líderes ocorrerá na quarta-feira (11) e na quinta-feira (12). O presidente turco Recep Tayyip Erdoğan e o secretário-geral da ONU, António Guterres, estão previstos na abertura. O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva também participará, conforme confirmação do governo brasileiro. Entre os nomes esperados estão ainda o primeiro-ministro britânico Andy Burnham e outras autoridades nacionais. A programação de alto nível prevê discursos, encontros bilaterais e mesas sobre eletrificação, indústria verde, financiamento, adaptação urbana e proteção das florestas. Além dos chefes de Estado, terão papéis importantes Murat Kurum, na presidência da conferência, Chris Bowen, na condução das negociações, e representantes de organizações internacionais, do setor privado e de comunidades afetadas pela mudança do clima. Leia também: Lula participará da COP31 na Turquia O Brasil chega à COP31 depois de sediar a COP30, em Belém, e pretende manter protagonismo nas negociações. Lula participará da cúpula de 11 e 12 de novembro e deverá defender medidas concretas de transição energética, combate ao desmatamento e financiamento da proteção florestal. A presidência brasileira da COP30 levará à conferência propostas de mapas do caminho para o afastamento dos combustíveis fósseis e para a reversão do desmatamento. O governo também pretende ampliar o apoio ao Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre (TFFF) e apresentar resultados de políticas ambientais brasileiras. O Pavilhão Brasil será o principal espaço nacional na Zona Azul, área reservada às negociações oficiais. Organizado pelo Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, pela presidência da COP30 e pela ApexBrasil, reunirá governos, povos indígenas, comunidades tradicionais, empresas, universidades e organizações sociais. A programação inclui debates sobre energia eólica, combustíveis sustentáveis, financiamento verde, mercados de carbono, agroecologia, cidades resilientes, proteção indígena e uso de tecnologia na política climática. A inauguração do pavilhão está prevista para segunda-feira (9). artigo.texto: New Dem regulators plan to take on Georgia Power’s data center gas boom Georgia residents are angry at the state’s unchecked data center boom and rising electric bills — and they voted accordingly in last week’s election. Democrats won every statewide race in Georgia, including two seats on the Public Service Commission. Republicans had held a majority at the powerful utility regulator for 30 years. The winning candidates, Commissioner-elect Shelia Edwards and reelected Commissioner Peter Hubbard, have made clear that their top priority is to rein in rising electricity bills from Georgia Power, the state’s biggest utility. That likely means the new Democratic majority will challenge Georgia Power’s plans to enact one of the largest fossil-fuel expansions in the nation. In December 2025, the Republican-led PSC approved Georgia Power’s plan to build nearly 10 gigawatts of new gas-fired power plants and batteries to serve proposed data centers. It did so despite recommendations from commission staff to approve only about one-third of that capacity right away, given the speculative nature of the data center growth projections that the utility used to justify its buildout. All three Democrats on the five-member commission have signaled opposition to those plans. The two Democrats already on the commission, Hubbard and Alicia Johnson, tried earlier this year to get the PSC to reconsider the planned gas buildout but were thwarted by the GOP majority. The five new gas-burning plants planned as part of that buildout could cost customers an estimated $50 billion to $60 billion over their multi-decade lifespan and lock in significant amounts of new greenhouse gas emissions, according to estimates from the Southern Environmental Law Center. Hubbard, who worked for 16 years in utility planning and renewable energy project development, has conducted his own analysis that found a “cost-optimized portfolio” prioritizing solar, batteries, and energy efficiency could meet expected demand and save billions of dollars compared to the utility’s gas-heavy approach. Georgia Power’s expensive gas buildout would exacerbate the affordability challenges its customers already face. The PSC has approved six rate hikes from Georgia Power in the past few years, increasing typical residential utility bills by 33%, or more than $500 a year on average. The utility, which earns a set rate of return on what regulators allow it to spend on power plants, has seen profits swell over that same time. “Georgia Power is making billions while Georgia families are struggling,” Edwards, who owns a communications consulting firm, said during an Oct. 28 press event hosted by the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, a nonprofit advocacy group. “Something is fundamentally wrong with that picture.” Controlling data center costs — and making them pay their own way In February, the PSC voted 3–2 against a motion brought by environmental advocates to reconsider the 10-GW gas buildout, with Hubbard and Johnson voting to block the expansion. The Democratic commissioners argued that the utility had failed to prove that data center growth justified the cost. Nor was their opposition enough to discourage Georgia Power. Just months later, in April, the utility submitted a new request to the PSC seeking permission to add somewhere between 2 GW and 6 GW of additional “dispatchable capacity resources.” Utility critics fear this new round will also tilt toward a preponderance of gas power plants instead of solar, batteries, or other cleaner options. Georgia Power says that its broader customer base will be insulated from cost increases related to its gas buildout, and that growing electricity sales will put “downward pressure” on customer rates. Last year, the all-Republican commission approved a rule that would allow Georgia Power to force data centers and other large customers to cover the costs of the new power plants and grid infrastructure built to serve them. Other utilities and state regulators have made similar pledges via “large load tariffs” meant to force data center developers to commit to paying a significant portion of their costs if they don’t get built or shut down early. “We know our customers depend on us to keep energy reliable and affordable for their homes and businesses,” Rick Anderson, the utility’s senior vice president and senior production officer, said in an April announcement. “As we continue to invest in diverse, flexible generation resources, we also continue to work with new large-load customers who are driving much of this growth on appropriate contracts that are designed to cover the cost to serve them.” But the utility’s critics say it has failed to prove that its contracts with data centers really do protect customers. They also contend that the Republican majority on the commission has rebuffed repeated demands for more transparency into how the requirements might be enforced. Those concerns were heightened earlier this year when OpenAI revealed its plans for a 3.2-GW data center in southeast Georgia. The PSC’s three Republican commissioners outvoted Hubbard and Johnson to approve that contract in August, despite concerns that Georgia Power had failed to publicly reveal the terms under which OpenAI would be held responsible for paying the cost of the utility’s investment in grid and power plant infrastructure to serve it. The few details that Georgia Power has since disclosed haven’t allayed those concerns, said Maggie Shober, research director at the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. “They have a statement saying, ‘The customer pays its full cost over the life of the contract,’ but no information on minimum bills, termination service, exit fees. It’s just, ‘Trust us, guys,’” she said. But trust is hard to come by these days. Last week’s election made clear just how large a swath of the public has turned against data centers. artigo.texto: NVIDIA has just come through a sharp pullback, with the stock down over the past month and year after a very large multiyear rise. This leaves a straightforward question for you as an investor: Are today's cash flows, and the ones buyers expect over time, enough to support the current share price after this reset? - Over the past 5 years, NVIDIA has returned roughly 5x. This means a lot of future cash generation is already embedded in expectations and needs to be weighed carefully against the recent slump. - Fresh scrutiny over AI data center regulation, export controls and the CEO misconduct probe can influence how quickly data center demand translates into cash inflows and how much capital NVIDIA may need to commit to maintain its position. - What if you looked at NVIDIA through its earnings instead? See what NVIDIA's 23.4x P/E says about the price. For investors, the debate is whether NVIDIA's recent price, after the sell off and rebound attempts, is adequately supported by the cash it produces and is expected to produce in the years ahead. If you want to test the same cash flow question you are asking of NVIDIA across a wider set of AI infrastructure plays, take a look at 53 AI infrastructure stocks. Is NVIDIA Still Cheap on Cash Flow? The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here focuses on the cash Nvidia can return to shareholders over time. On the latest twelve month view, Nvidia generated roughly $126.7b of free cash flow, and the model assumes those cash flows keep growing rather than shrinking from that base. Projected free cash flows step up materially into the early 2030s, then slow into a more measured second stage as the business matures in the model. That path helps explain why the DCF outcome sits substantially above the current share price of $186.64, even after the recent pullback. The Democratic midterm sweep, and the renewed focus on AI data center regulation it triggered, helps explain why the market price can still sit below what these cash flow projections support. NVIDIA's valuation puzzle only really comes into focus once you spell out the futures that might justify it. artigo.texto: BYD Yangwang Altior Debuts as Ultra-Luxury Flagship Sedan – 1,000 km Range, 5.6-Metre Length and Limited Production BYD's premium Yangwang brand has unveiled the Altior in Abu Dhabi, challenging established luxury carmakers with an imposing executive sedan featuring coach doors, a lavish four-seat cabin and next-generation battery technology. Chinese automotive giant BYD has taken another significant step into the global ultra-luxury automobile market with the unveiling of the Yangwang Altior, a flagship executive sedan designed to compete with some of the world's most prestigious luxury cars. Unveiled in Abu Dhabi on November 7, 2026, the Altior represents Yangwang's latest attempt to establish itself as an alternative to established European luxury manufacturers, particularly Mercedes-Maybach, Bentley and Rolls-Royce. Measuring an imposing 5.6 metres in length, the new sedan combines an executive-focused interior, distinctive coach doors and BYD's latest battery technology. The manufacturer is initially accepting pre-orders for an exclusive four-seat limited edition, with production restricted to just 399 examples worldwide. The limited-edition model is expected to cost approximately 2.08 million yuan (around ₹2.8 crore, indicative), although the final selling price has not been confirmed. Yangwang Altior – Key Highlights Exterior Design – A 5.6-Metre Luxury Limousine The Altior's styling reflects Yangwang's ambition to move beyond conventional premium vehicles and compete in the chauffeur-driven luxury segment. Its imposing front fascia incorporates a gemstone-inspired grille, drawing design inspiration from traditional Chinese ceremonial vessels. The sedan also features an elaborate two-tone exterior finish, enclosed alloy-wheel styling and floating wheel-centre emblems. One of the most distinctive elements is its rear-hinged coach doors. Opening to almost 90 degrees, these doors are designed to provide more convenient access to the rear passenger compartment. Integrated umbrella storage adds another traditional luxury-car touch. The Altior's 3,500 mm wheelbase is particularly noteworthy. Rather than prioritising compact exterior dimensions, Yangwang has designed the vehicle around maximising passenger space and creating a commanding road presence. Its substantial width of 2,030 mm further reinforces its positioning as a full-size executive limousine. Interior – Four-Seat Executive Lounge Inside, the Altior takes a passenger-first approach, with its initial four-seat configuration emphasising rear-seat luxury rather than maximum seating capacity. Two individual rear seats are separated by an elaborate centre console, creating a private executive environment. The seats incorporate leg rests, while champagne-glass holders, rear-seat controls and electrically operated privacy sunshades further enhance the chauffeur-driven experience. The interior combines quilted upholstery with decorative wood and metallic trim. Yangwang has also incorporated Chinese design influences to differentiate the Altior from its European competitors. The first special edition, named Shanhe Dingyun, features an exclusive brown-and-white colour scheme with details including jade-decorated air vents, gold-finished speaker grilles and unique commemorative badges. A conventional five-seat configuration is planned for a later stage, potentially broadening the car's appeal beyond customers seeking a dedicated executive limousine. Battery Technology – Over 1,000 km Claimed Range Despite its emphasis on luxury, the Altior also serves as a showcase for BYD's battery development. The sedan incorporates the company's second-generation Blade Battery technology alongside its latest Flash Charging system. Yangwang has quoted a driving range exceeding 1,000 km under China's CLTC testing cycle. However, it is important to distinguish the claimed test-cycle figure from real-world driving performance. Actual range will depend on driving conditions, speed, climate control usage and other factors. Yangwang has not yet fully clarified the model's production powertrain configuration. Detailed specifications covering battery capacity, motor output and charging duration also remain to be officially established. Limited Edition – Just 399 Units Worldwide Yangwang has opened pre-orders in China for the four-seat Shanhe Dingyun limited edition, with customers required to pay a deposit of 300,000 yuan. Only 399 examples of this edition will be offered globally, giving it an exclusivity-driven positioning from the outset. The anticipated price of 2.08 million yuan would place the Altior considerably above mainstream luxury sedans, signalling that BYD intends to compete on exclusivity, technology and craftsmanship rather than affordability. Yangwang is also offering exclusive customer experiences, including private previews, dedicated purchase consultants and priority test drives. The company has not confirmed the Altior's broader international delivery schedule or an India launch. Auto Punditz Analysis – Can BYD Challenge Europe's Ultra-Luxury Dominance? The Yangwang Altior marks an important shift in BYD's global ambitions. While the Chinese manufacturer has established a strong presence in mass-market electric vehicles, its latest flagship demonstrates an effort to compete at the highest end of the automotive industry. Three developments stand out. - First, BYD is moving beyond volume-driven growth. The Altior is unlikely to generate substantial sales volumes, particularly with its limited-edition positioning. Instead, the vehicle could strengthen BYD's brand image and demonstrate its technological and manufacturing capabilities to affluent customers. - Second, Chinese manufacturers are increasingly challenging established luxury brands. Traditionally, the ultra-luxury segment has been dominated by European manufacturers whose reputations have been built over decades. artigo.texto: Yokohama-based EGI Battery KK launches its Japan Technical Center to strengthen R&D, materials science, and supply-chain capabilities to support advanced lithium-ion battery development, manufacturing, supplier partnerships and customer relationships across Asia Pacific. ANN ARBOR, Mich., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EGI Battery, a U.S.-owned lithium-ion battery cell company, today announces the establishment of EGI Battery KK, its Japanese subsidiary, and the official opening of its Japan Technical Center in Yokohama. Japan's history of battery innovation, advanced manufacturing know-how and experienced talent make it a strategic location to bolster EGI's technical operations. EGI Battery KK's Technical Center will initially focus on conducting research & development, evaluating advanced battery materials, and strengthening supplier relationships and technology partnerships to support EGI's advanced battery cell development and commercialization efforts. "Building better batteries takes more than a breakthrough in the lab. It takes capabilities to connect materials, engineering and manufacturing to produce batteries which enable our customers' technology," said Tom McGuckin, CEO of EGI Battery. "Establishing EGI Battery KK is a strategic investment in those capabilities. By connecting Japan's deep battery expertise with the manufacturing operations we are building in Michigan, we aim to bring the next generation of advanced lithium-ion batteries into production and expand what our customers can achieve." EGI Battery KK also establishes a local base for working directly with customers and partners across Asia Pacific. The team will help connect regional market needs with EGI's cell development and commercialization efforts. McGuckin added, "This regional presence deepens collaboration between our technical development activities and our customers' applications." Junji Tabuchi, President of EGI Battery KK, will lead the Yokohama operation, including its technical partnerships and regional business development activities. Tabuchi brings more than 35 years of lithium-ion battery experience across UBE Corporation, NEC TOKIN and E-One Moli Energy, including leadership of battery materials R&D at UBE. "The opportunity is not only to develop better battery materials, but to turn those advances into cells that can be manufactured reliably and meet demanding customer requirements," said Tabuchi. "Our initial focus is on materials, R&D and our supplier partnerships. We are intentionally building a strong technical foundation in Japan so we can move promising research and engineering into commercial production." As the Japan operations develop, EGI Battery KK plans to expand into cell design, with a focus on electrodes, and then battery manufacturing capabilities. These future capabilities will leverage the center's initial materials, supply-chain and R&D activities, strengthening EGI's ability to develop and validate new battery technologies. The Japan Technical Center complements EGI's manufacturing expansion in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Through a phased approach, EGI is building the production capabilities and technical expertise needed to manufacture advanced lithium-ion pouch cells at scale. The Japan operation's initial materials evaluation, R&D and supplier collaboration will support that work, strengthening the connection between battery innovation and U.S. production. About EGI Battery EGI Battery is a lithium-ion battery company delivering the power that makes the next generation of drones, robots, aircraft and vehicles possible. Its team brings decades of combined lithium-ion experience, from materials science and cell design to high-volume manufacturing, giving EGI the know-how to develop innovative cell technology and produce it at scale. To meet growing demand and build a more resilient battery supply, EGI is scaling manufacturing at its Zeeb Manufacturing Center in Ann Arbor, Michigan, where fill and formation is already running and full cell production begins in 2027, providing customers with a direct path to NDAA-compliant cells. The company also operates a technical center in Yokohama, Japan, dedicated to battery materials research and development. The Yokohama team evaluates advanced materials, builds partnerships with suppliers and technology companies, and serves as a local base for customers across Asia. Learn more at egibattery.com. SOURCE EGI Battery Inc.

artigo.texto: A Baterias Moura se aliou à chinesa CATL para produzir sistemas de armazenamento de energia em sua planta industrial em Belo Jardim (PE). Na unidade a empresa já fabrica baterias para veículos. A companhia brasileira é a maior fabricante de baterias do País. A CATL também é fabricante de baterias para veículos automotores, mas detém avançada tecnologia do chamado BESS (battery energy storage systems; sistema de amazenamento de energia em baterias) – a empresa é líder global de sistemas desse tipo. O objetivo da parceria é atender a demanda que será proporcionada com o inédito Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade (LRCAP) por meio de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia (SAEs), realizado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e voltado ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), a rede de produção, transmissão e distribuição de energia elétrica do país. O certame será realizado nos dias 2 de dezembro – atendendo critérios de conteúdo local – e 4 de dezembro – para fornecedores internacionais. Há um número recorde de cadastrados para participar do certame: mais de 6 mil projetos, totalizando 296 GW em capacidade. A contratação do governo no leilão pode chegar a 4 GW, segundo fontes do mercado. A previsão de investimento da Baterias Moura para o projeto em Belo jardim é de R$ 200 milhões e prevê a ampliação da planta. Spartacus Pedrosa, diretor de operações de lítio do grupo, a estimativa é de que em meados do ano que vem a fábrica já possa fornecer sistemas para participantes do leilão baseados em armazenamento de energia. O executivo ressaltou ainda que a parceria prevê atingir as exigências de conteúdo local dos sistemas para atender o leilão. A Moura anunciou atender em 8 GWh às empresas participantes do leilão. A empresa brasileira já possui linhas de baterias baseadas em sistemas de armazenamento, mas são voltadas para clientes industriais, comerciais e condomínios. Agora, amplia a atuação com atendimento ao Sistema Interligado Nacional. Ressalta-se que com a chinesa CATL a Baterias Moura já desenvolvia projeto de eletrificação de veículos.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis set to pass sweeping data center regulations MINNEAPOLIS (FOX 9) - Minneapolis leaders appear close to a compromise on data centers as the city's temporary pause on construction nears its Nov. 21 end. What the proposed Minneapolis rules would do What we know: The proposal discussed at a Minneapolis City Council Committee of the Whole meeting would allow data centers only downtown or in the North Loop. They could only go into existing buildings, with minimal modifications allowed. In an attempt to address the potential for noise pollution, computers will have to be 20 feet away from exterior building walls. Local perspective: The plan would cap data centers at 150,000 square feet. Cities cannot place a limit on energy or water use, but under these new regulations companies would have to disclose that information to the city. "This is nothing other than keeping control for governing these data centers within us rather than farming it out to the state of Minnesota," said Councilmember Michael Rainville. By the numbers: The city says downtown has eight data centers serving tech companies right now. Many more data centers serving onsite computing needs of existing businesses exist around the city, according to city staff. Council members said they heard from Xcel Energy that there is interest in up to eight more data center projects downtown. Why the council remains sharply divided Why you should care: The council is split in half, with one side pushing for a full ban and the other pointing to downtown's high vacancy rate and seeing data centers as part of the solution. City staff said 30 percent of Downtown Minneapolis stands empty, which leaves residents to carry a disproportionate amount of the city’s property tax burden. The other side: "A complete ban on data centers is tone deaf. Tone deaf to the benefit to our labor – skilled labor. Tone deaf to our residents increased property tax burden. And tone deaf to the revenue problem that we have right here in our city," said Council member Elizabeth Schaffer. "What's tone deaf is saying that people want data centers," said Council member Soren Stevenson. "No data center in Minneapolis. That's easy. That's the easiest vote I ever had." Big picture view: Some council members who want a ban said the midterms were largely a referendum on data centers. "What we're talking about is actually the tone deaf proposal," said Council member Robin Wonsley. "It is very clear that our residents do not want to see this in their neighborhoods, in their community and in our city." What happens before the moratorium ends The council passed a six-month moratorium in May. That moratorium expires Nov. 21. Data centers could again move in with little oversight if the new rules do not pass. What's next: On Thursday, Nov. 12, the council will vote on the proposal. If council members stick with the plan discussed Monday, Nov. 9, the mayor's spokesperson tells FOX 9 Mayor Frey will support it. The Source: FOX 9 report from Emily Pofahl and Minneapolis City Council discussion.

artigo.texto: Riot Platforms is likely to see significant upside from its new powered land lease, according to Jefferies. The investment firm upgraded the digital infrastructure stock to buy from hold. It also hiked its price target to $28 from $13, implying 59% upside from Monday's close. "We are upgrading RIOT to BUY on a Corsicana lease with highly favorable economics (avg. 33% yield)," analyst Jonathan Petersen said in a note to clients. "The powered land lease lets RIOT monetize the site with less execution and financing risk. It also cuts capex to $6M per IT [megawatts] versus $11-15M for a typical data center build." RIOT YTD mountain RIOT year to date The powered land lease will be valid for 15 years, beginning in September 2027. The agreement will earn 33% average yield per year at half the usual capital, he added. Riot can fund the project with project debt or by a tenant in exchange for a rent credit. "We see RIOT's Corsicana deal as a reset for the market," the analyst wrote. "Pairing ready power with the tenant's modular solution improves speed to market, while the powered-land structure reduces RIOT's capital needs and shifts meaningful execution risk to the tenant." Jefferies' call falls in line with consensus on Wall Street. All 23 analysts covering Riot have a buy or strong buy on the stock, LSEG data shows. Shares have jumped 39% year to date.

artigo.texto: COP31 reacende debate sobre emissões de data centers Estudo estima até 54 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ em 403 instalações nos EUA; ONU cobra transparência ambiental da indústria de IA. Um estudo conduzido por pesquisadores de Harvard e outras instituições estima que 403 data centers de hiperescala nos Estados Unidos consumiram entre 68 e 99 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, com emissões associadas de 37 milhões a 54 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂). Os resultados colocam em evidência o impacto ambiental da infraestrutura computacional em meio à realização da COP31, que começou em 9 de novembro, em Antália, na Turquia. A conferência, que prossegue até 20 de novembro, terá sessões específicas sobre consumo energético de data centers, uso de fontes renováveis e medição dos impactos ambientais da IA. Entre elas estão eventos organizados pela União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT), pela Agência Internacional de Energias Renováveis (IRENA) e pela UNESCO. Os números fazem parte do estudo Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of U.S. Hyperscale Data Centers, divulgado em junho de 2026 na plataforma científica arXiv. A pesquisa foi elaborada por Gianluca Guidi, Francesca Dominici e outros pesquisadores. O levantamento considera diferentes cenários de utilização da capacidade instalada e apresenta estimativas de consumo e emissões, não medições diretas de cada empreendimento. O trabalho foi disponibilizado como preprint, ou seja, ainda sem conclusão do processo de revisão por pares. Data centers apresentam intensidade de carbono acima da média No cenário central da pesquisa, o consumo elétrico das 403 instalações correspondeu a aproximadamente 1,8% de toda a eletricidade utilizada nos Estados Unidos durante o período analisado. Os pesquisadores estimaram que 54% da geração de eletricidade atribuída ao funcionamento desses data centers teve origem em combustíveis fósseis. A intensidade média de carbono calculada foi de 545 gramas de CO₂ por quilowatt-hora (kWh), aproximadamente 48% acima da média de 370 gramas por kWh registrada na rede elétrica norte-americana. O indicador relaciona a quantidade de dióxido de carbono emitida à eletricidade consumida. A diferença identificada pelos pesquisadores está associada às características das fontes de geração que abastecem as instalações analisadas. Para chegar aos resultados, os autores combinaram informações sobre os data centers com dados do sistema elétrico dos Estados Unidos, incluindo registros da Agência de Proteção Ambiental (EPA). A metodologia considera diferentes níveis de utilização dos equipamentos, uma vez que a capacidade computacional disponível não opera necessariamente de forma integral. Os resultados mostram a importância da localização dos empreendimentos e da composição da matriz elétrica para a avaliação das emissões associadas à infraestrutura digital. COP31 terá debate específico sobre energia para data centers A programação da COP31 prevê, para 16 de novembro, uma sessão dedicada à utilização de energia renovável na infraestrutura de IA. O evento, intitulado Renewable Energy for AI: Green Data Centres for the Twin Transition, será organizado pela IRENA e pela Global Renewables Alliance, das 12h às 13h, no pavilhão Global Renewables Hub. O encontro discutirá os riscos da dependência de combustíveis fósseis, a contratação de eletricidade renovável e a necessidade de ampliar a capacidade de geração para atender ao crescimento dos data centers. A agenda também prevê a apresentação de princípios propostos pela IRENA para caracterizar data centers abastecidos por fontes renováveis. Entre os critérios estão a correspondência entre o consumo e a geração de energia renovável em termos de localização e horário, a rastreabilidade da eletricidade contratada e a comprovação de que os investimentos contribuem para ampliar a oferta de geração limpa. O debate abordará ainda o planejamento das redes elétricas e os mecanismos de contratação e investimento necessários para atender às novas cargas computacionais. Esses temas se relacionam diretamente aos resultados do estudo norte-americano, que identificou intensidade de carbono superior à média nacional no consumo elétrico atribuído aos data centers analisados. UIT e presidência da COP31 discutirão transparência da IA Também em 16 de novembro, a presidência da COP31 e a UIT realizarão uma mesa-redonda de alto nível sobre IA e sustentabilidade, das 9h às 11h. A sessão integra a iniciativa Green Digital Action e tem entre seus objetivos ampliar a transparência sobre o consumo de recursos pela IA e criar mecanismos de acompanhamento de seus impactos ambientais. A programação está dividida em quatro temas: medição, transparência e responsabilização; infraestrutura sustentável e economia circular; capacitação profissional; e utilização da IA em ações climáticas. O encontro também prevê o lançamento do Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge, iniciativa destinada a reunir compromissos voluntários de governos, empresas e outras organizações sobre o desenvolvimento e a utilização sustentável da IA. A proposta abrange critérios relacionados à concepção, aquisição, alimentação energética, implantação, medição e gestão de sistemas de IA. Para 17 de novembro, a programação da UIT e da UNESCO prevê outra sessão sobre IA sustentável e infraestrutura digital, relacionada às metas nacionais de redução de emissões e adaptação às mudanças climáticas. Os encontros integram a programação temática e os eventos associados à conferência. Sua realização não equivale à aprovação de novas obrigações internacionais para operadores de data centers. artigo.texto: 1 in 4 data centers sits in a water-stressed area — here’s what that means for nearby communities When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. AI has become integrated into our lives whether we like it or not. Despite big tech forcing schools to choose and lawsuits highlighting its dangers, the controversial technology is here to stay. New research published in Environmental Science & Technology puts specific AI concerns on a global map, highlighting 9,347 identified data centers, with roughly a quarter located in areas where water demand would exceed available supply for at least one month a year. The water has to come from somewhere Data centers use water to remove heat from their equipment. In evaporative cooling systems, some of that water evaporates rather than returning to the local water system. Electricity generation and hardware manufacturing add an indirect water footprint, too, according to the Pacific Institute. Where and when that consumption happens matters. The institute warns that data center water demand peaks during hot, dry periods, when supplies may be constrained, and other users also need more. Meeting those peaks can require additional utility infrastructure and spending. "They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms," study lead author Lorenzo Rosa said in an American Chemical Society release. That makes data center construction relevant to people who may never pay for an AI subscription. Before approving a facility, a community needs to understand whether its water system can accommodate a large new customer during a dry summer. Cities and municipalities are the largest water users, accounting for nearly 41% of the facilities studied, while agriculture is the primary user, accounting for another 28%, according to the American Chemical Society. A yearly average can miss the pressure The Potomac River basin offers a useful example. An analysis by the Interstate Commission on the Potomac River Basin describes current average data center water consumption in the Washington metropolitan area as relatively small. Its estimated 2025 average was about 4 million gallons a day, with peak-day consumption of approximately 15 million gallons. Cooling choices help explain the variation. Around 40% of facilities in the analysis rely exclusively on air cooling, while many others take advantage of cooler winter weather to reduce cooling demands. The commission cautions that approaches using less water often require more energy. For residents, an annual consumption figure only answers part of the question. They also need to know how much water a facility could require during the hottest days, when local supplies may already be under pressure. What communities deserve to know The same global study also examined existing data center locations under a scenario of 3°C of global warming relative to around 1900. The share exposed to water shortages rose to roughly a third. That projection applies future climate conditions to the facilities identified in the study; it doesn't account for where additional data centers might be built. Better disclosure would make proposed projects easier to assess. The Pacific Institute identifies a lack of standardized reporting on data center size, location and water use as an obstacle for communities and water managers. Residents deserve clear answers about a proposed facility's water source, expected summer demand and plans for drought. They also deserve to know who would pay for any necessary infrastructure upgrades. What communities can do now If a data center is proposed near your home, get answers now. Start with your local planning board or water utility and ask where its cooling water would come from, how much it could use on the hottest days, and what would happen during a drought. Be direct and ask who would pay for any water-system upgrades, too, and whether the operator would be required to make its water use public. Those details can help residents assess a project before approval. To learn more about the infrastructure behind AI, start with Google's data center water reporting or Microsoft's local environmental fact sheets. These disclosures can help you understand water use where facilities operate, though they won't tell you the footprint of your individual chats.

artigo.texto: A conclusão da instalação, comissionamento e energização do sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) ocorreu em meio a um aumento na demanda de eletricidade na província de Quang Ninh. Durante os meses de verão de 2026, a capacidade de carga máxima da cidade deverá atingir aproximadamente 1.200-1.400 MW, em comparação com um pico de 1.186 MW em 2025. Geração flexível de energia a partir de sistemas de armazenamento de baterias. Até o final de outubro de 2026, a Quang Ninh Power Company concluiu a instalação, o comissionamento e a energização de três Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (BESS). Com suas capacidades flexíveis de armazenamento e geração de energia, espera-se que esses sistemas ajudem a equilibrar a carga, melhorar a estabilidade da rede e fornecer à empresa uma ferramenta adicional para responder proativamente às flutuações cada vez maiores na demanda de eletricidade, concretizando gradualmente o objetivo de construir uma rede inteligente. Antecipando a tendência de armazenamento de energia, a Quang Ninh Power Company coordenou estreitamente com a Northern Power Corporation e empreiteiras para concluir a instalação, os testes de aceitação e a energização de três sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) nas subestações de 110 kV Trang Bach (comuna de Hoang Que), Gieng Day (110 kV) e Uong Bi (110 kV). Cada sistema tem capacidade de 5 a 10 MW e capacidade de armazenamento de 10 a 20 MWh. Diferentemente dos sistemas de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS) convencionais, o BESS é um sistema de armazenamento de energia em larga escala conectado diretamente à rede elétrica. O sistema pode ser recarregado em momentos apropriados e gerar eletricidade novamente quando necessário. O BESS pode ser concebido como um sistema de "armazenamento de energia" bidirecional. Quando a carga é baixa ou as condições do sistema permitem, o BESS armazena eletricidade; quando a demanda aumenta ou a rede precisa de suporte, o sistema gera eletricidade novamente. Portanto, o BESS pode contribuir para suavizar a curva de carga, reduzir a pressão durante os horários de pico e aumentar a flexibilidade na operação do sistema elétrico. A longo prazo, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) não substituem as fontes tradicionais de geração de energia ou os projetos de rede, mas sim desempenham um papel complementar, ajudando o sistema a utilizar a infraestrutura existente de forma mais eficiente. A eficácia do equipamento depende do local de instalação, da escala de potência, da capacidade de armazenamento, do método de controle e da coordenação com a central de despacho. Portanto, antes do comissionamento, os planos operacionais precisam ser calculados especificamente com base nas características de carga, capacidade de transmissão e requisitos de segurança de cada área. Isso também serve de base para que a Companhia de Energia de Quang Ninh avalie gradualmente a eficácia real, aprimore os procedimentos técnicos e prepare as condições necessárias para a operação dos sistemas no futuro. O Sr. Vu Viet Hong, Vice-Diretor da Empresa de Redes de Alta Tensão (Companhia de Energia de Quang Ninh), afirmou: Para adotar e dominar a nova tecnologia, a unidade coordenou com todas as partes envolvidas em todo o processo, desde a construção e aceitação até a conexão à rede elétrica. Em particular, os funcionários que operam e manipulam diretamente a rede elétrica nas subestações de 110 kV participaram diretamente do processo de testes pós-conexão, assimilando os procedimentos para lidar com situações reais sob a orientação de especialistas. Procedimentos operacionais, de resposta a incidentes, de manutenção e de assistência técnica também foram desenvolvidos para garantir que o sistema opere com segurança e estabilidade. Segundo o Ministério da Indústria e Comércio , o progresso dos projetos de energia no âmbito do Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII ainda é lento. Se os projetos de geração e transmissão de energia continuarem a sofrer atrasos, o sistema elétrico nacional poderá enfrentar um déficit de aproximadamente 4.256 MW de capacidade e 2,9 bilhões de kWh de eletricidade em 2027. Prevê-se que o déficit continue a aumentar no período de 2028 a 2030, concentrando-se principalmente no Norte. Em 2027, essa região poderá enfrentar um déficit de aproximadamente 5.680 MW de capacidade; em 2030, o déficit deverá atingir 13.026 MW. As previsões acima indicam que a implementação de soluções para aumentar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico é absolutamente essencial. Diante do aumento contínuo da demanda, especialmente em parques industriais, zonas econômicas , instalações de produção industrial e áreas e destinos turísticos na província de Quang Ninh, investir, concluir e preparar a entrada em operação do sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) é crucial para garantir um fornecimento de energia seguro, estável e contínuo. Quando estrategicamente posicionados e integrados a sistemas de controle e monitoramento, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) podem auxiliar na regulação de energia, respondendo melhor às flutuações de carga e utilizando de forma eficiente a infraestrutura elétrica existente. O sistema também tem o potencial de suportar a integração de fontes de energia renováveis, aumentando a adaptabilidade da rede às mudanças de potência e carga. O Sr. Le Ba Quyen, Vice-Diretor da Companhia de Energia de Quang Ninh, afirmou: "A empresa continua a coordenar-se com os níveis, setores e unidades relevantes para pesquisar e avaliar as necessidades, selecionar locais, escalas e planos operacionais para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias que sejam adequados às características da rede elétrica em cada área. Ao mesmo tempo, garante os requisitos de segurança elétrica, prevenção e controle de incêndios, eficiência do investimento e capacidade de integração com o sistema elétrico existente. artigo.texto: As opposition to building artificial intelligence (AI) data centers spreads across the United States, struggling small towns are betting their survival on luring those facilities. Major U.S. cities are tightening rules on data centers over heavy power consumption, noise, and environmental concerns. By contrast, rural towns where manufacturing has collapsed and populations are shrinking—unlike affluent suburbs—see data centers as the only tax base left to keep schools and roads running. The Washington Post (WP) reported on the 8th (local time) that the midterm elections held on the 3rd featured 41 local ballot measures across 10 states that could restrict data center development. Of those, 40 measures, or 97.6%, produced outcomes favorable to limiting data center construction. In network exit polls, 76% among respondents said they opposed building a new data center where they live. Fifty-seven percent said AI will do more harm than good to society. In Piqua, Ohio, residents banned a large data center that Meta planned to build for $1 billion (about 1.3566 trillion won) and recalled officials who had backed the project. In Texas, where data centers have clustered, Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on a moratorium on new construction, was elected governor. Even amid nationwide pushback, the tiny city of Harwood, North Dakota, with a population of 845, chose the opposite path. On the 3rd, Harwood residents voted down a ballot measure that would have required independent reviews and public hearings for large industrial projects, with 105 votes in favor and 325 against. It is seen as 75.6% of voters rejecting additional rules that could slow data center development. Residents backed the project on the calculation that once the data center is completed, the city's property tax revenue would grow to six times the 2024 level. Harwood's population is 845—about one-twenty-fourth the size of a Korean eup (20,000 people). The town has little industrial base beyond a few bars and grain elevators. Most residents commute to Fargo, North Dakota's largest city nearby. On Harwood's outskirts, Texas-based developer Applied Digital is building a data center of about 167,000 square meters with a $3 billion (about 4.09 trillion won) investment. Harwood Mayor Blake Henke has sparred with neighboring Fargo over annexing the data center site since the project began. He concluded that even if Harwood refused, the center could go up on land under Fargo's jurisdiction right next door. In that case, Harwood would bear the noise and traffic while Fargo collected the taxes. "If the data center is going to end up in essentially the same spot anyway, we'd rather receive the tax breaks and the revenue," Henke told WP. The city estimated annual property taxes from the completed facility at $1.65 million (about 2.2 billion won), roughly six times Harwood's 2024 property tax take. Applied Digital has also pledged more than 200 full-time jobs. It has already contributed funds to the city fire department and a park warming shelter. Across U.S. small towns hollowed out by industrial decline, data centers are seen as relief pitchers that can stave off extinction. Ellendale, a rural town of about 1,100 in the same state of North Dakota, embraced Applied Digital before Harwood did. The company is now expanding a data center campus there with a $5 billion (about 6.82 trillion won) investment. Mayor Don Flaherty said that if the campus grows to three buildings with up to 530 megawatts (MW), the number of full-time jobs will rise to 300 to 350—close to one-third of the current population. Ellendale's assessed value stood at $3.5 million (about 4.7 billion won) at the end of 2025, and the city projected that figure would more than double within a few years. "By 2028–2029, Applied Digital will pay more than $25 million (about 3.39 billion won) a year in property taxes and become North Dakota's largest property taxpayer," Flaherty said. There are also cases where attracting data centers has transformed public infrastructure. Quincy, an agricultural city about 240 kilometers east of Seattle in the northwest, used to grow potatoes. But over the past 20 years, more than 30 tech firms followed Microsoft in seeking cheap land and abundant power, completely changing the city's finances. An analysis by local outlet the Spokesman-Review of the city's audit reports found that Quincy's annual total revenue jumped from $6 million (about 810 million won) in 2006 to $47 million (about 6.4 billion won) in 2024. The population also grew from about 5,300 two decades ago to about 8,200. Data centers now account for 57% of Quincy's total local government tax revenue. With the expanded funds, the city built a new hospital, high school, fire station, and library. In rural Mecklenburg County, Virginia, a former correctional site that once produced no tax revenue became the highest-taxed property after Microsoft arrived in 2010. Data centers now support about 45% of the county's general fund. In Richland Parish, a rural area in northeastern Louisiana considered one of the poorest parts of the United States, data centers are shaking up the local economy. According to the New York Times (NYT), Meta announced in 2024 that it would build the $10 billion Hyperion data center there. In July this year, it raised the investment to more than $50 billion (about 67.83 trillion won). As construction ramped up, Richland collected $38.7 million (about 5.25 billion won) in sales taxes just in the first quarter this year from materials and equipment purchases. With tax revenue surging, annual bonuses for teachers in Richland jumped more than fivefold from about $10,000 last year to more than $50,000 (about 68 million won) this year. Still, attracting data centers does not yield only rosy outcomes. Communities face internal rifts, and rising incomes bring side effects. artigo.texto: Microsoft: restrição a componentes chineses pode afetar expansão dos data centers de IA (Divulgação/Getty Images) Editor de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 10 de novembro de 2026 às 14h38. Segundo a Reuters, a Microsoft tenta convencer o governo Trump a abandonar um plano de restrição a transceptores ópticos chineses usados em data centers de IA. Documentos do ITI alertam para o risco de interrupções no abastecimento. A Counterpoint estima que fornecedores chineses respondam por quase dois terços das unidades globais e cerca de 60% da receita de transceptores datacom. A discussão regulatória e o projeto S.5548 ainda não equivalem a uma proibição geral em vigor. A Microsoft pressiona o governo de Donald Trump para abandonar um plano de restrição a componentes chineses usados em data centers de inteligência artificial. O alvo são os transceptores ópticos, peças que conectam equipamentos por fibra óptica. Segundo a agência, representantes da empresa discutiram os riscos para o abastecimento com integrantes da Casa Branca em setembro. A Microsoft não comentou a reportagem, e a Casa Branca e a Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC) não responderam de imediato. Os transceptores convertem sinais elétricos em luz e fazem o caminho inverso na recepção. Na prática, permitem que servidores e outros equipamentos troquem grandes volumes de dados em alta velocidade. São parte da infraestrutura que precisa acompanhar a instalação dos processadores de IA. A chinesa Zhongji Innolight, fabricante desses componentes, está entre os nomes centrais dessa cadeia. A dependência vai além de uma companhia: segundo a Counterpoint Research, fornecedores chineses respondem por quase dois terços das unidades vendidas globalmente e por cerca de 60% da receita do segmento de transceptores para comunicação de dados. Na avaliação da consultoria, as americanas Coherent e Lumentum não conseguiriam substituir os volumes de Innolight e Eoptolink em um prazo de 12 a 24 meses. O obstáculo envolve capacidade industrial, encapsulamento dos componentes e escala de produção. O debate já aparece em documentos públicos. Em carta de 13 de agosto à FCC, o Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), associação do setor de tecnologia, pediu que os transceptores não fossem incluídos na chamada Covered List, relação de equipamentos e serviços considerados uma ameaça à segurança nacional dos EUA. A entidade alertou para os efeitos de interrupções no fornecimento sobre novos data centers e a liderança americana em IA. Caso a agência avance, o ITI defende que a medida se limite a fabricantes já presentes na lista, em vez de alcançar todos os produtos fabricados fora dos Estados Unidos. Há divergências sobre a resposta adequada à dependência. Em análise publicada em maio, Luke Hogg, da Foundation for American Innovation, defendeu uma transição para reduzir a exposição aos fornecedores chineses. O texto reconhece que a retirada imediata desses componentes prejudicaria a expansão da infraestrutura e propõe um horizonte até 2030 para a mudança. O tamanho dos investimentos ajuda a explicar a preocupação com novos gargalos. No trimestre encerrado em setembro, a Microsoft destinou US$ 45,2 bilhões a investimentos, incluindo arrendamentos, conforme seu balanço mais recente. Cerca de três quartos desse valor foram para ativos de vida curta, principalmente processadores e chips gráficos. Uma alternativa em discussão seria limitar a restrição aos transceptores de 3,2 terabits por segundo. Uma nota do Morgan Stanley citada pela agência prevê aumento da produção dessa geração em 2028 e adoção ampla em 2029. O recorte não foi anunciado pela FCC. Paralelamente à discussão regulatória, senadores apresentaram em 24 de setembro o projeto S.5548. A proposta bipartidária restringiria compras federais de determinados transceptores chineses para sistemas críticos e cita Innolight, Eoptolink e suas afiliadas. O texto prevê avaliação da capacidade de fornecedores americanos e de países aliados. As proibições passariam a valer cinco anos após eventual promulgação. Trata-se de um projeto de lei, não de uma regra em vigor nem de uma proibição geral de importação. É um dispositivo que transmite e recebe dados ao converter sinais elétricos em sinais de luz, e vice-versa, nas conexões por fibra óptica. A produção é concentrada. A Counterpoint avalia que concorrentes americanos não conseguiriam absorver os volumes de Innolight e Eoptolink em 12 a 24 meses. Não. A proposta foi apresentada no Senado e depende da tramitação legislativa. Seu foco são compras federais para sistemas críticos, com transição prevista no texto.

artigo.texto: The Norwegian government has cleared the zoning plan for Eiktyr Industrial Park in Orkland The approval provides a planning basis for Elinor Batteries’ proposed gigafactory on site Elinor is targeting 2030 for the start of operations, according to the latest municipal update Three years after announcing plans for a battery gigafactory in Norway, Elinor Batteries has reached a major planning milestone after the government approved the zoning plan for Eiktyr Industrial Park, where the battery project is planned. The proposal underwent years of planning and environmental impact assessments before the Norwegian Ministry of Local Government and Regional Development approved it. According to Elinor, the approved plan incorporates some changes to reduce the project’s environmental impacts, which will have minor implications for its planned development. Located in Orkland, the Eiktyr Industrial Park will host complementary industries that can share infrastructure, resources and energy, including Elinor’s Gigafactory project. Elinor produced its first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells in partnership with the research institute SINTEF at its Trondheim laboratory. The company plans to manufacture batteries for stationary energy storage at Eiktyr Industrial Park. According to Orkland municipality, Elinor is targeting 2030 to start operations. In 2024, Elinor announced a partnership with China’s Morlus Technology. At the time, Elinor said, “The agreement means that Elinor will be ready with its own batteries for commercial sale in Europe within six months – currently produced at Morlus' factory in China.” The gigafactory project will be located near Norway’s tech capital, Trondheim, connecting the site to the research and development community. This, as per Elinor, will create opportunities for collaboration across the battery value chain. “Eiktry brings together the scale, renewable power and proximity to leading technology environments that battery manufacturing requires,” said Elior Batteries CEO Anne Fredrik Lånke. Elinor Batteries is backed by Valinor, a Norwegian family-owned investment company. With zoning approval in place, Lånke said the project has secured political approval at every level, from local to national. The ‘large-scale’ manufacturing at Eiktyr will cater to the European demand for energy systems, transport, and industry, added the CEO.

artigo.texto: Battery energy storage systems are becoming essential infrastructure for a grid that increasingly depends on variable renewable generation. Their ability to respond quickly to changes in supply and demand makes storage uniquely valuable: batteries absorb excess generation, discharge when demand rises, and provide balancing services that help keep the grid stable. But as storage takes on a larger role, the definition of a successful project is changing with it. A battery energy storage system is no longer just a collection of batteries, inverters and electrical equipment. Modern BESS projects (Figure 1) run on software platforms, remote connectivity, operational technology (OT), market interfaces and a growing web of vendors and contractors. Any one of those systems or relationships can determine whether an asset is actually available when it’s needed. COMMENTARY That makes resilience part of the economics of storage, not just an engineering concern. Developers, owners and operators now have to ask not only whether a system can deliver its rated capacity, but whether they can maintain visibility into the asset, keep control of it, and restore operations quickly when something goes wrong. Availability is a Business Metric For storage, availability has direct financial consequences. Assets increasingly participate in energy and ancillary services markets where operators commit to delivering power at specific times. Miss that commitment, and the cost isn’t just lost production—depending on the market and contract structure, it can mean penalties or having to buy replacement energy at whatever the market is charging at that moment. That reframes how owners and operators need to think about resilience. Preventing an incident matters, but so does how fast an organization can detect a problem, understand its impact, regain control and bring the asset back online. No connected infrastructure is immune to equipment failure, software bugs, communications outages, human error or cyber incidents. Operators should plan on disruptions happening at some point in an asset’s operating life, not treat them as a remote possibility. The first hours after an incident matter most. Teams need to figure out what happened, which systems or accounts are affected, and how to restore the asset safely—and every hour of uncertainty adds to both the operational and financial exposure. Visibility is the Blind Spot One of the largest operational blind spots in battery storage today is visibility (Figure 2): who can access what, and what can they actually do once they’re connected? A modern BESS environment typically involves an asset owner, an operator, OEMs, integrators, software providers, maintenance teams and other contractors—often with dozens of people across multiple organizations holding some form of access to the systems around a single asset. That access is usually necessary; specialists need it to diagnose problems, perform maintenance and manage different parts of the system. But it raises a question that operators don’t always have a ready answer to. That question matters most for assets that can be dispatched remotely. The same speed that makes batteries valuable to the grid means the credentials and systems capable of changing their behavior need to be tightly controlled. With the right access, charging or discharging behavior can be changed in seconds. If that access is compromised, the consequence isn’t confined to an IT environment—it becomes a physical, operational event. The December 29, 2025 attack on Poland’s grid is a preview of what that looks like at scale. According to CERT Polska’s incident report and a joint alert from CISA and the Department of Energy, attackers used compromised edge devices to reach operational technology at more than 30 wind and solar sites and a combined heat and power plant serving nearly half a million customers. They deployed wiper malware, damaged remote terminal units and other field equipment, and severed the communication link between the sites and their grid operators. Generation itself was never interrupted—CERT Polska was explicit that current electricity production was not affected—but operators lost the ability to see and remotely control a fleet of distributed assets for a period of time. That distinction is the whole point. An asset doesn’t have to be physically damaged or taken offline to become an operational problem. If operators lose visibility into what an asset is doing, or lose the ability to control it as intended, its value to the grid is compromised regardless of whether the battery itself is fine. The risk also compounds at the fleet level. Grid stability increasingly depends on how many separate resources are coordinated and dispatched together. A problem at one small battery is a limited event. The Poland incident shows what coordinated disruption across dozens of sites in the same region looks like—which is why resilience has to be assessed at both the asset and the portfolio level, not asset by asset in isolation. Third-Party Access Needs an Owner BESS projects rarely operate within the boundaries of a single company, which makes third-party access one of the most important—and most neglected—parts of this problem. Vendors and contractors need access throughout the asset lifecycle, from commissioning and integration through routine maintenance and emergency troubleshooting. The trouble is that access granted for commissioning often stays active long after the project is in normal operation, unreviewed and unrevoked. Owners and operators should be able to answer, at any time: which external organizations have access to a given asset, which individuals within those organizations are authorized, what privileges they hold, and whether those privileges are still needed. artigo.texto: - Blockchain e IA: tecnologias serão utilizadas para registrar informações ambientais e estimar emissões dos veículos. - Créditos de carbono: projeto busca criar mecanismos transparentes para quantificar emissões e viabilizar sua monetização. - Participação da indústria: iniciativa envolve o Inmetro, universidades e fabricantes de veículos no âmbito do programa Rota 2030. O Instituto Nacional de Metrologia, Qualidade e Tecnologia (Inmetro) está desenvolvendo uma solução que combina blockchain e inteligência artificial para monitorar a emissão de poluentes de veículos no Brasil. A tecnologia faz parte do projeto Descarbonize.ai, iniciativa vinculada ao programa Rota 2030 que busca tornar o transporte rodoviário mais eficiente e sustentável. A proposta prevê a criação de uma plataforma capaz de coletar dados de automóveis, calcular sua eficiência energética e registrar informações ambientais em blockchain. O sistema também pretende viabilizar novos mecanismos de remuneração pelo compartilhamento de dados e pela redução das emissões de carbono, conectando motoristas, montadoras e empresas interessadas nessas informações. O projeto reúne o Inmetro, universidades federais e fabricantes como Volkswagen Caminhões e Ônibus, Peugeot Citroën e FCA Fiat Chrysler. Anunciada originalmente em 2024, a iniciativa segue entre os projetos de pesquisa registrados pela Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB) para o período de 2025 a 2026. Blockchain do Inmetro poderá registrar emissões de veículos e viabilizar créditos de carbono O projeto, denominado Descarbonize.ai: Sistema Integrado para Análise, Monetização e Descarbonização do Tráfego Veicular, pretende utilizar sensores conectados aos automóveis para coletar informações sobre consumo de energia, funcionamento dos motores e emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Esses dados serão processados por modelos de inteligência artificial capazes de estimar a quantidade de CO₂ emitida pelos veículos em diferentes condições de uso. A blockchain entra como uma camada de rastreabilidade, permitindo registrar informações e facilitar a verificação de sua integridade, característica importante para aplicações relacionadas ao mercado de carbono. Ao apresentar sua agenda tecnológica para a COP30, em novembro de 2025, o Inmetro destacou uma solução que combina inteligência artificial, processamento de dados na borda da rede e blockchain. Segundo o instituto, a proposta permite estimar emissões de veículos a combustão, híbridos e elétricos, oferecendo uma base tecnológica para a geração transparente de créditos de carbono. Motoristas poderão receber créditos digitais por compartilhar dados Outra possibilidade explorada pelo projeto envolve a criação de incentivos econômicos para motoristas que compartilhem informações geradas por seus veículos. A proposta considera a utilização de criptocréditos registrados em blockchain, que poderiam ser negociados com empresas interessadas nos dados coletados. Em entrevista divulgada em janeiro de 2024, Wilson Souza de Mello, pesquisador do Laboratório de Informática do Inmetro, explicou que o compartilhamento dessas informações poderia criar modelos de negócios envolvendo montadoras, seguradoras, distribuidoras de combustíveis e concessionárias de rodovias. Os créditos digitais funcionariam como uma forma de remuneração pela disponibilização dos dados. A iniciativa, entretanto, ainda não representa a distribuição de criptomoedas pelo governo brasileiro. Não foram identificados anúncios oficiais sobre o lançamento de um token negociável, uma rede blockchain específica ou o início de pagamentos aos motoristas. Esses mecanismos permanecem entre as possibilidades de aplicação da tecnologia. Projeto avança em universidades e pode ajudar indústria automotiva O desenvolvimento do Descarbonize.ai envolve pesquisadores do Inmetro, da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN) e da Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB). O trabalho integra o Rota 2030, programa federal voltado ao desenvolvimento tecnológico, à eficiência energética e à competitividade da indústria automobilística. Em outubro de 2025, pesquisadores das instituições apresentaram um estudo sobre estimativa de emissões de CO₂ em veículos a combustão por meio de redes neurais artificiais. O trabalho utiliza informações obtidas pelos sistemas eletrônicos dos automóveis e técnicas de inteligência artificial para calcular emissões e avaliar a incerteza das estimativas. A UFPB também mantém o Descarbonize.ai em seu catálogo de projetos de pesquisa para 2025 e 2026, com aplicações previstas em monitoramento ambiental, inventários de emissões e apoio à precificação do carbono. O Inmetro informou que uma etapa do programa Rota 2030 contempla R$ 18 milhões para projetos colaborativos, sem atribuir integralmente esse valor ao Descarbonize.ai. A utilização de blockchain nesse contexto representa uma aplicação da tecnologia além das criptomoedas. Embora o projeto ainda dependa de desenvolvimento e validação para aplicações comerciais, a proposta busca conectar dados veiculares, rastreabilidade digital e mecanismos econômicos de descarbonização, criando novas possibilidades para o setor automotivo brasileiro.
