artigo.texto: PowerCo's battery gigafactory in Sagunto (Valencia) has made progress in the construction of its cleanrooms and It plans to begin its industrial activity throughout of 2027, once the alliance with the Asian firm Gotion to operate the plant through a joint venture is finalized within an estimated period of six to eight months. According to company sources, the agreement between PowerCo and Gotion, announced on September 28, is structured as a joint venture. It is subject to the usual conditions for this type of transaction, including the necessary regulatory and administrative approvals. The factory is expected to begin production soon. effectively by the end of 2027. Corporate structure and investment The Sagunto gigafactory will be transferred to this new company, in which PowerCo will have majority controlThe company will retain 51% of the capital, while Gotion will assume the remaining 49% with a financial contribution of 1.100 billion euros. Current work in Sagunto has focused on finishing the cleanrooms, key spaces where the cells will be manufactured, and on the internal development of the industrial complex. Once these phases are completed, work will begin on... the entry and installation of the machinery and the rest of the production teams. It is planned for 2027 a phased start-up of the factoryFirst, the machinery, systems, and other facilities will be activated and verified. Then, the first test and validation cells will be manufactured, a necessary step before achieving a stable start to mass production. In parallel, PowerCo has indicated that it will intensify the staff training and development. The company's stated objective is to begin operations with an activity that, in its words, is 'competitive and ready to scale from day one'. Production capacity and technology Of the four planned production blocks, the first two have already been built. These two buildings will have a combined capacity of 30 GWh per year when operating at full capacity. This volume will allow for the supply of batteries for an average of between 350.000 and 400.000 electric vehicles each year, depending on the model, size and capacity of the batteries, as well as the cell configuration. The plant will begin by producing LFP cellsThese are based on lithium iron phosphate. However, PowerCo's standard cell supports various chemical compositions. The company envisions configurations ranging from LFP and sodium-ion to NMC, based on nickel, manganese, and cobalt, and even solid-state technologies. The Sagunto gigafactory is part of the network of large battery plants promoted by PowerCo. It is one of the three strategic facilities of the company, along with its first factory in Salzgitter, Germany, and another plant in St. Thomas, Canada. The goal is to develop an industry that the company considers 'solid, competitive and sustainable' in Europe. In the first phase of Sagunto, which includes two production blocks, 2,3 million euros have been allocated of investment. Currently, the plant has its own team of 414 people, which will be expanded as the start of production approaches. Opportunity for battery recycling The development of the gigafactory also opens the door to an associated recycling industry in the Valencian Community. Professor Antonio García, head of the battery group at the CMT Institute of the Polytechnic University of València (UPV)He pointed out that there is an opportunity to create a specific cell recycling activity in the territory and to integrate it into the value chain. García explained that recycling can be done directly. In that case, the cell components are separated and reused after treatment to assemble a new unit. Another option is so-called second use, which converts the batteries into energy storage devices for other applications, such as their integration into systems associated with photovoltaic panels. Electric vehicle penetration and infrastructure PowerCo's project aligns with the progressive increase of electric vehicles in the market. However, García has warned that one of the major challenges in the Valencian Community, in Spain, and in Europe as a whole is achieving a sufficient level of charging infrastructure to support mass electrification. For now, he noted, the percentage of electric vehicles in the total vehicle fleet remains low. Iberdrola has reported that it has over 2.200 public charging points in operation in the Valencian Community. Half of these are located in the province of Alicante, while more than 800 operate in the province of Valencia, and Castellón has already reached 200. The high-power charging points are managed by Iberdrola | bp pulse, the alliance created in December 2023 between Iberdrola and bp. bp has established itself as one of the leading operators of ultra-fast charging at service stations in Spain. Power grid and supply for industry The expansion of electric vehicles and new industrial projects, such as the Sagunto gigafactory and the Ford plant in Almussafes, demands a robust electricity grid. Expert Manuel Alcázar, from the Institute of Energy Engineering (IIE) at the UPV, has warned that the distribution network must adapt to increased industrial demand. According to Alcázar, it will be necessary reinforce lines, substations and transformer centers to connect new high-power consumers. However, he stressed that in the cases of Ford, which will create a joint venture with Geely in 2027 to manage the Almussafes plant and maximize its use at the lowest cost, and PowerCo, no significant grid connection problems are anticipated. The expert also warned that a potential closure of nuclear power plants would pose an additional risk. In his opinion, it would lead to a significant increase in energy prices, with direct consequences for the competitiveness and location of industrial activity. artigo.texto: For much of the past year, the debate among AI leaders has been whether to slow the pace of artificial-intelligence development. Last week, those outside of that select community finally had their say. Voters of all stripes chose to pull hard on the only lever available to them. Building data centers in the U.S. just became even more difficult, but perhaps as important, voters issued a challenge to the AI billionaires behind them. Victorious Democrats must now contend with the outcome while ensuring U.S. AI labs remain competitive on the global stage. In China, the bottleneck is in finding enough cutting-edge chips to fill its AI factories. In the U.S., the challenge is building enough factories to hold all of its chips. Which scarcity proves the greater handicap in the AI race remains to be seen.

artigo.texto: NGEL’s 10 GW/40 GWh tender divides the battery storage capacity into 7 blocks across 3 phases Suppliers will be required to provide comprehensive maintenance under a long-term service agreement The procurement call specifies LFP-based containerized battery systems with grid-forming PCS India’s NTPC Green Energy Limited (NGEL), the green energy arm of state-owned utility NTPC Limited, has invited bids for battery energy storage systems (BESS) with a stated project capacity of 10 GW/40 GWh. A tender of this magnitude signals that battery storage is now moving towards large-scale procurement by government entities. Recently, Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) issued a call for 4 GW/16 GWh standalone BESS (see SECI Invites Bids For 4 GW/16 GWh Standalone BESS). The tender covers the supply of lithium iron phosphate (LFP)-based battery containers and grid-forming power conversion systems (PCS). Winning bidders will also be responsible for supervising erection, installation, and commissioning at project sites, up to the PCS output terminals. The selected suppliers will be responsible for comprehensive service and maintenance for 15 years from the commissioning of each project under a long-term service agreement (LTSA). The international competitive bidding process covers a total deliverable capacity of 40.58 GWh, divided into seven blocks across three phases. Bidders can participate in one or more blocks and phases. However, they must quote for the full capacity of a selected block. The seven blocks range in capacity from 4.56 GWh to 6.8 GWh. Phase 1 comprises three blocks with a combined capacity of 17.42 GWh, while Phase 2 covers 4.56 GWh. The remaining 18.6 GWh is scheduled under Phase 3. It is open to experienced battery manufacturers as well as Indian companies meeting specified alternative qualification routes. These include Indian companies with a track record in BESS deployment, solar or wind power projects, or industrial and electrical substation projects, provided they associate with a qualified battery container manufacturer where required. For direct battery system suppliers, the technical qualification criteria include manufacturing and supplying at least 4,000 MWh of containerized battery systems through a maximum of 10 orders over the preceding three years. At least one order must cover 500 MWh. NGEL launched the tender on November 9, 2026. Bids must be submitted by December 8, 2026. India recently announced a new INR 14,500 crore viability gap funding (VGF) scheme to support 92 GWh of energy storage capacity, along with INR 2,814 crore to help develop domestic lithium and nickel processing capabilities (see India Steps Up Battery Localization With Two New Schemes).

artigo.texto: EXCLUSIVO: Jogo indie brasileiro aborda o trabalho do padre Julio Lancellotti, que voltou às redes sociais Datavault AI e Biochar Now combinam créditos de remoção de carbono segurados com tecnologia patenteada de tokenização Por Dino A Datavault AI Inc. ('Datavault' ou 'Empresa') (Nasdaq: DVLT) anunciou hoje uma colaboração estratégica global com a Biochar Now para expandir a distribuição de créditos de remoção de carbono verificados e segurados, por meio da tecnologia patenteada de tokenização da Datavault e de suas capacidades globais de marketing e distribuição. A parceria visa conectar os créditos de remoção de carbono da Biochar Now a uma rede mais ampla de compradores, ao mesmo tempo em que fortalece a transparência, a rastreabilidade e a responsabilidade nos mercados de carbono. Nos termos do acordo, a Datavault AI fornecerá acesso à sua tecnologia de tokenização de créditos de carbono, incluindo a patente norte-americana nº 12.443.977 e pedidos de patente relacionados que ainda estão em tramitação. A empresa também apoiará a geração de demanda global, o desenvolvimento de compradores, o marketing e a distribuição dos créditos de carbono elegíveis da Biochar Now, além de buscar a listagem desses ativos em plataformas de negociação parceiras, atuais e futuras. A Biochar Now remunerará a Datavault AI pelo uso de sua tecnologia e serviços; os termos financeiros específicos não foram divulgados. A colaboração une duas competências complementares: a remoção física de carbono, a verificação por terceiros e o programa de seguro de créditos de carbono da Biochar Now, somados à tecnologia de tokenização, troca de dados e capacidades de distribuição da Datavault AI. Juntas, as empresas pretendem tornar os créditos de remoção de carbono mais acessíveis aos compradores, reforçando, ao mesmo tempo, a documentação referente à sua autenticidade, titularidade e baixa aposentadoria do crédito. Os créditos elegíveis passam por verificação de terceiros e são rastreados no sistema proprietário 'Insured Carbon' (Carbono Segurado) da Biochar Now. O programa da Biochar Now, baseado em seguros, opera em substituição a um registro tradicional. Os créditos que atendem aos requisitos são segurados por meio de uma seguradora cativa pertencente à Biochar Now, estando sujeitos aos termos, limites e exclusões da apólice. 'Esta parceria reflete nosso foco em transformar a tecnologia e a propriedade intelectual da Datavault em oportunidades comerciais significativas', afirmou Teri Gallo, Diretora de Operações (COO) da Datavault. 'Estamos priorizando parcerias que potencializem nossas capacidades existentes, expandam nosso alcance de mercado e estabeleçam novos caminhos para o crescimento da receita.' 'Acreditamos que a mensagem dos eleitores é a de que o mundo não quer mais atrasos no enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. É necessária uma remoção real de carbono, uma responsabilidade efetiva e uma forma mais eficiente de conectar créditos de remoção de carbono confiáveis a compradores', disse James Gaspard, fundador e CEO da Biochar Now. 'Passamos anos desenvolvendo nossa tecnologia de produção patenteada, processos de verificação independentes e um programa de créditos de carbono segurados. A parceria com a Datavault nos permite gerar demanda por nossos créditos e criar um caminho para que os licenciados da nossa tecnologia alcancem compradores no mercado. Acreditamos que essa combinação pode ajudar a estabelecer um padrão mais elevado de qualidade e transparência para os créditos de carbono.' Criando um canal para os licenciados da Biochar Now O acordo foi estruturado para ir além da produção própria de remoção de carbono da Biochar Now. Por meio de uma estrutura de integração, projetos elegíveis operados por licenciados da tecnologia da Biochar Now poderão ser incorporados à parceria, desde que atendam aos requisitos de verificação, seguro e integração. Até a data deste comunicado, nenhum projeto de licenciados foi aceito, embora discussões estejam em andamento, com a Biochar Now encaminhando seus licenciados para a Datavault. Para a Biochar Now, essa estrutura cria uma oportunidade de ampliar o alcance de sua tecnologia patenteada, ao mesmo tempo em que auxilia os licenciados a levar créditos de carbono segurados e elegíveis a uma base global mais ampla de compradores. Conectando dados ambientais A parceria também contempla oportunidades para disponibilizar dados ambientais e de créditos de carbono, autorizados e de fonte primária da Biochar Now por meio do Information Data Exchange (IDE) da Datavault AI. A Biochar Now também terá acesso às funcionalidades DataValue e DataScore da Datavault para esses dados. A iniciativa visa conectar a remoção física de carbono a informações confiáveis e rastreáveis nos mercados de carbono e na produção de biochar. 'James e eu trabalhamos em estreita colaboração para concretizar este acordo; ele desenvolveu um modelo inovador para enfrentar os desafios do mercado de créditos de carbono', disse Teri Gallo, Diretora de Operações (COO) da Datavault. A Biochar Now combina a remoção física de carbono, verificação por terceiros e seguro para créditos que atendam aos requisitos. Nosso papel é facilitar o acesso a esses créditos para os compradores por meio da distribuição via plataforma, geração de demanda e marketing, ao mesmo tempo em que aplicamos nossa tecnologia para reforçar a transparência, a rastreabilidade e a proteção contra alegações fraudulentas ou duplicadas. Acreditamos que a combinação de remoção de carbono, proteção por seguro e responsabilidade digital pode tornar os créditos de carbono mais acessíveis aos compradores." Promovendo um mercado de carbono mais confiável e acessível A parceria entre a Biochar Now e a Datavault foi concebida para atender a ambos os lados do mercado de créditos de carbono: a necessidade de uma remoção de carbono documentada e a demanda por uma infraestrutura que conecte esses créditos aos compradores. The project uses solar trackers and TP580HG10NB bifacial modules, is expected to generate about 810 million units of electricity a year and mitigate around 103,820 tonnes of carbon emissions annually. With the commissioning, Tata Power Renewable Energy's utility-scale renewable portfolio has reached 12 GW, comprising about 7.2 GW operational, including 5.8 GW of solar and 1.3 GW of wind, another 4.9 GW at various stages of implementation and 0.7 GWh of battery energy storage. The company also disclosed 60 MWh of battery energy storage in operation across three locations in Mumbai at Mahalaxmi, Saki and Mankhurd, with a 200 MWh deployment across ten locations in the city approved by the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission in April 2025.

artigo.texto: Mills County to decide on adding data centers to zoning ordinance A zoning consultant spoke to the Mills County Planning and Zoning Commission on Tuesday night about what it may look like to add data centers to the county's ordinance. Ten counties in Iowa have data center ordinances. Mills County is not one of them. And as of right now, a data center is not coming to the county. Whether it's on the internet or in the headlines, data centers are a hot topic. "We have seen problems with communities having problems with the light pollution," said Mills County resident Jack Goodman. Like many others, Goodman has no interest in living near one. "We need to protect our environment here. We need to protect everything that is Mills County," he said. Goodman was one of many who spoke at the public meeting the Mills County Planning and Zoning Commission held Tuesday night. "Currently, there's (no) allowable land use in Mills County, so we would not be permitting any of those projects," Zoning consultant Matt Wyant said. And while there were some very strong opinions at the meeting, not everyone was against data centers as a whole. "There's enough data centers already operating. We should go study and visit some of those and see how they've worked at other places. I'm sure we can learn what not to do and what to do," said Christopher Weide. Wyant also says data centers can bring benefits to communities. "At the end of it, it's economic development. So you have growth in your county; there's going to be jobs included with that," Wyant said. He also said there are guardrails in place. "We are now under tight constraints from the state legislature when it comes to budget growth that we can have... so there may be the proper place for a data center to be located in a rural environment," Wyant said. As for Goodman, he's hopeful his voice will be heard. "These are good people. They live here, they care about our community, and I hope that they do listen to us residents," Goodman said. Over the next month, the planning and zoning commission will review materials that Wyant provided to them. The commission's next meeting is in December. artigo.texto: For most of the past decade, energy storage developers have handled battery procurement themselves, building that expertise in-house, project after project. That is no longer the only path into the market. Large loads, including data centers and other big electricity users, now contract directly with construction firms to build storage systems themselves, bypassing developers entirely, and some of those construction firms have never built one before. Those buyers face a choice: hire developers who already have the expertise, or build that expertise in-house under real time pressure. Either path carries the same exposure if buyers skip the fundamentals below. This shift poses the biggest risk facing storage buyers heading into 2027. Quality assurance, cell technology, sourcing rules, tariffs and financing standards are all shifting at once, often within the same procurement cycle. Buyers who succeed next year will fund quality assurance as a defined budget line item. Quality Assurance Cannot Stop at the Cell Cell and module manufacturing has matured, and automation keeps defect rates low—but not zero—at that stage. System integration has not kept pace. Wiring, thermal management and fire suppression still depend heavily on manual assembly. That dependency concentrates problems in exactly those areas. “System-level” also extends further than the container itself. It covers the network architecture tying a system together, the design of backup power for that network and how the system integrates its uninterruptible power supply. A factory audit limited to cell quality assurance never touches any of that. Intertek CEA’s factory audits (Figures 1, 2, and 3) back this up. System-level defects (Figure 4) accounted for 75% of quality findings across our 2025 inspections, compared with 15% at the cell level and 10% at the module level. Within system-level findings, 47% involved balance-of-system issues such as coolant leaks or malfunctioning alarms. Another 42% involved enclosure problems like water ingress, and 11% involved failed performance tests. A buyer who audits only the cell supplier checks the part of the system least likely to fail. Bigger Cells Carry Thinner Track Records That industry-wide track record took years to build. Cell formats keep growing, and the newest, largest cells have not had the same runway to earn it. A few years ago, 280 amp-hour cells set the standard. Then came 314 amp-hour cells. Manufacturers now ship cells rated at 500 amp-hours and beyond, with some exceeding 1,300. Larger cells need fewer connections, fewer weld points and less material. That appeal makes sense, but a bigger cell does not automatically perform better. A cell’s manufacturing maturity, R&D investment and third-party testing history matter more than its rated capacity. Buyers should ask how long a cell design has stayed in production and whether independent testing backs the manufacturer’s claims. Responsibility for thermal performance splits between two parties, and buyers should know which owns which piece. The cell manufacturer supplies the heat-load data the cell generates. The system integrator then designs the cooling system around that data, whether that means a larger cooling unit, cooling built into the module itself, or some combination. If the heat-load data is wrong—because of a mistake by the OEM or a miscommunication about how the battery will be used—the integrator will design an undersized cooling system. That gap typically will not surface until the system operates in the field. A separate risk exists even when the heat-load data is accurate: using the battery beyond its approved use case can overheat it, because the cooling system was sized only for that narrower, approved operating envelope. This shift also complicates projects built in phases if a different cell is used in later phases. Battery racks with different cell sizes balance differently. Mixing cell formats across a phased expansion can strain a system’s battery management and asset-tracking practices. Buyers augmenting existing systems need this built into the design from the start, not discovered or retrofitted afterward. Supply Chain Diversification Now Carries a Compliance Requirement Cell technology is one axis of risk. Where that cell comes from is another. Tariffs are pushing manufacturing away from single-country concentration, and that diversification now affects tax credit eligibility as well as sourcing strategy. Section 48E investment tax credit rules require a minimum share of a storage project’s cost to trace to non-prohibited-foreign-entity sources. That threshold sits at 55% for projects beginning construction in 2026 and rises five percentage points annually, reaching 75% by 2030. Falling short of that threshold disqualifies the credit outright. Full bill-of-materials traceability, down to sub-tier components, no longer counts as a nice-to-have. The compliance test requires it. Buyers should also build backup suppliers into procurement contracts before a primary source falls out of compliance, rather than after. Regulators Have Frozen New Inverter Authorizations Buyers relying on foreign-produced power inverters face a related problem. Regulators froze new equipment authorizations for foreign-produced power inverters with remote communication capability starting in late July, then narrowed the scope in August to utility-interactive inverters specifically, while exempting inverters that qualify for the Section 45X domestic manufacturing tax credit. That freeze still covers storage inverters as well as solar. Previously authorized models remain unaffected, but any project specifying a model that has not yet cleared authorization needs a contingency. The same discipline that protects against losing a cell supplier’s compliance status applies here: line up a backup before a project needs one, not after a shipment stalls. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Eleitor americano barra data centers e o Redata tenta atrair as obras para o Brasil, e a COP31 vai falar muito sobre isso Publicado 08/11/2026 • 19:44 | Atualizado há 11 horas Nano Banana 3 Placas contra data centers em rua residencial dos Estados Unidos, onde eleitores rejeitaram projetos em consultas locais na terça-feira (3) Duas fileiras de fardos de feno, a de cima soletrando "no data" e a de baixo "centers", com três deles pintados com a bandeira americana, ilustram a reportagem da agência Stateline sobre a terça-feira (3), dia em que eleitores de dez estados rejeitaram, em quase todas as consultas locais, a instalação de data centers perto de casa. O recado de beira de estrada interessa ao Brasil porque o Redata, regime de isenção de impostos para esses prédios de servidores sancionado em setembro, é a oferta nacional a quem ficou sem endereço, e interessa ainda mais na semana em que a COP31, a conferência do clima da ONU, abre em Antalya, na Turquia, na segunda-feira (9). O rastreador Data Centers on the Ballot contou 38 consultas em que prevaleceram restrições e uma única derrota, em Harwood, na Dakota do Norte. Na boca de urna da NBC, 56% dos eleitores disseram que a inteligência artificial e os data centers pesaram muito ou bastante no voto para o Congresso. O mercado entendeu o recado: as ações de Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet e Meta subiram na quarta-feira (4), mas o ganho foi em boa parte desfeito na quinta-feira (5), quando a Nvidia caiu 9,3% e a Dell, 15%. Na quarta-feira (4), no evento WSJ Tech, a presidente da Meta, Dina Powell McCormick, afirmou que será muito difícil construir novos data centers nos Estados Unidos e que todo hyperscaler, como se chamam as gigantes de nuvem, se pergunta se precisa construir fora do país. A consultoria STL Partners, citada pela CNBC, soma US$ 77 bilhões (R$ 413 bilhões, pelo câmbio de 29/10) em projetos americanos adiados ou cancelados por oposição local e US$ 42 bilhões na Europa. Carlos Barrera, presidente da Atlas Renewable Energy, disse à Fortune que a América Latina pode ser uma válvula de escape para a falta de capacidade nos Estados Unidos, o que dá ao Redata uma freguesia em potencial antes mesmo de ele funcionar. A presidência turca da COP31, com a Austrália à frente das negociações, publicou o Compromisso de Inteligência Artificial de Antalya, de adesão voluntária, que pede energia de baixa emissão nos data centers e relatórios sobre o impacto ambiental da IA, e que reconhece que o consumo de eletricidade dessas instalações subiu 50% em 2025. O Google já se mexeu: anunciou na quinta-feira (5) um data center em Wyoming que pagará por 100% da energia que consumir e será refrigerado a ar, para poupar a água local, segundo a Barron’s. Evan Tachovsky, do World Resources Institute, avaliou que o texto aponta a direção certa, mas não prevê responsabilização de empresas e governos. O Brasil chega a essa mesa com uma matriz de quase 87% de fontes renováveis e eletricidade que custa menos da metade da americana, com 60% dos dados do país processados no exterior, segundo o Ministério do Desenvolvimento. A lei 15.504 suspende por cinco anos tributos federais como PIS/Cofins e IPI sobre equipamentos, exige que 10% da capacidade atenda o mercado interno e que 2% do valor dos bens volte em pesquisa e desenvolvimento, mas o regime ainda não opera porque depende de decreto. A Fazenda resiste a incluir o gás natural entre as fontes aceitas, nove frentes parlamentares e 32 entidades pediram a Lula, em carta de outubro, que publique o texto com gás e deixe os pontos técnicos para depois, e o presidente já disse que quem vier terá de investir na construção de energia renovável. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, disse em outubro que o governo trabalha para concluir a regulamentação até o fim do ano. Quem espera o decreto já sentiu o custo, pois, segundo a Elea Data Centers, os investimentos em novos data centers caíram para cerca de R$ 2 bilhões em 2025, menos de um décimo da média anual de R$ 25 bilhões entre 2020 e 2024, e a empresa atribui a queda à demora do Redata. O diretor-geral do ONS, Marcio Rea, disse em setembro que os pedidos de conexão somam quase 20 gigawatts, cerca de 30% da energia do país, enquanto a projeção do próprio órgão para a carga dos data centers em 2030 é de 3,5 gigawatts, o que sugere que boa parte da fila é intenção e não obra. A obra mais adiantada, o Data Center Pecém, do TikTok, no Ceará, com 300 megawatts e R$ 50 bilhões na primeira etapa de um plano que chega a R$ 200 bilhões até 2036, mostra o obstáculo da licença. Em setembro, na quinta-feira (10), o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União foram à Justiça para impedir que ele opere antes de uma consulta ao povo indígena Anacé e de um estudo de impacto ambiental, porque, segundo a ação, foi enquadrado como empreendimento de baixo ou médio impacto numa região que depende de poços e tem histórico de escassez de água. A Omnia, responsável pelo projeto, afirma que o licenciamento segue o rito regular conduzido pela Semace, órgão ambiental do Ceará. A mesma ação cita 120 geradores a diesel, detalhe que entraria no relatório de impactos previsto no compromisso de Antalya, se o Brasil aderir. Leia todas as colunas de AI-451. artigo.texto: Google avança com centro de dados de 17 mil milhões A empresa prepara o seu primeiro centro de dados no Wyoming, mesmo depois de os eleitores norte-americanos terem rejeitado 40 das 41 propostas relacionadas com novas instalações. Neste artigo encontras: O Google vai avançar com um investimento de 17 mil milhões de dólares, cerca de 15,7 mil milhões de euros, numa conversão aproximada, para construir um centro de dados no Wyoming, nos Estados Unidos. A decisão surge numa altura em que a expansão da inteligência artificial enfrenta uma oposição crescente devido ao consumo de eletricidade, à utilização de água, ao ruído e ao impacto destas instalações nas comunidades locais. Google mantém plano apesar da reação política O projeto será desenvolvido em Laramie County com o apoio de quatro parceiros: Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power e Related Digital. A escolha do Wyoming é vista como favorável para a empresa. O estado apoiou maioritariamente Donald Trump nas eleições presidenciais de 2024, mas esse apoio político não elimina as preocupações das populações diretamente afetadas pelo centro de dados. Nas recentes eleições intercalares norte-americanas, candidatos críticos de novos centros de dados venceram disputas importantes no Texas e na Geórgia. No total, apenas uma das 41 medidas submetidas a votação acabou por beneficiar os interesses da indústria. O resultado mostra que a resistência aos centros de dados está a ganhar peso político nos Estados Unidos, precisamente quando as empresas tecnológicas tentam aumentar a capacidade necessária para serviços de inteligência artificial. Centro de dados terá capacidade energética de 702 MW O complexo deverá incluir uma instalação de células de combustível com 702 megawatts de capacidade. O sistema será fornecido pela Bloom Energy e contratado através da American Electric Power. As células vão produzir eletricidade a partir de gás natural. O projeto prevê ainda a captura e armazenamento de carbono, com o dióxido de carbono a ser transportado para armazenamento subterrâneo permanente num local operado pela Tallgrass Energy. O Google afirma que este acordo elevará para quase 1 gigawatt a sua capacidade contratada de captura de carbono nos Estados Unidos. A empresa também deverá recorrer a geradores a gás operados pela Tallgrass Energy e pela Black Hills Energy. Google promete reduzir consumo de água O consumo de água é uma das principais críticas dirigidas aos grandes centros de dados. Para limitar esse impacto, o Google planeia utilizar sistemas de arrefecimento a ar no Wyoming, em vez de soluções evaporativas que exigem grandes quantidades de água. A empresa comprometeu-se também a apoiar programas locais de reposição de recursos hídricos e garante que pagará integralmente a eletricidade utilizada pelo centro. Segundo o Google, a infraestrutura adicional diretamente causada pelo projeto será igualmente financiada pela empresa. A promessa pretende responder às preocupações sobre a pressão que o centro poderá colocar nas redes elétricas e nos serviços públicos. Impacto económico ainda gera dúvidas O Google estima que o investimento poderá gerar centenas de milhões de dólares em impostos sobre a propriedade para Laramie County e para o School District 1. A tecnológica promete ainda apoiar o ensino de ciência e tecnologia, a formação profissional, o empreendedorismo e as profissões técnicas no Wyoming. Apesar disso, os residentes querem respostas mais concretas sobre o número de empregos criados, os benefícios económicos permanentes e os efeitos acumulados de outros projetos semelhantes na região. Mais de 200 habitantes já participaram no processo de consulta. A construção do primeiro centro de dados do Google no Wyoming avança, mas terá de provar que os benefícios da inteligência artificial compensam os custos energéticos e ambientais para a comunidade. Fonte: TechRadar

artigo.texto: On November 5, 2026, OpenAI published a National Community Compact, a set of public promises for the data centers it plans to build across the United States. The timing and the vocabulary tell the story. As TechRadar reported, the company wants to build more AI infrastructure while Americans are increasingly saying no, and The Information has tracked the same tension. The OpenAI data center problem is no longer a zoning footnote. It is a political fight. The compact commits OpenAI to pay the full cost of electricity and grid infrastructure for campuses it owns and operates. It promises community input, published construction plans, no nondisclosure agreements with public officials at future sites, and a water plan plus a noise study for every location. It also introduces a new label. OpenAI now wants to call its data centers “compute campuses.” Is that enough? Our read is that the pledges are real and the money commitments matter, but a rename and a communications push cannot settle a dispute about power bills, water and who decides. Local resistance was already measurable before the announcement, as we covered when voters put the AI data center boom on notice. This analysis walks through what OpenAI confirmed, what it left open, what the market is pricing in and where the fight probably goes next. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the National Community Compact Actually Promises Start with what OpenAI itself confirmed. The National Community Compact dates to November 5, 2026, and it frames a set of commitments for data-center campuses that OpenAI owns and operates. That scope matters. A pledge covering owned-and-operated sites says nothing by itself about facilities run by partners or landlords, and a large share of AI capacity gets built through such arrangements. The confirmed list is short and concrete. OpenAI says it will pay the full cost of electricity and grid infrastructure for those campuses. It says it will solicit community input and publish construction plans. It says it will not use nondisclosure agreements with public officials for future sites. And it says each site will come with a water plan and a noise study. Each item answers a specific complaint that has dogged hyperscale builds. Residents have objected that power costs get shifted onto household bills. Councils have complained that deals were negotiated in secret. Neighbors have raised noise and water draw. By addressing all three, OpenAI shows it has read the objections correctly. The open question is whether a corporate pledge can substitute for binding local rules. The company also stated that it will keep pursuing U.S. data-center expansion despite the heightened political scrutiny. That sentence is the real context for everything else. The compact is not a retreat. It is a plan to keep building under new terms, which is why critics and supporters will both read it as a negotiating position rather than a final settlement. The Pay-Its-Own-Way Pledge on Power and Grid Costs The headline promise of the new OpenAI data center policy is financial. OpenAI says it will cover the full cost of electricity and grid infrastructure for the campuses it owns and operates. CNBC framed the move as a response to the election, reporting that OpenAI would pay for data center power after the vote showed public concern about AI. Why lead with power? Electricity is the most politically portable grievance. A voter who never sees a server rack still sees a utility bill. When a large new load connects to a regional grid, the fear is that upgrade costs spread across all ratepayers. A pledge to carry those costs directly tells that voter the bill will not land on their kitchen table. The pledge has limits that readers should keep in view. It applies to campuses OpenAI owns and operates. It is a company commitment, not a tariff approved by a state regulator. And the fact sheet from the announcement does not describe how compliance would be verified or what happens if a project is scaled back. Those details decide whether the promise protects ratepayers or merely reassures them. Still, the commitment is a meaningful concession. Paying the full grid bill raises OpenAI’s cost of building each campus, and that cost sits on top of an already heavy capital program. Few companies volunteer to raise their own cost of expansion unless they believe the political price of not doing so is higher. Why OpenAI Now Says Compute Campuses The second headline item is vocabulary. OpenAI plans to call its data centers “compute campuses.” An OpenAI spokesperson explained the choice this way: “Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we’re building for AI.” The word campus borrows from universities and corporate parks, places that suggest jobs, landscaping and civic presence. The phrase data center, by contrast, has picked up associations with humming warehouses, diesel backup generators and thin payrolls. Rebranding is an old public-relations move, and this one is easy to read. How the press received the rename Reception has been skeptical. Business Insider’s headline on the topic put it bluntly: good luck trying to rebrand data centers. The headline signals what many readers already suspect, that swapping one noun for another is the oldest trick in the brand playbook. The comparison is fair as far as it goes, but it also understates one point. Words do shape how a project gets described in a council meeting. If officials and local press adopt the new phrase, it changes the first impression of a proposal. The catch is that the first impression lasts only until the first question about power, water or noise. After that, the substance of the answers does the work. Altman, Brockman and Friar on the Backlash OpenAI’s senior executives have addressed the resistance directly, and their remarks reveal how the company diagnoses the problem.

artigo.texto: City of Eagan sues data center company Eagan Capital over "temporary chillers" The City of Eagan is suing Eagan Capital, a data center company in business along Pilot Knob Road, alleging they've been operating "temporary chillers" without proper permits. This comes months after Eagan Capital sued the city over a data center moratorium, calling it "unlawful." This latest lawsuit focuses on "chillers," which cool the data center and prevent overheating. During a city council meeting on Nov. 2, Mayor Mike Maguire announced the legal action and claimed the company was operating "without the required permits and approvals". The court document shows aerial pictures from 2025 showing no chillers on the property and from 2026 showing the chillers in place. In May, a representative for Eagan Capital told the council the company didn't think they needed a permit for installing the chillers but applied for one as soon as they were notified. The representative also said Eagan Capital designed a sound barrier around them. The city denied an interim use permit and later denied an application for a mechanical permit for permanent chillers in part because "data centers are not a permitted principal use in the Research and Development zoning district," the lawsuit explains. "There is a neighborhood just north of that facility in the Lawn Oak and Pilot Knob area that has waited a long time for this process to take place," said Maguire. "We appreciate the patience of that neighborhood." The city also alleges in the lawsuit, despite the sound barrier, that noise levels are beyond code. Denn lives across the street from the facility and hopes the court rules in favor of the city. He told WCCO the noise from the center is constant. "It's just a dull roar all the time, very uncomfortable," Denn said. "We have a patio that is down the hill from the chillers and they just make a lot of noise 24/7; [it] never goes away."

artigo.texto: Editor's note; With opinion polls registering widespread distrust by local residents in data centers, the foundation asked an expert to review best practices to both avoid the pitfalls and realize the opportunities. These comments were delivered at a recent colloquy in Roanoke. I want to start in New Carlisle, a town of about 1,800 people in St. Joseph County, which recently found itself negotiating with the largest company on earth — and doing so, at first, in secret. When Amazon's $11-billion data center campus came to New Carlisle, members of the Town Council signed nondisclosure agreements. The agreements barred them from disclosing what they called "nonpublic information relating to Amazon." The town's residents, in other words, were not permitted to know the terms of a deal that would reshape their water system, their roads, and their tax base for a generation — until the deal was essentially done. The reported terms, when they emerged, were these: a 10-year, 50-percent abatement on real property taxes, and an 85 percent exemption on enterprise technology equipment for 35 years. Thirty-five years. There are children in New Carlisle today who will be grandparents before that exemption expires. Alongside it, a $114 million water and sewer agreement and a $7 million contribution to roads and an interchange. Now, I am not here to tell you that New Carlisle got a bad deal. I am here to tell you something more unsettling: For a long time, nobody in a position to judge was allowed to know whether it was a good deal or a bad one. And that is the subject of my talk: the complete contract. I come at this as a Public Choice economist in the tradition of James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock. Public Choice begins with a simple, almost rude assumption: People in politics behave like people everywhere else. They pursue their own interests. A mayor wants to announce a jobs triumph before the next election. A company wants the lowest cost and the least scrutiny. A bureaucrat wants a bigger budget and a quieter life. None of them is paid, day to day, to maximize something called "the public interest." That sounds cynical. It is actually optimistic, because it tells us what to do. If you cannot rely on goodwill, you must rely on rules. And a contract between a municipality and a data center is the most important rule a town will write in a generation. A complete contract is one that answers, in advance, four questions: who pays for what, who bears the risk when things go wrong, how do we measure compliance and what happens at the end. An incomplete contract is not a neutral document. It is an invitation. Tullock taught us about rent-seeking: the art of getting rich not by producing something, but by persuading government to give you something. Every gap in a contract is a future rent-seeking opportunity, and the party with the lawyers will find it. So let us walk through the four places where these contracts are most often left incomplete — power, water, noise and land — and see what completeness looks like. First, power. A data center is, electrically speaking, a small city that never sleeps. A single large campus can draw several hundred megawatts — the equivalent of a few hundred thousand homes — and it wants that power on Day One. The question is who pays for the wires, the substations and the generation to serve it. Left vague, the answer defaults to: everybody else, through their electric bills. Ohio gave us the cautionary version of the good answer. Under a tariff approved by the state's utility commission, large data centers must commit to paying for at least 85% of their contracted load, for eight years, with a three-year exit fee and full reimbursement if they cancel a project after the utility has built for them. Think about what that does. It means a company cannot reserve a gigawatt of capacity, watch the utility build a substation, and then walk away leaving ratepayers holding the bill. The risk sits with the party that created it. Indiana produced a structurally elegant variant: in the AWS–NIPSCO arrangement, the data center load is served through a separate generation company, ring-fenced from the ordinary rate base, with roughly a billion dollars in bill credits over 15 years flowing back. The principle is what matters: the load that causes the cost is the load that pays for it. And Virginia gave us the warning about what happens when nobody writes the number down at all. The state's data center sales-tax exemption was projected, back in 2008, to cost about $1.5 million a year. By fiscal year 2025 it cost $1.9 billion. That is not a rounding error; that is fiscal illusion — a benefit that grows in the dark because no one put a cap, a sunset, or a review date in the original deal. A complete contract has an expiration date. An incomplete one has a surprise. Second, water. A data center that cools with water can drink like a town. And water contracts are where good intentions go to evaporate. Goodyear, Arizona, is my favorite story, because it is a story of a second chance. Microsoft originally promised to pretreat its cooling water on site and return roughly 5 million gallons a day to the city's surface-water plant, where it would become drinking water. It was a beautiful promise. It failed, almost immediately, over regulatory trouble. The city renegotiated: Microsoft would pay $36 million toward a $90 million expansion of the 157th Avenue treatment plant, post a $5 million assurance for the sewer line, fund a city coordinator, and — critically — air-cool its later buildings instead of evaporating water. Goodyear got real concessions. But notice the arithmetic: $36 million of a $90 million plant. The residents still carry the majority of a facility sized partly for Microsoft. Renegotiation after construction has begun is negotiation with one hand tied. artigo.texto: Standalone four-hour system adds 600 MWh of contracted storage capacity WASHINGTON, November 10, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Lydian Energy ("Lydian"), an Excelsior Energy Capital-backed developer, owner, and operator of energy infrastructure projects, today announced that its Faraday battery energy storage system (BESS) in Utah County, Utah, has reached commercial operation. The 150 MW/600 MWh project began operating on September 18, 2026. Faraday is contracted via a Schedule 34 contract in support of Meta's Eagle Mountain data center operations. A standalone, four-hour lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery system, Faraday BESS delivers 600 MWh of contracted storage capacity to PacifiCorp under a long-term energy storage agreement, supporting grid reliability in Utah. The project is situated on an approximately eight-acre site adjacent to the 525 MW Faraday solar facility and shares that facility's substation and interconnection, allowing Lydian to add storage using existing infrastructure. Lydian took Faraday BESS from mobilization to commercial operation in approximately 10 months. Faraday BESS is expected to pay approximately $9 million in property tax over the course of the project life. "Faraday BESS shows what a mature platform like Lydian's can deliver," said Kim Smith, Chief Operating Officer of Lydian. "Bringing it online on an extremely tight timeline took close coordination across our own team and our supply chain, construction, and financing partners, from acquisition through commissioning. When a wildfire threatened the area in June, our team put safety first while keeping the project on track. Faraday BESS enhances PacifiCorp's reliable, contracted capacity for Utah customers." "Storage is an essential part of a resilient grid. It gives utilities the flexibility to respond when conditions change, from extreme weather to unexpected outage," said Amanda Yang, Director of Clean and Renewable Energy at Meta. "Our investments in new energy resources are helping projects like Faraday BESS reach the grid, and that's a role we want to keep playing as we support our Eagle Mountain Data Center." "Excelsior backed Lydian because we recognized that a disciplined, execution-driven team could build a leading energy infrastructure platform," said Chris Moakley, Managing Partner at Excelsior Energy Capital and Chair of the Board of Lydian Energy. "As demand for reliable, domestically produced power continues to grow, storage projects like Faraday BESS will play a larger role in keeping the grid dependable."

artigo.texto: CATL is exploring lithium-air battery research that carries a theoretical range of up to 2,000 km (1,243 miles) on one charge, and Yahoo Autos reported the story under a headline that calls CATL the world’s biggest EV battery maker. The figure comes from a theoretical specific energy of roughly 3,500 Wh/kg. That is a lab-side projection, not a measurement from a finished battery pack. The distinction matters because the number travels faster than its caveats. Reporting describes the CATL lithium-air battery as exploratory, experimental research. No tested 1,243-mile vehicle exists. No announced production battery exists either, and the available coverage identifies no confirmed CATL quote, no price, no vehicle partner and no production schedule. This piece looks at the story from the hardware side. We already published an earlier breakdown of the CATL lithium-air cell, so here we focus on how the 3,500 Wh/kg figure turns into a range claim, which engineering steps stand between theory and a car, and what buyers, suppliers and investors can reasonably do with the news today, November 09, 2026. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The CATL Lithium-Air Battery Claim in Plain Terms Strip away the headlines and the story has four moving parts. First, CATL is the battery maker at the center of it. Second, the chemistry is lithium-air, sometimes called air-breathing, which uses oxygen from the surrounding air as a reactant. Third, the theoretical specific energy sits at about 3,500 to 3,505 Wh/kg. Fourth, that figure converts into a theoretical range of up to 2,000 km, or 1,243 miles. What the story does not contain is just as important. Nobody has shown a car driving 1,243 miles on this chemistry. Nobody has published a complete automotive pack specification. CATL has not named a product, and the phrase lithium-air battery describes a chemistry family, not an officially announced CATL product line. Readers who skim only the number could walk away believing a showroom model is coming. Readers who read the verbs get a different picture. Outlets use words like explores and theoretical, and they frame the work as research. That is the honest reading, and it is the one this article follows. The takeaway for anyone tracking battery hardware: treat the 2,000 km figure as a ceiling that physics might allow under ideal conditions. It is not a forecast of what drivers will see. What 3,500 Wh/kg Means and Where It Stops Specific energy measures how much energy a battery stores per kilogram of mass. A higher number means a lighter battery for the same range, or a longer range for the same weight. The 3,500 Wh/kg figure attached to the CATL lithium-air battery means one kilogram of the theoretical active material could, in principle, deliver 3.5 kWh. That is simple arithmetic from the reported figure. The word theoretical carries most of the weight in that sentence. Theoretical specific energy usually describes the chemistry on paper, before engineers add the housing, the electrolyte, the current collectors, the cooling, the safety systems and the air-handling hardware a real pack requires. Every one of those parts adds mass, and every gram added lowers the number a driver actually benefits from. The table below separates what the reporting states from what it leaves open. The range depends on battery mass, usable energy, vehicle efficiency, durability and recharge performance. Change any one of those inputs and the 1,243-mile figure moves. A heavier car, a colder day or a faster highway speed would all cut it, and none of those variables appears in the reporting. How a Lithium-Air Cell Differs From Lithium-Ion A conventional lithium-ion cell stores everything it needs inside a sealed package. The lithium-bearing anode and cathode materials both live in the cell, and the cell carries the mass of both. Charging and discharging shuttles lithium ions between them. That design has powered phones, laptops and nearly every electric car on sale. A lithium-air cell swaps the heavy cathode for an air electrode. Instead of hauling all of its reactants, the cell draws oxygen from the surrounding air. Dropping the stored cathode material is where the large theoretical gain comes from. The cost is complexity, because the cell now depends on an air electrode and an oxygen-management system rather than a sealed block of solid materials. Reports say the theoretical energy density would sit several times above the figures commonly associated with emerging solid-state batteries. Those reports also warn against treating it as a verified cell specification. For context on where solid-state work stands in the lab, see our coverage of a solid-state coating that kept 82.3% capacity after 300 cycles. That result shows how slowly even the more mature next-generation chemistry moves from a paper to a product. Think of it as two different engineering problems. Lithium-ion is a packaging and materials-refinement problem. Lithium-air is a systems problem, because the battery must breathe, filter and protect itself while the car keeps moving. Why Outlets Framed the Same Story Four Different Ways Coverage of the CATL lithium-air battery split along a clear line. Some outlets led with the big number. Others led with the caveat. Reading them side by side shows how much a headline can change what a reader believes happened. Yahoo Autos framed the story as an exploration of a theoretical 1,243-mile range, which matches the fact pattern. EVXL went further in the cautious direction, with a headline arguing that CATL’s lithium-air research is not a 1,243-mile EV battery. ShiftDelete used a similar tone, describing the 2,000 km figure as one that remains theoretical. Interesting Engineering ran a more aggressive headline. artigo.texto: In 2020, Virginia passed the Clean Energy Act to combat the disproportionate amount of carbon pollution the state's energy sector produces: an estimated third of Virginia's total carbon pollution. The main goal of the Act was to see energy reach net-zero emissions by 2050. Dominion Energy, one of Virginia's primary electric utility companies, has undertaken renewable projects in accordance with the Act, including the country’s largest offshore wind farm. Coincidentally, Dominion has not stopped investing in fossil fuels, as shown by its development of a gas plant in Chesterfield County and ongoing plans to develop one in Cumberland County. In a quote shared with WHRO’s Mallory Noe-Payne, Jeremy Slayton, a Dominion spokesperson, explained how “[O]n the hottest and coldest days of the year, when people are running their air conditioning, they’re running their heater, and that demand goes up and up and up.” Slayton also added, “if we can’t meet that demand, that means there will be blackouts”. This rhetoric not only misplaces blame on the average homeowner but also establishes the basis for Dominion’s plans to develop up to eight new gas plants within the next decade. These will be known as peaker plants, which are used selectively when energy demand is exhausted within Dominion’s pre-established grid. There is a caveat to the purpose of peaker plants, however, and that is their main purpose as energy sources for data centers. On Aug. 27, Prince Edward County hosted a public meeting with AVAIO Digital, a company planning to develop a data center on the 280 acres of Hit Park, located just three miles from Longwood’s campus. AVAIO is in the early stages of planning but has already established data centers in Appomattox and Caroline counties, as well as Arkansas, California and Mississippi. As listed on their website, the company is committed to cleaner, more sustainable data centers. Instead of using an influx of water to cool equipment, they use a closed-loop system wherein the water does not evaporate and is not discharged. The center is expected to require only 30,000 gallons of water per day compared to the average data center’s three to five million gallons per day, according to the Virginia Conservation Network. The largest disadvantage to such a system is that it will also need an estimated 300 megawatts of energy, which would require further development to strengthen the site’s connection to Dominion’s power grid, as Hit Park currently lacks necessary power access. AVAIO addressed the upfront costs associated with data centers, informing the community that they would pay all of the expected monetary costs of development as well as minimize the effects on the environment. The company detailed plans to uplift local conservation efforts and offset their carbon footprint to reach net zero. They attempted to make their plans palatable by noting data centers have been around since streaming and the internet but failed to reflect on the recent acceleration in data center development being due to advancements in generative AI. AVAIO also assured attendees they would be paying more than their fair share to Dominion but again failed to address the stress data centers place on energy grids—stress that will lead to the average person paying the price. More information about AVAIO’s plans is organized on Prince Edward County’s FAQ webpage.

artigo.texto: Data centers go 0-for-21 on the ballot By Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal Ohio voters sharply rejected data centers in this year’s election. Around Ohio, 18 communities voted on whether to curb or ban data center developments. In all 18 communities, voters decided that, yes, that would be a good idea. In most, the results were resounding — like Harlem Globetrotters vs. Washington Generals resounding. City leaders in Wilmington, the county seat of Clinton County, asked voters to rezone four parcels to allow data center development. Roughly 80 percent of voters rejected all four. In the Lake County Village of Perry, more than 87 percent of voters backed an initiative requiring data centers that accept tax incentives to take out a bond, operating kind of like an insurance policy, to back up their promises of local tax revenue. Voters in Piqua prohibited data centers within city limits by a 2-to-1 margin and didn’t stop there. They also recalled three city commissioners — including the mayor and vice-mayor — for approving a Meta data center in November last year. From Conneaut in far northeastern Ashtabula County to Trenton in Southwestern Butler County, nine communities passed initiatives modeled on the statewide data center moratorium Conserve Ohio organizers are trying to put on the ballot in 2027. That initiative would amend the state constitution to prohibit any data center drawing more than 25 megawatts a month. In a press release, Conserve Ohio congratulated communities who voted against data center development, and warned elected officials that “You cannot look away now.” “The above election results demonstrate that when communities have a say regarding the construction of a hyperscale data center in their local area, they overwhelmingly say no,” the group wrote. “Your oath is invoked. Stop the self-dealing, corporate fealty, and greed. Represent and serve the people who elected you.” Conserve Ohio urged Ohio citizens to push state lawmakers to pass a 12-month moratorium on any data center development in Ohio during the lame duck session between now and the end of the year. Upper Sandusky Angela Huffman is a sixth-generation farmer in northwest Ohio, and she heads up the national watchdog group Farm Action, which focuses on corporate consolidation in the food and agriculture sector. She explained data centers came onto their radar about a year ago, because of concerns about their impact on farmland. “And then lo and behold,” Huffman said, “I read in the newspaper back in June of this year that a data center, a nearly $1 billion data center, was proposed here right outside Upper Sandusky, which is about 10 miles from my farm.” Upper Sandusky is the county seat of Wyandot County, but it’s a small city with a population of less than 7,000 residents. In June, the company Smartland Energy proposed building a 150-megawatt natural gas plant on a 46-acre parcel. The idea was to build the powerplant first and then sell the power directly to a data center client on an adjacent 100-acre parcel. Smartland emphasized it “would not build, own or run” the data center, and that the eventual end-user would still need city approval and hadn’t been pre-selected. Huffman and other organizers began collecting signatures to oppose the project, and unlike many petition drives, she said their job was relatively easy. “Really our challenge was just finding ways to get in front of people,” she said. “They already knew about the issue. They were already concerned about data centers. So fortunately, we didn’t have to first educate or raise awareness and educate about what the problem was. They already knew. We just had to get their names on these petitions in time.” Huffman noted construction of a Louis Dreyfus Company soybean processing plant was already stretching local infrastructure, and a data center adding to the strain was a daunting prospect. When Upper Sandusky voters went into the booth last Tuesday, nearly 77 percent of them approved a city charter amendment banning data centers within city limits. Looking forward In a Facebook post last Thursday, Smartland Energy seemingly acknowledged its project doesn’t have a future in Upper Sandusky. The company thanked the community and reiterated its belief in their proposal. “At the same time,” it stated, “we value and respect the democratic process and the outcome of the charter amendment vote.” “Our team will take some time to come together, reflect on this process, and discuss the outcome,” Smartland added. “If there is ever anything further to share, this will be the first place we communicate it.” The drubbing data centers took in Ohio last Tuesday didn’t stop at the state line. Around the country, 47 initiatives were on the ballot to restrict data centers. Election officials are still counting votes for two of those contests, but according to the website Data Centers on the Ballot, 44 jurisdictions rejected data centers and just one welcomed them – that one was in Harwood, North Dakota (population 940). The day after the election, data center industry group Infrastructure for America released what it called a “good actor pledge”. It’s members, including Compass, Digital Realty, QTS and Vantage, committed to operate transparently, invest in their communities, and not be a drain on local power and water infrastructure. Ohio Capital Journal sent an email to the Data Center Coalition seeking comment about Ohio’s results, but got no response. To Huffman, the election results underscore the importance of communities having a voice in major developments like data centers. She stressed that she doesn’t oppose AI or development generally, but the way the industry has been operating feels “predatory.” Between tax abatements for developers, and the lack of local protections or input, “it’s really been tilted in favor of big tech,” she said, “at the expense of Ohio.” “I think that’s where a lot of the pushback started,” Huffman added. “If this had been more of a le

artigo.texto: Leilão de baterias atrai mais de 6 mil projetos e movimenta setor elétrico BNDES destinará R$ 30 bilhões a empreendimentos com componentes nacionais, em certame que marca a entrada do armazenamento em larga escala no sistema brasileiro Atualizado Pela primeira vez, o sistema elétrico brasileiro está em via de investir bilhões de reais em tecnologias para armazenamento de energia. Com isso, se insere na tendência global. Apenas no segmento de baterias, em 2025 a capacidade instalada no mundo atingiu 108 GW (gigawatts), volume 40% superior ao de 2024 e 11 vezes maior que o de 2021, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, na sigla em inglês). O movimento foi impulsionado pela China, Estados Unidos e Europa. “Baterias são a tecnologia que mais cresce no mundo”, diz Donato Filho, CEO da consultoria Volt Robotics. O Brasil, devido à matriz majoritariamente hidráulica, também conta com as hidrelétricas reversíveis (com dois reservatórios). No entanto, esse mercado ainda é incipiente. Somente no fim de setembro, portaria do Ministério de Minas e Energia as incluiu nos leilões para contratação de reserva de capacidade a serem realizados em 2027, 2028 e 2029. As baterias, no entanto, já têm leilão marcado para o início de dezembro de 2026. Segundo o Plano Decenal de Expansão da Energia (PDE) 2036, elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e em consulta pública até o fechamento desta edição, ao final deste período o país deverá contar com 9,2 GW em capacidade de armazenamento. Deste total, 7,2 GW em baterias e 2 GW em hidrelétricas reversíveis. A função do armazenamento é acumular energia elétrica em momentos em que há excesso de produção para utilizá-la em períodos de escassez. Como registra o PDE 2035, “as tecnologias de armazenamento constituem um recurso estratégico para o provimento de capacidade e para a ampliação da flexibilidade operativa do sistema”. Para o período, o PDE estima uma expansão de 100 GW na capacidade instalada do país, totalizando 359 GW. Essa expansão viria da construção de usinas convencionais e de soluções de armazenamento. A diferença entre as hidrelétricas reversíveis e sistemas de baterias, também chamados de BESS (batery energy storage system), é que as primeiras demandam de sete a oito anos para entrar em operação, só podem ser erguidas em locais onde há reservatórios, são mais lentas para ligar e desligar, podem acumular energia por muitas horas e demoram também horas para descarregar essa mesma energia. Além disso, contribuem para o abastecimento em períodos de estiagem. Já os BESS são mais ágeis: podem ser erguidos em um a dois anos, acumulam energia em poucas horas e a descarregam em períodos de tempo mais curtos, como quatro a oito horas. Além de beneficiar a potência, tornam a operação do sistema mais flexível. Por isso, os BESS são particularmente adequados a parques eólicos e solares, que contam com excesso de produção quando o vento sopra e o sol está a pino, mas sofrem com a escassez de insumo nos outros períodos. Isso provoca dois problemas: excesso ou escassez de energia. As duas situações são perniciosas, pois podem provocar apagões de energia e problemas de variação de tensão e de frequência. Isso obriga o Operador Nacional do Sistema (ONS) a determinar o corte da produção das renováveis quando há excesso (curtailment) ou aumentar a produção das térmicas e das hidrelétricas quando há escassez, a um preço maior. A questão é acentuada pelo comportamento do consumo: menor durante o dia, quando a produção é farta, e maior no início da noite, quando há escassez. “O problema é que esses cortes não são ressarcidos. Nós temos contratos, não recebemos o que não geramos e, às vezes, somos até multados”, diz Rodrigo Sauaia, CEO da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), referindo-se ao curtailment. “Temos que colocar o consumidor como protagonista e induzi-lo a mudar o horário de carga”, afirma Luiz Eduardo Barata Ferreira, presidente da Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia (FNCE). A expansão dos BESS tem sido beneficiada pela queda nos preços, que a partir de 2010 recuaram de mais de US$ 1.000/kWh (kilowatt/hora) para uma média global de US$ 108/kWh, conta Sauaia. Por isso, eles já são utilizados em projetos de média tensão, como indústrias, comércios e hospitais em substituição aos geradores convencionais. “Estamos vivendo uma onda que chega a 1 GW em projetos de menor porte e carga de média tensão”, diz Markus Vlasits, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). A exceção é a subestação de Registro (SP), da ISA Energia Brasil, primeiro BESS de grande porte no Brasil, inaugurado em 2022, com 90 MW de potência e 60 MWh de energia. Agora, o setor elétrico prepara-se para introduzir os BESS no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Pela primeira vez na história, em dezembro eles serão objeto de leilão específico organizado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e pela Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) para reserva de capacidade (LRCAP - Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade) na forma de potência. Isto significa que os projetos vencedores serão acoplados a subestações ligadas às linhas de transmissão de alta tensão do SIN, aumentando a potência e dotando o sistema de maior flexibilidade operacional. O leilão foi dividido em duas etapas. A primeira, no dia 2 de dezembro, para projetos com componentes nacionais. A segunda, no dia 4 de dezembro, para equipamentos nacionais e estrangeiros. Os primeiros contarão com financiamento de R$ 30 bilhões do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), via Finame. Para os demais, o financiamento ainda está indefinido. Mas, como diz Donato Filho, “no momento há muitos recursos externos para projetos ligados à energia renovável”. “O acesso ao financiamento do Finame, associado a critérios de conteúdo local, pode fazer do leilão de baterias também um instrumento de política industrial. artigo.texto: Entering Q4, the sodium-ion battery industry chain has reached the most critical delivery verification period of the year. SMM data shows that in October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY, while hard carbon anode production pulled back slightly by 4% MoM but surged 186% YoY—the high YoY growth rates confirm that the industry remains on a zero-to-one volume expansion trajectory, but the mediocre MoM performance reveals another reality: the pace of capacity ramp-up has generally lagged market expectations, with a clear time lag between order growth and actual delivery. On the pricing side, NFPP cathode quotes diverged, precursors hovered near cost lines, and iron phosphate supply-demand tension stayed high. The two-way squeeze of cost pressure and order losses below cost is reshaping the industry's competitive landscape. 1. Cathode Materials: Production Up 3% MoM, Capacity Release Falls Short of Expectations, Orders Accelerating Toward Top-Tier Players 1. Supply side: Ramp-up hindered, delivery capability supplemented by "outsourcing + toll processing" In October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY. The overall market operated steadily, but capacity release falling short of expectations was the most prominent contradiction this month. Although 10 kt-class new lines gradually entered commissioning, compounded by line switchovers and equipment changes, actual output still failed to meet the original ramp-up targets. Some enterprises improved delivery capability through outsourced processing and other means; once downstream processes are fully connected after mid-November, monthly capacity is expected to reach the kt level. 2. Demand side: Clear divergence, growth concentrated in small power and energy storage The demand side showed significant divergence: in October, some enterprises shipped only in the hundreds of mt, while November orders have already increased to several hundred mt and will be delivered in batches, with growth mainly coming from small power and some energy storage orders. However, it is worth noting that if lithium carbonate prices continue to weaken, December market conditions may fall short of November—some clients' new orders have already shown losses below cost, and downstream willingness to take orders has clearly declined. From the perspective of enterprise operations, the trend of orders concentrating toward top-tier players is becoming increasingly evident: industry leaders have orders on hand exceeding 1 kt, while their in-house monthly capacity is only several hundred mt and cannot fully cover demand, requiring a dual-line approach of "in-house production + toll processing" to ensure delivery. 3. Price side: NFPP quotes diverge, with cost pressure centered on iron phosphate October NFPP quotes remained relatively stable, with mainstream transaction prices concentrated at 24,000-27,000 yuan/mt. In the short term, there is clearly no room for price increases, nor for price cuts, and prices have entered a stalemate range. Cost-side pressure remains concentrated in the iron phosphate segment. Although phosphoric acid prices have pulled back from 12,000 yuan/mt to around 9,000 yuan/mt, iron phosphate prices remain at approximately 16,000 yuan/mt due to tight supply and demand, significantly above the reasonable range of 12,000-13,000 yuan/mt. Persistently high raw material costs are pushing downstream material enterprises to accelerate self-built iron phosphate production lines or form joint ventures with phosphorus chemical companies, advancing industry chain integration. In the precursor segment, mainstream transaction prices are 19,000-20,000 yuan/mt, with large orders as low as 17,000-18,000 yuan/mt, already essentially at cost levels. Enterprises generally adopt tiered pricing to secure major clients. 4. Competitive landscape: Tier differentiation accelerates, market exit approaches From the competitive landscape perspective, tier differentiation within the industry is accelerating. Top-tier cathode enterprises with planned capacity of 10 kt-level projects are coming online successively, steadily expanding their leading edge. Small and mid-sized startups are under pressure due to tightening financing environments and delayed production line construction, with some enterprises' publicly claimed capacity still lagging behind actual production. Another noteworthy signal: NFPP precursor enterprises generally show low willingness to cross over into cathode production, mainly due to concerns about direct competition with downstream clients—this has objectively maintained the existing competitive boundaries in the cathode segment. Looking ahead: Q4 cathode shipments may show a "high-then-low" trend, with prices remaining weak under the dual squeeze of cost support and inverted order losses. Top-tier players with scale capacity, integrated costs, and quality client structures will benefit first, and industry consolidation and concentration are expected to accelerate. artigo.texto: [SMM ESS Flash] A Revolta da Alemanha comissiona a primeira bateria doméstica de íons de sódio de 10 kWh, alocação de 2026 esgotada A startup Revolta, sediada em Frankfurt, instalou e comissionou a primeira bateria doméstica de íons de sódio de 10 kWh da Alemanha em uma propriedade perto de Aschaffenburg, um sistema com tensão nominal de 450 V composto por cinco módulos de 2 kWh combinados com um inversor SMA. Cada módulo pesa 18,7 kg, com classificação de proteção IP64 e densidade de energia de 107 Wh/kg e 141 Wh/l, carrega e descarrega a 0,4 C, o que corresponde a cerca de 2,5 horas, e a configuração de 10 kWh entrega uma potência máxima de cerca de 4 kW; a propriedade também abriga cerca de 20 kW de energia solar fotovoltaica e uma pequena central hidrelétrica convertida de um antigo moinho. A empresa enquadra a instalação como o início de seu lançamento comercial, permanecendo ainda em estágio piloto, com mais sistemas piloto em locais selecionados de clientes na Alemanha planejados para as próximas semanas e medidores gratuitos fornecidos para coletar dados operacionais; os módulos são listados a EUR 599 cada e o conjunto de cinco módulos de 10 kWh a EUR 2.995, com a alocação de 2026 esgotada e reservas abertas para 2027. Potência nominal, vida útil de ciclo e números de eficiência não foram divulgados, e os primeiros dados operacionais reais de armazenamento doméstico de íons de sódio na Alemanha fornecerão amostras de validação para desempenho em baixas temperaturas e segurança.

artigo.texto: Anthropic compra equipamentos para geração de energia para data centers de IA em negócio de US$ 3,4 bi, diz jornal Segundo o Financial Times, trata-se da maior aquisição individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração de energia já realizada por um laboratório de inteligência artificial A Anthropic concordou em pagar US$ 3,4 bilhões por geradores movidos a gás natural destinados a data centers, informou o Financial Times. Segundo o jornal, trata-se da maior aquisição individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração de energia já realizada por um laboratório de inteligência artificial. De acordo com a publicação, no fim de setembro a empresa adquiriu compromissos de fornecimento de 1,7 gigawatt em geradores de alta potência da OnePWR Solutions, fornecedora de equipamentos sediada em San Antonio, no Texas, sem, contudo, comprar a própria companhia. Inicialmente, a Anthropic planejava comprar energia da OnePWR, mas posteriormente decidiu assumir os pedidos de geradores da Caterpillar feitos pela fornecedora, acrescentou o jornal. A aquisição é o mais recente sinal de que os laboratórios de IA estão avançando cada vez mais sobre o setor de energia e eliminando intermediários na corrida para garantir equipamentos de geração de eletricidade, cuja oferta é escassa. - Em meio a dúvidas sobre IA: Vendedor misterioso coloca US$ 500 milhões em dívidas de data centers à venda O negócio também reflete o esforço da Anthropic para obter maior controle sobre a infraestrutura que sustenta suas operações de inteligência artificial, depois de depender fortemente de parceiros para garantir energia, chips, centros de dados e terrenos. Na segunda-feira, a empresa afirmou que pretende gastar mais de US$ 895 bilhões nos próximos anos, sendo a maior parte desse montante destinada a custos de capacidade computacional e infraestrutura. A OnePWR e a Anthropic se recusaram a comentar o assunto ao Financial Times e não responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de manifestação da Bloomberg.
