artigo.texto: AMD pronta para expansão de data centers na América Latina Região representa menos de 2% do mercado mundial de servidores, mas quase 8% dos gastos com nuvem, segundo executivo da fabricante. A AMD prevê uma expansão dos investimentos em data centers na América Latina, impulsionada pela demanda por IA e pela necessidade de manter determinadas cargas de trabalho em infraestrutura local. Segundo Nicolás Cánovas, líder da fabricante para a região, a América Latina representa menos de 2% do mercado mundial de servidores, mas responde por quase 8% dos gastos globais com serviços de nuvem. Os indicadores foram apresentados durante o AMD Partner Summit 2026, realizado entre 9 e 11 de novembro, na região de São Paulo. O encontro reúne representantes de cerca de 70 empresas parceiras e marca os 30 anos de atuação da companhia no Brasil. Para Cánovas, a diferença entre os dois indicadores mostra que a região expandiu sua capacidade computacional principalmente pela contratação de serviços de nuvem, sem desenvolver infraestrutura local na mesma proporção. “A América Latina, além de continuar crescendo como uma região focada em nuvem, terá que desenvolver seus próprios data centers para hospedar as cargas de trabalho e as informações sensíveis”, afirmou. Segundo o executivo, a tendência é de maior utilização de arquiteturas híbridas, que combinam serviços de nuvem e servidores próprios conforme os requisitos de cada aplicação. Os percentuais apresentados por Cánovas não vieram acompanhados do detalhamento das bases estatísticas utilizadas. Atualmente, a AMD registra crescimento das vendas para infraestrutura de processamento. No terceiro trimestre de 2026, a receita global da fabricante alcançou US$ 13,4 bilhões, alta anual de 45%. O segmento de data centers respondeu por US$ 8,5 bilhões, crescimento de 97% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025, impulsionado pelas vendas de processadores EPYC e aceleradores Instinct. Energia e Redata entram na avaliação dos investimentos A disponibilidade de energia, os custos operacionais e as condições regulatórias estão entre os fatores apontados pela AMD para a expansão da infraestrutura computacional na América Latina. Cánovas afirmou que as restrições de espaço físico e de acesso à energia em mercados como Estados Unidos e Europa contribuem para ampliar o interesse pela região. O executivo destacou a importância de políticas públicas, marcos regulatórios e oferta de energia limpa para viabilizar novos projetos. Questionado sobre o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), Sergio Santos, diretor-geral da AMD Brasil, manifestou apoio a iniciativas de incentivo à produção local e à atração de tecnologia. “Qualquer programa do governo que incentive a produção local e traga mais tecnologia para o país é sempre bem-vindo”, declarou. Santos também apontou a composição da matriz energética brasileira como um fator considerado nas decisões de investimento e afirmou esperar que projetos em discussão comecem a se materializar em 2027. AMD quadruplica eficiência energética em IA A necessidade de ampliar o processamento sem aumentar proporcionalmente o consumo de eletricidade também orienta o desenvolvimento de produtos da AMD. Em comunicado divulgado em agosto, a fabricante informou ter alcançado, até meados de 2026, uma melhora estimada de quatro vezes na eficiência energética de seus sistemas de IA em relação a 2024. O resultado superou a meta intermediária de três vezes estabelecida para o período. A companhia trabalha com o objetivo de ampliar em 20 vezes a eficiência energética de sistemas de IA em nível de rack até 2030, considerando cargas de treinamento e inferência e utilizando 2024 como referência. Nas projeções apresentadas pela AMD, dois racks de sua futura arquitetura poderão oferecer capacidade computacional equivalente à de 570 racks de referência de 2024. Para a carga de treinamento utilizada no estudo, a fabricante estima uma redução de 20 vezes no consumo elétrico durante o uso e de até 28 vezes na intensidade de carbono. A estratégia envolve mudanças nos processadores, nas memórias, nas interconexões, no software e na arquitetura dos sistemas. Durante o Partner Summit, Santos relacionou a evolução dos processadores à possibilidade de modernizar instalações existentes e liberar capacidade elétrica para novas aplicações de IA. Segundo o executivo, dependendo da carga de trabalho, as soluções da AMD permitem consolidar até 11 servidores antigos em um único equipamento. No ano anterior, a relação apresentada pela fabricante era de sete para um. “Dependendo da carga de trabalho utilizada por uma empresa ou por um hyperescaler, podemos fazer uma consolidação de até 11 para um”, afirmou. Santos explicou que o aumento da densidade de processamento pode reduzir a quantidade de equipamentos necessários, a ocupação física e os custos de refrigeração. A companhia também considera métricas como desempenho por watt, desempenho por dólar e custos de licenciamento nas avaliações de infraestrutura. AMD amplia participação e rede de canais no Brasil Além dos investimentos em infraestrutura, a AMD está expandindo sua atuação no mercado corporativo brasileiro, especialmente entre pequenas e médias empresas. Segundo Santos, a companhia contratou mais de 12 profissionais para reforçar sua equipe de canais e ampliou seu programa de parceiros comerciais, buscando maior integração com as redes de distribuição de fabricantes como HP, Dell e Lenovo. A estratégia está associada à adoção de IA pelas empresas, incluindo aplicações executadas em servidores e computadores com processamento local. “A IA vai muito além do nosso chip. Ela faz parte do ecossistema”, afirmou Santos. O executivo destacou que a comercialização dessas soluções exige que revendedores e integradores ofereçam serviços de implementação, segurança e suporte técnico, além do fornecimento de equipamentos. “Se você vende apenas a caixa, qualquer cliente pode procurar na internet e comprar mais

artigo.texto: Engine manufacturer Cummins (NYSE:CMI) fell short of the market's revenue expectations in Q3 2026, but sales rose 13.5% year on year to $9.44 billion. Its non-GAAP profit of $8.25 per share was 0.7% above analysts' consensus estimates. Is now the time to buy CMI? Find out in our full research report (it's free). Cummins (CMI) Q3 2026 highlights: - Revenue $9.44 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $9.96 billion (13.5% year-on-year growth, 5.2% miss) - Adjusted EPS $8.25 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $8.20 (0.7% beat) - Adjusted EBITDA $1.82 billion vs analyst estimates of $1.86 billion (19.3% margin, 2.4% miss) - Operating margin 15.3%, up from 10.2% in the same quarter last year - Market capitalization $61.75 billion StockStory's take Cummins delivered third quarter results that disappointed Wall Street's revenue expectations, triggering a negative market reaction. Management attributed the shortfall to a combination of ongoing supply chain constraints in its Power Systems segment and weaker-than-anticipated demand for North American pickup truck engines. CEO Jennifer Rumsey highlighted that robust demand for data center power solutions and heavy-duty truck engines partially offset these headwinds, stating, "order intake in the third quarter exceeded what we thought it would be," but bottlenecks limited shipments, especially in Power Systems and Distribution. Looking forward, management's guidance is built on continued strength in power generation—especially driven by data center customers in North America, China, and Asia-Pacific. The company expects to recover most delayed shipments in the next quarter and is expanding manufacturing capacity for future demand. However, CEO Jennifer Rumsey cautioned that uncertainty around EPA regulations and elevated diesel prices could moderate pickup truck engine sales, while CFO Mark Smith flagged that supply chain and regulatory factors will impact the pace of new product transitions. Key insights from management's remarks Management pointed to strong data center-related orders, supply chain challenges, and evolving regulatory dynamics as key themes shaping the quarter's performance and their updated outlook. - Data center power demand: Cummins saw exceptionally strong demand for power generation equipment from data center operators, with multi-year orders extending into 2028. This trend is global, with accelerated growth in China and the Asia-Pacific region, not just North America. - Supply chain bottlenecks: Delays from a key supplier in Power Systems constrained shipments, resulting in lower-than-anticipated revenues in that segment and Distribution. Management expects these issues to be largely resolved in the next quarter, allowing delayed deliveries to catch up. - North American truck uncertainty: Weaker-than-expected demand for pickup truck engines was attributed to elevated diesel prices and interest rates, as well as regulatory uncertainty surrounding upcoming EPA emissions rules. Customers are delaying some purchases as they await clarity on Non-Conformance Penalties (NCPs) and the phased transition to 2027-compliant products. - Product launches and feedback: Cummins completed the "Forever Rising Tour," showcasing its upcoming X15, X10, and natural gas X15N engines to customers. Feedback was positive, particularly regarding reliability and drivability, supporting confidence in the 2027 product launch schedule. - Investment in capacity and new technologies: The company opened a new manufacturing facility for cooling systems and is expanding production to meet rising demand, especially for smaller generator sets. This includes investment in battery energy storage systems (BESS) for data centers, marking Cummins' largest deployment to date.

artigo.texto: MEMPHIS, TN — Elon Musk says two additional data centers tied to SpaceXAI’s expanding artificial intelligence operation in the Memphis area are expected to begin operating before the end of the year. The announcement comes as the rapid growth of the facilities faces increasing scrutiny from residents and city officials concerned about the effects of large-scale data center development. The two sites, known as Gun Range and Spam, are part of the company’s Colossus 2 computing complex. Musk said Gun Range is expected to become operational by the end of November, with Spam scheduled to follow in December. Those dates are projections from Musk and have not been independently confirmed. The names reflect the properties’ previous uses. Gun Range was formerly a police and fire training facility, while Spam was a warehouse that stored products made by Hormel Foods. Both properties are in Southaven, Mississippi, across the state line from Memphis. Together, the two facilities are expected to house approximately 420,000 Nvidia GB300 graphics processing units. Musk indicated that Gun Range would contain about 220,000 chips configured to train artificial intelligence models. Spam is expected to house approximately 200,000 chips designed to handle inference, the process of responding to requests from users and running already-trained AI systems. The new buildings will expand Colossus 2, which already includes facilities known as Macrohard, Macroharder and Minihard. Musk has said the broader Colossus 2 complex is expected to contain approximately 1.2 million Nvidia Blackwell chips by the end of 2026. The company uses the computing infrastructure to support its Grok artificial intelligence platform. The expansion follows the launch of the original Colossus supercomputer in 2024 at a former Electrolux manufacturing facility in South Memphis. The company later expanded its operations into the Whitehaven area and Southaven. Musk has also said he has been spending several days a week in Memphis overseeing construction. The projects have drawn opposition from nearby residents who have raised concerns about pollution, noise, electricity demand and water use. In April, the NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against xAI and subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that the companies operated methane gas turbines without required permits at the Southaven site. A federal judge recently rejected the companies’ request to dismiss the lawsuit, allowing the case to proceed. Meanwhile, the Memphis City Council approved a 135-day pause on new data center permitting after rejecting a proposed yearlong moratorium. The measure is intended to give city officials time to develop land-use and siting rules addressing neighborhood protections, infrastructure and environmental concerns. It does not stop existing facilities from operating or automatically halt projects with protected approvals. The latest expansion highlights the challenge facing communities across the Mid-South as technology companies move quickly to build the infrastructure needed for artificial intelligence while residents and local governments seek greater oversight of the projects. Há dois anos, escrevi nesta coluna sobre a pegada de carbono das baterias de íons de lítio. O título Pegada de carbono das baterias – parte 1: do 8 ao 80 era uma provocação para mostrar como diferentes estudos podiam chegar a resultados muito diferentes para uma mesma tecnologia, dependendo das premissas adotadas e, principalmente, dos dados utilizados. Naquele momento, um dos pontos que mais me chamou a atenção estava no grafite utilizado nas baterias. Quem acompanha as discussões sobre veículos elétricos provavelmente já se acostumou a ouvir que a bateria é o grande vilão ambiental do carro elétrico. A afirmação é simplista e há uma questão interessante por trás dela. Quanto realmente sabemos sobre as emissões associadas à fabricação das baterias? A resposta depende muito da qualidade dos inventários utilizados nas avaliações de ciclo de vida. Em 2024, esta coluna já havia destacado diferenças expressivas nos dados disponíveis para a produção de grafite. Um dos problemas estava relacionado à produção de grafite sintético em rotas industriais amplamente utilizadas na China, entre elas o processo Acheson. A produção exige temperaturas muito elevadas e grande consumo de eletricidade. Além disso, os cadinhos de grafite utilizados no processo sofrem desgaste e precisam ser substituídos. Quando esse material não é corretamente contabilizado, uma parcela relevante das emissões simplesmente desaparece do cálculo. Naquele artigo, mostrei que algumas bases de dados utilizadas em avaliações de ciclo de vida apresentavam valores de emissões para o grafite muito inferiores aos encontrados quando o processo industrial era representado de maneira mais completa. Era uma questão metodológica, mas com consequências práticas. Se o inventário de um dos principais materiais da bateria está errado, a pegada de carbono atribuída à bateria também estará. Na época, era razoável tratar o assunto como uma hipótese que precisava de melhores dados. Agora, esses dados começam a surgir e permitem avaliar com mais segurança o peso do grafite na pegada de carbono das baterias. Um estudo publicado por pesquisadores alemães no Journal of Energy Storage (PUSHPENDRA et al, 2026) utilizou dados industriais primários, revisitando justamente o problema do grafite. O resultado é relevante porque mostra que a escolha do inventário utilizado na avaliação pode alterar significativamente a pegada de carbono atribuída à bateria. Em uma célula NMC622 analisada pelos pesquisadores, composta por níquel, manganês e cobalto na proporção 6:2:2, a pegada de carbono passou de aproximadamente 58 para 93 kgCO₂e/kWh quando os dados de grafite foram atualizados com dados industriais primários. Um aumento de cerca de 60%. Embora o estudo tenha sido conduzido com uma célula do tipo níquel-manganês-cobalto, suas conclusões são relevantes também para as baterias LFP (lítio-ferro-fosfato), hoje amplamente utilizadas em veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento estacionário. Isso porque ambas as tecnologias utilizam predominantemente grafite no ânodo. Em outras palavras, mesmo quando se eliminam metais críticos como níquel e cobalto do cátodo, a origem e o processo produtivo do grafite continuam exercendo influência decisiva sobre a pegada de carbono da bateria. Observe ainda que não se trata de uma diferença marginal. É o tipo de alteração que pode mudar a conclusão de uma análise de ciclo de vida. O resultado também não apareceu do nada. Um estudo publicado por CARRÈRE et al. (2024) no mesmo periódico já havia identificado forte subestimação nos dados disponíveis para o grafite sintético de grau-bateria. Outros trabalhos publicados nos últimos anos chegaram a conclusões semelhantes, apontando que os inventários utilizados em muitas avaliações ainda dependem de dados antigos, secundários ou que não representam adequadamente as rotas industriais atuais. O que isso tudo significa? Frequentemente, vemos números sobre “uma bateria emite determinada quantidade de CO₂ por kWh”, “um veículo elétrico compensa sua fabricação depois de tantos quilômetros” ou “determinado modelo apresenta determinada vantagem sobre um veículo a combustão”. Nada disso é tão simples. O grafite é um bom exemplo de como uma variável aparentemente secundária pode alterar o resultado final. Por isso, quando se pretende calcular a pegada de carbono de uma bateria, escolher um número médio da literatura e simplesmente multiplicá-lo pela capacidade em kWh pode produzir uma falsa sensação de precisão. Uma bateria de 50 kWh não carrega consigo uma etiqueta dizendo quantas toneladas de CO₂ foram emitidas para fabricá-la. Esse número precisa ser construído a partir da cadeia de produção. Se queremos comparar tecnologias de propulsão, precisamos comparar sistemas completos. O veículo elétrico tem emissões associadas à mineração, ao processamento de materiais, à fabricação da bateria, à geração de eletricidade e ao uso. O veículo a combustão tem sua própria cadeia de petróleo, refino, distribuição e combustão. Quando utiliza biocombustíveis, entram também na conta as emissões e remoções associadas à produção de biomassa, ao processamento industrial e à logística envolvida. Híbridos acrescentam uma combinação adicional de componentes, combustíveis e fontes de energia. A pergunta relevante não é qual tecnologia parece mais limpa. É qual delas apresenta menor impacto quando colocamos todas as etapas na conta. E, para responder, precisamos de bons dados. Meu artigo de 2024 não pretendia dizer que todas as baterias tinham uma determinada pegada de carbono. A questão era justamente a incerteza. artigo.texto: BMW Group has contracted Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution (LGES) in the US as additional cell suppliers for its Gen6 high-voltage batteries. Following the nominations, the car maker will receive European-produced cells from CATL, EVE Energy, and Samsung SDI, whilst LGES will deliver cells within the US. The appointments follow the company's "local for local" principle, whereby components are acquired close to vehicle assembly locations wherever possible. Both manufacturers will supply BMW Group from their established regional plants beginning in the late 2020s. BMW stated that targeted localisation across Europe, Asia, and North America reduces transit distances and bolsters supply security, while a globally diversified network supports flexibility and resilience. Assembly of the Gen6 high-voltage batteries will take place at five newly constructed facilities adjacent to vehicle plants in Debrecen, Hungary; Shenyang, China; Woodruff, US; San Luis Potosí, Mexico; and Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Lower Bavaria, Germany. Series production of the batteries commenced in Shenyang last month. Following Debrecen and Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Shenyang is the third location in the new global production network for Gen6 battery technology. BMW added that localising industrial value creation remains highly complex, particularly for cell production, requiring heavy investment and supply arrangements with global technology leaders willing to set up operations locally. It added that fostering regional battery ecosystems over the long term depends on feasible political regulations and attractive local conditions for the necessary industrialisation periods. The group also retains internal development, production, and recycling capabilities at three Bavarian competence centres. The Battery Cell Competence Centre in Munich investigates new cell technologies, whereas the Cell Manufacturing Competence Centre in Parsdorf tests near-series cells and evaluates high-quality, resource-efficient production. In Salching, German circular economy service provider Encory will construct and operate the Cell Recycling Competence Centre, recovering raw materials using BMW's direct recycling method to reintegrate into production. BMW purchasing and supplier network management board member Nicolai Martin said: "We aim to ensure our products' global competitiveness and to be successful in different markets. To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets. Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US." "BMW Group adds Samsung SDI and LGES as battery suppliers" was originally created and published by Just Auto, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: Microsoft President Brad Smith talks data centers, Millionaires Tax WASHINGTON STATE — Microsoft President Brad Smith acknowledged tech companies will need to brace for further legislation to limit data centers, amid a growing wave of pushback against the facilities. In his first comments since Election Day, Smith addressed the fact that 40 of 41 local ballot measures across the country were approved to limit data centers. “We are going to see more legislation. We're going to see state legislation across the country. We're going to see federal legislation across the country. I don't know how many of those bills will pass, but I think at some level, the best thing for our industry to recognize is usually to give people confidence that things will be done in a responsible way,” Smith said in an interview on the Microsoft campus in Redmond on Monday morning. “Everyone who wants to build a data center has to do it responsibly. I think that's the message.” Smith says the company’s internal polling suggests 15% of the public wants to build data centers, another 15% don’t want them built at all, and 70% say they want them built responsibly. Smith points to the story in Quincy, Washington, where Microsoft broke ground on a new data center and tax revenue in Grant County skyrocketed, leading to the construction of a new school, hospital, police station and fire station. “The poverty rate’s been cut in half. The property taxes that people pay have fallen, but property tax revenue has grown 12-fold, basically because of data centers,” he said. “When we started 20 years ago, Quincy, Washington, had one traffic light. Now it has two. There are ways to do this.” Smith and Microsoft also dipped their toes into the state elections, funding a political action committee called “Washington Needs to Compete." Smith had sounded alarm bells prior to the vote, suggesting a payroll tax in the future would be like “waving a flag” asking businesses to move jobs out of state. The PAC aired ads during Seahawks games but stopped short of taking a position on the Millionaires Tax, and Gov. Bob Ferguson was reportedly upset about it all. On Monday, Smith said, “The public has voted, it's offered its point of view, and that tax has been upheld, and barring a change from the Supreme Court, we should all assume it's going to become part of Washington state law as we go forward.” “I think everybody in the state worries about affordability. We do. Our employees do. Everybody does. We also need to recognize that when taxes rise on businesses, businesses inevitably pass those costs on to consumers, and so ongoing tax increases are making the state less affordable,” he added. As for his relationship with Ferguson, Smith said, “We have long worked with Bob Ferguson. We work with him as attorney general. We work with him as governor. I think the state is fortunate to have him as a governor. I look forward to working to support him. I especially look forward to working with him and our leaders in Olympia. Let's go forward in a way that really focuses on budget stability, affordability for our people, the creation of new businesses and jobs for our economy.” Ferguson, along with Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, has indicated the payroll tax is off the table with the approval of the Millionaires Tax.

artigo.texto: O Acre deu um importante passo em direção à certificação internacional de seus créditos de carbono. Na terça-feira, 10, em Antalya, na Turquia, a governadora Mailza Assis participou de uma reunião com a ART Trees, entidade responsável pela validação de projetos de carbono, para discutir o progresso da auditoria necessária ao reconhecimento dos créditos jurisdicionais do estado. A reunião ocorreu durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31). O encontro é um desdobramento das articulações realizadas em junho, durante a Semana de Ação Climática em Londres, onde Mailza se encontrou com Mary Grady, presidente da ART Trees. Também participaram da reunião Neide de Lima, presidente do Instituto de Mudanças Climáticas e Regulação de Serviços Ambientais (IMC), Victor Hugo Rondon, consultor internacional de mercados de carbono, Madson Cameli, chefe de gabinete, e Lúcia Madrid, diretora associada da ART. O principal objetivo da reunião foi atualizar o status da auditoria e alinhar procedimentos para avançar na certificação. O reconhecimento internacional permitirá ao Acre registrar créditos de carbono jurisdicionais, facilitando futuras negociações no mercado internacional. Mailza expressou sua gratidão pela disponibilidade da ART e reiterou o compromisso do governo em concluir o processo, afirmando que “estamos colocando um grande esforço, por meio do IMC, para concluir esse processo, que será muito importante para o desenvolvimento do Acre.” A auditoria está sendo conduzida por uma empresa independente que segue os critérios do padrão internacional ART Trees, que estabelece normas para a contabilização e verificação de reduções de emissões decorrentes do desmatamento e degradação florestal. Neide Lima destacou a importância de cumprir todos os requisitos previstos para a conclusão satisfatória da etapa, com o Acre atualmente na oitava de 11 etapas do processo de certificação. Entre os próximos passos, estão a finalização das verificações técnicas e a submissão dos resultados ao conselho deliberativo da ART. Uma nova fase da auditoria está prevista para o primeiro trimestre de 2027, quando auditores visitarão comunidades no Acre para realizar verificações. Neide também ressaltou a dimensão social do processo, enfatizando que os recursos obtidos com a comercialização dos créditos devem contribuir para o desenvolvimento das comunidades locais. Victor Hugo Rondon sublinhou a necessidade de assegurar que todas as exigências internacionais sejam cumpridas, levando em conta as prioridades sociais e ambientais do governo acreano. A Companhia de Desenvolvimento de Serviços Ambientais (CDSA) também será envolvida nas próximas etapas, especialmente nas estratégias relacionadas às negociações dos créditos certificados. O governo do Acre espera que a certificação abra oportunidades para atrair investimentos em agricultura familiar, extrativismo sustentável e iniciativas de preservação ambiental. A certificação envolve uma avaliação independente para assegurar que os resultados ambientais atendam aos requisitos estabelecidos, com cada crédito de carbono representando uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e) cuja emissão foi reduzida ou removida. O IMC continua promovendo agendas estratégicas durante a COP31, defendendo a valorização das comunidades e apresentando projetos de desenvolvimento sustentável para ampliar o diálogo com governos, investidores e instituições internacionais. artigo.texto: WASHINGTON – Microsoft and other companies and trade groups have pressed the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump to halt plans to bar imports from China of a key component used in artificial intelligence data centers, three people familiar with the situation said. In August, the Trump administration was reported to be seeking a ban on U.S. imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within data centers. The concern is that they could be used by Beijing to steal data, install malware or disrupt service at U.S. data centers. Microsoft has 35 data centers under construction in the U.S. and another 134 planned, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company that tracks data center development. It is one of a group of companies and trade groups making the case to the Trump administration that such a ban could irreparably damage the U.S. edge over China in the AI race by further slowing the data center rollout, the sources said.

artigo.texto: Normally this newsletter is dedicated to local San Diego issues. But allow me, for a moment, to fixate on members of Congress. They’re actually doing something – though how good it will be, on the whole, is up for debate. A contingent of Democrats and Republicans just wrote the country’s biggest set of permitting reforms in years, and they’re trying to pass it before Democrats take over, following the “blue wave” midterm elections. The reforms would accelerate permitting for energy and transmission projects while also limiting environmental review, and put the onus on data center developers to pay for all their own energy costs. The Senate got enough votes Monday to limit debate on the so-called BAAJA or Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and move it forward for a final vote. The bill could have big implications for the data center proposed on U.S. Navy land near downtown San Diego. This 400-plus-page law would force data centers, rather than taxpayers, to pay for all their costs – both the power and the upgrades to the local power grid to keep it running. While California lawmakers passed similar laws on data centers this last session, they don’t apply to San Diego’s proposed project. The state doesn’t have jurisdiction over land owned by the U.S. Navy. For that reason, among others, San Diego Rep. Scott Peters, along with clean energy proponents and developers and labor leaders, urged fellow Democrats to support the bill generated by the currently Republican-controlled Congress. “Democrats say they want to lower utility costs and combat climate change. Research shows the bipartisan permitting package would do both,” Peters told Politico recently. If you’d like to go deeper, David Roberts, a clean energy journalist and host of the Volts podcast, spent two hours unpacking its main reforms, chief among them allowing both electric transmission lines (the biggest powerlines carrying energy across state lines) and natural gas pipelines to be built much faster. Electricity demand by Americans had been stagnant until the recent business of building data centers to fuel artificial intelligence coupled with electrification of cars and buildings exploded. But it takes 10 to 15 years to actually build a new transmission line, the highways of the power grid that can carry power from state to state. Whole regions of the country are beginning to hit their limit in terms of how much power they can get to customers during heat waves, for example. The culprit? Many backers of the bill say it’s long, arduous permitting processes making it difficult to expand energy grid infrastructure. Without transmission lines, it’s a lot harder to bring new clean energy projects online, dispatch their power to places that need it and really transition the grid off of fossil fuels. The kicker is, BAAJA also makes it easier to build things like natural gas pipelines which are not good for the climate. (That’s because natural gas is a fossil fuel burning as almost pure methane, a huge climate heater-upper). But that’s how lawmakers were able to make this a bipartisan deal. In any good compromise, neither side is happy. The bet, as Roberts put it, is that both energy sources (Republicans favoring fossil fuels and Democrats favoring clean energy) would be on more equal footing to compete for energy proliferation. To speed up their permitting, both would get to bypass, in large part, the National Environmental Protection Act, which requires an analysis of a project’s environmental impacts. (Projects would still be subject to laws like the Clean Water Act, however.) Environmental groups like the Center for Biological Diversity have decried this law for that reason. Daniel Palken, Roberts’ guest who works for the oil-exec-owned Arnold Ventures, says that if this bill passes, it would allow a fair amount more drilling for oil and gas especially on federal land. The Rhodium Group, an independent research think tank based in New York City, did a bunch of modeling on what the outcome of the bill reforms might be – and the conclusion was to take some bad with the good. The researchers’ paper said that the bill would allow for up to 249 gigawatts of clean resources to be built through 2040 – a 50 percent increase to average U.S. electricity demand now. Liquified natural gas production, mainly to be exported outside the U.S., would increase by up to 15 percent. They estimate that tradeoff, in the best case scenario for the climate, would reduce economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 149 million metric tons by 2040. That’s like taking 32 million cars off the road for one year. But it’s not as astounding as it sounds. Humanity as a whole needs to reduce greenhouse gas emission by 1,350 billion metric tons to have a 50 percent shot at reducing global warming by 2 degrees Celsius – a level of warming the United Nations predicts will still cause near total destruction of the world’s coral reefs and intensify drought, sea level rise and extreme heat on millions. The U.S. is the biggest emitter, especially if you include our offshoring of much of our manufacturing demand. But it’s a start, I guess. In Other News - Rep. The two-way squeeze of cost pressure and order losses below cost is reshaping the industry's competitive landscape. 1. Persistently high raw material costs are pushing downstream material enterprises to accelerate self-built iron phosphate production lines or form joint ventures with phosphorus chemical companies, advancing industry chain integration. artigo.texto: Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure. Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure. President Donald Trump said Monday he is fully behind bipartisan legislation that could lower Americans' electricity bills by requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs of expanding the nation's electrical grid. "We are behind it 100%," Trump told reporters when asked about the legislation. Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act as electricity demand grows rapidly across the country, driven in part by the explosion of artificial intelligence and data centers. The legislation would speed up federal approval of energy infrastructure projects while requiring large data centers to contribute more toward the costs of expanding the electrical grid. An analysis by Grid Strategies estimates that, under the legislation, data centers would pay an additional $35 billion toward transmission infrastructure over the next decade, compared with what they would otherwise pay under current policies. A separate analysis from Rhodium Group estimates the bill could save the average American household between $50 and $78 a year on electricity by 2040, compared with what households would otherwise pay without the legislation. Both analyses examined an earlier version of the bill, before lawmakers released amendments Saturday. The savings are projections, not guaranteed reductions from today's electricity bills. "This bill has specific provisions related to data centers where they pay more. In fact, they pay more than their fair share. Intentionally to enable them to pay for more of the grid and then other rate payers, you and me. And homes and businesses. We would all pay relatively less," said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies. How the legislation would work Energy experts say the country faces an infrastructure bottleneck as electricity demand grows. Building the power plants and transmission lines needed to keep up can take years, with federal permitting among the obstacles. The legislation aims to speed up that process by setting stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and making it easier to approve new transmission lines. It would also give states additional options to require data centers to pay more than the cost of serving them and use the additional revenue to reduce electricity costs for other customers. States including Virginia, Ohio and Florida have already approved special electricity rate structures designed to make large power users shoulder more of the infrastructure costs associated with serving them. Why the bill faces opposition The legislation would also make it easier to approve fossil fuel projects, drawing opposition from environmental groups. Critics warn it could weaken federal safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge new projects. The bill was negotiated by four senators: Republicans Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah, and Democrats Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four lawmakers released amendments Saturday aimed at addressing some of those concerns, including strengthening consultation with Native American tribes and giving states more opportunities to weigh in on proposed projects. Major industry groups representing renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies support the legislation. The bill also includes a provision that Whitehouse says would prevent the Trump administration from continuing to pay offshore wind developers to abandon their projects. The administration has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements, according to the Associated Press. Despite endorsing the legislation, Trump continued criticizing wind energy Monday, telling reporters that "wind turbines are a major loser." Will Congress pass it? The bill's future remains uncertain despite bipartisan support and the president's endorsement. Some Democrats helped write the legislation and want it passed now, while others, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, are pushing for changes. Jeffries' office said last week that the legislation "falls short" in several areas. The debate comes just days after Democrats won control of Congress, giving them more leverage to negotiate energy legislation when the new Congress takes office in January. The Senate scheduled a procedural vote for Monday evening on whether to advance a legislative vehicle for the permitting proposal. The vote requires 60 senators to move forward and would not constitute final passage of the legislation.

artigo.texto: Letter: Hearing on Proposed Data Center Ban Nov. 12 I am writing to make residents aware of two important opportunities to make their voice heard in the next week. Ban Data Centers – Hearing on Thursday, November 12th at 7:00 p.m. Zoom Link At our Town Council meeting on Oct 5, we voted to refer a zoning bylaw amendment to the Planning Board and the Council’s Community Resources Committee that would ban data centers in all zones in Amherst. This zoning amendment had a total of nine council sponsors (over half of the council, myself included) because we recognize the harmful impacts of data centers on host communities. Please see this document compiled by Amherst for the People for more information, including information specifically relevant to the Amherst context. At the Planning Board/CRC hearing held on Oct. 22, members of the Planning Board and CRC discussed the possibility of recommending that this amendment be converted into a moratorium on data centers, which would allow the town time to study and create regulations around data centers. If you are against data centers in Amherst, please attend the next hearing at the Planning Board/CRC to let them know that we want a ban only. Here are some key points: - We don’t need to waste town staff time on studying how to regulate data centers, because we don’t want them in our community. - The measure that was brought to the Planning Board and CRC to study was a ban – and it was supported by over half of the council because the people we represent also don’t want data centers in our community. FY28 Budget Hearing – Monday, Nov. 16, 6:30 p.m. (Town Hall or Zoom) On Monday, November 16th, the Town Council will hold a public forum on the budget for next year. It is essential that residents weigh in on their priorities now, because the Finance Committee is working on budget guidelines that the Council will vote on in early December. The Finance Committee and Town Manager always increase each department’s budget by the same percentage, which has led to major budget cuts in our schools and the chronic underfunding of CRESS, our civilian responders – among other issues. Please attend the budget hearing to make your voice heard. Equality is not the same as equity. The finance committee and the council should carefully consider the needs of each department when creating the budget guidelines. It’s really important to understand that if residents don’t speak out and impact the budget guidelines now, it will be very hard if not impossible to make any changes next year – even if the percent increase voted for the schools and other key departments lead to cuts. If you have any questions or concerns, please feel free to contact me directly at canomartina@amherstma.gov Amber Cano-Martin Amber Cano-Martin is an Amherst Town Councilor representing District 2.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA PSI detalha a receita de seus data centers por trás de suas ambições de pesquisa em IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A TechCrunch informou em 10 de novembro de 2026 que a Physical Superintelligence obtém sua receita atual usando suas ferramentas para otimizar data centers, enquanto busca construir, no longo prazo, um negócio baseado na descoberta de fenômenos físicos com auxílio de IA. O CEO Matt Pines descreveu o objetivo como transformar avanços da física teórica em tecnologias concretas. Os data centers são o primeiro campo de provas dessa abordagem, onde os sistemas de pesquisa em IA da PSI, que ela chama de físicos virtuais, podem atuar em sistemas físicos reais sujeitos a restrições operacionais mensuráveis. A PSI é uma empresa de benefício público, com segurança, verificação, desenvolvimento responsável e amplo benefício público estabelecidos em seu estatuto. Em sua página da empresa, informa ter mais de 25 pesquisadores e engenheiros e ter captado mais de US$ 58 milhões, em uma rodada liderada pela Breakthrough Energy Ventures. Data centers como campo de provas comercial O trabalho atual de otimização simula calor, energia, água e som, relacionando o desempenho das instalações e seu impacto nas comunidades à física de cada local. Em sua página sobre sua visão, a PSI afirma que constrói modelos de alta fidelidade de instalações em operação para que os físicos virtuais possam examinar o sistema por completo, identificar restrições ocultas e testar intervenções. Os resultados pretendidos incluem maior densidade computacional, uso mais eficiente da energia, melhor gestão térmica e maior eficiência de capital. As campanhas comerciais também fornecem subsídios para a pesquisa. Segundo a PSI, instalações em operação impõem restrições que não seriam propostas em simulações, e cada campanha treina os físicos virtuais usados nas campanhas seguintes. Assim, o negócio de data centers cumpre duas funções: gerar receita no presente e fornecer restrições práticas que ajudam a aprimorar o sistema de pesquisa. Um sistema de pesquisa baseado em verificação Pines descreveu um sistema de pesquisa eficaz como uma combinação de estruturas de software em torno de modelos, ferramentas, sistemas de memória e infraestrutura de simulação, que permite explorar um problema em amplitude e profundidade, considerando uma ampla variedade de alternativas. A PSI formaliza esse processo como uma Campanha Autônoma, um esforço contínuo que vai da definição do problema à formulação de hipóteses, verificação, experimentação, engenharia e implantação. Cada campanha tem marcos mensuráveis, etapas rigorosas de verificação e um caminho para a aplicação, enquanto os pesquisadores humanos escolhem as missões e os critérios de sucesso. A arquitetura separa a geração de candidatos da verificação. Entre as verificações estão as leis de conservação, a simetria, a consistência dimensional, a demonstração formal, a simulação, os gêmeos digitais — contrapartes virtuais de sistemas físicos — e as medições físicas. A PSI afirma que os verificadores que certificam um resultado também podem se tornar funções de recompensa, ou sinais de treinamento, para os físicos virtuais usados posteriormente, vinculando diretamente a avaliação ao aprimoramento do sistema. O anúncio de pesquisa de 6 de novembro de 2026 da PSI fornece um exemplo. A empresa afirmou que seu sistema desenvolvido internamente, executando um modelo da Anthropic que ainda não era público na época, produziu uma demonstração completa da conjectura de Aaronson–Ambainis no terceiro dia de uma execução; o Lean, um assistente de demonstração que verifica cada etapa, aceitou o resultado e, posteriormente, aceitou uma versão final após duas melhorias. Em aberto desde 2008, a conjectura trata das situações em que computadores quânticos podem ser exponencialmente mais rápidos do que computadores convencionais ao processar entradas aleatórias. David Turturean liderou o trabalho com acesso antecipado ao Claude Fable 5.2, que a Anthropic apresentou publicamente em 9 de novembro de 2026. A validação física continua sendo o teste comercial A demonstração também ilustra um limite à comercialização. A matemática e a ciência da computação podem expressar resultados em código validado, mas a física e as ciências da vida ainda exigem contato experimental com a natureza. Pines disse que a PSI está trabalhando em formas eficientes de validar resultados computacionais por meio de experimentos, resumindo a diferença com a observação de que “a natureza também tem voz nos seus modelos da realidade”. Pines também disse que a física teórica ainda não é, em sua maior parte, domínio das máquinas, apesar de ter apresentado aos investidores, de seis a nove meses antes, uma tese mais contundente, embora condicional. Essa ressalva é importante para os negócios da PSI: sua receita atual depende da otimização de instalações, enquanto sua ambição mais ampla exige descobertas validadas que possam se tornar dispositivos ou outras tecnologias. Pines relacionou um fato da natureza validado à possibilidade de construir um dispositivo com capacidades antes indisponíveis. Para a PSI, portanto, a questão comercial é saber se seu processo de geração e verificação pode produzir repetidamente resultados confirmados por experimentos, permitindo que o mesmo sistema de pesquisa passe da otimização da infraestrutura de IA à criação de tecnologias baseadas em nova física.

artigo.texto: A new global network will launch at the UN climate summit COP31 on 12 November in Antalya, Türkiye, aiming to tackle fragmentation in carbon markets and help channel more investment into climate projects, particularly in developing countries. Convened by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Global Carbon Market Network will seek to strengthen links between carbon and capital markets, improve transparency and credibility, and facilitate cross-border transactions. Carbon markets remain fragmented across different standards, registries and trading systems. Concerns over credit quality, transparency and double counting have weakened confidence and constrained market development, particularly in developing economies. Ahead of the official launch, UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno expressed hope that the Network would help make carbon pricing a more effective tool for reducing emissions and mobilizing climate finance for developing countries. Connecting fragmented carbon markets “Carbon markets can play a role in putting a price on emissions and mobilizing finance for climate action, but their effectiveness depends on trust, integrity and functioning market infrastructure,” said Nan Li Collins, UNCTAD’s Director of Investment and Enterprise and Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative. The Network will promote cooperation among exchanges and market institutions, including technical work on market integrity, measuring and verifying emissions reductions, and digital technologies to improve transparency and reduce transaction costs. Why it matters now Carbon pricing is expanding. Emissions trading systems and carbon taxes now cover nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than $107 billion in public revenue in 2025. The UNCTAD-convened Network will not create a new carbon market or standard. Instead, it aims to connect existing markets and initiatives, including voluntary and compliance markets. Voluntary carbon markets have particular potential to channel private investment across borders. UNCTAD research shows that most voluntary carbon credits are generated by projects in developing countries and sold to buyers in developed countries. Stronger links between markets could help build confidence in these transactions and expand financing for projects that reduce or remove emissions in developing countries. Who is participating and what’s next? The Network’s initial activities include capacity-building programmes, market-practice benchmarking, a global synthesis report on the state of carbon markets, and engagement with emissions trading system regulators on technical and interoperability issues. Founding members span Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America.

artigo.texto: Analog chipmaker Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) beat Wall Street's revenue expectations in calendar Q3 2026 (fiscal Q2 2027), with sales up 42.2% year on year to $1.62 billion. On the other hand, next quarter's revenue guidance of $1.61 billion was less impressive, coming in 1.4% below analysts' estimates. Its non-GAAP profit of $0.97 per share was 3.4% above analysts' consensus estimates. Revenue $1.62 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $1.61 billion (42.2% year-on-year growth, 0.8% beat) Adjusted EPS $0.97 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $0.94 (3.4% beat) Adjusted operating income $639.9 million vs analyst estimates of $628.9 million (39.5% margin, 1.8% beat) Revenue guidance $1.61 billion at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, below analyst estimates of $1.63 billion Adjusted EPS guidance $0.91 at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, below analyst estimates of $0.95 Operating margin 28.6%, up from 7.8% in the same quarter last year Inventory days outstanding 184, up from 175 in the previous quarter Market capitalization $35.21 billion StockStory's take Microchip Technology's latest quarter saw sales climb on robust demand in industrial and data center end markets, with management attributing growth to new design wins and strength across key verticals. However, the market reacted negatively to the results, reflecting concerns over the sustainability of these gains. CEO Steve Sanghi noted that several non-recurring items, including licensing revenue and a distribution price adjustment, boosted reported sales. He emphasized, "Industrial and data center end markets were the two biggest drivers of our growth." The company also faced rising inventory levels as it prepared for future customer needs. Looking ahead, Microchip Technology's guidance reflects cautious optimism tempered by supply chain constraints and seasonal factors. Management highlighted that some high-margin orders in advanced products cannot be fulfilled this quarter due to extended lead times at foundries and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) suppliers. Sanghi explained, "Our net sales guidance is lower than what we would have expected a quarter ago," citing both the absence of last quarter's one-time items and supply limitations. The company expects incremental capacity additions and a gradual improvement in fulfillment, but does not anticipate a swift normalization of gross margins given ongoing supplier price increases and operational bottlenecks. Key insights from management's remarks Management credited broad-based design win momentum, particularly in data center and industrial applications, for the quarter's growth. Non-recurring revenue items and evolving supply chain dynamics contributed to deviations from consensus expectations. Industrial and data center momentum: Management pointed to strong demand and recent design wins in industrial automation, robotics, and data center infrastructure, with the data center segment now representing nearly 17% of sales. The company is ramping next-generation PCIe Gen 6 switch and retimer products, highlighting 24 design wins that will scale revenue over the next year. Impact of non-recurring items: The quarter benefited from approximately $53 million in one-time revenue from licensing, pricing changes on channel inventory, and a customer contract. CFO Eric Bjornholt clarified these items carried 100% gross margin but are not expected to repeat, creating a less favorable comparison for the coming quarter. Supply chain bottlenecks: CEO Steve Sanghi described persistent constraints at both internal fabrication sites and external OSAT partners, with the AI sector crowding out capacity for legacy and analog products. Lead times for many core products have lengthened from 4-8 weeks to as long as 32 weeks, affecting the timing of high-margin shipments. Inventory management and production shifts: Inventory days outstanding increased as Microchip received high-value wafers in anticipation of demand and shifted some production internally to offset external bottlenecks. The company is qualifying new OSAT partners and rebalancing its internal versus external manufacturing strategy but expects these transitions to take several quarters. Acquisitions and portfolio expansion: Microchip completed the acquisitions of Hailo (AI edge computing) and VORAGO (aerospace and defense), integrating these into existing business units. While these deals will add to operating expenses in the short term, management expects them to accelerate the roadmap in AI and provide high-margin opportunities in aerospace and defense. Drivers of future performance Microchip's forward outlook is shaped by ongoing supply constraints, pricing pressures from suppliers, and the need to balance capacity with persistent demand across end markets. Supply chain and capacity expansion: Management stressed that lead times remain extended due to capacity constraints at foundries and OSAT partners, impacting fulfillment of high-margin products. While incremental internal and external capacity additions are planned for the coming quarters, the timing of improvements remains uncertain, and some backlog will spill into future periods. Supplier price increases and margin headwinds: Sanghi acknowledged that further price hikes from foundry and OSAT suppliers starting in January will pressure gross margins. While Microchip is reluctant to push another immediate price increase to customers, the company will need to assess whether these costs can be absorbed or passed on, with a long-term gross margin target of 65%. Diversified end-market demand: Despite concerns about an overheated data center market, management highlighted steady momentum in industrial, aerospace and defense, automotive, and communication segments. The company's relatively modest exposure to data center revenue, compared to peers, leaves it less vulnerable to a slowdown in that sector, while broad-based design wins are expected to support growth. artigo.texto: South Korean defense and technology giant Hanwha Ocean plans to advance the power and control system for its Floating Data Center (FDC). The company announced on Friday that it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with ABB, a transnational corporation specializing in electrification and automation, for this purpose. Hanwha Ocean introduced the FDC at the Gastech Exhibition & Conference 2026 in September. The solution is designed to operate offshore, generating its own power and using seawater-based cooling systems to improve energy efficiency. Now, under the new deal with ABB, Hanwha Ocean will lead the basic design and power system configuration, establish design criteria for LNG engine-based power generation, and assess equipment layouts and suitability for offshore conditions. ABB, in turn, will analyze power system reliability and power quality based on Hanwha Ocean’s design and conduct technical reviews to improve efficiency amid fluctuating demand in the offshore environment. “AI data centers can experience rapid fluctuations in power demand during computing operations. Together, we will develop technologies to adjust LNG engine output in response to these changes and maintain stable operation of power equipment,” Hanwha Ocean shared on social media. Through this collaboration, Hanwha Ocean aims to extend its offshore engineering and construction capabilities into digital infrastructure and continue strengthening the core technologies behind FDCs.

artigo.texto: Cincinnati council hears study on how to regulate data centers CINCINNATI (WXIX) - The City of Cincinnati is considering how to regulate data centers. A presentation Tuesday in council gave an overview of how data centers could be installed in the city. The city ordered a study to help guide council as members consider how to handle data centers if more are brought into the city. What the study found The Department of City Planning and Engagement representatives acknowledged that data centers may be a piece of important infrastructure, but not everyone wants them around. “We all use the internet. We use social media, we do Google search ... All of that uses data from data centers, so if we want to do that, we need data centers,” Councilman Mark Jeffreys said. About 400 people provided the city with feedback on the issue. “The primary message that we received from community members was a strong desire to see the zoning code prohibit data centers as a land use,” said Sophia Ferries-Rowe with the Cincinnati Department of City Planning and Engagement. The department said 28 data centers currently operate within the Greater Cincinnati area, with nine directly in the city. If more arrive, residents are concerned about increased heat, noise, energy bills and water utility bills, the study found. The study also found that more data centers could create jobs and help support local infrastructure, but they may have negative environmental impacts on carbon emissions. RELATED | Data centers multiply across Ohio, raising questions about costs and benefits Water use and costs “Why should citizens and property owners pay higher water bills to protect a billion dollar company?” Stephan Pryor said. Representatives with the Metropolitan Sewer District and Greater Cincinnati Water Works suggested that existing regulations already control how companies use water. They said the city could implement a reuse system that would allow water that is not fully treated to be rerouted directly to data centers and other uses not related to drinking water. They told Councilman Evan Nolan that it would require new infrastructure. “That could be expensive,” Nolan said. “Could be, yes, but other places in the country have had private investment,” said Scott Bessler, with the Metropolitan Sewer District. PREVIOUSLY | Cincinnati considers temporary halt on new data centers Next steps As the study continues, local leaders still have questions about how much energy and water current data centers use before setting any guidelines. “We need to put a cost associated with those, and if another data center is proposed to be built, we need to know what that cost is so we can offset it. It shouldn’t be on ratepayers,” Jeffreys said. The next step is more research, and city departments will put forth recommendations for the zoning rules. Another public engagement session will follow, and the recommendations will be refined before going before council. See a spelling or grammatical error in our story? Please click here to report it. artigo.texto: Cabinet tackles grid congestion with large-scale energy storage The Dutch government wants to expand energy storage to ease pressure on the country’s overloaded electricity grid. Published on November 9, 2026 According to the government, more energy storage is needed to ensure that renewable electricity remains available when there is little wind or solar power being generated. It therefore aims to increase battery storage capacity in the Netherlands to 110 gigawatt-hours (GWh) by 2040, more than 50 times the level at the end of 2025. The expansion should also help reduce pressure on the electricity grid. Climate and Energy Minister Stientje van Veldhoven and State Secretary Jo-Annes de Bat announced the plans in a letter to the Dutch House of Representatives. To make the expansion possible, the government has reached agreements with grid operators, industry association Energy Storage NL, regional and local authorities, and the Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM). These agreements are set out in a joint Energy Storage Policy Agenda. Batteries to ease pressure on the grid The expansion is intended, among other things, to reduce pressure on the electricity grid. In many parts of the Netherlands, the grid is so congested that businesses and households have to wait for a new or upgraded connection. This is also holding back the construction of new homes. By storing electricity when demand is low and making it available during peak periods, batteries can help relieve pressure on the grid. According to the government, grid-friendly energy storage could also reduce the need for investments in expanding the electricity grid. Faster permitting The 25 action points include measures to speed up the permitting process for large-scale battery projects. Grid operators, the energy storage sector and regional authorities will need to work more closely together to achieve this. The parties are also working on agreements concerning the conditions and compensation for energy storage. One example is the use of flexible grid contracts, under which large batteries are connected subject to conditions that take into account the available capacity on the electricity grid. Compensation for households Large-scale batteries are not the only way to help stabilise the electricity grid. Households can also receive compensation if they help manage peak demand using their home batteries, heat pumps or electric vehicle chargers. Since November 1, households in the provinces of Gelderland, Utrecht, Flevoland and North Brabant have been able to participate in the scheme through a number of energy suppliers. The scheme is expected to be extended to the rest of the Netherlands in 2027.

artigo.texto: COLUMBUS, Ohio — The push against data centers has been well-documented. One independent tracker counts nearly 150 data center moratoriums in place all across the state. Opponents are concerned about a wide variety of issues, including the impact the centers have on the environment and their utility bills. At the same time, supporters point to the fact that those data centers are bringing billions of dollars in investment and new opportunities for construction workers. As data centers continue to expand across Ohio, so does the demand for the workers needed to build them. “We’ve got in-house architecture and engineering, licensed and stamped in all 50 states,” said Will Goodin, vice president of project development for Terrapin Construction Group. Terrapin Construction Group designs data centers across the country with four separate projects currently in Ohio. “And that’s inclusive of mechanical, electrical, plumbing as well as engineering, civil, so site work and structural work as well,” Goodin said. He said the growing number of data center projects is creating more business for his company, making over $100 million from design, construction and procurement of HVAC equipment this year, and they’re on track to triple that next year. “We’ve seen a huge uptick in not only design but also a lot of pre-construction, a lot of construction specifically in the data center asset class,” Goodin said. And it’s not just the construction crews. Goodin said demand for the specialized equipment needed to build these facilities is also high, with some supplies taking months to arrive. “There’s huge lead times depending on the types of equipment that you’re looking to source for your project. Anywhere from 18- to 50-plus weeks for any number of transfer switches, switch gears, chillers, things of that nature,” Goodin said. That demand creates opportunities for a wide range of skilled trades, including electricians, mechanical contractors, framers and carpenters. Goodin said the steady pipeline of projects is providing job security for his company and the subcontractors it relies on. But he recognizes the industry is not without controversy. “Depending on who you ask, it’s kind of a loaded, complicated issue but we’re very excited to be a resource for folks who are looking to get into this business and are expanding their current operations,” Goodin said. Across Ohio, communities are pushing back against data center development. As more communities consider putting development on pause, the question becomes: How many jobs do these facilities actually create once construction is over? Case Western Reserve University Economics Professor Jonathan Ernest said the initial construction phase can provide a significant employment boost. But he said once it’s built, that changes. “There are fewer people onsite for the longterm with lots of jobs in an area. So we’re not likely to get entire cities that are built around the one plant that everyone works at we’re not likely to get that with data centers because they don’t need that many capacity of people on site for the long run,” said Ernest. So, while the construction boom is creating opportunities for Ohio’s skilled trades, Ernest said communities should take a closer look at what those projects will mean for the local workforce once the facilities are up and running. According to the U.S. Data Center Map, there are 26 data centers currently being constructed, with another 54 in the planning phase.

artigo.texto: UK has no plans to slow down AI data center construction The country’s growth minister said the data centers will continue as “essential infrastructure” projects. As the US deals with the fallout associated with the ongoing demand for data centers, the UK is looking to capitalize on it instead, according to one of the country's ministers. Dan Tomlinson, the UK's minister for growth, told the The Financial Times that data center construction will continue as "essential infrastructure." Tomlinson told FT that AI is becoming more widely used throughout the UK's economy, meaning the country will need more data centers to support that growth. However, the minister added that data center construction in the UK will have to invest in local communities and create jobs to receive government support. Tomlinson also told FT that the UK government has taken away some lessons from the "free-for-all in parts of the US" with data center construction and that the country would take a more nuanced approach with better oversight. According to the UK Compute Roadmap, a policy paper detailing how the country can meet AI's growing power demands, the UK needs to have at least a computing capacity of 6GW from data centers by 2030. The UK previously made it easier for data centers to earn approvals, thanks to the "AI Growth Zones" initiative introduced by former prime minister Keir Starmer in 2025. However, UK residents have taken to protesting on sites of planned data center construction. Across the Atlantic, a majority of American voters said they're in favor of restricting the rapid pace of data center construction in local ballot results.

artigo.texto: Invinity Energy Systems plc (AIM: IES), a leading global producer of vanadium flow batteries operating in the UK and Canada, has unveiled a major upgrade to its Endurium vanadium flow battery platform, now available for general purchase. The upgraded Endurium module offers a 50% rise in energy capacity and a 33% enhancement in peak power output, along with several engineering advancements. This upgrade supports further product cost reductions and enhances project economics for customers, marking a key milestone in the company’s ongoing cost reduction initiative. Key Points - Invinity Energy Systems plc (AIM: IES) is a top global manufacturer of vanadium flow batteries with facilities in the UK and Canada. - The new Endurium module is now commercially available, delivering 50% more energy capacity and 33% higher peak power output. - Enhancements include increased electrolyte volume, upgraded electrical and power distribution systems, and refined fluid management and control algorithms. - Investors should monitor upcoming product roadmap milestones and progress on the company’s cost reduction and margin enhancement goals. Endurium’s 50% Energy Capacity Increase Driven by Multiple Engineering Enhancements The improved performance of the upgraded Endurium module results from a series of engineering modifications rather than a single change. Invinity highlights the expansion of electrolyte capacity, enhancements to electrical and power distribution subsystems, and advancements in fluid management and control system algorithms as key factors. Collectively, these improvements significantly boost power and energy density, reducing the number of modules needed to deliver the same electrical output as before. The upgraded Endurium is now available for customers seeking large-scale, long-duration energy storage solutions. Reduced Module Count Lowers Installation and Lifecycle Expenses for Clients A major commercial benefit of the upgrade is that fewer Endurium modules are required to meet specific energy storage needs, cutting equipment and space demands. Invinity notes this leads to decreased installation and lifecycle costs, enhancing project economics. The Endurium platform is designed for heavy-duty, high-throughput use and built to last 30 years or more without degradation or fire risk—advantages over lithium-ion alternatives. These features are particularly valuable for customers in renewable energy and grid infrastructure sectors seeking durable, long-lasting storage assets. Upgrade Advances Company’s Cost Reduction Program Reaffirmed to Shareholders Invinity links the Endurium upgrade directly to its ongoing product cost reduction program, recently reaffirmed to shareholders. The development was achieved by Invinity’s internal product development and R&D teams. CEO Jonathan Marren called the upgrade "another milestone" and noted further enhancements remain on the product roadmap, with continued emphasis on cost reduction, margin improvement, and strengthening Endurium’s market position as the company grows. The announcement did not disclose specific financial details, cost savings, or margin targets.

artigo.texto: Eletronet investe R$ 25 milhões em novo data center em São Paulo Com obras iniciadas, ELET1 terá 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW; lançamento está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. A Eletronet, empresa da Axia Energia (antiga Eletrobras), anunciou investimento de R$ 25 milhões na construção de um novo data center em São Paulo. Batizada de ELET1, a unidade terá 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW. As obras já começaram, e o lançamento está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto prevê uma segunda fase de expansão, na qual a potência poderá chegar a 1 MW, cujo prazo de entrega ainda não foi definido. A instalação ampliará a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão, com atendimento a provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações, provedores de internet (ISPs) e hyperscalers. Interconexão e migração da infraestrutura O ELET1 abrigará o ponto de interconexão (PIX) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo. Segundo a empresa, a unidade ficará em uma região com concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo. O projeto também contempla a migração da infraestrutura instalada no atual data center da companhia em São Paulo. A Eletronet afirma que a transferência será planejada para preservar a continuidade dos serviços. “Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais”, afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet (na foto acima). Segundo o executivo, o investimento acompanha o avanço de aplicações em nuvem, inteligência artificial, streaming e serviços digitais, que demandam suporte a volumes crescentes de dados. Energia e redundância Entre os recursos previstos para o ELET1 estão dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVA, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predial (BMS) e monitoramento contínuo. A unidade também contará com um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência. “Mais capacidade precisa vir acompanhada de eficiência, resiliência e previsibilidade operacional. Por isso, o ELET1 foi concebido com uma arquitetura que otimiza o uso dos recursos e oferece mais flexibilidade à operação”, afirma Emerson Hioki, diretor de tecnologia da Eletronet. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Confira o resumo que a OESTE.IA, a IA da Revista Oeste, fez pra você A Noruega decidiu suspender temporariamente novas reservas de conexão de data centers à rede elétrica para avaliar a crescente demanda de energia dessas instalações, impulsionada pela expansão da inteligência artificial. A medida foi anunciada pela operadora do sistema elétrico, Statnett, nesta segunda-feira, 9, e deve durar até, no máximo, 1º de agosto de 2027. A Noruega vai suspender temporariamente novas reservas de conexão de data centers à rede elétrica. A decisão busca avaliar como o país vai lidar com a demanda de energia dessas instalações, que vem crescendo com a expansão da inteligência artificial (IA). A operadora do sistema elétrico norueguês, Statnett, anunciou a medida nesta segunda-feira, 9, em comunicado. A previsão é que a suspensão termine, no máximo, em 1º de agosto de 2027. Receba nossas atualizações Leia também: “Nvidia investiga suspeita de espionagem envolvendo CEO“ A construção de data centers avança em diversos países. Empresas de tecnologia investem centenas de bilhões de dólares em estruturas destinadas à operação e ao treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial. A expansão, contudo, também provoca resistência de comunidades nos Estados Unidos e na Europa, principalmente por causa da demanda por terrenos e eletricidade e do possível aumento das tarifas de energia. O ministro da Digitalização da Noruega, Torgeir Micaelsen, defendeu o controle sobre a expansão dessas instalações. “Queremos data centers na Noruega, mas não podemos aceitar todos os tipos de data centers”, afirmou a jornalistas nesta segunda-feira. “Portanto, precisamos controlar o crescimento e garantir que a Noruega receba os data centers de que realmente necessita, aqueles que proporcionam os maiores benefícios para a sociedade.” Demanda supera o consumo máximo do país Segundo dados da Statnett, os data centers já conectados à rede norueguesa somam 800 megawatts (MW) de capacidade. Outros 4.200 MW têm reserva de conexão, enquanto 9.100 MW aguardam na fila por capacidade. Além desses pedidos, empresas solicitaram conexão para mais 18 mil MW. Com isso, a demanda total à espera de acesso chega a 27.100 MW. O volume supera o consumo máximo de energia da Noruega, que fica pouco acima de 25 mil MW. Os números ajudam a dimensionar a pressão que os novos empreendimentos podem exercer sobre o sistema elétrico do país. Um relatório recente do Conselho Norueguês de Tecnologia também questionou os benefícios econômicos dessas instalações. Segundo o documento, os data centers geram poucos empregos permanentes depois da conclusão das obras. O conselho informou ainda que 90% dessas estruturas pertencem a empresas estrangeiras. + Entenda mais de Mundo em Oeste
