artigo.texto: Data centers may be willing to be double charged for grid infrastructure, so long as those costs are paired with policy that makes it easier to build in the U.S. Tucked inside the Senate’s bipartisan permitting reform bill are provisions that would upend decades of federal power rules by directing data centers and crypto miners to pay for both the new transmission lines needed to serve them, as well as the cost of using the existing grid. Historically, charging a customer twice for the same capacity was considered an illegal practice. But that could change, as data centers disproportionately drive up demand for electricity across the U.S. and hyperscalers promise not to saddle other customers with the bill. The shift reflects a fraught moment in the race to power artificial intelligence, especially heading into the midterm elections next week. Energy affordability is top of mind for many voters across the U.S., whose opinion of data centers has soured dramatically this year, according to the latest polling by POLITICO. Half of Americans now oppose data centers being built within three miles of their home, up from 28% in January. Their concerns are rooted in rising utility bills, water use, air pollution, and AI’s impact on jobs and the broader economy. Controversial projects are affecting local races, including in states like New Mexico, Utah, and Wisconsin. “I think the data center industry will take this deal because they’ve already acknowledged that they need to cover their costs,” Tyson Slocum, director of Public Citizen’s energy program, told Latitude Media. “And at the end of the day, the bill will make it a lot easier to build the gas and renewable infrastructure needed to serve data centers.” President Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of data centers that underpin the global AI race, who says the U.S. needs to win against China, launched a voluntary ratepayer protection pledge in March. Tech giants, AI labs, and major utilities signed it, with the tech companies promising to either build or buy generation to power new data centers and pay for any new grid infrastructure to serve them. Trading extra cash for speed The Senate permitting deal, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, aims to actually enforce that pledge. And so far, at least two industry groups that represent companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft have endorsed the legislation: the Corporate Energy Buyers Association and the Electricity Customer Alliance. However, the Data Center Coalition has not endorsed the bill. The group told Latitude Media in a statement that it’s still reviewing the legislation with its members. Amazon, Google, and Meta didn’t respond to a request for comment. Microsoft declined to comment. CEBA in a statement described BAAJA as a “generational opportunity” to build out U.S. energy through faster infrastructure permitting and improved transmission planning. Jeff Dennis, executive director of ECA — which represents tech companies and residential and industrial customers — said BAAJA strikes a balance between encouraging the build out of larger transmission lines in a more financially disciplined way, while setting the stage for long-term affordability. He noted that data center developers have already said they expect to pay their own costs, and then some. “They are willing to pay more than their own costs to make sure other customers are treated fairly,” Dennis said. BAAJA would require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to rewrite a 1994 policy that allowed electricity customers to pay either the “embedded” costs of the existing grid, or the “incremental” cost of its expansion — not both. Instead, computational loads larger than 20 megawatts would be forced to pay both. States could charge a “surplus” on top of that, in order to lower other customers’ utility bills, and discriminate against data centers by treating them as a “less favorable” customer class to other large industrial, manufacturing, or commercial loads. The bill also would mandate that utilities hold data centers liable for capital costs, even if they exit agreements early for any reason, to make sure ratepayers aren’t left on the hook. Dennis said a final bill must ensure that data centers aren’t forced to shoulder so much of the costs that they ultimately decide to build off-grid. Some projects are already going that route, including those backed by Microsoft and Amazon, mainly powered by gas turbines and engines and backup diesel generators. “That could pose negative impacts to customers and removes a lot of investment in the grid we all rely on,” he said. A Senate aide told Latitude Media that key negotiators are working on a managers’ amendment to BAAJA, although it’s unclear whether it would revise the ratepayer protection section of the bill. Nidhi Thakar, CEBA’s senior vice president for policy, said the group supports BAAJA in its current form, but acknowledged there is some concern among its data center members about how much they’ll be forced to pay. “A lot of this will have to get worked out in a FERC rulemaking,” Thakar said. “That is where the deep details on how to allocate costs for new transmission lines will occur. So that rulemaking will be very critical.” The Senate is set to vote on the permitting bill on Nov. 9, the week after the midterm elections.

artigo.texto: As Toyota's luxury brand Lexus rolls out electric versions of its midsize-plus ES sedan, competition is heating up in Korea's 70 million won EV segment. The 70 million won range is expected to see fast-growing demand because it preserves a premium image while still qualifying for subsidies. But most of the key models at this price point, including the ES EVs, are equipped with batteries from China's CATL, leaving Korean battery makers on the sidelines. According to the auto industry on the 10th, Lexus on the 13th of last month launched the all-electric ES350e and ES500e and the hybrid ES350h as part of the new eighth-generation ES in the Korean market. The ES is a core Lexus model that made its global debut in 1989. The new ES is the fully redesigned eighth generation, the first full change in eight years since 2018. Until now, the ES was sold only with internal-combustion and hybrid powertrains, but starting with this eighth generation Lexus has dropped the combustion-engine model and added an EV. The entry-level Premium trim of the ES350e is priced at 71.6 million won. That is 1.3 million won cheaper than the ES350h Premium trim at 72.9 million won. Because EVs carry costly batteries, they are often pricier than comparable combustion or hybrid models. Lexus appears to have set the EV's starting price below the hybrid to quickly gain share on price competitiveness. Lexus also priced the higher-spec ES500e Premium in the 77 million won range. The ES350e is a front-wheel-drive model with a single motor, while the ES500e is all-wheel drive with dual motors. The ES500e's range is 435 km per charge, shorter than the ES350e's 478 km, but it outmuscles the ES350e with 347 horsepower versus 227 horsepower. After Lexus priced the new ES EVs in the lower-than-expected 70 million won range, domestic consumer interest surged. Industry sources say total orders for the new ES, including one month of preorders, have reached about 5,000 units. EVs—the ES350e and ES500e—account for roughly half. Rivals starting in the 70 million won range include Volvo's midsize-plus ES90 sedan, Polestar's midsize-plus SUV Polestar 3, and BMW's midsize SUV iX3. Tesla's midsize SUV Model Y, which dominates the Korean market, starts at 49.99 million won for the base rear-wheel-drive Premium, while the all-wheel-drive Model Y L Premium sells for 72.99 million won. Automakers are clustering new models in the 70 million won bracket because policy changes on subsidies are seen as boosting demand at this price point. Currently, EVs priced under 85 million won qualify for subsidies, but the government plans to lower the threshold to under 80 million won starting next year. In addition, vehicles priced 80 million won or more must carry green license plates if purchased as corporate cars. Price a car in the 60 million won range or lower and its premium image fades; move into the 80 million won range and you risk losing subsidies and being required to use green plates, among other drawbacks. As a result, import brands are concentrating on the 70 million won segment to protect brand value while reaping multiple practical benefits. The problem is that batteries in EVs priced in the 70 million won range are effectively dominated by China's CATL. CATL is the world's No. 1 supplier, with a 39.1% cumulative share of the global EV battery market from January through September this year. The Lexus ES350e and ES500e, Volvo ES90, and Polestar 3 all use CATL's LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries. For the Model Y, the Long Range and Performance trims use LG Energy Solution's NCM batteries, but the cheaper rear-wheel-drive trim also uses CATL's LFP battery. The BMW iX3 is equipped with batteries from China's EVE Energy. Automakers are largely sourcing batteries from CATL and other Chinese makers because they are relatively inexpensive. NCM batteries, the mainstay of Korean suppliers such as LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI, offer higher energy density and longer range but cost more due to pricey cobalt and nickel. LFP batteries, by contrast, use iron and phosphorus as main materials and can be procured at lower cost. Battery industry officials worry that LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On—the three Korean players—will keep losing share at home to Chinese batteries. The high-end premium EV segment has limited room to expand, and domestic automakers such as Hyundai Motor are struggling to grow EV sales. "To make matters worse, after BYD, Chinese EV makers such as Zeekr and Xpeng are entering Korea one after another, further squeezing Hyundai Motor and Kia," a battery industry source said. "Korean battery makers' recent focus on the energy storage system (ESS) market also reflects their judgment that it will be hard to win back EV leadership from Chinese companies anytime soon."

artigo.texto: Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) turned up in two big data center announcements on Nov. 5. NTT DATA said it had agreed to deploy 900 megawatts of the fuel cell maker's onsite power across data center projects around the world. And Alphabet's Google said Bloom would build the fuel cells for a 702-megawatt plant powering its first data center in Wyoming, a $17 billion project. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The stock had a bad day anyway. Shares ended at $167.52, off around 16%, amid worries that rising opposition to new data centers after the Nov. 3 midterms might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. The growth stock is still up over 90% this year. But it now sits about 52% below the $345.85 record close it set on June 22. How much new business did Bloom win on Nov. 5? Less than the headlines may suggest, because just one of the two deals is new. I think the other still matters, though, and the stock looks much more reasonably priced than it did in October. Image source: The Motley Fool. Google's fuel cells were ordered in January Google won't buy the fuel cells itself. American Electric Power plans to invest around $4 billion in the 702-megawatt project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, the utility said on Oct. 14. It'll sell the plant's output to Google under a 20-year power purchase agreement, and it expects the plant to be fully running by late 2028. The fuel cell order came months earlier. In January, an AEP subsidiary agreed to buy solid oxide fuel cells for around $2.65 billion for a plant near Cheyenne. The purchase used most of an option for 900 extra megawatts under AEP's 2024 supply deal with Bloom. For a sense of scale, that one order is worth over half of Bloom's full-year revenue forecast of $4.4 billion to $4.6 billion for 2026. So, Google's news didn't add to Bloom's orders. The fuel cells were bought in January, and AEP had already named Google as the plant's customer in October. That still means something, I think. A fuel cell order backed by a 20-year power contract with Google looks more likely to become revenue on time than one linked to an unnamed buyer. NTT DATA is the new business NTT DATA's deal is the new business, and the companies called it Bloom's biggest international project so far. NTT's data center arm plans to use the fuel cells as its main power source, with the relationship meant to reach gigawatt scale across its global portfolio. What the release didn't say matters, too. It gave no dollar value, no project locations, and no timeline beyond first shipments starting in 2027. This deal shouldn't show up in Bloom's 2026 revenue, and Bloom hasn't said how much of it falls in 2027 or later. But 900 megawatts is a lot of fuel cells -- nearly a full year of output at the 1 gigawatt of annual production capacity Bloom's Fremont, California, plant had going into 2026. The company planned to double that capacity by year-end. Bloom needs deals like this, because its quarter-to-quarter growth slowed sharply in the third quarter. Second-quarter revenue of $1.07 billion was 42% above the first quarter's $751 million. Third-quarter revenue then climbed 16% sequentially to $1.24 billion, up 138% year over year. And October's raised outlook (management's third raise this year) implies a sequential gain of 9% to 25% in the fourth quarter. That's still strong growth. Keeping it up into 2027 and 2028, though, depends on deals like NTT DATA's moving from announcement to shipment. Is the price finally reasonable? Based on the midpoint of management's adjusted earnings forecast for 2026 ($3.10 to $3.40 a share), Bloom stock cost around 52 times earnings at its Nov. 5 close. The same forecast had it at around 67 times earnings at the $217.77 close on Oct. 22. On next year's expected earnings, shares now trade at around 31 times earnings. Still, 52 times earnings is a premium price. It assumes Bloom keeps growing quickly well past this year. But Bloom landed a big new deal on Nov. 5 as its shares got much cheaper. Of course, a slower U.S. data center build-out might delay some deliveries. And October's weak spot hasn't gone away. Bloom's operations burned $27 million in cash in the third quarter, mostly because it booked revenue faster than it could bill customers for it. Is Bloom stock worth buying after a 16% one-day drop? I'd consider buying some shares at this price, a few at a time. And I'd maybe add more when billing catches up with revenue. Should you buy stock in Bloom Energy right now? artigo.texto: Lubbock residents urge council to pass data center moratorium City council hosts first public hearing over proposed 90-day moratorium LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - Residents urged the Lubbock City Council to pass a 90-day data center moratorium during the first of two public hearings on the proposal. The proposed moratorium followed a successful citizen petition organized through SAVE Lubbock this past summer. Residents raise concerns Fabian Mata, a north Lubbock resident, told city council Tuesday afternoon he does not trust the city to enforce its ordinances. “We don’t trust you when you say you’re going to put 1,000, 2,000, 5,000 feet [setback] in the data centers in north Lubbock because you don’t enforce any of the ordinances,” Mata said. Natalie Miller of the North and East Lubbock Coalition said while the moratorium proposal isn’t exactly what citizens asked for, she hopes council respects their wishes. “Citizens of Lubbock asked for 18 months. There was a compromise for 90 days, and that’s what the law would allow for. And so, we accepted that answer, and now we’re just asking to simply honor that,” Miller said. Zoning recommendations At its meeting last week, the Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended that Lubbock require specific zoning for AI factories. The proposed rules would address landscaping, setbacks, noise and pollution limits, and data center decommissioning. Stephen Sanders of SAVE Lubbock said residents should be heard. “We don’t want a data center in those communities at all. But if we have to have one, it needs to be 1,000 foot setback,” Sanders said. The commission’s recommendations for large-scale data centers are scheduled to come before the council Dec. 1. Some residents said a moratorium would come too late because the Lubbock Economic Development Alliance has already approved a new data center inside city limits. That facility is smaller than the large-scale data centers the city is considering regulating. “We had no opportunity to say no because LEDA and you all had already spoken about it,” Stephanie Smith said. The second public hearing on the moratorium is set for Dec. 10, when council will have its first opportunity to vote on it. “Usually it’s the industry comes in first and then we study. We’re just saying let’s study this first, right?” Miller said. Copyright 2026 KCBD. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Gangues organizadas roubam caminhões carregados de componentes para data centers: prejuízo já soma US$ 100 milhões A febre da IA transformou servidores, chips e memórias em alvos milionários nos EUA, gerando perdas que ultrapassam US$ 110,6 milhões desde junho O avanço da inteligência artificial gerou uma onda de crimes sofisticados contra o setor de tecnologia. Quadrilhas organizadas estão interceptando caminhões para roubar cargas valiosas de componentes para data centers, como servidores, cabos de cobre e chips de memória. Com ataques altamente planejados antes dos veículos deixarem os depósitos, os prejuízos com os roubos já somam US$ 110,6 milhões desde junho, registrando perdas que variam entre US$ 2 milhões e US$ 38 milhões por ocorrência. A corrida do ouro da inteligência artificial está recriando uma espécie de "Velho Oeste do século XXI", reunindo todos os elementos de um faroeste clássico. De um lado, estão as minas de ouro — os data centers — e investidores com bolsos cheios, dispostos a comprar as pás e todo o material necessário para extrair o metal precioso, que agora assume a forma de dados. Faltavam apenas os saqueadores de estradas para completar o cenário, mas eles acabaram de chegar. Desta vez, a diligência é um caminhão semirreboque carregado de peças para equipar data centers. Conforme revelou a emissora norte-americana NBC News, a nova carga cobiçada reúne servidores, cabos de cobre para instalações e chips de memória. E as quadrilhas não improvisam: escolhem a carga de maneira calculada muito antes de o veículo deixar o depósito e o interceptam antes que chegue ao destino final. Prejuízos passam de US$ 100 milhões desde junho Estima-se que, desde 3 de junho, os roubos registrados de cargas de tecnologia somaram **US$ 110,6 milhões**. Segundo levantamento da FreightWaves com Scott Cornell, presidente da Associação para a Proteção de Ativos Transportados (TAPA Americas) e executivo especialista em crimes de transporte na SPG Cargo & Logistics, os prejuízos em cada ataque variam entre **US$ 2 milhões e US$ 38 milhões**. Announces Intent to Launch Exchange Offer to Acquire Up to $50,000,000 of Outstanding Shares for Cash and New Preferred Shares Company Moves to Address Significant Gap Between Market Value and Balance Sheet Strength LAS VEGAS , Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it intends to commence an exchange offer to purchase up to 192,307,692 shares of its Class A Common Stock, $0.001 par value per share ("Common Stock") in exchange for units (the "Units") consisting of (a) $2.00 in cash and (b) one share of preferred stock with a stated value of $24.00 per share (the "Preferred Stock"), per 100 shares of Common Stock. The Preferred Stock will be entitled to receive an annual dividend of 12.00%. Stockholders will be able to exchange blocks of 100 shares of Common Stock for one Unit consisting of (a) $2.00 in cash and (b) one share of Preferred Stock which values the Common Stock at $0.26 per share and represents an 82% premium to the November 6, 2026, closing price of $0.1429. The exchange offer will require that a minimum of 100 million shares of Common Stock be tendered by common stockholders. The Company will seek to list the Preferred Stock on the NYSE American. If the application to list the Preferred Stock is approved by the NYSE American, trading in the Preferred Stock is expected to commence within a 30-day period after the approval of listing. The Company expects to formally launch the proposed exchange offer around November 17, 2026, subject to board approval, regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. The proposed exchange offer reflects Hyperscale's view that its current market valuation does not accurately reflect the strength of its balance sheet, including its holdings of cash and Bitcoin. Milton "Todd" Ault III, Executive Chairman of Hyperscale Data, stated: "We believe there is a material disconnect between the intrinsic value of Hyperscale and where our Common Stock is currently trading. "The exchange offer is intended to provide shareholders with an opportunity for liquidity and an instrument that will allow stockholders to participate in the long-term growth of the Company while receiving a fixed payment. The exchange offer will, if consummated, also allow the Company to repurchase a meaningful percentage of its shares at what we believe are significantly undervalued levels. We believe this is a disciplined and shareholder-focused use of capital." Details regarding the proposed exchange offer and instructions for stockholders interested in participating will be provided in the Offer to Exchange and related documents, which will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC") and distributed to the Company stockholders. The exchange offer will not be made to any person in any jurisdiction in which either the exchange offer, or solicitation or sale thereof, is unlawful. This press release is for informational purposes only and shall not constitute an offer to buy or sell Common Stock or any other securities. Any solicitation of offers to buy the Common Stock will only be made pursuant to an Offer to Exchange and related materials to be sent to the Company stockholders on the commencement of the exchange offer. Company stockholders should read such materials carefully when they become available because they will contain important information, including the terms and conditions of the proposed exchange offer. The tender offer documents will be available without charge at the SEC's website at http://www.sec.gov and will be delivered without charge to all stockholders of the Company who so request it. It is anticipated that the exchange offer will be made pursuant to the exemption from registration requirements of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, contained in Section 3(a)(9) thereof. Under that exemption, if Common Stock exchanged is freely tradeable, the Preferred Stock received in exchange therefor will be freely tradeable. If the Common Stock is restricted, the Preferred Stock will be restricted to the same degree. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. artigo.texto: On one of the hottest nights of the year, South Australia‘s big batteries ran out of charge before the evening peak ended. That night shows why the next question for Australia’s grid isn’t how many batteries we build, but how long they can run. Australia has built big batteries at record pace. The grid-scale fleet in the National Electricity Market (NEM) now holds about 17.7 GWh of storage, yet it averages just 2.3 hours of discharge at full power.[1] HiTHIUM, a battery manufacturer focused solely on energy storage, thinks that number needs to grow. Its answer is the ∞Power 6.9 MWh, a system it describes as the world’s first battery built from the cell up for eight hours. A battery that runs out at 8pm is useful. A battery that runs past midnight is infrastructure. TL;DR - Duration is the new pressure point: Most of Australia’s grid batteries hold two hours or less, but high-price events are expected to stretch from about 1.5 hours today to 5–10 hours by the 2040s. - Policy is already moving to eight hours: NSW and South Australia now contract storage that can run for eight hours or more. - HiTHIUM has built for that standard: Its ∞Power 6.9 MWh uses a dedicated 1,300 Ah cell designed for eight-hour discharge, backed by a 25-year design life. What happened in South Australia on 26 January 2026? South Australia had the quarter’s most expensive evening, and its batteries ran low before the evening ended. The Australian Energy Regulator (AER) set out what happened in its report on significant electricity prices.[2] Parts of Adelaide passed 44°C. Evening demand topped 3,100 MW, within 300 MW of the state’s record. Wind output fell to around 337 MW, about 12% of installed capacity. Prices ran high from 6:30pm to 10:30pm, peaking at $20,158/MWh for a 30-minute period. AEMO declared an actual lack of reserve from 8:30pm to 9:45pm. Batteries delivered plenty of power early in the evening. But from around 7:50pm, operators began withdrawing offers, mostly citing state of charge. By 8:55pm, battery offers had fallen below 100 MW, down from an average of 839 MW when high prices began. The AER attributed the evening’s prices to more than heat alone: high demand, low wind, network constraints and rebidding all played a part. Yet much of that rebidding was itself a duration story — Neoen shifted 130–200 MW at Blyth toward the high-priced evening hours as its forecast state of charge fell, and Vena Energy withdrew 40 MW at Tailem Bend. The heat continued overnight. When prices spiked again the next morning, the AER found very little battery capacity was on offer. The batteries did their job. They simply couldn’t last long enough. A battery that starts discharging at 6:30pm with eight hours of storage could, in principle, keep going until 2:30am— through the morning spike that followed. The AER found that across that quarter, prices above $5,000/MWh added $63/MWh to South Australia’s average wholesale price.[2] Why is battery duration becoming the big question? The grid’s hardest hours are getting longer, while most of the battery fleet was built for short bursts. A battery’s duration is how many hours it can discharge at full power. A 100 MW / 200 MWh battery is a two-hour battery. Two-hour systems make up 5.2 GW of the NEM’s 7.3 GW of operating battery capacity, Modo Energy’s July 2026 long-duration outlook found.[3] Those batteries were designed for a grid with sharp, brief price spikes. That grid is changing. In the same analysis, Modo forecasts that price events above $300/MWh will lengthen from about 1.5 hours today to between five and 10 hours by the 2040s. The reliability outlook points the same way. Modo’s reading of AEMO’s 2026 Electricity Statement of Opportunities is that most shortfall events will run longer than four hours by 2030.[4] The existing fleet and pipeline can already cover shorter events. The industry has moved to four hours. Is that enough? Developers have already stretched duration. Four hours is now the default for new NEM battery investment, according to Modo Energy’s analysis of duration trends.[5] The future pipeline holds 24.4 GW of four-hour-or-longer capacity, but only 2.6 GW at eight hours, Modo’s July outlook shows. Four hours would have covered the high-price window on 26 January. It would not have covered the next morning, when batteries that had discharged overnight had little left to offer. As coal retires, the grid needs storage that can cover a whole evening and still have something left. How do Australia’s storage schemes treat duration? Australia’s storage schemes don’t agree on how long is long enough. National tenders mostly buy four-hour batteries, while NSW and South Australia now write eight hours into their contracts, and WA’s requirement is climbing towards seven. NSW: the country’s biggest long-duration tender In February 2026, ASL awarded LTESAs to six battery projects totalling 1.17 GW / 11.98 GWh, all eight hours or longer.[6] The largest, Neoen’s Great Western Battery, has a nominal duration of 10.6 hours.[7] The round took NSW’s contracted storage to 30 GWh. A further 12 GWh tender has been scheduled to start in Q2 2026, with another 12 GWh in 2027. South Australia: four-hour batteries derated to fit South Australia’s first FERM round shows what an eight-hour rule does to a fleet built around shorter durations. Modo Energy’s analysis found that the six winning batteries hold 1,334 MW of nameplate capacity but commit only 517 MW to the scheme.[8] That’s because four-hour batteries had to derate their power to stretch their energy across eight hours. The state still expects its large-scale battery capacity to grow from 1.1 GW to 2.5 GW.[9] Derating works. But it means buying more inverters, transformers and grid connection than the firm power you actually get. National tenders still default to four hours The federal CIS has been the biggest driver of new batteries, and it mostly buys four hours. Tender 8 projects needed at least two hours of storage

artigo.texto: Anthropic has spent billions developing Claude, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence models. Now it's preparing to spend a staggering amount of money to make sure Claude has somewhere to run. In its recent IPO filing, Anthropic disclosed approximately $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all related to computing and infrastructure. About $447.5 billion of those commitments are expected to come due by the end of 2030. But Anthropic isn't simply buying computing capacity from Amazon and Alphabet anymore. It's also pursuing dedicated data center infrastructure, including arrangements in which third parties develop facilities that Anthropic leases and operates through specialized partners. Anthropic isn't necessarily constructing or owning the buildings itself. And its filing doesn't identify most of the companies that will build and equip those facilities. Still, some interesting publicly traded companies do this type of work and offer investors exposure to data center construction. Sterling Infrastructure: Preparing the ground Before installing a server, someone has to prepare the site. My pick in this realm is Sterling Infrastructure (STRL +14.97%), which provides site development services for large industrial projects, including data centers and semiconductor manufacturing facilities. Sterling performs excavation and grading at construction sites and prepares infrastructure to support large buildings. Its electrical contracting business adds another source of revenue from complex construction projects. Business is booming. In the third quarter, Sterling's E-Infrastructure Solutions segment generated $1.30 billion in revenue, an increase of 212% from a year earlier. That segment accounted for 83% of the company's total quarterly revenue. Sterling also reported $4.14 billion in signed backlog and another $2 billion in unsigned awards. Management says its broader pipeline of identified work, including future project phases, approaches $8 billion. STRL Sterling Infrastructure NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Quanta Services: Delivering the electricity Data centers need power, and a lot of it. Quanta Services (PWR +9.35%) provides transmission lines, substations, and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the power grid. AI data centers aren't the only customers demanding more electricity. Utilities are investing in grid modernization, while industrial facilities and other large electricity users need additional capacity. That gives Quanta a much broader opportunity than any single AI company's expansion plans. Revenue in the third quarter was $12.01 billion, up 57% from a year ago. Its Electric segment generated $9.80 billion, accounting for nearly 82% of total revenue. Meanwhile, Quanta's total backlog reached a record $63.7 billion, providing substantial visibility into future work. PWR Quanta Services NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Vertiv: Keeping the chips cool AI chips and servers generate a lot of heat as they work together on AI tasks. And without a way to cool off, they won't work for long. Vertiv Holdings (VRT +9.63%) makes liquid cooling systems that help solve that problem, as well as power equipment and related infrastructure for data centers. The company's Q3 revenue was $4.31 billion, up an impressive 61% from a year ago. Organic orders more than doubled, and adjusted operating margin increased 290 basis points to 25.2%. The company's deferred revenue also reached $4.12 billion at the end of September, compared with $1.81 billion at the end of 2025. That reflects payments received for products and services that haven't yet been recognized as revenue. Converting that demand into completed deliveries remains important. VRT Vertiv NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Three stocks to buy to invest in AI infrastructure Anthropic's filing makes clear that expanding computing capacity involves considerably more than purchasing advanced chips. It requires land, construction, electricity, cooling equipment, and specialized contractors. Sterling, Quanta, and Vertiv each participate in a different part of that process. While none is identified as an Anthropic contractor in the filing, all three serve customers beyond Anthropic. That's why they're worth examining.

artigo.texto: AI data centers raise questions about water use, cooling Artificial intelligence can answer a question in seconds, but behind that speed is a physical network of computers, power lines and, in many cases, water. Data centers running AI generate enormous amounts of heat and keeping that equipment cool can place new demands on local water supplies, especially during hot weather or drought. Shirley Clarke, a Penn State Harrisburg professor, said cooling is a major issue. “The biggest part that people need to know about air and water is this issue around cooling the computer chips that we use, which take a tremendous amount of water depending on what cooling system we use,” Clarke said. How data centers stay cool When an AI program summarizes a document or answers a question, that work happens on computers housed in data centers. Those computers use electricity, and as they work, their chips give off heat. How that heat is removed can make a major difference in how much water a facility needs. One common method uses water that moves through tubes near the chips to carry heat away. In some systems, that water circulates in a closed loop. But the water can become too warm to reuse directly, so some facilities use cooling towers, where water is sent outside and allowed to evaporate. That breaks the closed loop and requires new water to be added. Another option uses fans to move air across equipment, which uses very little water but can require more electricity on very hot days. Experts say the amount of water used can vary widely depending on the model, the length of the response, the location, the weather, the cooling system and the electricity supply. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that all U.S. data centers — not just those running AI — directly consumed about 17 billion gallons of water in 2023. Questions for local communities For communities considering a data center, the biggest questions are where the facility would get its water, how much it would need on average and on the hottest days, and what happens when supplies are low. “You know, does it go to the residents to do what? Shower, to clean, to drink, to cook? Or does it go to the data center or is there a balance in there? And that's what many of the parties are going to have to be dealing with and the water systems are gonna have to deal with,” Clarke said. Location also matters. A facility drawing from a small stream or heavily used groundwater source may raise different concerns than one served by a larger supply. Groundwater can also replenish slowly, and even where water is available, a utility may need new pipes, pumps or treatment capacity. There is also debate about using treated wastewater for industrial cooling instead of drinking-water supplies. “The other problem we have with this really is we're just not equipped for it. Oftentimes the data centers are not built next to the treatment plants. So now we'd be looking at running another set of infrastructure to get the wastewater to that,” Clarke said. The question, experts say, is not whether every data center uses the same amount of water. They do not. The question for each community is how a proposed facility will be cooled, where its water and electricity will come from, and what protections will be in place when supplies are under stress.

artigo.texto: Mundo Indonésios protestam contra data centers por falta de água Enfrentando uma seca severa e escassez de água para necessidades básicas como cozinhar e tomar banho, os habitantes da ilha de Batam, na Indonésia, manifestam-se contra a rápida instalação de ‘data centers’ que impulsionam o avanço da inteligência artificial. A região vem sofrendo uma seca prolongada, intensificada pelo fenômeno climático El Niño, segundo o responsável pelo serviço local de abastecimento de água, em depoimento à AFP. Como em outras nações, a população atribui a culpa aos ‘data centers’, que são instalações que mantêm aplicativos e ferramentas de IA em funcionamento e utilizam água para resfriar seus equipamentos. Juniardi Adinda Sembiring Gurukinayan, comerciante local de 54 anos, relatou que inicialmente a chegada dessa indústria parecia positiva para Batam, mas com os cortes recentes no fornecimento de água, os moradores enfrentam dificuldades como ficar sem banho em algumas ocasiões. Ele destaca: “Não podemos preparar arroz sem água, nem cozinhar verduras”. Em um período crítico, dezenas de moradores realizaram protestos diante do Nongsa Digital Park, um complexo de ‘data centers’ e outras instalações que foi designado como zona econômica especial. Os residentes creem que a escassez hídrica está relacionada à construção dessas instalações, afirmou Juniardi. A seca causou uma queda acentuada no nível do reservatório próximo a Nongsa, enquanto uma pane elétrica agravou as interrupções no abastecimento, explicou Ginda Alamsyah, porta-voz da empresa operadora de água Air Batam Hilir. Esse parque tecnológico é abastecido por outro reservatório, o de Duriangkang, conforme fonte do setor industrial. Em setembro, as autoridades orientaram os empreendedores a instalarem sistemas para dessalinização da água do mar para uso na refrigeração, evitando assim a pressão sobre os recursos locais. Empresas como BW Digital, com sede em Singapura, DayOne e Princeton Digital Group operam ou planejam operar no Nongsa Digital Park. Gaw Capital Partners, com sede em Hong Kong, declarou estar ciente das preocupações dos moradores e que seus centros de dados adotam tecnologias eficientes e energias renováveis para minimizar impactos, incluindo sistemas de circuito fechado que reutilizam água. Na cidade costeira vizinha de Mata Ikan, moradores têm utilizado água do mar para higiene pessoal após evacuações, relata o manifestante Rahmat, de 52 anos. Sulastri, de 38 anos, conta que a crise hídrica, que já dura um ano e piorou nos últimos seis meses, faz com que precise usar água engarrafada para lavar utensílios domésticos. O governo disponibilizou água por meio de caminhões-pipa, porém a qualidade foi criticada por moradores, pois estava malcheirosa e com coloração amarelada. Autoridades locais não responderam aos questionamentos da AFP sobre a situação. O prefeito de Batam, Amsakar Achmad, afirmou que as interrupções no abastecimento não são consequência dos data centers, mas sim de fatores climáticos. A rápida expansão tecnológica e seus desafios Relatório da KPMG indica que a capacidade dos ‘data centers’ no sudeste asiático deve triplicar entre 2025 e 2030, o que poderá aumentar a pressão sobre recursos hídricos e energéticos, já fortemente dependentes de combustíveis fósseis. A Indonésia e a Malásia viram crescimento acelerado destes centros, especialmente após Singapura suspender novos projetos temporariamente. Ginda ressalta que a empresa de água apoia o desenvolvimento desde que haja gestão eficiente, incluindo melhorias nos reservatórios de Batam e técnicas como semeadura de nuvens para combater a seca. Impactos e mobilizações na Malásia Na região de Johor, considerada um grande polo emergente para infraestrutura de IA, a capacidade dos ‘data centers’ aumentou consideravelmente, causando preocupações ambientais. Projeções do governo indicam que até 2035 esses centros poderão consumir um terço da energia total da Malásia. Moradores protestam contra poluição por poeira e alagamentos provocados pela proximidade das instalações a áreas residenciais, enfatizando que a situação está em um momento crítico, segundo Mohd Fadhil Md Din, da Universidade Tecnológica da Malásia. Em Kota Damansara, um projeto de ‘data center’ foi suspenso após forte oposição da comunidade, com mais de 9.000 assinaturas em petição e pressões políticas. Jahaidi Harun, aposentado de 72 anos, destacou que além do barulho, o consumo elevado de água é sentido por todos quando não chove por um período prolongado.

artigo.texto: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has defended the anti-data center movement. He argues that slower compute growth would buy time to harden the world against AI-driven cyber and bio risks. The timing matters for markets. AI chip stocks and Bitcoin miners that now rent power to AI labs depend on a fast data center buildout. Why Buterin Isn't Worried About the Anti-Data Center Movement Buterin said in an X post on Nov. 8 that he disagrees with the strong emotional reaction to anti-data center groups. His case rests on algorithmic progress. By his estimate, whatever bigger data centers could do in two years, today's will manage in four, or sooner. Even extreme success for the anti-data center movement would therefore cause nothing close to a disaster, the Ethereum co-founder argued. Cybersecurity problems are already visible, he noted, and bio risks may follow soon. The world needs every bit of time to prepare. He added that science faces many bottlenecks besides AI. As a result, delaying AI by one year would slow research by far less. Buterin stressed that his view needs no doomer claims about recursive self-improvement (RSI), where AI systems upgrade themselves. The post fits his recent warnings. At Devcon 8, he said AI could crack crypto by finding shortcuts through its cryptography. Who Pays if the AI Buildout Slows? The anti-data center movement has spread from protests to policy. Sen. Bernie Sanders has called for a national data center moratorium after Democrats won Congress. In Europe, several hundred activists occupied a Microsoft construction site in Amsterdam on Nov. 6, Al Jazeera reported. Police detained 150 to 200 people. However, not everyone agrees with Buterin. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink has warned that halting data center construction would push the US into recession. Bitcoin miners carry their own exposure. Riot Platforms sold most of its Bitcoin to fund Texas AI data centers. The state's governor-elect has pledged a permit freeze. Still, Buterin said that even if the anti-data center movement's success proved net-bad, it would be no worse than many other political fights. For AI-linked assets, the debate is shifting from whether the buildout continues to how fast. artigo.texto: All eyes were on Texas during the midterms, and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, especially the neoclouds, took a beating when a Democrat governor won the state. The main fear is that increased AI regulations will make it harder to build data centers in the future, and existing projects may get delayed. It's a legitimate concern, and Texas isn't the only state that was affected. Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona also saw Democratic victories, and they have been instrumental states for the AI boom. Bears will argue that Democratic victories can turn into a major bottleneck for AI as construction projects are delayed or canceled. Here's what investors should consider. Governors still answer to the House and Senate While governor victories capture headlines, each governor must still answer to their state's House and Senate. Those two political arms introduce more variety that can result in gridlock instead of sweeping AI regulations. Here's how it varies for the four states that have played a vital role in artificial intelligence: - Texas: Republicans lost the House but have the Senate. - Ohio: Republicans maintained the House and the Senate. - Georgia: Republicans lost the House but have the Senate. - Arizona: Democrats won the House and the Senate. Ohio has the best political profile for tech companies. A gridlock essentially lets existing data center projects continue. Texas and Georgia can still create a gridlock due to Republicans controlling the Senate, but their political leverage isn't as good as Ohio's. Data centers in Arizona won't face the same political gridlock since Democrats have secured the House and the Senate. Arizona Democrats are in the best position to act swiftly. Job cuts are a real risk Although activism and protests toward data centers have gotten louder in recent months, delaying and canceling these projects comes with downsides that extend beyond lost innovation. While an anti-big tech stance may cause people to look the other way when hyperscalers face roadblocks, those same data center delays and cancellations have a real impact on jobs. Politicians on both sides of the aisle love to tout job growth. For instance, former President Biden was enthusiastic about a $3.3 billion data center in Wisconsin since it could create 2,000 permanent jobs once built. If many data centers are delayed or canceled, it can lead to thousands of people losing their jobs. While regulation may become stricter, kneecapping the industry also translates into lost jobs. Democrats may not care as much about GDP during this cycle since Trump is still the president, but slowing down AI infrastructure can result in negative GDP growth, since it's the main catalyst powering the economy. A negative GDP growth reading won't be a good look. The Democrats can introduce measures that make their voters happy without uprooting the entire AI trade. Local engagement will become more valuable Good PR will be incredibly valuable for neoclouds as the Democrats gain more control of the government in January. Investors can expect to see companies take more steps to financially support local communities beyond new jobs. These initiatives can help them win over residents and provide tangible benefits to the entire community. Part of that may mean reduced tax breaks, a point of contention that was gaining steam before the midterm results. Some tech companies are also acquiring old infrastructure and converting it into AI data centers. For instance, Terawulf is turning a retired coal plant into an AI data center. Those types of changes are less disruptive and let AI data center developers focus on job creation. If more neoclouds and colocation developers take this approach, it will be harder for Democrats to issue sweeping changes that stall out the industry. Investors should pay attention to how data center developers are enhancing local communities, because winning over locals will reduce uncertainty with their gigawatt pipelines.

artigo.texto: The dust from the midterms had hardly settled Wednesday when OpenAI leaders began reckoning with an urgent question: would the outcome make it harder to secure the vast amounts of computing power the company needs to keep growing? During a Q&A with employees, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman fielded questions about data centers and public sentiment on AI, according to people familiar with the matter. A day earlier, a wave of data-center opposition had helped candidates promising to freeze development win statehouses in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Michigan—all major states for data-center sites. Altman acknowledged that the public is concerned about water use and said that whatever the reason, he understood why people might not want to live near data centers, the people said. At one point, he mused that the company should perhaps look to build data centers in the desert. Meanwhile, senior leaders were busy discussing whether the company would need to reset expectations for its data-center capacity next year, The Wall Street Journal previously reported. And employees involved in OpenAI’s data-center development were exchanging intelligence on newly elected Democratic politicians in key states and discussing how best to engage with them, according to messages viewed by the Journal. Across Silicon Valley, similar scenes played out as tech companies that have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to the artificial-intelligence race, and carefully cultivated relationships with AI-friendly officials at all levels of government, rushed to plan for a changed reality. Overnight, they found themselves facing the prospect of blanket moratoriums, tighter environmental regulations and longer review timelines, along with potential new AI-safety regulations that could further bog them down. The tech investor Brad Gerstner said on the “All-In” podcast that as much as 35% of the U.S. data-center construction planned for next year is now at risk. Executives in charge of government relations for so-called hyperscaler companies moved quickly to open lines of communication with incoming governors and their transition teams, seeking an understanding of how their campaign-trail rhetoric would translate into policy actions. Dina Powell McCormick, who as president of Meta Platforms oversees its AI-infrastructure operations, said at the WSJ Tech conference Wednesday night that the company had already found one incoming governor prepared to parley. “We did have a governor that won last night who did make data centers a big part of their platform say, ‘As soon as we get past the inauguration, let’s meet, because we don’t want to lose this investment in our town. We don’t want these jobs to go elsewhere,’ ” she said. But on the whole, Powell McCormick said, Meta assumes that building data centers in the U.S. is “going to be harder” and getting new ones done from scratch will be “very challenging.” She said Meta and other tech companies are increasingly considering building new data centers outside the U.S. as one way around the new hurdles. Another avenue, she said, is to scale up existing data centers, where surrounding communities that have seen benefits in the form of job creation and tax revenue don’t require as much persuasion. To have any hope of winning over the public, Powell McCormick said, the AI industry will have to get much better at talking about its product and the potential societal benefits. “I think we have to double and triple down on telling the story,” she said. OpenAI President Greg Brockman , also speaking at the conference, echoed that point, saying, “We need to do a better job of really communicating to local communities about why data centers are something that can be beneficial to them.” On Thursday, OpenAI became the latest AI giant to unveil a broad commitment governing how it approaches building new data centers. The company said it would not require public officials to sign nondisclosure agreements to engage in data-center negotiations and that it would solicit community input and provide clear public information about the energy, water and noise impacts of its infrastructure investments. Anthropic, in an S-1 filing last week for a planned initial public offering, previewed for investors the risk that local and state governments might adopt data-center moratoriums. “Such moratoriums, or similar actions, could delay or prevent the construction or expansion of facilities on which we depend for compute,” the filing said. Anthropic said it was pursuing projects in several “non-U.S. jurisdictions” as part of a plan to “reduce concentration risks associated with operating a significant portion of our compute infrastructure in the United States.” The S-1 detailed approximately $895.4 billion of AI computing and infrastructure commitments through 2045. The company has separately announced plans to build data centers in Texas and New York, with sites coming online this year. artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Sells Remaining Bitcoin Reserves to Reduce Debt and Fund Michigan AI Data Center LAS VEGAS , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that as of November 8th, 2026, it had sold all of its remaining Bitcoin reserves at approximately $76,000 per Bitcoin. The Company sold approximately 211.56 Bitcoin and received gross proceeds of approximately $16.0 million. Since the Company initially sold a portion of its Bitcoin reserve in late July of 2026, the Company has sold approximately 1,113 Bitcoin for approximate proceeds of $74.4 million. Hyperscale Data is using the proceeds to pay down debt and fund the continued development of its Michigan AI data center. "Our highest priority is to energize the first 10 megawatts of critical IT capacity at our Michigan data center in December," said Will Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data. "We believe bringing that capacity online is our quickest path to profitability. Selling our Bitcoin reserves reduces our exposure to Bitcoin price swings and gives us cash to pay down debt and fund the work in Michigan. We believe that's the best use of this capital for all our stockholders." Hyperscale Data continues to mine Bitcoin at its Montana mining site. Going forward, the Company expects any Bitcoin it holds on its balance sheet to come primarily from its own mining operations. The Company expects to file its Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, on or before Monday, November 23. In light of the recently announced proposed exchange offer for its Class A common stock (the "Exchange Offer"), the Company also expects to move its virtual Investor Day from November 12 to November 23. Management expects to update investors on debt reduction and progress toward the December energization target. When the Company commences the Exchange Offer, it will file the offer documents with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Stockholders should read those documents when available. They will be accessible free of charge at www.sec.gov. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. artigo.texto: Anthropic's S-1 Says It Will Expand Its Data Center Footprint. Here's Who Could Pour the Concrete, Wire the Power, and Cool the Chips. Anthropic has spent billions developing Claude, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence models. Now it's preparing to spend a staggering amount of money to make sure Claude has somewhere to run. In its recent IPO filing, Anthropic disclosed approximately $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all related to computing and infrastructure. About $447.5 billion of those commitments are expected to come due by the end of 2030. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » But Anthropic isn't simply buying computing capacity from Amazon and Alphabet anymore. It's also pursuing dedicated data center infrastructure, including arrangements in which third parties develop facilities that Anthropic leases and operates through specialized partners. Anthropic isn't necessarily constructing or owning the buildings itself. And its filing doesn't identify most of the companies that will build and equip those facilities. Still, some interesting publicly traded companies do this type of work and offer investors exposure to data center construction. Sterling Infrastructure: Preparing the ground Before installing a server, someone has to prepare the site. My pick in this realm is Sterling Infrastructure (NASDAQ: STRL), which provides site development services for large industrial projects, including data centers and semiconductor manufacturing facilities. Sterling performs excavation and grading at construction sites and prepares infrastructure to support large buildings. Its electrical contracting business adds another source of revenue from complex construction projects. Business is booming. In the third quarter, Sterling's E-Infrastructure Solutions segment generated $1.30 billion in revenue, an increase of 212% from a year earlier. That segment accounted for 83% of the company's total quarterly revenue. Sterling also reported $4.14 billion in signed backlog and another $2 billion in unsigned awards. Management says its broader pipeline of identified work, including future project phases, approaches $8 billion. Quanta Services: Delivering the electricity Data centers need power, and a lot of it. Quanta Services (NYSE: PWR) provides transmission lines, substations, and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the power grid. AI data centers aren't the only customers demanding more electricity. Utilities are investing in grid modernization, while industrial facilities and other large electricity users need additional capacity. That gives Quanta a much broader opportunity than any single AI company's expansion plans.

artigo.texto: Byhmgard signs loan agreement with Signet Bank for the financing of the SW Power battery storage plant in Rīga, 15 MW / 30 MWh Byhmgard AB (publ) ("Byhmgard" or the "Company") announces that its wholly owned project company SW Power SIA (the "Project Company") has signed a loan agreement with Signet Bank AS for a project loan of just over EUR 3.0 million, corresponding to 50 percent of the financing of the Company's battery storage plant at Ata iela in Rīga, Latvia (the "Plant"). The total financing requirement for the Plant amounts to approximately EUR 6.1 million (approximately SEK 67 million). The remaining 50 percent is intended to be financed largely through the Company's wholly owned subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB, which in turn owns all shares in the Project Company, acquiring battery systems on a payment plan and contributing them to the Project Company as a contribution in kind. This credit is guaranteed with support from the financing agreement with Middelborg AS and Gimle Invest AS announced by the Company on 11 March 2026. The loan from Signet Bank is sized to be serviced by the group's revenue from energy arbitrage, which the Company estimates at approximately EUR 20 million over 20 years, with a further potential of approximately EUR 33 million from balancing and capacity services to the state-owned transmission system operator Augstsprieguma tīkls (AST). As previously announced, commercial operation is planned for the second quarter of 2027. Financing The financing requirement of approximately EUR 6.1 million is financed half by a project loan from Signet Bank AS, Rīga, secured on the Plant and the Project Company. The loan is disbursed against costs incurred during construction and is repaid monthly from autumn 2027. The other half is intended to be financed through the Company's subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB, which in turn owns all shares in the Project Company, acquiring battery systems on credit and contributing them to the Project Company as a contribution in kind. The battery systems make up most of the portion of financing provided by Byhmgard Invest AB, and the balance, approximately 30 percent, is contributed in cash by Byhmgard Invest AB. The credit for Byhmgard Invest AB's acquisition of the battery systems is supported by guarantees from Middelborg AS and Gimle Invest AS in accordance with the financing agreement announced on 11 March 2026, under which these parties undertake to cover the part of the project cost not financed by bank debt. The financing of the Company's second plant in Rīga, SW Battery SIA, is being finalised and is intended to follow the same structure. Revenue calculation The loan from Signet Bank is sized on estimated revenue from energy arbitrage, that is trading on the Nord Pool day-ahead and intraday markets. According to the Company's revenue analysis, the Plant is estimated to generate revenue of approximately EUR 20 million over the period 2027 to 2047, which meets the bank's coverage requirement for interest and repayments. The Company's revenue analysis is based on historical price spreads on the Nord Pool day-ahead market for Latvia, one full charging cycle per day, assumptions on efficiency, degradation and availability, and an assumed price development over the period. Once the Plant has been approved for balancing and capacity services with the state-owned transmission system operator in Latvia (AST), further revenue of approximately EUR 33 million is estimated based on external market assessments that Byhmgard has requested from local third-party market participants. These calculations indicate total revenue of approximately EUR 53 million for the period 2027 to 2047 in the electricity, balancing and capacity markets. Any revenue from balancing and capacity services is, however, not necessary for the payment of interest and repayments on the loan. Estimated revenue varies with price spreads in the electricity market and in the balancing and capacity markets, and the actual outcome is expected to fall within the range of EUR 20 million to EUR 53 million. All amounts are estimated revenue before operating costs. The plant and timeline The Project Company is wholly owned by Byhmgard through its subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB. The Plant has a grid connection of 14.99 MW and consists of six liquid-cooled lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery containers with two hours of storage, approximately 30 MWh. Land rights and the environmental decision have been obtained, and the grid connection agreement has been entered into. As previously announced, the Project Company has signed an EPC agreement with Latvijas Energoceltnieks (LEC) and an operation and maintenance agreement with Alstra Energy AB. LEC will only commence its work under the EPC agreement after Byhmgard issues a notice to proceed. Notice to proceed to LEC is issued when the building permit is registered with the relevant authority in Rīga. The building permit is expected to be obtained in mid-November 2026. Costs for LEC's work, approximately EUR 0.6 million, begin to accrue when the notice to proceed is issued and are included in the total investment of approximately EUR 6.1 million. Costs for Alstra Energy AB's work, approximately EUR 70 thousand per year, begin to accrue once operation has commenced and are included in the Plant's operating costs. Delivery of the battery systems to Rīga is expected in spring 2027 and commercial operation in the second quarter of 2027. An application for approval for ancillary services is planned to be submitted thereafter. CEO comment "The loan agreement is a decisive step in the financing of our first own plant, and we are closer to our goal of moving from delivering battery systems to owning and operating them. The loan is sized on estimated revenue from energy arbitrage, which gives a robust base, while potential ancillary services to AST may provide a substantial upside. artigo.texto: State clean energy programs and the communities they’re meant to serve want the same thing. Both want more resilient, more affordable, cleaner power. And yet, across solar and storage programs throughout the U.S. Northeast, projects stall, applications bounce back and forth, and entire counties opt out of battery storage altogether. This is not because anyone disagrees on the goal, but because the two sides are speaking different languages about cost, risk, and timeline. COMMENTARY The disconnect is a translation and timing problem, and underneath it, a fluency problem: clean energy is still young enough as an industry that we haven’t built a shared, baseline understanding of how it works, which is exactly the vacuum fear and misinformation grow fastest in. The technical, financial, and safety information communities need almost always exists somewhere; it just doesn’t arrive in a form, on a timeline, or in a language that matches the person who has to act on it. The Technical Handoff Gap Consider a state clean energy incentive program that requires applications to meet a minimum technical requirement, such as a shading threshold verified through third-party modeling software. Programs like this are purposely built to require licensed contractors, rather than homeowners, to submit on a project’s behalf. In practice, though, the person doing the actual submitting inside that contractor’s office is often administrative staff, handling documentation and portal logistics rather than the shading analysis itself. The friction shows up when an application gets flagged for revision. If a shading model overestimated sun exposure, if a battery specification sheet vaguely says it’s UL listed, or if a site location on a drawing is off, the fix requires looping back to whoever built the original technical analysis, understanding what needs to change, and resubmitting. For an administrative submitter without training to read these types of documents, it could be a multi-week round trip, and every round trip pushes a project’s timeline further from the one the applicant was promised. The review requirement is holding a consistent technical bar as intended, but it is colliding with an industry that hasn’t yet agreed on what baseline fluency should look like. As the technology moves from niche to standard, programs need to better explain their requirements, and applicants and communities need to get better at asking questions. The Bandwidth and Fit Gap Some states have built entire portfolios of clean energy incentive programs, including production-based solar incentives, demand-reduction standards that reward market participation, dedicated resilience programs, and more. We’ve worked directly on application reviews and feasibility studies for programs like these, as well as supported the people weighing whether to pursue them, including town officials, church administrators, and facility managers. Across nearly every one of those conversations, we found real interest and need, but simply not enough bandwidth to figure out which program actually solves their problem. These aren’t organizations with dedicated energy staff. Most of the people making these decisions have the same relationship to electricity most people do: they know what it costs, not how it works. They know their power went out last summer, or that heating bills wiped out half their annual budget, but they don’t have a working sense of peak demand, energy arbitrage, or how a given program lines up with either problem. For example, many states have built resilience-specific tracks alongside their standard incentive programs. Local leaders recognize that a community hub (Figure 1) worried about outages needs a different program than a homeowner just trying to lower a bill. But the program simply existing isn’t the same as someone knowing it’s the right fit. The real work is helping someone who’s never had to think about kilowatts vs. kilowatt-hours figure out which program they need. The Trust and Visibility Gap A string of BESS fires, layered on top of a wave of unrelated lithium-ion fires involving e-bikes and scooters, has created a perception problem for the industry. The largely negative image of battery storage that many community members hold is hard for any single conversation to undo, especially in dense urban areas or in smaller communities served by volunteer fire departments. Faced with that uncertainty, it was faster and safer for many municipalities to pass a moratorium than to build out permitting and zoning frameworks on their own, and the result was close to a domino effect, with moratoria spreading across counties and towns statewide. The irony is that most states had already responded substantively, not just rhetorically. They published model laws, a customizable zoning and permitting template local governments could adopt directly. These outlines stood up to a peer review program that puts technical experts in front of every project above a size threshold, reviewing design drawings, vetting proposed equipment, confirming fire suppression systems are in place, and checking third-party test reports, emergency response plans, and hazard mitigation analyses. Projects receiving state incentive awards go through this layer of scrutiny as a condition of funding. Very few communities living near these proposed projects seem to know that layer exists, which means a state-level solution and a community-level fear are running in parallel, as if unaware of each other. Information and trust broke down because nobody built a shared understanding before it was urgently needed. Developers typically don’t live in the communities where they’re proposing projects, which raises a fair question on both sides: How does that engagement avoid feeling staged, and how is a community supposed to know what to ask for or how to respond? What is Required There’s a version of developer-community engagement that gets this sequencing right from the start

artigo.texto: Washington County to consider yearlong pause on data centers The Washington County Quorum Court held a County Services Committee meeting on Monday. One of the issues discussed at Monday's meeting was a proposed yearlong moratorium on data centers in Washington County. The committee debated the item and discussed amendments that would be made to the original draft. The item was passed by the committee and will move to quorum court for a formal discussion and potential vote. The next Washington County Quorum Court meeting is scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 19. Evelyn Rios Stafford, the Justice of the Peace for District 12, is one of the supporters of the moratorium. She said that the proposed moratorium would allow time for the quorum court to look over planning and zoning rules. "We've heard a lot of concerns over the last year from residents of our county. They see data centers opening up in other places. And they are concerned about the amount of electricity they use, the amount of water. Is it going to raise people's utility bills? Are they going to create noise if they come into our county? And so I think we need to take the time and take a pause in order to see what we need to do to protect our residents," Rios Stafford said. According to Rios Stafford, there are currently no plans for data centers in Washington County.

artigo.texto: North Dakota Town Bucks Backlash, Welcomes Data Center In a year when voters across the country largely tried to slam the brakes on new data centers, one tiny North Dakota town hit the gas, the Washington Post reports. Residents of Harwood, population 845, rejected a ballot measure that would have forced independent reviews and public hearings for big industrial projects, effectively clearing the way for a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot data center on the edge of town. The measure failed by roughly 3-to-1, Fortune reports, even as national exit polls showed 76% of voters opposed to new data centers in their communities and most skeptical of AI's impact. Harwood's mayor argued the project was inevitable—if not in Harwood, it would likely still have ended up nearby—that the town should be the one to capture its projected $1.65 million in annual property taxes and 200 or so new jobs. Opponents warned of environmental risks, noise, and future cleanup costs—but were decisively outvoted.
