artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., Marisa Wanzeller e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA As negociações dentro do governo em torno do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) avançaram, segundo relataram interlocutores à Agência iNFRA. No entanto, há alguns aspectos relacionados ao setor elétrico que ainda precisam ser pacificados, dentre eles, a possível exigência de aquisição de energia nova para abastecimento dos data centers. A expectativa é que o decreto seja publicado ainda em novembro, após a participação do presidente Lula na COP31, na Turquia. O setor aguarda o governo definir se será necessário que os empreendimentos comprem energia de usinas novas, construídas para o seu abastecimento, ou recém-construídas, conforme o conceito de “adicionalidade energética”. O tema divide agentes no setor. Outra negociação ainda na mesa é quanto à cobrança de encargos dos data centers. Segundo interlocutores, os investidores querem ser isentos do pagamento da CDE (Conta de Desenvolvimento Energético) por meio da celebração de contratos de autoprodução por equiparação. Também é esperada a lista de fontes de geração que serão aceitas, com expectativas do segmento de gás natural para que a molécula seja incluída. Adicionalidade A exigência de novas usinas para atender os data centers não é um consenso. De um lado, há empresas que veem na adicionalidade uma possibilidade de expansão dos negócios. Do outro, há geradores com usinas que ficarão descontratadas que miram esse mercado e avaliam que erguer novas plantas de geração tiraria a competitividade dos projetos e acarretaria custos para o sistema elétrico. Na última sexta-feira (6), o presidente Lula falou sobre o tema e defendeu que os empreendimentos de data centers construam suas usinas. O presidente disse que os centros consomem muita energia e que “quem vier investir [que] construa a sua própria energia”. Ele continuou: “Não vai ser a energia do povo que vai ser usada para data center”. A preocupação está em linha com o que se observa em países onde o desenvolvimento de data centers já está mais avançado, como os Estados Unidos. Lá, a população viu a conta de energia aumentar em algumas regiões. Autoprodução Também circula nos bastidores que o Ministério da Fazenda levou à mesa de discussão uma proposta para que os empreendimentos sejam enquadrados como autoprodutores de energia. Dessa forma, os data centers ficariam isentos do pagamento da CDE – a conta que reúne os custos dos subsídios do setor elétrico. Com a possibilidade aventada, os técnicos do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) fazem agora o cálculo dos impactos dessa renúncia. Eles analisam se é possível “reduzir os danos”, disseram fontes. Na autoprodução por equiparação, o consumidor da energia se torna acionista da SPE (Sociedade de Propósito Específico) da usina. Dessa forma, é equiparado ao autoprodutor “clássico” – que investiu em geração própria para atender ao empreendimento consumidor. Gás natural Quanto às fontes de suprimento, a resistência de parte do governo federal à inclusão do gás natural está menor, segundo pessoas a par das tratativas. Agora, a tendência é que o decreto contemple o insumo, ainda que com condicionantes, como compensação pelas emissões de carbono. Os secretários-executivos dos ministérios de Minas e Energia, da Fazenda, da Indústria e Comércio e da Casa Civil reuniram-se na última semana, ocasião em que o MME defendeu o gás natural. Interlocutores afirmam que a Fazenda – que vinha travando a entrada do gás – passou a admitir a possibilidade de incluir a fonte. Falta, agora, fechar o modelo das condicionantes. No MME, a intenção é que as compensações de carbono mantenham os projetos de gás viáveis. No setor, no entanto, os agentes estão preocupados com os termos, que podem onerar os investimentos e acabar restringindo, na prática, a implementação de térmicas a gás para abastecer os data centers. Algumas possíveis formas de compensação aventadas nos bastidores são o uso de tecnologia de CCUS (Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono, na sigla em inglês) ou a aquisição de créditos de carbono. Riscos Agentes ligados ao segmento de gás natural vinham demonstrando temor com a possibilidade de o gás ficar totalmente fora da regulamentação do Redata. Agora, admitem que esse risco é menor, mas ainda agem com cautela e dizem que será preciso ver os termos impostos pelo governo nas condicionantes. Uma regulamentação restritiva por causa das condicionantes, segundo um executivo, pode afastar investimentos em térmicas colocalizadas com data centers e pressionar as tarifas de energia. Isso porque os centros de dados poderiam ter de usar energia da rede nos horários com escassez de energia renovável, aumentando a demanda por potência. Caso o decreto vete ou restrinja o gás, o setor cogita buscar alterar os termos da regulamentação via Congresso. Isso poderia ser feito por meio de um PDL (Projeto de Decreto Legislativo). “Ficou claro que o Legislativo, ao aprovar o Redata, não quis restringir nenhum combustível de baixa emissão, como o gás natural”, comentou um agente termelétrico. Por outro lado, os geradores renováveis apontam que as termelétricas a gás natural emitem mais carbono do que os limites estabelecidos internacionalmente, de aproximadamente 0,10 tonelada de gás carbônico por MWh (megawatt-hora). Dessa forma, essas usinas não se enquadrariam na exigência da lei. Atraso O diretor de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais da Brasscom (Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil), Sergio Sgobbi, diz que a demora na regulamentação tem afastado os investidores, que estão buscando outras alternativas. artigo.texto: A new database of local government meeting records puts a hard number on something planners have heard in hearing rooms all year. Prophecy Gov, a San Francisco AI startup, operates a tool called American Sentiment, and it classified 90.5% of 10,202 public comments about data centers as negative, according to TechRadar’s coverage of the report. The comments came from 906 public meetings held by 417 local governments across 48 states during 2026. Headline writers boiled that down to “America hates data centers.” That phrase is headline wording, not an on-record statement from a named person, and the data does not say 90.5% of Americans oppose data centers. It says that when residents speak at the microphone, they mostly speak against. The finding arrives in a year when siting fights have moved from zoning footnotes to front-page politics. Our earlier look at the 41 data center ballot measures that put the AI boom on notice covered the voting side. This story covers the hearing-room side, and for anyone who buys or builds cloud capacity, it matters just as much. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What American Sentiment Actually Measured American Sentiment is a database, not a survey. Prophecy Gov collected public comments made at local government meetings, then classified each one by tone. The comments were not solicited, weighted, or balanced against a population sample. Residents chose to speak, and the tool recorded what they said. That design has real strengths. Public comment is where land-use decisions get shaped, and local boards often cite what they hear from residents when they vote on rezoning, tax abatements, or utility agreements. A dataset of 10,202 comments across 48 states gives researchers something they rarely had before: a searchable record of the arguments people actually make in the room. The classification split is stark. Beyond the 90.5% negative share, 7% of comments expressed support for a potential nearby data center, and 2.5% asked questions. Those three buckets account for the whole dataset. In other words, almost nobody in these meetings arrived undecided and left with a neutral note on the record. TechRadar framed the result with the “America hates data centers” headline, and other outlets echoed the sentiment. The underlying dataset is more careful than the headline. It measures comment tone at 2026 meetings, nothing more. Keep that boundary in mind through the rest of this analysis, because the gap between “comments” and “public opinion” is where most of the debate will happen. The Numbers at a Glance The table below collects every figure reported so far from the American Sentiment database. No price data, technical specifications, or named speaker quotes have surfaced in the coverage, so this is the full quantitative picture as of November 09, 2026. Two details deserve a second look. First, the 73% figure describes meetings, not comments, so it measures how often a hearing featured zero supporters. Second, water is named as the top concern, but the reports available so far do not give a percentage for it. Anyone citing a specific water share is guessing. Why 90.5% Is Not a National Poll The most important caveat is also the simplest. The dataset measures the comments collected, and those comments are not a representative national opinion poll. A poll draws a sample that mirrors the population. A public comment period draws whoever shows up, and showing up takes time, motivation, and often a personal stake. Who shows up at the microphone People who live next to a proposed site have the strongest reason to attend. They worry about noise, traffic, property values, and power lines. People who might benefit from a data center, such as future employees, local suppliers, or residents who like lower property tax rates, have a diffuse stake and little reason to give up an evening. That asymmetry is old, and planners know it well. The self-selection problem cuts both ways Self-selection inflates opposition in the raw numbers, but it does not make the opposition fake. Local boards act on what they hear. If 9 in 10 speakers oppose a project, elected officials feel that pressure whether or not a silent majority would have voted differently. For developers, the comment record matters as a political force even if it fails as a statistical sample. The sensible reading: American Sentiment tells us what local decision-makers are hearing, not what the country thinks. Those are different questions, and only the first one drives permit votes. The 7% Support Gap and the 73% of Empty Support Benches Seven percent of comments backed a nearby data center. That sounds small, and in raw terms it is. Using the reported shares, it works out to roughly 714 supportive comments out of 10,202. The more telling number is the meeting-level one: 73% of tracked meetings had no supporters at all. Run the arithmetic and the picture sharpens. About 661 of the 906 meetings featured no one speaking in favor, which leaves roughly 245 meetings with at least one supportive voice. In those 245 hearings, supporters were still outnumbered overall, since the 90.5% negative share holds across the whole dataset. total_comments = 10202 meetings = 906 negative = total_comments * 0.905 # ~9,233 support = total_comments * 0.07 # ~714 questions = total_comments * 0.025 # ~255 mention_ai = total_comments * 0.21 # ~2,142 no_support_meetings = meetings * 0.73 # ~661 with_support = meetings - no_support_meetings # ~245 comments_per_meeting = total_comments / meetings # ~11.3 These counts are our own rounding of the reported percentages, so treat them as approximations rather than figures published by Prophecy Gov. They still show the scale: a few hundred supportive comments set against more than nine thousand negative ones. The practical lesson for the industry is blunt. artigo.texto: KINGSTON, N.Y. — The city is seeking city residents to apply to serve on its new Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Task Force. Mayor Steve Noble’s office said task force members will review the city Zoning Working Group’s proposal and “offer their perspectives to ensure the city’s form-based code adequately addresses land-use, environmental, and thermal runaway safety challenges associated with commercial battery arrays.” The BESS Task Force will consist of 10 members, including two City Council members, City staff, representatives from the Conservation Advisory Council and Climate Smart Action Committee, and two City residents appointed by Common Council President Andrea Shaut. City residents interested in applying can complete a short application https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/CWZCNB9. The application deadline is Monday, Nov. 16. In October, the city’s Common Council voted unanimously to create the task force with a goal of drafting zoning regulations for utility-scale battery energy storage systems after proposals for such facilities have caused controversy in neighboring communities. Such facilities consist of lithium-iron-phosphate battery cells packaged into modules, about the size of oversized briefcases, which are then put into racks and stored in containers resembling shipping containers. The facilities require proximity to a utility’s substation. The five proposals in Ulster County — three in the town of Ulster, one in Saugerties and one in New Paltz — are all proposed near a Central Hudson substation. So far, no utility-scale battery energy storage systems have been proposed within city limits, and lawmakers have even questioned the feasibility of locating such a facility within city limits. Proposed lithium-ion battery energy storage projects, including the three projects proposed in the neighboring town of Ulster, have met with controversy across the county. Two of those projects, on Hurley Avenue in the town of Ulster, are close to the city line Mission Clean Energy has proposed a 120-megawatt lithium-ion battery facility on a 7.3-acre site at 463-465 Hurley Ave. That project is about 500 feet west of the controversial Terra-Gen site at the former John A. Coleman Catholic High School, where the Town Board is being asked to approve a 250-megawatt lithium-ion facility on 15 acres. In the town of Ulster, board members are also reviewing a proposal from BayWa r.e. for a 150-megawatt lithium-ion battery facility on Frank Sottile Boulevard. It would be on about 10.4 acres adjacent to the former town landfill, with a new substation constructed on the other side of the road. It would be adjacent to a residential neighborhood and the 164-unit Ulster Gardens apartment complex. In the town of Saugerties, Key Capture Energy has proposed a 100-megawatt facility on Tomson’s Road near a Central Hudson substation that has met with opposition from residents and calls from Saugerties village officials for a moratorium on such projects and most recently led to sparring between members of the public and a Saugerties Town Board member at an October Town Board meeting. For questions about the Kingston BESS Task Force, email Shaut at ashaut@kingston-ny.gov.

artigo.texto: CATL and Dongfeng reportedly signed a group-level agreement on ultra-fast charging and battery swapping on October 29, 2026. Separate talks over Shenxing III’s first vehicle launch were reported as unsettled on November 3, so the agreement and the battery’s potential debut are distinct developments. China EV Signal reported the agreement’s scope, while CarNewsChina reported the status of the launch talks. A charging time is useful only when you know the starting and ending charge levels. What the CATL-Dongfeng agreement covers The reported agreement concerns cooperation on ultra-fast charging and battery swapping. The separate negotiations concern first-launch rights for Shenxing III, CATL’s lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. CarNewsChina said those talks had begun in the second quarter of 2026 and were still unsettled in its November 3 report. How CATL explains Shenxing III’s design In a technical presentation, CATL compares Shenxing III cells measuring 300 millimeters with “common” 400-millimeter cells. Its presenter says shortening a cell by 100 millimeters cuts heat generation by 20%. A separate report attributed another figure to CATL: a 20% improvement in thermal efficiency from its cooling system. Thermal efficiency and heat generation are different measures. In the presentation, CATL also puts the cells’ internal resistance at 0.25 milliohms and claims they retain more than 90% of their capacity after 1,000 ultra-fast charging cycles. What CATL’s charging times say CATL claims Shenxing III can charge from 10% to 35% in one minute and from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes 44 seconds. The company also claims a 10C equivalent charging rate, with peaks of 15C. Just Auto reported these figures. The 6-minute-27-second result has two reported endpoints: Just Auto and Híbridos y Eléctricos give 10% to 98%, while InsideEVs reports 10% to 90%. CATL’s separate cold-weather claim is a charge from 20% to 98% in about nine minutes at −30°C, as reported by Just Auto.

artigo.texto: Deutsche Bank and Rabobank are backing an €835 million (about $936 million) financing package to help energy storage company Return expand its battery storage business in Germany. The deal will support new projects as the country works to integrate more wind and solar power into its electricity system. The portfolio facility initially covers three battery energy storage projects with a combined capacity of 117 megawatts (MW). More eligible projects can be added as they reach financial close. The financing combines support for physical battery assets with Return’s Virtual Flexibility Portfolio (VFP). This model connects multiple storage facilities into one virtual system. Energy companies can access flexible electricity capacity through a single platform. The transaction involves several financial and technical advisers. Rabobank acted as financial adviser, while White & Case advised the lenders. Other firms involved included Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, Baker McKenzie, Baringa, DNV, EY, EY-Parthenon, and Marsh. The deal comes as Germany’s battery storage market grows. It also shows how private finance helps build the infrastructure for a power system with more renewable energy. A Financing Framework for Germany’s Battery Expansion The €835 million facility gives Return a way to finance several battery projects under one structure instead of arranging separate financing for every site. This approach could help speed up project development. Eligible facilities can access funding as they progress toward financial close, without having to restart the financing process each time. The initial portfolio includes three projects in Germany with a combined power capacity of 117 MW. Return stated that, with four-hour batteries running two full cycles each day, the facilities could provide enough electricity yearly to power around 100,000 German households. The company plans to add more projects to the financing framework through 2027. Return also has wider growth plans for the German market. It aims to install at least 1 gigawatt (GW) of battery storage capacity each year from 2027. The company estimates that this would require annual investment of €750 million to €1.2 billion, depending on market conditions. The financing is therefore part of a much larger expansion plan. The company has not said that the full €835 million will be used only for the three projects in the initial portfolio. Daniel Witvoet, CFO at Return, remarked: “As demand for energy flexibility grows, we need to scale not just our battery storage capacity, but also the way we finance it. By bringing together physical infrastructure financing and our virtual flexibility model, we can expand more efficiently and respond to our customers’ evolving needs. This is an important step towards our ambition to become a leading independent provider of energy flexibility in Germany.” Why Germany Needs More Battery Storage Germany is adding more wind and solar power to its electricity mix. However, these sources do not produce power at a steady rate. Solar generation changes with daylight and weather, while wind output can rise or fall depending on conditions. Battery storage can help manage these changes. It can store electricity when supply is high and prices are low, then release it when demand rises or renewable generation falls. This can help balance the grid and make better use of clean electricity. Germany’s Federal Network Agency explains that battery systems can respond to electricity market prices, support grid stability, and improve the use of renewable power. The need for this flexibility is becoming clearer as storage projects move through the development pipeline. According to data published by Germany’s Federal Network Agency in August 2026, network operators received 18,158 battery storage connection applications in 2025. These requests represented about 573.5 GW of planned power capacity and 1,583 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy capacity. However, these figures do not represent projects that are certain to be built. Developers sometimes submit applications for the same project at several possible locations. The regulator noted that only one location may ultimately be selected. A more advanced measure is the number of grid connection offers. In 2025, network operators issued 1,937 offers covering 54.2 GW of power capacity and 142.4 GWh of energy capacity. These offers provide a clearer picture of project progress because they are binding proposals for connection agreements. Even so, projects still need to secure financing, complete construction, and meet other requirements before they can operate. Germany’s Storage Pipeline Reflects a Growing Market Germany’s battery storage market has expanded as renewable energy has gained a larger role in power generation. Fraunhofer ISE reported that, in 2025, wind and solar power generated more electricity than any other source in Germany’s public electricity mix. The shift increases the need for storage and other flexible resources that can help match supply with demand. The International Energy Agency has also identified utility-scale battery storage as an important part of Germany’s energy transition. Large batteries can provide services such as frequency response and reserves, helping the grid remain stable as the electricity mix changes. Globally, battery storage is growing quickly as well. The IEA’s Global Energy Review 2026 reported that 108 GW of new battery storage capacity was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024. Global installed capacity was 11 times higher than in 2021. These trends are creating opportunities for developers, utilities, and financial institutions. However, the scale of Germany’s connection requests also shows that grid access and project delivery remain important challenges. artigo.texto: The Korea Overseas Infrastructure & Urban Development Corporation (KIND) will jointly develop an energy storage system (ESS) project in Ireland with Shinhan Asset Management, Hyosung Heavy Industries and Irish developer Lumcloon Energy. KIND said on the 11th that it signed a memorandum of understanding with the three companies at the Embassy of Ireland in Seoul on the 10th to jointly develop the ESS project and to pursue overseas infrastructure projects together. The agreement covers an ESS project being developed in the Coolpowra area of County Galway, Ireland. KIND and Shinhan Asset Management agreed to build a strategic cooperation framework with Hyosung Heavy Industries and Lumcloon Energy for the development of and investment in the project. The partners agreed to pursue grid connection for the large-scale ESS and to cooperate across the entire development process, from project permitting and transmission grid connection to deal structuring and financing. If the project moves ahead, it will stabilize output from renewable sources such as wind power and improve both the flexibility of electricity supply and grid stability, the parties to the agreement said. Ireland is expanding its use of renewable energy in response to rising electricity demand and the need to secure grid stability. The country is positioned to tap wind resources along the Atlantic coast, while the need to expand energy storage infrastructure to cope with the intermittency of renewable power is also growing. "Ireland is a market where the importance of grid stability and energy storage infrastructure is growing, driven by the expansion of renewable energy and rising large-scale power demand from facilities such as data centers," a KIND official said. "Using this memorandum of understanding as a starting point, we will work closely with local partners and Korean EPC companies to advance project development, and contribute to expanding Ireland's stable power infrastructure and to broadening Korean companies' entry into the European market."

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA Sete associações do setor elétrico enviaram carta ao governo federal solicitando apoio à aprovação do PL 3.716/2026, que propõe alterar as regras de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias no âmbito da reserva de capacidade. O documento pede prioridade na tramitação da proposta para garantir segurança jurídica à realização do primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade voltado a baterias. A carta é assinada pela ABEEólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), ABIHV (Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde), Abrage (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica), Abragel (Associação Brasileira de Geração de Energia Limpa), Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Absolar (Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica) e Apine (Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica). O projeto, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim, prevê a revogação do dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004 que determina o rateio dos custos da contratação de baterias exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração. As entidades defendem que o custeio siga critérios semelhantes aos aplicados às demais tecnologias contratadas para a reserva de capacidade, considerando que o serviço beneficia todo o sistema elétrico. Segundo as associações, a concentração dos custos nos geradores não impede seu repasse aos consumidores, uma vez que os encargos podem ser incorporados aos preços da energia. “Esse encargo será incorporado aos preços da energia, conforme as condições contratuais e de mercado, e repercutirá nos custos de produção de bens e serviços, possivelmente de forma opaca ou pouco clara”, afirmam as entidades na carta. As associações também alertam que a manutenção das regras atuais pode elevar os riscos dos empreendimentos, encarecer as contratações e provocar questionamentos administrativos e judiciais, com possíveis impactos sobre o cronograma do certame. A carta foi encaminhada a seis ministros, incluindo os titulares de Minas e Energia, Fazenda e Casa Civil, e solicita articulação do Executivo para a aprovação do projeto.

artigo.texto: Editor’s note: This month, we offer views from the left and right on issues around artificial intelligence. To our columnists: What’s your take on the growing use of AI in our society and how it will likely impact our region? Do local communities have a responsibility to oppose or support the data centers that power AI? by Carl Mumpower and Bill Branyon On the right Carl Mumpower: Let’s answer the last question first. Support for local AI data centers? Not an issue. We’re too expensive. Poor counties will win that lottery. But there could be an upside to being neighborly. When the Terminators start showing up, it’ll give antifa a productive mission. On the rest, with one exclusion, we’re stuck with speculation. The exception? Western North Carolina is blessed to exist on a self-correcting planet. Anything coming from man will thus (1) contain built-in limitations and (2) hide opportunities amid the miseries. In other words, AI is going to bring our region good and bad, dependably countered by the law of unintended consequences. Some of the AI good will include: complex, lightning-speed answers to questions; extraordinary efficiency potential for business, industry and government; unprecedented information access and research simplification; vastly expanded automated manufacturing capacity; hyperefficient bookkeeping, record and data keeping; reduced costs and better patient care through dramatically expanded medical best-practice protocols; crime reduction through universally shared antisocial-behavior tracking and accountability enforcement; and personalization abilities that will find AI behaving more pleasantly than most humans. The bad? Autonomy, liberty and anonymity will be at increased risk; our capacity to militarily kill one another will be gravely expanded; a good number of people — through job obsolescence — will have to become mechanics, plumbers, nurses or something else useful that AI can’t do; without care, education will become less about learning and more about figuring out how to disguise the use of AI to shortcut assignments; surveillance will expand far beyond our imagination in all urban settings; and socialism and the Chinese Communist governance model will be unleashed, while democracy will have to struggle mightily toward self-preservation. Things to remember as we construct our anticipatory anxiety script? AOL’s anticipated internet dominance; premature assertions about the demise of paper; Y2K disaster presumptions; catastrophic climate change forecasts; COVID-19 protocol assurances; hysterical MAGA outcome predictions; the end of decayed dinosaur carcasses as a source of petroleum; and the notion that LED light bulbs would last 20 years. Further considerations? Watch out — it turns out that AI is lazy. It digs down as few layers as necessary to produce a “satisfactory” answer to most questions and service requests. Birthed out of the hands of man, we should’ve seen this one coming. Back in the ’80s, John Naisbitt’s book Megatrends: Ten New Directions Transforming Our Lives was all the rage. Among his suggestions was that the future would find us living in a high-tech, high-touch world. He got the first part right. AI — crafted toward an appealing personality — may finally add a softer texture to our heretofore increasingly low-touch crabbiness. There’s one more little teeny-weeny problem. AI is also sociopathic. Various dictionaries define the term as lacking a sense of morality, conscience and/or social accountability. Considering the international cast of characters crafting AI’s springboard, should we be concerned with HAL’s sociopathic potentials? You bet. It is my pleasure to gift you with this human intelligence-generated chew toy. “With artificial intelligence we are summoning the demon.” — Elon Musk On the left Bill Branyon: “I’m sorry, Dave. I’m afraid I can’t do that,” said HAL the computer as it refused to save Dave the astronaut in 2001: A Space Odyssey. Then came Star Trek’s relentless Borg, Matrix movies, I Robot’s endless hordes and scores of other such movies to get us in the habit of fearing AI. Then Bill Gates piggybacked on this cinematic dread by insisting, “We have to acknowledge that AI is almost uniquely dangerous because it’s unbounded in how good it will get.” Elon “USAID murderer” Musk added that AI is a “fundamental risk to the existence of human civilization.” Then Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger made the misanthropic statement that there’s a greater than 10% chance that “AI could kill all humans … within the next decade.” What bonkers bravado it takes for those tech bros to claim they can dominate in a few years what evolution took 3.8 billion years to create: humanity. On the other hand, what could be a better sales pitch than blaring that AI is so powerful it’ll destroy everyone? The snake-oil bros are either consciously or unconsciously hustling us. AI is probably about 10% amazing substance and 90% hubristic hype. Perhaps that’s why there’s such a rush to attach some concrete substance to it in the form of building thousands of gigantic data centers? A Michigan Advance article republished in The Washington Post says yes to that question, contending that the scurry to build data centers will make tech bro CEOs even more billions. Yet, as Martin Kushler notes in the article, when you Google data-center products, “you frankly get a bunch of nebulous buzzwords like ‘cloud computing’ … ‘high-performance computing’ and ‘edge services.’” So “for the small investors at the bottom, one has to wonder whether this is a 21st-century ‘tulip mania’” — a reference to the 1634-37 Dutch frenzy for new colors of tulips that inspired the first speculative bubble in history. Now, even AI-obsessed Jeff Bezos contends AI “is a kind of industrial bubble.” How many millions of people will it financially destroy when it pops? artigo.texto: Greeneville Municipal Planners Tuesday morning will be asked to consider recommending a six month Data Center moratorium to the full City Council. The matter is on the agenda for the 9:30 am meeting of the Planning Commission in the G. Thomas Love Boardroom in the GEA building. PROPOSAL If approved by the Planning Commission, the recommendation would be forwarded to the Greeneville City Council for consideration of an ordinance placing a temporary six (6) month moratorium on the establishment, construction, expansion, relocation, or operation of data centers within the Town of Greeneville. BACKGROUND The Zoning Ordinance does not currently define data centers or provide standards for their review. Radio Greeneville News first told you that on October 13, 2026, the Planning Commission approved a process todevelop data center regulations and requested the Town Attorney’s review of a moratorium. The Town Attorney has now prepared the draft ordinance (Seen below). During the moratorium, no permits or approvals would be issued for data centers. Existing operations, accessory computer equipment, and telecommunications and broadband facilities are not affected. STAFF RECOMMENDATION The planning staff recommends that the Planning Commission recommend approval of the data center moratorium ordinance to the City Council for adoption, allowing the Commission time to develop permanent data center regulations through its workshop sessions. artigo.texto: Neighbors protest data center developments in Fayette County PIPERTON, Tenn. (WMC) - Residents in Fayette County packed a city meeting Tuesday night to push back against potential data center developments in their quiet, rural community. Neighbors in and around Piperton, Tennessee, gathered at city hall, turning a local planning commission meeting into an open town hall. While no data center proposals were officially on the agenda, Piperton’s city manager says several rules will be in place before any project is considered. Even still, some residents want to make sure data centers never come their way. “I hope that you look at me as your neighbor in Fayette County and say, ‘I won’t do it to you,’ and I hope you know that I wouldn’t do it to you, and I hope the commission and our leadership can look at each of us and know that they won’t do it to us either,” said Laura Kate Jordan. “So, not just talking about the coding of what’s coming, but first and foremost, we’re not allowing this. Not at all. This is not coming here, and we’re not doing it.” Much of the pushback centers around land near I-269 and Macon Road, where residents say they recently spotted survey crews. artigo.texto: BYD planeja investir R$ 1 bi em nova fábrica no Brasil Nova unidade da montadora chinesa produzirá vans elétricas e caminhões; empreendimento deve criar 2.000 empregos A montadora chinesa BYD planeja investir R$ 1 bilhão na instalação de uma nova fábrica de vans elétricas e caminhões no Brasil. O empreendimento deve criar 2.000 empregos, de 2028 a 2029. As informações foram divulgadas pela CNN Brasil nesta 2ª feira (9.nov.2026). Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro disputam a instalação da unidade. A fabricante ainda não definiu a localização e considera os incentivos oferecidos pelos governos estaduais para decidir onde realizará o investimento. Os modelos que serão fabricados no novo complexo também não foram anunciados. A BYD, no entanto, apresentará os caminhões elétricos eT35 e eT75 na Fenatran, feira do setor de transportes que começa nesta 2ª feira (9.nov), em São Paulo. A montadora levará ainda uma versão do eT23 adaptada para o transporte de bebidas. BYD NO BRASIL O projeto faz parte da expansão industrial da BYD no país, iniciada com a abertura do complexo automotivo de Camaçari, na Bahia. Com a nova unidade, a empresa pretende ampliar a atuação no mercado de veículos comerciais e competir com fabricantes tradicionais de vans movidas a diesel. Com investimento anunciado de R$ 11,3 bilhões, o complexo de Camaçari é responsável pela produção dos modelos de carros Dolphin Mini, King, Song Pro e Atto 2. A BYD pretende ampliar a capacidade anual da unidade para 300.000 veículos na próxima etapa de expansão da empresa no país. Em balanço divulgado em 5 de novembro, a montadora informou que a fábrica baiana já ultrapassou a marca de 150 mil veículos produzidos e conta com 9.500 empregos diretos desde a inauguração, em outubro de 2025.

artigo.texto: The Edmond City Council voted unanimously on Monday night to extend the city’s existing moratorium on data centers through June 30, 2027. The council approved the extension in a 5-0 vote during its Nov. 9 meeting. The moratorium temporarily prevents the city from accepting rezoning and building permit applications that would allow data centers to be built, expanded or operated within Edmond. City officials said the extension will provide additional time to evaluate potential regulations and land-use considerations related to data centers. The moratorium will remain in effect through June 30, 2027, unless the city takes further action.

artigo.texto: Trending BOARDMAN -- Don't be quick to dismiss data centers. There's room for talk, understanding and opportunity. That’s the message from an organization of business, union and educational leaders that emerged Monday to promote data center development in the Mahoning Valley. The co-founders of Mahoning Valley Coalition for a 21st Century Economy -- the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber and the Western Reserve Building Trades -- said at a news conference that education and conversation are needed to understand how the high-tech facilities can benefit the region and its economy. Their effort is backed by 29 entities -- from Youngstown State University and Brilex Industries to the Cafaro Company and SoftBank Group. "We now have an opportunity, if we do this right, to reverse decades of brain drain, create a 21st century economy that helps us retain our best and brightest, and be the destination for other people's best and brightest," said Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Regional Chamber. The group's initiative comes as some Valley communities have rejected data center development. Moratoriums have been enacted in Niles, McDonald, Girard, Warren, Newton Falls, Vienna, Howland, Braceville, Boardman, Cortland and Ellsworth Township. Voters in Hubbard voted to ban data centers in last week’s general election. "Come to mutual agreements without moratoriums," Coviello said. "The indirect impact of moratoriums on the data center industry is it sends a message out to all industries that one slight thing and you might slap a moratorium on my industry or my business. "When you say no to data centers, you say no to Hynes Industries. You say no to Wheatland Tube. You say no to Foxconn." The Ohio Supreme Court recently backed the village of Lordstown in a zoning issue involving a data center developer. During her campaign, Gov.-elect Amy Acton said she supported a conditional moratorium on data centers. She set six standards a developer must meet before coming into the state. "As we start talking about bans and moratoriums and different things like that, that’s not the right way to go," said Marty Loney, president of the Western Reserve Building Trades. "What we don’t understand, or what we don’t have, is then an avenue to be able to sit down with these companies and make those community benefit agreements where it works for everybody." Loney said the monetary benefits to the Valley are considerable. "Everybody talks about temporary jobs, right?" he said. "An average-sized data center is about 1,700 construction jobs over a several-year period. That to me doesn’t sound temporary. That sounds like community benefits for our tax base. "It’s a great way for young folks to have a great future here in the Valley." He said the new coalition is designed to deliver accurate information to the public and to dispel fears. "What we can’t lose sight of, though, is that people have legitimate concerns. ... We can't allow a small group of critics to dictate what's best for our local area." Rick Organ, CEO of Austintown-based Hynes Industries, told the audience that the century-old steel company has evolved and grown. Data centers have played a role. "It has profoundly impacted our business in a positive way," he said. "Over the course of the past two years, we have invested over $30 million in our business. We’ve doubled down to produce components and parts into the data center marketplace. "We’ve been in it for a number of years. It represented about 10% of our business as recently as two years ago. Today, it represents 40% of our business." Besides Hynes Industries, supporting the initiative are BBM Railway Equipment; Brilex Industries; Cafaro Company; Discover Global; Edge City; Foxconn; HBK CPAs & Consultants; HSH Contractor; Humtown Products; McDonald Industrial Development; Methodica Capital; North Jackson Commerce Park; Ohio Business Roundtable; Oppidan; Platz Realty Group; QUICKmed; Roemer Industries Inc.; Sharon Tube; SoftBank Group; Sunbelt Solomon; Taylor-Winfield Technologies; Top Property Holdings; Warren Area Chamber of Commerce Economic Development Foundation; Warren Area Chamber of Commerce Education, Civic and Cultural Foundation; Western Reserve Port Authority; Wheatland Tube; Youngstown State University; and Zekelman Industries. Covielli said he and Loney have already met with Boardman Township's zoning commission and the Trumbull County Council of Governments. "We want to continue to offer ourselves to be available to come and speak to any public body that wants to receive our information, our handouts and also to ask us questions directly," he said. That includes trips to communities opposed to data centers. "We’ll certainly go everywhere that we are welcome to go and meet with folks."

artigo.texto: Vanderburgh County data center committee hosts meeting Tuesday EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Residents from across Vanderburgh County spoke out about data centers at a public forum hosted by the Vanderburgh County Data Center Committee Tuesday at Ivy Tech’s auditorium. Most who spoke opposed data centers. Others backed them, saying the facilities would bring jobs and strengthen the community. The committee decided at its last meeting to hold the forum, making a point to hold at least one. Water, noise and security concerns Opponents cited concerns about water usage, noise, data security and environmental impact. Several questioned whether data centers are needed at all. Leann Rippy said she wants answers about the county’s water supply. “A geologist told us that all of our water is going to be dried up within 5 mile radius and within a short period of time. The data center representatives say different. Who’s correct? Who’s going to fix our water well if it’s damaged or drained?” Beverly White-Rowley urged the committee to reject data centers outright. “If you love your family, just say absolutely not to data centers. We don’t need any more data. I can find out about you and you and you and you and everyone in here on the Internet today. I don’t need to know all your dirt.” Many opponents spoke two or even three times, arguing data centers should not be in the county. Supporters point to jobs Supporters said data centers would create work. Ryan McRoberts said construction alone would employ many people. “These data centers will provide hundreds and thousands of jobs for construction over the next couple of years. They will also provide dozens and dozens of maintenance jobs after the facility is up and going.” Money questions Some opponents said data center supporters stand to profit. Kaleb Brown said the people speaking in favor have a financial stake. “The only people who’ve had anything positive to say about this data center all have financial gain to make from the situation. They all have construction businesses. The only people that are for this have a financial incentive. When does the money stop? I guarantee you every single person sitting in this chair makes more money than I do.” What’s next A moratorium on data centers has been in place for the past few months while the committee researches their impacts. The committee is preparing a report and recommendation for the Vanderburgh County commissioners. Committee officials said they will consider all of the public comment as they prepare for their next meeting, scheduled for Nov. 17. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Feds ask for proposals for industrial use of Hanford land. Data centers possible The Department of Energy issued a request for industry proposals Friday to use up to 3,700 acres of unneeded Hanford nuclear site land in Eastern Washington for industrial projects. The uses to be considered could include data centers or other computing capabilities, new energy generation, advanced manufacturing or development of critical materials. The land under consideration includes 1,876 acres of federal land along Route 4 South to the south of Energy Northwest’s commercial nuclear power plant, but on the other side of Route 4. It is immediately north of former Hanford land transferred by DOE to the Tri-Cities community in 2015 for industrial development through the efforts of the Tri-City Development Council. That acreage is listed by DOE as “available” and the remaining 1,249 acres is to the west of that tract and is listed by DOE as potentially available. DOE could enter into one or more long-term realty agreements at those sites, with all funding for work to come from those holding the new agreements. “With our Hanford team delivering historic cleanup progress, now is the time to invest in a community that has shouldered the burden of the past for far too long,” said Tim Walsh, DOE assistant secretary for environmental management. “At a site where too many see only challenges, I see opportunities for revitalization and new generational and life-changing jobs as we clean the legacy of the past to power a future built on affordable American energy, high-paying jobs, innovation and enduring economic vitality,” he said. Under the American Energy Hubs initiative, DOE is repurposing land once needed for wartime use, including developing nuclear weapons during World War II and the Cold War, for industrial use. The Hanford nuclear site adjacent to Richland was used from World War II through the Cold War to produce almost two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear weapons program. Hanford industrial land use plan The Tri-City Development Council sees the request for industry proposals, which DOE calls a “Request for Offer,” as closely aligning with the community’s vision for using some Hanford land for industrial development of base-load energy generation, such as new nuclear energy. The Comprehensive Land Use Plan for the Hanford site calls for most of the DOE land to be used for preservation and conservation. A limited portion, about 10%, is designated for industrial development to help replace Hanford jobs as environmental cleanup is completed. Now environmental cleanup is underway on radioactive and hazardous chemical waste and contamination at places around the site, with much of the site’s land never used for plutonium production or waste disposal. Most of the remaining Hanford cleanup is north of the area being considered for industrial development. TRIDEC sees the types of projects that could be considered, including nuclear energy projects, advanced manufacturing, data centers or related industries, as a good fit, especially for nearby Richland, said David Reeploeg, TRIDEC vice president of federal programs. “They have the potential to create a lot of additional good-paying jobs (and) further grow and diversity our economy,” he said. “We’re really excited about DOE now taking the next step into making this a reality.” As any plans proceed, TRIDEC wants to work closely with tribes, which have cultural resources they want to protect and treaty rights at Hanford, Reeploeg said. “We look forward to working collaboratively with the Tri-Cities community and the best of private industry as we accelerate cleanup and explore the art of the possible,” said Ray Geimer, the DOE manager for Hanford. “Exploring these opportunities is the next logical step for a site that is advancing cleanup and for a community that has always been all in on the all-of-the above American energy and innovation.” Protecting Richland power Proposals for the industrial land will be evaluated for technological readiness, financial viability and detailed plans to complete regulatory and permitting requirements. Consideration also will be given to compatibility with existing local redevelopment plans and potential partnerships with tribal and local businesses, according to DOE. Responses from interested businesses are due Jan. 29. Applicants who are selected will be responsible for building, operating and decommissioning each project and must secure utility interconnection agreements, according to DOE. Applicants may propose projects on all or a portion of available land, and DOE may consider multiple projects. It also says that project owners must adhere to President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which is designed to protect local power users as data centers are built. Companies would be responsible for new power generation resources and the cost of all power delivery infrastructure. The Hanford site is positioned to attract major private development because of its skilled trade workforce, DOE’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in Richland, its economic development leaders and community attitudes, according to DOE. Nuclear power center “We feel like there’s the potential for any number of different types of development on this land,” Reeploeg said. “We’re especially excited about the potential for new nuclear, whether it’s expanding what Energy Northwest is already planning on doing or other potential new nuclear opportunities.” Energy Northwest is working with Amazon to deploy an X-energy reactor, a small advanced nuclear reactor, on the land it leases near Richland. New energy generation could be combined with energy-intensive industries, whether that is data centers or advanced manufacturing, he said. DOE’s request for proposals give an opportunity to create a master plan for the development for best use of industrial resources, he said. artigo.texto: Bolivar city council discusses possible data center moratorium BOLIVAR, Tenn. (WBBJ) - Bolivar City Council members discussed a possible moratorium related to data centers as they consider how such a facility could affect the community. Mayor Julian McTizic said an inquiry was made about a potential data center at the city’s industrial complex, but it did not lead to a property sale. “The council just decided not to take any action but also make sure we do some studies on what it will look like for a data center to be in our community,” McTizic said. McTizic said multiple people have expressed interest in coming to the community, although he has not recruited data centers. Some community members have raised questions about the potential financial and environmental effects of a data center. Bolivar sits along the Hatchie River, which Councilwoman Caroline Miller described as an important local resource. “We are here on the Hatchie River. That’s one of our greatest resources,” Miller said. “We have water and, you know, we want to maintain that. We want to honor that.” City leaders said they want to stay ahead of the issue, be transparent and keep the community informed as they consider potential interest in a data center before property is purchased. Members of the public were given an opportunity to address the council during the meeting, but no one spoke. Copyright 2026 WBBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A corrida pelo avanço dos modelos de inteligência artificial provocou um salto dramático na demanda por recursos hídricos ao redor do mundo. Empreendimentos de grande porte chegam a retirar 5 milhões de galões de água por dia para evitar o superaquecimento de servidores, sobrecarregando o abastecimento público em regiões castigadas pela estiagem. Por que os chips de inteligência artificial exigem tanta água? O processamento ininterrupto de redes neurais profundas exige milhares de placas de processamento gráfico operando em capacidade máxima. Essa densidade de circuitos concentrada em gabinetes fechados gera um volume de calor residual que inviabiliza o uso exclusivo de ventiladores convencionais de ar. Para resfriar essa infraestrutura com baixo custo financeiro, a indústria adota torres de arrefecimento evaporativo. Nesse processo, o calor das máquinas é transferido para a água líquida, que evapora na atmosfera e impede o derretimento dos semicondutores durante as operações de cálculo. Quanto representa o consumo diário de 5 milhões de galões na prática? A retirada contínua de água potável por um único galpão tecnológico altera de forma profunda a disponibilidade hídrica dos municípios vizinhos às centrais de dados. Para mensurar a proporção desse impacto frente ao uso humano e urbano tradicional, examine o comparativo volumétrico estruturado na tabela a seguir: Como a evaporação nas torres sobrecarrega bacias e lençóis freáticos? Ao contrário do uso doméstico, em que a água consumida retorna à rede coletora como esgoto para ser tratado, o resfriamento de computadores consome a água de forma consuntiva definitiva. Cerca de 80% do volume captado se transforma em vapor e se dissipa com as correntes de vento, sem recarregar o rio ou aquífero de origem. Esse esvaziamento silencioso dos mananciais foi detalhado pelo Environmental and Energy Study Institute ao analisar o impacto hídrico de servidores. Em regiões agrícolas de clima semiárido, a captação maciça rebaixa o nível dos poços artesianos e compromete a irrigação de lavouras vizinhas durante o verão. Conflito pelo Acesso à Água A instalação de polos tecnológicos em áreas com risco de seca gera disputas administrativas por outorgas públicas, obrigando prefeituras a escolher entre a atração de investimentos e a segurança de abastecimento da população. Leia também: A ilha brasileira que existe há 435 anos e conquista quem procura uma vida mais tranquila perto do mar Quais alternativas de engenharia reduzem o gasto de água nas instalações? Para mitigar a dependência de reservatórios potáveis e responder a novas exigências regulatórias, projetistas desenvolvem métodos térmicos que operam em circuito fechado ou aproveitam fontes residuais. Entre as principais tecnologias disponíveis para substituir as torres evaporativas convencionais, destacam-se as seguintes frentes: - ❄️ Sistemas em circuito fechado: Radiadores que recirculam o mesmo líquido em tubulações seladas, impedindo a perda de vapor para o ar. - 🔬 Imersão direta em fluido dielétrico: Servidores submersos em óleo mineral sintético que conduz o calor sem contato com água líquida. - 🚰 Água de reuso industrial: Utilização de efluentes sanitários tratados de estações municipais no lugar de água potável encanada. Quais são as principais dúvidas sobre o uso de água na inteligência artificial? O consumo oculto gerado pelo uso de ferramentas digitais no dia a dia levanta questionamentos sobre a pegada ecológica dos servidores. Veja os esclarecimentos a seguir: Perguntas Frequentes Esclareça o impacto ambiental dos centros de dados A expansão da infraestrutura digital global depende da superação do desperdício de água potável no resfriamento mecânico. A adoção de circuitos fechados e o uso de águas residuais tratadas são os caminhos necessários para viabilizar a tecnologia sem esgotar bacias essenciais à sobrevivência das cidades.

A Prefeitura de Campo Grande abriu pregão eletrônico para contratar a locação de uma solução de alta disponibilidade de data center em contêiner, com entrega da estrutura, operação ininterrupta e manutenção integral. O aviso do Pregão Eletrônico nº 186/2026, da Secretaria Especial de Licitações e Contratos (Selc), saiu no Diogrande de segunda-feira (9). As propostas podem ser enviadas até as 7h44 de 25 de novembro, e a disputa de preços começa às 7h45. O contrato, pedido pela Agência Municipal de Tecnologia da Informação e Inovação (Agetec), inclui manutenção preventiva, preditiva e corretiva, fornecimento de peças e insumos e suporte técnico completo. Segundo o aviso, o objetivo é “garantir a estabilidade, segurança e escalabilidade do ambiente tecnológico municipal”. artigo.texto: City of Boise approves emergency moratorium on large data centers Boise, Idaho (CBS2) — The city of Boise has approved an emergency moratorium that temporarily pauses the development of large data centers within city limits. The ordinance, passed Tuesday evening during a city Council meeting, halts new applications for data centers for up to six months. It applies to facilities larger than 100,000 square feet or those with a projected power demand of at least 20 megawatts at full buildout. City leaders said concerns about potential impacts on water resources, energy use and land development led to the decision. They also mentioned the rise of moratoriums across 44 other states. Boise residents weighed in on the proposed moratorium with the majority of feedback in support of the moratorium. “These data centers use a tremendous amount of water and as our state goes through this predicted drought through the winter, i feel it's incredibly important to have guidelines in place before more data centers move in and take up what little resources we have,” Boise resident, Kyle Chandler said during Tuesday meeting. Another Boise resident urged leaders to consider long-term impacts. “We must understand that every decision we make, not only the impact it has on us here and now, but on the next seven generations to come,” the resident said. “I don't hear anybody talking about the future, i hear people trying to make a profit quick and dirty," she said. City leaders said they would take the next months to revise Boise's city code as well as restrictions and guidelines they would want to put in place in regard to large data centers, with public feedback from the community. Council members also discussed the importance of county and state level elected officials dong their part to put those guidelines in place. Council members voted unanimously on the moratorium, and the ordinance is set to go into effect immediately.

artigo.texto: Google Adds TPU 8tx, 8i Max for Enterprise AI Google Cloud is expanding its TPU lineup with one chip for secure AI workloads and another for higher-capacity inference with large context windows. To meet growing demand for AI inference, Google Cloud on Monday beefed up its Tensor Processing Unit family with two new chips: a more secure version of its TPU 8t accelerator and a higher-capacity version of its TPU 8i inference chip. The new processors are designed to address two emerging enterprise requirements: stronger protection for sensitive AI workloads and better performance for agentic AI applications with large context windows, said Mark Lohmeyer, vice president and general manager of AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud. The announcements build on Google Cloud’s eighth-generation TPU chips introduced in April. At that time, the company launched TPU 8t for training, which it said delivers up to 2.7 times better training performance than the prior generation, and TPU 8i for inference, which it said offers 80% better inference price-performance. TPU 8tx Adds Security; TPU 8i Max Boosts Capacity One of the new accelerators, TPU 8tx, is built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and adds hardware-level encryption for secure inference and small-scale training. The chip is paired with custom AMD CPU hosts to help protect and isolate sensitive data and model weights, even while inference is actively running, Lohmeyer said during a media briefing. Google Cloud also introduced TPU 8i Max, a variant aimed at enterprises running increasingly agentic workloads with large context windows. Lohmeyer said the chip is intended to address memory constraints by effectively “adding more lanes to the highway.” To create TPU 8i Max, Google Cloud combined two TPU 8i chips into a single package, doubling compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i, the company said. TPU 8i Max delivers 384 GB of high-bandwidth memory, Lohmeyer said. “We’re just seeing tremendous demand for the TPU platform and systems,” Lohmeyer said during the briefing. He added that Google Cloud is also seeing a broadening of AI use cases, including demand for confidential computing and for agentic inference with very large context windows while maintaining strong performance. Custom TPUs Could Sharpen Google Cloud’s Edge Dave McCarthy, group vice president at IDC, said Google Cloud’s move toward more specialized custom AI chips could help it further differentiate itself from rival cloud providers. “The fact that Google was able to launch the 8i and 8t earlier this year, and now they’re coming out with these new ones within the same calendar year, is just showing the pace of innovation,” McCarthy said. “They’re showing their commitment to R&D to build this stuff. And if what they’re saying is true – twice the bandwidth, all these new features – that’s showing they’re potentially outpacing the competition in terms of new product releases.” McCarthy described confidential computing as an emerging requirement for AI workloads. Cloud providers have traditionally focused on protecting data in transit and at rest, he said, whereas confidential computing is intended to protect data in use. “If Google can come out with a strong confidential compute story, it kind of gives them a little bit of an edge,” said McCarthy, adding that Nvidia is still developing its strategy in this area. Google Cloud also said TPU 8i Max allows more silicon to fit within an existing rack footprint, enabling significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt in its data centers. That could help Google Cloud increase capacity without adding more racks or building more data centers, at least in the near term, potentially easing some of the capacity pressures facing the industry, McCarthy said. More broadly, McCarthy said Google Cloud’s strategy of continually enhancing its silicon and making TPUs available through other providers could expand the company’s market reach while creating an additional revenue stream. Oracle recently announced it would make TPU chips available to customers of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. During the media briefing, Lohmeyer also said Google Cloud would allow select customers to deploy the TPU 8tx in their own data centers.

artigo.texto: The Washington County Chamber of Commerce will host its next Eggs and Issues program on Wednesday, December 2, featuring a discussion about the growth of the data center industry and lessons learned in Loudoun County, Virginia. The program, titled “Data Centers: The Loudoun County Experience,” will feature Joe Kroboth, deputy county administrator for Loudoun County. Breakfast will begin at 6:45 a.m., with the program starting at 7:30 a.m. at Hagerstown Community College in Rooms 211 and 213 of the Career Programs Building. Kroboth brings experience from both sides of the regional data center discussion. He spent seven years as public works director in Washington County, Maryland, before serving 14 years as deputy county administrator in Loudoun County, which is widely known as the “Data Center Capital of the World.” Loudoun County was among the first communities in the country to embrace the data center industry. Today, the county has more than 230 data center facilities operating or in development. The industry has brought significant economic benefits to Loudoun County. Data centers account for nearly 40% of the county’s tax base and generate approximately $1.3 billion in annual tax revenue. County officials say the revenue has helped lower property tax rates for residents every year since 2016. However, the growth has also brought challenges, including concerns about noise, backup diesel generators, electric transmission lines and the placement of facilities near residential neighborhoods. Loudoun County is now revisiting some of its land-use regulations and development standards based on lessons learned over the past two decades. Kroboth will share his firsthand perspective on the opportunities and challenges associated with data center development, including what has worked, what has not and what communities should consider before making decisions with long-term consequences. The Chamber says the program is intended to provide community leaders and residents with an opportunity to learn from a county with extensive experience in the industry. The Chamber is not advocating for or against data center development but hopes to provide a balanced discussion as interest in the industry grows in Washington County and the surrounding region. A question-and-answer session will follow Kroboth’s presentation. Registration is available at www.hagerstown.org. The event will be held at Hagerstown Community College, 11400 Robinwood Drive in Hagerstown. Attendees should use Parking Lot F.

artigo.texto: TIM vai conectar fábrica e carros da BYD TIM Brasil vai conectar fábricas e carros da BYD A TIM Brasil e a BYD fecharam acordo que permitirá à montadora chinesa ampliar a disponibilidade e a gama de serviços digitais em seus veículos, além de conectar a infraestrutura de seu complexo industrial em Camaçari (BA) com tecnologia 4G e 5G. A parceria prevê a instalação de uma rede celular privativa - exclusiva para a BYD - cobrindo as linhas de produção da montadora na Bahia. As empresas não divulgaram o valor a ser investido. “Nós estamos falando de máquinas, equipamentos, sistemas, controles, acessos, pessoas, carros. É um ecossistema geral. [...] É uma infraestrutura ‘outdoor’ [externa] e uma ‘indoor’ [interna] que ela [TIM] terá essa responsabilidade de tocar: a fábrica e essa interação com todos os sistemas de operação, de industrialização, de controles”, explicou Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da BYD do Brasil, em entrevista ao Valor. A expectativa é de que a rede privativa contribua para aumentar a eficiência da cadeia de suprimentos, além de conectar os trabalhadores espalhados pelo complexo industrial, já em atividade, que deverá ter 2,2 milhões de metros quadrados de área construída, num terreno de 4,6 milhões de metros quadrados. “Temos atualmente 9.520 colaboradores, [...] mas hoje, durante as 24 horas de um dia, você tem ali 14 mil, 15 mil pessoas transitando dentro do nosso parque industrial”, contabiliza Baldy. Para além do nicho de redes privativas, a parceria com a montadora marca também a mais recente investida da TIM no chamado mercado de serviços B2B2C, aqueles em que uma empresa presta serviço a outra companhia, que por sua vez atende o consumidor final. A operadora conecta mais de 630 mil veículos à internet, como parte de um acordo anunciado em 2020 com a Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA), que posteriormente incorporou o grupo PSA, transformando-se na Stellantis. “Hoje já estamos emplacando, essencialmente, 60% das vendas de carros conectados”, diz Alberto Griselli, diretor-presidente da TIM Brasil. A frota de carros eletrificados (elétricos e híbridos) da BYD que circula no país soma quase 400 mil veículos, segundo estimativa da própria montadora. A partir do acordo com a TIM Brasil, cuja cobertura 4G abrange 100% dos municípios brasileiros e a 5G alcança 1.171 cidades, toda essa base de veículos será beneficiada, afirma Baldy. Serviços disponíveis via smartphone para clientes da BYD - como controle do ar-condicionado, abertura e fechamento das portas, aquecimento dos bancos e localização do veículo - terão sua área de cobertura ampliada. Além disso, haverá novas opções de interatividade. A cobrança pelos serviços de conectividade não será feita do usuário final, mas da montadora, como parte de um modelo de negócios B2B2C. Dentro da estratégia da TIM para o mercado corporativo, a Internet dos Veículos (IoV) - uma variante da Internet das Coisas (IoT) - é uma forma de a operadora monetizar seu investimento na cobertura móvel de rodovias. Ao fim do segundo trimestre, a TIM contabilizava mais de 13,7 mil quilômetros em rodovias cobertas. Uma alternativa natural para ampliar essa cobertura seria recorrer a uma parceria com uma operadora de satélites, o que permitiria alcançar regiões remotas do país onde não chegam as redes terrestres de telecomunicações. “Estamos negociando [uma parceria], sim, pois essa tecnologia é complementar à nossa”, adianta Griselli. A operadora recebeu em 22 de outubro autorização da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) para testes e aplicações comerciais de sistemas D2D - que permitem a conexão direta entre celulares e satélites - dentro do ambiente regulatório experimental (“sandbox”) criado pela agência, com vigência prevista até 22 de abril de 2029, explica Rafael Pistono Vitalino, sócio especialista em regulação do escritório PDK Advogados.

artigo.texto: The Oakland City Council voted unanimously to extend the city's current data center moratorium for nearly a year, keeping restrictions in place that were originally set to expire next week. The decision was met with a standing ovation inside City Hall, as council members approved a 10-month extension to give municipal staff more time to study data center development, energy use, and environmental impacts while drafting potential new regulations. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are "We need more research and that’s what the community asked for. They want to know the risk of water going up and PG&E going up, and they deserve that," said Tonisha Scott, an Oakland resident. Public commenters at the meeting voiced strong concerns regarding transparency and resource consumption. "We pay taxes here! … and whatever goes on in Oakland, we are supposed to know about it!" said one public commenter. City officials plan to host community meetings over the coming months to allow residents to weigh in. "The importance of extending the moratorium is to give the city the adequate amount of time for our staff… to come back to the council with some firm guidelines," said District 3 City Councilmember Carroll Fife. Local While the extension provides a temporary pause, some community advocates view it as a stepping stone toward a permanent ban. "This is really a first step for a lot of the communities…," said Zoe Jonick, an organizer with 350 Bay Area, a climate group that has advocated for similar local moratoriums across the region. "You heard that a lot at the meeting tonight in Oakland… where a lot of people said yes we want this extended 10 more months, but really we want it extended forever," Jonick added. Oakland's original 45-day moratorium was slated to expire on Nov. 20. Tuesday's vote extends the restrictions through Oct. 5 of next year.

artigo.texto: Grupos da América Latina defenderam a criação de regulamentações específicas para definirem o escopo da expansão dos centros de dados (data centers) e garantir proteção às regiões que recebem essas infraestruturas. A demanda foi apresentada durante o segundo seminário realizado pelo Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet (Lapin), que ocorre em Fortaleza, no Brasil. O encontro, com duração de três dias, reúne pesquisadores, jornalistas, ativistas e representantes de comunidades de diferentes países da América Latina para discutir os impactos do rápido crescimento da infraestrutura digital. Um dos principais pontos do debate é a diferença entre a velocidade com que esses projetos avançam e a capacidade das regulamentações existentes de avaliar seus impactos. Os participantes defendem procedimentos de autorização mais rigorosos e transparentes, que garantam a participação das populações afetadas. Segundo eles, sem essas medidas, os custos ambientais e sociais podem recair inteiramente sobre as comunidades locais, enquanto os benefícios ficam concentrados em outras regiões. Entre os principais temas discutidos estão o consumo de água e energia, a transição energética, o racismo ambiental e o chamado "extrativismo digital". Os centros de dados são infraestruturas físicas essenciais para o funcionamento de serviços online e sistemas de inteligência artificial, mas exigem recursos naturais e grandes áreas para sua instalação. Por isso, conforme destacado durante o seminário em Fortaleza, o planejamento desses empreendimentos não deve ser tratado apenas como uma questão tecnológica, mas também ambiental e social. artigo.texto: Google has taken over an unfinished data-center project in southeastern Wyoming from Crusoe, according to The Hans India, which ran the story under a headline that calls Crusoe a $30.9 billion AI startup. Crusoe confirmed the sale on Friday, November 6, 2026. Google announced plans to invest $17 billion in the Wyoming campus. Neither side has disclosed what Google paid for the site. That last point trips up a lot of coverage. The $17 billion is Google’s planned investment in the campus, not the purchase price, and the price itself stays private. Our first report on the Google Crusoe Wyoming data center deal laid out the basic facts on the day. This analysis asks a different question: what does the handover say about who controls AI compute, and why did a developer that did the early work on the site end up passing it to a company it had reportedly pitched as a customer? We separate what Crusoe and Google confirmed from what reports attribute to people familiar with the matter. Two tables below sort the numbers and the open claims. The later sections cover the AI-model angle (why new model generations push big buyers toward owning sites), a comparison of the ways a hyperscaler can secure capacity, the market impact, and five predictions. Every figure comes from the November 6 reporting. Where a detail is missing, we say so instead of filling the gap. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Crusoe Confirmed on November 6 The confirmed core is short. Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based AI-infrastructure company, sold its unfinished southeastern Wyoming data-center project to Google. The company confirmed the sale on Friday, November 6, 2026. Google announced it will invest $17 billion in the campus. The acquisition price was not disclosed. Crusoe’s contribution before the sale is also on the record. Its pre-development work covered site selection, government approvals, and a power strategy. Those three items matter more than they sound. A large AI campus needs land, regulatory sign-off, and a credible answer to where the electricity comes from. Developers who hold all three can sell a site to a buyer with deeper pockets, and that is the position Crusoe held on Friday. Headlines framed the deal in different ways. TechCrunch titled its piece “Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google”, which signals a project in difficulty. Bloomberg went with “Google Takes Over Wyoming Data Center That Crusoe Had Pitched”, which points to the customer relationship. Yahoo Finance chose “Google buys Wyoming data center site as hyperscalers move to own AI capacity”, a trend framing. Each headline emphasizes a different reading of one transaction, and none of them replaces a statement from the companies on why the deal happened. Treat the word “troubled” as TechCrunch’s characterization. The reasons behind the takeover remain unconfirmed, a point we return to below. Related guides: Readers who want something to keep after this story can start with npm audit for Node.js projects, one of our guides in the same area, and the Shattered guides hub groups the rest by task, with the comparisons that explain the trade-offs behind each recommendation. The Numbers That Get Mixed Up Four dollar figures circulate around this story, and they measure four different things. Readers who skim headlines often merge them into one imagined price. The table separates them. A little arithmetic puts the scale in view. Google’s planned $17 billion equals roughly 55 percent of Crusoe’s $30.9 billion valuation. The September $3.9 billion round equals about 12.6 percent of that valuation. Those ratios compare a spending plan with a company’s worth, so they illustrate size and do not describe the economics of the deal. As NewsBytes put it in its headline, the price stayed undisclosed, and any estimate of Crusoe’s gain or loss on the site is guesswork. The Markets Insider write-up of the deal called it a $17 billion expansion, which is accurate for Google’s side. It does not mean Google wrote a $17 billion check to Crusoe. Most of that money, if Google follows through, goes to construction, equipment, and power infrastructure over the life of the build. Why “AI Startup” Is the Wrong Label for Crusoe The headline on The Hans India story calls Crusoe an AI startup. The reporting itself describes something narrower. Crusoe develops AI infrastructure and data centers. Its work in Wyoming involved land, permits, and power, not models, chatbots, or software products. The label matters because it changes how readers judge the news. An AI-software startup that loses a contract tells you about demand for its product. An infrastructure developer that hands a site to a customer tells you about construction cost, delivery schedules, and who carries risk. Those are different businesses with different yardsticks. Infrastructure firms get measured in megawatts delivered and dates met, and software firms get measured in users and benchmark scores. It also changes the valuation story. A $30.9 billion price tag on a software company would rest on revenue multiples. A $30.9 billion valuation on a developer of AI campuses rests on the market’s belief that contracted capacity will get built and filled. Losing one project does not break that belief, but delays and cost overruns at any single site test it. Readers who see “startup” may picture a fragile newcomer. The reports describe an eight-year-old company that raised $3.9 billion in a single round only two months ago. The Unconfirmed Reasons Behind the Takeover Two explanations dominate the reporting, and neither comes from an identified on-record Google statement. The first says Google took over because it raised concerns about Crusoe’s construction costs and timeline.
