artigo.texto: O primeiro leilão brasileiro de armazenamento em baterias recebeu 6.091 cadastros, um recorde para contratação de projetos no setor elétrico segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Os certames estão marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro e somam 296.807 megawatts de potência inscrita. O leilão de 2 de dezembro exige componentes nacionais e terá financiamento de R$ 30 bilhões do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) via Finame. A etapa de 4 de dezembro aceita equipamentos importados, mas ainda não tem linha de crédito público definida. A diferença entre as duas datas transforma o certame em disputa de política industrial, não apenas em compra de reserva de capacidade. O banco público cria demanda para fabricação e montagem de baterias, produção de componentes, engenharia e serviços tecnológicos no país, segundo avaliação de Rosana Santos, diretora-executiva do Instituto E+ Transição Energética. A corrida global ajuda a explicar a pressa brasileira em ter capacidade própria de armazenamento. Em 2025, o mundo instalou 108 gigawatts de baterias, alta de 40% sobre 2024 e volume 11 vezes maior que o de 2021, puxado por China, Estados Unidos e Europa, segundo o relatório Global Energy Review 2026 da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA). No Brasil, as hidrelétricas não suprem sozinhas a flexibilidade operacional que o sistema elétrico ganha com sistemas químicos de armazenamento. Os conjuntos de baterias entram em operação em um a dois anos e descarregam energia em ciclos de quatro a oito horas, enquanto usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis levam de sete a oito anos para ficar prontas. Esses sistemas ajudam a aproveitar o excesso de geração eólica e solar e a reduzir cortes de geração (curtailment) que hoje não são ressarcidos aos produtores. Rodrigo Sauaia, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), afirma que os geradores deixam de receber pelo que não injetam na rede e enfrentam prejuízos financeiros. A queda internacional dos custos também viabilizou os sistemas de baterias no mercado brasileiro. Desde 2010, o preço médio global caiu de mais de US$ 1.000 por quilowatt-hora para cerca de US$ 108 por quilowatt-hora em 2025, de acordo com levantamento anual da consultoria BloombergNEF. A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou os editais em 27 de outubro e reduziu o investimento de referência de R$ 9,8 milhões por megawatt para R$ 6 milhões por megawatt. As garantias de proposta e de fiel cumprimento também caíram, o que diminui a barreira de entrada e amplia a competição. Os contratos valem por 15 anos, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. A bateria precisa garantir potência por quatro horas a cada ciclo diário, com receita anual ajustada pelo desempenho efetivo. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE) calcula que a rede básica possui cerca de 56 gigawatts de margem de conexão para baterias, com base em nota técnica do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) e da EPE. Esse volume supera em até 12 vezes a necessidade estimada para o período de 2028 a 2030. Nos pontos com bônus locacional, a folga chega a 13,7 gigawatts, concentrada principalmente na Bahia, no Piauí, no Ceará e no norte de Minas Gerais. Para a ABSAE, a infraestrutura de transmissão não deve ser gargalo para os primeiros leilões. Os preços-teto ficaram em R$ 1,76 milhão por megawatt-ano no leilão com exigência de conteúdo nacional e R$ 1,58 milhão no certame aberto a importados. A associação considera os valores alinhados às projeções do mercado e suficientes para atrair investidores qualificados. Os 6.091 projetos cadastrados ainda passarão por análise e habilitação técnica conduzida pela EPE antes da disputa. A proporção final entre equipamentos fabricados no país e sistemas importados nos leilões de dezembro definirá o alcance industrial do financiamento público.

artigo.texto: A resistência à instalação de novos data centers, uma infraestrutura que cria poucos empregos e consome energia e água em volumes gigantescos, está a aumentar em todo o mundo. O exemplo mais recente ocorreu na semana passada nas eleições intercalares nos EUA, onde os candidatos com posições contrárias à instalação de data centers somaram vitórias. Nas sondagens realizadas nesse dia, o eleitorado confirmou que a questão foi determinante para o seu sentido de voto. Além dos danos ambientais, as populações queixam-se do aumento dos preços da eletricidade nas zonas onde foram instalados os centros de dados. Nas dezenas de referendos locais realizados no mesmo dia nos EUA, apenas num caso os eleitores deram a vitória à posição da indústria. Estes megacentros de dados são usados para alimentar modelos de inteligência artificial das grandes empresas tecnológicas. A oposição à construção dos grandes data centers alastra à Europa e o governo norueguês deu o exemplo ao anunciar esta segunda-feira a suspensão de novos pedidos de ligação à rede elétrica por parte destes data centers. A Noruega produz hoje mais energia do que a que consome, mas as estimativas apontam para um défice futuro por causa dos data centers, com a consequente subida do preço da eletricidade. O total de pedidos de ligação feitos este ano ascende aos 26 mil megawatts de nova capacidade, o que é mais do que a capacidade instalada na Noruega, com os data centers a representarem 75% dos pedidos, afirmou o ministro da Energia Terje Aasland, citado pela Reuters. A decisão do Governo, anunciada pelo operador da rede elétrica Statnett, foi justificada pelo ministro da Digitalização Torgeir Micaelsen com o objetivo de “obter um maior controlo sobre o crescimento dos centros de dados e garantir que dispomos dos centros de dados de que realmente precisamos”. Ficam assim suspensos temporariamente os novos pedidos de ligação e o futuro regime de licenças irá favorecer data centers que prestem serviços às áreas da defesa, da polícia e da preparação para emergências, aos serviços de saúde e a outras infraestruturas críticas, tais como a rede móvel e o sistema financeiro, afirmou Micaelsen. De fora ou com restrições acrescidas no acesso a terrenos e eletricidade ficarão as grandes empresas que operam as clouds e também as empresas de criptomoedas. E os novos data centers terão de pagar os custos da rede, podendo ser obrigados a construir centrais elétricas a gás, incluindo sistemas de captura e armazenamento de carbono, para produzirem a sua própria eletricidade, afirmou o governo. Também a Dinamarca aprovou no mês passado no Parlamento uma lei que empurra os data centers para o fim da fila de prioridades no que toca ao acesso à rede elétrica, atrás dos serviços de saúde e segurança, da rede de carregamento de carros elétricos e das habitações.

artigo.texto: Iniciativa transforma benefícios ambientais da reciclagem em créditos de carbono e gera renda para cooperativas de catadores; projeto será apresentado em painéis sobre sustentabilidade e justiça climática na Turquia O Ministério Público de Mato Grosso do Sul (MPMS) levará à 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31) uma experiência que une reciclagem, geração de créditos de carbono e inclusão social. O Projeto Reciclarbono, apoiado pela instituição e finalista dos Prêmios CNMP 2026 e J.Ex., estará entre as iniciativas brasileiras apresentadas nos debates sobre soluções ambientais. A conferência será realizada em Antália, na Turquia. O MPMS será representado pelo promotor de Justiça Luciano Furtado Loubet, integrante do Núcleo Ambiental da instituição e presidente da Associação Brasileira dos Membros do Ministério Público de Meio Ambiente (Abrampa). Loubet foi convidado a compartilhar experiências desenvolvidas no Brasil em painéis sobre gestão de resíduos, economia circular, cidades sustentáveis e justiça climática. Entre os destaques está o debate internacional “The Informal Sector Enabling Climate Action”, promovido pela Zero Waste Foundation e pelo Climate High-Level Champions’ Office. A Abrampa participará como palestrante na Zona Azul da COP31, área destinada às negociações e aos eventos oficiais da conferência. Projeto transforma reciclagem em créditos de carbono Desenvolvido em parceria com instituições públicas e acadêmicas, o Reciclarbono transforma os benefícios ambientais gerados pela reciclagem em créditos de carbono. O valor obtido é convertido em renda para cooperativas e associações de catadores. A iniciativa busca associar a redução dos impactos ambientais à valorização dos trabalhadores da reciclagem, aproximando a economia circular das estratégias de enfrentamento às mudanças climáticas. Debates incluem gestão de resíduos e cidades sustentáveis A programação da COP31 também prevê discussões sobre encerramento de lixões, combate à poluição marinha, economia circular de baixo carbono e gestão de resíduos sólidos. Os painéis incluem ainda experiências municipais para a construção de cidades sustentáveis e temas relacionados à segurança jurídica de políticas climáticas. A participação do MPMS e da Abrampa amplia a presença de experiências brasileiras nos debates internacionais sobre sustentabilidade, inclusão social e políticas públicas ambientais, levando iniciativas acompanhadas em Mato Grosso do Sul para a discussão global sobre mudanças climáticas. artigo.texto: Woodbury County Zoning Commission hears data center concerns in Salix SALIX, Iowa (KTIV) - Woodbury County Zoning Commission continued their tour of Woodbury County, Monday Nov. 9, this time in Salix for one of their data center town halls. Back in June, the Woodbury County Board of Supervisors passed a 12-month moratorium on all potential data centers in the county. And now, the county’s zoning commission is looking for public input on what requirements or regulations they would like to see added to a county data center ordinance. That ordinance would only affect unincorporated areas in the county not incorporated cities or towns. Monday, the commission heard from residents in Salix. There, people voiced their concerns about data centers affecting the environment, water quality, local roads, and noise pollution. Overall, many asked the commission to take their time to creating regulations. “To my mind, the costs and risks far outweigh the benefits. While we do not want woodbury county closed to business the goal would be to ensure that if a hyper scale data center were to be proposed in this county, its residents would be protected from harm,” said Janet Yanek, a concerned resident. Some residents did acknowledge that they aren’t fully against data centers, they just ask the county to have enough regulations in place so they don’t impact residents. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with data centers if they are in the right spot. I think that resources are a big thing to look at and keeping the costs on the companies that are building them is also a big thing to look at. But keeping the residents first is the biggest things in my eyes,” said Preston Zemanek, a concerned resident. The zoning commission plans to hold another town hall in Correctionville on January 18th. That location has yet to be determined. If you are a resident of Woodbury County and would like to submit your input, you can email dpriestley@woodburycountyiowa.gov or reach out to the Woodbury County Planning and Zoning at 620 Douglas Street, Sixth Floor, Sioux City, IA 51101. artigo.texto: Eletronet aporta R$ 25 milhões em novo Data Center em SP Nomeado ELET1, o Data Center terá capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência de 0,5 MW, podendo ser expandida para 1 MW. Lançamento é previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. A Eletronet, uma empresa Axia Energia, anunciou o ELET1, seu novo Data Center em São Paulo, que ampliará a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão da companhia e fornecerá mais escala ao atendimento de provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações e provedores de Internet (ISPs), e hyperscalers. Com investimento de R$ 25 milhões, o centro terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW, podendo chegar a 1 MW na segunda fase de expansão. Com as obras já iniciadas, a previsão de lançamento é para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto acompanha o aumento da procura de empresas dos segmentos de cloud, streaming e telecomunicações por infraestrutura de Data Center em regiões estratégicas de São Paulo, com alta disponibilidade e acesso a um amplo ecossistema de conteúdo. O ELET1 estará em uma localização com elevada concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo. O Data Center também abrigará o PIX (Ponto de Interconexão) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo, o maior ponto de troca de tráfego de Internet do mundo, tanto em volume quanto em número de participantes. O PIX da companhia se destaca por liderar o volume de tráfego de download entre as operadoras participantes do IX.br São Paulo. Para os clientes, estar nesse ambiente aumenta as possibilidades de conexão com diferentes redes e provedores de serviços digitais. “O ELET1 representa um passo estratégico para fortalecer nossa atuação no segmento de Data Centers. Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais”, afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet. Segundo ele, o projeto acompanha o avanço de aplicações em nuvem, inteligência artificial, streaming e serviços digitais, que exigem suporte para volumes cada vez maiores de dados. “Queremos ir além das necessidades atuais e antecipar os próximos ciclos do mercado, fortalecendo nossa capacidade de conectar clientes, redes e ecossistemas digitais”, diz. Com segurança, tecnologia de última geração e resiliência operacional entre os pilares da iniciativa, o ELET1 seguirá as melhores práticas globais de infraestrutura, com soluções voltadas à proteção física e lógica, alinhadas às diretrizes da norma ISO 27001. O Data Center também contará com aplicações modernas e práticas de gestão ambiental e energética, tendo como referência os padrões ISO 14001, ISO 50001 e LEED, apoiando no melhor desempenho energético e na redução do PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness). Entre os recursos previstos estão dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVA, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predial (BMS) atualizado, monitoramento contínuo e um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência.

artigo.texto: NYSERDA Awards Nearly $13 Million to 15 Innovative Energy Storage Projects New York's NYSERDA is distributing nearly $13 million across 15 long duration and advanced battery storage projects, from compressed air to sodium-ion, with grid-scale demonstrations among the goals. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) announced on November 6, 2026 that nearly $13 million has been awarded to 15 projects. The funds come from the Power Generation and Storage Innovation program. They support product development and demonstration of battery storage solutions, including long duration systems. Storage is drawing funding in other markets, as shown by India's approval of a 92 GWh storage program and Anchor Energy Partners' â¬75 million target for its first storage fund. A program focused on alternatives to lithium-ion The program competitively awards funding to long duration energy storage (LDES) projects and other under-utilized alternatives to traditional lithium-ion batteries that have yet to be commercialized. The selected solutions include new designs with a duration of more than 10 hours at rated power. According to NYSERDA, they target grid congestion, hosting capacity constraints and lithium-ion siting limitations. Doreen M. Harris, president and CEO of NYSERDA, says investing in next-generation energy storage technologies is critical to building a flexible and resilient grid. In her view, the projects would advance solutions able to deliver power when it is needed most and help lower costs. The agency highlights three focus areas: enhanced inherent design safety, material innovations for more efficient and longer-lasting battery cells, and diversified battery material composition to improve safety and local supply chains. From compressed air to sodium-ion Aestus Energy Storage LLC receives over $590,000 for a subscale test of approximately 35 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of two alumina-silica ceramic heat sink materials. The materials are intended for the design of a 20 megawatt-hour (MWh) Advanced Compressed Air Energy Storage (A-CAES) system for utility-scale applications. Alsym Energy, Inc. gets over $290,000 to design and test a 10 kWh prototype non-flammable sodium-ion battery energy storage system, in partnership with the Rochester Institute of Technology's Battery Development Center. AlphaEn Corporation receives over $350,000 for a modular, roll-to-roll lithium metal electrode manufacturing platform that uses recycled lithium from retired assets. Daqus Energy, Inc. is awarded nearly $1 million for a completely metal-free organic cathode for lithium-ion batteries, in partnership with Binghamton University's Northeast Center for Chemical Energy Storage. Graphenix Development (GDI) receives over $700,000 to combine 100% silicon anodes with sulfur cathodes. IBEX Materials Inc. gets $750,000 for a silicon-rich, graphite-free anode integrated with solid-state electrolytes. InfinitEnergy, Inc. is awarded $250,000 for solid-state batteries designed to operate without external mechanical pressure. Inlyte and Sprocket receive the largest amounts Inlyte Energy receives over $2.4 million, the largest amount among the winners listed. The funding is meant to deploy an iron-sodium battery of more than 10 hours to address substation peak load growth and distribution-level resilience challenges. Sprocket Power, Inc. gets over $1 million to demonstrate direct current fast charging stations fed from an underground Vanadium Redox Flow Battery. LiBAMA Power Corporation receives over $400,000 to develop and test advanced metal anodes with Elementium, a nonflammable electrolyte supplier. LiNova Energy, Inc. gets nearly $720,000 for a lithium-ion battery with critical-mineral-free polymer cathodes. Orion Polymer Corp. is awarded $250,000 to demonstrate the technical viability of its membranes for lithium sulfur batteries through a prototype pouch cell. Respire Energy, Inc. receives over $850,000 to further develop its metal-air battery with Binghamton University, Intertek and Bettergy Corp. - Gas42.5 % - Nuclear17.2 % - Coal14.2 % - Wind10.3 % - Solar10.1 % - Hydro3.9 % - Bioenergy1.0 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: As ações da AAON Inc (NASDAQ:AAON) subiram aproximadamente 22% nas negociações pré-mercado de terça-feira, após a fabricante de equipamentos de aquecimento, ventilação e ar condicionado (HVAC) divulgar resultados do terceiro trimestre e receita acima das expectativas dos analistas, além de elevar sua projeção financeira para o ano de 2026. A empresa reportou lucro ajustado de US$ 0,83 por ação, superando a estimativa de consenso dos analistas de US$ 0,56 em US$ 0,27. A receita trimestral aumentou 84,1% em relação ao ano anterior, atingindo o recorde de US$ 707,4 milhões, comparada a US$ 384,2 milhões no mesmo período de 2025 e às expectativas dos analistas de US$ 599,7 milhões. O aumento da receita refletiu a demanda pelas linhas de produtos AAON e BASX da empresa, maior produção e maior utilização da capacidade produtiva recentemente ampliada. A receita do terceiro trimestre subiu 84,1%, atingindo o recorde de US$ 707,4 milhões A AAON reportou vendas líquidas de US$ 707,4 milhões no terceiro trimestre, representando um aumento de US$ 323,2 milhões em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. O resultado superou a estimativa consensual dos analistas em aproximadamente US$ 107,7 milhões. O lucro ajustado por ação atingiu US$ 0,83, em comparação com as expectativas do mercado de US$ 0,56, refletindo a maior receita e o melhor desempenho operacional da empresa durante o trimestre. O lucro bruto aumentou 76,4%, atingindo US$ 188,5 milhões, enquanto a margem bruta alcançou 26,7%, uma melhoria de 60 pontos base em comparação com o segundo trimestre. O lucro operacional mais que dobrou, aumentando 129,3% para US$ 100 milhões. A empresa atribuiu os resultados ao aumento da produção, às medidas de precificação e à maior utilização de suas instalações fabris. A receita da BASX aumentou 218,3%, impulsionada pela demanda por data centers A AAON registrou crescimento de receita em ambas as suas principais marcas de produtos. As vendas de produtos da marca AAON aumentaram 19,6%, atingindo US$ 310,2 milhões, enquanto a receita da marca BASX subiu 218,3%, para US$ 397,2 milhões. O aumento na receita da BASX refletiu a demanda por equipamentos de refrigeração e controle ambiental utilizados em centros de dados, incluindo instalações operadas por grandes provedores de computação em nuvem. A expansão da capacidade de produção da empresa também contribuiu para sua capacidade de atender a pedidos adicionais de clientes durante o trimestre. Os analistas da William Blair destacaram o desempenho da unidade de negócios BASX, observando que os pedidos aceleraram durante o terceiro trimestre. Os analistas disseram que as encomendas do quarto trimestre deveriam “igualar ou superar” o “resultado excepcionalmente forte de 586 milhões de dólares do ano anterior”. Segundo sua avaliação, a demanda foi sustentada por pedidos repetidos de clientes de computação em hiperescala e pela adição de novos clientes. AAON eleva sua previsão de crescimento de vendas para 2026 para 72% a 75% Após a divulgação dos resultados trimestrais, a AAON aumentou sua previsão de crescimento das vendas líquidas para o ano de 2026 para entre 72% e 75%, em comparação com a previsão anterior de 55% a 60%. O ponto médio da faixa revisada é de 73,5%, representando um aumento de 16 pontos percentuais em relação ao ponto médio da previsão anterior. A empresa também atualizou suas expectativas de rentabilidade e despesas operacionais. A AAON agora prevê uma margem bruta anual de aproximadamente 26%, em comparação com a projeção anterior de 25% a 26%. Prevê-se que as despesas com vendas, gerais e administrativas representem aproximadamente 13% das vendas, em comparação com a previsão anterior de 13% a 14%. A revisão das perspectivas reflete as expectativas da administração em relação à atividade de produção, à demanda por produtos e aos custos operacionais durante o restante do ano. Analistas destacam o crescimento dos pedidos e a melhoria das margens Analistas da William Blair afirmaram que a AAON “superou dois obstáculos importantes” com seu relatório financeiro do terceiro trimestre. O primeiro fator foi uma aceleração nos pedidos da BASX, impulsionada pela demanda de operadores de data centers e por novos relacionamentos com clientes. O segundo fator foi a melhoria na margem bruta, que os analistas atribuíram a ações de precificação e maiores volumes de produção. A empresa indicou que as ações da AAON poderiam atingir US$ 100 sob uma estrutura de avaliação que aplica 18 vezes o EBITDA projetado para 2027 ao negócio da marca AAON e de 10 a 11 vezes o EBITDA estimado para 2027 da BASX. A avaliação representa a análise dos analistas, e não uma previsão da empresa ou um preço futuro garantido das ações. A William Blair também identificou uma melhoria adicional na margem bruta em 2027 como um “fator essencial para a criação de mais valor”. Os comentários refletem as expectativas da empresa em relação ao desempenho operacional futuro da companhia e à contribuição de suas duas principais linhas de produtos. AAON reformula resultados do primeiro semestre após identificação de erros contábeis Juntamente com os resultados do terceiro trimestre, a AAON divulgou que identificou erros em suas demonstrações financeiras referentes ao primeiro e segundo trimestres de 2026. Os erros foram descobertos durante a preparação do relatório financeiro do terceiro trimestre da empresa. Como resultado, a AAON revisou seus resultados financeiros do primeiro semestre, aumentando as vendas líquidas anteriormente divulgadas em US$ 10,7 milhões e o lucro diluído por ação em US$ 0,09. A empresa também identificou uma deficiência material em seu controle interno sobre os relatórios financeiros. A AAON afirmou estar implementando medidas destinadas a corrigir as deficiências de controle identificadas. artigo.texto: Missoula company CubCloud AI has sued the city of Missoula over a recent zoning change that blocks data center development within the city limits, citing the state’s Right to Compute Act. The company, represented by the Arizona-based Goldwater Institute through the Big Sky Legal Project, argues in the lawsuit filed Nov. 4 that the city’s rules preventing it from expanding its business are not supported by a “compelling governmental interest,” nor are they narrowly tailored as required by the Right to Compute Act. “The City’s new ordinance targets data centers because it considers them the wrong type of business,” said the Goldwater Institute’s Dave Roland in a press release. “The fact that the ordinance’s blanket restrictions sweep in CubCloud shows they are not narrowly tailored toward protecting the public from excessive noise, light, pollution, etc., as the Right to Compute Act requires.” Missoula City Attorney Ryan Sudbury told Montana Free Press that, as of Monday morning, the city had not been served with the lawsuit but that he was aware of the case. Sudbury said city officials had internal discussions about the Right to Compute Act while crafting the zoning amendment and that the city plans to defend the change. “Nobody knows what the law is intended to do or what it means,” Sudbury said. “It has not been tested in court. … If we get served, we will defend the city’s action.” The Montana Legislature passed the Right to Compute Act in 2025. The law links the development of computational resources, such as data centers, to constitutional rights, including property and freedom of expression. As with other constitutional rights, government infringement of the right to compute is limited except when driven by a compelling governmental interest, such as the preservation of public health and safety. While some local governments have argued the law prevents them from regulating data centers, others, including Missoula County, have moved forward with crafting new rules. Large data center proposals have received significant pushback from residents. Missoula County’s recently released data center study found even small-scale operations can have some significant impacts on energy demand, water use and air and water pollution. The city adopted a new zoning code in late 2025 that went into effect earlier this year. While the new code allowed data centers in heavy industrial areas — which are not included on the zoning map — the rules inadvertently permitted data centers citywide if they took up less than 50% of a facility. The amendment approved in October closed that loophole by revising the definition of a data center and regulating the facilities based on how the equipment is used rather than how much floor space it occupies. CubCloud AI was founded about a year ago and has 18 employees, according to the complaint. The business provides private computational resources, remote data processing, server hosting and cloud computing services. CubCloud operates a facility on Kestrel Drive near the Missoula Montana Airport that previously met the city’s requirements because the computational resources occupied about 20% of the floor area, the complaint said. Joshua Rhines, CubCloud CEO, planned to build a new stand-alone building on the site that would house additional computing resources. Under the city’s updated rules, the business could not build similar facilities on its existing site or anywhere else within city limits. The complaint argues the facilities do not generate noise, odors, physical intrusions or other adverse conditions that would constitute a nuisance or unreasonably interfere with neighboring properties. The complaint argues the zoning amendment violates the Right to Compute Act by restricting the company’s ability to own or use computational resources and is not supported by a compelling government interest. Even if a compelling government interest was identified, the rule is not narrowly tailored to fulfill that interest, the complaint states. The Goldwater Institute is a public policy research and litigation organization focused on limited government, individual liberty and free speech, according to its website. The organization has partnered with the Montana-based Frontier Institute, a conservative think tank, on the Big Sky Legal Project to provide free legal services to Montanans “whose rights are being violated by federal, state, or local government.” Missoula City Council Member Kristen Jordan argued last month that the zoning code is insufficient to prevent data center development, which could be approved through a rezoning request. artigo.texto: BHP World's largest miner by market cap A new report from DLA Piper indicates that price volatility in critical minerals is holding back a significant share of energy storage projects, according to Mining.com. The study, based on interviews with 550 participants across the energy storage, investment and mining sectors, found that 23% said projects that had appeared viable were deferred or cancelled because of unpredictable commodity prices shaped by tariffs, wars and other geopolitical tensions. A further 12% of respondents described price volatility as a dealbreaker for project development. DLA Piper natural resources partner Alex Jones said unpredictable pricing pressures were producing a cascading effect across the sector, weakening investor confidence, limiting financing and structuring, and contributing to delays, repricing and, in some cases, abandoned projects. The report identifies the reluctance to commit capital amid uncertain and volatile future commodity prices as the leading obstacle to investment. More than half of respondents called price volatility a major constraint on mining or processing investment, with consequences felt across the project lifecycle. Among them, 28% reported difficulty securing bankable long-term offtake agreements, 27% had postponed investment decisions and 26% faced a higher cost of capital. The impact varies by region. Participants in the United Kingdom and the United States reported the strongest effects, with 16% and 18% respectively calling volatility a dealbreaker for project development. German participants stood apart, being the only group to say volatility was not a dealbreaker, with just 8% treating it as a major problem. Australian participants viewed volatility as one of several material considerations rather than a major roadblock. DLA Piper partner Oliver Wright suggested that capital is likely to concentrate in regions seen as offering execution credibility and proximity to supply chains and demand, as developers seek locations where they can exercise more control and stay closer to the supply chain through market cycles. Companies are increasingly adopting vertical integration to limit exposure to volatile commodity markets and to pricing benchmarks influenced by China, the report found. At least 37% of surveyed developers and 32% of mining and raw materials producers have taken this route, which lets businesses control more stages of production, from extraction and refining to manufacturing and recycling. Wright said companies had long depended on supply chains they did not control, and that recent volatility had demonstrated how quickly pricing and supply terms can change. He said developers and miners are now working to hold the parts of the chain they rely on most, from mine through refinery to recycling plant, so that an upstream squeeze no longer disrupts operations. Participants are also reconsidering how prices are set. Some 37% believe component-linked pricing would work better than raw material spot prices, while 48% of mining and raw materials producers favor long-term fixed pricing with periodic resets. Rare Earth Americas chief executive and president Donald S. Swartz II said in the report that strategic mineral supply chains carry value beyond the daily spot price. Wright added that the industry is expected to shift what contracts are priced against, whether component-linked pricing, price floors or hybrid structures. The three stocks that follow are only a starter set from this theme, and the fuller screen surfaced 44 more businesses with equally compelling stories that are not covered below. "Although MasTec highlights record backlog tied to AI and cloud related data center work, there is a risk that customers slow or resize these projects as power availability, permitting or technology choices evolve, which could leave MasTec with underutilized capacity and pressure future revenue and EBITDA if awards are delayed or repriced." The key question is what happens to MasTec's profitability if that long pipeline of high complexity work shifts in timing or mix. Most revenue comes from Clean Energy and Infrastructure at about US$6.1b, Power Delivery at US$5.2b, Communications at US$3.4b, and Pipeline Infrastructure at US$2.7b. artigo.texto: The CRU published a decision on the initial procurement of Long Duration Energy Storage (“LDES”): Long Duration Energy Storage Decision Paper. This follows an earlier consultation, which we looked at in our insights blog post: Energy update: Long Duration Energy Storage. The CRU now approves the core framework for the initial procurement of up to 500 MW through a technology-neutral, service-based procurement, progressed through the ECP connection process (for more detail, see our briefing: New Connection Policy for Onshore Generators and Storage). EirGrid proposes a two-stage procurement: qualification followed by a tender phase. Which projects can participate? To qualify, projects must have: - a minimum four hours’ import and export duration on the transmission system, - a 1:1 ratio of maximum export capacity (“MEC”) to maximum import capacity, - a minimum capacity of 20 MW for hybrid projects or 75 MW for standalone projects, - a maximum capacity of 100 MW, and - round-trip efficiency of at least 75%. At qualification stage, projects must hold a connection offer at 110 kV or above. At tender stage, projects must have a connection agreement, planning consent for the facility and grid connection, evidence of land rights for the grid connection, maps and AutoCAD drawings of the grid infrastructure, and a detailed connection programme. Co-located sites must have at least 30 MW of TSO-connected renewable generation, with separate market registration and sub-metering. How will projects be selected? At qualification stage, company and project requirements will be assessed on a pass/fail basis. Company requirements include financial turnover (to be confirmed through further consultation), relevant experience and cyber-security requirements. Qualifying tenders will be scored on cost (50%), impact (30%) and connection method (20%). - Impact scoring evaluates a project’s ability to reduce renewable dispatch down and remain available to provide wider system value, using data from hourly ECP modelling. - Connection method scoring is intended to incentivise efficient use of grid. EirGrid’s proposal is that new standalone transmission connections will receive zero points, while the maximum of 20 points will be given to existing standalone connections at tender closing date or to hybrid connection arrangements (with at least 30 MW of renewable generation). EirGrid does not propose MEC sharing for this initial procurement, considering it infeasible within the required timeframe. We touch on some of the issues in our insights blog post: Energy Update: Sharing Maximum Export Capacity at electricity grid connection points. Highest-ranked projects will progress to a Best and Final Offer stage and a Deliverability Assessment, aspects of which are to be further consulted upon. What revenue support will be available? Service duration will be ten years. The CRU has approved in principle a competitively bid revenue floor, subject to an LCOS-informed bid limit. EirGrid proposes that the floor be set on a pay-as-bid basis and remain fixed over the contract term, subject to indexation, with a true-up payment where eligible market revenues fall below it. The storage asset will retain 70% of revenues above the floor, with 30% shared with consumers. EirGrid proposes returning the consumer share through transmission use-of-system charges. The cost of electricity bought for charging (and therefore the round-trip efficiency losses) will be netted off against gross eligible market revenues, but the asset’s other operating, commercial and financing costs will not be deducted. Open-book accounting will be required. EirGrid proposes quarterly interim settlements and annual reconciliation. Full approval of this framework remains subject to EirGrid demonstrating its effective interaction with other mechanisms, as noted further below. How will assets operate? Contracted assets will retain full SEM market access, subject to Trading Envelope compliance. The CRU supports the Trading Envelope model in principle and has approved initial issuance of dynamic import/export limits at 10:00 on the day before the Trading Day. EirGrid must publish a Trading Envelope methodology in advance of the tender and house the methodology and issuance timing in a protocol document so that any material changes are subject to public consultation and CRU approval. The CRU supports in principle non-compliance charges (for taking positions outside a Trading Envelope) and a Trading Non-Activity Scalar (which would reduce the floor for insufficient participation or cycling). Methodologies remain to be consulted on, including treatment of inactivity caused by TSO instructions or Trading Envelope limits. Next steps Many of the revenue and operational design features are subject to final approval by the CRU following demonstration by EirGrid that these mechanisms operate together as a coherent and financeable package providing effective incentives for assets to operate and deliver system value. Before tenders are invited, EirGrid must consult on and finalise the Trading Envelope methodology, Trading Non-Activity Scalar, Deliverability Assessment methodology, contractual arrangements and governance and change-control provisions. The consultation on contractual arrangements is to include timelines. Before contracts are awarded, EirGrid is required to notify the CRU of the proposed selected portfolio, aggregate volume and expected costs.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›Tata Power Deploys 60 MWh BESS Across Three Locations in Mumbai Tata Power Deploys 60 MWh BESS Across Three Locations in Mumbai Tata Power has operationalised 60 MWh of BESS across Mahalaxmi, Saki and Mankhurd in Mumbai, with the installations serving a distribution network covering over 8 lakh consumers and supporting peak demand management. November 10, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Tata Power has operationalised 60 MWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) across Mahalaxmi, Saki and Mankhurd to strengthen Mumbai’s electricity distribution network, which serves over 8 lakh consumers. The installations store electricity during lower-cost solar generation hours and discharge it during evening peak demand, helping optimise power procurement costs, improve energy utilisation and reduce dependence on expensive peak-hour electricity, the company stated. Equipped with fast-response and high ramp-rate capabilities, the systems support dynamic load management and enable the distribution network to respond to fluctuations in demand. Operating at approximately 1–1.5 cycles per day, the installations also support peak load management and power procurement optimisation. The decentralised, grid-connected systems provide localised energy storage and dispatch capabilities, while their black-start functionality supports grid restoration during power system disturbances. The operational capacity forms part of Tata Power’s larger plan to modernise Mumbai’s electricity infrastructure. In April 2025, the company received approval from the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) to deploy 200 MWh of BESS across 10 strategic locations in the city. The larger deployment is aimed at strengthening grid stability, managing peak demand, improving reactive power management and supporting faster restoration of electricity supply to critical infrastructure, including hospitals, Metro services, airports and data centres, the company stated. artigo.texto: Power Where Are the Biggest U.S. BESS Projects Being Built? U.S battery energy storage systems, virtually unknown at a utility-scale only a few years ago, are growing larger, representing construction investments in the U.S. Released Monday, November 09, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Eric Funderburk for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary U.S. battery energy storage systems are growing larger, often exceeding hundreds of megawatts in capacity and racking up substantial construction investments. A Big Market The deployment of battery energy storge systems (BESS) across the U.S. has represented a major shift in the U.S. power sector, opening the door to a utility-scale power source that was virtually unknown only a few years ago. And that door has opened in a big way. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) in August reported that nearly 52 gigawatts (GW) of battery energy storage was deployed in the U.S. at the end of June 2026, with 8.3 GW of that coming in the first half of 2026 alone. A previous article from Industrial Info Resources noted that $3.8 billion worth of standalone BESS projects were lined up to break ground in September. In addition to standalone battery facilities, dozens of BESS units are lined up to accompany solar installations, evening out power supply at times when solar power isn't actively being generated. Industrial Info Resources data show more than 1,400 U.S. BESS projects, valued at nearly $642 billion, either underway or on the planning table, although these frequently include solar power and a handful of wind projects accompanying the battery storage. Current construction represents more than $25.5 billion in investments. The Bigger, the Better? So where are the largest BESS projects currently being built in the U.S., and what is driving this $25 billion in current construction? One BESS installation rises to the top of the list: Intersect Power's Darden Clean Energy Project in Fresno, California. This massive 1,150-megawatt (MW) battery installation will be able to match the output of the accompanying 1,150-MW solar power plant at maximum discharge for a period of up to four hours with its 4,600-megawatt-hour discharge rating. The BESS unit plans to employ Tesla's lithium-ion-phosphate (LFP) battery technology and is expected to begin operating in 2028. Subscribers can access details of the project, including construction timelines, key contact details, and equipment and service needs on both the solar BESS components of the project, by clicking here. Battery storage also is a major component of the Steel River Energy Center being built near Osceola, Arkansas, which will feature 720-MW/2,880-MWh of battery capacity at full buildout. Work is underway on the first two phases of construction, which will add 480 MW of battery capacity to accommodate 1,000 MW of solar generation. A third phase of construction to add more solar generation along with an additional 240 MW of battery energy storage capacity is planned to get started at a later date. Work is just getting started on SB Energy's Libra hybrid energy center in which 700 MW of solar capacity is equally matched a 700-MW/2,800-MWh BESS unit. SB Energy has employed SOLV Energy to construct the project on federal lands managed by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM) near Yerington, Nevada. The project has a targeted in-service of 2028. Oregon a Prime BESS Destination Planned BESS builds are a more slippery target, but a few substantial projects seem to likely to move forward, including an anticipated 1,400 MW of battery storage at an Oregon project backed by Amazon. Ownership of the Sunstone solar/BESS project in northeastern Oregon was transferred to a subsidiary of Amazon earlier this year, but drawing on Amazon's substantial resources and a hard deadline of November 2027 to get moving on construction, the project seems likely to move forward. The first two phases of construction will add a combined 400 MW of BESS capacity, while a projected third phase would add a massive 800 MW of additional battery energy storage, although work on this final phase remains a few years out. Another substantial BESS project is on the books for Sherman County, Oregon, in the form of the Buckley solar/BESS facility, which could begin construction next year. The project planned by Boise, Idaho-based Clenera Renewable Energy would include 1,200 MW of solar and matching 1,200 MW of battery capacity with a four-hour discharge time. Substations, transmission tie-ins and all manner of equipment are part of the project, so an anticipated completion date of early 2029 could prove somewhat optimistic, depending on when construction kicks off and the pace at which is performed. Key Takeaways - BESS capacities are growing larger, often matching the solar generation capacity it frequently accompanies. - Oregon is the destination for two substantial BESS projects, each planned to add 1,200 MW or more of battery capacity. artigo.texto: Last week, Ohio had more data center-related measures on the ballot than any other state, and voters from Piqua to Grove City, Conneaut to Urbana, overwhelmingly voted to restrict the hyperscale developments. Barry Blankenship started leading a data center resistance group in Trenton in southwest Ohio after two projects were proposed near his home. He says the ballot measure results send a message to local leaders about where residents stand. “That shows when the power of the people comes together, we can beat money and we can beat big tech,” Blankenship said. Note: election results are unofficial until confirmed by each county’s Board of Elections. Find more detailed information about local results below. The Ohio Newsroom’s Erin Gottsacker spoke with WVXU Environment Reporter Isabel Nissley about the types of ballot measures voters considered and what the results say about public sentiment. On why voters favored restricting data center developments Nissley: Data centers really connected to this larger election issue of affordability. The computing facilities require massive amounts of electricity, which is driving up energy costs statewide, and people in several communities told me they're already having to make tough choices with their finances. They're scared for what they'll have to cut next if electricity bills keep climbing up. Other people say they don't want this resource-guzzling big tech infrastructure as a neighbor. They say they're worried about data centers' noise, pollution, water use, a lack of transparency about projects from government officials and more. Those concerns are bipartisan, and they drove Ohioans to the polls to deliver an overwhelming rebuke of data centers last week. Ballot measures to limit the developments passed with a large margin of support statewide, from Sunbury in central Ohio, which passed a ban on large facilities with 79% of the vote, to Perry in Northeast Ohio, which approved restrictions with 87% of voters in favor. On how Ohio election results compared with other parts of the country Nissley: About a dozen other states had data center-related measures on the ballot, and like in Ohio, many passed with large margins of support. What's different here is the number of data centers. There are more than 200 projects planned or under construction in Ohio. That's the fifth highest number in the nation. On the impact on future developments Nissley: Organizers say last week's vote is just the start of getting more restrictions on data centers in Ohio. A statewide coalition made up of lawyers and everyday people worked with the dozen plus communities to draft ballot language. Now, Conserve Ohio says it's looking to expand its efforts in more communities and help more people amend their city charters to ban data centers. The group is also collecting signatures for a statewide petition to amend the Ohio Constitution to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers. In terms of projects that are permitted or under construction, it looks like they'll largely proceed as planned. But future projects won't have as easy of a path forward if they're allowed to build at all. On the consequences of limiting data center development Nissley: Organizations like the Ohio Chamber of Commerce see data centers as major economic drivers. A Chamber of Commerce Research Foundation study says $40 billion have been and will be invested in data centers around the state through 2030, as well as jobs and state and local tax revenue. With new restrictions on these projects, they say communities will lose out and suffer economically. How ballot measures fared Data center ballot measures ranged from outright bans, to new regulations, to recalls of elected officials who supported data centers. Southwest Ohio City of Trenton: a charter amendment to prohibit the construction of data centers over 25 megawatts within city limits passed with 80% of the vote. City of Piqua: a charter amendment to ban the construction of data centers larger than 25 megawatts of peak power demand passed with 67% of the vote. City of Piqua: recall of commissioners in the city’s 1st, 3rd and 5th wards. All three were recalled with at least 70% of the vote. City of Urbana: a charter amendment to ban the construction of data centers larger than 7.5 megawatts of peak power demand passed with 77% of the vote. City of Urbana: a recall of Mayor Bill Bean passed with 73% of the vote. City of Wilmington: four referendums to reverse the February rezoning of four parcels totaling more than 500 acres near U.S. 68 from “rural residential” to “light industrial” adjacent to proposed data center campus. Each zone change was reversed with support from at least 79% of voters. Monroe Township (Adams County): a resolution establishing a zoning review process for “higher-impact development” passed with 60% of the vote. Sprigg (Adams County): a resolution establishing a zoning review process for “higher-impact development” passed with 53% of the vote. Northeast Ohio City of Hubbard: a blanket ban on all data centers in the city passed with 76% of the vote. City of Conneaut: a charter amendment prohibiting data centers larger than 25 megawatts in the city passed with 64% of the vote. Village of Perry: an ordinance requiring that data center development companies seeking tax incentives provide financial backing to commitments around jobs and tax revenue. Developers must post a bond to back those claims before receiving any incentives. The measure also implements noise requirements. It passed with 87% of the vote. Village of Monroeville: a pro-data center ballot issue FAILED with 87% of the vote. It was an advisory ballot question regarding an ordinance to allow data center development in the village. Because it is advisory, this question does not mandate the village to take any particular action but informs them of community sentiment. artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council advances data center plan, lays out rules Minneapolis leaders moved a data center ordinance ahead as members remained split over tax relief, oversight and environmental concerns. The Minneapolis City Council moved the ordinance forward Monday, with the city’s moratorium set to end in two weeks. The proposal is headed to a full council vote later this week. There were more than 1,600 public comments as the council debated the rules. The ordinance would require data centers to be downtown, 150,000 square feet or smaller and only in existing office space. Other restrictions included that data centers cannot be the primary use of a building or be on the first two floors. Supporters said the projects could help as downtown property values slump and the tax base falls. “I have heard some say that the economic benefit of these small-scale data centers is wishful thinking; I beg to differ,” Minneapolis City Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer said. “Will small-scale data centers be a cure-all for revenue generation?” Shaffer asked. “I’ve already said no. Is it a step in the right direction for some revenue generation and property tax relief? Yes.” Councilmember Aurin Chowdhury backed an all-out ban, but that effort failed Monday. Chowdhury said residents wanted stronger limits and raised concerns about environmental effects. “What I hear from my constituents is, ‘Don’t sell us out to big tech, don’t sell it out to this industry that oftentimes tries to go around the rules and find loopholes,'” Chowdhury said. “It could have absolutely gone further,” Chowdhury added. “Residents asked for far more.” The council also failed to approve an overlay district that would have required future data center projects to get council approval. Mayor Jacob Frey’s office said he did not support that step but does support the ordinance the full council will take up later this week. His office shared the following: “The Mayor had been in conversation with council members ahead of today’s meeting. He supports the regulatory framework that was approved today.”

artigo.texto: HARRISBURG, PA — Four Chester County lawmakers are backing legislation that would require large Pennsylvania data centers to secure additional electricity capacity, disclose water consumption and commit to substantial local economic benefits, introducing new statewide oversight as communities confront the infrastructure demands of large-scale computing facilities. House Bill 2888, introduced Nov. 4 and referred to the House Energy Committee, would establish energy, environmental, employment and public-reporting requirements for hyperscale data centers. Chester County Democratic Reps. Chris Pielli, Kristine Howard, Melissa Shusterman and Danielle Friel Otten are among its co-sponsors. The legislation would create state-level obligations for qualifying facilities while preserving municipal authority over zoning and land use, a distinction relevant to ongoing data-center development disputes in East Whiteland, East Brandywine and other Chester County municipalities. Under the proposal, operators of new hyperscale data centers would be required to develop plans for obtaining sufficient additional electricity capacity to meet their facilities’ full demand. The legislation also establishes escalating requirements for clean, reliable electricity generation, with alternative compliance payments available under specified circumstances. Operators would have to certify that changes to their energy plans would not impose additional costs on other electricity customers, addressing concerns about how major new power demands could affect the broader electric system. The bill generally defines hyperscale data centers by electricity demand, including facilities requiring at least 20 megawatts of power when served by utilities with peak loads of 2,500 megawatts or more. Affiliated or colocated facilities could be considered together when determining whether the threshold applies. Water consumption would face additional scrutiny. Qualifying operators would have to submit water-management and sustainability plans to state agencies and disclose annual electricity and water consumption. Depending on a project’s location and potential environmental effects, water plans could require hydrogeological studies, baseline monitoring and corrective measures to protect high-quality waterways, public drinking-water sources and nearby tributaries. The legislation would also establish minimum economic commitments for new or expanding facilities. Covered projects would be required to submit community-benefit plans providing for at least $250 million in investment, 200 construction jobs paying prevailing wages and 50 permanent positions paying at least 125% of Pennsylvania’s average statewide wage. Those requirements would apply to qualifying facilities beginning operations, expanding or making new investments after the legislation took effect. Developers would also be required to negotiate in good faith with host municipalities over community impacts, including noise, traffic, lighting, emergency-response demands and visual screening. Negotiations would additionally address local financial contributions and annual reporting, creating a formal process for municipalities to seek commitments from developers beyond existing zoning procedures. The proposed law would not eliminate local zoning authority or independently authorize or prohibit individual data-center projects. Municipal governments would retain their existing responsibilities for land-use decisions. State oversight would instead supplement those local processes through separate operating, environmental and economic-development requirements. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and Department of Community and Economic Development would administer portions of the proposed framework. After a 60-day period to correct violations, regulators could assess civil penalties reaching $25,000 per day for continuing noncompliance. Unresolved false or materially misleading submissions could trigger penalties of up to $50,000 per day. The bill’s reporting requirements would extend to qualifying data centers already operating in Pennsylvania, while its community-benefit obligations would focus on new operations, expansions and investments following enactment. For Chester County, the proposal would add a potential statewide regulatory framework to a development issue already generating local debate over land use, infrastructure capacity and municipal oversight. Its legislative prospects remain uncertain. House Bill 2888 was referred to the House Energy Committee on Nov. 4 and has not received a committee or floor vote. Pennsylvania’s 2025-26 legislative session ends Nov. 30, leaving less than a month for lawmakers to advance the measure. If the bill does not pass before the session concludes, it would need to be reintroduced in the next legislative session to receive further consideration. For now, the proposed energy, water and community-benefit requirements remain legislative proposals rather than enforceable obligations on Pennsylvania data-center operators. artigo.texto: Power Entergy Powers Up Texas, Louisiana for Data Centers Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $33 billion of projects from Entergy, with nearly $16 billion attributed to grassroot developments Released Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Entergy is turning to Texas and Louisiana to build out some of its highest-profile power-generation and transmission projects, including several attached to data centers. Powering Up the Pelican State Entergy Incorporated, a utility that serves parts of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Arkansas, is taking a bigger role in powering up the data center market, while scrambling to reinforce a regional power grid under growing stress. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $33 billion worth of active and proposed projects from Entergy, nearly $16 billion of which is attributed to grassroot developments. According to Industrial Info Resources data, more than 50% of the total investment is attributed to projects in Texas and Louisiana. In a quarterly earnings-related conference call last week, Andrew Marsh, the chief executive officer of Entergy, said his company has more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines planned, "primarily in Louisiana and Texas, 85% of which are 500-kilovolt lines. Approximately 70% of the investment is already approved." Last month, the Louisiana Public Service Commission (LPSC) approved Entergy's Babel-to-Webre Transmission Project, a 147-mile line connecting the company's Babel Substation in South Toledo Bend, Texas, which already is under development, to the existing Webre Substation in New Orleans. The project is part of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator's (MISO) 2025 Transmission Expansion Plan (MTEP25), which comprises 432 transmission projects intended to support rapid load growth and improve system reliability. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the Babel-to-Webre project in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Project Database, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in reports on the transmission line and substation. Marsh also said the U.S. Gulf Coast was a hotspot for its power-generation business: "We also have nine plants in regulatory review in Louisiana, with schedules to support decisions later this year. We have an additional four plants that are in our supply plan, but later in the cycle. That leaves eight units that are available for new growth opportunities." Hyperscalers are among the customers for Entergy's power-generation projects in Louisiana, Marsh said: "We have been innovative in expanding our investment by accessing less-traditional markets. For example, in October, we closed on our second build-to-suit lease" for a unit addition at its Waterford Power Station in Killona, Louisiana, which is being developed partly to service Facebook parent Meta Platforms Incorporated's Hyperion Data Center in Rayville, Louisiana, the first phase of which is under construction. Subscribers can learn more from detailed reports on the Waterford addition and the first phase of Hyperion. Subscribers also can consult a full list of project reports for Meta's nearly $79 billion worth of data center projects in Louisiana. By the Numbers - More than $33 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from Entergy - More than 50%: Share of the total investment attributed to projects in Texas and Louisiana - $940.3 million: Entergy's third-quarter net income, a 35.5% year-over-year increase Shaking Hands with Google Renewable energy also is in Entergy's project mix, including one project intended to serve a data center: the Cypress Solar & Battery Storage Project in Wright, Arkansas, which is designed to generate 600 megawatts (MW) from photovoltaic (PV) panels provided by Canadian Solar Incorporated and store up to 350 MW in a battery energy-storage system (BESS) unit. The Cypress complex will serve Google parent Alphabet Incorporated's West Memphis Data Center, nicknamed "Project Pyramid," a $10 billion investment across five buildings. To ward off public criticism surrounding data center growth, Google agreed to cover all power and infrastructure costs, including $600 million in new grid enhancements. The grid enhancements include a 250-MW BESS unit at the Driver Solar Plant in Osceola, Arkansas, and the 100-MW, standalone Jones Mill BESS unit in Malvern, Arkansas. Both projects are owned by Entergy. Subscribers can learn more from detailed project reports on Cypress, Driver and Jones Mill. Subscribers also can consult a list of reports for projects related to the West Memphis Data Center. Entergy reported consolidated operating revenues of $4.37 billion for third-quarter 2026, a 14.7% increase from the same period last year. Net income stood at $940.3 million, a 35.5% increase. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from Entergy. artigo.texto: Anthropic proposes IPO price as data center communities ask who benefits Company could be valued at up to $1.4 trillion; residents near projects seek a direct financial stake GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY) - Anthropic, the company behind the AI assistant Claude, proposed a share price of $70 to $78 on Tuesday for its initial public offering. Communities that host data centers are questioning whether the economic benefits last beyond construction. At the high end, the offering could raise up to $64 billion. The stock sale could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion. The sale has not happened yet. Data centers need land, power and approvals The industry’s growth depends on more data centers. Those projects require land, electricity, infrastructure and local approvals. Janine Yorio, CEO of Community Digital Technologies, works with residents near data center projects. She said there is a difference between building the facilities and sharing in the wealth they generate. “Part of the reason why people were so upset about data centers is because they see billions of dollars being poured into their local community to build them,” Yorio said. “But then the local prosperity ends there. After construction stops, there are very few jobs for local workers.” Tax revenue does not necessarily reach homeowners Data centers can generate tax revenue. Those benefits do not necessarily reach individual homeowners. Communities are pushing for residents to have a more direct financial stake in projects built near them. They also want more control over what gets built and who pays the price. As communities question the impacts, developers may face more pressure to offer benefits beyond tax revenue. Yorio said approaches used in the past may not be enough. “Developers have already tried lots of different things. They’ve tried giving towns new schools and paying taxes. And even that hasn’t been enough,” Yorio said. “So the next step is to talk to the neighbors like potential partners and offer them a piece of the upside. People want to understand that they are not going to get left behind by the AI economy that’s being built in their neighborhood.” Payments and ownership stakes Possible benefits include direct payments or ownership stakes for homeowners near data centers. There is no guarantee developers would agree. Copyright 2026 WBAY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de […] 10 de novembro de 2026, às 17:42 Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de sua linha pesada desenvolvida para atender às exigências elétricas cada vez mais complexas de máquinas agrícolas. Segundo levantamento da Companhia Nacional de Abastecimento (Conab), a safra brasileira de grãos 2026/27 poderá alcançar 367,1 milhões de toneladas, alta de 1,4% sobre o ciclo anterior. A área prevista de plantio chega a 85,4 milhões de hectares, expansão de 2,3%. Ao mesmo tempo, a Anfavea registra queda de 15,8% nas vendas de máquinas agrícolas de janeiro a agosto de 2026. Com a renovação mais lenta, preservar a disponibilidade dos equipamentos ganha peso na gestão da safra. A indisponibilidade de uma máquina pode exigir socorro, reparos e reprogramação de atividades, além de afetar o ritmo de outros equipamentos envolvidos no plantio ou na colheita. Ao apresentar a M100HA, a Moura reforça sua atuação em soluções de energia para o agronegócio, com suporte de sua rede nacional de pós-venda e destinação ambientalmente adequada das baterias ao fim da vida útil. “No campo, a produtividade não depende apenas da capacidade da máquina, mas de ela estar disponível quando o clima permite operar. Uma falha na partida pode interromper uma frente de trabalho inteira. Por isso, a escolha da bateria deve considerar o motor, as condições de uso e a instalação elétrica”, afirma Felipe Godoy, Diretor de Negócios Corporativos e Novos Mercados da Rede Moura. Além do esforço exigido na partida de motores a diesel, tratores e colheitadeiras incorporam atualmente computadores de bordo, GPS, telemetria, sensores e iluminação auxiliar. Esses recursos exigem conexões elétricas confiáveis. Com o motor ligado, o sistema de geração assume o fornecimento de energia. À bateria cabe garantir a corrente de partida e as funções previstas no projeto. A M100HA é uma bateria chumbo-ácido de 12 volts e 100 ampères-hora, com corrente de partida a frio de 930 ampères. Um de seus diferenciais é o posicionamento dos terminais, adequado aos chicotes originais de determinadas máquinas agrícolas. Quando a aplicação é compatível, a configuração dispensa extensões, emendas e esforços indevidos nos cabos, fatores que podem comprometer conexões sob vibração. A estrutura interna também contempla proteção e sustentação das placas, além de ligas de chumbo e separadores de alta retenção, recursos voltados à resistência mecânica e à durabilidade. Esses elementos são relevantes para máquinas submetidas à trepidação e ao uso intensivo no campo. A escolha exige observar as especificações do equipamento e não dispensa manutenção preventiva. artigo.texto: Power DTE Boosts Spending Outlook, Eyes Data Center Growth Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion worth of active and proposed projects from DTE Released Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary DTE Energy is raising its five-year investment plan in an effort to boost lower-carbon resources, including battery storage, and to cater to the U.S. data center market. Leaning into a Changing Economy DTE Energy Company is shifting its focus to some of the most energy-hungry parts of the U.S. economy: The Detroit, Michigan-based power provider announced last week it plans to sell off a non-utility subsidiary for $3 billion, so it can focus more on its regulated electric utility and fund a newly revamped five-year investment plan. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion worth of active and proposed projects from DTE. Last week, DTE raised its five-year investment plan, which covers 2027-31, to $44.2 billion. Specifically, the company aims to invest $39 billion at its DTE Electric subsidiary and $5.2 billion in its gas operations; the previous, 2026-30 investment plan totaled $34.5 billion, with $30 billion for DTE Electric and $4.5 billion for gas operations. The DTE Electric investment "includes approximately $23 billion of cleaner generation investment, supporting cleaner and more affordable energy for our customers while meeting demand growth," said Joi Harris, the chief executive officer of DTE, in a quarterly earnings-related conference call. "The plan includes 7.6 gigawatts (GW) of new solar and wind resources, 2.1 GW of new combined-cycle natural gas generation, and 2.7 GW of energy storage." According to Industrial Info Resources data, battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects account for more than $1.8 billion of DTE's active project slate. The two highest-valued projects both are just south of Detroit: the 350-megawatt (MW) Monroe I Energy Center in Monroe and the 200-MW Fermi Energy Center in Newport. Both are set to begin construction in the spring of 2027. artigo.texto: Data centers need power – lower income, rural residents pay the price By Caitlin Hayes, Cornell Chronicle As the engines of artificial intelligence, large data centers can consume as much power as medium-sized cities, straining grids and prompting expensive upgrades to U.S. energy infrastructure. New research finds that residents, and especially lower-income and rural residents, are disproportionately bearing the costs. In the study, published Nov. 9 in Nature Energy, Cornell researchers analyzed growth in energy demand and infrastructure projects for four major U.S. power grids from 2020 to 2025 and found that data centers have hiked wholesale energy prices and on average paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth – $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill in 2025. The remaining $5.13 billion, or 62%, fell largely on residents, with the lowest income households seeing extra energy costs up to 28% of their incomes. “We were trying to answer a very simple question: With the booming of data centers, who pays for that expansion and who benefits?” said Fengqi You, the Roxanne E. and Michael J. Zak Professor in Energy Systems Engineering in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering. “It’s not just a question of generating enough electricity but of whether the rules for paying for the grid are keeping pace with who is driving new demand.” The research is the first multi-region, long-term assessment of how data center development impacts infrastructure growth and how costs are distributed across communities. It comes amidst a boom in data center construction. The researchers found that transmission investment in energy infrastructure projects increased from $2 billion in 2020 to $34 billion in 2025, with data centers driving much of that rise. Debates are ongoing – from local communities to state governments to Congress – about who picks up the bill as growth accelerates; data centers are projected to consume between 8% and 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, with 70% to 80% of that attributed to AI. With first author and postdoctoral researcher Cheng Feng, You also looked at data centers’ economic benefits, finding that each gigawatt of data center capacity can create 15,000 jobs across the economy, with an average 2,700 jobs directly associated with the data center (although not necessarily all on-site). “In a lot of discussions right now, people take one side or the other, completely yes on data centers or completely no,” said You, director of the Cornell AI for Sustainability Initiative. “But there are benefits and costs, and the key issue in the end is how to balance the trade-offs.” Sharing the cost of power infrastructure The team analyzed data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers, as well as power-price records, rate filings from utilities, power-line plans, and federal household and job data. The major grids they studied encompass regions with the largest clusters of data centers, including the southern San Francisco Bay area; north Texas around Dallas-Fort Worth; the Midwest; and the mid-Atlantic region, including northern Virginia, where the biggest concentration of data centers has been built to date. State incentives for data centers have provided returns on the investments, if inconsistently, the researchers found. Some states, such as California, reaped $180 in worker income for every dollar spent, while Virginia increased income $2 for every dollar invested. The researchers determined that the presence of an existing, qualified workforce was a stronger indicator of high returns than the amount of incentive spending. Data centers also increased wholesale electricity prices, the amounts utilities pay regional power markets before delivering the electricity to homes. In the most-affected hubs, data center growth raised those prices by nearly 10% or more by 2025. In Virginia, the costs jumped 15% and in California’s southern Bay Area, 20%. In contrast, residents in New York and New England, where data center construction has been limited, have not seen clear price increases due to data center expansion, the researchers found. “I think that means we’re at a good starting point in New York to think about the next steps,” You said. “Economic benefits, job benefits, investment, fairly allocating the costs – these are the dimensions and trade-offs we need to consider.” A key problem is how the costs of new infrastructure projects are currently shared: The allocation is often based on previous patterns of energy consumption. “It’s kind of a chicken-and-egg problem,” You said. “Because if you’re going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there’s no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they’re not using energy. So with this model of relying on past consumption, households end up taking on much of the infrastructure costs.” Many more rural and lower-income residents saw proportionally higher bills; the share of rural families shouldering a high energy burden – spending more than 6% of their incomes on energy – rose 76% more than among urban residents. The authors cite a national survey finding that rural residents are also less likely to use AI tools like ChatGPT than urban residents. The impact on energy bills also has a wide geographical reach. For example, residents in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio help pay for grid upgrades linked to data center growth in Virginia, the researchers said. “You do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure,” You said. “The grid connects communities across states, and cost-sharing rules connect them financially.” Using insights from the data, You and Feng recommend changes to cost-sharing rules and strategies to lower burdens. In all four regions, they found that, if data centers cut back power use during 22 of the region’s peak demand hours each year, they would relieve strain on the grid and minimize the need to expand.
