artigo.texto: Protect Kansas circulating 3-part petition to ban hyperscale data centers TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - Both Topeka and Shawnee County now have a moratorium in place for data centers. Similar to what we just saw happen in Emporia, the group Protect Kansas is collecting signatures to ban hyperscale data centers. Even with moratoriums in Shawnee County and the city of Topeka, Protect Kansas is taking matters into their own hands. “The city can change their moratorium at any time. They’ve let us know that they could vote that in and change that any day,” Colleen Campbell, Protect Kansas co-founder, said. The petition is broken into 3 parts: - No data centers over 25 megawatts - Preventing Topeka from supplying water to data centers outside city limits - “No annexing the data centers from the county into the city,” Campbell said. “So it’s not completely banning data centers. It’s just saying, ‘hey, we don’t want these hyperscale ones that use a lot of resources,’” Campbell said. It’s not just about protecting people in the city. “The county doesn’t have any recourse for a petition or any kind of way for them to have their voices heard,” Campbell said. The petition needs 6,000 signatures that can be verified by the city clerk. “The city council actually has a chance to just accept the petition as is so they can go ahead and make it as law,” Campbell said. If city council doesn’t accept it, the petition could be challenged in court or put it to a public vote. Though the moratoriums are in place, Protect Kansas wants this to go beyond the expiration dates. “This gives us long-term protection, and it’s really mirroring what the moratorium has already done, so we’re just looking for that longer-term, more solid protection,” Campbell said. WIBW reached out to the city for comment on the petition, but the city has not responded. The Shawnee County moratorium expires at the end of Feb. 2027, and the Topeka data center moratorium expires in mid-July 2027. Copyright 2026 WIBW. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Maine developer revives plan to turn former Jay paper mill into AI data center JAY (WGME) -- A local developer has revived plans to turn a former paper mill in Jay into an AI data center, teaming up with the same national partner that pulled out of the original project in June. The local developer intends to file permit applications with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection to redevelop a portion of the former Androscoggin Paper Mill in Jay into a data center. Six years ago, a wood pulp digester exploded at the paper mill in Jay, eventually leading to the closing of the mill and a loss of 170 jobs. The $550 million facility Sentinel Data Centers wants to build wouldn't bring back all those jobs, but it could significantly ease some of the tax burden in Jay. "If we have nothing there, we have no tax base, and we have a property just sitting there with really no purpose,” Jay resident Jason Mancine said. “So, I think it's an opportunity." "I think it's a good idea,” Jay resident Elizabeth Bates said. “If not that, something else. They should do something with it." Some people in town say they're concerned about all the electricity and water data centers use. - Also read: After Mills vetoes statewide pause, Maine towns move to halt data center projects locally Town leaders say it would be about the same as what the paper mill used, and they don't expect much of an environmental impact change. "It's a former industrial site, so it's not as though we're putting this in the middle of a forested wetland or something like that," Jay Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere said. "I understand people's concerns about environmental impacts, but I think it would be miniscule compared to what paper mills were," Mancine said. CBS13 reached out to the developer and was told they are not commenting at this time. Earlier this year, Governor Janet Mills vetoed a moratorium on data centers after lawmakers refused to carve out an exception for the Town of Jay. Governor-Elect Hannah Pingree has said she would sign a bill to ban new data centers in Maine. "I don't know how that will play out," LaFreniere said. "My hope personally is that what they're coming out with at the state level will be met by this developer anyway." Developers plan to hold a public meeting at the Jay mill site in one month to talk about the impact of water and electricity use by the proposed data center.

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações aprovou R$ 46,3 milhões do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) para o projeto Prisma, plataforma que usa inteligência artificial para distribuir o processamento de dados entre infraestruturas, inclusive mini data centers, segundo o ministério em 9 de novembro de 2026. O Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), de Campinas (SP), executa o projeto, e a Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep) gere os recursos. O prazo é de 36 meses, contados a partir do convênio entre as duas instituições. Leia também - João Pessoa já sedia data center que vai quadruplicar de tamanho; Nordeste tem vantagem de US$ 17,4 bilhões no setor, aponta Redata - Brasil lidera expansão de data centers na América Latina - IA pressiona consumo de energia dos data centers O que o projeto Prisma prevê Segundo o Ministério das Comunicações, a plataforma deve decidir com IA onde e como os dados serão processados, distribuindo recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Os objetivos são reduzir o consumo e os custos de energia, cortar custos operacionais, acelerar o acesso à informação e proteger dados estratégicos. Os mini data centers são instalações menores, que processam dados mais perto de onde são gerados. O projeto prevê estimular a expansão dessas unidades em diversas regiões do país, sem informar quantidade nem localização. - Setores atendidos: saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. - Energia: soluções de armazenamento de eletricidade, para dar mais autonomia e continuidade aos serviços. - Segurança e governança: padrões internacionais de segurança e diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). De onde vem o dinheiro O Funttel é um fundo de natureza contábil, alimentado por contribuição de 0,5% sobre a receita bruta das prestadoras de serviços de telecomunicações, segundo o Ministério das Comunicações. Nos últimos anos, o fundo destinou mais de R$ 362 milhões a empresas do setor, segundo a pasta. O Prisma já aparecia entre os projetos do pacote de cerca de R$ 104 milhões do Funttel para o CPQD, anunciado em março de 2026 para 6G, nuvem e IA, com execução entre 2026 e 2028. O comunicado de 9 de novembro não informa se os R$ 46,3 milhões fazem parte desse total. O que dizem os envolvidos Frederico de Siqueira Filho, ministro das Comunicações, afirmou que investir em tecnologia nacional garante ao Brasil mais autonomia para proteger informações e reduz a dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior. Gustavo Correa Lima, diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, destacou que a arquitetura permite “maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”, ou seja, nas unidades próximas a quem gera a informação. Joana Meirelles, superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, citou o objetivo de disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional segura e sustentável. O que falta para o projeto sair do papel O aporte mostra a direção do governo, que é a de levar processamento para perto dos usuários com tecnologia desenvolvida no país. O que falta para isso se concretizar são os detalhes de execução. O comunicado não informa se o convênio entre Finep e CPQD já foi assinado, em quais regiões os mini data centers serão instalados, quantas unidades serão e quantos empregos o projeto gera. No Prisma, o ponto em aberto é a execução do convênio.

artigo.texto: RWE has started construction of its first battery energy storage system (BESS) in Italy. The 62.5 MW Ragusa battery will be located in Sicily. It will consist of 42 containers with lithium-ion batteries, being able to deliver its maximum output for four hours. This corresponds to a nominal storage capacity of 262.5 MWh. Commissioning is scheduled for the end of 2027. Sopna Sury, CEO RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said: “The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone. We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun. In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilising the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most. Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21 000 households for four hours. We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system.” Ragusa battery will provide balancing energy to stabilise the electricity grid. It also features the technology necessary to provide new grid forming services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). In addition to the batteries, RWE will build the associated grid infrastructure. This includes a high-voltage transformer to connect to the 150-kV grid. artigo.texto: ProLogium and Rimac Technology Advance Next-Generation EV Battery Development Paris, France, October 12, 2026 – ProLogium today announced progress in its collaboration with Rimac Technology on next-generation electric vehicle battery pack development. The companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in September 2025 to develop a next-generation battery platform and have completed a battery pack concept mockup, which will be displayed at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The next phase will focus on developing a functional battery segment to establish a basis for testing the thermal management and cell-integration concepts and support battery pack applications in the battery electric vehicle (BEV) market. The collaboration combines ProLogium’s next-generation cell technology with Rimac Technology’s battery system development expertise, focusing on a pouch cell-to-pack architecture. Through a staged development path from concept mockup to functional battery segment, full-scale functional battery pack and in-vehicle testing, the companies will progressively evaluate cell and system integration approaches, connecting next-generation cell technology with automotive product development. From Concept Mockup to Functional Hardware Bringing cell technology into automotive applications requires more than cell-level performance. It also involves addressing thermal management, cell integration and battery pack architecture at the system level. With battery pack integration at its core, the collaboration brings together cell technology and systems engineering to examine the design requirements for next-generation batteries in automotive applications. The completed concept mockup is an initial milestone in this development process. The ongoing development will move the project from a conceptual representation toward functional hardware, using a battery segment as the platform for subsequent testing. This work will assess the feasibility of thermal management and cell-integration concepts and inform full-scale battery pack development. By developing a battery segment before expanding to a full-scale system, the companies will gather test results and design feedback at each stage to assess whether the integration approach can meet automotive battery-systems requirements. Vincent Yang, Founder and CEO of ProLogium, said: Since jointly announcing our collaboration with Rimac Technology at IAA in 2025, both teams have continued to advance the project, translating our shared technical vision into concrete engineering development work. ”What we are presenting at the Paris Motor Show is the baseline of that collaboration. Building on the completed concept mockup and the functional segments currently in development, we are preparing to move into the development and production of a functional battery progressing toward a full-scale battery pack and subsequent vehicle integration validation. Bringing next-generation batteries to the automotive market requires more than cell technology. It also takes the engineering expertise to integrate those cells into a battery pack with optimized architecture and thermal management. We look forward to combining our technical strengths through hardware development and testing to address the engineering challenges of automotive integration and translate the value of next-generation cell technology into solutions that can be adopted in vehicles.” Daniel Kišić, Principal Product Architect of Rimac Technology said: Rimac Technology is developing a scalable cell-to-pack integration technology for solid-state pouch cells, designed to meet and exceed the requirements the automotive industry is expected to set over the coming decade. ”A wide range of integration solutions is currently being evaluated and tested in parallel on functional battery segments, covering thermal management, swelling management, cell integration and system-level design. Some of these solutions are oriented towards maximum energy density and reduced space and weight, while others are oriented towards delivering performance. The work starts from vehicle-level requirements and aims to improve every aspect of the battery design by reducing complexity, combining functions and reducing weight. It does so with cost in mind, while still delivering state-of-the-art charging times and power output. Once validated at vehicle level, the solution is expected to deliver significant weight savings, improving driving efficiency and extending range. OEMs could then choose between more energy on board at the same weight, a smaller and lighter battery for the same range, or any combination in between.” A Clear Pathway to Full-Scale Battery Packs and In-Vehicle Testing According to Rimac Technology’s current development roadmap, the functional battery segment currently in development is planned for display at CES 2027, with the full-scale functional battery pack identified as a development milestone for the second half of 2027. Subsequent targets include in-vehicle and public-road testing in the second half of 2028.These stages will progressively expand the scope of validation, from assessing integration concepts in a functional battery segment to a full-scale battery pack, followed by vehicle installation and road testing to evaluate system performance in an automotive environment. At the Paris Motor Show, the companies will present the concept mockup stage of the collaboration and outline the next steps in functional hardware development and integration validation. By combining cell technology with battery systems engineering, ProLogium and Rimac Technology will continue to advance next-generation battery integration technology development from concept design toward automotive applications. artigo.texto: On Wednesday afternoon, Jamie Robins strolled up to the entrance of Google’s UK headquarters in Kings Cross, London. He brandished a letter containing details of a petition signed by almost 55,000 people, calling for Google to abandon plans to build a large new data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London. Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site. Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility. Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them, hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US, people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works. Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour. Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week. In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner. “There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.” The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake. Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.) The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget. “We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.” Google says the objections are grounded in misconceptions about its plans. The company claims it will achieve a net gain in biodiversity by retaining habitat and transplanting endangered plants to another location; and that it will offset the emissions by financing new sources of renewable energy generation, with a view to becoming carbon-neutral by 2030. Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.” Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.” There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions. In the US, some states have instituted permitting freezes and data center moratoria, and pro-data center candidates were roundly crushed in this week’s midterm elections. In the UK, Foxglove recently succeeded in a legal challenge that forced the government to withdraw planning permission for a data center to the west of London. Thurrock Council tells WIRED it expects to rule on Google’s initial planning application early next year. After that, the company will need to come up with a more granular plan for developing the site, which will be subject to another lengthy vetting process. The protesters say they intend to make life hard for Google at every step. “These planning campaigns can go on for years,” says Robins. “It’s a war of attrition.”

artigo.texto: Power PPL Pours Capital into PJM as Data Center Plans Grow Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $7 billion worth of active and proposed projects from PPL, nearly half of which is attributed to grassroot projects Released Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary PPL expects growing energy demand from data centers in the PJM region will necessitate the development of more gas-fired and T&D capacity. Data Dominates the Agenda PPL Corporation, an important energy provider on the PJM Interconnection, is building out its gas-fired power-generation capacity to meet the ever-growing demand from data centers--especially in Kentucky and Pennsylvania, which have emerged as investment hotspots for the company. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $7 billion worth of active and proposed projects from PPL, nearly half of which is attributed to grassroot projects. Companywide, PPL plans to raise its base capital expenditures for 2027 through 2030 to $25 billion, which is $2 billion more than the 2026-29 plan. In Kentucky alone, the company's spending is set to increase from $2.3 billion in 2026 to $3.6 billion in 2027. "Through 2032, additional capital investment opportunities could reach a total of $12 billion to $16 billion," in addition to the amount projected through 2030, said Vince Sorgi, the chief executive officer of PPL, in a quarterly earnings-related conference call. "This includes additional regulated generation investment in Kentucky required to meet continued increases in potential demand growth." The increased spending in Kentucky is attributed largely to the proposed construction of a 645-megawatt (MW), natural gas-fired, combined-cycle (NGCC) turbine, subject to regulatory approval. But that approval could be a tough process: The Kentucky Public Service Commission (KPSC) has denied several requests from PPL in recent years to add new gas-fired capacity. However, KPSC did grant a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) in October 2025 for the proposed Unit 6 at Mill Creek Power Station in Louisville, Kentucky, which also is a 645-MW, NGCC unit. Louisville Gas and Electric Company (LG&E), a PPL subsidiary, owns Mill Creek and is developing the project, which is set to follow the ongoing construction of the 621-MW Unit 5. PPL expects Unit 5 will be completed sometime in the second half of 2027. Together, the two new units would nearly double capacity at Mill Creek, which has an operational output of at least 1,361.7 MW. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the Mill Creek developments in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a plant profile and detailed project reports on Unit 5 and Unit 6. Concurrent with the Mill Creek 6 approval, the KPSC granted a CPCN to PPL's proposed, 621-MW unit addition at the E.W. Brown Power Station in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, which currently has an output of at least 1,457.6 MW. Subscribers can learn more from a detailed plant profile and project report. By the Numbers - More than $7 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from PPL - $25 billion: The company's base capital expenditures for 2027 through 2030 - $12 billion to $16 billion: Additional capital investment opportunities from 2031 to 2032 Keystone State Key to Growth Sorgi announced in the earnings call that Invitium Energy, a joint venture between PPL Corporation (with a 51% stake) and Blackstone Infrastructure (49%), "signed a letter of intent (LOI) with Quality Technology Services (QTS) to be their generation solution provider in portions of Pennsylvania. Under that LOI, we have agreed with QTS on all key commercial terms for approximately 2 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity for its Salem Township Data Center project, with a 20-year initial term allowing for multiple five-year renewals." According to Industrial Info Resources data, the Salem Data Center, which is located in Luzerne County, comprises 12 buildings and more than $10 billion of investment value. Sorgi also noted PPL's large load tariffs "require data centers to cover the cost of serving them, so existing customers don't bear that burden." Subscribers can learn more from a plant profile and a detailed list of project reports. Through Invitium, PPL has proposed the Luzerne County Power Station, which is designed to generate at least 1.5 GW for data centers in the area. The company also is looking into additional transmission and distribution (T&D) capacity to support the load growth. Subscribers can learn more about the Luzerne County Power Station from a detailed project report. PPL's net earnings for the third quarter were reported to be $367 million, a 15.4% increase from third-quarter 2025. Operating revenues stood at $2.5 billion, an 11.5% increase. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from PPL. artigo.texto: A chinesa Trina Storage avalia instalar uma fábrica de baterias no Brasil, mas só deve decidir depois de conhecer o tamanho do mercado aberto pelos primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia do país, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Em entrevista ao Canal Solar, a líder de Vendas da empresa para a América do Sul, Mariana Goudel, disse que a companhia já apresentou cotações para projetos que somam mais de 50 GWh de capacidade. O número reúne negociações em diferentes estágios, e não contratos fechados. «Tem um plano em andamento, sim, da Trina, onde a gente quer trazer uma fábrica nos próximos anos», afirmou a executiva, sem informar prazo nem valor de investimento. Segundo ela, apressar a fábrica para atender à primeira contratação poderia comprometer a execução e a qualidade dos equipamentos. Conteúdo local no primeiro leilão Os editais foram aprovados na semana passada pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). O leilão de 2 de dezembro exige conteúdo nacional, e o de 4 de dezembro é de ampla concorrência. Para o primeiro, a Trina pretende combinar equipamentos importados com componentes feitos no Brasil: a parte de corrente alternada, ligada à conversão de energia, terá produção local, enquanto a de corrente contínua será importada. Os sistemas oferecidos têm duração de quatro horas. A empresa também busca o credenciamento no BNDES para acessar linhas de financiamento, incluindo o Fundo Clima, que a executiva compara ao papel que o banco teve na expansão das cadeias eólica e solar. Entre os potenciais compradores estão geradoras, transmissoras, fundos de investimento e grupos estrangeiros. Ambição de metade do mercado Não é a primeira vez que a Trina mostra apetite pelo leilão. Em agosto, durante a feira Intersolar South America, Goudel disse à pv magazine Brasil que o objetivo da empresa era «levar 50% do leilão», com a plataforma Elementa 3, e citou uma carteira de mais de 50 clientes no país, com mais de 100 GWh em projetos em discussão. A expectativa do setor é que os leilões de dezembro inaugurem uma nova fase para o armazenamento no Brasil, hoje puxado por aplicações em comércio, indústria e áreas remotas. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento (Absae) projetava, na mesma feira, demanda de 4 a 5 GW nos certames. Para cumprir as exigências de nacionalização, a JA ESS também estuda parceiros locais, a CATL reforçou a parceria com a Moura e a Jinko ESS assinou memorando com a UCB.

artigo.texto: What to know: - Romulus City Council unanimously passed a 180-day data center moratorium. - Romulus Mayor Robert McCraight said the city currently has no data centers and has not received any data center proposals, but the moratorium will allow the Romulus Planning Commission to consider regulations. - The moratorium was amended to apply to all data centers. ROMULUS, Mich. — Romulus City Council voted unanimously to impose a 180-day moratorium on data center proposals while the city studies how to regulate the facilities. The moratorium takes effect immediately. It was initially proposed for data centers with an electrical demand of at least one gigawatt, but council members amended it to apply to all data centers. The resolution directs the Romulus Planning Commission to study how to measure data centers’ electrical demand and environmental impacts and consider appropriate zoning regulations. Mayor Robert McCraight said the pause will give officials time to develop an ordinance. “It’ll allow a little bit of time to draft an ordinance. It’ll give us some time to pull in some information, pull in some third parties, and give us expert opinions and not just pass legislation, good legislation,” McCraight said. McCraight said Romulus currently has no data centers and has not received any proposals. Some residents called for a complete ban. Resident Kelly Babowicz said a moratorium was not enough. “A moratorium on data centers is not sufficient for our city. Instead, we need to push for a complete ban on these facilities,” Babowicz said. Councilwoman Kathleen Abdo and Councilman William Wadsworth also suggested looking into an outright ban. McCraight said the city should consider whether smaller data centers could support local industry, including Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport. “There may be some need for data centers on a smaller level to support industry,” McCraight said. “DTW may need a data center to support their industries. So we don’t know. We need to look at all those facets before we pass legislation.”

artigo.texto: Next week, much of the industry will gather in Las Vegas for RE+ to talk about what gets built next. It’s an important conversation, but I’d encourage asset owners to bring a second question with them: what more can we get from what’s already been built? This question matters more than ever as electricity demand climbs and customers feel it on their monthly bill. EIA expects consumption to grow another 3.1% in 2027, driven largely by data centers and other commercial loads, while residential customers will pay nearly 5% more for power this year. The industry is working hard to add capacity, but getting it built takes time. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and GridTracker, the median project built in 2025 spent more than five years moving from interconnection request to commercial operation and only 13% of the capacity that requested interconnection between 2000 and 2020 had come online by the end of 2025. New generation is essential, but the fleet already operating is an opportunity we can’t afford to pass up. With nearly 52 gigawatts (GW) of utility-scale battery storage operating in the U.S. as of mid-2026, the installed base is too large to overlook and performance across it varies widely. When a battery energy storage system (BESS) falls short, the instinct is often to blame the battery and reach for augmentation or replacement, but in many cases the bottleneck is the controls, software and integration around it. Operating assets are under more pressure Higher prices should raise the value of delivering power when and where the grid needs it, yet revenues for many operating assets are moving in the other direction. In ERCOT, the average battery earned 84% less in 2025 than at its 2023 peak, as more storage competed for the same services. With incentive economics shifting too, asset managers face real pressure to get more from existing assets. At the same time, utilities are leaning on storage for grid stability. As more gas units face revenue pressure and retirement, the grid loses the spinning mass that provides inertia in the first moments of a disturbance. Grid-forming inverters can replace that inertia, often by upgrading existing storage rather than building new. Providing that support, alongside peak shaving, load shifting and voltage and frequency regulation, takes controls that respond faster than many legacy SCADA and EMS platforms were built to handle. Compliance requirements are moving just as quickly, with FERC Order No. 901 directing NERC to develop new reliability standards for inverter-based resources, including batteries, through 2030. Many plants operating today were designed before those requirements existed, increasing the importance of controls that can evolve as grid codes change. The same logic also applies to solar and wind plants. Once control functions are proven in the field they can easily be applied to other assets across the whole market. The battery isn’t always the bottleneck A recent Gridmatic study of 30 California batteries shows what’s at stake, with fleetwide availability averaging just under 80% and execution and bidding strategy driving a wide gap between top and bottom performers. Had every asset matched the leader, the group would have earned an estimated $98 million more over two years. The lesson isn't that every performance gap can be solved with software. It's that owners shouldn't assume the battery itself is the limiting factor. Before committing additional capital, owners should examine the full system: controls, software, market strategy, integration and plant-level coordination alongside battery health and hardware performance. Think about the smartphone in your pocket. Its hardware may be several years old, but software updates can improve how it performs and add capabilities that weren’t available when you bought it. Storage assets aren't so different: the physical equipment may still have years of useful life, while the controls and software around it can evolve to meet new market and grid requirements. A modern energy management and plant control platform layered onto existing assets can help owners: - Respond faster and more precisely to grid signals and market opportunities - Meet new grid code requirements through software rather than hardware - Expand operational flexibility and support additional value streams - Maximize usable energy through balancing and intelligent power allocation - Extend the competitive life of existing assets A controls retrofit in practice We saw this firsthand in the U.K., where our team, then part of Wärtsilä, worked with Zenobē to retrofit an existing 100 MW/100 MWh battery site with a new GEMS power plant controller. The upgrade took over energy management, secured grid compliance and added stateful grid-code functions such as de-load, along with control for multiple tenants sharing one point of interconnection. The batteries stayed in place, but the site gained new capabilities and is better prepared for future requirements. That same approach translates to U.S. markets, where interconnection rules and local regulations are evolving quickly. New deployments will remain critical, but the next wave of value may come from making today’s fleet work harder. As the industry gathers at RE+, owners should ask not just what they need to build next, but what more the assets already on the grid could deliver. Before replacing hardware or adding capacity, diagnose the whole plant. The constraint may not be the battery cells.

artigo.texto: FIRST ON FOX: A new analysis from a conservative AI safety group found that deep-red counties with large data centers or proposed projects shifted further toward Democrats in last week's midterm elections than comparable counties without such projects. Humans First’s analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, examined public election returns and data-center project records in 1,540 counties across 16 states. The memo used several comparisons to measure what the group describes as a "data center penalty." Across all counties examined, those hosting large data centers shifted an additional 2.2 percentage points toward Democrats compared with non-host counties in the same states. The pattern appeared in 14 of the 16 states and 25 of the 27 governor and Senate races examined. Restricting the analysis to deep-red counties — those President Donald Trump won by at least 20 points in 2024 — produced a 2.1-point raw gap between counties hosting large data centers and comparable counties without projects. Among deep-red counties with projects still in the proposal stage, the gap was 1.1 percentage points after accounting for past voting patterns, rural or urban status, population size, racial and ethnic makeup and recent voting trends. TEA PARTY FOUNDER LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE 'DATA CENTER REVOLT' AGAINST AI DATA CENTER EXPANSION The group identified 114 proposed large data center projects across 92 deep-red counties, potentially setting up more local fights. The memo found that Republican vote totals fell an additional 1.1% in deep-red host counties compared with comparable counties without large data centers, while Democratic vote totals showed no significant change. The memo cautioned that its findings show an association rather than proof that data centers caused voters to change their behavior. County-level results also cannot determine whether Republicans switched their votes or simply stayed home. "Our analysis looked at how counties with data centers voted and how those counties moved to the left," Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer told Fox News Digital. "I think this happened for the reason I’ve been warning conservatives and Republicans about for some time: People engage politically when issues affect them personally. There’s nothing more personal than your pocketbook, your health care, your kids and family, your home and your community. A data center involves all of those things, which is why I believe these counties moved away from Republicans," she continued. Humans First’s September "Data Center Revolt" bus tour made 35 stops in 27 states, including 14 stops in the states covered by the analysis. Nine of those stops were in deep-red counties, all of which hosted a large data center project. Those nine counties shifted 2.2 points further toward Democrats after the analysis accounted for its controls, compared with a 0.75-point shift among deep-red host counties overall. The group said those same nine counties showed no comparable gap from 2020 to 2024. The findings do not establish whether the group's visits influenced voting behavior or whether those counties already had stronger opposition to data center development. Separately, voters favored restrictions on data center development or rejected measures supporting such projects in 46 of 47 local data center ballot measures in 2026, according to Ballotpedia. The measures included different types of proposals, including restrictions on development and advisory questions. Kremer said this is a local control issue, stressing that Republicans should focus on protecting property rights and ensuring people have control over how things affect their lives. "Whether you’re talking about AI technology or the infrastructure needed to build AI data centers, the American people have not had a seat at the table," Kremer said. "They haven’t had a say in how the technology affects them or how the data center buildout affects their communities. In many places across the country, developers and companies have gone in and cut deals behind closed doors, under a cloak of darkness, using nondisclosure agreements and shell companies. By the time people in the community find out about the project, it’s too late to stop it." "These projects affect the quality of life and how much money people have. They can increase the cost of electricity and water, while tax abatements are given to trillion-dollar companies — some of the wealthiest companies in the world. That is money coming out of the pockets of the American people," she continued. Kremer added, "When you talk about Iran and gas prices, tariffs and now the AI data center buildout, all of these costs are coming out of people’s pockets. That’s when people engage politically, and I think that’s what we saw last Tuesday." The concerns come amid a broader debate over how data centers should pay for the electricity and grid infrastructure they require. The Energy Department estimates data centers used 4.7% of U.S. electricity in 2024 and, in its reference case, could account for 11.8% by 2030. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has directed regional grid operators to address safeguards against shifting the costs of serving large electricity users onto other customers. Those developments do not establish that data centers caused higher household rates in the counties examined by Humans First. Tax incentives also vary by state. The National Conference of State Legislatures reported that at least 38 states offer incentives specifically for data centers, including equipment-tax exemptions and, in some states, exemptions involving electricity or property taxes. The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group, says such incentives are similar to those offered to other capital-intensive industries and argues that data centers generate jobs, investment and tax revenue. Humans First does not support a nationwide or statewide moratorium on data centers, but Kremer said individual communities should be free to approve

artigo.texto: The Rural Shift in Data Center Development As pressure on power, land, and permitting intensifies, more data centers are moving to rural areas, making remote sites a growing part of future development. Traditionally, key considerations when selecting a data center site have included access to power, proximity to end-user concentrations, and the availability of high-performance network infrastructure. Those factors help explain why data centers have historically been built in or near urban areas rather than in remote regions. Recent developments, however, suggest that this pattern is changing. Two-thirds of new US data center projects are targeting rural locations, marking a shift away from the longstanding concentration of facilities in major hubs such as Northern Virginia, Texas, and California. The change is not limited to the United States. Hyperscalers are also evaluating remote parts of South America as potential locations for the next generation of data centers. That shift raises two questions: Why are remote regions gaining prominence as data center sites, and does this represent a lasting change in site-selection strategy? Why Rural Sites Are Gaining Appeal Rural areas present distinct challenges as data center sites. They are often farther from end users, which can increase latency, and power and network infrastructure may be less developed or located farther away. At the same time, rural settings can offer advantages that may outweigh those drawbacks for some operators. One of the biggest is land availability. Securing enough land for a data center in or near an urban area can be difficult and expensive because undeveloped parcels are limited. In many rural markets, that constraint is less severe. Community opposition may also be more limited in less densely developed areas. Permitting can be simpler, too, because lower levels of surrounding development often mean fewer barriers to new construction. Power Constraints Are Reshaping Site Selection Another factor behind the shift toward less developed areas is the growing importance of on-site power generation. In a market where public power grids, including those in wealthy, highly developed regions, cannot always meet the capacity needs of new data centers, operators are increasingly exploring self-generated power. That can include dedicated generation assets or on-site plants. From that perspective, limited access to existing grid infrastructure in remote regions becomes less of a constraint. Fiber Is Still a Challenge, but a Manageable One On-site power does not solve every problem. Data centers still need access to high-performance network infrastructure, which, in most cases, means fiber-optic cables. Many rural areas currently have limited fiber access. Still, networking may be easier to address than power. Extending fiber is typically less expensive and less complex than building long-distance power infrastructure or developing major on-site generation capacity. In many cases, if existing fiber is available within a few hundred miles of a proposed site, connecting to it can be economically viable. Rural Data Centers Are Not New, but the Scale Is Although nearly nine-tenths of existing data centers remain concentrated in developed areas, the idea of placing facilities in rural regions is not new. Amazon, for example, explored the feasibility of data centers in Chile and Argentina more than eight years ago, and the discussion of rural data center development dates back at least a decade. What is different now is the level of execution. Over the past few years, operators have begun breaking ground on rural projects on a greater scale, driven by changing dynamics around power sourcing, land availability, and community response. Why the Shift to Rural Data Centers May Continue The factors that make rural locations more attractive are unlikely to disappear soon, suggesting that the industry will continue to expand into less-developed areas. That does not mean every new data center will be built far from cities. Urban sites will remain important for facilities that require ultra-low latency or whose scale does not justify the infrastructure investment needed to support a remote site. Even so, rural development appears to be shifting from exception to mainstream strategy. If constraints on power, land, and local opposition persist, a larger share of the industry’s next wave of large-scale projects is likely to be sited outside traditional metro hubs.

artigo.texto: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises AMD has begun shipping sixth-gen Epyc servers and is rolling out Helion AI racks, signaling a bigger push into enterprise and agentic AI infrastructure. AMD said Tuesday that its sixth-generation Epyc SP7 server processor is now generally available and that hardware makers have begun shipping servers powered by the new chip. The company also said the first Helion racks for agentic AI, which hardware vendors build from an AMD blueprint, will become available throughout this month. The new SP7 processor, which features up to 256 cores, is the first of four sixth-generation Epyc CPUs to become available. The other three are expected in 2027, AMD said. The broader family of sixth-generation processors, much of which is code-named “Venice,” is designed for enterprise, cloud, high-performance computing, and AI workloads, including agentic AI. AMD said it is seeing strong demand for the new chip. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su said early demand for Venice is the strongest AMD has seen for any new generation of Epyc processors. Su said AMD began revenue shipments of Venice during the third quarter and that hardware makers have committed to more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than the number committed for Turin, AMD’s fifth-generation Epyc chip. AMD is working to capture more market share in CPUs, GPUs, and overall AI infrastructure as it competes with rivals amid surging AI demand. AMD is directly challenging market leader Nvidia in GPUs and rack-scale systems, while Nvidia is taking on AMD with its own CPU. Arm has also introduced its own Arm-based CPU to compete with Intel and AMD’s x86 processors, and cloud providers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure have built their own custom AI accelerators and Arm-based CPUs. Sixth-Gen Epyc Targets AI Infrastructure as Helion Comes Online During the earnings call, Su said Venice delivers significantly better performance per watt, per core, and per dollar than any other x86 or Arm server CPU. AMD said systems based on the new Epyc SP7 processor deliver up to 3.7 times more performance than an Nvidia Vera CPU-based system and up to 2.2 times the performance of an Intel Xeon 6980P system. Agentic AI is driving demand for server CPUs, which play three distinct roles for the emerging workload: general-purpose services, GPU host nodes, and agent sandboxes. While GPUs handle inference, organizations still need a large number of CPUs to orchestrate the workflow, from invoking tools to retrieving data. AMD introduced Helion in October as an open rack-scale design for agentic AI. Hardware partners include Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Cisco. Helion racks, built for agentic AI, are different from AMD’s Helios racks, which are designed for large-scale inference, frontier model training, and fine-tuning. AMD said Helion will come in three versions: - Helion Liquid, a CPU-only, liquid-cooled rack designed to operate side by side with a Helios rack for large-scale agentic AI deployments; - Helion Air, a CPU-only rack designed to expand agent capacity within existing air-cooled data centers; and - AMD Helion Air Inference, an air-cooled rack that combines CPUs and GPUs for inference. AMD also said Meta is preparing to deploy sixth-generation AMD Epyc CPU-based platforms at scale and that Microsoft Azure’s Azure HDv2 service for AI data processing is now in preview. Why Venice Matters to Enterprise Data Centers Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Venice is an important launch for AMD and for enterprises. Enterprise CIOs have fixed power budgets in their data centers and need infrastructure that supports not only traditional workloads today, but also agentic AI in the years ahead, Kimball said. With up to 256 cores, Venice lets companies run traditional workloads on fewer servers, freeing up space for AI infrastructure. Servers running sixth-generation Epyc processors today are also well suited to support agentic workloads in the future because of the CPU’s high core count and large cache and memory, Kimball noted. “It’s huge for those enterprise organizations that are in the beginning stages of the AI-ification of their business,” he said.

artigo.texto: CATL unveils dual-battery system to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification CATL (HKEX: 3750) has unveiled a dual-electric range extension battery for heavy-duty trucks, pairing a swappable main battery with an independent on-board battery as it expands its push in freight electrification. The world’s largest EV battery maker introduced the system in Beijing on Tuesday, alongside upgrades to its Qiji battery-swapping system aimed at reducing fleets’ energy replenishment and battery costs. The system consists of 2 independent battery systems: a standardized, chassis-mounted swappable main battery and a 77-kWh range-extension battery behind the cab. The latter supports 3C charging and provides backup power. Drivers of conventional battery-swapping trucks typically return to swap stations with about 30% charge remaining to avoid running out of power en route, leaving part of their leased battery capacity unused, CATL said. With the backup battery, the system can increase the main battery’s depth of discharge (DOD) from about 70% to more than 95%, allowing trucks to return to a swap station with less than 5% charge remaining in the main battery. The system can switch power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining uninterrupted power and providing redundancy under demanding operating conditions, the company said. It uses what CATL calls a “1+X” architecture. The main battery remains standardized for compatibility with the Qiji swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be tailored to requirements such as low-temperature performance, high energy density or high power. The 2 battery systems can be upgraded independently. The range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an on-board asset, while the main battery can be leased flexibly according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental expenses during idle periods. Alongside the new system, Qiji introduced the 260# and 300# standardized swappable batteries, with capacities of 432 kWh and 513 kWh, respectively, complementing its existing 75# battery. The new-generation Qiji station can complete a battery swap in 5 minutes and reduces construction costs by 10%, CATL said. It requires no excavation pit and can be deployed in as little as 5 days. The company also changed the billing method for its battery-as-a-service (BaaS) offering, charging customers for net energy charged rather than energy discharged, allowing them to retain the benefits of regenerative braking. The change can reduce per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%, further improving the economics of operating electric heavy-duty trucks, according to CATL. The company plans to have 900 heavy-duty truck battery-swap stations operating by the end of 2026 and expand to 2,000 by 2027. Its long-term goal is to deploy 10,000 stations across China with partners. Agreements covering 13,000 vehicles were signed at the event, with orders for battery-swapping products from major logistics companies including SF Holding and China Postal Express & Logistics. The launch comes amid a rapid increase in new energy vehicle (NEV) penetration in China’s heavy-duty truck market. New energy heavy-duty trucks accounted for 50% of the segment in September, up from 29% a year earlier, according to China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) analysis of compulsory traffic insurance data. CATL launched its Qiji Energy heavy-duty truck battery-swapping solution in June 2023 and introduced the 75# standardized swappable truck battery in May 2025, expanding its presence in logistics. On June 30 this year, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement with J&T Express to provide swappable batteries, swap-station equipment, and operation and maintenance services for more than 5,000 heavy-duty trucks. Beyond the dual-electric range extension system, CATL also unveiled truck batteries for different transport applications, including ultra-light and ultra-thin packs mounted behind the cab, as well as chassis-mounted batteries for short-haul and long-haul operations. artigo.texto: Resumo - Governo federal destina R$ 46,3 milhões ao desenvolvimento da plataforma Prisma - Projeto usa inteligência artificial para distribuir dados entre mini data centers - Finep administra os recursos; o CPQD fica responsável pela execução do convênio - Prazo de execução previsto é de 36 meses após a assinatura do acordo - Expectativa é reduzir gastos de energia e aumentar a proteção de dados estratégicos Ao Prisma, plataforma criada para administrar e repartir informações entre mini data centers espalhados pelo território nacional, a União aplicará R$ 46,3 milhões. O Ministério das Comunicações divulgou os detalhes nesta segunda-feira (9). Para definir onde e de que maneira os dados serão processados, a tecnologia se apoiará em inteligência artificial. Na prática, o sistema identifica o melhor destino para cada conjunto de dados e distribui de forma automática os recursos computacionais entre as diferentes infraestruturas. Com isso, o Executivo projeta queda nos gastos com energia e nos custos operacionais, além de acesso mais rápido às informações e maior proteção dos dados considerados estratégicos. Quem administra e executa o projeto Caberá à Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep) administrar os recursos, enquanto o Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD) se encarregará da execução. Assim, a partir da data em que as duas instituições assinarem o convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação, começa a contar o prazo definido, de 36 meses. Aposta em soberania digital Por fim, o tratamento de dados no país ganhará mais autonomia e soberania com a medida, na avaliação de Frederico Filho, ministro das Comunicações. Em nota, ele declarou: ‘Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior’.

artigo.texto: Estimated read time: 5-6 minutes - A Salem forum debated data centers' impact on Utah County communities and environment. - Volition's CEO defended its data center project amid concerns over pollution and resources. - Grassroots group Speak Up Utah seeks 7,000 signatures for a referendum on data center policies. SALEM, Utah County — A packed room at the Salem Community Center on Monday night heard from a panel of policymakers, technology leaders, conservation advocates and data center developers as Utahns wrestle with a growing question: Can data centers be developed responsibly? The discussion focused on transparency, community involvement and accountability as large-scale data center projects continue to move forward across despite mounting public concerns. Kieren McCord, civil and construction engineering professor at Brigham Young University, said communities should understand the various technologies available when evaluating proposed projects. "There's a lot of nuance in the types of mechanical cooling systems that you can use; there's a lot of nuance in the types of power generation, and those decisions are often made early on in the process," McCord said. "Knowing the options in each of those categories makes you able to ask for things, because maybe, maybe you just think 'No data center whatsoever.' But maybe you think, 'Yes, under the right conditions.'" One project at the center of the discussion was Volition, a data center development initially proposed near the mouth of Spanish Fork Canyon. The project is now planned for a site across I-15. Volition CEO Jeff Chavez said the new location is farther from existing homes. He said there are no plans for future residential development nearby. Chavez defended the project against concerns about pollution and resource consumption, arguing that Volition's model differs from many traditional data centers. "We have no electricity from the grid, no wasted water (and) a really strong economic return to the community," Chavez said. "We have no request for incentives. We meet all air emissions requirements." Grow the Flow executive director Ben Abbott said it should be required that all data centers are built with clean energy. "We can't sacrifice our air quality," Abbott said. "It used to be when the wind blew, that's when the inversion would clear out. Now, when the wind blows, we get pollution from Great Salt Lake because there are 1,200 square miles of exposed lakebed. So we also have to make sure that we aren't moving backwards when it comes to water conservation and security." Chavez also said data center operators should do more to reduce the visual impact of their facilities and make commitments to local communities. "Companies like ours can also volunteer and say, 'Here's our commitment,'" Chavez said. "'We will not work with nefarious companies. We do not work with surveillance, we do not work with the Department of War (and) we do not work with the Chinese.'" Members of the grassroots organization Speak Up Utah attended the event and said they are leading an effort to overturn Spanish Fork's recently approved data center ordinance through a referendum. The group has raised concerns about public input, air quality impacts and data privacy, among other issues. Chavez said Volition does not currently have a response to the referendum effort, adding that city leaders were well informed throughout the approval process and that many concerns had been addressed. "We really don't have a response to the referendum, because I think everything we did in the city, open hearings, the open houses that brought in several hundred people (and) website that details all of this site, we feel like the city is pretty well informed," he said. Carol-Lyn Jardine with grassroots organization Conserve Utah Valley said one of the main goals of the forum was informing residents about key issues with data centers before the Utah County Commission votes on a new policy. A previous planning commission meeting received a lot of attention after a physical altercation between an audience member and law enforcement. "While we're considering what the impacts are on people, on the environment, on the land (and) on water, and if we don't invite all voices to the table to have those kinds of conversations, we find that the rhetoric just gets dialed up on both sides," Jardine said. "When we can bring people together and have real dialogue where folks get to ask their hard questions and people who are looking at these projects get to hear the real concerns of residents, we can find more positive outcomes." Silicon Slopes CEO Clint Betts argued that industry and political leaders have not adequately explained the benefits data centers bring to Utah communities. "I can tell you who benefits from having a data center in your community: Elon Musk, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta and the Department of War," Betts said. "Why do we need them?" Chavez countered that data centers support many technologies people use every day, from streaming services and videoconferencing platforms to emerging artificial intelligence tools. "There is an infinite number of systems that we rely on today because of data processing through a computer in a data center," Chavez said. "There's a lot of things that superintelligence and high-density computing is doing that is changing. Medicine is changing. Industry is making things much more efficient." Speak Up Utah organizers said they are seeking roughly 7,000 signatures to qualify their referendum effort. The group is hosting informational and signature-gathering events at the Spanish Fork Public Library.

artigo.texto: Os desafios dos Sistemas de Armazenamento Hidráulico no Brasil Os SAH são empreendimentos intensivos em capital e de prazo de maturação Atualizado O Setor Elétrico Brasileiro (SEB) atravessa um período sensível de mudanças estruturais, marcada pela expansão acelerada das fontes renováveis variáveis e da geração distribuída. Segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional (EPE, 2025) as fontes renováveis responderam por 86,8% da geração elétrica, enquanto eólica e solar alcançaram 26,4% do total. A capacidade instalada de energia eólica chegou a 34,7 GW e a fotovoltaica a 64,8 GW, dos quais a micro e minigeração distribuída correspondeu por 45 GW com 7,2 milhões de unidades consumidoras. Essa transição energética altera a composição de energias renováveis, mas aumenta a necessidade de deslocar a geração de outras fontes ao longo do dia, exigindo, cada vez mais potência e flexibilidade para manter o equilíbrio entre demanda e oferta. Nesse contexto de transição, a expansão do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) não pode adicionar apenas energia e potência, mas precisa ter flexibilidade para deslocar excedentes de energia no tempo. Assim, o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) projeta um aumento dos cortes de geração por razões energéticas, ou seja, excesso de oferta, à medida que a expansão renovável e dos recursos energéticos distribuídos cresce mais rapidamente do que a demanda diurna. Armazenamento, potência e flexibilidade passam a ser atributos centrais e estratégicos para a expansão do SIN. A promulgação da Lei nº 15.269/2025 e as das regulamentações associadas ganham relevância para a superação dos problemas, através da construção de um arcabouço regulatório que reconhece o armazenamento no planejamento, estabelece regras de outorga, diferencia os Sistemas de Armazenamento Hidráulico (SAH) e orienta seus mecanismos competitivos de contratação. O desafio agora é transformar essas diretrizes investimentos. Os SAH podem efetivamente contribuir para integração das fontes solar e eólica, redução de restrições de geração, atendimento à ponta, resiliência energética, serviços ancilares, flexibilização e eventual postergação de investimentos em transmissão. Seu principal atributo é deslocar a geração de energia no tempo, já que consomem energia para bombeamento quando a eletricidade é abundante e ajudam a produzir energia quando é mais necessária. Em relação às baterias, os SAH apresentam vantagens quando são necessários grandes volumes de energia e períodos de armazenamento mais longos. As tecnologias tendem, portanto, a ser complementares: as baterias podem atender as necessidades de curta duração e resposta rápida, enquanto os SAH podem realizar ciclos diários prolongados e deslocamentos de maior duração (semanais, mensais ou sazonais). A evolução do planejamento ilustra essa mudança de escala. No Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE) de 2034 foi estimada 400 MW, já no PDE 2035, a necessidade chegou a aproximadamente 7 GW e, no PDE 2036, a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) passou a distinguir o armazenamento de curta e de longa duração. A Lei nº 15.269/2025 estabeleceu a sua base institucional ao reconhecer o armazenamento como atividade regulável, determinar sua consideração no planejamento e prever tratamento específico para os SAH. Ademais, abriu espaço para procedimentos de licenciamento de empreendimentos estratégicos distintos e reconheceu o valor sistêmico desse sistema de armazenamento. As Resoluções Normativas ANEEL nºs 1.161/2026 e 1.162/2026 deram tratamento a diferentes configurações de SAH incluindo do tipo ciclo fechado e intervenções associadas a usinas hidroelétricas existentes. As Resoluções CNPE nºs 7/2026 e 8/2026, por sua vez, orientaram a identificação de projetos e a estruturação de mecanismos competitivos para a contratação dos SAH. Recentemente, a Portaria Normativa MME nº 143/2026 estabeleceu o cronograma estimado de leilões para 2027 a 2029 e previu a possibilidade de participação de SAH nos Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade (LRCap) na forma de potência. A perspectiva de contratação deixa, assim, de ser apenas uma diretriz regulatória e passa a estar associada a uma programação concreta de leilões, ainda condicionada às necessidades de potência identificadas pela EPE. A fim de dar mais consistência e fundamentação à contratação via leilões, a EPE estruturou uma metodologia de cadastramento de projetos para subsidiar a definição do desenho dos futuros leilões. Isto porque o armazenamento hidrológico, diferentemente das baterias, não constitui, por si só, um produto homogêneo. Um SAH voltado a ciclos diários atende a uma necessidade distinta daquele destinado a deslocar excedentes por vários dias. Potência, duração, rampas, frequência de acionamento, ciclos sucessivos e requisitos de controle de frequência e tensão influenciam projetos e seus custos. O edital deverá estabelecer atributos e premissas operacionais claros, permitindo comparar projetos em bases equivalentes e precificar riscos a partir de referências comuns. Para os SAH, o padrão de utilização também afeta dimensionamento, manutenção e risco. Portanto, o contrato deve definir tanto a potência disponível quanto as condições de sua utilização. A alocação de riscos é igualmente decisiva. O risco de construção é do empreendedor, enquanto questões diretamente determinadas pela necessidade do sistema, como o acionamento para bombeamento, precisam de regras claras de liquidação. Também será necessário definir o tratamento da energia consumida no bombeamento, sua exposição ao Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças (PLD) e interação com o Mecanismo de Realocação de Energia (MRE). É importante que o consumo associado ao bombeamento não seja confundido com o risco hidrológico compartilhado pelo MRE e que geração e bombeamento tenham tratamento contábil específico na Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE), além de evitar dupla incidência da compensação financeira pelo uso dos recursos hídricos. artigo.texto: Most of Virginia’s spending on economic development incentives over a recent 10-year period went to data centers in the form of a tax break, according to a report released this week. Data centers are eligible for a state sales and use tax exemption on computer equipment and software, provided they meet certain investment and job-creation criteria. That exemption — which was the topic of extensive debate during the past General Assembly — accounted for about $4.1 billion of the $6.8 billion that the commonwealth put toward economic incentives between fiscal years 2016 and 2025, or about 60%, according to the report from the state’s Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission. The data center exemption constitutes the majority of that 10-year period even though reliable spending data for the data center tax exemption is only available since fiscal year 2021, according to the report. “Better information on the tax savings because of the data center exemption and because of data center growth in the state has resulted in dramatic increases in spending estimates on the exemption beginning in fiscal year ’21,” Ellen Miller, the commission’s chief economic development and quantitative analyst, said Monday while presenting the report to state lawmakers. The report noted that tax exemptions averaged $812 million in the five years since and totaled an estimated $1.4 billion in fiscal year 2025. It also said the exemption policy created 29 jobs for every $1 million of tax revenue that data centers didn’t have to pay and that for every $1 that Virginia spent on the exemption tax incentive, the state received 22 cents in revenue. Miller noted that the report does not include local impacts such as a county’s business personal property taxes. She said that as long as localities have not set their tax rates very low, data centers “should be generating a good amount of revenue for the locality.” Virginia has been dubbed the “data center capital of the world” due to Northern Virginia’s outsized quantity of the buildings full of computer servers that power the online world. The industry is expanding in Southside and Southwest Virginia, with multiple projects either publicly announced or rumored to be in motion. Appalachian Power has said it is seeing “explosive” demand for electricity from large potential customers, “primarily” data centers. Another finding from the new audit and review commission report: The data center tax exemption is not as influential as previously thought when it comes to data center companies choosing whether to set up or expand in Virginia. Previous reports attributed 90% of data center location and expansion decisions to the existence of Virginia’s sales tax exemption, the commission said. The latest report revises that downward, saying about 50% of such decisions were made based on the exemption. Miller said the change was due to more recent research on the impact of sales tax exemptions. Other economic development incentives from Virginia include different types of tax incentives, grants and programs that offer loans and gap funding. The data center exemption is 16 times bigger than the next largest incentive, a program that helps eligible manufacturers save on income taxes. Business savings from tax incentives other than the data center exemption have totaled about $175 million annually since fiscal year 2023, according to the report. Although grants make up just 16% of economic development incentive spending, they offer higher economic benefits than the data center exemption in part because they’re invested in industries such as manufacturing that have a greater impact on the economy through the goods they produce and the wages they pay, according to the report. For every $1 million that Virginia spends on grant awards, 131 jobs are created, and the state receives $1.29 in revenue for every $1 spent on grants, according to the report.

artigo.texto: Do carbono medido ao ganho ambiental comprovado: O desafio do SBCE Medir emissões não é, por si só, comprovar ganho ambiental. A partir da nova portaria do SBCE, o artigo propõe critérios para que a prova científica sustente conclusões jurídicas legítimas. segunda-feira, 9 de novembro de 2026 Atualizado às 17:21 Introdução Uma indústria divulga um inventário de emissões verificado por terceira parte. Um projeto florestal documenta o aumento do carbono armazenado na vegetação. Os dois resultados são relevantes. Mas bastam para afirmar que houve redução adicional de emissões ou ganho ambiental comprovado? Não necessariamente. O inventário quantifica emissões em determinado perímetro; o levantamento de biomassa descreve um atributo da vegetação. Nenhuma dessas evidências, isoladamente, demonstra causalidade, recuperação da biodiversidade ou saldo ecológico líquido. Essa distinção tem efeitos concretos sobre certificações, decisões de investimento e confiança nas informações ambientais. É nesse contexto que ganha relevância a portaria SEMC/MF 3.199, de 28 de outubro de 2026, publicada no dia seguinte. Ao escalonar as obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação - MRV no SBCE - Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa, a norma cria condições para produzir informações climáticas comparáveis e sujeitas a controle. Não fixa, de imediato, limites individuais de emissão nem impõe aquisição generalizada de créditos. Mas torna urgente uma pergunta para a regulação climática: o que cada metodologia permite reconhecer, juridicamente, como resultado ambiental comprovado? A resposta exige congruência entre o fato a demonstrar, a aptidão do método e a extensão da conclusão extraída da evidência. 1. A portaria 3.199/26 e a regulação orientada por evidências A portaria organiza três momentos sucessivos em cada etapa setorial. No primeiro ano (A1), prevê a apresentação do plano de monitoramento; no segundo (A2), a mensuração das emissões e remoções segundo o plano aprovado; a partir do terceiro (A3), a mensuração continua e passa a ser acompanhada da apresentação do relatório verificado referente ao ano anterior (art. 2º). O primeiro grupo começa em 2027; os demais têm início previsto até 2029 e até 2031, respectivamente (art. 3º). Conteúdo, formato e prazos de entrega ainda serão detalhados em atos próprios, editados com a antecedência mínima estabelecida pelo parágrafo único do art. 2º. O escalonamento não equivale a enquadramento automático pelo CNAE. Os §§ 2º e 3º do art. 3º exigem considerar as atividades, fontes e instalações efetivamente abrangidas. Além disso, a lei 15.042/24 prevê, no art. 30, patamares superiores a 10 mil toneladas de CO2 equivalente por ano para as obrigações de plano e relato e superiores a 25 mil para a conciliação periódica, observadas as condições legais e a regulamentação. A portaria organiza o calendário do MRV; não antecipa, por si, as obrigações de entrega de ativos decorrentes de um plano de alocação. A sequência normativa é coerente. O art. 29 prevê os deveres dos operadores; o art. 32 disciplina o relato anual e sua avaliação de conformidade; e o art. 30, § 2º, condiciona a aplicação das obrigações às atividades para as quais existam metodologias consolidadas de MRV. O art. 5º, V, por sua vez, exige uma estrutura confiável, consistente e transparente, apta a assegurar a integridade e a comparabilidade das informações. A qualidade da mensuração deixa, assim, de ser um detalhe instrumental: integra as condições jurídicas para operacionalizar deveres quantitativos. A própria lei separa, contudo, etapas que poderiam parecer equivalentes. Segundo o art. 1º, § 5º, remoções superiores às emissões não se convertem automaticamente em Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs). O art. 44 condiciona o reconhecimento desses ativos a metodologia credenciada, mensuração e relato, verificação independente e inscrição no Registro Central. Inventariar emissões, verificar declarações e reconhecer um resultado apto a gerar ativo regulado são operações diferentes. O legislador não atribui efeitos idênticos a informações que respondem a finalidades distintas. 2. O que os estudos científicos demonstram - E o que não demonstram A distinção entre informação mensurada e efeito efetivamente atribuível a uma intervenção não é apenas teórica. Probst e colaboradores (2024), em síntese publicada na Nature Communications, examinaram estudos de avaliação rigorosa referentes a 2.346 projetos de mitigação. Estimaram que menos de 16% dos créditos emitidos nos projetos avaliados correspondiam a reduções efetivas de emissões. O percentual varia entre modalidades e não representa todo o universo de projetos. Mais importante: a pesquisa examina a integridade do creditamento e da adicionalidade, não a acurácia geral dos inventários corporativos que o SBCE passará a exigir. Em direção complementar, Swinfield e colaboradores (2026) reuniram seis avaliações independentes de 44 projetos REDD+. Em 36 deles, as estimativas apontaram redução do desmatamento; ainda assim, o desmatamento evitado reivindicado superou, no agregado, em 10,7 vezes aquele sustentado pelas avaliações independentes. O resultado não autoriza afirmar que a conservação financiada por esses mecanismos seja inútil. Evidencia algo mais preciso: um benefício pode ser real sem que sua magnitude declarada esteja causalmente demonstrada. Linhas de base, áreas de comparação e modelos contrafactuais afetam decisivamente essa atribuição. Outro limite aparece quando se altera o objeto da pergunta. Ong e colaboradores (2026), na Nature Climate Change, examinaram 133 projetos de desmatamento evitado por meio de cinco indicadores de integridade ecológica e controles comparáveis. Predominaram resultados mistos, insignificantes ou negativos segundo os indicadores adotados.
