artigo.texto: A Nvidia fechou o trimestre encerrado em julho de 2026 com receita de US$ 96,2 bilhões, avanço de 106% sobre igual intervalo do ano anterior, e mais de 92% desse montante veio de um único segmento: os data centers. Mais de nove décimos do faturamento dependem de um só tipo de cliente — quem compra capacidade de computação para inteligência artificial. A comparação recorrente com os vendedores de pás da corrida do ouro tem fundamento: a companhia não precisa acertar qual modelo de IA vai dominar, porque vende o equipamento que praticamente todos os concorrentes precisam comprar. Microsoft, Google e Meta figuram entre as empresas cujas tecnologias rodam sobre processadores da Nvidia, conforme a fonte. Data centers respondem por mais de 92% da receita Fundada em 1993, na Califórnia, a Nvidia começou projetando processadores gráficos para computadores pessoais e videogames. O salto veio quando a mesma arquitetura usada para renderizar imagens se mostrou eficiente em tarefas de cálculo pesado — sobretudo o treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial. GPU é a sigla de unidade de processamento gráfico: o chip projetado para executar milhares de contas em paralelo, e não em sequência. Semicondutor, por sua vez, é o material cuja condução elétrica é controlada para processar informação; no vocabulário do setor, o termo virou sinônimo do próprio chip. Projeta o chip, mas não tem fábrica A Nvidia opera no modelo fabless — desenha o produto e entrega a fabricação a terceiros. Quem produz a maior parte dos chips avançados é a taiwanesa TSMC. O arranjo dispensa fábricas próprias e cria um elo único na cadeia: um problema na produção taiwanesa chega rápido ao volume de vendas, enquanto o clima entre China e Taiwan segue no radar. Do videogame ao data center O peso do portfólio não está em cada item isolado, e sim na integração: chip, rede e software são vendidos como um sistema. CUDA, o ambiente de programação da empresa, amarra o desenvolvedor ao seu ecossistema — e essa combinação é o que dificulta a substituição por um fornecedor alternativo. A concorrência inclui os próprios clientes A AMD, com a linha Instinct, é a rival mais direta no mercado de aceleradores para IA e servidores. Do outro lado aparece a Huawei: os processadores Ascend ganharam espaço como alternativa chinesa aos chips americanos, movimento reforçado pelas restrições de exportação impostas por Washington. Google e Amazon, dois grandes compradores, desenvolvem silício próprio — TPUs no caso do Google e a linha Trainium na nuvem AWS — para cortar custos e reduzir dependência de terceiros. A Intel segue na disputa por processadores de servidor. Quatro riscos que a concentração escancara - Fornecedor único: a produção concentrada na TSMC transforma qualquer ruptura em risco de entrega. - Geopolítica: as limitações dos EUA à exportação de chips avançados para a China fecham parte de um mercado relevante e estimulam alternativas locais. - Ciclo de gastos: se o investimento em data centers perder ritmo, a demanda pelos processadores recua junto. - Clientes verticalizados: quanto mais os chips próprios de Google, Amazon e outros avançarem, maior a pressão sobre preço e participação de mercado da Nvidia. O episódio que derrubou as ações Um suposto caso de espionagem chinesa envolvendo o fundador e CEO Jensen Huang deu origem a uma investigação, derrubou os papéis e recolocou no debate a vulnerabilidade das gigantes de IA depois de valorizações bilionárias. A reação tende a anteceder qualquer conclusão da apuração — e diz menos sobre o mérito do caso do que sobre o volume de expectativa embutido no preço. O que muda para quem acompanha a empresa Com a receita praticamente toda atrelada a um único destino, o balanço da Nvidia passa a espelhar o ciclo de investimento das grandes plataformas de nuvem. Um arrefecimento desses gastos não reduz apenas a taxa de crescimento: atinge quase toda a base de receita de uma vez. Historicamente, empresas com faturamento concentrado em um único cliente final costumam apresentar resultados mais sensíveis a revisões de orçamento do setor. Para quem acompanha o papel, dois indicadores carregam mais informação do que a cotação do dia: a evolução da receita de data centers e o grau de adoção dos chips próprios desenvolvidos pelos clientes. O primeiro mede a força do ciclo; o segundo antecipa a pressão competitiva que pode corroer preço e participação.

artigo.texto: Céu noturno: rastros de satélites podem interferir em imagens captadas por observatórios astronômicos (Freepik) Redatora Publicado em 9 de novembro de 2026 às 12h00. A expansão de data centers no espaço pode transformar a aparência do céu noturno e prejudicar pesquisas astronômicas realizadas na Terra. Cientistas alertam que projetos envolvendo centenas de milhares de satélites poderão aumentar a poluição luminosa e dificultar a observação de estrelas, galáxias e outros objetos celestes. O problema já afeta o Observatório Vera C. Rubin, no Chile, onde satélites deixam rastros luminosos nas imagens captadas pelos telescópios. A instalação iniciou em 2026 um levantamento do Universo previsto para durar dez anos. Segundo informações do The Wall Street Journal, astrônomos temem que a expansão das megaconstelações de satélites comprometa parte das observações científicas. O próprio Observatório Vera C. Rubin reconhece que os rastros provocados por satélites representam um desafio para suas pesquisas. Os satélites refletem a luz solar em direção à Terra. Quando atravessam o campo de visão de um telescópio, podem deixar faixas brilhantes nas imagens. Esses rastros dificultam a identificação de objetos celestes e podem comprometer informações utilizadas em pesquisas astronômicas. Segundo Jonathan McDowell, astrofísico que acompanha lançamentos orbitais, existem atualmente mais de 17 mil satélites ativos ao redor da Terra. Há uma década, eram aproximadamente mil. O pesquisador estima que esse número possa ultrapassar 100 mil nos próximos dez anos. Para J. Anthony Tyson, cientista-chefe do Observatório Rubin, a proliferação de satélites representa uma ameaça ao trabalho científico desenvolvido na instalação. Atualmente, grande parte dos satélites em órbita é utilizada para telecomunicações, incluindo o fornecimento de internet pela Starlink, da SpaceX. Entretanto, empresas como SpaceX, Google, Blue Origin e Cowboy Space anunciaram projetos relacionados à instalação de centros de processamento de dados no espaço. Essas estruturas poderiam exigir grandes quantidades de satélites para realizar operações computacionais fora da Terra. A SpaceX apresentou planos para um sistema orbital chamado Starmind, que poderia reunir mais de um milhão de satélites. A empresa também descreveu equipamentos com até 1.500 metros quadrados de área. Já a Cowboy Space apresentou projetos de satélites com aproximadamente 4.800 metros quadrados. As dimensões são superiores às dos satélites Starlink atuais, que possuem cerca de quatro metros quadrados. Uma das preocupações dos pesquisadores envolve o posicionamento dos futuros satélites em órbitas que permitam maior exposição à luz solar. Essas configurações poderiam manter os equipamentos iluminados durante longos períodos, aumentando a quantidade de luz refletida em direção à Terra. Samantha Lawler, professora da Universidade de Regina, no Canadá, alerta que satélites destinados a data centers orbitais poderiam apresentar brilho comparável ao de Vênus. Segundo a pesquisadora, centenas de milhares desses equipamentos poderiam dificultar a visualização da Via Láctea e de estrelas menos brilhantes em determinados horários. Hanno Rein, professor da Universidade de Toronto, também estudou os possíveis efeitos da expansão das constelações. De acordo com suas projeções, parte dos pontos luminosos observados no céu poderia corresponder a satélites artificiais, e não a estrelas. Shane Ross, professor de engenharia da Virginia Tech, desenvolveu uma simulação para representar como uma grande constelação de satélites poderia aparecer vista da superfície terrestre. O modelo mostra milhares de pontos luminosos distribuídos em uma faixa que atravessa o céu, de um horizonte ao outro. A projeção considera um cenário com centenas de milhares de satélites e ilustra como a concentração desses equipamentos poderia alterar a paisagem noturna. A União Astronômica Internacional (IAU) recomenda que os satélites sejam suficientemente pouco brilhantes para não serem visíveis a olho nu. As orientações buscam reduzir a interferência das constelações nas observações astronômicas. Apesar disso, não existem limites regulatórios gerais para o brilho visível dos satélites, segundo as informações apresentadas pelo Observatório Rubin. A SpaceX já adotou medidas voluntárias para reduzir o brilho dos equipamentos Starlink. Tyson afirma que a empresa mantém conversas com pesquisadores sobre o problema há quase uma década. O observatório também relata contatos com outras companhias do setor. Mesmo com essas iniciativas, o crescimento das constelações continua sendo motivo de preocupação. O Observatório Vera C. Rubin iniciou em 2026 um levantamento de dez anos destinado a investigar diferentes fenômenos do Universo. Entre os objetivos estão o estudo da matéria escura, a identificação de asteroides e o acompanhamento de mudanças no céu. A presença crescente de satélites pode dificultar a coleta de imagens e a identificação de objetos menos brilhantes. Tyson teme que a expansão das megaconstelações prejudique a continuidade das observações planejadas. Além dos rastros luminosos nas fotografias, o cientista alerta para a possibilidade de um aumento generalizado do brilho do céu, caso grandes quantidades de satélites sejam colocadas em órbita.

artigo.texto: Opposition to AI data center helped to fuel the nationwide "blue wave" on Election Night for Democrats at the ballot box. This summer, New York became the first in the nation to pass a one-year statewide moratorium on new data center construction. The push continues for Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign more restrictive legislation that passed the state legislature back in June. “Seeing the wins across New York state and the country is a signal that many of the things we’ve been talking about are incredibly popular,” said Democratic state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez. Gonzalez’s Responsible Data Center Development Act passed the state legislature in June. The following month, Hochul signed the nation’s first one-year moratorium on new data centers in New York state. Advocates maintain Gonzalez’s measure covers a broader range of large facilities starting at 20 megawatts or more. The governor’s moratorium has a threshold of 50 megawatts or more. Gonzalez believes data centers helping to fuel turnout nationwide makes her case stronger in having Hochul sign her legislation. “I absolutely think that’s the case,” she said. “We always knew that data centers was a bipartisan issue across the country, but even in New York state. A recent poll said that 63% of New Yorkers would support our moratorium being extended at the end of the one year.” In a statement to Spectrum News 1, a spokesperson for Hochul’s office said in part: "New Yorkers across the state have made abundantly clear that the rapid growth of AI and data centers cannot come at their expense. Governor Hochul listened, acted and is proud to have delivered the first data center moratorium in the nation. The Governor will continue to strengthen protections around artificial intelligence that will put New Yorker's and their future first." Critics argue stricter guidelines on data centers will come at an economic expense, with some states missing out on investments. Political expert Grant Reeher says it will depend on if this issue gets worked out on the national level. “If it remains something states are taking different positions, I think the states that aren’t doing it will pay some sort of economic price,” he said. Reeher says he believes what we’ve witnessed at the ballot box in reference to data centers is a “physical proxy” about voters’ much more “general anxiety about the future when it comes to AI.” In a CBS 60 Minutes interview on Sunday, President Donald Trump explained why he’s an advocate for AI data centers. “The level of power of winning that race is very important,” said Trump. “China has no problem with data centers. China has no problem with electricity. By the way, neither do we because I’m demanding that they build their own electric plant.” Despite the arguments, Gonzalez is continuing to advocate. In August, she embarked on a statewide data center tour. On Tuesday, her tour will stop at the First Unitarian Church of Rochester. The event is in partnership with Democratic state Sen. Samara Brouk.

artigo.texto: Jefferson County leaders hold workshop to discuss potential data center impacts Commissioners have seven more months before the county’s data center moratorium, which was put in place this summer, is up MONTICELLO, Fla. (WCTV) - Jefferson County residents and leaders are discussing the potential impacts of data centers as the county’s 12-month moratorium remains in place. County Manager Doug Baber said the workshop on Monday was an opportunity for commissioners to hear from experts about the potential impacts of data centers. “Data centers have been known as the boogeyman for quite a while, and I don’t disagree with a lot of that stuff because it’s unknown,” Baber said. “We want to make sure we bring in the experts on both sides of the field to talk about how much water it would use, how much electricity it would demand, how many acres they would have to have, how many jobs they create per acre.” Attorneys and professors from Florida State University and the University of Florida were among several experts sharing their knowledge, including the potential costs of studying the impacts. Andrew Fay, an attorney with the Digital Infrastructure Industry Group at Greenberg Traurig, discussed the cost of engineering studies needed to help commissioners make informed decisions. “The cost for the engineering studies for the expertise to make a decision on the impacts for water, the impacts that maybe the noise will have on the area, the light, the impact to the natural environment that it could be built in, all are extremely expensive and can be extremely time-consuming,” Fay said. Experts discussed both the potential jobs data centers could bring and concerns about light, noise and water. More news out of the Big Bend: Those concerns resonated with District Four Commissioner Austin Hosford, who pointed to issues residents have already raised about the Trulieve cannabis facility in the county. “Just right off the top, hearing the issues in these other places Texas, Virginia, light, noise, and water. I know how aware y’all are of what we’ve been dealing with in Jefferson County; we’ve got a major operation that has caused light, noise, and water problems for quite a lot of people, so that jumps off to me big time,” Hosford said. Residents also had a chance to ask questions and share their concerns, with many worried a data center could change the county’s rural character. Jefferson County is known for its natural resources, including the Wacissa River and springs. Some residents questioned whether the community has the resources to support a data center. “We don’t have the baseline to support it. Tallahassee could. We just don’t have it. I don’t see how it benefits us long term. I’m not opposed to data centers; I just don’t see how our county could support the construction of it or even the employment that we really want from it,” Jefferson County resident Tracy Place Allison II said. Baber also said there have been no applications for data centers in Jefferson County. No action was taken Monday night. Commissioners have seven more months before the county’s data center moratorium, which was put in place this summer, is up. artigo.texto: Oklahoma City extends moratorium on data center projects OKLAHOMA CITY, Okla. (KOKH) — Oklahoma City is keeping its pause on data centers development requests in place. The city council voted on Tuesday to extend a moratorium on new rezoning requests for data center projects through the end of next year or when the zoning code is updated, whichever comes first. A moratorium was already place through the end of this year, with the exception of one project. "We originally approved this in April and then in May. We hired a consultant to help us looking at our code to see what kind of updates or changes we might make. We have since approved one item...a hyperscale data center that was already in process, approved the zoning, and have a CBA that we're still going to negotiate with them. We feel like there's just a lot more information that we can collect working with our consultant and what we'll learn in this process," said City Manager Craig Freeman. On October 27, the city council approved a rezoning request for the hyperscale data center Freeman was referring to. Many OKC residents were not happy with that decision, including Le'Shauhndin Kirkendoll. On Tuesday she demonstrated to the city council what she says living next to a data center would sound like by playing the noise on her phone during her allotted public comment time. "This really is a time for comments. I think you've made your point. Are you going to speak anymore? If not, we'll move on," Mayor David Holt said. "Within, 90 seconds, 30, 60 seconds Holt was already irritated and annoyed with the noise quality. But that's what our elected officials are wanting to force the constituents to live with for whatever reason," Kirkendoll told FOX 25. Kirkendoll said she has been showing up to city council meetings to advocate for those who can't, since they are held every other Tuesday morning. "I've heard a lot of people in opposition for the data centers. I haven't heard one person that wants the data center in their neighborhood," she said. Kirkendoll said she was glad to see the moratorium extended. "I also hope that they implement some type of construction hold, because Oklahoma just needs to pump the brakes a little bit until we can get a bigger picture of what's going on," she said. As for the data center campus the city council already approved a rezoning request for, the next step will be to finish negotiating the community benefits agreement.

The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force have maintained that the 56,000-square-foot laboratory and data center under construction in Kīhei is not expected to be a significant added strain on the region’s infrastructure. But federal officials still won’t say how much water the project is expected to use. The nearly $100 million facility at Līpoa, the mixed-used development formerly known as the Maui Research and Technology Park, is intended to consolidate some of the military’s operations on the island into one location. It is being engineered to meet high federal energy and water-efficiency benchmarks, according to a 2022 environmental assessment. However, no specific details about the facility’s projected water usage have been made public, nor has that information been shared with county officials who make decisions about whether to approve applications for new construction projects in the area. Those decisions are based, in part, on where and to what extent the island’s water infrastructure can handle new development. Typically, plans for new development would prompt the Maui Department of Water Supply to reevaluate the subdivision’s water meter reservation and adjust it as necessary, according to a department statement provided Monday by county spokesperson Lila Lawrence. The military’s data center project was granted a federal exemption, so the department has not reviewed the subdivision since December 2022 — when there were no proposed buildings or other permit plans — and the water meter reservation was determined based on the lot’s square footage, according to the department. Water is already limited in South Maui, which receives almost all of its water from the ʻĪao and Waiheʻe aquifers in Central Maui. The Central-South Maui water system has for years been operating dangerously close to capacity, and Kīhei residents are often subjected to water conservation advisories due to dry conditions and issues related to the region’s aging infrastructure. Projects like the nearly 1,000-unit Ledcor South Maui Properties, the 652-unit Mākena Mauka project and the 1,150-unit Honua‘ula project — also known as Wailea 670 — have come under fire in part because of concerns about the availability of potable water. Given those challenges, no building project’s anticipated water consumption should be hidden from the public, said Hina Kneubuhl, an organizer with Protect Haleakalā, a collective of Hawaiian cultural practitioners, environmentalists, community leaders and others working to protect culturally significant landscapes. “I’m tired of these kinds of things being opaque. It’s not fair,” she said. “We’re living on an island with limited water and power resources. How is it just or fair to keep those kinds of figures from the public, and how can County Council members or the Planning Commission or anybody involved in making decisions make an informed decision without that kind of information?” Kelly King, who was recently elected to represent South Maui on the Maui County Council, said her decision-making related to future development projects would absolutely be affected by whether she has access to information about the military facility’s water consumption. “But I think that we shouldn’t just sit back and wait for information that may not be forthcoming. I think we need to actually call them into the chambers,” she said. “They need to come clean and tell us what they are doing.” She added, “The scrutiny for all the development is going to get much, much more detailed, I think, and the community is going to want more answers before the council makes any more moves.” When asked directly about the Kīhei project’s anticipated water usage, a spokesperson for the U.S. Space Force provided an emailed response from department representatives that did not include specific figures. Instead, representatives shared information about some of the water efficiency measures planned for the new facility. In its environmental assessment, Air Force officials did not consider the project’s impact on future development that had not already been approved, and it only considered developments in the neighboring community. Department of Land and Natural Resources spokesperson Andrew Laurence said the DLNR administrators and staff who submitted comments on the project’s environmental review four years ago are no longer with the agency, he said, “so we can’t speak to the reviews that were conducted in 2022.” At least some of the new facility’s hardware will be cooled using a permanently sealed system that continuously recirculates the same water, and there is projected to be a minimal increase in water demand compared to the military’s current leased facility in Kīhei, according to information provided by U.S. Space Force spokesperson Bradley Sturk. “This slight difference is solely due to additional standard restroom space required to consolidate personnel from multiple commercial leased buildings into a single building,” according to the department statement emailed by Sturk. artigo.texto: O mercado regulado de carbono do Brasil pode acrescentar 5,8% ao Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) até 2040 e 8,5% até 2050, segundo estimativas do Banco Mundial divulgadas pelo Ministério da Fazenda. A projeção também aponta uma redução de 27% nas emissões dos setores submetidos ao sistema até meados do século. Os números foram apresentados pela Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono (SEMC), vinculada ao Ministério da Fazenda, durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), em Antália, na Turquia. O encontro ocorre até 20 de novembro e marca a apresentação dos resultados da primeira etapa de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). Criado pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o SBCE estabelece um limite para as emissões de gases de efeito estufa de empresas de setores regulados. As companhias recebem cotas de emissão, que diminuem gradualmente ao longo dos anos e podem ser negociadas entre os participantes do mercado. O objetivo é criar um incentivo econômico para que as empresas reduzam a poluição. Quem emitir menos do que o limite poderá negociar cotas excedentes com outras companhias que precisem delas. Mercado regulado de carbono terá adesão gradual Em outubro, o Ministério da Fazenda divulgou o cronograma para que os setores industriais iniciem o monitoramento das emissões e cumpram as exigências de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (MRV). O conjunto de procedimentos determina como as empresas devem medir, registrar e comprovar a quantidade de gases de efeito estufa que lançam na atmosfera. As regras alcançam operadores com emissões a partir de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente por ano. Segundo o governo, esse grupo representa menos de 1% das empresas brasileiras. A secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis, afirmou que o sistema oferece previsibilidade regulatória para atrair investimentos sustentáveis. A expectativa do governo é que a implementação do mercado contribua para a modernização industrial e para a transição a uma economia de baixo carbono. Coalizão liderada pelo Brasil reúne 42,2% das emissões globais A participação brasileira na COP31 também marca o primeiro ano da Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono (OCCCM), iniciativa apresentada pelo país durante a COP30, em Belém (PA). Presidido pelo Brasil e copresidido pela China e pela União Europeia, o grupo reúne jurisdições responsáveis por 42,2% das emissões globais de gases de efeito estufa e por US$ 49 trilhões do Produto Interno Bruto mundial. O Plano de Trabalho 2026-2027 da coalizão foi aprovado em setembro, em Wuhan, na China. Durante a COP31, a delegação brasileira conduz uma reunião de alto nível e prevê a entrada de novos participantes. Também está prevista a assinatura de um Memorando de Entendimento para a adesão do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB). Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, a instituição será o primeiro banco multilateral de desenvolvimento sediado na Ásia a integrar formalmente a governança da coalizão. Desmatamento na Amazônia e no Cerrado recua O Brasil também apresenta na conferência dados recentes sobre a redução do desmatamento. Segundo o Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros (BiomasBR), do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), a taxa de desmatamento na Amazônia caiu 41,8% no período 2025/2026, para 3.335 quilômetros quadrados. O resultado é o menor da série histórica, iniciada em 1988. No Cerrado, a redução foi de 23,8%, com área desmatada de 5.516,69 quilômetros quadrados. De acordo com os dados apresentados pelo governo, esse é o menor índice desde 2001. O Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SEEG), iniciativa do Observatório do Clima, atribui à contenção da perda de vegetação uma contribuição para a queda de 6% nas emissões brutas do Brasil em 2025.

artigo.texto: [SMM ESS Flash] A Revolta da Alemanha comissiona a primeira bateria doméstica de íons de sódio de 10 kWh, alocação de 2026 esgotada A startup Revolta, sediada em Frankfurt, instalou e comissionou a primeira bateria doméstica de íons de sódio de 10 kWh da Alemanha em uma propriedade perto de Aschaffenburg, um sistema com tensão nominal de 450 V composto por cinco módulos de 2 kWh combinados com um inversor SMA. Cada módulo pesa 18,7 kg, com classificação de proteção IP64 e densidade de energia de 107 Wh/kg e 141 Wh/l, carrega e descarrega a 0,4 C, o que corresponde a cerca de 2,5 horas, e a configuração de 10 kWh entrega uma potência máxima de cerca de 4 kW; a propriedade também abriga cerca de 20 kW de energia solar fotovoltaica e uma pequena central hidrelétrica convertida de um antigo moinho. A empresa enquadra a instalação como o início de seu lançamento comercial, permanecendo ainda em estágio piloto, com mais sistemas piloto em locais selecionados de clientes na Alemanha planejados para as próximas semanas e medidores gratuitos fornecidos para coletar dados operacionais; os módulos são listados a EUR 599 cada e o conjunto de cinco módulos de 10 kWh a EUR 2.995, com a alocação de 2026 esgotada e reservas abertas para 2027. Potência nominal, vida útil de ciclo e números de eficiência não foram divulgados, e os primeiros dados operacionais reais de armazenamento doméstico de íons de sódio na Alemanha fornecerão amostras de validação para desempenho em baixas temperaturas e segurança.

artigo.texto: After pushback, Ottawa voters approve 10-year moratorium on data centers Ottawa residents voted overwhelmingly to impose a 10-year moratorium on data centers, joining a national trend of communities restricting data centers on the November Ballot. After pushback, Ottawa voters approve 10-year moratorium on data centers Ottawa residents voted overwhelmingly to impose a 10-year moratorium on data centers, joining a national trend of communities restricting data centers on the November Ballot. Ottawa, Kansas, residents voted by over 70% to approve a 10-year moratorium on data centers following a lengthy back-and-forth between county residents, city officials, and third party spending. It started when a proposal for a data center popped up just on the outside of Ottawa. Franklin County resident, Jessica Christopher, brought her concerns to the city. "When they had discussed putting up this 450 megawatt or whatever data center, it was going to be about a mile from my house," Christopher said. Christopher and other residents began to feel their concerns about the project were not being met. So they started petitioning to let voters weigh in on the issue, under Kansas law. "We rallied the troops. We went and did a few drive-thru events. And when I was sitting there counting the last ones, we had 1031 (signatures)," Christopher said. Despite gathering significant support, Christopher said the group faced obstacles. City officials argued the petition could not make it onto the ballot, as it was an administrative issue and not a legislative. That's when Ottawa residents, including Michael Lewis, sued the city. "We filed for a writ of mandamus, which what that says is that's compelling your elected officials to do their job since their job was to put it on the ballot or accept it. They didn't do their job. The district clerk or district court judge ruled that, yes, the citizens do deserve to be heard," Lewis said. The efforts surrounding the issue led to the formation of Ottawa United, a group of residents focused on the issue of data centers. "It was a mix between Republicans and Democrats and a bunch of unaffiliated voters. And we all just came together for a common good, which is why we named it Ottawa United," Chirstopher said. The campaign also faced challenges from outside influences. KMBC 9 uncovered tens of thousands of dollars in campaign filings from a Virginia-based political action committee, called the Defend US PAC. The PAC spending focused on urging residents to vote no on data center issues in Kansas communities, including in Ottawa and Emporia. "There was at least five or six different mailers that showed up at the doors. We had text messages come in every week," Lewis said. On election day, voters approved the moratorium in Ottawa by just over 70%. "I broke down, it was amazing. It was the thing that I have made that I am the proudest of, other than my children," Christopher said. Ottawa joins other Kansas communities, and communities across the U.S., in addressing the controversial issue of data center development. "It was kind of nice not only winning for our community, but also pushing back to the big money interests, saying that we're not for sale," Lewis said.

artigo.texto: 09/11/2026 Sete associações do setor elétrico afirmam que os custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias serão repassados aos consumidores de qualquer forma, mesmo que a cobrança seja concentrada nos agentes de geração. Com esse argumento, as entidades solicitaram ao governo federal apoio à tramitação e à aprovação do Projeto de Lei nº 3.716/2026, que propõe retirar dos geradores de energia elétrica a obrigação exclusiva de custear a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias como reserva de capacidade. Em carta conjunta encaminhada a ministros, as entidades defenderam que a reserva de capacidade assegura a disponibilidade de potência nos momentos em que o sistema elétrico necessita, contribuindo para a segurança do abastecimento e beneficiando o conjunto dos usuários. Por essa razão, avaliam que o custeio deve observar critérios compatíveis com a natureza sistêmica do serviço, sem estabelecer um tratamento diferente daquele aplicado às demais tecnologias contratadas para a mesma finalidade. As associações argumentam que concentrar a cobrança nos geradores não elimina o custo para os consumidores, já que o encargo tende a ser incorporado aos preços da energia, conforme as condições contratuais e de mercado, com reflexos sobre os custos de produção de bens e serviços. As entidades também mencionam que a área técnica da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) já tratou da possibilidade de repasse desses custos aos contratos regulados pela agência. O documento aponta ainda que a incerteza sobre a dimensão dos encargos e a possibilidade de recuperação dos valores pode elevar os riscos dos empreendimentos e os custos de contratação, sem gerar benefícios efetivos para a sociedade. Leilão de baterias e segurança jurídica As associações também alertam para os possíveis efeitos da indefinição sobre o custeio no primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade voltado a sistemas de armazenamento por baterias. Segundo o documento, a manutenção da controvérsia pode provocar questionamentos administrativos e judiciais, com impactos sobre o cronograma do certame, a implantação dos projetos e os investimentos na cadeia de equipamentos, engenharia e serviços. O grupo destaca a importância desses investimentos para o desenvolvimento da cadeia industrial brasileira, incluindo requisitos de fabricação nacional. Na avaliação das entidades, a aprovação do PL 3.716/2026 pode reduzir incertezas regulatórias e criar condições mais favoráveis à consolidação do mercado brasileiro de armazenamento de energia, contribuindo para a segurança do abastecimento e a competitividade da economia. As associações pediram aos ministros a priorização da tramitação da proposta e a articulação com as lideranças do Poder Executivo Federal para viabilizar uma solução sobre a distribuição dos custos e preservar as condições para a realização do leilão. A carta conjunta foi encaminhada à ministra-chefe da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior; ao ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira; ao ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti; ao ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Márcio Fernando Elias Rosa; ao ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan; e ao ministro-chefe da Secretaria de Relações Institucionais da Presidência da República, José Guimarães. São signatários do documento Elbia Gannoum, presidente-executiva da Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica); Fernando Delgado, diretora-executiva da Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (ABIHV); Marisete Pereira, presidente-executiva da Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica (Abrage); Alessandra Carvalho, presidente-executiva da Associação Brasileira de Geração de Energia Limpa (Abragel); Fábio Lima, diretor-executivo da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia(Absae); Rodrigo Sauaia, presidente-executivo da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar); e Rui Altieri, diretor-presidente da Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). Além da carta conjunta, as associações encaminharam uma solicitação individual de reunião institucional ao ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti, para tratar do PL. Fonte: MegaWhat

artigo.texto: I'm a firm believer in investing in what you know—and what you use. During a recent visit to my parents' New Hampshire property, my brother and I tackled overdue maintenance, and having the right equipment on hand was critical to finish the work in the limited time we had. He and I rented both a compact track loader (CTL, not pictured) and a bulldozer (pictured above) from United Rentals (NYSE: URI) to push through some of the heavier work. For those who may not be familiar with the company, United Rentals can quickly deploy heavy equipment to a remote site. Here's why I believe it sets up well for a defined-risk, moderately bullish options trade. The good news is that United Rentals is currently trading at a below-market forward multiple — both on a Price-to-Earnings (P/E) basis, currently ~17.3x forward estimates of ~$61.10/share, and on an Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) basis at ~8.8x $9.25 billion in FYE2027 EBITDA. This despite the fact that the company is compounding revenues, earnings, and EBITDA at a noticeably faster clip than the cap-weighted S&P 500. Effectively, one can buy superior, market-beating growth at a discounted market multiple. The recent third-quarter earnings confirmed this trajectory. URI delivered a beat and raise, pointing to robust underlying demand across its end markets, and the sell-side is scrambling to catch up, revising its forward estimates upward. Improving earnings estimates is one of the most reliable, time-tested short-term investment factors. Stocks with positive estimate revisions tend to meaningfully outperform those burdened with declining estimates in the short term. The macro backdrop provides a sturdy foundation for this growth. We are in the midst of a broader nonresidential construction recovery, which has driven an environment of improving and resilient rental rates. Although admittedly a potential slowdown in data center construction could become a future headwind, broader infrastructure demand remains robust. A balanced view requires acknowledging the risks. While URI looks cheap relative to the broader market, it is not exactly cheap relative to its own history. The stock is currently trading roughly 20% to 25% above its five-year average multiple. One could easily argue that the historical multiple was simply too cheap for a business of this quality, scale, and capital efficiency. Still, mean reversion back to historical levels of "cheapness" remains a downside risk. This brings us to the options market. When you have a stock with solid momentum, fundamentals, and positive estimate revisions, but you're hesitant to pay a premium to its historical valuation, outright unhedged equity accumulation isn't always the optimal route. Instead, selling cash-covered puts offers a highly strategic entry mechanism. The trade With URI's implied volatility currently hovering in the 42% to 45% range, the options market is pricing in enough movement to offer a decent premium. By selling a cash-covered put, we acknowledge both the good and the bad. It respects the aggressive growth, market share capture, and the recent beat-and-raise quarter, while appropriately hedging against the risk of that elevated historical multiple. If the stock continues its upward march, the puts expire worthless, and we pocket a high-probability yield that easily beats fixed income. If the stock pulls back—perhaps toward that 5-year average multiple—we are assigned the shares at a lower effective cost basis, which, if it happens, we could lower even further by writing upside covered calls against it. (This approach to entering a stock, then writing covered calls if assigned, is sometimes referred to as "the wheel strategy"). So either we acquire an attractive stock at a price we dictate (the short strike, less the premium collected for selling it) or we simply collect premium for assuming that risk if the stock does not decline. For a company that provides the literal heavy lifting for infrastructure growth, that's a structural advantage worth trading. artigo.texto: UK singer-songwriter Bess Atwell is back with a bold new chapter. Her fourth studio album, 'Cut a Figure', is officially set to land on 5th February 2027 via Nettwerk. Alongside the announcement, Atwell has treated fans to the striking lead single 'Glass', complete with a brand-new music video and news of a sprawling 2027 world tour. Following her acclaimed 2024 record 'Light Sleeper', which was produced by Aaron Dessner, Atwell sought a drastic change of scenery. A spontaneous nine-month relocation to Quebec, Canada, provided the distance she needed to craft her most fiercely honest work yet. Ditching some of her usual creative habits, she eventually teamed up with renowned producer Chris Coady—known for his work with Beach House, DIIV, and Foals—in Los Angeles to bring the project to life. The shift in her approach was highly intentional. “The songs I really enjoyed performing from my last record were the rare moments where I put down any instruments, and it was just me singing to my audience, which can be a bit scary,” she says. “But those were the songs that seemed to connect the most, and where I felt most free to actually live with the song and what it was about.” The album’s emotional anchor is undoubtedly the new single, 'Glass'. Powered by a cathartic indie-pop arrangement and crystalline vocals, it tackles the paradox of vulnerability. Bess explains, "I knew I wanted to name the album after a line in this song as it feels like the heart of the record. Sometimes, an eagerness to be seen and understood can have the opposite effect - you can be so transparent that you end up invisible. When I was a teenager, I was really into doing 'personality tests'. One test had you imagine a cube and then describe it (the cube supposedly representing how you express yourself). All my friends and family pictured various different sizes and colours, while I saw a transparent glass box floating in space." 'Cut a Figure' sees Atwell turning the lens inward, processing long-held anger, untangling toxic dynamics, and exploring her own health struggles. From the Eighties-tinged bite of 'The Act' to the shimmering analogue synths of 'Tonight I Am Allowed', the record is a defiant, self-accepting shedding of people-pleasing tendencies. Be sure to stream 'Glass' on your favourite digital platforms today and check out the brilliant new video. To stay updated on the upcoming album and secure tickets for her upcoming 2027 world tour, follow Bess Atwell on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and X.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBM.resumo: A Eletronet anuncia o ELET1, seu novo Data Center em São Paulo, que ampliará a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão da companhia e fornecerá mais escala ao atendimento de provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações e provedores de Internet (ISPs), e hyperscalers. Com investimento de R$ 25 milhões, o centro terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW, podendo chegar a 1 MW na segunda fase de expansão. Com as obras já iniciadas, a previsão de lançamento é para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto acompanha o aumento da procura de empresas dos segmentos de cloud, streaming e telecomunicações por infraestrutura de Data Center em regiões estratégicas de São Paulo, com alta disponibilidade e acesso a um amplo ecossistema de conteúdo. O ELET1 estará em uma localização com elevada concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo.  O Data Center também abrigará o PIX (Ponto de Interconexão) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo, o maior ponto de troca de tráfego de Internet do mundo, tanto em volume quanto em número de participantes. O PIX da companhia se destaca por liderar o volume de tráfego de download entre as operadoras participantes do IX.br São Paulo. Para os clientes, estar nesse ambiente aumenta as possibilidades de conexão com diferentes redes e provedores de serviços digitais. “O ELET1 representa um passo estratégico para fortalecer nossa atuação no segmento de Data Centers. Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais”, afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet. Segundo ele, o projeto acompanha o avanço de aplicações em nuvem, inteligência artificial, streaming e serviços digitais, que exigem suporte para volumes cada vez maiores de dados. “Queremos ir além das necessidades atuais e antecipar os próximos ciclos do mercado, fortalecendo nossa capacidade de conectar clientes, redes e ecossistemas digitais”, diz. Com segurança, tecnologia de última geração e resiliência operacional entre os pilares da iniciativa, o ELET1 seguirá as melhores práticas globais de infraestrutura, com soluções voltadas à proteção física e lógica, alinhadas às diretrizes da norma ISO 27001. O Data Center também contará com aplicações modernas e práticas de gestão ambiental e energética, tendo como referência os padrões ISO 14001, ISO 50001 e LEED, apoiando no melhor desempenho energético e na redução do PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness). Entre os recursos previstos estão dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVA, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predial (BMS) atualizado, monitoramento contínuo e um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência. “Mais capacidade precisa vir acompanhada de eficiência, resiliência e previsibilidade operacional. Por isso, o ELET1 foi concebido com uma arquitetura que otimiza o uso dos recursos e oferece mais flexibilidade à operação. A modernização dos sistemas críticos também nos permitirá atender a diferentes perfis de uso e níveis de demanda, mantendo o ambiente preparado para operações críticas”, afirma Emerson Hioki, Chief Technology Officer (CTO) da Eletronet. O ELET1 integra a estratégia da Eletronet de fortalecer sua atuação em Data Centers e complementa a expansão de sua rede nacional de fibra óptica. A nova unidade também contempla a migração da infraestrutura atualmente instalada no Data Center da companhia em São Paulo para o novo ambiente, em um processo planejado para preservar a continuidade dos serviços.

artigo.texto: Genoa residents seek to restrict data centers as push to limit them grows across Ohio Residents say a potential project could affect quality of life, but getting the issue on the ballot could be difficult GENOA, Ohio (WTVG) - Some residents in the village of Genoa are joining a growing push across Ohio to restrict large-scale data centers. They face obstacles in their effort to stop a potential project. According to Ohio State University, 18 Ohio communities have had ballot issues related to data center development. Voters sided against data centers in each case, often by a wide margin. Genoa residents who want similar restrictions could have difficulty getting the issue on the ballot. Marc Hanneman of Residents Against Genoa Environmental Destruction said residents want to take action. “If we sit back and let it roll over us, we’ll get it,” Hanneman said. Residents are concerned about a potential data center on 430 acres south of State Route 163 along Reiman Road. Hanneman said residents worry about the effect on water resources and wildlife. They also worry about noise and light pollution a project near residential neighborhoods could bring. “If we stand up and exercise our rights as citizens and residents of this community — that is [a] peaceful, loving community — we might just turn them away,” Hanneman said. The village annexed the property three years ago, which led to studies of what could be built on the empty fields. “I wish they’d slow down, moratorium, re-zone it. We could put it into apartments, we could put it into residential, we could do a lot of things… greenhouse, warehouse,” Hanneman said. Residents looking to stop a possible data center face a key challenge. Some Ohio communities have added bans or restrictions to their charters. Genoa does not have a charter, so residents are looking into creating one. “We’re looking into a charter, turning our village into a charter,” Hanneman said. Hanneman said a charter could give the community a way to put guardrails in place. Residents are also joining a statewide effort with Conserve Ohio to petition for a ban on large-scale data centers. Hanneman’s group plans to collect signatures Friday at the Genoa Retirement Center from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. near the potential project site. Hanneman said the group also conducted exit polling after the recent election. “92% is against a data center coming into Genoa,” Hanneman said. “This is registered voters coming from the polls saying that they don’t want it.” Latest Local News | First Alert Weather | Crime | National | 13abc Originals Copyright 2026 WTVG. artigo.texto: CATL's 2,000-Kilometre EV Battery Claim Faces Severe Engineering Reality Check Chinese battery giant CATL is advancing research into lithium-air technology that theoretically promises electric vehicles a range of 2,000 kilometres, but formidable engineering hurdles keep the innovation confined to the laboratory. Chief editor: Ken Kariuki 0701401086 Chinese battery giant CATL is advancing research into lithium-air technology that theoretically promises electric vehicles a range of 2,000 kilometres on a single charge, but material scientists warn that formidable engineering hurdles keep the innovation confined to the laboratory. The prospect of a 2,000-kilometre range relies on the extraordinary theoretical energy density of lithium-air cells, which can reach up to 3,505 watt-hours per kilogramme. While this figure dwarfs the 200 to 300 Wh/kg capacity of current lithium-ion packs, translating the chemistry from a controlled cell environment to a mass-produced, safe, and durable automotive battery pack remains a monumental challenge that experts estimate is at least a decade away from commercial viability. The Chemistry of Air-Breathing Cells Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries that rely on heavy, expensive transition metals like cobalt, nickel, and manganese for the cathode, lithium-air batteries use oxygen drawn directly from the ambient atmosphere as the cathode reactant. During discharge, lithium ions from the anode combine with oxygen to form lithium peroxide or lithium oxide, releasing energy in the process. This fundamental shift in chemistry eliminates the need for heavy metal oxides, drastically reducing the weight and potentially the raw material cost of the cell. Because the cathode reactant is not stored inside the battery casing but is instead continuously drawn from the environment, the theoretical specific energy of the system approaches that of gasoline, making it the holy grail of electrochemical storage. The 2,000-Kilometre Theoretical Gap Recent industry reports highlighting CATL's research have generated immense excitement, frequently citing the 2,000-kilometre range figure. However, this metric is derived from the theoretical limit of the raw chemical cell under perfect laboratory conditions. In a real-world electric vehicle, the battery cell represents only a fraction of the total system weight. A functional battery pack requires heavy thermal management systems, reinforced casings, complex wiring, and safety buffers. When the 3,505 Wh/kg cell-level figure is adjusted for pack-level integration, the effective energy density drops precipitously. Furthermore, the 2,000-kilometre claim assumes a highly efficient vehicle chassis and optimal driving conditions, ignoring the immense energy demands of highway speeds, climate control, and varying topographies. Furthermore, the immense weight of the required air filtration systems and protective casing means that a pack-level energy density of 1,000 Wh/kg is currently viewed as the absolute maximum achievable ceiling for commercial automotive applications within the next decade. Formidable Engineering Hurdles The transition from theory to reality is blocked by severe material science constraints that have plagued lithium-air research for decades. Engineers must overcome a matrix of chemical and physical limitations: - Moisture and Air Contamination: Lithium metal reacts violently with water. An air-breathing battery requires complex, heavy filtration membranes to let oxygen in while keeping atmospheric moisture and carbon dioxide out, which negates a significant portion of the weight savings. - Dendrite Formation: During the charging cycle, lithium ions tend to form needle-like structures called dendrites on the anode. These microscopic spikes can pierce the internal separator, causing catastrophic short circuits and thermal runaway. - Oxygen Electrode Degradation: The chemical byproducts of the oxygen reduction reaction are highly corrosive. They rapidly degrade the porous carbon cathode and the liquid electrolyte, leading to a severe loss of capacity over time. - Poor Cycle Life: While modern lithium-ion packs easily endure 1,500 to 2,000 charge cycles, practical lithium-air cells currently struggle to maintain stability beyond a few dozen cycles before failing entirely. Industry Timelines and Commercial Reality CATL's dominance in the global EV supply chain means its research directions heavily influence long-term industry pivots. The company is actively exploring various post-lithium-ion chemistries, including solid-state and condensed matter batteries, which offer more immediate, albeit less spectacular, improvements in safety and energy density. For the automotive sector, the lithium-air breakthrough represents a vital horizon for the post-2035 era, rather than an imminent product launch. Consumers waiting for a 2,000-kilometre EV will need to rely on incremental advancements in silicon-anode technology and semi-solid-state architectures for the foreseeable future. Until material scientists can solve the cycle-life and moisture-sensitivity paradoxes, the 2,000-kilometre battery will remain a brilliant theoretical benchmark rather than a driveway reality. Automotive executives remain highly skeptical of near-term integration, noting that the supply chain for specialized lithium metal anodes and solid electrolytes is virtually nonexistent at the scale required for global vehicle production. Consequently, legacy automakers and EV startups alike are focusing their immediate capital expenditure on incremental improvements to high-nickel cathode formulations. How did this story land? artigo.texto: Desenvolve SP e Möbius lançam fundo de R$ 70 milhões para provedores e data centers FIDC terá R$ 50 milhões da agência paulista e R$ 20 milhões da gestora para recebíveis, equipamentos e operações de consolidação. A Desenvolve SP e a Möbius Capital lançaram um Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios (FIDC) de R$ 70 milhões destinado ao financiamento de infraestrutura digital no Estado de São Paulo. O fundo tem como público provedores regionais de internet e data centers de pequeno porte e poderá financiar a compra de equipamentos, antecipar recebíveis e apoiar operações de fusão e aquisição. A estrutura conta com R$ 50 milhões subscritos pela Desenvolve SP em cotas seniores e R$ 20 milhões pela Möbius Capital em cotas subordinadas. O comunicado não informa quando os recursos estarão disponíveis para contratação nem detalha taxas, prazos ou limites de crédito por empresa. Uma das modalidades previstas é a antecipação de recebíveis dos provedores, originados em contratos com clientes pessoas físicas e jurídicas. O fundo também poderá investir em operações de crédito para a aquisição de equipamentos de infraestrutura tecnológica e para a expansão das empresas, incluindo compras e fusões de negócios do setor. “Temos um histórico de realizar financiamento para aquisições de provedores de internet, operações via mercado de capitais para fomentar o crescimento de empresas do setor, além de dar apoio no avanço da profissionalização e governança dessas companhias”, afirma Roberto Savaris, sócio e fundador da Möbius Capital. Segundo o anúncio, o fundo pretende ampliar o acesso ao crédito em regiões subatendidas, especialmente nas cidades do interior paulista. Entre os objetivos estão a expansão da conectividade em localidades com baixa penetração e a ampliação do acesso à infraestrutura de data centers. Composição de recursos públicos e privados A Desenvolve SP é a agência de fomento do Estado de São Paulo, vinculada à Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico. Seu diretor-presidente, Ricardo Brito, relacionou a participação no fundo à estratégia de combinar recursos públicos e privados. “Nossa meta é ampliar o acesso ao crédito e facilitar recursos para negócios inovadores. Por meio do blended finance, conseguimos atrair investimento privado, potencializar o impacto do recurso público e alcançar mais empreendedores”, afirmou Brito. Os valores anunciados correspondem a recursos subscritos. O material divulgado não esclarece se os R$ 70 milhões já foram integralizados. A Möbius Capital foi uma das gestoras selecionadas na chamada pública da Desenvolve SP para FIDCs e Fundos de Investimento em Participações (FIPs). O processo incluiu a apresentação de uma Carta-Consulta com informações sobre a tese de investimento, estrutura, estratégia, governança, equipe, histórico e valor solicitado. Após a análise de elegibilidade e uma apresentação presencial, a proposta passou pela diligência da gestora e do fundo. Concluída essa etapa, o Comitê de Investimentos da Desenvolve SP aprovou o compromisso de investimento. Na sequência, foram implementados os termos e condições do compromisso, conforme os processos internos da agência. O comunicado não detalha os critérios de acesso ao financiamento pelas empresas interessadas. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Expansão de data centers – A Noruega decidiu interromper temporariamente a concessão de novas conexões elétricas para data centers. A medida, anunciada pela operadora estatal Statnett, busca evitar uma sobrecarga na rede diante do crescimento acelerado dos projetos no país. A previsão é que a restrição permaneça em vigor até, no máximo, 1º de agosto de 2027. A expansão dessas estruturas ocorre em escala global, impulsionada pelos investimentos de empresas de tecnologia em infraestrutura para desenvolver e operar sistemas de inteligência artificial. O avanço, porém, também provoca resistência de comunidades na Europa e nos Estados Unidos, principalmente pela demanda por terrenos e eletricidade e pelos possíveis impactos nas tarifas de energia. LEIA: IA permite que hackers ataquem empresas em diferentes países “Queremos data centers na Noruega, mas não podemos aceitar todos os tipos de data centers” afirmou o ministro da Digitalização, Torgeir Micaelsen. “Portanto, precisamos controlar o crescimento e garantir que a Noruega receba os data centers de que realmente necessita, aqueles que proporcionam os maiores benefícios para a sociedade.” De acordo com a Statnett, 800 megawatts (MW) de capacidade de data centers já estão conectados à rede. Outros 4.200 MW têm reservas aprovadas, enquanto 9.100 MW aguardam disponibilidade. Há ainda pedidos adicionais para conectar 18 mil MW. Somados, os projetos pendentes representam 27.100 MW, volume superior ao pico de consumo de eletricidade da Noruega, que ultrapassa pouco os 25 mil MW. Um relatório recente do Conselho Norueguês de Tecnologia também apontou limitações econômicas do setor. Segundo o documento, os data centers geram poucos empregos permanentes após a conclusão das obras e cerca de 90% das instalações pertencem a empresas estrangeiras. artigo.texto: A data center owner specifies 400 pieces of owner-furnished, contractor-installed equipment. The purchase orders go out. The manufacturers confirm ship dates. The construction schedule is built around those dates. Six months later, a generator arrives at the jobsite with undocumented damage. Nobody knows when it happened. Nobody knows who touched it last. The vendor says it left the factory clean. The carrier has no record of an incident. The site crew is pointing fingers. This is the accountability gap. And it costs the industry more than most owners realize before they've lived through it. The OFCI model creates accountability risk by design Owner-furnished, contractor-installed programs make financial sense. Owners can leverage their purchasing power, standardize equipment across a portfolio, maintain direct relationships with manufacturers, and build a data record that — if captured correctly — can improve how future programs are planned and executed. On paper, it looks like control. In practice, most OFCI programs distribute that equipment across a chain of custody that nobody fully owns. A manufacturer ships to a freight forwarder. The freight forwarder hands off to a carrier. The carrier delivers to a warehouse. The warehouse holds it until the GC is ready. The GC coordinates final delivery. The installation crew takes it from there. At each handoff, responsibility technically transfers. But accountability rarely does. Each party documents what they received, in whatever format their own system requires, and hands the equipment forward. If something is missing, damaged, or mislabeled, the discovery almost always comes late, usually at the point in the project when it causes the most disruption. The data problem underneath the accountability problem Most owners believe their OFCI equipment is being tracked. In many cases, it is; loosely, across multiple systems, with inconsistent standards and no shared source of truth. A manufacturer has a ship date in their ERP. A carrier has a delivery confirmation in their TMS. A warehouse has a receiving record in their WMS. The owner's project team has a schedule in their construction management platform. None of these systems talk to each other. The data lives in silos, and nobody is reconciling it in real time. When the project team needs to know where a piece of critical equipment is, they start making phone calls. When they need to know its condition, they hope someone took photos. When a discrepancy surfaces, they spend days reconstructing a chain of events from fragmented records. That is not visibility. It is archaeology. Research has found that US construction professionals spend an average of 14 hours per week on non-optimal activities such as searching for project data, correcting mistakes, and managing rework. That is 35% of their working hours. For the US construction sector at large, this accounted for over $177 billion in excess costs in 2018. What the gap actually costs The damage is rarely dramatic. It accumulates in the places that are hardest to measure. A generator arrives at the jobsite before the pad is ready. The site team has nowhere to put it, so it sits on the trailer longer than planned. That costs money. When the pad is finally ready, the equipment needs to be repositioned. That costs more money. If it was sitting in an uncontrolled environment, there may be questions about condition. That costs time. A switchgear unit ships with components missing — a configuration issue at the manufacturer that nobody caught on the way out. The project team discovers it during installation. Replacement parts have a 14-week lead time. The schedule absorbs the hit. None of these costs appear on a single line item. But they accumulate, and they all count toward the total cost of ownership for a program that looked predictable on paper. A pallet of equipment arrives at a warehouse and is logged as received. When it is released to the jobsite three months later, three pieces are missing. Nobody knows if they were missing at receipt or left during storage. The warehouse record is a single line item. The investigation goes nowhere. Each of these incidents has a specific cause. But the underlying condition is always the same: nobody owned that equipment at the moment the problem was created. A joint study by PlanGrid and FMI found that roughly 48% of US construction rework is directly attributable to inaccurate, inaccessible, and incompatible project data, costing the industry more than $31.3 billion annually. Chain of custody is a process, not a document The common solution to accountability gaps is paperwork. Bills of lading. Receiving records. Inspection checklists. These create documentation, but documentation is not the same as accountability. A receiving record captures what the warehouse accepted. It does not necessarily capture condition. A bill of lading records that a delivery was made. It does not capture what the driver saw when they opened the trailer. A checklist completed quickly and filed away creates a paper trail that is almost impossible to use as evidence when something goes wrong months later. Research bears this out. Project teams with centralized, easy-to-locate documentation are twice as likely to feel confident proving which party was responsible when a dispute arises. Teams whose documentation lives in email threads, text messages, and phone calls report the lowest confidence. Documentation structure determines whether it can actually be used. Real chain of custody means every touchpoint captures the same data — condition, serial numbers, quantities, photographs — in a format that feeds a single record the owner can actually use. Exceptions get flagged in real time, not discovered months later. And one party owns the continuity of that record across the entire chain, not just their piece of it. artigo.texto: Envision and ju:niz Energy Extend Partnership With 442 MWh Battery Storage in Bavaria The Smareg 13 project in VÃ¶hringen becomes the third joint project for the two groups. According to them, it relies on the Gen 8 platform, four-hour storage and a low-noise design. Envision Energy and ju:niz Energy are expanding their partnership with Smareg 13 (VÃ¶hringen II), a 442 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bavaria. According to the two groups' press release, it is their third joint project, bringing the total volume of their collaboration to nearly 600 MWh. Elsewhere in Europe, other players are developing smaller capacities, such as PGE Dystrybucja, which secured a grant for a 4 MW energy storage system in Lutomiersk. Storage also remains in focus across the Rhine on the gas side, where German gas storage is at a record low and the INES organisation is calling for reform. A developer and operator role for ju:niz Energy ju:niz Energy is responsible for the development, financing and realization of Smareg 13. The company will operate the system over the long term. The project forms part of its German BESS portfolio, which the company says is growing. The site is located adjacent to the operational Smareg 12 facility. According to the press release, the project would strengthen storage capacity in Bavaria and provide greater flexibility and balancing capability as Germany integrates a growing share of renewable energy. Envision's Gen 8 platform at the core of the project Smareg 13 will deploy Envision's Gen 8 BESS platform, which combines four-hour energy storage, advanced battery technology and grid-forming capabilities. The two companies say its low-noise design allows deployment in acoustically sensitive environments. According to the press release, this feature addresses one of the key site challenges. Henry Peng, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of the EU and LATAM regions, says the group is moving forward with a significantly larger project before its first two projects have completed delivery. He sees this as evidence of Envision's role as a long-term technology partner. According to him, the company is also expanding its local capabilities in Germany. Vural Oezcan, chief operating officer (COO) at ju:niz Energy, says the project combines a very advanced development status with four-hour storage technology. He expects Smareg 13 to contribute to flexibility and system stability. He adds that Envision has proven to be a strong technology partner in the existing cooperation. artigo.texto: Fort Worth considers 90-day pause on data center development as residents raise concerns Fort Worth is considering new restrictions on where and how data centers can be built, including a potential 90-day pause on new development, as residents raise concerns about the impact on their neighborhoods. Tuesday marked the first of two public hearings required before the city can move forward with the proposed moratorium. The next hearing is tentatively scheduled for Jan. 12, with a possible vote in February. Dozens of residents brought their concerns directly to city leaders Tuesday, citing potential effects on the environment, quality of life, and the pace of development. "There's environmental concerns ... where I live, just about a mile away there's a data center in the works so I am concerned for my own quality of life but even more so for others," resident Ellis Maxwell said. "Data center developments are being very much rushed, rushed through the process," Brian Patman said. "So they are very much being pushed through before there is any regulation available to sort of rein them in." A city commission led by TCU Director of the Institute for Environmental Studies Michael Slattery presented its findings Tuesday after months of studying the potential impact of data centers on power, water and nearby communities. "The questions we looked at came out from a number of sources, one of which was the surveys that we got to look at … about 1,500 surveys that came back to the city from residences … and just lots and lots of conversations," Slattery said. The commission presented 19 recommendations, including requiring non-evaporative, closed-loop cooling systems to conserve water, zoning standards to protect residential neighborhoods, noise limits that account for surrounding areas and a pilot study of low-frequency noise. "I think it would give the city a roadmap on how to move forward," Slattery said. "Our city has an opportunity to be the city that did not just react to this technology, but has helped to understand it. That starts with doing what you asked us to do, get the facts, say them plainly, and say when you don't know." Maxwell said he hopes the proposed moratorium leads to lasting changes. "I want to make clear with the moratorium that it's not just a moment to sort of give us this concession and then wait for public pressure to die down, but that it's actually something that we're going to continue speaking out," Maxwell said.

artigo.texto: - Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz criticizes MIDA's role in data center decisions. - Schultz cites public concerns and process flaws in the Stratos Project's approval. - Reforms may include giving local governments more authority over data center approvals. SALT LAKE CITY — Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz agrees that the general public had "fair concerns" regarding the Stratos Project as the massive data center project, led by celebrity businessman Kevin O'Leary, was going through the state approval process. That's why he bemoans how those concerns and the whole process were handled. "You have Kevin O'Leary saying, China this and China that and whatever else, and I wanted to bang my head against the wall as that was happening. ... I've never been more frustrated than that," said Schultz, R-Hooper, recalling the drama during a joint Deseret News/KSL editorial board meeting on Monday. O'Leary worked out a framework for the data center proposal in a remote area of Box Elder County with the Military Installation Development Authority, a board made up of government appointees. It seeks to bolster the U.S. military's access to artificial intelligence and cloud-computing capabilities. Box Elder County leaders carried out additional votes to move it forward. One of the leaders who voted in favor said they felt pressured to accept it to avoid costly lawsuits. They could have rejected it and "the project area would not exist," MIDA executive director Dan Hemmert said last month. Project officials recently filed a new water application, which states the facility would include 11 data center building clusters along with a 7.5-gigawatt generation facility comprised of 15 500-megawatt combined-cycle natural gas power plants. It plans to use a little more than 1,700 acre-feet annually from Salt Wells Spring Stream. Meanwhile, multiple Utah residents who opposed the project have sued O'Leary and Fox News in recent months, claiming that the billionaire defamed them by falsely claiming they were agents of the Chinese government during interviews with the network for objecting to the plan. While O'Leary has sought a dismissal in at least one of the suits, the whole series of events was difficult to watch and proved that process adjustments are needed for data centers, Schultz said. "The thing that broke down on that was the process. That's where it went awry," he said. "Really getting back to fundamentally following the process on these controversial issues will help alleviate those concerns." A 'huge mistake' Data center reform may be one of the priorities during the 2027 legislative session, which is expected to be different following a drastic change in the Utah Legislature, said Schultz and Senate President-elect Evan Vickers, R-Cedar City. Senate President Stuart Adams, who serves as the MIDA board chair, was ousted in the Republican primary. Republicans also lost a supermajority in the House of Representatives for the first time in decades, the Associated Press projected on Monday. It's unclear how much of that was tied to data centers, but top state leaders acknowledged that it may have factored in lost public trust. Reforms to data center policy may start with giving local governments a greater say when it comes to approving data centers. Utah stepped up to oversee data centers when it became clear that they could overwhelm the state's energy grid without coordination between local governments, Schultz explained. However, he believes the recent backlash shows that the current process is broken. "MIDA should never be doing data centers," he said. "That was a huge mistake. ... I think it's important to know that and recognize that and make sure that doesn't happen again." Gardner Policy Institute noted in August, which could help affordability challenges — likely another key subject next year. That's on top of environmental concerns, which typically include urban heat, water consumption, and strains on electricity grids, the Yale School of Environment points out. The state, Vickers said, has already passed requirements tied to utility rates and water consumption. Modern facilities might be able to offset additional concerns, but the debate over pros and cons should be taken up on a local level. It's something that might require local entities to break down each request to see if it's the right fit. "If you can go through this process and check those boxes, it really comes down to a local decision," he said. "Do you want it or don't you?" Other adjustments? Utah may also examine other concerns, such as the rate of tax increments handed out for projects, Schultz noted. He and Vickers spoke on the issue weeks after fellow state lawmakers grilled Hemmert on the Stratos Project during interim meetings at the Utah Capitol.
