artigo.texto: Publicidade O desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial e de data centers no mundo tem colocado um grande desafio para os países, incluindo o Brasil, em termos de estrutura. De acordo com o Itaú BBA, a necessidade de grandes fontes de energia e de sistemas robustos de distribuição que a estrutura demanda pode ser especialmente favorável para a WEG (WEGE3) aqui no país. A avaliação veio depois de uma reunião entre o banco e a Scala, uma das maiores desenvolvedoras de data centers de grande escala da América Latina. Segundo a empresa, o Brasil possui uma vantagem importante em se tratando da disponibilidade de energia elétrica, especialmente, quando comparado a mercados norte-americanos, com maiores restrições de oferta de energia. Para a WEG, a demanda elevada de equipamentos e a oferta de fornecedores locais ainda limitada e com prazos de entrega longos, coloca a companhia em uma posição favorável para capturar os benefícios desse ciclo de investimentos. Após “sell-off” com midterms em meio a temores de IA, bancões recomendam compra A forte correção das ações ligadas à inteligência artificial após as eleições legislativas nos Estados Unidos abriu oportunidades de compra em diversos segmentos do setor JBS, Minerva e MBRF: como será o 3º trimestre dos frigoríficos? Melhora no cenário internacional e pressão no Brasil podem gerar efeitos diversos Atualmente, a companhia já fornece boa parte dos equipamentos que compõem a cadeia elétrica de um data center, enquanto a oferta de fornecedores locais ainda é bastante limitada. Por esse motivo, também, o BBA reforçou a WEG como sua principal escolha no segmento de transportes e bens de capital. Além disso, reforçou a recomendação outperform (desempenho acima da média do mercado), com preço-alvo de R$ 56. Continua depois da publicidade Cenário favorável De acordo com a administração da Scala, o projeto planejado próximo a Porto Alegre, o Scala AI City, já obteve autorização da ANEEL para dispor de 5 GW de energia elétrica, o que dá suporte ao potencial desenvolvimento do projeto ao longo do tempo. Segundo a empresa, um projeto de 1 GW pode exigir a disponibilidade de transformadores em aproximadamente oito meses. Ao mesmo tempo, os prazos de entrega de alguns equipamentos elétricos podem chegar a até três anos. Para a administração da Scala, uma empresa que já possua capacidade produtiva instalada no país, como a WEG, teria vantagem competitiva em relação aos concorrentes que ainda precisem estruturar suas operações locais. Continua depois da publicidade Fabricantes de equipamentos, como a Vertiv, também têm sido negociados no mercado a múltiplos de avaliação superiores aos das empresas operadoras de data centers. Isso sugere, segundo os analistas do BBA, que o mercado pode atribuir um valor relativamente maior às empresas que fornecem os equipamentos necessários para a expansão dessa infraestrutura do que às próprias empresas responsáveis por operar os data centers. Amparo fiscal Atualmente, os servidores dos data centers, estão sujeitos a uma carga tributária efetiva de aproximadamente 70% no Brasil. Esses equipamentos representam cerca de 80% do investimento total em bens de capital de um data center. Continua depois da publicidade De acordo com a administração da Scala, essa mesma carga tributária tem sido a justificativa para que cerca de 40% das cargas de trabalho brasileiras ainda sejam executadas no exterior. Estimativas do BBA apontam que o Redata, o programa que estimula investimentos em centros de dados no Brasil, poderia reduzir essa carga tributária para aproximadamente 20%, tornando mais atrativa a realização desses investimentos diretamente no Brasil. Os analistas explicam que, na prática, uma redução da tributação sobre servidores diminuiria o custo de implantação dos data centers no país. Com isso, empresas que hoje preferem instalar sua infraestrutura no exterior poderiam passar a considerar o Brasil uma alternativa economicamente mais interessante. Continua depois da publicidade

artigo.texto: Romulus City Council voted to temporarily ban data centers, discuss Flock cameras ROMULUS, Mich. (FOX 2) - The City of Romulus is getting ahead of the data center debate before it even begins, as they are temporarily banned before they even open. Data Centers and Flock, oh my! Big picture view: Data Centers and Flock cameras were the hot topic of discussion at Romulus City Hall on Monday. Residents joined the meeting expressing a number of environmental concerns and that they do not need one in their neighborhood. Meanwhile, the city council stressed that nothing has been proposed. A six-month moratorium would prevent them from even looking at proposals or applications, so the city council voted unanimously for the moratorium. Besides Data Centers, Flock cameras became another topic of discussion. The city has twenty up and running with thirty more scheduled to go up. Residents at the meeting questioned how they are being funded. Residents asked: Is it paid for by the city's Tax Increment Finance Authority, also known as ‘TIFA Board?’ Or was it the police department? Some say the original contract with Flock was for $47,500 but allege a short time later it was $90,000. What they're saying: When FOX 2 asked Mayor Robert McCraight about this discrepancy in October, he said it was a "typo by a clerical person." "It’s just a way to clean it up. We want to make sure everybody’s on board and on the same page," he said. "The TIFA Board knew what they were voting on to support and help alleviate some of that drain or general fun which is public safety dollars. But Romulus is a different community. We housed DTW. We talked about it before with 30-million travelers. That’s more than Disneyland and the Magic Kingdom. "So when you talk about 60–70 percent of the violent crime in Romulus is committed by people who don’t live here, we need to use tools to push that number down and our accredited police department is doing such. But we’re always going to look at one's venues. Is that the best technology that we have right now? It seems like. Can we get better? Absolutely." Watch FOX 2 Detroit LIVE The Source: FOX 2 attended the Romulus City Council meeting for details in this report.

artigo.texto: Harrisburg data center offers insight into technology and community concerns A Harrisburg data center operated by Alerify provides a closer look at the technology behind the cloud, as concerns grow over the development of larger hyperscale data centers in Pennsylvania. Video above: Top news stories from News 8 at 5 p.m. Inside a smaller data center "This data center here isn’t one of those large AI hyperscale data centers. It's actually only 2,500 square feet. And it fits in this commercial building right behind me," said Andy Kochanowski, CEO of Alerify, during a tour of the facility. Kochanowski explained that customers trust the center with their data and equipment, emphasizing the importance of security. "Customers trust us with their data and their equipment, and they don’t want anybody, you know, getting into it," Kochanowski said. Inside the facility, the hum of machines and air conditioning systems is constant. "That noise, is that all of the machines and everything?" asked News 8's Maegan Summers during the tour. "That noise is at some of the machines, but mainly it's the air conditioning systems to keep the equipment cool," Kochanowski said. The center houses computer servers and data storage rented by various customers, essentially serving as the physical form of the cloud. "It's almost like your personal belongings when you put them in storage. But we're doing it for computer equipment. So that's called co-location," Kochanowski said. "Virtual server hosting is basically, instead of owning equipment, you want to create a private server up in the cloud. This is the cloud," he added. Cooling and power demands The facility operates at about 50% capacity, with aisles of equipment rotated between hot and cold zones to regulate temperatures. "It's comfortable in here. It’s probably like 71 or 69. Yeah. So it's reasonable. But if you come in here, it’s probably going to feel like a temperature difference," Kochanowski said. Between cooling the building and powering the machines, the data center uses 40,000 to 80,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month. Despite its relatively small size — about 2,500 square feet, comparable to a tennis court — larger hyperscale data centers can span hundreds of thousands of square feet. One such center being built in Lancaster is 850 times larger than the Harrisburg facility. "We've seen more of these hyperscale data centers start to come up. Do you think that they're necessary?" Summers asked. "They need to go somewhere. You know, obviously I'm a consumer. I have a home. I don't want to see my electric rates go up either. And I don't want to deal with the noise. But they do need to go somewhere," Kochanowski said. Community concerns about hyperscale centers The rapid development of hyperscale data centers has sparked concerns among community groups like Lancaster Stands Up. Taylor Enterline, a member of the group, outlined their worries about the environmental and community impact. "The electric grid. What happens when there's a blackout? If there's a blackout, the data center is going to keep running. They have all these backup generators. But where does the help come from? For our neighbors, our biggest one is water. Our beautiful Susquehanna, down the road, is sacred. It's beautiful. How are we protecting our water?" Enterline said. Enterline suggested state-level regulations on hyperscale data centers and artificial intelligence, as well as community benefit agreements to hold developers accountable. "Testing and control. Right. We're not just like testing beforehand. We're testing during and we're testing afterwards. And if they are not following through on that, who is holding them accountable? Who knows if these large, you know, monstrosities of AI hyperscale data centers are going to be needed in five to 10 years? Who's responsible for shutting those down, cleaning them up? It should not be on the community who didn’t want them in the first place," Enterline said. Exploring more efficient practices As a smaller data center owner, Kochanowski shared his perspective on environmentally friendly practices, including partnering with Penn State students to develop more efficient air conditioning systems. "There are a lot of dilapidated, old foundries and steel mills that already have the power into those places but are just barren. We have to redo something like that versus starting brand new. We also need to be very conscientious of the noise, especially in communities. And the power draw, you know, to the extent they can produce their own power, that's great," Kochanowski said. He also highlighted the benefits of closed-loop cooling systems for water conservation. "I think that’s the best way to go, honestly. I mean, to the extent you can recirculate that water through that computer equipment and not have to continue to tap the challenges making that water cool itself down before it cycles back through," Kochanowski said. The future of data centers Looking ahead, Kochanowski predicted continued growth in the data center industry but noted that advancements in equipment could reduce the need for large facilities. "I think it's going to continue to grow. The question becomes whether or not the equipment needed shrinks. Then it may not be as big an issue in the future as what it is today," Kochanowski said.

artigo.texto: Community Corner ‘Nobody Here Asked For This’: Protestors Rally Against South Brunswick Data Center Advocates want the DEP to reject the air permit for the 341,000-square-foot AI data center in South Brunswick. SOUTH BRUNSWICK, NJ — More than 150 people packed Christ Congregation in Princeton on Friday to push back against a 341,000-square-foot AI data center going up on Route 1 in South Brunswick. The town hall came three days before the state’s deadline for public comment on the project’s air permit. Residents from South Brunswick, Princeton, Franklin and other nearby towns attended. Advocates were on hand to help them file comments with the state Department of Environmental Protection. Sentinel Data Centers, the developer, has applied to the DEP for an air permit to run 12 diesel generators at the site, which is on the former Princeton Nurseries property. Organizers said 20 generators are planned in total once the facility is fully running. Find out what's happening in South Brunswickfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The public comment period closes Monday. “A lot of people are still in shock that their local officials could approve something like this. They’re mad, and they’re ready to fight back. No one wants to breathe in toxic fumes from a data center,” said Ben Dziobek, executive director of Climate Revolution Action Network. Find out what's happening in South Brunswickfor free with the latest updates from Patch. “Nobody here asked for this facility, and nobody here is going to benefit from it,” Dziobek said. “If Governor Mikie Sherrill and Commissioner Ed Potosnak approve these diesel generators, they’re going to do it over the objections of thousands of people who will have to live with the consequences.” Charlie Kratovil, senior organizer at Food & Water Watch New Jersey, called on the state to reject the application. “The Bloomberg data center’s application for permission to pollute using a dozen dirty diesel generators is an immediate threat to our air, water, and climate,” Kratovil said. “We need Governor Sherrill to protect New Jersey by denying this permit and issuing a strong moratorium on data center construction.” Steven Donziger, an environmental and human rights attorney, talked about possible legal challenges to the project. “I’ve spent decades taking on some of the most powerful corporations in the world, and one thing I’ve learned is that no corporation is above the law,” Donziger said. “Bloomberg and Sentinel Data Centers should not be allowed to put corporate profits ahead of the health and safety of New Jersey families. Residents have every right to challenge this project, demand accountability, and pursue every legal avenue available to protect their communities.” The DEP held a public hearing on Sentinel’s application in late September. The department later extended the comment period after state Sen. Andrew Zwicker asked for more time for residents to weigh in. The final decision rests with DEP Commissioner Ed Potosnak. Before Sherrill appointed him to lead the department, Potosnak served on the Franklin Township Council and led the New Jersey League of Conservation Voters. The project has drawn opposition from residents, U.S. Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-12th District, and Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-12th District. The Princeton Mayor and Council and students at Princeton University have also come out against it. High school and college students planned a protest for 1 p.m. Saturday, outside the South Brunswick Municipal Building at 540 Ridge Road, less than 24 hours after the town hall. Climate Revolution Action Network organized the protest with the South Brunswick High School Democrats, New Jersey High School Democrats, Union County High School Democrats, College Democrats of New Jersey and TCNJ Democrats. Residents who want to comment before Monday’s deadline can use Climate Revolution Action Network’s template letter at climaterevolutionnj.org/sbdc. artigo.texto: Com bilhões de dólares injetados em novos data centers nos Estados Unidos, as comunidades locais questionam o retorno real desses investimentos bilionários em infraestrutura de energia, terrenos e equipamentos. O impacto real no mercado de trabalho Embora exijam aportes massivos, essas instalações costumam empregar apenas algumas dezenas de profissionais diretamente, como engenheiros, técnicos de TI e seguranças. Essa baixa contratação direta tem alimentado o ceticismo e gerado oposição comunitária em estados como Texas e Ohio, resultando em atrasos ou cancelamentos de US$ 156 bilhões em projetos apenas no ano de 2025. Uma pesquisa realizada por especialistas em economia urbana e mercado imobiliário analisou 1.584 data centers inaugurados entre 2000 e 2023 para entender se essas estruturas realmente fomentam postos de trabalho na região. A análise cruzou dados de localização, capacidade de consumo de energia e registros federais de emprego, comparando os municípios beneficiados com localidades semelhantes que não receberam os centros. Como e quando os empregos surgem Os dados indicam que, em média, de 1.000 a 1.300 postos de trabalho indiretos são criados nos municípios entre três e cinco anos após a abertura do primeiro centro. Nos dois primeiros anos, o cenário no mercado de trabalho permanece praticamente inalterado, excluindo o setor de construção civil. O estudo aponta que cada megawatt adicional de capacidade está associado a cerca de 7,4 empregos locais extras após cinco anos. Considerando expansões futuras, a estimativa cai para aproximadamente 2,7 postos de trabalho fora da construção por megawatt de capacidade final. Onde os novos postos se concentram Diferente do esperado, o crescimento das vagas não se reflete no comércio varejista ou em restaurantes. A expansão está fortemente concentrada nos setores imobiliário, de serviços profissionais e técnicos, além de transporte e armazenagem. Apesar de gerarem empregos indiretos, os pesquisadores ressaltam que os impactos ambientais e estruturais, como o consumo elevado de água e energia, além dos incentivos fiscais recebidos, mantêm o debate aberto sobre a viabilidade dessas instalações para as cidades.

artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council moved forward with a ban on giving tax incentives to data center developers on Monday. The ordinance, proposed by Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman, was approved unanimously by the council in a study session and will go to a future regular meeting for an official vote. Recommended Stories Aurora’s city code allows the city to use retail tax revenue and construction material use tax revenue generated by qualifying development projects to help finance public improvements and attract businesses. It also allows the city to waive sales or use taxes for certain developers. The ordinance, if passed at a future regular meeting, would prohibit data center incentives entirely. “There is an unprecedented amount of money behind data centers largely driven by AI and they do not need our tax dollars,” Coffman said about his proposed ordinance Monday. No councilmembers opposed the ordinance, but several brought up concerns or alternative proposals. The council already has the ability to vote on every sales and use tax incentive, including those for data centers, Councilmember Alison Coombs said, adding that if the council does not want to give incentives to a data center, it can vote against them. If the council wants to have a broader conversation about whether its oversight procedures work well, that conversation should go to a policy committee, Coombs said. Coffman countered that the process, which happens in executive sessions, is not transparent to the public. “I don’t think it’s wise to bind the hand of future councils,” Councilmember Curtis Gardner said, adding that creating a sweeping rule for one industry “is not a good way to do governance.” Four tax incentives have been issued for data centers totaling $83 million. As of earlier this year, about $9 million had been paid out against that potential, City Manager Jason Batchelor said. After some debate, the mayor stood firm on his proposal, saying he was putting it forward for a recorded vote as-is. “If somebody else wants to have a discussion on process and procedure, you’re welcome to do that, but you will vote on this issue,” Coffman said. None of the councilmembers present opposed the ordinance. Data centers have been a major topic of discussion in recent council meetings, during which the council has passed several data center regulations but twice denied a data center moratorium. Dozens of residents have attended recent meetings to oppose data centers in Aurora, specifically the Trident Data Center from Vantage Data Centers, which was planned for an area near Green Valley Ranch communities.

artigo.texto: The deployment of renewable energies is advancing at a historic pace. However, as they become more prevalent in the energy system, large-scale storage systems are required to prevent electricity generated during solar and wind production peaks from being lost. Global investment in these technologies continues to grow., and in the most dynamic markets, about 80% of new large-scale developments already combine solar energy with battery systems. Nevertheless, the international supply chain faces major challenges due to dependence on metals such as lithium and cobalt. To diversify these solutions, the scientific community has turned its attention to a highly abundant resource: saltwater from the seas. This search for new formulas complements stationary storage methods investigating everyday, low-impact materials, such as sand batteries for thermal storage. This opens up a range of solutions that allow renewable energy generation to be decoupled from the time of consumption. Although the development of lithium-ion batteries marked a historic turning point in the electrification of transportation and electronics, for which the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded in 2019, grid storage requires innovation in other areas. One of the most promising technologies in this field is seawater batteries (SWBs), which are currently in the research phase and have great potential in terms of storage. They represent a technological shift because they use the salts present in the aquatic environment—specifically sodium ions (Naâº)—as the active material for storing energy. Rather than being sealed cells from start to finish, they have an open part that interacts with the seawater and oxygen in the environment. When charged with renewable electricity, the battery traps sodium from the saltwater and accumulates it at its negative pole. When discharging, the process naturally reverses, returning the sodium to the sea and releasing the stored electricity to the grid. To keep this reaction stable and prevent water from degrading the internal components, these cells use a NASICON-type solid separator (sodium super-ionic conductor), a high-strength ceramic material. Unlike conventional plastic membranes, this ceramic component acts as a selective filter, allowing only sodium ions to pass through. This prevents two common problems associated with equipment submerged in seawater: the build-up of encrusted salts (scaling) and the adhesion of algae or microorganisms (fouling). A three-in-one solution: renewable energy, water reuse, and carbon capture Seawater batteries’ greatest potential lies in their ability to integrate various sustainability-contributing applications within a single operating cycle: - Integrated water desalination: By combining the NASICON ceramic separator with a complementary membrane to capture chloride, the battery separates the salt from seawater while simultaneously storing electricity. This advantage is strategic for coastal regions subjected to periods of water stress. According to the Spanish Desalination and Reuse Association (AEDyR), Spain is leading the way in water reuse in Europe with rates between 10% and 13% of the flow treated through advanced systems, highlighting the energy efficiency of water treatment. - Passive COâ capture: During discharge, the system naturally generates sodium hydroxide. This alkaline substance spontaneously reacts with the carbon dioxide (COâ) dissolved in seawater and with minerals such as calcium or magnesium, causing the gas to transform into stable solid carbonates. This carbon sequestration mechanism operates without the need for heat or additional energy consumption. The road towards industrial scale Testing in laboratories and research centers has progressed from tiny button batteries to larger prototypes assembled in independent modules. This modular structure allows cells to be stacked like blocks, enabling adaptation to industrial facilities, docks, and generation parks at sea. The European Union is seeking to increase its capacity in this environment. Although technical challenges remain to advance its commercial implementation, seawater battery research demonstrates how innovation can expand energy storage alternatives. Exploring new materials, resources, and applications creates opportunities for developing more efficient and sustainable solutions that can complement the advancement of renewable energies and utilize available resources more effectively.

artigo.texto: Rivian and Redwood Materials Expand Partnership to Span the Lifecycle of the Battery Redwood will now recycle Rivian’s battery scrap and end-of-life packs as well as provide energy storage for its manufacturing plant IRVINE, Calif.–(BUSINESS WIRE)–American automaker Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) and energy technology company Redwood Materials today announced a major expansion of their partnership, establishing Redwood as one of Rivian’s key partners to enabling end-to-end energy solutions—recycling Rivian’s production scrap and end-of-life EV batteries, as well as providing stationary battery storage at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. Through the partnership, Redwood collects Rivian EV battery packs through Rivian’s nationwide network of service centers when they are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. Redwood then evaluates each battery pack to determine whether to repurpose it for energy storage—deployed directly at Rivian’s manufacturing facilities or at other locations—or to recycle it. Redwood will now also recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian’s manufacturing operations. This new scope of the partnership builds on the existing work, announced in April 2026, that is deploying 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage from repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker’s manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. RJ Scaringe, Rivian Founder and CEO, said: Giving Rivian battery packs a second life in stationary storage is a massive unlock for the energy transition, “By partnering with JB and the Redwood team, we’re turning retired EV batteries into a powerful tool to make the grid more reliable and lower energy costs for everyone.” JB Straubel, Redwood Materials Founder and CEO, said: Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials, “Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.” When EV batteries reach the end of their useful lives in vehicles, they often still have substantial useful energy capacity for second-life applications, such as stationary storage. Energy storage applications with repurposed batteries can ease stress on the grid during periods of high electricity demand, improving grid reliability while reducing energy costs for the user, as well as the grid at large. During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, these packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. When paired with Rivian—and other—EV battery packs, Redwood’s proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving. Once batteries are no longer useful in energy storage applications, or where scrap is generated during manufacturing, they can be recycled. Redwood’s advanced process is capable of recycling and recovering critical minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper at rates exceeding 95 percent, encouraging the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the United States. This expanded partnership reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. As grid connections take years to secure and conventional infrastructure remains supply-constrained, companies increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem—recovering materials, managing recycling, and deploying storage as a single system rather than separate vendors. Rivian’s work with Redwood is a model for that approach: one partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery, built to move faster than the grid alone can. artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) autorizou o acesso de 645 MW de demanda à Rede Básica de transmissão para de projeto da Casa dos Ventos no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, em Caucaia, no Ceará. A conexão está prevista para ocorrer por meio da futura subestação Pecém III a partir de 1° de dezembro de 2028, mas depende da conclusão de obras de transmissão e de adequações técnicas no sistema elétrico regional. O empreendimento está vinculado à empresa Pecém VDB 1, cuja participação integral foi adquirida pela Casa dos Ventos junto à Voltalia. A operação, submetida e aprovada pelo Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade), envolveu os direitos de acesso à infraestrutura de transmissão necessários ao desenvolvimento de projetos de data centers no complexo cearense. O pedido de acesso do Pecém VDB 1 foi originalmente apresentado pela Voltalia Energia do Brasil ao Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), em fevereiro de 2026, sendo que o ativo fazia parte do Complexo Industrial Projeto Amônia Verde de Pecém. Posteriormente, a Casa dos Ventos adquiriu a participação integral na empresa Pecém VDB 1, com o objetivo de aproveitar os direitos de conexão para desenvolver projetos de data centers. Conexão depende de obras na transmissão O parecer do ONS aponta que a conexão do data center à Rede Básica será feita por meio de dois circuitos na linha de transmissão de 500 kV entre Pecém II e Pacatuba, na futura Subestação Pecém III. A ligação envolve instalações de duas transmissoras, a STN e a Axia, antiga Chesf, e depende de uma intervenção na subestação Pacatuba, com prazo contratual para entrar em operação até 30 de junho de 2029. O ONS condicionou a viabilidade da conexão à entrada em operação de um conjunto de obras de transmissão na região Nordeste. Entre elas estão a Subestação Morada Nova, Teresina IV e Cratéus, além de obras associadas, contratadas no leilão de transmissão de 2024 e com prazo de conclusão até junho de 2029. A lista inclui ainda oito compensadores síncronos, equipamentos que ajudam a controlar a tensão da rede. Três foram contratados no leilão de transmissão de 2025 e outros cinco estão previstos no planejamento do setor. Estrutura de conexão compartilhada Para viabilizar a conexão, serão implantados quatro trechos de linha de transmissão em 500 kV, com aproximadamente 3,35 quilômetros de extensão, para conectar a futura subestação Pecém III à linha entre Pecém II e Pacatuba. A estrutura compartilhada também atenderá outras quatro unidades consumidoras, data centers demominados Pecém VDB 2, Pecém VDB 3, Pecém VDB 4 e Pecém VDB 5.

artigo.texto: Jefferson County residents weigh extending data center moratorium at public meeting MONTICELLO, Fla. -- Jefferson County residents and leaders gathered for a public workshop to weigh the potential impacts of data centers and to discuss whether the county’s one-year moratorium should continue. County leaders said the workshop was intended to give both commissioners and the public a clearer understanding of how data centers could affect the area, including electricity and water consumption, runoff and noise. The meeting was also framed as an educational session, not a vote on any specific project. “You should always be concerned about anything that we are not very sure about. That’s the reason for this workshop, Tonight their not voting on anything the board of county commissioners is just educating themselves as well as the public so that they can make an informed decision once the moratorium expires in June of 2027,” said Doug Baber, county manager for Jefferson County. Some residents voiced skepticism about whether data centers would be a good fit for the community, including concerns about who would ultimately pay for the infrastructure and utility demands associated with large facilities. “People in the community were paying for the data centers utility usage and I need to know..My light bills are high enough, I don’t need to pay for a billionaires data center,” said Mary Harris, a Jefferson County resident. Jefferson County leaders agreed on June 18 to a one-year moratorium on data centers to allow time to consider their impact. Baber said the technology and the public perception around it can shift quickly. “Data centers change every day, through the good on some things, the bad on other things and a lot of times their the boogie man. So the things that you don’t know and you don’t respect often you think the worst of,” Baber said. During the workshop, electricity usage and the size of potential facilities were among the sticking points discussed. The forum also gave county commissioners and residents a chance to consider possible guardrails for data centers moving forward, as environmental concerns continue to be raised statewide about the pros and cons of data centers locating near neighborhoods.

artigo.texto: A massive data center development proposed in Sutton could bring nearly $28 million a year in property tax revenue to the Massachusetts town, but the project is already drawing concerns from residents about its potential impact on their community. The proposal calls for a 10-building data center campus off Boston and Providence roads. Each building would be roughly 250,000 square feet, bringing the development to approximately 2.5 million square feet at full build-out — the equivalent of about 43 football fields of floor space. Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The project is associated with the Kraft Group and Unified Global Packaging Group, which owns the property. The development could represent approximately $16.75 billion in investment and require about 900 megawatts of electricity at full build-out, according to the town's preliminary review. That amount of power would put the proposal among the larger data center developments being planned nationwide. For Sutton, the financial implications could be significant. Town projections estimate the first two buildings could generate about $10.4 million in annual property taxes by fiscal year 2031. Once all 10 buildings are assessed, the town estimates annual property tax revenue could reach approximately $27.8 million by fiscal year 2035. The town's financial modeling also predicts that the average single-family homeowner could pay approximately $5,800 less annually by fiscal year 2035 than under the town's projected tax bills without the development. The possibility of financial relief comes as Sutton projects a structural budget deficit that could grow to approximately $9.1 million by fiscal year 2033 without corrective action. But some residents say the potential financial benefits do not outweigh their concerns. Neighbors raised questions Tuesday about noise, water and electricity use, generators, traffic and potential costs for municipal services. The town's review identifies several of those issues as areas requiring further study, including water supply, wastewater, noise, lighting, traffic and emergency response. "This is just the very, very beginning of this," Jonathan Anderson, chair of the Sutton Select Board, told residents. No final approval has been granted. Town officials expect additional technical review and negotiations over zoning regulations and a community benefits agreement. A zoning change would require a Planning Board hearing and approval by a two-thirds vote at Town Meeting. Residents made clear Tuesday that scrutiny of the proposal is just beginning. "I have a 3-year-old grandson," longtime resident Mario Giamie told NBC10 Boston. "And I'm not going to subject him to this if I can fight it, and I will fight it."

artigo.texto: From Nov. 9 to 20, Antalya, Türkiye, is hosting the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31). Its main themes are climate finance, adaptation, the energy transition, reducing the energy intensity of buildings and reporting on commitments made. Since the first days of its independence, Kazakhstan has been an active and responsible participant in global processes on sustainable development and climate change: it signed and ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2009 and subsequently joined the Paris Agreement in 2016. This was preceded by extensive expert and analytical work by the Ministry of Environmental Protection, renamed the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources in 2021, with support from the World Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Development Program (UNDP), national experts and the National Chamber of Entrepreneurs of Kazakhstan. Today, Kazakhstan positions itself as a leader in advancing the green energy transition not only in Central Asia but also across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Kazakhstan was the first country in the region to adopt a Strategy for Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060. This year, by Sept. 1 order of the Prime Minister, a Plan of Organizational Measures for implementing the Strategy was approved. The plan will help integrate decarbonization principles into all areas of the national economy, including sectoral planning systems and the monitoring, reporting and accounting of greenhouse gas emissions on an innovative, digital basis. The initiative of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to harness the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) is especially relevant to resetting the country’s national emissions trading system. Speaking at the BRICS+ summit on Sept. 13, he again underlined the role of AI in global development and noted that “Kazakhstan regards AI as a strategic priority and is ready to use its advanced computing infrastructure, as well as national and UN digital centers, to expand effective cooperation” for the country’s sustainable development. COP31 experts note a revival of global carbon trading, particularly in the submission of projects to the voluntary carbon market, which undergo a multi-stage review by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM). As regards the regulated greenhouse gas market – existing national emissions trading systems and their participation in global carbon trading – discussions continue on avoiding double counting and on building the necessary carbon infrastructure. Among Asian countries, Kazakhstan was one of the first to launch an emissions trading system (KazETS). It covers 220 installations in the six basic sectors of the economy and is now undergoing a transformation through the development and introduction of auctioning and of production benchmarks drawing on EU and OECD experience. At the same time, full participation of Kazakh enterprises in global carbon trading and access to the carbon markets of other countries require, first and foremost: a gradual phase-out of free allowances; a higher price per tonne of greenhouse gases; the transfer of the existing MRV (monitoring, reporting and verification) system to a digital platform. For Kazakh exporters, the absence of a modern, internationally recognised infrastructure for monitoring, reporting and verifying CO₂ emissions, and of verifiers accredited in line with international requirements, is currently a serious challenge. At the same time, the experience of leading carbon market players and platforms such as Sylvera, BeZero Carbon, Isometric and Calyx Global shows that AI makes it possible to assess the integrity and risks of carbon projects, to evaluate the carbon footprint and the contribution of enterprises and sectors to the Sustainable Development Goals, and to build digital solutions, including under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. At COP31, the National Pavilion of Kazakhstan will also present a number of digital solutions for resetting the national ETS and creating a regional digital climate hub with the support of the UNFCCC. We hope that this initiative, developed by experts of Astana Hub together with Green Academy, the University of Central Asia and the Kunayev Institute of Mining, with the support of the Swedish company Planboo and SagtaAI, will be supported by the delegations of the Central Asian countries and included in the outcome document of COP31. The author is Professor Dr. Bakhyt Yessekina, a member of the Green Council under the President of Kazakhstan. Yessekina is the head of the Green Academy Scientific Research and Education Center. artigo.texto: Mercado global de etiquetas para fios: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Mercado de etiquetas para fios até 2035: demanda por cabeamento de data centers impulsiona o crescimento Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Etiquetas para Fios, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de etiquetas para fios é um componente essencial, ainda que muitas vezes negligenciado, do setor mais amplo de soluções de identificação elétrica e industrial. No período de análise de 2026, o mercado se caracteriza por demanda estável, sustentada por exigências obrigatórias de segurança, conformidade e eficiência operacional nos setores de infraestrutura, manufatura e tecnologia. Este relatório oferece uma avaliação abrangente do estado atual do mercado, de suas cadeias de suprimento complexas e da dinâmica competitiva entre fornecedores globais de materiais e fabricantes especializados. As trajetórias de crescimento estão fundamentalmente atreladas ao investimento global em eletrificação, expansão de data centers, automação industrial e infraestrutura de energia renovável. O mercado não é monolítico: segmenta-se por tipo de material, tecnologia de impressão e indústria de uso final, cada qual com drivers de demanda e cenários competitivos próprios. Embora a sensibilidade a preço continue sendo um fator, a proposta de valor das etiquetas para fios está cada vez mais ligada à durabilidade, à legibilidade e à integração com sistemas digitais de gestão de ativos. O período de análise até 2035 prevê um mercado em evolução, respondendo à integração tecnológica e às pressões por sustentabilidade. Este relatório oferece uma base granular e orientada por dados para que as partes interessadas compreendam os fluxos de volume e valor, identifiquem oportunidades estratégicas e naveguem pelos desafios logísticos e competitivos que definirão o desenvolvimento do mercado na próxima década. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de etiquetas para fios até 2035 pressupõe expansão contínua em ritmo moderado, com valor e volume globais crescendo de forma constante a partir da base de 2025. A demanda é ancorada por exigências obrigatórias de identificação em instalações elétricas, cablagem de dados e telecomunicações e painéis de controle industrial, nos quais as etiquetas apoiam a conformidade com normas de segurança, a eficiência da manutenção e a rastreabilidade. O driver concreto mais forte é a rápida expansão de data centers e de infraestrutura de cablagem de alta densidade, que exige grandes volumes de marcadores de fios duráveis e legíveis para instalação, comissionamento e manutenção contínua. A automação industrial e a fabricação de painéis de controle acrescentam demanda, à medida que montadores de painéis e integradores de sistemas especificam etiquetas que atendem às normas UL, IEC e outras. Instalações de energia renovável, incluindo parques solares e eólicos, contribuem com crescimento incremental por meio de suas extensas redes de fiação. Do lado da oferta, o mercado permanece fragmentado, com fornecedores globais de materiais e conversores especializados competindo em desempenho de material, durabilidade da impressão e velocidade de personalização. A volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas para polímeros e adesivos representa um risco persistente de margem, enquanto a transição para impressão digital e kits de etiquetas pré-impressas está remodelando os canais de distribuição. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico mantém a maior participação no consumo, apoiada pela fabricação de eletrônicos e pelo investimento em infraestrutura, enquanto a América do Norte e a Europa priorizam produtos de alto desempenho e certificados. A previsão aponta para um índice de mercado de 142 em 2035 (2025=100), equivalente a uma CAGR de 3,6%, com potencial de alta decorrente da aceleração dos gastos com data centers e eletrificação e risco de baixa associado à fraqueza industrial cíclica. Drivers e restrições da demanda Principais drivers de demanda - A rápida construção de data centers e a cablagem de fibra e cobre de alta densidade exigem etiquetas para fios duráveis e legíveis para instalação e manutenção. - As normas de segurança elétrica e conformidade exigem identificação clara de fios em instalações industriais, comerciais e de infraestrutura. - A automação industrial e a fabricação de painéis de controle ampliam a demanda por marcadores de fios pré-impressos e imprimíveis. - Instalações de energia renovável, incluindo parques solares e eólicos, envolvem extensas redes de fiação que exigem etiquetagem. - O crescimento da fabricação de chicotes automotivos e aeroespaciais aumenta as exigências de rastreabilidade e identificação. - A automação predial e os sistemas inteligentes de gestão de instalações impulsionam a demanda por cabeamento estruturado e etiquetagem. Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - A volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas de polímeros e adesivos pressiona as margens dos fabricantes e pode adiar decisões de compra. - A concorrência de produtores regionais de baixo custo limita o poder de precificação em segmentos sensíveis a preço. - A adoção de sistemas digitais e de gestão de ativos baseados em RFID pode reduzir a demanda por alguns tipos convencionais de etiquetas. - A fraqueza cíclica da produção industrial e da construção pode reduzir temporariamente o consumo de etiquetas para fios. artigo.texto: A corrida pela inteligência artificial está criando um novo desafio nos Estados Unidos: encontrar energia suficiente para manter os grandes centros de processamento de dados em funcionamento. Com a demanda por eletricidade crescendo rapidamente e as conexões à rede convencional demorando anos, empresas começaram a apostar em uma alternativa pouco comum: reaproveitar motores de aviões aposentados para gerar energia. A estratégia foi apresentada pelo jornal The New York Times. De acordo com a publicação, companhias especializadas estão retirando turbinas de aeronaves antigas e adaptando os equipamentos para funcionar como geradores elétricos. A solução tem atraído principalmente empresas que precisam colocar data centers em operação sem esperar pela conclusão de obras de infraestrutura energética. Um dos principais motivos para essa escolha é o tempo de instalação. Segundo Audun Martinsen, analista da consultoria Rystad Energy ouvido pelo jornal, conectar uma estrutura de 100 megawatts à rede elétrica pode levar cerca de sete anos. Com turbinas adaptadas, esse prazo poderia cair para aproximadamente dois anos. A diferença é importante para as empresas de inteligência artificial, que precisam ampliar rapidamente sua capacidade computacional. Os data centers consomem grandes volumes de eletricidade e dependem de fornecimento contínuo para manter servidores, sistemas de processamento e equipamentos de refrigeração funcionando. Motores militares poderiam gerar 40 mil megawatts O potencial dessa tecnologia também aparece em um levantamento da Administração de Informação de Energia dos Estados Unidos. Em janeiro, o órgão estimou que os motores de aproximadamente 4 mil aeronaves militares aposentadas, armazenadas em uma base no deserto de Tucson, poderiam alcançar uma capacidade de geração de cerca de 40 mil megawatts. O volume seria maior do que toda a capacidade de geração de energia do estado do Arizona. A estimativa ajuda a dimensionar o interesse pelo reaproveitamento desses equipamentos. Originalmente projetados para impulsionar aeronaves, os motores podem passar por adaptações para operar como turbinas geradoras de eletricidade. xAI e OpenAI já utilizam turbinas adaptadas Entre as empresas que recorreram a essa alternativa está a xAI, companhia de inteligência artificial de Elon Musk. Segundo o The New York Times, oito turbinas convertidas de motores de aeronaves foram instaladas no Mississippi para ajudar no abastecimento do data center Colossus 2, em Memphis. A presença dos equipamentos foi identificada pelo jornal a partir de licenças estaduais e imagens de satélite. A OpenAI também utilizou uma solução semelhante em seu primeiro complexo Stargate, localizado em Abilene, no Texas. Em 2025, a empresa recorreu a turbinas a gás para ampliar a oferta de eletricidade necessária ao funcionamento da estrutura. O movimento acompanha a expansão dos investimentos em inteligência artificial. Com a disputa por capacidade de processamento cada vez maior, as empresas buscam alternativas para evitar que a falta de energia atrase a construção e a operação de novos centros de dados. Organizações ambientais apontam riscos de poluição Apesar da rapidez na instalação, o uso de motores adaptados tem provocado críticas de organizações ambientais e moradores das regiões próximas aos empreendimentos. As principais preocupações envolvem a eficiência energética dos equipamentos e a emissão de poluentes. No Mississippi, o Centro de Direito Ambiental do Sul (SELC) contestou a autorização para o funcionamento das turbinas utilizadas pela xAI. A entidade questionou a documentação apresentada pelo fabricante e afirmou que não havia comprovação suficiente de que os equipamentos atendiam às exigências ambientais relacionadas à emissão de substâncias como o formaldeído. O grupo também acusou a empresa de apresentar estimativas abaixo do esperado para a quantidade de poluentes liberados. Patrick Anderson, advogado do SELC, criticou a escolha de uma tecnologia considerada mais poluente justamente por empresas que estão na linha de frente do desenvolvimento tecnológico. Na avaliação dele, a expansão da inteligência artificial deveria ser acompanhada por soluções de geração de energia menos prejudiciais ao meio ambiente. Outro problema apontado é que turbinas adaptadas de motores de aviões podem apresentar eficiência inferior à de equipamentos projetados especificamente para usinas a gás natural. Com isso, seria necessário utilizar mais unidades para produzir a mesma quantidade de eletricidade. A utilização desses motores mostra o tamanho do desafio energético provocado pela expansão da inteligência artificial. Enquanto as empresas tentam garantir eletricidade em menos tempo para ampliar seus data centers, cresce também a discussão sobre os impactos ambientais das soluções escolhidas para sustentar essa expansão. Compartilhe este conteúdo do Diário da Guanabara, o melhor site de notícias do Estado do Rio.

artigo.texto: Company proposing battery storage facility, data center infrastructure site in South Bend SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WSBT) — An energy center development could be in South Bend's future. The company nextNRG is planning to develop 27 acres into a data center infrastructure, battery storage, and pharmaceutical site. The multi-million-dollar proposal is in its early stages and the deal has not officially been closed. The proposed development, would be called the Lone Wolf Energy Center. The company nextNRG is planning to acquire 33-acres located on Lone Wolf Drive near the Toll Road and US 31 on South Bend's Northwest side. This announcement came as a surprise for neighbors who live nearby. “Well, I'm very shocked first of all. What is going on, Will it affect us? So, we're, I'm sure most of my neighbors out here are going to be very not happy. You know, they're upset already that no one contacts them and stuff,” said Tom Bayer. 27 acres would be used for data center infrastructure and battery storage. It's expected to support up to 70 megawatts of capacity, but could potentially go up to 100 megawatts. But it leaves neighbors with concerns about the potential long-term effects of this development. “So we'd like to know, are we protected? I heard about water issues, you know, I've heard about noise, which noise pollution, you know. So, there's a lot of issues that haven't been come forward to us," said Bayer. The city of South Bend says they have also had no communication with NextNRG and said in a statement: "The City learned of NextNRG’s involvement and the larger project scope from Inside Indiana Business on Friday. If accurate, the city will hold this project to protections and standards in the Neighborhood’s-First framework, including zero local incentives or subsidies and a requirement that the developer pay its own way for any infrastructure and energy needs." The existing 50,000 square-foot building would be leased separately to a pharmaceutical company for 10-years. NextNRG says the proposed acquisition remains subject to negotiation and execution of transaction documents. Meaning the deal has not officially closed for the $22 million purchase. WSBT sent a list of questions to NextNRG: What does the timeline look like for this project? - What does the timeline look like for this project? - How will the company address potential noise, emissions, water use, and traffic from this project? - Why is this location being chosen in South Bend? - What can those who live in South Bend expect from the company and completion of this data center? - How does the size of this data center and impact compare to other locations the company owns? - Some residents are calling for transparency about this project. Do you plan to hold a public, in-person meeting to address potential concerns? - What are the potential costs of this project? NextNRG response: Statement: NextNRG was founded to make energy smarter and cleaner, and the Lone Wolf Energy Center in South Bend is designed to meet growing technology demand without putting the cost on the community. When our November 5 announcement referred to a data center, it meant the amount of power the site can support, not the development of a traditional hyperscale facility. Lone Wolf aims to generate its own power on site to support compact, modular computing units, so it won’t strain the local grid, raise utility rates, draw on local water or seek local tax incentives. The project remains in its early stages, with negotiations ongoing and no final agreements in place. We look forward to working alongside South Bend residents to pioneer a greener model that the community can be proud of as we spearhead the future of energy, together. FAQ Is NextNRG building a data center in South Bend? No. Lone Wolf is intended as an energy project that will generate power on site and use it to support modular computing units. These are container-sized systems set on concrete pads, with no large building, no water use and no major construction. Our announcement used the term “data center” to describe the site’s power capacity, not the type of facility. How is modular computing different from a traditional data center? Modular computing units are compact, quiet, and self-contained. They have their own cooling systems, need only limited construction, and run at a fraction of the scale of hyperscale campuses, which can span millions of square feet, draw hundreds of megawatts from the local grid, and use large amounts of water for cooling. Will this affect my utility bills, water or taxes? Lone Wolf is designed to produce its own power, so it is not expected to strain the grid or raise residents’ utility rates. It does not draw on local water and is not seeking local tax incentives. It is expected to add to the local tax base, not take from it. How will this impact the surrounding community? Lone Wolf would add to South Bend’s tax base and bring local construction jobs to the area. Because the project will generate its own power, it would reduce reliance on the local grid and would not increase residents’ utility rates. It would also not draw on local water or rely on local tax incentives, and construction would be limited to site preparation. Where does the project stand? The project is in its early stages, with negotiations ongoing and no final agreements in place. NextNRG looks forward to working openly with residents as plans develop. It’s unclear what the timeline is or when the approval process could be finalized.

artigo.texto: Proposed Auburndale data center draws scrutiny over power demand, water use and impact AUBURNDALE, Fla. - Hundreds packed a public workshop Tuesday night as Auburndale residents and local leaders challenged developers over the massive power and water demands of a proposed hyperscale data center. Auburndale technology center proposal The backstory: The proposed data center would sit on 75 acres along Pace Road. The project is part of the Florida High Tech Corridor, an innovation district established about 30 years ago. In December 2023, Auburndale city commissioners approved a new land-use designation and rezoning for the property, allowing for industrial and certain technology uses, including a data center. Construction on the first two of four approved buildings began in early 2024. The property was purchased in December 2025 by Pace Road DC Development LLC, the company behind the current proposal. Some current commissioners acknowledged they were not in office when the original land-use and zoning decisions were made. City Commissioner Sean Levy said, "I will not allow a rubber stamp process to jeopardize our resources, economy or the peace of our schools." Power grid and water concerns By the numbers: One of the biggest questions surrounding the project is how much electricity it could require. TECO would supply the power, with demand expected to start at 350 megawatts and eventually increase to 700 megawatts. That's enough electricity to power an estimated 350,000 to 500,000 homes. Residents also raised questions about water use and noise. Teresa Detweiler said, "People put their whole life savings into their property and homeownership, and you have a data center that's coming in and your property drops by 10 percent." Polk County economic impact The other side: The developer estimates the facility would use more than 4,600 gallons of potable water per day, compared with as much as 10,000 gallons for a warehouse of the same size. The company says it plans to use a closed-loop cooling system and limit noise at the property line to 50 decibels, about the level of a quiet office. They are also projecting 292 permanent jobs and say the project will not receive financial incentives. The first two buildings are expected to be operational by 2029. State utility cost regulations What's next: The developer submitted a building permit application and interior retrofit site plan on November 4. The city still needs to review those plans. There are also questions about who will pay for the electricity and infrastructure needed to serve the data center. Florida Senate Bill 484, signed into law this year, requires data centers to cover their electricity and infrastructure costs rather than pass them on to other ratepayers. However, TECO still needs approval from the Florida Public Service Commission for its new tariff, which will govern how those costs are charged. The Source: FOX 13 attended the public workshop and heard from Auburndale city commissioners, residents, the developer, Pace Road DC Development LLC, and TECO. Project details and estimates were presented during the workshop.

artigo.texto: China has officially connected the world’s largest liquid air energy storage (LAES) facility to the electricity grid in Golmud, Qinghai Province, marking a major development in long-duration energy storage technology. The 60 MW project is located in the Qaidam Basin, adjacent to a large solar power facility, and is designed to improve renewable energy integration and grid stability. The facility aims to address the challenge of balancing electricity supply and demand as solar and wind generation fluctuate throughout the day. It uses surplus electricity generated during periods of high renewable energy production to store energy for later use when demand increases. The storage process begins with ordinary air, which is purified and compressed using a multi-stage centrifugal compressor. During compression, the system captures and stores the generated heat in insulated tanks. The compressed air is then cooled to approximately minus 194 degrees Celsius, converting it into liquid form. This liquid air is stored in large tanks under near-atmospheric pressure until electricity is required. When power demand rises, the stored liquid air is pumped and heated before being converted back into gas. The expanding gas drives turbines, generating electricity that can be supplied to the grid. This process allows the facility to store surplus renewable energy and release it during periods of higher electricity consumption. The project can absorb approximately 600 MWh of surplus electricity per day and is expected to deliver around 180 GWh of electricity annually. Its capacity could support the electricity requirements of tens of thousands of households while helping reduce the challenges associated with intermittent renewable energy generation. Unlike conventional battery storage systems that depend on minerals such as lithium, liquid air energy storage uses ordinary atmospheric air as its primary storage medium. It also does not require specific underground geological formations, making the technology more flexible in terms of project locations and deployment. Another important feature of the facility is its 100% domestic equipment localization rate. The project uses locally developed intellectual property, equipment and manufacturing supply chains, highlighting China’s efforts to strengthen its domestic energy storage industry. The commissioning of the Golmud facility represents an important milestone for large-scale energy storage. Its operational performance is expected to provide valuable experience for future projects and demonstrate how long-duration storage technologies can support renewable energy expansion, improve grid flexibility and strengthen electricity supply reliability. artigo.texto: Quincy data center tour offers lessons as Montana weighs development QUINCY, Wash. — As Montana debates data center development, midterm election voters are making it clear they want a say in what comes next. NBC Montana’s Laurel Staples visited one of the nation’s largest data center hubs to see how the technology is changing and what Montana could learn from it. Eight data center campuses operate in Quincy, Washington, where Montana Tech’s Robert Morris, who serves on Montana’s Energy Task Force, joined NBC Montana for a tour. Morris, who has four decades of experience in the industry, said newer facilities are becoming more efficient in how they use electricity. “More of the power goes right to the servers rather than the cooling systems and the power system itself,” Morris said. Water use is another key question. “They’ve gone from evaporative coolers that use utility supply or civil supply of water to air-cool chillers, which use no external water for cooling,” Morris said. Newer cooling technologies can reduce water use, but city officials say data centers account for about 5% to 8% of Quincy’s water use. Before entering the facility, Morris pointed to transmission lines carrying hydropower from the Columbia River system into the regional grid part of a vital energy corridor which connects to the Colstrip Plant in Montana. He also used a phone app to take a rough, uncalibrated sound reading near the campus. The app fluctuated between about 70 and 100 decibels, a range that spans from a vacuum cleaner to a loud power lawn mower. For Morris, it’s another data point in a broader effort to give communities facts as they consider data center development. “My approach is to not pick sides but to bring data. And that’s what I try to do. It is very emotionally charged, and data centers are not right for every place. But let’s understand what the real facts are, and then each community can make its own choice.” Morris said. Inside Sabey Data Centers’ newest building, representatives described a colocation model in which customers from different industries store data at the facility. Those customers include health care and agriculture businesses. One example shared during the tour was how farmers use stored data to track soil composition and apple inventory. The tour showed how the facility manages heat from its servers. Warm air moves through a ceiling plenum to a cooling area, where fans pull it across chilled coils. The cooled air then returns to the server hall. The liquid used in the cooling process is sent to outdoor chillers to be cooled and reused, according to company representatives. Morris said the newest building reflects how quickly the technology has advanced. He also noted that the air chillers were quiet during the visit. Morris said Quincy also offers a lesson in planning. He said data center developers, local leaders and Grant County Public Utility District worked together on infrastructure, which he said was paid for by the data center. In a second report, NBC Montana will examine how data center development has affected Quincy and what the community’s experience could mean for Montana.

artigo.texto: Trending LANSING -- Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed a petition for rehearing before the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) in case U-22058, wherein the Commission approved DTE's special contracts to service a Google hyperscale data center in Van Buren Township. The Attorney General repeatedly demonstrates in her petition where DTE failed to meet its legal burdens, the MPSC ruled in error by applying incorrect standards of review and acting without reason or regard for ratepayer protections, and how the consequences of both are unnecessary risks of cost-shifting from DTE and Google to the utility's household, business, and other classes of customers. Attorney General Nessel raises in her petition several proposals for strengthening DTE's cost recoveries from Google, establishing sufficient cost and benefit tracking mechanisms, and ensuring adequate cost backstops by Google and DTE that won't ultimately fall on DTE's existing ratepaying customers. "These are massive, twenty-year, billion-dollar contracts between one of the wealthiest businesses on the planet, and one of the most powerful companies in the State," said Attorney General Nessel. "The MPSC simply didn't do their job here – failing to protect DTE's existing residential and business customers, and accepting lousy contracts with weak terms to yet again appease a utility they're supposed to keep in check. Sweetheart deals for data centers and unaccountable utilities run amok is not responsible government, and it's not good business for the State. In this petition we've outlined serious concerns about how these contracts set up DTE customers to be burned." Among the Attorney General's most significant concerns is the MPSC's decision to adopt DTE's contract-long "aggregation" approach to assessing projected ratepayer benefits against the utility's actual costs to serve the Google data center. This decision presumably accepts years-long periods where DTE's other customers will directly subsidize the operation of the hypserscale data center, and the MPSC itself concedes this will certainly happen, at least for a four-year period from 2035 to 2038. DTE proposed to the MPSC a 20-year term-long "aggregation" standard for evaluating costs and benefits to and from its other customers, and assumes only to evaluate or demonstrate whether other customers bore any net-negative cost of serving the Google data center in view of the entire 20-year term, indicating that DTE expects its other customers to pay costs to support the data center and makes difficult any challenge to those costs until the contract term concludes. The MPSC order establishes the precedent and the expectation for their acceptance of DTE passing on data center costs to other ratepayers in any number of years under the presumption of a longer-term benefit that has not been adequately supported throughout the case and that may not ever be realized. "The most shocking part of these contracts is that DTE and the MPSC are seemingly signing off on unknown ratepayer costs to support the Google data center, as long as DTE's benefit projections can keep pace for 20 years" added Attorney General Nessel. "It's imperative to keep DTE from charging Michigan households their own costs to fuel Google's data center, and that we insist that costs and benefits be accounted for and reconciled annually. This aggregation standard, on a twenty-year contract, simply swings the doors wide open for customer cost-shifting, and that's how the data center crash-lands onto your electric bill." The MPSC additionally adopted a collateral cap limiting Google and parent company Alphabet's liability for costs of service, which the Attorney General urges the MPSC to reject outright on rehearing. As it did when considering the DTE contracts to service the Oracle and Open AI data center in Saline, the MPSC also ignored in this case significant transmission costs identified by the Attorney General that DTE has refused to account for in its contracts and assessments. For these reasons, and more articulated within the petition, the Attorney General asserts the MPSC's order demonstrates a litany of errors, such as by applying an incorrect burden of proof and an incorrect standard of review, by failing to meaningfully engage with or outright ignoring important arguments from the Attorney General's briefing, and by repeatedly defaulting to acceptance of DTE's proposed terms despite DTE's failures to support the reasonableness and prudence of those terms. The consequence of these errors, argues Attorney General Nessel, is the imposition of mistaken and unnecessary cost-shifting risks onto Michigan ratepayers. The Attorney General argues that, given DTE's repeated failure throughout the contested case to meet its burden of proof under Michigan law, the MPSC must adopt on rehearing the recommendations made in her petition or instead reject the contracts outright.

artigo.texto: Microsoft pressiona Trump contra veto a componentes chineses para data centers | Vero NotíciasMicrosoft pressiona Trump contra veto a componentes chineses para data centers A Microsoft pressiona o governo de Donald Trump a abandonar os planos de proibir a importação de transceptores ópticos chineses, componentes essenciais para data centers de inteligência artificial. A empresa alerta que a medida pode atrasar a expansão da infraestrutura tecnológica dos EUA. A gigante de tecnologia possui 35 data centers em construção e outros 134 planejados no país. A empresa argumenta que a proibição pode comprometer a cadeia de suprimentos e deixar chips de IA sem utilização por falta de componentes para conectá-los. O governo americano avalia o veto por preocupações de segurança nacional, incluindo riscos de espionagem e ataques cibernéticos atribuídos à China. A Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC) trabalha na restrição, enquanto empresas do setor alertam para possíveis prejuízos à competitividade. O bitcoin recuava 1,94% nesta terça-feira (10), a US$ 73.570, às 17h15, segundo a Binance. Durante o dia, atingiu o menor nível desde agosto. O ethereum caía 3,93%, cotado a US$ 2.051,06. A queda ocorreu após dados de inflação dos Estados Unidos reforçarem expectativas de aumento dos juros em dezembro. Antes da divulgação, o diretor do Federal Reserve, Christopher Waller, havia defendido considerar uma alta de 0,5 ponto percentual. O dólar comercial subiu 1,48% nesta terça-feira (10) e fechou a R$ 5,58, maior cotação de 2026. A moeda norte-americana também atingiu o patamar mais elevado desde 31 de julho de 2025. A alta ocorreu após a inflação ao consumidor dos Estados Unidos avançar 0,4% em outubro, acima dos 0,3% esperados pelo mercado. O indicador influencia as decisões do Federal Reserve sobre os juros americanos. A Anthropic pretende captar até US$ 62,5 bilhões em sua oferta pública inicial de ações, com preço entre US$ 70 e US$ 78 por papel. A operação pode avaliar a desenvolvedora de IA em aproximadamente US$ 1,03 trilhão. A companhia colocou à venda cerca de 801,4 milhões de ações da Classe A. A avaliação total considera também outras classes de papéis e a possibilidade de compras adicionais pelos bancos responsáveis pela oferta. Deputados afirmaram nesta terça-feira (10), após reunião com o ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, que não há negociação para adiar a reforma tributária. Segundo eles, o governo mantém o início da CBS em janeiro de 2027. O presidente da Frente Parlamentar do Empreendedorismo, deputado Joaquim Passarinho (PL-PA), disse que a prioridade é implementar a mudança. A CBS substituirá PIS e Cofins, enquanto a CNI defende adiar o início para 2028. A Petrobras registrou lucro líquido de R$ 39,75 bilhões no terceiro trimestre de 2026, alta de 21,5% na comparação anual. O balanço foi divulgado nesta terça-feira (10). A receita da estatal somou R$ 169,3 bilhões, crescimento de 32,4% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. A produção de petróleo também avançou, com aumento de 11,9%.

artigo.texto: Karpowership acquires UK 100MWh BESS site for development The Turkish renewable energy company has bought a fully consented plot near Birmingham in the UK's Midlands for a 100MWh BESS installation. Anglo Renewables has sold a fully consented 50MW/100MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) project near Birmingham to Kinetics Energies for an undisclosed sum. The 2-hour project, dubbed Kitwell, is expected to connect to the grid in 2028. Northamptonshire-based Anglo Renewables is a micro-business (having a turnover of less than £1 million annually) that enters into agreements with landowners and steers appropriate permitting for change of land use and planning permission for battery energy storage system or solar PV installations. In the case of the Kitwell site, it is presumed any agreement between the landowner and Anglo Renewables passes to Kinetics Energies, part of Karpowership, the Turkish energy group. The head of commercial at Karpowership and CEO of Kinetics Energies, Mehmet Katmer, said: "Battery storage has an important role to play in keeping the grid flexible and reliable, and we look forward to delivering an operating BESS project as part of our strategy to deliver 800MW of low and zero carbon assets across Europe." In England and Wales, BESS sites are not considered to be nationally significant infrastructure regardless of their size, and permission for development is subject to approval by the relevant local planning authority. artigo.texto: Ohio Chamber study: Data centers added more than $9B to state economy in 2025 COLUMBUS, Ohio (WSYX) — Ohio’s growing data center industry added more than $9 billion to the state’s economy last year, according to a new study commissioned by the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. The study found that data centers and the construction needed to build them supported nearly 70,000 jobs in Ohio last year. About 14,000 people work directly in the data center industry, with average pay and benefits of about $148,000 a year, the report said. Looking ahead, the study estimated that planned construction and equipment spending through 2030 could support more than 257,000 jobs for a year. The report also examined the fiscal impact of incentives and investment tied to the industry. It said the state gave up more than $1.5 billion in tax revenue, but that the investment has generated a $2.7 billion fiscal surplus.
