artigo.texto: Statesboro’s city government, through City Attorney Cain Smith, filed a response Oct. 19-21 in Bulloch County Superior Court to a lawsuit seeking to reverse the city’s Aug. 18 rezoning of a 27-acre tract on Burkhalter Road to “O” or office at the request of data center developers. Meanwhile, Smith says that processing by the city of any further application by the property owner and potential developer, 4AM Development LLC, for a special use permit required for a data center “would continue to be stayed.” In other words, unless the court upholds the zoning or until it issues some other go-ahead, the mayor and council apparently won’t be holding a hearing to consider issuing a permit, even if 4AM Development, whose publicly identified partners are Bobby Bagwell and Charles C. Way, try to submit a completed application. The Data Centers Ordinance, enacted in June by a 3-1 vote of City Council as an amendment to the Statesboro Unified Development Code, allows data centers as a special use in four non-residential zoning classifications. However, “special use” means that a data center will not be automatically allowed. Instead, plans for any particular site must meet special requirements for a permit to be issued by the council on a majority vote. Way and Bagwell, whose company reportedly includes two other investors, propose locating a 230,000-square-foot data center on the site at 6539 Burkhalter Road, and have applied to Georgia Power for an up to 99-megawatt electrical supply. City Council’s Aug. 18 vote approving the rezoning from “R-4” high-density residential to “O” was 3-2, including the mayor’s tiebreaker. Original complaint But on Sept. 17, the nonprofit organization Coastal Communities United and 11 named individuals, including some adjacent property owners and other nearby residents, filed a petition in the county Superior Court for review of the rezoning and a declaratory judgment against the city’s action. Although worded in some ways like a standard lawsuit, the “petition for review” signed by attorney Robert Abney Fricks Sr. of Warner Robins identified his clients as petitioners rather than plaintiffs. But it named both the city, as a municipal corporation, and 4AM Development as defendants. It asserted that the petitioners would suffer damages “to be determined” but asserted no monetary amounts. In the closing paragraphs of the 30-page complaint, the petitioners asked that the court declare the city zoning decision “invalid, void or stricken.” Citing a provision of state law, the complaint also asserts that filing such a challenge should “stay all legal proceedings in furtherance of the action.” 4AM’s previous answer As previously reported, 4 AM Development LLC, though William J. Keogh III, of the Augusta-based Hull Barrett law firm, then replied with an Oct. 6 "motion to dismiss and request for expedited hearing.” Points of that motion were reported by the Statesboro Herald in an Oct. 12 story. At that time city officials had not filed a separate answer, but Smith said the city would have to do so or face a “default judgment” and would answer by a 30-day deadline from having been served notice of the suit. Notice had been served Sept. 21 at City Hall. The city’s answer, signed by Smith as submitted to the court Oct. 19 and stamped at the clerk of court’s office Oct. 21, runs to 16 pages. It parallels the 4AM Development response in some ways, such as by asserting that the nonprofit organization and the 11 property owners or neighbors at various distances from the site lack legal standing to challenge the zoning decision. The city’s answer But the city’s response differs from the developers’ in other ways, such as by asserting a defense of sovereign immunity. The city’s “first defense” is simply: “The Petition fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted and thus should be dismissed.” The “second defense” is that the petitioners allegedly lack standing. “Petitioner Coastal Community United should be dismissed from this action,” Smith has asserted in the city’s written answer. “An organization cannot obtain standing merely by asserting its members’ rights. It must establish a cognizable violation of its own rights under an available standing theory.” He cites the 2025 opinion of the Georgia Supreme Court in a case called Republican National Committee v. Eternal Vigilance Action Inc. in support of this. Smith then cites the state high court in a different decision, from 2006, as holding “that a plaintiff cannot avoid zoning-standing requirements merely by seeking equitable relief or asserting an interest in enforcing zoning laws.” The city’s fourth defense, the one claiming sovereign immunity, is aimed at an assertion in the petitioners’ complaint that the rezoning decision amounts to an “inverse condemnation” by reduction of nearby property values. “Petitioners do not allege and cannot show that private property has been taken for public use, nor does the City maintain any control or interest in the rezoned property; the city is therefore immune from claims for inverse condemnation,” the answer asserts. The city’s “fourth defense” briefly echoes a point of the developers’ motion, that petitioners “are barred from making a Constitutional attack for the first time before the Superior Court.” In other words, the defendants assert that the citizens should have stated a constitutional basis for their objections during the rezoning hearings. But then the city’s “fifth defense” claims that the petitioners’ complaints “are not ripe for adjudication” because the data center project “cannot be undertaken without the issuance of a special use permit by the Mayor and Council.” The city’s answer continues through 12 stated “defenses,” most very short and direct. But the 12th goes on to list 115 specific points from the petitioners’ complaints as “denied” or “admitted.” It ends with a request to the court dismiss the petition and require the petitioners to pay all costs of the act

artigo.texto: The Case for Prefabricated Power in AI Data Centers Key Highlights - Prefabricated power modules integrate critical electrical systems into factory-tested, cohesive solutions. - Off-site assembly can cut deployment timelines in half compared to traditional construction. - Factory testing reduces on-site complexity, commissioning delays and unexpected construction costs. - Modular infrastructure enables flexible capital investment and more efficient long-term operations. - Power skids and outdoor modules offer deployment flexibility for different site requirements. The AI boom has placed data center operators in a historic squeeze. CTOs and infrastructure managers are under pressure to bring massive, high-density computing capacity online faster than ever, even as the grid struggles to keep up. And as demands intensify, there’s very little room for error. The question now is how the industry can scale AI infrastructure without putting reliability, power availability, and the grid itself at risk. In this high-stakes environment, power-related challenges represent a massive business risk. They remain the leading cause of impactful data center outages and cost the world’s 500 largest companies an estimated $1.4 trillion annually. That makes the way power infrastructure is designed, built and deployed more important than ever. The industry is beginning to rethink the traditional approach to building power infrastructure. To scale rapidly without compromising reliability, the industry is shifting toward prefabricated, factory-tested power modules. By moving complex electrical assembly off-site, operators can balance the competing demands of deployment speed, financial risk, and total cost of ownership. The Technical Reality: A Power Module Is a Cohesive System A prefabricated power module is more than a group of components assembled on a metal floor. It’s an integrated system that is engineered and tested to operate as a single unit. In a typical deployment, a weather-proof outdoor module or an indoor structural skid houses: - Medium Voltage (MV) Switchgear: The entry point for utility power, providing robust protection and control. - Low Voltage (LV) Distribution Switchboards: Directs large blocks of power to the server rooms. - High-Efficiency UPS Systems: Industrial-grade systems operating at optimized efficiency to minimize energy waste. - Energy Storage: Long-life valve regulated lead‐acid (VRLA) or high-density Lithium-Ion battery cabinets. - Auxiliary Systems: Factory-installed direct expansion (DX) cooling, clean-agent fire suppression, security cameras, and comprehensive environmental monitoring. The critical engineering value lies in factory-level integration. When these systems are designed, wired, piped, and programmed under controlled factory conditions, the complex electrical and digital interactions between them are fully validated before shipping. For example, coordination between an MV switchgear’s circuit breaker trip settings, a UPS’s transient response, and a Lithium-Ion battery’s management system is highly sensitive. Resolving a communication mismatch or tight clearance issue on-site during commissioning can delay a project by weeks. Resolving it on the factory floor, where engineers have specialized diagnostics and direct manufacturer support, takes hours instead of weeks and eliminates on-site construction errors. Balancing the Tradeoffs: Speed vs. Cost vs. Risk Infrastructure buyers prioritize outcomes differently. Hyperscalers might value pure speed to market, while colocation providers and enterprise operators may be highly sensitive to upfront CapEx, long-term OpEx, or project risk. Prefabricated modular infrastructure shifts the traditional trade-off curve across all three variables: 1. Speed: Accelerating Time-to-Market For AI developers chasing first-mover advantages, speed is often the primary metric. By moving much of the electrical work off-site, prefabricated power modules can significantly shorten deployment timelines. For example, Schneider Electric’s power skids can be operational in half the time of traditional “stick-built” electrical rooms. A new research paper co-authored with hyperscale developer Compass Datacenters also highlights the quantitative deployment efficiency gains of shifting from traditional white space builds to prefabricated modular IT pods. According to the study performed at a Compass hyperscale data center campus, prefabricated modular pods shorten onsite installation time from 75.5 hours to just 15 hours per pod, delivering an 80% reduction in onsite installation duration. By shifting critical assembly, integration and verification to a controlled factory environment, data center operators can reduce on-site labor and complexity while bringing AI compute capacity online faster. 2. Risk: Shifting Complexity Off-Site On-site construction is inherently unpredictable, plagued by weather delays, labor shortages, and variable craft quality. Shifting assembly to an ISO-certified manufacturing facility replaces field variables with standardized quality control. Factory-tested validation ensures that the module arrives as a "plug-and-play" asset, eliminating unexpected construction expenses and ensuring the system works flawlessly from day one. 3. Cost: Granular CapEx, Reduced OpEx, and Environmental Impact From a financial perspective, modular construction also gives operators more flexibility with capital. Instead of building massive, over-engineered structures on day one to accommodate growth that may not happen for years, they can add capacity as demand materializes. That means capital can be deployed when it is actually needed, rather than tying up millions in infrastructure long before the servers — and the revenue they generate — are ready. There are operational savings, too. Pre-engineered systems can be paired with cloud-based monitoring and intelligent management platforms that give operators a much clearer view of system health in

artigo.texto: Publicidade O Ministério das Comunicações informou nesta segunda-feira (9) que o governo federal planeja investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma de gerenciamento e distribuição de dados entre mini data centers no Brasil. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados, distribuindo automaticamente os recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Na prática, o Executivo espera que a tecnologia reduza gastos com energia e custos operacionais, acelere o acesso às informações e aumente a proteção de dados estratégicos. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), e o projeto será executado pelo Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD). O prazo de execução é de 36 meses, a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Filho, afirmou que o projeto possibilitará maior autonomia e soberania no tratamento de dados no País. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirmou em nota.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›NHPC Floats Tender for BESS Integration with 1,200 MW Jalaun Solar Park in UP NHPC Floats Tender for BESS Integration with 1,200 MW Jalaun Solar Park in UP NHPC has invited bids to develop battery energy storage systems and supply solar-plus-BESS power using 1,200 MW of existing solar capacity at Jalaun Solar Park in Uttar Pradesh. November 09, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey NHPC has floated a tender for setting up Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and supply of Solar-plus-BESS power utilising the 1200 MW Solar Project at Jalaun Solar Park of Bundelkhand Saur Urja (BSUL), Uttar Pradesh. BSUL intends to integrate BESS with the existing solar power of 2,419 Million Units (MU) in Solar + BESS configuration to meet the firm and dispatchable power requirement of the end procurer. Bidders need to pay INR 30 lakh (plus GST) for each Block. They also need to deposit INR 10 crore as bid security. The last date for submission of bids is December 12, 2026. The techno-commercial bids will be opened on December 16, 2026. The project developer will be selected through Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) based on a composite solar-plus-BESS tariff under two configurations. Configuration I involves scheduling 300 MW of solar power during solar hours and 800 MW/4,800 MWh of BESS capacity during non-solar hours. Configuration II involves scheduling 600 MW of solar power during solar hours and 800 MW/3,200 MWh of BESS capacity. Developers can bid for either or both configurations, with the final selection depending on the buying entity's requirements. The selected BESS developer will set up battery storage infrastructure across four blocks near three 33/400 kV pooling substations close to Jalaun Solar Park. The developer will procure solar power generated from these blocks and supply the combined solar-plus-BESS power to the designated delivery point at the ISTS CTUIL substation. Bidders can submit offers for Configuration-I, Configuration-II or both, with each location comprising 75 MW solar capacity and 200 MW/1,200 MWh of BESS under Configuration-I, or 150 MW solar capacity and 200 MW/800 MWh of BESS under Configuration-II. Bidders can secure up to 50 percent of the total contracted capacity, with allocation limited to a maximum of two locations across either or both configurations. For Configuration-I, bidders must have a minimum net worth of INR 353.20 crore per block, while the requirement for Configuration-II is INR 261.20 crore per block. To demonstrate liquidity, bidders must meet at least one of three criteria: minimum annual turnover of INR 176.60 crore per block for Configuration-I or INR 130.60 crore for Configuration-II; PBDIT of INR 35.32 crore or INR 26.12 crore per block, respectively; or an in-principle bank sanction for a fund-based credit line of INR 44.15 crore per block for Configuration-I or INR 32.65 crore for Configuration-II. artigo.texto: Analysis: One of the biggest challenges when it comes to wind and solar power is how to store this energy for later use Energy storage is arguably the biggest challenge in green energy adoption. It is critical if we are to balance our national grid and reduce dependency on imported energy. Currently, we are wasting 15% of green energy produced in Ireland, which is enough to power 660,000 homes. This is primarily caused by high generation of wind farms at night when demand is low. This creates a problem that is simple in concept, but extremely challenging at a national grid level: how do we store this energy for later use? Ireland has some examples of success in this regard. We have created multiple large scale batteries including pumped hydro storage in the Wicklow mountains and one of the world's largest fly wheel systems at Moneypoint in Clare. These types of storage differ from the lithium-ion batteries that power most of our devices. They essentially store energy by moving mass. Both have different strengths and weaknesses, but if we are to meet our emissions targets and secure our energy security more storage using different forms of technology is needed. Rust battery A recently launched project in partnership with US company Form Energy and Irish company FuturEnergy will use a new approach to storage in the form of the Ballynahone Energy Storage iron-air battery project. The battery system will be located southwest of Buncrana, near the Trillick substation in Co Donegal and will create 1,000 MWh which could power approximately 87,000 homes for 24 hours. While grid scale battery systems are not unusual, the technology used in Donegal is unique and very different to more common lithium ion systems. This battery technology, in the simplest terms, is able to draw electricity from iron as it rusts (oxidises). Recharging the battery reverses this chemical reaction. Because the battery is mainly made of iron, air and water they are very cheap to manufacture and easy to recycle at end of life, which is approximately 20 to 30 years of use. The graph compares the cost of different energy storage technologies per kilowatt-hour, highlighting a wide range of expenses across various systems. Iron-air batteries by Form Energy emerge as the most cost-effective option at an estimated €30 per kWh, while standard lithium-ion (LFP) and pumped hydro systems occupy the mid-range. In stark contrast, mechanical flywheels stand out as significantly more expensive than the rest, but are useful in specific grid balancing applications. The very low cost of storage makes this look like the ideal solution. So what's the catch? As with all technological solutions, there are advantages and disadvantages. These need to be carefully considered, especially when technology has not yet been widely proven beyond manufacturer testing. One of the main draw backs for iron air batteries is the amount of energy lost during a charge and discharge cycle. This is often referred to as round trip efficiency. Early reports suggest that iron air can achieve approximately 50% efficiency which means that half the electricity used to charge the battery is lost. By comparison, lithium ion can achieve 85-95% efficiency in grid scale use and pumped hydro can achieve approximately 75% efficiency. Iron air also has a lower discharge rate than lithium ion. It is designed to discharge over 50 to 100 hours. You could consider iron air like a tractor that can draw a large load of electricity to the grid slowly, where lithium ion is the expensive sports car that can get there quickly, but with a much smaller load. These are two very different technologies used for different energy needs. Both of these battery types, in addition to a wide range of other energy storage devices, will be needed in order to create a reliable green energy system that can cope with intermittent generation. While the round trip efficiency issue remains, it is important to remember that oil and gas electricity generation ranges from 40-60% efficient and results in considerable CO2 emissions. No energy generation or storage option is perfect, and we cannot afford to allow perfect to be the enemy of the good when it comes to securing Ireland’s energy independence. artigo.texto: A new battery energy storage system (BESS) being built on the former coal power station at Fiddler’s Ferry has passed a major milestone, with the installation of key electrical equipment. The site is owned by SSE Renewables, with infrastructure specialists OCU Energy and Fluence building the 150 MW BESS. When complete, it will be capable of providing power for approximately 250 000 homes for a two-hour period at a time. An SSE Renewables spokesperson previously said: “Similar to our Ferrybridge project, our grid scale battery at Fiddler’s Ferry will be built on what was a former SSE-owned coal-fired power station and highlights the transition away from fossil fuels towards a net-zero future.” Kiosk buildings, which will house electrical relays, switchgear, control panels, and communication systems, are now in place, fabricated by RSK Group companies AJ Engineering & Construction Services and Northern Engineering & Welding Co. (NEWCo). AJ Engineering & Construction Services Pre-Construction Manager, Lee Binks, said: “When fully operational, the BESS site will store power for release back to the UK national grid when it is needed the most – helping to manage peaks of energy demand and supporting a transition away from fossil fuels. “We have designed, fabricated and cladded two auxiliary transformer buildings and one portable relay room for the site in a modular format, reducing the time spent on site. These buildings provide compact, weatherproof enclosures that house the equipment that ultimately connects the battery system to the national grid. In addition to this, we have fabricated and erected the switch room, which is a structural steel portal frame building with insulated cladding. “Usually, for the aux buildings and portable relay rooms, these types of small buildings are manufactured using glass reinforced plastic or brick and built on site. To speed up delivery and reduce complexity, we built them off-site using fabricated steel modules. They were then transported to the site and lifted into place, already cladded and ready for fit-out.” Binks explained that because they are widely used in both the water and the en-ergy sectors, they are in high demand, and lead times for their procurement can be significant. He concluded: “Having been built with steel and cladding, the kiosks were ready to be installed on site within six weeks. Normally this team of structural designers, detailers, fabricators, steel erectors and site management would have to do this on-site. By building the kiosks off-site, we have avoided adding further complexity to an already busy construction site.” Fellow RSK company, Acies, carried out the connection design on the structural frame for the switch room, working in collaboration with AJ Engineering while it carried out the modelling of the building. With the kiosks in place, OCU Group will begin the fit-out process of the internal equipment that will connect the site to the national grid. It is expected to be operational in 2027. artigo.texto: The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission recently approved AES Indiana’s plan to serve a Google data center in a contested case that highlights the complex challenges regulators and utilities face in allocating system costs for large computational loads. According to the Oct. 7 order, AES will acquire or build new generation, storage and grid infrastructure for a 390-MW data center planned for Monrovia, a town Southwest of Indianapolis, at an estimated project cost of about $737 million. The new generation, storage and transmission assets included in the Monrovia Project will go into the utility’s rate base. AES says its electric service agreement with Google is designed to ensure the revenues will be sufficient to “reimburse at least 100%” of the project’s incremental direct costs. But the contract itself is heavily redacted, and an estimated $74 million in network upgrades has been explicitly allocated to all customers as a reliability need, prompting criticism from consumer advocates that the arrangement is shifting costs onto other ratepayers. What are ‘reasonably allocable’ costs? Indiana state law requires large load customers to reimburse at least 80% of project costs “reasonably allocable” to them. Claire Wayner, a senior associate at the clean energy nonprofit RMI, said in an interview that while local projects are fairly easy to trace back to a specific data center, broader regional system upgrades raise more complex questions about who benefits and how costs are allocated across jurisdictions. “Maybe they're upgrading a part of the grid that they were going to have to upgrade anyway because it's aging infrastructure,” Wayner said. “If that's the case, they should have to demonstrate that, and then maybe cross socialization makes sense.” But, she continued, “If that upgrade was not going to be built without the data center, without benefits modeling or just a demonstration of the benefits to the rest of the zone, it's difficult to make the claim that all ratepayers in that zone should pay for it.” AES Indiana will serve Google’s data center from its portfolio of shared generation and battery assets. The new generation and storage assets built to meet the additional demand will be owned through a subsidiary by the utility and go into its rate base. In testimony to the commission, a utility representative said the transmission infrastructure included in the Monrovia Project falls into three basic categories: interconnection infrastructure for the generation and storage; “direct connection” infrastructure for connecting the data center to the system; and network upgrades necessary “primarily” to serve Google “but also to meet other customer demand or energy needs.” Google will pay about $32 million upfront for the direct connection, but $73.8 million in network upgrades will be included in AES Indiana’s transmission rate base and recovered through future rates from all customers, including residential ones. Commissioners approved the proposal 5-0, saying in their order that “although the Customer may be the impetus for the network upgrades being made, this does not preclude the upgrades from providing system-wide benefits.” “Network upgrades, as the name implies, are upgrades or additions to the transmission network intended to provide reliability, resiliency, and stability to the system at large,” it said. “Just as the Customer will be allocated a portion of the existing network transmission infrastructure, it is reasonable for existing customers to also be allocated a portion of the network upgrades.” The Midcontinent Independent System Operator approved some of the network upgrades, which include a new substation, citing reliability and load growth. Although the order says the portfolio proposed in AES’ filing is for 390 MW of new load with 460 MW of new 4-hour storage and 130 MW of solar generation, the substation planned for the project is designed for 1,200 MW of load, creating opportunity for future expansion at the site. The generation and storage resources consist of one 200-MW and one 130-MW battery energy storage system, called Foundry Works and Hardy Hills, respectively, as well as a 130-MW solar facility paired with a 130-MW BESS called Crosstrack. Their cost is redacted in the case filings. ‘Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts’ Ben Inskeep, program director at the Citizens Action Coalition, a consumer advocacy group that intervened in the case, sees the deal as running counter to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed earlier this year by tech companies and utilities, including Google and AES Indiana. “These network upgrades are specifically driven by the Google data center,” Inskeep told Utility Dive in an interview. “Instead of making the cost causer pay, AES Indiana has decided to spread the costs out to other ratepayers, and our commission has unfortunately approved that.” Ben Gavelek, a spokesperson for the commission, declined to comment on the deal. Google did not respond to requests for comment. Claire Rice, a spokesperson for AES Indiana, said in an email that although the transmission assets are being allocated through the normal cost-of-service process, Google’s rate includes a “separate incremental-cost test designed to recover the incremental costs required to serve Google, including the network upgrades.” “Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts,” she added. Many of the exact terms of the service agreement, including monthly energy and demand charges and riders, are redacted in the public record. Parts of other contracts underpinning the deal are also confidential. The assets will be included in future base rate case filings. Until those new rates are established, the utility plans to recover those costs through its Environmental Cost Recovery and netted with contract revenues. The commission’s order says AES Indiana’s accounting and ratemaking proposals enable it to “match” the project

artigo.texto: The Lead In: City Council coin toss, Harmony data center, Townies’ future, and Albert Lea tax aid Pine Island City Council seat, Townies Future, Harmony Data Center, Albert Lea Tax abatement ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – A city council seat is up for grabs. The future of a popular restaurant space will be decided. A data center discussion comes to a head. And a Freeborn County town could help a local company expand. Here is The Lead In, for Nov. 8-14, 2026. Pine Island: Tie for council seat to be settled by coin flip or draw Last Tuesday’s election saw several candidates win decisively in their races. The race for Pine Island City Council is a different story. According to the unofficial results, Tosca Wohl won 809 votes, or 27.9%, to claim the first of two open council seats. However, the second seat ended in a tie between incumbent Delana Weis and challenger Dominick Pahl, each earning 711 votes. According to the City of Pine Island, the decision will come down to a coin toss or drawing from a hat. It will occur at a special council meeting on Thursday, Nov. 12, at 6 p.m. at City Hall. Rochester: Park Board to decide Soldiers Field clubhouse concessions The Rochester Park Board is scheduled to make a decision on the future of concessions at the Soldiers Field Memorial Park clubhouse. Rochester Parks and Recreation is recommending Uni Uni Bubble Tea and Old Abe Coffee Shop to replace Townies Philly Kitchen + Bar as the clubhouse concessions operator. The city announced the recommendation Friday. The city said it also received a proposal for Townies to retain the space, but parks and recreation officials decided to move in a different direction. The city said Uni Uni Bubble Tea and Old Abe Coffee Shop’s proposal stood out for menu options, ideas and approach to serving customers. Townies said it was informed of the decision less than half an hour before the city sent out the announcement. In mid-July, the restaurant temporarily closed after multiple employees quit due to a broken air conditioning system, something the restaurant looked to the city to fix. Townies responded to the news on Facebook Friday, thanking the community for its support over the years. The restaurant also said that while it is closing its doors, it is not staying silent. A Townies customer started a petition on Saturday calling on the Park Board to keep the restaurant at its location. As of 11 p.m. Sunday, the petition has more than 2,000 signatures. On social media, Townies General Manager Tim Nela asked customers to attend the meeting to show support for the restaurant. The Park Board will make a final decision Tuesday at 4:30 p.m. at the Maintenance Center. Harmony: council to review data center ordinance The Harmony City Council is preparing to consider final language on its proposed data center ordinance at its meeting Tuesday at 7 p.m. at the community center. The review follows months of discussions among councilmembers and the community about how to address a possible data center in the region. According to the city, the goal is to protect public health and welfare, as well as the environment around the town. The proposed ordinance would limit data centers to a new industrial technology zone in the city and limit each data center to 55 megawatts of power. Any building would have to sit at least 500 feet from residential areas. Evaporative cooling, which uses large amounts of water, would also be banned. Unlike the planned Google data center development in Pine Island, there has been no public announcement about a specific project in Harmony. However, the city website says there has been interest from developers. Albert Lea: council to vote on tax abatement and loans for company expansion In Freeborn County, the Albert Lea City Council will vote on assisting a local business expansion with a tax abatement and loans. The council will vote on providing D & S Holdings of Albert Lea with three forms of financial aid for a $2 million expansion of Pro Manufacturing on 209th Street. The aid includes: - A tax abatement starting in 2028 that would last 10 years and not exceed $129,000. - A forgivable loan of $50,000 if the expansion brings in at least five new jobs maintained over five years. - A $300,000 loan at zero percent interest to be paid over 10 years. The loans come from a fund created for assisting businesses with job creation. The goal of the financial assistance is to increase both the number of jobs in town and the local tax base. The council will take up the items at its regular meeting Monday at 7 p.m. at City Hall. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. Copyright 2026 KTTC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A Botetourt County resident’s lawsuit alleging that the county’s board of supervisors violated the state’s open meetings and open records law when it greenlit a Google data center campus is legally sufficient to move forward, a circuit judge ruled Tuesday. But after nearly three hours, which featured some testimony and a lot of arguments about the case’s merits, substitute Judge Michael Doucette said court schedule issues forced him to postpone a further hearing on the matter until next week. Robert Dallas, who lives near the Botetourt Center at Greenfield site, filed suit Nov. 2, seeking to invalidate the county’s economic development performance agreement with the limited liability company behind the project. His case alleges that the county violated the Virginia Freedom of Information Act when it approved documentation advancing the Google project. Dallas’s suit also asks the court to “rescind all actions” carried out in connection with the June 2025 document. Respondents in the case are the county, its board of supervisors, its economic development authority and Google-owned Helio Capital LLC. Julian Harf, representing the county, elicited testimony showing that Google has transferred $2.5 million of a promised $4 million to the county, helping pay for ambulances, fire trucks, heart monitors, body cameras and more. Further testimony showed ground clearing work has already started. Harf used the testimony to help support a plea filed in response to the suit. He asked the court to find that even if Dallas’ allegations are true, his case is legally insufficient. “Remedies” for a FOIA violation “do not include rescission” of the agreement and its effects, Hart said. An invalidated agreement would not be the court’s problem, said John Fishwick, who leads Dallas’ legal team. Google, the county and Helio could work out those ramifications among themselves, Fishwick said. FOIA law calls for a hearing within seven days of a suit’s filing, but it took eight before Doucette could be available. By the time the recently retired Nelson County judge decided in the plaintiff’s favor, the hearing time had bumped up against an already scheduled criminal court docket that included several cases in which jail sentences could be ended. “I won’t force an inmate to spend one more day in jail,” he said as he told those gathered in the courtroom that the trial would be set for 9 a.m. Monday. It was unclear why Botetourt County Circuit Judge Joel Branscom was unavailable to hear the case. According to the suit, the county’s board of supervisors did not disclose on its published agenda that it would be discussing the agreement or a resolution to enact it in a closed meeting on June 24, 2025. After the board returned to public session, it voted 5-0, with no discussion, to approve the resolution and the agreement, after they were added to the agenda during the meeting as so-called “walk-on” items, the case alleges. After a recess, the board returned to address another walk-on item — announcing the data center project. Yet another item that hadn’t appeared on the agenda was a board resolution approving Google’s agreement with the Western Virginia Water Authority, Dallas alleges. Harf and Helio’s lawyer, Graham Bryant, told the court that information on the agenda denoted an economic development project in the industrial park, which they argued was the most the board needed to disclose, to protect the negotiations. Harf said that county officials discussed the matter in detail after the vote, and any violation committed was “technical.” Fishwick said the board sneaked the matter into its meeting that day, part of an atmosphere of secrecy it had developed. “They treat FOIA like it’s a little technical thing, and they can run roughshod,” Fishwick said, adding that the supervisors’ later announcement of the project was more of a “cheerleading session” than an information share.

artigo.texto: Residents of Jacumba Hot Springs gathered Monday night at the community center for their monthly Jacumba Community Sponsor Group meeting. But one agenda item dominated the discussion – preliminary plans for a data center north of Interstate 8. For years, back country residents in communities like Jacumba have fought large energy projects. Most recently, the Jacumba and Boulevard communities battled two solar and battery energy storage projects that the County Board of Supervisors ultimately approved. “At the end of the day, we’re going to represent ourselves at that table,” said Jeff Osborne, the community group’s current chair. “We’re going to ask for things. We’re gonna ask for representation. We hope to get some response on this specific topic of data centers from the supervisors soon so we can have some indication. Because this is kind of a whole new thing.” There are few things these days that have inflamed communities more than data centers. The massive buildings powering the AI boom can have huge impacts on local land use, water and power. “I’m pro business. I was a contractor for 30 years. But something like that out here in the mountains,” said Ray Tiffany, a longtime Jacumba resident. “It’s just not right.” Osborne first heard about the data center plans after members of the Boulevard Community Planning Group were tipped off by a local landowner. The Jacumba group confirmed the proposal through County records obtained under the California Public Records Act. The tentative plans come from the Spain-based renewable energy company, IGNIS. Tahir Fazal, an IGNIS representative, said in an interview with KPBS that the company is in the early phases of deciding whether to do the project. “We have not done an application, so this project right now is nothing more than a consultation to the county to assess what the permitting path will be, to assess whether there are any limitations that are in place for this project,” Fazal said. Fazal said if the company does decide to pursue the project, it will do community outreach. “We're gonna be transparent on this, as we progress, with the community,” Fazal said. “Right now, I cannot give you an accurate answer on when we will take action on the application. As I mentioned, we are evaluating the guidelines that we received.” The project would ultimately need approval from the San Diego County Board of Supervisors, a county spokesperson confirmed Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Do ronco ao silêncio: qual a diferença entre dirigir um carro elétrico e um a combustão? César Urnhani, piloto e especialista automotivo, mostra quais são essas diferenças e dá dicas para quem está fazendo essa transição. Crédito: Estadão Gerando resumo A TIM fechou um contrato com a BYD para fornecer internet a toda a frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil, além do seu polo industrial. Com a parceria, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades onde a operadora oferece cobertura. A previsão é de que cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa contem com essa conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. Assim, a BYD busca avançar no desenvolvimento de novas funcionalidades que envolvam serviços conectados. Com o crescimento de serviços como inteligência artificial e uso de funções como mapas e streaming a bordo, um carro já tem consumo de dados quase equiparável a de um plano básico pós-pago, tipo ‘controle’. Do lado da TIM, o negócio representa uma expansão no setor automotivo, onde já oferece conexão para cerca de 630 mil veículos. A tele italiana possui uma parceria com a antiga Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA) – hoje parte do grupo Stellantis – para fornecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em veículos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram no Brasil. Essa é a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina, com 4,6 milhões de m². O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, garantindo uma rede preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e as demandas tecnológicas do complexo.

artigo.texto: A expansão de data centers para inteligência artificial, que mobiliza trilhões de dólares no mundo inteiro, enfrenta resistência crescente da opinião pública e, sobretudo, de eleitores. Nas eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos, realizadas na última terça-feira, dia 3 de novembro, eleitores rejeitaram ou restringiram projetos em dezenas de municípios de dez estados americanos. Pelo menos 38 de 41 medidas locais sobre o tema resultaram em veto ou limitações, mandando um recado que atravessa linhas partidárias e já repercute em mercados e na estratégia das empresas de tecnologia. Pesquisas de boca de urna, como a da NBC News, mostram que 57% dos eleitores acreditam que a IA fará mais mal do que bem à sociedade e que 76% se opõem à construção de data centers em suas comunidades. Uma pesquisa Gallup de março registrou 71% de oposição a instalações locais. O tema une preocupações com contas de energia mais altas, uso intensivo de água, ruído, poluição e baixa geração de empregos. No encontro Future of AI (Futuro da IA), do Financial Times, realizado nesta quinta-feira, 05 de novembro, em Londres, executivos admitiram que o próprio setor contribuiu para a hostilidade. O codiretor executivo da Prometheus, Vik Bajaj, diz que a reação não se explica apenas por resistência à tecnologia. “Como categoria profissional, passamos dois anos dizendo às pessoas, de maneira bastante irresponsável, que a IA mudaria o futuro do trabalho para pior, que elas perderiam o emprego, que seus filhos perderiam o emprego, que seus netos viveriam em um mundo irreconhecível. E, no último ano, também estivemos flertando com a ideia de que se trata de uma crise existencial”, afirma Bajaj. O fundador da Niantic Spatial, John Hanke, reconhece que o ritmo de construção foi acelerado demais. “E parte disso foi feito com a cabeça enterrada na areia”, diz. A ex-chefe de políticas globais da DeepMind e diretora do Projeto de IA e Geopolítica da Universidade de Cambridge, Verity Harding, observa que os data centers se tornaram o alvo concreto de ansiedades mais amplas sobre a tecnologia. “De certa forma, só podemos culpar a nós mesmos”, afirma. Os impactos locais são concretos. Data centers de grande porte consomem energia equivalente à de dezenas de milhares de residências e exigem volumes significativos de água para resfriamento. No primeiro trimestre de 2026, ao menos 75 projetos avaliados em cerca de US$ 130 bilhões foram bloqueados ou atrasados por oposição comunitária, segundo o Data Center Watch. Em 2025 e 2026, o volume acumulado de empreendimentos afetados chega a centenas de bilhões de dólares. A resistência não se limita aos Estados Unidos. Há protestos na Índia, no Japão e na Europa. No Brasil, o Ministério Público e a Defensoria Pública pedem a paralisação de obras em Pecém (CE), voltadas ao TikTok, até que haja consulta à comunidade indígena e estudo de impacto ambiental. Há ações semelhantes envolvendo projetos em Belém do Pará e Campinas, além de questionamentos sobre o uso de água no Espírito Santo. O setor brasileiro ainda é pequeno em capacidade global, mas cresceu rapidamente. Gargalos de energia já reduziram a carteira de projetos viáveis, segundo análise da Rystad Energy, de cerca de 21 GW para aproximadamente 7 GW. No Brasil, o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) condiciona incentivos à eficiência hídrica e a energia renovável ou de baixa emissão, mas o acesso à rede permanece o principal entrave. As empresas respondem com mudanças. Nos Estados Unidos, OpenAI, Amazon e Microsoft anunciaram o fim de acordos de confidencialidade controversos. Mais de 200 companhias aderiram a um compromisso não vinculante da gestão Trump para que custos de eletricidade dos data centers não sejam repassados aos consumidores. O chefe da divisão de novas energias da Chevron, Jeff Gustavson, afirma que o relacionamento com as comunidades decide o sucesso dos projetos. “Se você não consegue administrar esse relacionamento, se as comunidades não se beneficiam desses investimentos, você enfrentará oposição”, diz Gustavson. O diretor-executivo da britânica Virtus Data Centres, Adam Eaton, diz que a visibilidade aumentou com a IA e que o setor precisa informar melhor as comunidades. A expansão continua necessária para atender à demanda por modelos e serviços de IA, mas o resultado das urnas e das mobilizações locais indica que o ritmo e as condições dependerão cada vez mais da capacidade de demonstrar benefícios concretos e reduzir impactos sobre energia, água e vizinhança. – Com informações de agências internacionais e do UOL/Folha de S. Paulo.

artigo.texto: Indonesia requires support from developed countries and private partnerships to ensure climate financing is accessible. Benefits for local communities are a key priority. 11 Nov 2026 10:47 WIB · Lingkungan AFP ANTALYA, KOMPAS – The Indonesian government has reaffirmed its readiness to actively develop the carbon market as a strategic instrument to accelerate climate action and mobilize sustainable financing. This initiative has moved beyond mere ambition and has entered a phase of tangible implementation, with the preparation of regulations for carbon economic value and the offering of high-integrity carbon projects to global investors. President's Special Envoy for Climate and Energy Hashim Djojohadikusumo emphasized that Indonesia's natural wealth, encompassing forests, peatlands, mangroves, and oceans, is not merely a collection of resources but a national heritage and a significant contribution to the health of the planet. To maximize this potential, the government is enhancing carbon market governance through Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 and developing a national carbon unit registry system (SRUK) to ensure transparency and investment certainty. "Indonesia views the carbon market as a strategic instrument to accelerate climate action, achieve our NDC targets, and mobilize sustainable financing," Hashim emphasized in a keynote speech during the discussion session titled "Unlocking Indonesia's Carbon Market Potential for Climate Action and Sustainable Finance" on Tuesday (10/11/2026) at the Indonesian pavilion at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the Climate Change Convention (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey. Hashim added that the development of a credible carbon market must deliver tangible environmental benefits and attract long-term investments, with a key requirement being the availability of a robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) system. In the maritime sector, Deputy Minister of Marine Affairs and Fisheries Irwan Meilano emphasized the urgency of incorporating the ocean into climate solutions, given the long-standing impacts felt by fishing communities and coastal ecosystems. The Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries is currently working on reforesting 600,000 hectares of mangroves and optimizing seagrass beds as part of its efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change. "The challenge before us is no longer ambition; it's implementation," Irwan said at the same event. As a tactical step, Irwan stated that the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries will soon issue derivative regulations to implement the national carbon policy. The ministry is scheduled to launch a ministerial regulation on the economic value of carbon on November 18-19. Simultaneously, the government will also present three candidate blue carbon project sites to potential partners and investors. Furthermore, Hashim and Irwan agreed that the commercialization and preservation of carbon ecosystems must not overlook the welfare of surrounding communities. Hashim emphasized that conservation and natural restoration must create meaningful economic opportunities for local residents living alongside these ecosystems. In line with this, Irwan also emphasized the importance of support from developed countries and private partnerships to ensure climate funding is easily accessible. "We need straightforward access to funding, support for mobilizing private investment, and partnerships that transform good projects into viable investment models, while ensuring that the benefits reach local communities," he stated. During a press conference on Tuesday, COP31 Negotiation Presidency Chris Bowen set an ambitious target to increase global electrification levels to 35 percent by 2035. This initiative is seen as an essential requirement and the only way to prevent global temperatures from rising more than 1.5 degrees Celsius amid the threats of a global polycrisis. "We are meeting in a time of polycrisis, when the world is under immense pressure. Unlike previous COPs, we are now confronted with the rise of artificial intelligence and the pressures it places on energy networks. At the same time, the climate crisis has not disappeared; in fact, it is worsening," Bowen stated. Coinciding with Energy and Transport Day at COP31, Bowen emphasized the importance of accelerating electrification as a key solution to various crises. Currently, the global electrification rate stands at just 23 percent, a slow increase from 17 percent in 2005 and 19 percent in 2015. For years, the global electrification rate has increased by an average of only 0.3 percent per year. To achieve a leap target of 35 percent within less than a decade, the COP31 presidency is urging participating countries to sign an electrification pledge and engage in consultations to ensure this target is included in the conference's final decision. We want people to leave here saying, ‘Yes, things changed at COP31.’ Murat Kurum, COP31 President COP31 President Murat Kurum emphasized during the same press conference that electrification is a central theme of COP31. The presidency is advocating for the expanded use of clean energy-based electricity in the transportation, building, and industrial sectors to reduce dependence on the vulnerability of supply and prices of imported fossil fuels. The crisis in the global energy market has served as a harsh lesson for many countries. According to Kurum, from March to August 2026, fuel-importing nations will face an additional cost surge of approximately $330 billion due to price volatility. With the increasing affordability of electrical technology, electrification is seen as a golden opportunity to enhance energy security while also reducing emissions. artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: Repórter Publicado em 8 de novembro de 2026 às 09h28. A Anthropic, desenvolvedora de IA, investiu US$ 3,4 bilhões para garantir fornecimento de energia a seus data centers através de geradores a gás. O acordo com a OnePWR Solutions é a maior compra individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração elétrica por uma empresa de IA, refletindo a crescente demanda por eletricidade com a expansão de data centers. A empresa assegurou equipamentos encomendados anteriormente, evitando preços mais altos. A Anthropic, desenvolvedora da inteligência artificial Claude, fechou um acordo de US$ 3,4 bilhões para garantir o fornecimento de energia a seus data centers. A empresa assumiu encomendas de geradores a gás com capacidade total de 1,7 gigawatt (GW), em uma tentativa de reduzir a dependência de fornecedores de eletricidade. A operação, concluída no fim de setembro com a americana OnePWR Solutions, foi revelada pelo Financial Times. Segundo o jornal, trata-se da maior compra individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração elétrica por uma desenvolvedora de IA. O negócio mostra como a demanda por eletricidade está alterando a estratégia das empresas de tecnologia. Com a expansão dos data centers, a procura por turbinas e geradores a gás aumentou, e os prazos de fabricação de novos equipamentos passaram a se estender por anos. Em vez de depender exclusivamente de concessionárias e fornecedores especializados, companhias de inteligência artificial começaram a investir diretamente na infraestrutura necessária para manter suas operações. A OnePWR havia encomendado os geradores à Caterpillar dois anos antes, mas precisava de financiamento para concluir a compra. Inicialmente, a Anthropic pretendia contratar a empresa como fornecedora, mas decidiu assumir diretamente os pedidos, segundo uma pessoa familiarizada com a negociação ouvida pelo FT. Com isso, a desenvolvedora do Claude garantiu acesso a equipamentos encomendados antes da alta dos preços, com entregas previstas para o curto prazo e os próximos dois anos. A Anthropic não comprou a OnePWR. O acordo incluiu serviços de engenharia e construção necessários para instalar os geradores, sem transferência de funcionários da fornecedora. As empresas não comentaram a transação. A disputa por equipamentos de energia também levou outras gigantes da tecnologia a ampliar seus investimentos no setor. A xAI, empresa de Elon Musk controlada pela SpaceX, comprou turbinas móveis a gás por US$ 2 bilhões neste ano. Já a Alphabet, controladora do Google, adquiriu a desenvolvedora de energia Intersect no fim de 2025. O investimento em geradores ocorre enquanto a Anthropic amplia seus compromissos financeiros para sustentar a expansão da inteligência artificial. A empresa informou que possui quase US$ 900 bilhões em compromissos de capacidade computacional até 2045. Até então, vinha recorrendo principalmente a parceiros para garantir acesso a chips, terrenos, data centers e eletricidade. A companhia também se prepara para uma possível abertura de capital ainda em novembro, em uma operação que pode estar entre as maiores da história, segundo o Financial Times. Os planos de expansão, porém, enfrentam desafios financeiros. A Blackstone alertou investidores de que pode receber uma classificação de crédito especulativa, inferior ao grau de investimento anteriormente esperado. Glossário O que é geradores a gás? Equipamentos que geram energia elétrica a partir de combustível a gás, usados para fornecer energia a data centers e outras instalações. O que é OnePWR Solutions? Empresa americana que forneceu geradores a gás à Anthropic como parte de um acordo de US$ 3,4 bilhões para garantir energia aos data centers de IA. O que é data centers? Instalações que abrigam servidores e equipamentos de computação, essenciais para operar serviços de IA e nuvem. O que significa turbinas móveis a gás? artigo.texto: Energy storage is expanding across Europe, but its growth remains constrained by obstacles that extend beyond technology. This is the conclusion of Energy Storage Deployment in the EU: Drivers, Barriers and Policy Pathways, published by the Joint Research Centre (JRC), the European Commission’s science and knowledge service. The analysis identifies grid connection delays as the most widespread barrier, while regulatory uncertainty and unpredictable revenues limit projects’ ability to secure financing. The report combines market data, policy analysis and a stakeholder consultation that received 19 responses. The JRC treats these contributions as qualitative evidence rather than a statistically representative sample. Grid connections remain the main bottleneck Insufficient capacity at targeted connection points and lengthy procedures for securing connection agreements are delaying new installations. In the report’s stakeholder consultation, insufficient grid capacity received an average severity rating of 4.1 out of 5, followed by long lead times for connection agreements, at 3.9 out of 5. The study also highlights how applications for projects that fail to progress, or reserve several potential locations, can block capacity for developments that are ready to proceed. Measures examined include prioritising projects that demonstrate maturity, improving transparency on available grid capacity and simplifying administrative procedures. Flexible connection agreements offer another route to earlier grid access. However, they may impose temporary network access restrictions that developers must account for in their business models. Predictable revenues are critical to financing The JRC warns that projects relying exclusively on market revenues still face difficulties attracting financing in many countries. Price volatility and uncertainty over future income make it harder for lenders to assess projects’ ability to repay debt. There is also a risk that the entry of additional batteries and other flexible resources will erode some revenue opportunities, particularly in markets vulnerable to saturation. The report identifies long-term contracts, capacity and flexibility remuneration mechanisms, and agreements combining renewable generation with storage as ways to improve revenue predictability. It also examines tolling agreements, under which a counterparty pays an agreed fee for commercial use of a storage facility. These arrangements can support financing, although they transfer part of the risk to the counterparty and require an assessment of its creditworthiness. Regulation still limits the value storage can capture Fragmentation across national markets represents another obstacle. The report highlights double charging when storage withdraws electricity from and injects it into the grid, high network tariffs and incomplete rules for participation in certain markets. It also finds that some services storage can provide, such as relieving local grid congestion, do not always receive adequate remuneration. The JRC therefore argues that policies should reward measurable contributions to the electricity system—including duration, availability and security of supply—while maintaining technology neutrality. Co-location with renewables creates opportunities The report highlights the potential of installing batteries alongside solar or wind farms. These configurations can share infrastructure, capture electricity that might otherwise be curtailed and shift delivery to higher-value hours. Power purchase agreements combining renewable generation and storage can provide an electricity supply profile better aligned with buyers’ requirements. However, securing financing requires clear contractual provisions on revenue allocation, operational responsibilities and risk sharing. Modelling points to 172 GW of EU storage needs by 2030 The report cites PRIMES modelling results that put the European Union’s power sector storage requirements at 172 GW by 2030, combining batteries and pumped hydropower. For 2040, projected requirements range from 213 GW to 275 GW, depending on the scenario. These figures represent modelled system requirements, rather than a specific binding storage deployment target. The JRC concludes that accelerating deployment requires action on permitting, grid connections, market rules and revenue stability. Falling technology costs support growth, but converting that potential into operating projects also depends on a framework that enables developers to finance and connect their assets.

artigo.texto: Turkey approves more than 33 GW of energy storage projects — Deutsche Welle Turkey, which is hosting the UN climate summit COP31 in Antalya, has approved more than 33 GW of battery energy storage projects since 2022. According to Deutsche Welle, these capacities could supply electricity to more than 27 million households. Storage systems are intended to complement the rapid growth of wind and solar generation. These sources currently provide 22% of Turkey's electricity, compared with 4.5% ten years ago. Solar energy's share of the country's installed power generation capacity grew from about 0.1% in 2014 to nearly 21% at the beginning of 2026. Dependence on coal At the same time, coal-fired electricity generation in Turkey has increased by about one-third over the past decade. In 2024, the country surpassed Germany and Poland in coal generation capacity; these countries had previously had the largest such capacities in Europe, but they have begun to decline. Turkey has still not set a date for a complete phaseout of coal. According to the German climate campaign Beyond Fossil Fuels, about 97% of new coal projects in the country have been cancelled over the past ten years. However, in June, Turkish authorities announced plans to expand one of the largest coal-fired power plants and nearly double its capacity. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. The Climate Action Tracker think tank notes that Turkey's current climate target allows emissions to increase until 2038. In the organization's view, this complicates the country's achievement of its carbon neutrality target by 2053. Electrification and fuel imports According to Efe Baysal, head of the Turkish team of the environmental network 350.org, Turkey imports 95% of its natural gas, 83% of its crude oil, and 60% of its coal. In September, the country launched the global “35x35” initiative, which envisages increasing the level of electrification of the world's economies from just over 20% to 35% by 2035. The initiative includes replacing fossil fuels with electricity in transport, buildings, and industry. At the same time, according to Climate Action Tracker's assessment, Turkey's national energy plan provides for the electrification of only about 25% of total energy consumption by 2035.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de ventiladores de resfriamento: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de ventiladores de resfriamento até 2035: demanda por refrigeração de data centers impulsiona expansão Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de ventiladores de resfriamento, o setor inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de ventiladores de resfriamento é um componente crítico do ecossistema mais amplo de gestão térmica, sustentando a integridade operacional e a eficiência de uma vasta gama de tecnologias industriais, comerciais e de consumo. No período de análise de 2026, o mercado se caracteriza por demanda robusta, impulsionada pelo crescimento contínuo do processamento de dados, da eletrificação e da manufatura avançada, embora enfrente pressões simultâneas decorrentes da reconfiguração das cadeias de suprimento e da volatilidade dos custos de matérias-primas. A transição para projetos de ventiladores mais eficientes em energia, inteligentes e específicos para cada aplicação está remodelando a dinâmica competitiva e favorecendo empresas com forte capacidade de P&D e cadeias de suprimento verticalmente integradas. Este relatório traz uma avaliação abrangente do estado atual do mercado, das principais forças de oferta e demanda, dos fluxos comerciais e dos mecanismos de formação de preços, culminando em uma previsão estratégica até 2035 que delineia os caminhos de crescimento e os desafios a serem enfrentados. A evolução do mercado está indissociavelmente ligada a megatendências globais, como digitalização, exigências de sustentabilidade e automação industrial. Essas forças não apenas ampliam o mercado endereçável, como também ditam uma mudança nas especificações dos produtos em direção a maior desempenho, menor ruído acústico e maior conectividade. O cenário competitivo está se fragmentando, e líderes consolidados em segmentos industriais amplos enfrentam concorrência intensificada de fabricantes especializados que atendem nichos de alto crescimento, como veículos elétricos e infraestrutura de energia renovável. Compreender a interação entre esses fatores tecnológicos, econômicos e geopolíticos é essencial para os agentes que buscam aproveitar oportunidades emergentes e mitigar riscos inerentes. Esta análise sintetiza dados proprietários, estatísticas comerciais e inteligência setorial para construir um retrato detalhado do mercado mundial de ventiladores de resfriamento. O horizonte de previsão até 2035 é estruturado a partir da análise da trajetória das principais indústrias de uso final, dos desdobramentos regulatórios e dos ciclos de inovação tecnológica. As implicações para fabricantes, fornecedores e investidores são profundas e exigem uma estratégia nuançada, que equilibre escala e especialização, gestão de custos e investimento em inovação, alcance global e proximidade com os mercados regionais. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de ventiladores de resfriamento até 2035 prevê expansão sustentada, apoiada pela demanda estrutural da infraestrutura de data centers, da modernização de sistemas HVAC e da automação industrial. O índice de mercado deve alcançar 142 em 2035 (2025=100), o que corresponde a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de aproximadamente 3,6% no período de previsão. Essa perspectiva pressupõe ausência de recessão global relevante, continuidade dos investimentos de capital em infraestrutura de nuvem e inteligência artificial e endurecimento gradual das normas de eficiência energética nas principais economias. Espera-se que a demanda por refrigeração de data centers seja o maior contribuinte individual para o crescimento incremental, à medida que operadores de hiperescala e de colocation ampliam a capacidade para atender cargas de IA, o que exige sistemas de ventiladores de alto fluxo de ar e alta eficiência. Os sistemas HVAC seguirão como o maior segmento em volume, com a demanda de reposição e as atualizações impulsionadas por normas para ventiladores de velocidade variável e baixo ruído sustentando o crescimento em valor. A demanda por ventilação industrial acompanhará a produção manufatureira e a atividade de mineração, com mercados emergentes na Ásia-Pacífico e na América Latina oferecendo potencial de alta. O resfriamento automotivo se beneficiará da eletrificação, já que a gestão térmica das baterias exige módulos adicionais de ventiladores, embora o crescimento da produção de veículos de passeio possa ser modesto. O resfriamento de eletrônicos de consumo terá demanda estável, puxada por dispositivos portáteis e hardware para jogos, enquanto equipamentos médicos e telecomunicações oferecem nichos menores, porém de alto valor. Do lado da oferta, a volatilidade dos custos de matérias-primas, especialmente cobre e aços especiais, segue como risco relevante, ao lado de interrupções logísticas e da incerteza na política comercial. Espera-se uma consolidação moderada do cenário competitivo, com os principais fabricantes investindo em tecnologias de ventiladores inteligentes que incorporam sensores integrados e conectividade IoT. No geral, a perspectiva-base é positiva, mas atenuada pela ciclicidade dos mercados industriais de uso final e pela pressão persistente sobre as margens nas negociações de preços com montadoras. artigo.texto: 9 de novembro de 2026, às 16:22 A TIM fechou um contrato com a BYD para fornecer internet a toda a frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil, além do seu polo industrial. Com a parceria, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades onde a operadora oferece cobertura. A previsão é de que cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa contem com essa conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. Assim, a BYD busca avançar no desenvolvimento de novas funcionalidades que envolvam serviços conectados. Com o crescimento de serviços como inteligência artificial e uso de funções como mapas e streaming a bordo, um carro já tem consumo de dados quase equiparável a de um plano básico pós-pago, tipo ‘controle’. Do lado da TIM, o negócio representa uma expansão no setor automotivo, onde já oferece conexão para cerca de 630 mil veículos. A tele italiana possui uma parceria com a antiga Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA) – hoje parte do grupo Stellantis – para fornecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em veículos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram no Brasil. O contrato entre a TIM e a BYD envolve também a implantação de infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da montadora em Camaçari, na Bahia. Essa é a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina, com 4,6 milhões de m². O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, garantindo uma rede preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e as demandas tecnológicas do complexo. artigo.texto: Scaling Power Electronics from Residential to Utility-Scale Energy Storage The article examines how power-conversion architecture, semiconductor selection, thermal management, protection, control, and grid integration must evolve as battery energy storage systems scale from residential installations to utility-scale plants. It focuses on the engineering implications of increasing power, voltage, current, and system complexity. November 09, 2026. By News Bureau Scaling a battery energy storage system (BESS) involves far more than increasing the power conversion system rating. It requires a coordinated evolution in electrical architecture, semiconductor topology, thermal management, protection, controls, and grid interconnection capability. BESS Application Segments BESS applications can broadly be classified into three segments: Each segment is characterised by distinct economic drivers, operating profiles, duty cycles, system requirements, technical constraints and control objectives. Electrical Architecture Residential: Integrated Solution The battery, converter and protection functions are integrated into a single enclosure. The primary objectives are compactness, safety, efficient power conversion, plug-and-play installation, low maintenance, uninterrupted power supply and a service life of 10–15 years. For example, Hoymiles HIS series converters along with LB series battery packs provide an integrated solution that simplifies installation and supports reliable long-term operation. C&I: Modular Architecture Power and energy are distributed across battery racks and multiple PCS units. Each section can be monitored, protected and maintained independently, while supervisory controls coordinate overall operation. Utility: High Power Subsystem At the multi-megawatt level, the PCS contains semiconductors, DC link capacitors, busbar, cooling, protection, sensors and control subsystems. Multiple PCS blocks share a medium voltage network and are coordinated through a BESS controller and power plant controller (PPC). The plant, rather than an individual PCS, becomes the controlled electrical resource. Power Conversion Topologies Residential: Integrated Converter Residential topologies use a two-stage conversion scheme: an isolated bidirectional DC-DC converter (e.g., dual active bridge) matching wide battery swing to a regulated high-voltage DC bus, feeding a single-phase full-bridge inverter. Moderate power throughput allows compact integration of passive LCL filter inductors and planar magnetics. C&I: Modular Converters Scaling to hundreds of kilowatts relies on paralleled three-phase two-level or three-level bridges. Paralleling requires active carrier interleaving to suppress AC ripple, common mode filtering to block zero-sequence circulating currents, and dynamic active/reactive current sharing loops. For example, the Hoymiles HESS-261 series supports modular design that allows multiple units to be connected in parallel to meet custom energy needs and easily scale up for future expansion. Utility: Multilevel High Current Topologies Utility PCS designs utilise three-level Neutral Point Clamped (NPC), Active NPC (ANPC), or T-type topologies. These lower the device dV/dt stress, reduce switching losses and shrink output LCL filter footprints. However, they demand active neutral point balancing algorithms, ultra-low stray inductance busbars and gate drives with multi-stage desaturation protection. DC Voltage and Current The selected DC link operating voltage influences the entire electromechanical stack, including switch conduction losses, conductor copper volume, creepage and clearance distances and switchgear arc extinction capability. Residential Traditional 48 V systems prioritise touch safety and simple pack balancing, but require heavy conductors. Higher voltage strings (200–500 V DC) drastically reduce I²R conduction losses and cabling weight, requiring integrated DC Arc Fault Circuit Interrupters (AFCI) and rapid shutdown. C&I Operating in the 100 kW to 1 MW range at lower voltages causes severe current penalties. Standardising on 800–1,000 V DC reduces cable size, cuts inverter conduction losses, and boosts round-trip efficiency (RTE). Utility Standard 1,500 V DC platforms maximise container energy density and minimise cabling over large field layouts. However, prospective short-circuit currents exceed 50–100 kA, creating high arc-flash energy and strict insulation requirements (As per IEC 62477-1). Fast-acting DC fuses or high-speed hybrid DC breakers are essential to clear non-zero-crossing faults. Semiconductor Technology Semiconductor selection balances switching losses, conduction losses, thermal impedance, switching frequency, and passive filter dimensions. Residential Operates at higher switching frequencies for silent operation and reduced filter size. Low-voltage topologies employ low R_DS(on) Si MOSFETs, whereas high-voltage strings use 650 V / 1,200 V SiC MOSFETs to reach peak efficiencies above 99 percent. C&I Operates between 4 kHz and 12 kHz. Converters use 1,200 V IGBT modules or hybrid configurations like Si IGBTs with SiC Schottky diodes to suppress diode reverse recovery losses affordably. Utility Operates between 1.5 kHz and 3.5 kHz to manage thermal dissipation. Power stages deploy high-power dual/half bridge modules. In three-level ANPC designs, hybrid configurations place fast SiC MOSFETs in high-frequency switching positions and low-V_CE(sat) Si IGBTs in 50/60 Hz line unfolding positions, maximising efficiency across wide power factor ranges. Hoymiles HPCS series string PCS comes with SiC technology, which offers higher efficiency. Thermal Management Thermal management becomes progressively more critical as BESS power increases. The fundamental requirement remains the same at every level. The heat generated by the battery and power electronics must be removed while maintaining the components within their allowable operating temperature range. Residential Residen
