artigo.texto: Data centers become a political flashpoint after midterms, putting AI industry on notice HOBART, Ind. - The message from voters was hard for the data center industry to ignore: communities want a say in what gets built in their backyards — and they're increasingly demanding answers before those projects move forward. Data center debate The backstory: President Donald Trump has been one of the biggest supporters of the data center boom, arguing these facilities will bring jobs, investment and economic prosperity to communities across the country. On August 31, in a post on Truth Social, Trump said in part, "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want data centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let data reign." "You have to convince your community how great these things," said Trump. "You can't fight it. You have to go with it. And you're going to make a tremendous amount of money. You're going to reduce taxes." But that message hasn't necessarily resonated with residents who are worried about the potential consequences of these massive developments. And those concerns became a political talking point during the midterm elections. The Associated Press reports Democrats who campaigned on tighter restrictions on data centers made significant gains in several key gubernatorial races, including Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa. In fact, 32 of the 34 winning gubernatorial candidates in races where AP called a winner supported stronger regulations or restrictions on data centers. Twelve supported outright bans or moratoriums. At the local level, the opposition was even more pronounced. An analysis by Redbud Consulting found voters approved restrictions in 44 of 45 completed local data center referendum elections across the country. And the opposition wasn't confined to one political party or one part of the country. The AP Voter Poll found roughly three-quarters of Americans opposed building a new data center in their community. For Wannie Park, founder and CEO of Pado AI, an energy orchestration software company that works with data centers, this backlash has been building for some time. "I think the dynamics of growth sometimes, which is what we're kind of going through, is oftentimes full brute force without thoughtfulness and good planning," said Park. "And I think with that, what you have is sort of what we have now, which is the backlash, right? Moratoriums and just people saying like, 'hey, let's take a breath here and figure out what's the right way to deploy this stuff.'" Park says the issue has become increasingly bipartisan, as residents question whether the economic benefits promised by developers are actually materializing. "People are saying, well, like, 'hey, I'm not getting what I thought I was getting' or ‘the economic development is not there’ or 'you're using up and polluting all our water' or ‘my rates are going up.’ Like all those types of things started to trickle in," said Park. Hobart meetings on data centers In northwest Indiana, Fox Chicago has reported increasingly heated public meetings in Hobart over proposed data center developments, with some residents even being removed after voicing their opposition. And the concerns being raised locally mirror what is happening across the country. On Fox News, Compass Data Centers CEO Chris Crosby acknowledged that not every developer has done a good job addressing those concerns. "I think it's fair. Their questions are real. Not everybody who develops and owns data centers does a good job of it. And, you know, there is a bar that needs to be raised," said Crosby. He says developers need to be more transparent, pay their own way when it comes to electricity and provide tangible benefits to the communities where they operate. Park agrees the industry needs a different approach. And he takes issue with the idea that opposing data center development means someone doesn't understand the importance of artificial intelligence. "I think that's just the wrong position, right?" Park argues the industry has been operating inefficiently, with opportunities to get more out of existing facilities rather than simply building more. He says older data centers could be repurposed, potentially reducing the need for some of the massive new construction projects being proposed. And he pushes back against the argument that slowing development automatically means America will fall behind China in the AI race. "I don't think it's that dire. Sometimes the industry kind of speaks to it like it's a binary. We have to build, build, or we're going to fall behind China or whatever. We're not going to lead. It's not that dire," said Park. What's next: Instead, Park says the next phase should focus on making better use of existing infrastructure and proving that these projects produce meaningful benefits. He also believes the political backlash is already affecting the industry's bottom line, with stricter regulations and uncertainty making investors and lenders more cautious about financing new developments. The Source: The information in this report came from statements by President Donald Trump, reporting and polling by The Associated Press, an analysis by Redbud Consulting, interviews with Pado AI CEO Wannie Park and Compass Data Centers CEO Chris Crosby, and previous FOX Chicago reporting on data center developments in Hobart, Indiana.

artigo.texto: A world leader in the provision of battery manufacturing assembly equipment, Gloucester-headquartered TBS Engineering plays a crucial role in keeping the vehicles and infrastructure used by millions of people up-and-running, right across the globe. SoGlos looks at five of its biggest customers and the products they power, from high-end cars like Porche, Bentley and Jaguar, to everyday essential infrastructure, like rail signals and telecoms. Exide With roots going all the way back to the 19th century, Exide is a US-founded company steeped in history, having made batteries used to launch torpedoes in World War Two, and by NASA to land on the moon in the 1960s. Now split from its former North American operations, the company supplies batteries for the automotive and energy sectors, operating from facilities across Europe and Asia Pacific as Exide Technologies. Bringing in annual revenue of around €1.6 billion, it supplies world-leading vehicle manufacturers from Citroen, Volkswagen and Mini, to Alfa Romeo, BMW and Jaguar, powered by TBS Engineering's state-of-the-art battery manufacturing assembly equipment. Clarios Clarios is a global giant in the automotive battery manufacturing sector, serving 1.5 million customers across more than 100 countries – and boasting the claim that one in three vehicles worldwide are powered by a Clarios battery. Bringing in $10.6 billion in annual revenue, a long list of renowned vehicle manufacturers use Clarios batteries, from Nissan, Renault and Skoda, to Porche, Bentley and Mercedes Benz. TBS Engineering has built up a strong partnership with Clarios, providing critical battery manufacturing assembly equipment that has accelerated capacity expansion for the company globally – a valued collaboration that was recognised with an award at the Clarios Supplier Summit in 2026. Enerya Served by TBS from its Mexico office, Enerya is dedicated to the manufacture of electrical batteries for the vehicle industry. Based in Nuevo León in Mexico, it's a leading North American brand, manufacturing batteries that power everything from passenger cars and commercial trucks, to motorcycles and marine vessels. TBS established its Mexico office in Monterrey in 2024, in order to provide its customers in the region with aftermarket spare parts, technical support, service, account management and streamlined logistics. East Penn A private, family-owned business operating the largest single-site lead battery manufacturing facility in the world, Pennsylvania company East Penn serves the North America and Asia Pacific markets. Making batteries for all types of vehicles, from cars and trucks, to boats, along with reserve power for things like rail signals and telecommunications, the company boasts annual revenue of around $3 billion. East Penn and TBS have a long-standing relationship which goes back to 1987, with Robert Flicker, COO of East Penn, saying of working with the Gloucester company: 'Their commitment to customer satisfaction and their willingness to work with their customers to provide the state-of-the-art equipment with high-level quality and standards makes them a great partner to satisfy our equipment needs.' Amara Raja Indian company Amara Raja Energy & Mobility manufactures a range of batteries for the automotive and industrial sectors, bringing in annual revenue of more than £1 billion. The company is the largest automotive battery manufacturer in India, supplying major auto manufacturers like Ford, Suzuki and more, while it also makes industrial batteries for sectors including telecoms, railways and defence. This year, TBS Engineering opens its TBS India office in Pune, Maharashtra, where it will provide aftermarket and technical support services for its clients in the region. To find out more about TBS Engineering, its global operations, and the equipment and services it provides for its customers, visit tbseng.co.uk.

artigo.texto: Frontier Institute announces lawsuit against Missoula’s data center zoning ordinance MISSOULA, Mont. — On Nov. 9, Frontier Institute announced attorneys from Arizona’s Goldwater Institute will represent CubCloud AI in a lawsuit regarding Missoula’s zoning regulations after the city passed an ordinance in October that would change the way it zones for data centers. “There’s a lot of things we should be requiring of data centers, I just don’t believe that what we’re doing should be in the same category of a multibillion-dollar facility,” Joshua Rhines, founder and CEO of CubCloud AI, said. The ordinance adopted by Missoula simply changed what is defined by a data center in regard to zoning. “It currently reads as a facility or portion of a facility housing network computer systems, servers and appliances and telecommunications equipment. It goes on. I simply would like to or propose that it read and slash or telecommunications,” Justin Ponton, the ward 2 city council member, said when he proposed the amendment back in October. The ordinance passed unanimously, and the addition of that one word may place protections on high-scale data centers. But, according to the lawsuit, it violates Montana’s Right to Compute Act and jeopardizes small tech businesses and their ability to grow in Montana. “Lawmakers go about regulating for data centers they need to make sure that they’re being thoughtful in the way they go about it. They can’t just enact sweeping bans on an entire category of technology without potentially sweeping in the little guys and these local small businesses like CubCloud who are real assets to our community,” Kendall Cotton, CEO and president of Frontier Institute, said. CubCloud AI is a local Missoula tech company founded on the belief that Montana had a need for local AI infrastructure and provides local organizations looking to implement AI an alternative to large-scale data centers like Microsoft or Meta. “You know it was never going to be like a hyperscale data center that would be 20 megawatts like Bonner or 100 megawatts or any of that it always planned to be like 2 or 3, you know obviously those plans are off the table right now you until we figure out what’s going on with ordinance here,” Rhines said. The city is aware of the lawsuit and issued this statement to NBC Montana regarding its current stance. It reads: “The city is aware of the lawsuit filed by CubCloud, however it has not been served the lawsuit as of the present moment. The city is aware of the Right to Compute Act. It is the city’s position that the Right to Compute Act does not give data center companies the right to locate wherever they please. The city plans to vigorously defend the City Council decision in this case. However, the city will not comment on the specifics of this case pending litigation.” CubCloud AI is not seeking a monetary settlement and simply is looking to work with the city to revise the current ordinance. “Our hope is we can have a productive dialogue and hopefully come out with an ordinance that addresses small business interest and saves the city from getting a Trojan horse situation which I think is probably why they passed the ordinance and their main fear,” Rhines said.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: (VCG/VCG/Getty Images) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 9 de novembro de 2026 às 10h01. A ByteDance, dona do TikTok, planeja expandir suas operações de data centers no Brasil. O primeiro complexo está em construção no Ceará, com investimentos bilionários, enquanto negociações avançam para uma segunda instalação voltada ao mercado brasileiro. O projeto enfrenta questionamentos jurídicos sobre licenciamento ambiental e consulta indígena. Com seu primeiro data center na América Latina ainda em construção, a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, já procura uma empresa para desenvolver a segunda fase do complexo no Pecém, no Ceará. Em paralelo, o grupo chinês abriu conversas preliminares sobre outra instalação, fora do complexo portuário, que atenderia clientes no Brasil, segundo a Bloomberg. A expansão no Pecém pode superar em porte a obra atual, estimada em US$ 10 bilhões e que terá demanda elétrica de cerca de 300 megawatts (MW). A segunda fase segue em avaliação, e o projeto voltado ao mercado brasileiro está em estágio inicial. As obras da primeira etapa começaram em janeiro de 2026. A Omnia, plataforma de data centers do Pátria Investimentos, desenvolve o projeto para a ByteDance em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos. A previsão informada pela Omnia à Reuters é iniciar a operação no terceiro trimestre de 2027 e ampliar as atividades gradualmente até 2029. O projeto original do Pecém foi anunciado em dezembro de 2025 com investimento estimado em cerca de R$ 200 bilhões para o complexo completo, previsto em fases. Na etapa em obras, os servidores terão 200 MW de capacidade de tecnologia da informação. A demanda elétrica total, próxima de 300 MW, inclui os sistemas que mantêm os equipamentos em funcionamento, como a refrigeração. A energia é uma parte do negócio que já tem contrato. Em maio, Omnia e Casa dos Ventos acertaram um fornecimento de 20 anos, avaliado em cerca de US$ 2 bilhões. A maior parte virá do complexo eólico Ibiapaba, no Ceará, com uma parcela menor de um parque no Piauí, segundo as empresas. Perto do Pecém, os cabos submarinos que chegam a Fortaleza dão ao estado conexões de fibra óptica com os Estados Unidos, a Europa e a África. O empreendimento em construção fica na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Pecém. O conselho federal que administra o regime aprovou o projeto da ByteDance para prestação de serviços exclusivamente ao mercado externo. Na prática, os servidores ficam no Ceará e processam dados para operações em outros países. Já a instalação em discussão fora do Pecém teria como destino o mercado brasileiro, segundo a Bloomberg. As conversas ocorrem enquanto o governo prepara as regras do Redata, regime federal sancionado em setembro que prevê incentivos tributários para equipamentos de data centers. Entre as contrapartidas previstas na lei estão critérios de eficiência hídrica e a oferta de pelo menos 10% da capacidade beneficiada ao mercado interno, compromisso que pode ser substituído por investimento adicional em pesquisa e inovação. Na sexta-feira, 6, a ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, disse que o governo espera anunciar a regulamentação na semana de 16 de novembro. Em setembro, o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União entraram com uma ação civil pública para impedir o início da operação antes de uma consulta livre, prévia e informada ao povo indígena Anacé e da elaboração de um estudo de impacto ambiental. Os órgãos também pedem que sejam avaliados os efeitos do empreendimento sobre a água, a rede elétrica e as comunidades do entorno. Em resposta à agência eixos, a Omnia afirmou que o licenciamento segue o rito da Superintendência Estadual do Meio Ambiente do Ceará (Semace) e que possui as autorizações válidas para as atividades que exerce. No início de novembro, o Fórum Nacional pela Democratização da Comunicação divulgou as conclusões de uma missão dos conselhos nacional e estadual de direitos humanos que recomendou a revisão do licenciamento e a consulta às comunidades afetadas.

artigo.texto: Ex-employee sues OnderLaw, claims assault, online campaign for Ferguson data center ST. LOUIS, Mo. (First Alert 4) -An ex-employee of OnderLaw is suing the law firm, claiming harassment and an online campaign to sway public perception of a proposed data center in Ferguson. The lawsuit, filed on Thursday, was filed by an ex-employee referred to in court documents as Jane Doe. The lawsuit names the defendants as OnderLaw and James ‘Jim’ Onder. Onder’s lawyer told First Alert 4 he is declining to comment for the story. First Alert 4 has also reached out to OnderLaw for comment. As of publication time, we have not heard back. Court records show Onder’s lawyer had filed to have the case sealed by the court. In a Friday ruling, Judge Heather Cunningham denied the request. The 30-page lawsuit alleges a series of sexually inappropriate actions taken by Onder against Doe, along with allegations he pressured her to participate in a campaign against Ferguson and its city council regarding a vote against his proposed data center. The lawsuit alleges OnderLaw discriminated against Doe after she exercised her workers’ compensation rights and that the company violated Missouri’s whistleblower protection act. Against Onder himself, Doe alleges assault and battery The Ferguson Project On May 4, Ferguson’s City Council rejected tax breaks for Onder’s proposed data center at the former Emerson campus. The project would have received $1.5 billion in tax breaks over the 15 years of the agreement. After the rejection by the City Council, Doe claims that Onder ordered her to create a negative campaign about the city and residents. Onder told Doe the campaign would be pushed through Meta to residents in Ferguson; the content would appear as real news stories and paint the city as overrun with crime, the lawsuit states. The lawsuit says that Onder told Doe this would get him back to the approval process through a loophole and his relationships with officials and leaders at the Port Authority. Days after the rejection, on May 7, Doe was in a closed-door meeting with Onder, a St. Louis County official and a crisis public relations consultant. In this meeting, Doe alleged Onder again detailed his campaign plan. During the meeting, Onder said he wanted to instill fear about safety in Ferguson with exaggerated stories, making the data center “the only way out for these people,” documents state. While planning the campaign, Doe claims that Onder mocked Black people. Doe said during one meeting, while discussing what graphics to use during a Ferguson town hall, Onder said: “They [Black people] can’t read, so it doesn’t matter.” Doe says after the May 7 meeting she told Onder and Lisa Frederick, who served as the Chief Operating Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and President for OnderLaw, she would not work on the Ferguson project. Doe says that Onder persisted and told OnderLaw Director of Special Projects, Don Bertelsmann, to use bots to manufacture comments about Ferguson on social media that would look like they were coming from ordinary people. Doe alleges Onder instructed Bertelsmann to use computers in his home lab to do the botting. Months earlier, in January 2026, Doe alleges she was given a 2025 expense folder by Bertelsmann, showing a charge on his personal credit card for two “labs”; one at his house and another at his father-in-law’s house, according to the lawsuit. Bertelsmann wanted a reimbursement of $8,000 for equipment, software and internet service, the lawsuit states. At the time, Doe alleges that Bertelsmann wouldn’t tell her what the labs were for. Months later, Onder directed Bertelsmann to use his home lab and the computers in it to run bots for the Ferguson campaign. Allegations of violating Missouri lobbying law The lawsuit states that Onder’s goal was to influence Ferguson’s City Council’s decision on the data center’s tax breaks by pushing down real residents with fake accounts. The lawsuit states that Onder’s campaign efforts violated Missouri’s Lobbying Law, which requires every lobbyist to register with the Missouri Ethics Commission and prohibits hiring a person not registered as a lobbyist by the state. According to the lawsuit, Onder knew that Bertelsmann was not a registered lobbyist but still hired him. Doe claims she refused to be part of the campaign, as well as her team. She says she reported the campaign to Faith Earley, who was the firm’s new COO. The reports were done in mid-May; Doe says she reported her concerns multiple times after. The suit shows a text message exchange between Onder and Doe, in which Onder says, “So I shouldn’t announce to the World the illegal bribes each one requested to buy their votes?” in reference to the Ferguson City Council. Doe alleges repeated instances of sexually inappropriate behavior Doe claims in the lawsuit that Onder began acting sexually inappropriately toward her shortly after she joined his law firm in early 2025. The first incident happened, she claims, on April 2 of that year. She says Onder had touched her leg and waist after sitting next to her at a business meeting at a local steakhouse. She alleges in the suit she tried to move away from Onder, but couldn’t escape his reach and he continued the contact. A month later, on May 3, she alleges Onder began grabbing at her waist during an afternoon work party at an area hotel. She says Onder kept advancing on her until she was backed up against a wall. The suit alleges Onder had been pulling her so close that “he looked ready to kiss her.” Doe alleges she only got away after another party guest entered the room. The next month, between June 4 and 6, Doe claims she was on a work trip for OnderLaw. During the trip, she says Onder inappropriately touched her during a conference dinner. She claims Onder again inappropriately touched her leg again on the car ride back to their hotel. Doe alleges Onder asked her to go to the bar with him, which she refused. artigo.texto: Building owners are turning to battery energy storage systems to lower energy costs, add resilience against grid disruptions and support decarbonization. Despite momentum, their adoption faces a number of persistent obstacles, said panelists at the Greenbuild conference last month. Nationwide, nearly 58 gigawatt-hours of on-site battery storage capacity was installed in 2025, the largest single year of new battery capacity on record, according to a report by the Urban Land Institute and UL Standards & Engagement, drawing on data from the American Clean Power Association. Looking ahead, the sector is expected to install 500 GWh of battery storage between 2026 and 2032, the report says. Notwithstanding the success of these models, several barriers are keeping the market from growing more quickly, according Jill Maltby-Abbott, senior environmental and sustainability standards engineer at UL Standards & Engagement, a panelist who contributed to the ULI and UL report. Location-specific challenges. Even when a project makes economic sense, it can be stopped by interconnection and permitting woes, unclear approvals, shifting local requirements and unfamiliarity with the technology, according to Maltby-Abbott. Even where interconnection and permitting processes exist, commercial-scale storage projects can take years to deliver, the report said. Long and unpredictable timelines can cause projects to accumulate soft costs — like time and money spent on community engagement or engineering fees — and be exposed to changing market conditions, incentive structures and regulatory requirements, adding to the financial risk of implementation, per the report. Risk thresholds. Another key consideration is how municipalities view the risk and governance of these assets, Maltby-Abbott said. “How are [municipalities] defining the [risk] thresholds that they’ll accept? It’s very much on a per-project, per-owner basis, and this is a challenge that a lot of people experience with multiple emerging technologies.” Concern over risk can lead to delays as local officials put up hurdles, Dean Apostoleris, practice leader of renewable energy development at Kimley-Horn, said at the conference. “What we see as a really big barrier in terms of penetration into new markets and, even in some situations, mature markets is resistance from the regulatory, zoning, land use and siting perspective of these batteries,” he said. Even in really population-dense markets, where storage development has been a priority for quite some time, there has only been increased adoption of on-site battery energy storage in the past five or so years, according to Apostoleris. “That issue stems from a lack of education and lack of knowledge about what battery energy storage really is,” he said. For example, New York state has established a mandate to procure 6 GW of battery energy storage by 2030, with Illinois and Massachusetts setting targets of 3 GW and 5,000 MW as well, respectively. But with those targets close to just three years away, New York only has 415 MW of battery storage installed, or 7% of its target, as of the presentation, Aposoleris said. State mandates aim to spur battery adoption but development "comes down to the local and community level,” Apostoleris said. “And a lot of these communities have not yet had the bandwidth, the knowledge or the education to implement some of these regulations.” “As a result, when you actually go to permit and construct BESS, ultimately the reviews and approvals are … preventing a lot of that mandate and that goal from being achieved,” he said. Fire risk. Of all the risks, fire is one of the first localities worry about, said Kara Kokernak, senior director of the ULI Lewis Center for Sustainability in Real Estate. “That is something that became very apparent” when conducting research for the report, she said. “That was tagged in most of our conversations, but having fire safety teams part of that education can help ease those concerns.” Because of this pushback, Apostoleris said, it can be much easier to implement these projects in jurisdictions that have already established BESS safety requirements and review processes, which provide more prescriptive guidance on how projects will be evaluated. He points to the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board as a good example. It “allows a lot of developers to push through their projects in a very prescriptive manner that reduces some of the risk that often comes with uncertainty of reviews and approvals they might have at the state level,” Apostoleris said. Even when requirements are stringent, this predictability can help project teams incorporate safety considerations earlier while supporting fire department preparedness and confidence in how potential incidents will be avoided or managed, the report says. Community engagement, or lack thereof, can often delay, constrain or stop otherwise viable projects, the report says. For that reason, early engagement, before formal filings, is a “consistent recommendation from those who have successfully navigated community opposition,” the report says. “This gives developers the opportunity to understand specific concerns, explain safety and emergency response approaches, and adjust the project so that community input is reflected in project planning from the start.”

artigo.texto: ZTE Powers High Efficiency AIDC with Robust Energy Infrastructure AI's growth depends on stable, efficient, green energy—the foundation powering every model training run and inference call. November 11, 2026 Sponsored by ZTE As the AI wave surges forward, computing power is reshaping industries at an unprecedented pace. Yet behind every model training run and every inference call, what truly sustains continuous computing output is a stable, efficient, and green energy foundation. As per-rack power consumption climbs from 10–20 kW to 100 kW, 600 kW, and even 1 MW, as air cooling approaches its engineering limits and losses in traditional power supply links become increasingly prominent, the benchmark for AIDC competition is shifting from "computing scale" to "computing efficiency". In this "energy efficiency battle" crucial to the sustainable development of computing power, ZTE is reconstructing the "energy foundation" of AIDC with a systematic approach—ensuring every kilowatt-hour is converted into tokens more efficiently. Computing Power Sprints Ahead, Electricity Becomes a "Scarce Resource" Computing demand is growing explosively, and electricity consumption in computing centers is rising rapidly. The problem goes far beyond total electricity use: traditional data centers typically have a per-rack power consumption of 10–20 kW, while in the AIDC era, high-density deployment of GPU clusters has become the norm. Per-rack loads are quickly exceeding 100 kW, and high-end intelligent computing scenarios can reach 600 kW or even 1 MW. The shortcomings of traditional power supply architectures are now exposed: significant losses occur across the multi-stage conversion chain from transformer to server, resulting in extra annual operating costs. Such architectures can no longer meet the needs of high-density racks, making power supply architecture innovation urgent. Cooling challenges are equally severe: the engineering limit of air cooling is approximately 20–30 kW per rack, beyond which cooling capacity drops sharply. When the heat flux density of GPU clusters far exceeds the boundaries of air cooling, liquid cooling is no longer an "option" but a "mainstream solution"—the core guarantee for high-value computing power to operate stably at full load. The competitive benchmark for AIDC is shifting from "computing scale" to "computing efficiency". The long-term development of AI computing power increasingly depends on the upper limit of energy supply and on the end-to-end conversion efficiency from Energy to Token. This is precisely the core proposition ZTE is addressing. 800V High-Voltage DC System: Tackling Power Loss from the Source ZTE's first answer is the 800V high-voltage DC system, a fundamental innovation in traditional power supply architecture. With an efficient topology design, DC/DC intelligent battery management, diverse application modes, and excellent scalability, it delivers high-density, high-efficiency, green, and reliable DC power supply, solving the core power supply challenges of high-density computing infrastructure. Intelligent management has also achieved a leap forward: it supports one-stop full-link management and full-system visibility and controllability, covering functions such as fault recording, temperature measurement at key locations, and selective protection simulation. Predictive maintenance is carried out across three levels—module faults, system faults, and battery lifespan—making O&M more worry-free. Relying on dual-standard compatibility and modular elastic design, the system can flexibly switch voltage standards (±400V/800V), supporting smooth transition between old and new scenarios. Capacity can be expanded on demand, reducing initial investment pressure. It fully covers centralized large-scale computing bases and distributed edge computing upgrade scenarios, meeting the needs of all types of customers, including operators, internet companies, and professional computing power investors. Megawatt-Level Liquid Cooling CDU: Innovation Breaks Through the "Thermal" Ceiling While efficiency on the power supply side leaps forward, the cooling side also requires capability reconstruction. ZTE has launched a cold plate liquid cooling CDU to achieve optimal cooling costs across the full lifecycle and all-weather cooling safety assurance for equipment rooms. The CDU has a single-unit cooling capacity of 1.5 MW, expandable to 2.4 MW, with flexible configuration of 2–5 CDU cabinets. Auxiliary modules can be selected on demand and upgraded as business grows, greatly reducing initial investment and later retrofit waste. Based on the integration of multiple sensors for flow, pressure, temperature, and more, the 1500 kW liquid cooling CDU achieves precise temperature control of ±0.5°C and pressure control of ±0.05 bar, ensuring stable operation of high-density equipment. It is equipped with health indicators and status visualization for intelligent O&M, and features multiple safety designs such as N+X redundant hot backup and dual power feeds, supporting 7×24-hour uninterrupted operation. The combination of 800V high-voltage DC and the 1500 kW liquid cooling CDU outlines an efficient "inbound" and "outbound" channel for AIDC: the power supply side delivers every kilowatt-hour to the server with minimum loss, while the cooling side expels heat with maximum efficiency, keeping PUE stably within 1.15. Real-world application is the only benchmark for validating technological effectiveness. The Nanjing Binjiang Data Center was among the first to deliver demonstration results from its upgrade and transformation: It implemented a liquid-cooling integrated solution with a power density of up to 60 kW, adopting high-efficiency HVDC power distribution and busway, 32°C air supply, and group control optimization, achieving a PUE of only 1.15. artigo.texto: New power equipment for AI sites is now booked into the 2030s, so developers are paying for anything that already exists. If you're betting on AI capacity arriving on schedule, the secondhand turbine market is where that schedule gets tested. Reuters reported on Monday, November 9, that utilities, developers and data center builders are combing the world for used gas turbines, reviving mothballed machines and converting retired jet engines into power generators. The reason is arithmetic. Global orders for gas turbines are above 100 GW, against annual manufacturing capacity of 60 to 70 GW, and new US units now take about six years on average to arrive, with delivery talks focused on 2030 to 2031. Grid connections are no faster. Reuters put US data center demand at roughly 17 GW this year and said it could triple by 2028, when expected power capacity of 87 GW would still trail the 129 GW the buildout needs. A developer who waits for a new turbine from GE Vernova, Siemens Energy or Mitsubishi Heavy Industries is waiting past the point where the chips it has already ordered will be obsolete. Per Reuters, well-maintained used units go for about $1.5 million to $1.7 million per megawatt, and refurbished ones around $1.3 million. New turbines cost $2 million to $2.5 million per megawatt. Reuters cited one deal as the sharpest example: two 14.5-megawatt turbines from Solar Turbines, a Caterpillar subsidiary, sold for $12.5 million, or about $430,000 per megawatt. A new equivalent would have cost around $35 million and taken five years. That discount is the bargain. The catch is that sellers know it. "That secondary market is very, very hot right now," EthosEnergy chief executive Ana Amicarella told Reuters, adding that the company has also seen "an escalation on the prices of what people are demanding." Darayus Pardivala of Sulzer's US aftermarket business said his team now gets a request "every few weeks" to find a used gas turbine for a data center. Crusoe has canceled its $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 jet-derived turbines from Boom Supersonic, walking back a plan once pitched as a fast workaround for the AI industry's power bottleneck. The move comes weeks after Crusoe raised $3.9 billion at a $30.9 billion valuation and dropped a Wyoming campus, and lands the same week Oracle filed a force... - why Crusoe canceled Boom Superpower turbine order - AI data centers alternative power generation solutions Frankly, a market where brokers get phone calls every few weeks is not a market that can rescue anyone at scale. Reuters itself noted that the secondhand route is unlikely to offset a meaningful share of the delays, since there is little excess supply to buy. Every working turbine that comes up for sale has a line behind it. Jet engines do the rest The more inventive supply comes from aviation. Crusoe, the AI infrastructure firm, ordered 13 aeroderivative turbines from ProEnergy in April, for about 650 MW. Aeroderivatives are built on jet engines from GE Aerospace, and ProEnergy takes used CF6-80C2 cores, the engine family that powered Boeing 747s, and mounts them on trailers as 48-megawatt units, according to Tom's Hardware. The same report said ProEnergy has delivered more than 1 GW of its PE6000 systems to just two data center customers. Wartsila, the Finnish engine maker, has taken a different route around the queue. Reuters said it has booked around 3 GW of orders from US data centers since spring last year for power units that run on gas engines instead of turbines. Siemens Energy has said more than 60% of its US gas turbine orders are now tied to AI data centers, as Tom's Hardware reported. The winners here are the less famous names. EthosEnergy, ReflowX, SVI Bremco, Sulzer and ProEnergy sit in the aftermarket, and none of them needed to build a new factory to benefit. Reuters also named FTAI Power and Boom among the firms trying to turn aircraft-engine know-how into data center power, according to the Runtime Wire summary of the piece. What the scramble says about AI timelines Look at what is being bought. Trailer-mounted jet engines and second-hand industrial turbines are bridge power: loud, less efficient and meant to run until a grid connection shows up. Nobody pays a premium for stopgap equipment unless the buildout schedule is already slipping, and a developer who locks up a used unit early can switch on capacity years ahead of rivals still in the new-equipment queue. That changes how you should read the capex headlines. Spending plans assume sites go live on time. A six-year wait for new turbines says the physical side of the boom is moving slower than the financial side, and that the companies with power in hand, bought used or built from an old airliner engine, are the ones whose timelines are real. artigo.texto: Funttel destina R$ 46,3 milhões ao CPQD para desenvolver tecnologia nacional de data centers Projeto Prisma, do Funttel, terá duração de 36 meses e usará inteligência artificial para distribuir processamento entre data centers. O Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) aprovou na sexta, 6, um investimento de R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma nacional de gerenciamento de data centers e infraestruturas de processamento distribuído. O projeto, denominado Prisma, será executado pelo CPQD, com recursos administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep). A iniciativa prevê o uso de inteligência artificial para definir onde os dados deverão ser processados e distribuir recursos computacionais entre diferentes instalações, incluindo mini data centers localizados em diversas regiões do país. O projeto terá duração de 36 meses, contados a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre o CPQD e a Finep. O comunicado não informa a data prevista para a assinatura do instrumento. A proposta busca desenvolver uma tecnologia nacional capaz de gerenciar ambientes distribuídos de processamento, com aplicações previstas em telecomunicações, saúde, defesa, segurança pública e educação. Inteligência artificial para distribuir processamento O Prisma utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar a infraestrutura mais adequada ao processamento de dados e realizar a distribuição dos recursos computacionais entre diferentes instalações. Uma das frentes do projeto é o uso de mini data centers em arquiteturas de computação de borda (edge computing), nas quais parte do processamento ocorre mais perto dos locais de geração e utilização das informações. Essa arquitetura permite reduzir a distância percorrida pelos dados entre os dispositivos e os centros de processamento, com potencial para diminuir o tempo de resposta de aplicações digitais. Para o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima, o processamento distribuído também permite ampliar o controle sobre as informações mantidas nessas estruturas. “Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”, afirmou. No setor de telecomunicações, a plataforma está prevista entre as soluções que poderão utilizar infraestrutura distribuída de processamento. Eficiência energética e continuidade dos serviços Outro objetivo do Prisma é desenvolver mecanismos para reduzir o consumo de energia e o impacto ambiental dos data centers. A proposta contempla o gerenciamento de recursos computacionais e soluções de armazenamento de energia elétrica para ampliar a autonomia das instalações em situações de instabilidade no fornecimento. Entre os resultados esperados estão a redução da pegada de carbono, o aumento da resiliência a falhas de energia e a proteção contra ataques cibernéticos. O projeto também prevê mecanismos de governança de informações críticas, observando padrões internacionais de segurança e as diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD). Funttel financiará desenvolvimento tecnológico Os recursos foram aprovados pelo Conselho Gestor do Funttel, fundo vinculado à política de desenvolvimento tecnológico das telecomunicações e cuja atuação envolve o Ministério das Comunicações. A Finep ficará responsável pela gestão financeira dos recursos, enquanto o CPQD executará as atividades de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação previstas no projeto. Segundo a superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, Joana Meirelles, a proposta é disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional para aplicações em diferentes setores. “O objetivo é desenvolver e disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional segura e sustentável para setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações”, afirmou. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, relacionou o investimento à ampliação da capacidade nacional de desenvolvimento tecnológico e à soberania nacional. “Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirma o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho. *Com assessoria de imprensa

artigo.texto: A City-County Council committee voted 11-2 Monday to recommend the full council reject about $113 million in tax breaks for data center developer DC Blox. The company previously won approval to build a two building campus on Indianapolis’ east side. The recommendation is not binding. The full council, which must also approve the tax abatements, is expected to vote in December. More than two dozen people spoke at the meeting in council chambers — nearly all opposed the tax deal. Indy Economic Development CEO Andrea Richter-Garry, whose organization negotiated the deal for the city, told the committee the project would bring in about $58 million to the local community during the abatement period: roughly $28 million in taxes plus the company’s $30 million pledge. DC Blox has not fully committed to building the $1.8 billion data center project at 305 Fintail Drive near Irvington. Asked by Councilor Andy Nielsen whether it would build the first building without the abatements, David Armistead, the company's senior vice president of sales, said it has no full tenant commitments on that building and none on the second, citing a court challenge to its land use approval. The Atlanta-based company said the project is planned to be built in two phases — a one-story, 70,000-square-foot building expected to be completed within two years, followed by a two-story, 250,000-square-foot building, in the next five years. The development would create hundreds of temporary construction jobs and 21 permanent positions. Data centers have become a major target of Indiana's economic development strategy, but the industry's need for electricity has put it at odds with a separate fight over rising utility costs. Gov. Mike Braun signed a law this year aimed at reining in utility rates, and critics argue large-scale power consumers like data centers make that harder. Members of the council’s Metropolitan and Economic Development Committee considered two abatements: a 10-year, 50% break on real property taxes on land and buildings, and a 10-year, 85% break on personal property taxes on high-tech equipment like servers. The site of the data center is on the border of two districts represented by two members of the City-County Council — Nielsen and Michael-Paul Hart. Nielsen rejected the plan. “The presentation we got is clear as mud,” he said. “It is speculative.” If the project is built as planned, the company said it would still pay about $28 million in property taxes during the abatement period. It also pledges $30 million for east side projects on top of the local taxes, including park and trail upgrades, a fire station and $5.7 million in redevelopment of Washington Square Mall. Councilor Hart, who sponsored the proposals, said the vote is about east side investment, not whether to allow a data center, which the Metropolitan Development Commission already approved. “You see convention centers in Noblesville and in Fishers — all those things are starting to take the people away from Indianapolis because we're not investing in our townships,” he said. “We're going to become a downtown of nothing if we don’t start doing it.” Residents who testified opposed the breaks. Sue Beecher, president of the Irvington Community Council, said the group voted unanimously against any abatements. Others cited concerns over contamination or said the company could afford to build the campus without tax breaks. DC Blox is one of three data centers in the city approved before the Metropolitan Development Commission voted in August to temporarily ban new developments in Marion County through 2027. The other approved centers are Sabey Data Centers’ $4.3 billion project in Decatur Township, which received more than $240 million in tax breaks in September, and Metrobloks’ project in Martindale-Brightwood. DC Blox is also planning to seek state incentives but the application is not yet complete. Eric Weddle is WFYI's education editor. Contact Eric at eweddle@wfyi.org or follow him on X at @ericweddle

artigo.texto: Changan and CATL to collaborate on 1,500 km solid state cells, establish 75 GWh battery lines Chinese automaker Changan has officially announced plans to deepen its partnership with battery giant CATL. The two firms have committed to expanding joint battery production capacity to 75 GWh and collaborating on solid-state batteries (SSBs) and sodium-ion cells. Like its previous statements on its in-house SSBs, Changan made its announcement on an interactive platform owned by the Shenzhen Stock Exchange. The automaker also expressed commitment to prospective industries, including humanoid robots and China’s “low-altitude economy”. More cells with CATL Changan and CATL are not new partners in China’s automotive sector, having established a joint venture (JV), CATL-Changan (时代长安, Times Changan), earlier in 2023. The JV supplies cells to Changan’s in-house NEV brands, including Avatr, Deepal, and Nevo. Libattery.net, a Chinese battery industry outlet, reports that CATL-Changan is on track to reach 50 GWh of battery production capacity, a plan Changan revealed at an investor relations event in May 2025. The announcement means CATL-Changan will receive an additional 25 GWh of capacity and new production lines. The JV plans to establish a 700,000-square-meter facility and invest 5 billion yuan (~750 million USD) in the expansion. According to Changan, the new facility will integrate the “latest generation of CATL battery tech” and supply cells to the automaker’s NEV brands. It’s planned to start operations in 2027 and meet the 25 GWh goal in three years. It will be situated in a high-tech zone between Chongqing City and Sichuan Province. The automaker expects the expansion to bring in annual revenue of 10 billion yuan (~1.5 billion USD), create 2,500 jobs, and generate 300 million yuan (~45 million USD) in tax revenue for the local community. Changan may also see this move as a way to cut costs. ZAKER News, a Chinese automotive outlet, reports that the Chongqing-based automaker is only earning 68 yuan (10 USD) per car, and is under heavy pressure to boost profits. A JV with CATL would give it access to cheap in-house cells, and avoid high acquisition costs for battery packs,which is one of the priciest components in an NEV. More on Changan’s SSBs Changan has joined the race for SSBs in China, announcing its Golden Bell (Jinzhongzhao) cells in November 2023. The automaker says it’s aiming for an energy density of 400 Wh/kg and claims it will be 70% safer than rivals because it uses “AI remote diagnosis technology”. It also claims the new Golden Bell cells will help EVs reach ranges over 1,500 km and says cell degradation won’t be noticeable for at least 600,000 km. Cell life will exceed 5,000 cycles, and Golden Bell packs will support 6C charging, enabling a 30-80% charge in 9 minutes. The automaker has also reiterated its development schedule for the Golden Bell cells, aiming for vehicle road tests in 2026 and ramping up to commercial production in 2027. artigo.texto: Fort Worth leaders receive data center recommendations that could lead to moratorium on development FORT WORTH, Texas - Fort Worth leaders could put a temporary moratorium on data center developments as the city learns how to manage the industry's growing impact. Fort Worth data center moratorium Local perspective: On Tuesday, November 10, the Fort Worth Data Center & Infrastructure Commission, a commission appointed by the Fort Worth City Council in August, delivered recommendations on data center development in the city. The commission gave 19 recommendations in total after studying four areas of data center development: electricity, water use, land use and neighborhood impacts, and economic impacts. Some of the commission's recommendations include: - Requiring closed-loop cooling systems to recirculate water rather than draw in new water - Increase the distance from homes to data centers from 50 feet to 350 feet - Enforce noise regulations on data centers The recommendations could lead to a 90-day moratorium on data center development in the city, something that has been in the works since the committee was created in August. Such a moratorium would allow the city to review the commission's recommendations and decide whether changes are needed to the city's zoning rules and development codes. You can find the commission's full report below. No action was taken on the commission's findings at Tuesday's meeting. What they're saying: Michael Slattery, the chair of the commission, tells FOX 4's Vania Castillo these recommendations would give the city a "roadmap" on how to move forward with data centers. "It would give data center developers much more certainty. It's certainly not going to please everybody, and I think ever does. And I think that I think it starts to put some certainty around how to move this forward," Slattery said. Some residents at Tuesday's city council meeting said the recommendations don't go far enough. "Two months is not enough time to consider all of the issues involved with a data center," resident Julie Waters said. "Today, you have an opportunity to save your seat in the next election. Listen to the cries of your people who have come before you, meeting after meeting, asking for a moratorium. If not for your people, then for then at least to wipe away the stain of corruption on your reputation and legacy." The backstory: Fort Worth leaders have been considering their position on data center development since this past summer. In early July, Fort Worth's zoning commission voted against new restrictions on future data center projects in the city, citing the need for more information on the rapidly-changing industry. Several days later, five Fort Worth City Council members called for a moratorium on data center construction. They say the pause would allow the city to discuss and refine regulations on data centers. That call led to the creation of the committee that gave today's findings. Fort Worth currently has four operating data centers, with at least four more in development. What's next: Fort Worth city staff say the next public hearing is planned for January 12, 2027. The earliest a data center moratorium could be enacted is February 2027. Officials noted that existing sites and projects already moving through the application pipeline would be exempt from the moratorium if the policy is formally adopted next year. The Source: Information in this story comes from a Fort Worth City Council meeting and previous FOX 4 reporting.

artigo.texto: Hazle Township residents press for tougher data center zoning limits on revised ordinance HAZLE TOWNSHIP, LUZERNE CO. (WOLF) — A packed auditorium at Hazleton Area High School Monday night, as Hazle Township residents voiced their concerns over a proposed 40-page zoning ordinance that could determine where data centers are allowed to be built. Township supervisors are considering revisions to the ordinance, including a designated overlay district for data center developments. But the proposal is drawing pushback from residents who say they want a say in how these projects could impact their community. The township recently posted an updated version of its proposed data center ordinance, dated November 5, along with a map showing a proposed area called the Energy and Technology Overlay District. Under the proposal, data centers would be allowed within that designated area without needing a special exception from the zoning hearing board. However, developers would still have to meet township requirements and obtain the necessary approvals. Residents raised concerns and suggested stronger protections, focusing on noise levels, decibel limits, and potential environmental impacts. The proposed data center zoning amendment would allow the residential setback requirement to be reduced to 500 feet. One resident spoke out in favor of increasing the setback requirement to provide greater protection for nearby residents. “The 1,250 feet requirement should be enforced, if this is going to go through. 500 feet is not enough to protect property and or people from the noise, the pollution, and the activities of an active data center area,” said Margaret. Another resident stressed the importance of giving residents a voice before any decisions are made on the amendment. “We believe residents deserve a meaningful opportunity to understand, question, and discuss the proposed regulations,” said Michael Reilly. One resident cited a statistic that 71% of people oppose local AI data centers, questioning why Project Hazelnut is still being considered and referencing a recent debate involving Governor Shapiro. “Governor Shapiro stood up at his debate, and say any community that’s not for this, they will not go through with these data centers. So, I don’t even know why we’re still having this conversation,” said Jane Tadlock. The revised amendment also outlines additional approval requirements for battery storage facilities and sets standards for roads, utilities, fire protection, noise and water systems. Developers would also need to complete necessary infrastructure improvements before buildings could be occupied. The board has until December 7 to finish the amendment process.

artigo.texto: Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB), IOI Corp Bhd and a consortium of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) have partnered to develop a 500 MW solar power project integrated with a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bahau, Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia. The project represents a major renewable energy investment, with TNB planning to inject up to RM424.4 million into the joint venture (JV). According to a filing with Bursa Malaysia, TNB’s subsidiary, TNB Renewables Sdn Bhd (TRe), has signed a shareholders’ agreement with IOI Corp’s subsidiary, Luminous Aspect Sdn Bhd, and CSP 500MW Sdn Bhd. The project will be developed through Bahau Energy Ventures Sdn Bhd, the joint venture established by the three partners. The proposed development will comprise a 500 MWac solar photovoltaic (PV) power plant and a 250 MW/1,000 MWh BESS. It will operate under Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS), which enables renewable energy developers to supply green electricity to corporate consumers. Under the agreed ownership structure, TRe will hold a 70% stake in the joint venture, making it the largest shareholder. Luminous Aspect will own 25%, while CSP will hold the remaining 5%. CSP represents a consortium of 12 SMEs that have established the special purpose company to participate in the development and implementation of the project. The JV has a maximum equity capitalisation of RM606.2 million. TRe will contribute RM424.4 million, while Luminous Aspect and CSP will invest RM151.5 million and RM30.3 million, respectively. The project financing is expected to combine shareholder equity and third-party project financing, with a debt-to-equity ratio of up to 80:20, subject to market conditions and funding availability. The project will be supported by TNB’s long-term renewable energy offtake agreement with DayOne Data Centres Ltd, a Singapore-headquartered digital infrastructure company. Under the agreement announced on June 11, 2025, DayOne is expected to procure up to 500 MWac of renewable energy over 21 years to support its data centre operations in Malaysia. TRe will act as the project’s asset manager and oversee engineering and procurement arrangements. Meanwhile, IOI will participate as an investor and provide the project site through a land lease arrangement. IOI Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Datuk Lee Yeow Chor said the partnership would support the company’s renewable energy portfolio and generate stable long-term recurring income. For TNB, the project is expected to strengthen its renewable energy portfolio and support Malaysia’s energy transition. The company highlighted growing corporate demand for renewable electricity and the implementation of CRESS as important factors supporting the project’s prospects. TNB also stated that the transaction is not expected to have a material impact on the group’s earnings per share, net assets per share or gearing for the current financial year. The eventual financial impact will depend on the final project cost, financing arrangements and commercial operations. The partnership also aligns with IOI’s Five-Year Strategic Roadmap for 2025–2029, which aims to expand its renewable energy business and strengthen its participation in Malaysia’s low-carbon energy transition. artigo.texto: The Bihar Electricity Regulatory Commission (BERC) has approved a proposal by Bihar State Power Holding Company Limited (BSPHCL) to procure 300 MW of solar power integrated with a four-hour Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), marking an important step towards strengthening the state’s renewable energy supply and improving electricity availability during peak demand periods. The approval will enable Bihar’s distribution companies, North Bihar Power Distribution Company Limited and South Bihar Power Distribution Company Limited, to secure renewable electricity through a long-term power procurement agreement for 25 years. The electricity will be procured through NHPC Limited, which will act as the intermediary procurer. SAEL Industries India Limited has been selected as the project developer to supply 300 MW of power from a larger 1,200 MW interstate transmission system-connected renewable energy project. Under the approved arrangement, the discovered tariff is ₹3.13 per kilowatt-hour, while NHPC will receive an additional trading margin of ₹0.07 per kilowatt-hour. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission had previously adopted the competitively discovered tariff in April 2026. The project includes a four-hour battery storage facility designed to provide 150 MW of firm electricity during evening peak demand hours, between 6:00 PM and midnight. This arrangement is expected to help Bihar manage its rising electricity demand and improve the reliability of power supply when solar generation is unavailable or reduced. The storage component will play an important role in shifting renewable electricity to periods when consumption is higher. The commission has also established strict performance requirements to ensure reliable electricity delivery. The developer must maintain at least 70 percent of the contracted peak capacity on a monthly basis and 85 percent annually. Failure to meet these requirements will attract financial penalties calculated at 1.5 times the applicable tariff rate for the shortfall. These provisions are intended to ensure that the project delivers the required electricity consistently. The regulatory approval was granted by a commission comprising Chairman Amir Subhani, Member Legal P. S. Yadav and Member Technical Manoj Kumar. While examining the petition, the commission considered the national Resource Adequacy framework and Bihar’s growing electricity requirements. It observed that the procurement would help the state address its Renewable Purchase Obligation requirements through FY 2029-30. The project is also expected to reduce Bihar’s dependence on expensive short-term electricity purchases, particularly during evening peak hours. By securing long-term renewable power supported by battery storage, distribution companies will have an additional source of reliable electricity, potentially reducing the need for load shedding and improving consumer supply conditions. SAEL Industries India Limited is expected to operationalise the project on or before June 30, 2028. Achieving this deadline will allow the state to benefit from transmission charge waivers, including a 25 percent waiver on interstate transmission charges for the solar component and a 100 percent waiver for electricity supplied from the co-located battery storage system. Additionally, BERC has approved a modified Power Sale Agreement incorporating consumer protection provisions. These provisions will account for potential tariff reductions arising from future changes in Goods and Services Tax rates. The decision is expected to support Bihar’s renewable energy transition while balancing electricity supply reliability, procurement costs and consumer interests.

artigo.texto: Nove ONGs, incluindo o Greenpeace, exigem suspensão de projetos de data centers no Brasil até que sejam feitos estudos de impacto e criadas leis rigorosas. Ações ocorreram em Fortaleza, Belém e Pindamonhangaba para alertar sobre os altos consumos de água e energia. Nove organizações da sociedade civil lançaram a mobilização nacional "Parem os mega data centers! O Brasil não é colônia das Big Techs". O grupo pede que nenhum projeto de centro de dados de hiperescala avance no país enquanto não houver estudos de impacto, licenciamento ambiental completo e uma lei que garanta participação das comunidades atingidas. O lançamento aconteceu em 6 de novembro com atos em Fortaleza (CE), Belém (PA) e Pindamonhangaba (SP), onde há projetos desse tipo. A iniciativa integra o Dia de Ação Global contra mega data centers, que mobilizou mais de 100 organizações de diferentes países nos dias 6 e 7 de novembro. - Nove ONGs assinam o manifesto: Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil. - As entidades exigem o fim das isenções fiscais concedidas ao setor pelo regime Redata. - Ações ocorreram em Fortaleza, Belém e Pindamonhangaba, cidades com projetos de data centers em andamento. - Os projetos consomem grandes volumes de energia e água, gerando preocupação com a fatura de luz e abastecimento. - O movimento faz parte de uma ação global que envolve mais de 100 organizações internacionais. Críticas à falta de transparência e impactos sociais As organizações pedem ainda o fim das isenções fiscais concedidas ao setor pelo Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). Esse regime foi sancionado em setembro e deve ser regulamentado pelo Governo Federal ainda neste ano. Na avaliação das entidades, o país oferece benefícios fiscais, energia e água a essas empresas antes de ter análise dos riscos, planejamento territorial, regras socioambientais e contrapartidas sobre a soberania digital. Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil, alertou para a interferência dos bilionários da tecnologia no processo eleitoral. "Acabamos de testemunhar a interferência dos bilionários da tecnologia no nosso processo eleitoral. Se por um lado precisamos regulamentar essas plataformas, por outro, precisamos impedi-las de construir suas casas de máquinas - os data centers - no nosso território da forma como têm feito, transferindo para a nossa população os seus custos socioambientais, sem ganho nenhum pro país", disse Catão. Vozes locais repudiam projetos na Amazônia e no Rio João Paulo Guimarães, ativista do Amazônia Sem Data Center, declarou: "É um absurdo um data center na Amazônia. O Pará já lidera números de mortes pelo calor extremo. Nós repudiamos esse projeto.". Mariana Ceres, ativista da Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, ressaltou a falta de participação social. "A principal questão para nós está na falta de transparência e total ausência de participação social. Em 2026, é inaceitável um empreendimento desse porte e com grande impacto ambiental, sem que haja um rigoroso licenciamento ambiental", afirmou Ceres. Andréa Camurça, coordenadora de Incidência Política do Instituto Terramar/CE, destacou a questão energética. "A ação é fundamental para que as vozes dos territórios cheguem ao mundo e denunciem a ofensiva das big techs sobre os bens comuns do Sul Global. Não podemos gerar insegurança energética num país que ainda enfrenta pobreza energética: queremos água e energia para o povo, não para big techs!", declarou Camurça. Polinho Mota, diretor do Data_labe, comentou sobre a situação no Rio de Janeiro. "Aqui no Rio de Janeiro estamos acompanhando a chegada de um mega empreendimento que vai afetar a vida de toda a população da cidade, mas que em momento nenhum ouviu o que tínhamos para falar. Por isso, junto com o Decodifica e Coding Rights, estamos enfrentando a falta de transparência e exigindo mais estudos de impacto", relatou Mota. Detalhes das ações em três capitais brasileiras As mobilizações no Brasil começaram no dia 6 pela manhã, em Belém. A campanha Amazônia Sem Data Center esteve na comunidade Residencial Miramar Shalon, para uma roda de conversa com os moradores que podem ser impactados pelo projeto BEL1, da Elea Data Centers e Axia Energia. No Ceará, onde o data center do TikTok está em fase avançada de construção, ativistas se reuniram para conversar com a população na orla da Praia de Iracema, em Fortaleza. A atividade foi realizada pelo Instituto Terramar e Greenpeace Brasil. Um caminhão de LED percorreu as ruas da cidade com informações sobre os impactos no aumento da conta de luz e na poluição sonora. O caminhão exibiu ainda o documentário "Inteligência Natural", realizado pela Coding Rights sobre o empreendimento que está sendo construído pelas empresas Omnia e Casa dos Ventos em território indígena Anacé, em Caucaia, na região metropolitana. Já em Pindamonhangaba, a ação foi organizada pelas Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba. Moradores da região se reuniram em uma praça de grande circulação para alertar a população sobre o projeto Riverhook Village 18, planejado para a cidade. O que são data centers e por que geram preocupação Os mega data centers, ou centros de dados de hiperescala, são complexos industriais voltados sobretudo ao treinamento de modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA) pelas grandes empresas de tecnologia, as Big Techs. Funcionam sem pausa, ocupam áreas extensas e consomem volumes muito altos de energia e água para refrigeração. Nas cidades que recebem esses projetos, a preocupação dos moradores vai do barulho contínuo das máquinas à pressão sobre o abastecimento de água e a conta de luz.

artigo.texto: Lydian Energy has brought its 150 MW/600 MWh Faraday battery energy storage system (BESS) into commercial operation in Utah County, adding four hours of contracted electricity storage capacity to the power infrastructure supporting Meta’s Eagle Mountain data center. The facility began operating on September 18, 2026, under a long-term energy storage agreement with PacifiCorp, according to Lydian’s November 10 announcement. The project adds battery storage alongside Lydian’s existing 525 MW Faraday solar facility, using the solar plant’s substation and grid interconnection rather than requiring a separate connection. The arrangement allows the developer to expand the site’s energy infrastructure while making use of existing grid facilities. Faraday BESS occupies approximately eight acres and uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery technology. Its 150 MW power rating and 600 MWh storage capacity provide a four-hour duration at full rated output. Lydian said it completed the project in approximately 10 months from mobilization to commercial operation. The project also establishes the first operating phase of a larger battery storage development at the site. Lydian is developing Faraday BESS 2, which could add another 375 MW/1,500 MWh by the fourth quarter of 2028. Battery storage supports Meta’s Eagle Mountain operations Faraday BESS operates under a Schedule 34 arrangement supporting Meta’s Eagle Mountain data center. PacifiCorp receives the project’s contracted storage capacity under a long-term agreement, placing the battery within a utility-contracted arrangement rather than making it an exclusively dedicated power supply physically connected to Meta’s campus. The project has a longer development history than its commercial operation announcement suggests. In January 2023, PacifiCorp executed a power purchase agreement for 525 MW of solar generation from Faraday Solar and a separate battery storage agreement for a 150 MW, four-hour system. A March 2023 filing before the Utah Public Service Commission identified the two agreements as serving a single Schedule 34 customer. At that time, PacifiCorp expected the solar facility to enter commercial operation on September 30, 2025, and the battery system on June 1, 2026. The battery ultimately began operating on September 18, 2026, approximately three and a half months after the original target recorded in that filing. Lydian’s reported 10-month construction and commissioning period refers to the period from mobilization, not the entire development history dating back to 2023. Meta subsequently identified its involvement directly. In a September 14, 2026, update, the company named Lydian’s 150 MW Faraday battery as part of its investments in energy resources supporting the Eagle Mountain data center. Meta said its Utah energy investments had added more than 1.7 GW of clean and renewable energy and 600 MWh of battery storage across 13 sites. It also said it pays the full costs of its data centers’ electricity use and funds new and upgraded infrastructure needed to support its operations. This arrangement connects three distinct participants. Lydian develops, owns and operates the battery, PacifiCorp contracts for its storage capacity, and Meta supports the energy arrangement as part of its strategy for the Eagle Mountain data center. Shared solar infrastructure supports the battery installation One of Faraday BESS’s most important infrastructure features is its integration with the existing Faraday solar facility. The battery occupies approximately eight acres adjacent to the solar development and shares its substation and grid interconnection. This allows Lydian to add a substantial storage installation without developing an entirely separate grid connection. The solar facility began commercial operation on September 30, 2025, under the associated PacifiCorp agreement. The battery’s September 2026 commissioning therefore adds storage to an existing generation site rather than establishing an entirely new energy development. The technical arrangement also requires an important distinction when assessing the site’s combined capacity. Faraday Solar has a stated capacity of 525 MW, while the battery can discharge at up to 150 MW. These ratings should not automatically be combined to suggest that the shared interconnection can export 675 MW simultaneously. The actual combined export capability depends on the approved interconnection limits and operating arrangements. Lydian has not disclosed the site’s detailed export constraints or how PacifiCorp coordinates solar generation and battery dispatch. Nevertheless, reusing the existing substation and interconnection provides a clear infrastructure advantage. It allows the developer to expand the site’s energy capabilities using facilities already established for the solar project. Faraday BESS 2 could add another 1.5 GWh Lydian is developing a second battery installation, Faraday BESS 2, at the Utah site. The proposed expansion would add up to 375 MW of power capacity and 1,500 MWh of storage, with commercial operation targeted for the fourth quarter of 2028. If completed at its announced maximum capacity, the second phase would increase the site’s combined battery storage to 525 MW and 2,100 MWh. That would establish a substantially larger storage development alongside the existing 525 MW Faraday solar facility. The expansion would also increase the amount of electricity that can be shifted across different periods, subject to charging availability, grid conditions and contractual dispatch requirements. However, Lydian has not disclosed Faraday BESS 2’s battery supplier, engineering and construction contractor, construction financing or detailed procurement schedule in its November 10 announcement. The second phase therefore remains a development target rather than an operational expansion. Its progress will depend on the remaining development, financing, procurement and construction requirements. C

artigo.texto: Not all technology companies stand to lose from a slowdown in data center construction. In fact, it could be exactly what Amazon needs to pull ahead, according to Jim Cramer . "If it's going to be slower, that does work for the incumbents, hence why I would buy Amazon," Jim said Monday morning on CNBC. A divide in the artificial intelligence trade has become increasingly apparent since last week's midterm elections , as growing opposition to new projects raises concerns about future infrastructure spending. Amazon shares have surged 7% since the election, including Monday's intraday gains. Other cloud incumbents such as Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet are solidly higher too. Meanwhile, semiconductor and neocloud stocks have suffered steep losses, with Micron tumbling 14.1%, Sandisk plunging 21.2% and CoreWeave falling 8.9%, when including Monday's intraday bounce-back rallies. The strength in hyperscalers has helped fuel a broader technology rebound following last week's sell-off. Despite weakness in Nvidia and other chipmakers, the Nasdaq has gained a combined 3.3% over Friday and Monday, recovering much of Thursday's 5.5% plunge. "I think the Amazon move is very right," Jim said. "I was talking about it going to $300." That would represent nearly 10% upside from current levels. The recent rally marks a turnaround for Amazon, which had slumped over the last few months as investors grew tired of enormous AI spending. The stock briefly got hot in late July and into August, following the forced unwind of Situational Awareness and an encouraging second-quarter earnings report . But after closing at $284 apiece on Aug. 3, shares lost more than 15% through the end of October, ending that month at roughly $240. Cramer argued that a slowdown in development could benefit established cloud providers, which already operate extensive data center networks and could have the corporate heft needed to navigate any new bureaucratic obstacles. He compared the situation to a yellow flag in Formula One racing. "Everyone has to go slower, no one's allowed to pass," he said. "If that's the case, that's Microsoft and that's Amazon winning." Demand for AI computing power isn't going away, even if new data centers become harder to build. Unlike smaller neocloud providers that rely on continued expansion to grow, Amazon and Microsoft already have massive infrastructure networks in place, positioning them to capture a larger share of demand as new capacity becomes harder to bring online. Jim also said that he likes that Amazon has been less reliant on neocloud providers to secure extra capacity to meet demand. A slower buildout would also ease pressure on the hyperscalers to keep accelerating capital spending, potentially allowing their free cash flow to recover and improving returns on their existing infrastructure investments. For investors, that makes the established hyperscalers better positioned to weather a slowdown than companies whose growth depends more directly on new data center construction.
