artigo.texto: How data center demand is reshaping electricity costs across the US By Lucas Winter for Shipley Energy Three years ago, U.S. utilities expected peak electricity demand to grow by about 24 gigawatts over the following five years. Their most recent forecasts put that figure at roughly 166 gigawatts, 6.9 times the earlier estimate, and about 90 gigawatts of the increase is tied to data centers. That growth is beginning to show up in electricity costs for businesses and households, though the effect looks very different depending on where a customer is located. Data centers used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the lab projects that share could reach 6.7% to 12% by 2028. The U.S. Energy Information Administration expects record national electricity sales in 2026, driven by data center development and manufacturing, with the average U.S. residential price rising from 17.3 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2025 to 18.2 cents in 2026. Whether data centers raise costs in a given area depends on three things: - How much spare power supply the region had before they arrived - How its electricity market recovers the cost of new demand - What rules regulators have set for very large customers Before looking at how those factors play out region by region, it helps to understand how data center demand turns into charges on an electricity bill. For instance, if you’re doing business in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Maryland, or D.C., capacity charges are now one of the fastest-growing parts of commercial electricity bills in the PJM region. Below, Shipley Energy explains what the latest auction results mean for your next budget. A large data center campus can need as much power as a small city, running around the clock. Grid operators and utilities have to secure generation and build transmission for that demand, often years before the facility opens. Those costs reach customers through three main channels. The first is capacity costs, which pay power plants to be available during the hours when demand peaks. Some regions buy this capacity through auctions held years in advance, so forecasts of future data center demand can raise prices before the facilities exist. The second is wholesale energy prices, which rise when added demand calls more expensive power plants into service. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas estimate that existing data centers have already raised wholesale electricity prices by 2% to 6% on average nationwide. The third is transmission and distribution, the lines and substations needed to deliver power to new load, which are often paid for by all customers in a utility’s territory. Because wholesale power typically makes up about half of the retail price of electricity, a given increase in wholesale prices reaches retail bills at roughly half its size. A Region-by-Region Look The same kind of demand growth is producing very different results across the country. PJM The grid operator serving 13 states and Washington, D.C., runs a capacity auction about three years ahead of delivery. Its clearing price rose from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024/2025 to $269.92 for 2025/2026, then hit a federally approved cap in each of the next three auctions. The 2028/2029 auction cleared at $325 per megawatt-day and still came in 6,831 megawatts short of PJM’s reliability requirement. PJM’s independent market monitor attributes about 46% of capacity costs across the last four auctions, or $29.4 billion, to data center demand. MISO The Midcontinent grid operator saw summer capacity prices reach a record $666.50 per megawatt-day for 2025/2026 as its surplus shrank. A year later, the picture shifted. Capacity offered into the 2026/2027 auction grew 3.4%, led by solar additions, and annualized prices fell to between $116 and $126 per megawatt-day, down from $212 to $217 the year before. Texas ERCOT has no capacity auction, so data center demand shows up mainly in wholesale prices during high-demand hours and in transmission spending. In August 2026, Gov. Greg Abbott directed state regulators and ERCOT to audit every data center seeking a grid connection before any project moves forward, citing more than 474 gigawatts of requests, more than five times the state’s record peak demand, with about 90% coming from data centers. Southeast Georgia Power’s pipeline of prospective large-load projects grew from about 16,000 megawatts in 2023 to roughly 69,000 megawatts by December 2025, about 80% of it from data centers. The utility and its regulators disagree on the electricity bill impact. Georgia Power projects that new large-load contracts will produce about $950 million a year in customer savings beginning in 2029, while state commission staff cautioned that the related generation buildout could add around $20 a month to residential bills. Pacific Northwest Data centers account for roughly 15% of the current load of Oregon’s investor-owned utilities, according to the state’s utility commission. Under a 2025 state law, Oregon regulators approved new rates for Portland General Electric in July 2026 that raised data center rates by an average of 29% while lowering residential rates by 1.3% and commercial rates by 2.1%. Surplus-Supply States In states that had extra generation before data centers arrived, new demand has often spread fixed grid costs across more customers. North Dakota saw electricity demand grow almost 40% while inflation-adjusted prices fell by about 3 cents per kilowatt-hour. Researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and The Brattle Group, who documented that pattern, describe the overall relationship between load growth and prices as mixed and uncertain in their 2026 update. Forecasts Versus What Gets Built Not every announced data center will be built, and forecasts disagree about how many will. artigo.texto: 247 – O governo federal planeja destinar R$ 46,3 milhões ao desenvolvimento de uma tecnologia nacional de inteligência artificial (IA) para gerenciar e distribuir dados entre pequenos centros de processamento de informações espalhados pelo Brasil. A iniciativa pretende modernizar a infraestrutura digital do país, reduzir custos operacionais e ampliar a autonomia brasileira no tratamento de informações estratégicas. O plano do Ministério das Comunicações prevê que o investimento seja direcionado ao desenvolvimento do projeto Prisma, uma plataforma capaz de identificar automaticamente onde e como os dados devem ser processados, utilizando inteligência artificial para otimizar a distribuição dos recursos computacionais. A proposta é permitir que diferentes estruturas de armazenamento e processamento de dados operem de maneira integrada, com maior eficiência na utilização de energia e capacidade computacional. O sistema deverá identificar as melhores condições para executar determinadas operações e distribuir as demandas entre os chamados mini data centers. Além da redução de despesas com energia elétrica e manutenção das operações, o governo espera que a plataforma acelere o acesso às informações e fortaleça a proteção de dados considerados estratégicos. Governo busca reduzir dependência de tecnologias estrangeiras Um dos principais objetivos do investimento é ampliar a soberania tecnológica brasileira, diminuindo a necessidade de utilização de soluções desenvolvidas fora do país para administrar infraestruturas digitais. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Filho, destacou que o desenvolvimento de tecnologias nacionais é fundamental para garantir maior autonomia no tratamento de informações e preparar o Brasil para os desafios da transformação digital. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirmou o ministro, em nota. A declaração coloca a redução da dependência tecnológica externa entre as prioridades do projeto, ao lado da modernização dos sistemas de processamento e da segurança das informações. A iniciativa também busca estimular o desenvolvimento de soluções brasileiras de inteligência artificial aplicadas à infraestrutura digital, área considerada estratégica para o armazenamento, a circulação e o processamento de grandes volumes de dados. Projeto será executado pelo CPQD e terá duração de 36 meses A administração dos R$ 46,3 milhões ficará sob responsabilidade da Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), instituição federal de fomento à pesquisa e à inovação. A execução técnica caberá ao Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD), instituição brasileira especializada em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação tecnológica. O prazo previsto para a realização do projeto é de 36 meses, contados a partir da assinatura do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD. Durante esse período, o trabalho será direcionado ao desenvolvimento da plataforma Prisma e de suas funcionalidades de gerenciamento inteligente de dados. A tecnologia deverá permitir que as demandas computacionais sejam distribuídas automaticamente entre diferentes infraestruturas, levando em consideração as condições necessárias ao processamento das informações. Inteligência artificial será utilizada para otimizar recursos O funcionamento previsto para o Prisma tem como elemento central a utilização de inteligência artificial na administração dos recursos computacionais. Em vez de concentrar necessariamente o processamento em uma única estrutura, a plataforma deverá avaliar a distribuição das demandas entre diferentes mini data centers, buscando melhorar o aproveitamento da capacidade disponível. Esse modelo poderá contribuir para reduzir o consumo de energia e os custos associados ao funcionamento dos equipamentos, além de tornar mais eficiente a circulação das informações. A proteção de dados estratégicos também integra os objetivos anunciados pelo Ministério das Comunicações. Ao desenvolver uma solução nacional de gerenciamento, o governo pretende fortalecer a capacidade brasileira de administrar informações em infraestruturas digitais.

artigo.texto: Solutions for Diverse Energy Applications As Australia expands renewable energy deployment, energy storage is increasingly important for grid flexibility, energy cost optimization and reliable power supply. OneMatrix Solution addresses utility-scale applications, including renewable energy projects, standalone grid-side storage and electricity market operations. Featuring flexible modular design and LONGiBank 3.0, it supports 2–8-hour duration and customized system configurations. Cluster-level independent management, AI-powered battery health diagnostics and intelligent O&M help improve operational efficiency and support long-term asset performance. The solution has received TÜV Rheinland certifications under IEC 62619, IEC 63056, and an IEC/EN 60730-1 Annex H report, reinforcing its safety credentials for international markets. Hi-MO One Pro supports C&I applications with flexible 2-24-hour configurations for solar-plus-storage, peak-valley arbitrage, and backup power. Featuring LONGi's proprietary iCCS and liquid-cooling technology, it supports grid-connected and off-grid operation, helping businesses optimize energy costs and enhance power supply security. OneNexus H2 and M5 serve remote areas, mining operations and other locations with limited grid access. By coordinating solar, battery storage and diesel generation, they help increase renewable energy utilization, reduce diesel dependence and strengthen power supply resilience. Project Experience Demonstrates Local Market Value In Strathalbyn, South Australia, the Lunio Energy BESS project was connected to the grid in September 2026. Comprising four LONGiBank 2.0 systems with a total capacity of 5 MW/20 MWh, the project participates in Australia's National Electricity Market (NEM), optimizing charging and discharging in response to electricity demand and market prices. Advancing LONGi ONE Through Localized Services LONGi continues to integrate proprietary technologies, system solutions and intelligent O&M under its LONGi ONE strategy, providing support from solution design and delivery through lifecycle operations. Through its "2830 Plan," LONGi aims to establish 30 comprehensive local service centers worldwide by the end of 2028, strengthening local responsiveness and lifecycle support. With its full-stack capabilities, diverse solution portfolio and expanding local service network, LONGi Energy Storage will continue working with Australian customers and partners to deliver flexible, reliable and sustainable energy solutions. artigo.texto: Tsunami democrata tira de Donald Trump o controle da Câmara e do Senado Oposição terá, no mínimo, 54 senadores, caminha para maioria robusta na Câmara e elege governadores em estados importantes e simbólicos. Crédito: Estadão O mercado financeiro focado em tecnologia não tem vivido seus melhores dias recentemente e o índice Nasdaq chegou a registrar sua maior queda diária desde abril de 2025 na última quinta-feira (5). A queda foi de 5,5% e resultou na redução de US$ 2,5 trilhões (R$ 13,4 trilhões em conversão direta) do valor de mercado das principais empresas do setor, influenciadas pelas midterms dos Estados Unidos. O motivo para esse derretimento abrupto tem relação com as recentes eleições de meio de mandato, as midterms norte-americanas. Na última rodada, a expressiva vitória do Partido Democrata contra o Partido Republicano no pleito acendeu o temor de que a expansão da inteligência artificial sofra mais regulações nas mãos dos democratas. A Nvidia, empresa mais poderosa do planeta e absoluta na venda de chips para servidores, viu suas ações caírem 9%. Com a rival direta, a AMD, a queda foi ainda mais chamativa e bateu nos 17%. O índice de semicondutores da Filadélfia (SOX) também registrou uma queda notória de 12%, o nível mais baixo dos últimos seis meses. O clima pesado não está restrito somente aos Estados Unidos e chega a outros países em um efeito cascata. Bolsas asiáticas, como a japonesa Nikkei e a sul-coreana Kospi, operaram em forte queda. O índice VIX, chamado de “termômetro do medo” em Wall Street, registrou seu maior salto desde 2024 e aumentou a apreensão dos acionistas. - 🪧Índice VIX (Termômetro do medo): essa é uma métrica de Wall Street que mede a expectativa de volatilidade do mercado para os próximos 30 dias. Quando o índice dispara, significa que há insegurança por parte de investidores e possibilidade de quedas na bolsa. IA pode esbarrar em decisões políticas Analistas do mercado financeiro mostram que o receio de acionistas e investidores é que os democratas façam força contra a construção de novos data centers em solo americano. Um dos motivos é o fato desses centros de dados exigirem grandes volumes de água para resfriar os servidores, além dos gastos em energia e o barulho. Uma estimativa do UBS aponta que quase 30% da capacidade adicional de data centers esperada para 2028 nos Estados Unidos tem risco de sofrer paralisações. Como o mercado de IA se expandiu rapidamente nos últimos anos, isso se tornou um empecilho para investidores da categoria, que demandam novas instalações para o treinamento dos modelos de IA. Gigantes responsáveis por essas tecnologias, como a Amazon e Alphabet (dona do Google) viram quedas de 2,2%. No caso da Microsoft, o recuo foi de 3,6%. Aliás, a companhia de Redmond já teria começado a apertar a supervisão de projetos terceirizados de data centers. Por falar em IA e problemas financeiros, o caso de infidelidade do CEO da Nvidia pode trazer grandes consequências à empresa e ao mercado global. Não esqueça de continuar ligado no TecMundo para acompanhar outros artigos como esse e não perder as principais informações da indústria de tecnologia. Com informações de Reuters.

artigo.texto: NHPC Limited has issued a tender on behalf of Bundelkhand Saur Urja Limited (BSUL) to select a Battery Energy Storage System Developer (BESSD) for developing two Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). NHPC's two BESS projects comprise a 300 MW/800 MW/4,800 MWh system and a 600 MW/800 MW/3,200 MWh system. It has sought bids until December 12, 2026. By seeking over 4 hours of supply during non-solar hours, the tender seeks to push the boundaries of solar plus storage in UP for the first time. BSUL is a joint venture between NHPC Limited and the Uttar Pradesh New and Renewable Energy Development Agency (UPNEDA). The selected developer will procure the entire solar energy generated by the existing solar plants, establish co-located BESS projects, and utilise the solar power to charge the BESS. The remaining solar power, along with the power discharged from the BESS, will be scheduled for supply. Scope of Work BSUL intends to integrate BESS with its existing solar power generation capacity to meet the firm and dispatchable power requirements of the End Procurer. It has invited proposals for setting up BESS projects that will use energy generated by the existing solar plants to charge the storage systems and schedule Solar-plus-BESS power under either of the two configurations. The projects are intended to meet the solar and non-solar hour power requirements of the Buying Entity/Distribution Companies (DISCOMs). Under the first configuration, the project involves scheduling 300 MW of solar capacity during solar hours, coupled with an 800 MW/4,800 MWh BESS for supplying power during non-solar hours. Under the second configuration, 600 MW of solar capacity will be scheduled during solar hours, supported by an 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS during non-solar hours. Under this framework, BSUL, acting as an Intermediary Procurer, has selected Coal India Limited (CIL) and NLC India Renewables Limited as Solar Power Developers (SPDs) to develop a total solar generation capacity of 1,200 MW across Tehsil Orai and Tehsil Madhogarh. BSUL will execute Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) to procure the entire 1,200 MW of solar power generated from the park. Integrating ESS With Solar Projects Energy Storage Systems (ESS) play a critical role in managing fluctuations in renewable energy generation and helping grid operators maintain reliability while facilitating the smooth integration of renewable energy into the grid. Additionally, ESS connected to Solar Photovoltaic (SPV) plants can enhance the utilisation of renewable energy transmission systems. It has been clarified that the BESSD will procure the entire power generated by the co-located solar projects in Jalaun Solar Park from the Solar Power Project Developer (SPPD), BSUL, at the tariff detailed hereunder.

artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries are moving into commercial production, supported by growing interest in diversified supply chains and reliable performance across a wide range of temperatures, according to new analysis from Wood Mackenzie. The report, Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow, examines developments in China, the United States, Germany and India. It finds that supply agreements now exceed 70 GWh, signalling growing confidence among downstream customers. Wood Mackenzie expects leading manufacturers to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by the end of 2026. However, parity at module and complete system level is not expected until after 2030. Supply security and temperature performance support adoption The consultancy identifies supply chain security, cycle life and a broad operating temperature range as key advantages of sodium-ion technology. Its performance in cold conditions strengthens its appeal for applications where low temperatures can affect battery operation. According to Ankita Chauhan, Director of Global Supply Chain and Integrated Power & Renewables Research at Wood Mackenzie, these characteristics, alongside geopolitical supply advantages, are driving near-term commercialisation. China leads manufacturing expansion China is leading the development of sodium-ion manufacturing capacity. Wood Mackenzie reports that BYD has 30 GWh of planned capacity in the country, while CATL is targeting at least 1 GWh of sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026. China, the United States and Europe have significant offtake agreements, while India remains at an early stage of commercial validation. Manufacturing capacity, however, is expanding ahead of demand. The consultancy estimates a learning rate of 18–20% for China during 2026–2035, reflecting the potential for costs to decline as production scales and manufacturers gain experience. Higher upfront investment, lower lifetime costs The analysis puts average global upfront costs for sodium-ion systems at US$229/kWh, compared with US$200/kWh for LFP. Despite this initial premium, it estimates that sodium-ion can deliver a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project. The projected savings stem from lower operating expenditure and avoiding capacity additions needed to compensate for battery degradation. According to Wood Mackenzie, system economics remain stable across storage durations of two to four hours. Near-term deployment nevertheless faces several obstacles. The report highlights Chinese export controls, India’s underdeveloped supply chain, slow gigafactory expansion in the United States and German trade policies as potential constraints on growth. Policy plays a central role in commercialisation Wood Mackenzie finds that taxation, trade measures and domestic manufacturing incentives are shaping sodium-ion deployment alongside technological progress. According to the report, China’s reintroduction of a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries in July 2026 exempts sodium-ion technology through the end of 2028. LFP batteries face a 2% levy from September 2026, rising to 4% from September 2027. In the United States, the consultancy identifies Section 301 tariffs of approximately 58% on Chinese energy storage cells as an incentive for domestic sodium-ion production, complemented by manufacturing credits under Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act. In Europe, carbon-footprint disclosure requirements under the EU Battery Regulation provide further support. India is developing local capacity through a US$1.25 billion incentive programme and duty exemptions on manufacturing equipment, the report notes. The economics could shift decisively between 2030 and 2035 Wood Mackenzie identifies 2030–2035 as the period when sodium-ion economics could become significantly more competitive. For projects being deployed today, however, it considers LFP the established, bankable choice for storage assets with durations of two to four hours. Sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine cell materials and establish a consistent operating track record. The consultancy therefore expects several battery technologies to coexist, each serving different applications and storage durations.

artigo.texto: ENERGY Governor’s energy council recommends data centers, large users cover grid costs Report offers 22 recommendations, including zero-carbon standard shift A council appointed by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is urging lawmakers to make data centers and other large power users pay for the grid costs they create, according to a report released this month. In April, Lujan Grisham established the 13-member Energy Affordability and Grid Reliability Council through an executive order to develop recommendations addressing energy affordability, grid reliability, infrastructure investment and economic development. State Economic Development Secretary Rob Black, acting Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Secretary Erin Taylor and Rep. Meredith Dixon, D-Albuquerque, were among the public officials appointed to the council. El Paso Electric President and CEO Kelly Tomblin and TXNM Energy President and CEO Don Tarry also serve on the council. The council’s report includes 22 recommendations to inform future legislative, regulatory and administrative actions. Among them: Large industrial customers should “bear costs attributable to serving them and existing customers should be held harmless from costs and financial risks caused by new large loads,” the report said. The report said the state Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department should develop a database of large electricity users, noting that industrial customers accounted for about 47% of New Mexico’s 2025 electricity sales, followed by commercial users at 30% and residential at 23%. “Meeting growing demand requires careful planning and prudent investment,” Tarry said in a statement announcing the report. The report notes that future energy demand is expected to grow, though the “scale, timing and location of that growth remain uncertain.” “New Mexico’s three major (investor-owned utilities) are all evaluating significant load growth scenarios, including growth from data centers, manufacturing, electrification of oil and gas operations and in other industrial processes, transportation electrification, and broader economic development,” the report said. Already, most New Mexicans have seen increases on their monthly electricity bills — under a staggered rate increase approved last year — to help cover the cost of system expansions for the Public Service Company of New Mexico. Lujan Grisham in 2019 signed into law the Energy Transition Act requiring utilities to go carbon-free by midcentury. The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission in May 2025 approved PNM’s phased-in rate increase request to help cover the costs of renewable energy buildout. That PRC approval hiked average monthly residential bills by roughly $12. The report also recommends that lawmakers shift the state’s renewable-energy standard to a “zero-carbon” standard, giving utilities more flexibility to meet clean energy targets with non-emitting resources such as nuclear power. The council’s report also suggests other measures, such as broadening the availability of energy infrastructure securitization for utilities, which would allow utilities to recover infrastructure costs via bonds backed by ratepayer revenue, thereby reducing financing costs and passing on savings to ratepayers. In a statement, Lujan Grisham said the recommendations “give us a path to protect ratepayers, bring more power onto the grid and keep our energy clean, all at the same time.” Added Dixon, “These recommendations give legislators a practical starting point for protecting customers while supporting responsible growth.” Justin Horwath covers tech and energy for the Journal. You can reach him at jhorwath@abqjournal.com.

artigo.texto: The Telangana Electricity Regulatory Commission (TGERC) has granted in-principle approval to state distribution companies, Telangana State Southern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGSPDCL) and Telangana State Northern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGNPDCL), to procure 7,300 MW of renewable energy along with advanced energy storage systems. The proposed procurement will involve long-term power supply agreements ranging from 15 to 25 years and aims to meet the state’s growing electricity demand while supporting national renewable energy targets. The approval follows a petition submitted by the distribution companies highlighting the need to strengthen Telangana’s future power supply. According to the Central Electricity Authority’s (CEA) Resource Adequacy Plan, the state’s annual energy requirement is expected to increase from 1,08,125 million units (MU) in FY 2026-27 to 1,77,219 MU by FY 2035-36. Peak electricity demand is also projected to rise by nearly 49.4% during this period. The distribution companies are also preparing for the expiry of several existing power purchase agreements, which could create gaps in energy availability and peak power supply. At the same time, meeting the Ministry of Power’s increasing Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO) targets has become important to avoid regulatory and financial penalties. The approved procurement plan includes four major renewable energy components. The first involves 800 MW of standalone wind power under a 25-year agreement. This capacity is expected to complement solar generation and improve the overall renewable energy supply profile. The second component covers 3,000 MW of solar power integrated with a 6,000 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), configured at 1,000 MW for six hours. The project will operate under a 25-year agreement, allowing electricity generated during periods of high solar availability to be stored and supplied during evening peak demand. The third component includes 2,000 MW of Renewable Energy Round-the-Clock (RE-RTC) power for 25 years. This arrangement is intended to provide a more consistent renewable electricity supply and support the state’s base-load requirements. Additionally, the plan includes 2,000 MWh of Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE), configured at 500 MW for four hours, under a 15-year agreement to address peak demand periods. During the public consultation process, consumer groups and industry stakeholders raised concerns about the procurement process, demand projections and the possible impact on electricity tariffs. Some participants questioned the initiation of tendering activities before obtaining formal regulatory approval. They also highlighted the importance of promoting distributed renewable energy projects and creating opportunities for local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). In response, TGERC directed the distribution companies to obtain prior approval from the Commission before initiating bidding for future long-term or medium-term power procurement. The Commission also clarified that DISCOMs can participate in competitive procurement processes conducted through the Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) or use state-level tendering mechanisms. The selection between these routes should be based on the most cost-effective landed tariff at the Telangana periphery. The approved renewable procurement is expected to strengthen the state’s energy security, reduce dependence on conventional power sources and limit consumer exposure to rising fuel-linked electricity costs.

artigo.texto: O presidente da Argentina, Javier Milei, propôs cortar de 25% para 15% o imposto corporativo para projetos de inteligência artificial com investimento mínimo de US$ 1 bilhão para transformar a Patagônia em polo de data centers. O Brasil já lidera a região nesse mercado. Em Los Toldos, na estepe patagônica, um data center de 12 MW já funciona com gás que seria queimado como subproduto da extração de petróleo de xisto, segundo o Financial Times, reproduzido pela Folha. Tomás Ocampo, fundador da Unblock Energy, planeja uma instalação de várias centenas de MW na zona rural argentina. Ele diz ter recebido uma enxurrada de ligações de investidores dos Estados Unidos após as eleições de meio de mandato americanas. "Antes de colocarmos data centers no oceano e no espaço, a Argentina faz muito sentido", disse Ocampo. Como fica o incentivo fiscal argentino O corte de imposto vale para projetos com investimento mínimo de US$ 1 bilhão e ainda depende de aprovação no Senado argentino, que também avalia o projeto Green Capital, em Chubut, com US$ 3 bilhões em 130 mil hectares. O consumo de eletricidade estimado é de 2,7 vezes todo o consumo de Buenos Aires em 2025, dado que já alimenta a resistência de moradores da região. Publicidade Não vamos regulamentar a inteligência artificial. Vamos deixá-la livre. A frase foi dita por Milei em reunião da Câmara de Comércio dos EUA. A oposição no Congresso argentino já modificou regras sobre compra de terras por estrangeiros e travou a autorização para que sistemas de IA administrem empresas sem presença humana. Como o Brasil já sai na frente O Brasil concentra 48% da capacidade de data centers em operação na América Latina e 71% de tudo que está em construção na região, segundo levantamento da Forbes Brasil. O país deve atrair US$ 33 bilhões até 2030. O país também concentra três das cinco maiores posições regionais em capacidade instalada, à frente de México, Chile e Colômbia. O avanço brasileiro pode render US$ 60 bilhões por ano até 2050, e o setor cresce no país enquanto trava nos Estados Unidos. A disputa pela água que data centers consomem também é tema no Brasil. Um estudo mostrou que as instalações de IA em São Paulo usam 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano, preocupação que também mobiliza moradores da Patagônia. O que acontece agora O projeto de incentivos segue em tramitação no Senado argentino, sem data certa de votação. O projeto de maior destaque de Milei na área, anunciado em outubro do ano passado, pode ter estagnado, segundo a Folha. O governo argentino não detalhou um novo cronograma. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, enquanto isso, seguem de olho nos dois países ao mesmo tempo.

artigo.texto: EU Close to Deal to Link UK Carbon Market After Brexit Split (Bloomberg) -- The European Union and the UK are in the final stages of a deal to link their emissions markets, a move that would boost liquidity and eventually save companies millions of euros in carbon border taxes. The agreement, to be announced at a key summit later this month, would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems, almost six years after Britain started its own cap-and-trade program in the wake of Brexit. Negotiators have already ironed out details on emissions caps, supply controls and free permits, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The treatment of financial derivatives is the only outstanding issue. The EU’s carbon market is the region’s key way to meet its carbon reduction goals. Started in 2005, the market imposes gradually shrinking emissions limits on around 10,000 facilities in sectors from steel and cement to fertilizers, power production and aviation. Once linked, it will allow mutual recognition of permits from both markets for compliance, helpful for companies with operations in both regions. The linkage deal is set to be one of the main deliverables at the Nov. 20 meeting of UK and EU leaders, alongside matching university tuition fees for students traveling between the two. Other areas of agreement include committing to minimizing the effect of their trade measures on vulnerable sectors like steel and electric cars, and deepening cooperation on cyber threats, Bloomberg reported last month. The European Commission declined to comment on the agreement, in line with its long-standing policy of not commenting on draft documents. The agreement will not automatically exempt the parties from their respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms, which put emissions costs on certain imported products to shield local producers against competitors from regions with laxer climate rules. Instead, it will pave the way for a waiver once the parties fulfill certain condition embedded in their domestic laws, the people said. The EU law sets two requirements for such a move: full linkage with its ETS and effective carbon pricing without preferential rebates. Once those are met, the EU will add the UK to a list of countries outside of the CBAM regulation scope via a delegated act. While the EU carbon border tax became operational this year, with the first compliance deadline set for September, the UK mechanism is to kick off at the start of 2027. UK carbon prices have already narrowed their discount to the EU ETS market since the two parties committed last year to establishing a link. The UK carbon contract for December closed at a £64.81 per ton on Friday while benchmark EU allowances were at €86.55. The price gap could shrink further over the next two years, as UK allowances move closer to EU permits, Moutaz Altaghlibi, Senior Energy Economist at ABN Amro wrote in a note on Nov. 5. That would mean UK firms having to pay more for permits. “Linking the systems should also improve liquidity, make carbon prices more consistent across Europe, and reduce CBAM-related costs and paperwork for trade between the UK and EU,” he said. Although the idea of re-linking carbon markets has been discussed for years, Britain’s current Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also working to bring the UK closer to Europe on a broader level. A key parameter in the agreement will be the cap on emissions in the UK ETS. The EU is set to recognize emissions caps in the British system in the 2028-2030 period, according to people with knowledge of the issue. From 2031, the annual UK issuance will be capped at 7.1% of permits to be issued in the EU ETS. The UK will also create its own Market Stability Reserve, a mechanism that the EU has had for more than a decade to automatically control the supply of carbon permits and alleviate a glut of allowances that emerged and weighed on prices. It will start with at least 29.5 million allowances when the deal enters into force. Before the start of 2030, a decision will be taken on adjustments to ensure that the amount of permits in the UK MSR corresponds to at least 6.7% of allowances in the EU ETS reserve in 2029. As part of the draft deal, negotiators have also agreed to keep rules aligned over time, with Britain obliged to integrate European rules into its law. The deal will need to be ratified by both the UK and the EU, in a procedure that involves the European Parliament and member states in the EU Council. It will enter into force a month after the last notification regarding the two other deliverables of the upcoming summit: an SPS agreement on sanitary and phytosanitary standards and a solution on a youth mobility scheme, known as YES. The parties may also choose to apply the deal on a provisional basis before its entry into force. ©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

artigo.texto: PRESS RELEASE: Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators. Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028. When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies. Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report Principal contributors: Glenn McGrath, Alex Mey

artigo.texto: BOISE, Idaho — No mega data centers are currently proposed within Boise city limits, but with large-scale projects emerging elsewhere in Idaho, Mayor Lauren McLean says she doesn't want to wait until one arrives to determine whether the city is prepared. In an interview with Idaho News 6 on Monday, McLean explained what prompted her call for a six-month moratorium on large data center development, what questions she wants answered and why she believes the city needs to act now. "A lot of people are asking that, and they're asking why now, but I wouldn't want them to ask tomorrow, why didn't you do it," McLean said. WATCH: Boise mayor explains preemptive data center pause McLean pointed to recent data center proposals in other Idaho communities as a major factor behind her decision. South of Boise, a developer has proposed a project involving nearly 3,700 acres of federal public land, including a 4 million-square-foot data center. Meta already operates a data center in Kuna, while city leaders in Pocatello recently rejected another large-scale proposal. McLean said developments like those have raised questions about whether Boise has adequate protections in place. "This is a preemptive step. We don't want to be too late, so we're going to get ahead of this and ask the questions we need to ask to make sure we're advocating for Boise," McLean said. Those questions extend beyond the environmental impacts of data centers to whether the facilities provide enough long-term economic benefits for the communities hosting them. "The impact that it would have on water, the power that's needed, the number of jobs that might or might not exist, and also the noise," McLean said. Under her proposal, Boise would temporarily prohibit new data centers larger than 100,000 square feet or requiring more than 20 megawatts of power. The city has no pending applications meeting those thresholds. The proposal also raises questions about how Boise evaluates major industrial development, particularly as the city supports Micron Technology's multi-billion-dollar semiconductor expansion. Like large data centers, semiconductor manufacturing requires significant electricity and water resources. Asked how Micron's expansion differs from the facilities she wants to study, McLean emphasized the company's commitment to permanent jobs and investment in Boise. "Micron is not a data center," McLean said. "Yes, they require water, power. They're investing in the community, and they're creating opportunity for our kids and grandkids to come home with high-paying jobs." Her response highlights another consideration the city intends to examine: whether the economic benefits of large data centers justify their demands on local infrastructure and resources. McLean said she wants Boise to attract companies that invest in the community and provide lasting employment opportunities. Rather than responding to a specific development application, McLean said the proposed moratorium would allow city officials to study potential impacts before deciding what long-term regulations may be necessary. She also wants residents involved in determining what protections the city should establish. "Part of the six months is going to be a conversation with the community. I want to hear from residents on what they expect," McLean said. Asked whether six months would provide enough time, McLean said the city intends to use the period to examine existing regulatory tools, identify potential gaps and determine what additional steps may be needed. The mayor also suggested Idaho communities need more support at the state level when evaluating large data center developments. "The state needs to create guardrails so that communities can advocate for themselves," McLean said. For now, McLean's proposal is less about responding to a project already seeking approval in Boise and more about determining what rules should be in place if one eventually arrives. The Boise City Council will hold a public hearing on the proposed moratorium Tuesday, Nov. 10, before considering whether to approve it.

artigo.texto: Phillips 66 stock adds SAF portal to carbon-market strategy Published on 11/10/2026 at 14:40 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS SAF Portal Broadens Phillips 66 Offering - The new platform lets companies buy sustainable aviation fuel environmental attributes through a book-and-claim model. - Customers receive documentation covering the emissions reductions linked to their purchases. - The initiative expands Phillips 66's sustainable aviation fuel sales and distribution strategy. Phillips 66 launched an Environmental Attributes Portal on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, giving companies a direct way to purchase environmental attributes linked to sustainable aviation fuel. Biofuels International Magazine reported that the platform is designed for businesses seeking to address emissions from business travel and upstream transportation. The portal uses a book-and-claim model. Companies can purchase the environmental attributes even when the physical sustainable aviation fuel is not available at their location, allowing the environmental benefit to be separated from the fuel's physical delivery. New Channel For SAF Customers Phillips 66 said the platform lets customers select the environmental attributes they want and complete purchases through flexible payment methods, including credit cards. There is no minimum purchase requirement, which broadens access beyond large-volume fuel buyers. After a purchase, customers receive an Environmental Attribute Document summarizing the associated carbon dioxide emissions reduction. That documentation can support internal emissions analysis and corporate reporting, making the portal a commercial tool as well as a transaction platform. Sunny Lopez, senior director of aviation and sustainable fuel sales at Phillips 66, said the company built the portal around its experience across feedstock sourcing, production, fuel delivery and distribution. The comments underline the company's effort to simplify access to SAF-related claims as corporate buyers face pressure to reduce transport emissions. Building A Broader SAF Platform The portal adds to Phillips 66's recent SAF initiatives. The company announced an agreement with Chooose in 2026 to integrate the technology provider's platform into existing SAF processes, with the aim of streamlining fuel delivery, distribution and documentation. For investors, the portal offers a route to serve sustainability demand without requiring every customer to take physical SAF at its operating locations. Its financial contribution will depend on transaction volumes, customer adoption and the availability of qualifying SAF attributes. The launch therefore supports Phillips 66's commercial positioning in renewable fuels, while the article does not provide revenue or earnings guidance for the portal. artigo.texto: The Nefer Benban Solar and BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) project in Egypt, developed by Infinity Power, secures US$127 million in financing to advance construction. The project is being developed by Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy, a special-purpose company owned by Infinity Power and HAU Energy and is designed to strengthen Egypt’s renewable electricity capacity and grid reliability. Meanwhile, Egypt’s Obelisk solar and battery project has begun operations, marking further progress in the country’s renewable energy expansion. The financing package includes a US$65 million construction bridge loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Meanwhile, Germany’s development finance institution, DEG, will provide an equal amount. Together, the funding will support a 200MW solar plant and a 120MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at Benban Solar Park near Aswan. Additionally, the EBRD identifies HAU Energy as the borrower, while Nefer Benban is the project company. The solar-storage development will combine daytime solar generation with battery storage that can release electricity during evening peak-demand periods. Therefore, the project is intended to help manage fluctuations in renewable generation and improve the reliability of electricity supplied to the national grid. The electricity will be sold to the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company (EETC) under a 25-year power purchase agreement. Project Scope and Technical Specifications The project will use solar PV panels to generate electricity. Meanwhile, the 120MWh battery system will store excess daytime output. It will then release the stored electricity when demand rises or solar generation declines. Project disclosures list the solar plant’s installed capacity at approximately 200MW. However, the EBRD’s November 2026 announcement specifies a 258.5MWp photovoltaic (PV) array. Additionally, the project is among Egypt’s early utility-scale developments combining solar generation with battery storage. The facility will store surplus daytime electricity and release it after sunset. Consequently, it will extend the availability of solar power beyond daylight hours. It is also expected to reduce fluctuations in renewable electricity supply. The project is located within the wider Benban Solar Park, one of Egypt’s major renewable energy hubs. Furthermore, the established site provides an opportunity to expand solar generation and integrate additional flexibility into the electricity grid. Financing Structure and Project Partners The US$127 million financing package comprises a US$65 million construction bridge loan from the EBRD and an equal contribution from DEG. Additionally, the funding will cover eligible development and construction costs. These include engineering, procurement, installation, testing and commissioning. However, the package represents construction debt financing, not the project’s total capital cost. The project has also secured a separate EBRD financing commitment of up to US$63.5 million for Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy. This comprises up to US$56 million from the bank’s own resources and US$7.5 million from the Clean Technology Fund. Additionally, the package supports the combined solar and storage development. However, the two financing arrangements represent separate facilities and should be reported separately when outlining the project’s total funding. Infinity Power is a joint venture between Infinity and Masdar. It focuses on developing renewable energy projects across Africa. Meanwhile, HAU Energy is an investment platform established to develop renewable energy projects in Egypt. It is associated with Hassan Allam Utilities, Meridiam and the EBRD. Additionally, Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy serves as the project-specific company for the Benban development. Construction Status and Expected Impact The financing is intended to support construction and commissioning activities of the Nefer Benban Solar Project. However, the financing announcement alone does not establish that the facility has completed construction or entered commercial operation. The EBRD’s project information describes the development as an implementation-stage investment, while its latest announcement confirms the planned solar and battery configuration. Once operational, the facility will supply electricity under a long-term power purchase agreement with EETC. Additionally, the battery system will release stored solar power during peak demand after sunset. Consequently, it will help the grid accommodate a greater share of variable renewable energy. The Nefer Benban Solar Project also supports Egypt’s energy transition goals. These include expanding private-sector renewable energy capacity and reducing reliance on fossil-fuel generation. However, its long-term contribution will depend on timely construction, successful commissioning and grid integration. Furthermore, its impact will depend on the facility’s operational performance. artigo.texto: Land & Expand: Texas’ AI Boom Meets a New Political Reality Key Highlights - Democrat Gina Hinojosa's election as Texas governor, alongside Democratic gains in the state House and statewide offices, raises the prospect of an extended data center permitting pause and new legislation in 2027. - Riot Platforms disclosed a 910 MW, approximately $28 billion lease with Anthropic at its Corsicana campus, while Hut 8 advanced its gigawatt-scale Beacon Point project. - CenterPoint Energy increased its 10-year capital plan to $70.7 billion as Greater Houston prepares for major industrial and data center electricity demand. - Fermi's proposed 222 MW TensorWave lease missed its closing deadline, while Microsoft declined to exercise an expansion option for capacity at Nscale's Texas project. - From San Antonio to Hudspeth County, developers increasingly face demands for greater transparency, water and power safeguards, and clearer community benefits. In DCF's Land & Expand series, we track where North American data center development is taking root, where it's accelerating, and the forces shaping which projects actually get built. Today we examine how Texas has become one of the clearest demonstrations of the extraordinary scale of AI infrastructure development — and of the challenges now facing the industry as it attempts to turn that investment into operating capacity. In the space of several weeks, the state has seen major new data center leases, expanded utility investment plans, new behind-the-meter generation proposals, and continued construction on large AI campuses. At the same time, regulators have tightened oversight, municipalities have adopted additional development controls, and several high-profile transactions have encountered financing or execution challenges. Then came the November 3 midterm elections. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democrat elected Texas governor since Ann Richards in 1990. Democrats also won the Texas House and the lieutenant governorship, although Republicans retained their majority in the state Senate. The results introduce a new political dimension to a data center market already undergoing substantial regulatory change. Hinojosa made the industry's rapid expansion a campaign issue, calling for a moratorium on new approvals until lawmakers establish stronger protections for communities, water supplies, electricity customers, and local decision-making. In a November 5 interview reported by Reuters, the governor-elect reaffirmed her intention to pause further approvals until those protections are in place. As Data Center Frontier reported in August, Texas was already moving toward a more restrictive regulatory framework under Abbott, who ordered audits of prospective data centers and suspended certain approvals pending the results. Hinojosa's election could extend that process and place new requirements on developers seeking to move projects forward. Yet the state's AI infrastructure market is hardly standing still. The emerging Texas story is not simply one of growth versus regulation. It is about a new set of conditions under which massive capital commitments, available power, established customers, and community acceptance may determine which developments actually reach operation. A $28 Billion Agreement Shows That Texas Is Still in Expansion Mode One of the largest recent transactions illustrates the continuing strength of demand. On November 4, Riot Platforms announced a 15-year, triple-net powered-land lease covering 910 MW of critical IT capacity at its Corsicana campus in Navarro County. Although Riot initially described its customer as a leading frontier AI laboratory, the company's quarterly SEC filing identifies Anthropic as the tenant. Riot estimates that the agreement represents approximately $28 billion in contractual revenue over its initial term, with an average of about $1.8 billion annually. The contract became effective November 4 after the applicable approvals and technical conditions were satisfied. The development model is noteworthy. Riot will provide land, powered pads, and high- and medium-voltage electrical infrastructure, while Anthropic will supply and operate its modular computing equipment. The lease covers a contiguous 332-acre site, with deliveries expected in three phases extending through July 2028. The first phase comprises 400 MW, followed by 200 MW and 310 MW. Under the agreement, Anthropic is responsible for electricity costs and other operating expenses, while Riot retains responsibility for the site's power infrastructure. Rent is structured around contracted capacity rather than actual computing utilization. The result is a substantially more defined commercial arrangement than a speculative gigawatt-scale development announcement. Nevertheless, construction, financing, commissioning, and scheduled delivery remain significant obligations. It is also an example of the changing role of former cryptocurrency infrastructure operators in the AI market. Sites originally assembled around access to large electrical loads are increasingly being repositioned to serve customers requiring high-density computing capacity. The transaction underscores the continuing appetite for large-scale Texas developments, extending the expansion trend documented in DCF's previous Land & Expand roundup. Riot's agreement was announced one day after Hinojosa's election victory. The timing is striking, although the transaction was negotiated and signed before the election and should not be interpreted as a response to its outcome. Instead, it demonstrates the simultaneous forces now shaping Texas: substantial demand for power-ready infrastructure and growing uncertainty over the rules governing future development. artigo.texto: BYD investirá R$ 1 bilhão para produzir vans e caminhões no Brasil Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro disputam a próxima unidade da fabricante chinesa, que prevê gerar dois mil empregos A BYD vai instalar uma nova fábrica no Brasil para produzir vans elétricas e caminhões. A coluna apurou com exclusividade para a CNN Brasil que o projeto prevê investimento de R$ 1 bilhão e a criação de 2 mil postos de trabalho entre 2028 e 2029, início da produção. Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro foram selecionados pela fabricante e disputam o investimento. A escolha final do estado ainda está em aberto porque virá acompanhada pelo pacote dos incentivos. O projeto marca a segunda fase da expansão industrial da BYD no país. Depois de colocar em operação a fábrica de automóveis de Camaçari, na Bahia. A greentech prepara a nova unidade voltada aos veículos comerciais. Com as vans elétricas, a montadora entra numa disputa com as clássicas, que vendem os modelos a diesel. Durante a semana, a SAIC, com a Volks Caminhões, exibirá sua defesa no segmento das vans, trazendo novidades. Na Fenatran, que começa nesta segunda (9) em São Paulo, a BYD vai trazer os caminhões elétricos eT35 e eT75, além de uma configuração do eT23 para o transporte de bebidas. O eT35 usa a bateria Blade, enquanto o eT75 é voltado à distribuição urbana e regional. Os modelos que sairão da nova fábrica ainda não foram detalhados e devem ser anunciados nos próximos meses. Na Bahia A fábrica de Camaçari ultrapassou 150 mil veículos produzidos e 9,5 mil empregos diretos pouco mais de um ano após a inauguração, segundo balanço divulgado pela montadora em 5 de novembro. O investimento anunciado para o complexo chegou a R$ 11,3 bilhões, ante os R$ 5,5 bilhões informados em julho. A unidade baiana, que produz Dolphin Mini, King, Song Pro e Atto 2, tem capacidade instalada de 150 mil veículos por ano, com previsão de chegar a 300 mil na próxima etapa. A BYD já concluiu as obras civis dos galpões de soldagem e pintura e realiza testes operacionais nas duas áreas. Mais de 1.100 profissionais foram contratados para atuar nessas estruturas, que permitirão incorporar novas etapas da fabricação em Camaçari. Quem vai crescer? A BYD levou seus concessionários a Mendoza, na Argentina, para mostrar os carros que vêm por aí. Mas o recado mais direto da convenção foi para os donos das lojas. Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da companhia, deixou claro que, na próxima rodada de expansão da rede no Brasil, vai crescer com a BYD quem mantiver a exclusividade entre as marcas chinesas. Na prática, o grupo que quiser abrir mais pontos de venda com a fabricante terá de deixar as rivais asiáticas fora do portfólio. No encontro, a montadora apresentou um plano com sete lançamentos e novos pontos de venda. Um dos SUVs já tem nome e ano para chegar. O Ti7, antecipado por esta coluna, é um híbrido plug-in boxy de sete lugares confirmado para 2027. Com carroceria de linhas quadradas e porte do Denza B5, ele coloca a BYD na disputa por compradores de modelos como o Jetour T2 e o GWM Haval H7. O Dolphin GT será o próximo nacional e nós já cravamos aqui na CNN sobre o híbrido plug-in flex, que será feito na Bahia em fevereiro.

artigo.texto: UK and EU officials are on the brink of an agreement that would link their carbon emissions markets, a move that would save companies millions of euros in carbon border taxes, as the diplomatic push for deeper EU-UK integration accelerates ahead of a key post-Brexit summit next week. The deal would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems. The UK’s post-Brexit emissions trading scheme was modelled on the EU’s. The UK’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, which is set to come into force early next year, is also based on the EU’s carbon border levy, a tax on imported industrial goods which are linked to high carbon emissions. Once the UK and EU emissions trading systems are linked, that would pave the way for them to be exempted from their respective CBAM laws. On Tuesday (10 November), UK trade minister Jonathan Reynolds and Europe minister Hamish Falconer held talks with EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to push for a UK inclusion in the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ initiative, that would allow UK firms to retain access to the EU’s industrial supply chain. Meetings with vice-president Stéphane Séjourne and defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius were also on the agenda.

artigo.texto: David Sacks Warns the AI Data Center Pipeline Could Dry Up. Here’s What’s at Stake A permitting fight could stall the buildings that every AI chip, cable, and cooling system needs. While chip stocks sank in a single month, one corner of the market barely flinched. Which suppliers are exposed, and who collects rent either… This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. David Sacks thinks the AI data center boom could run out of road within about two years. On the All-In podcast episode released November 7, which covered the midterm elections, the AI selloff, and what the hosts called a data center freeze, David Sacks said: “Nobody can make a $50 billion investment in conditions of uncertainty. I think by 2028 the pipeline will be closed or significantly reduced.” His argument rests on permitting. Sacks said the biggest danger is breaking ground and then, halfway through, getting “enjoined” or stopped by a worker strike or a community group. According to Sacks, governors in the largest data center states are “basically indicating that they favor a moratorium” until certain conditions are met. Why a Permitting Freeze Reaches Every Supplier A data center needs land, power, and a finished building before a single chip goes in. Broadcom’s chief executive made the same point on the company’s September call: “Before you get the chips out there, you have to get the data center shell in place and ready for production.” If the buildings stall, chip, networking, and cooling orders slow down after them. That dependency matters because each company in the chain is posting growth that assumes the expansion keeps going: - The company, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), reported Data Center revenue of $89.02B, up 117%, guided next quarter to $108.0B +/- 2%, and disclosed supply obligations of $279.00B in its latest earnings release filed with the SEC. - Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) sees fiscal 2028 AI semiconductor revenue reaching $230 billion. That target falls inside Sacks’s 2028 window. - Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET) grew revenue 58.5% and guided Q4 to $3.9B-$4.0B. It also disclosed that a limited number of large customers drive much of that revenue. - Vertiv (NYSE:VRT) reported organic orders up over 100%, and customers typically order 12 to 18 months ahead. The power, cooling, and networking names behind the data center buildings are a trade of their own, and we pulled together seven of them in a free report on the AI suppliers that aren’t chipmakers. Landlords Held Up While Chip Stocks Fell Over the month ending November 6, NVIDIA fell 21.4%, Broadcom 22%, Arista 20.86% and Vertiv 25.81%. Over the same month, Equinix (NASDAQ:EQIX) slipped only 1.85% and Digital Realty 3.47%. One explanation is that a freeze could help companies that already own permitted, powered sites. Equinix’s chief executive said, “If there are a number of projects canceled, then it only makes what is already scarce capacity much more of a scarce resource.” She added that across its 3 gigawatts of planned capacity, “the land, power and permitting are largely secured.” Digital Realty has 1.5 gigawatts under construction, 63% pre-leased, and a record $2.5 billion backlog that gives it visibility through 2027 and into 2028. Counterpoint: Permitting Outcomes Remain Unsettled Sacks’s view is a forecast. Proposed moratoriums can be narrowed, delayed, or dropped, and nobody knows yet how state policy will land. Vertiv’s chief executive called power, permitting, and labor pacing items that “are not slowing down growth.” NVIDIA expects fiscal 2028 revenue growth of approximately 70% and describes that outlook as limited by supply, with customer demand running higher. NVIDIA also cited top-five hyperscaler capex of nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027. What Retirement Investors Should Watch Next Many people own this trade without picking a single stock. A major Nasdaq-100 index fund’s prospectus notes significant exposure to the information technology sector, so a slowdown in AI spending would show up in many 401(k) and IRA balances. Four signals stand out: - State action: whether moratorium talk in the big data center states turns into passed rules or remains at the proposal stage. - Guidance checks: NVIDIA’s results against its $108.0B guide, and Broadcom’s against expected Q4 AI revenue of $21.7B. - Vertiv orders: customers order 12 to 18 months ahead, so a slowdown in orders would be one of the first signs that 2028 projects are being pushed back. - REIT pre-leasing and pricing: rising rents at Equinix and Digital Realty would suggest that scarcity is helping the landlords even as new construction slows down. If permitting tightens, investors with heavy index exposure to AI hardware should know which parts of the chain depend on new construction and which ones collect rent on capacity that is already built. artigo.texto: São Paulo lança fundo de R$ 70 milhões para ISPs e data centers de pequeno porte Iniciativa quer ampliar o acesso a crédito em regiões ainda subatendidas por data centers e redes de conectividade, sobretudo no interior paulista. Operações de fusão e aquisição (M&A) também estão contempladas. A Desenvolve SP e a gestora Möbius Capital lançaram um Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios (FIDC) de R$ 70 milhões para provedores de serviços de Internet (ISPs) e data centers de pequeno porte. O objetivo é ampliar o acesso a crédito e apoiar investimentos em infraestrutura digital no Estado de São Paulo. Com apoio do fundo, os provedores, em linhas gerais, poderão antecipar os recebíveis de seus clientes, tanto pessoas físicas como jurídicas, e investir em operações de crédito destinadas a financiar a compra de equipamentos de infraestrutura e projetos de expansão de redes. O FIDC também visa a ampliar o acesso a crédito em regiões ainda subatendidas por data centers e redes de conectividade, sobretudo no interior paulista. Operações de fusão e aquisição (M&A) também estão contempladas. O fundo é composto por R$ 50 milhões da Desenvolve SP, nas cotas seniores, e R$ 20 milhões da Möbius Capital, nas cotas subordinadas. “Nossa meta é ampliar o acesso ao crédito e facilitar recursos para negócios inovadores. Por meio do blended finance, conseguimos atrair investimento privado, potencializar o impacto do recurso público e alcançar mais empreendedores”, afirmou o diretor-presidente da Desenvolve SP, Ricardo Brito, em nota. Já a Möbius Capital foi selecionada por meio de uma chamada pública. Além de sua experiência no setor de infraestrutura digital, a gestora apresentou tese, estrutura, estratégia, governança, equipe, histórico e valor pleiteado para o desenho da linha de crédito. “Temos um histórico de realizar financiamento para aquisições de provedores de Internet, operações via mercado de capitais para fomentar o crescimento de empresas do setor, além de dar apoio no avanço da profissionalização e governança dessas companhias”, destacou Roberto Savaris, sócio e fundador da Möbius.

artigo.texto: - A 60 MW/600 MWh liquid air energy storage (LAES) plant in Golmud, Qinghai province, was synchronised to the grid on 30 October and has started producing power. - Developer China Green Development Investment Group (CGDG) says it is the largest grid-connected liquid air storage installation in the world, by both power rating and energy capacity. All major equipment was made in China, giving the project a localisation rate of 100%. The plant shows a route to long-duration storage that needs neither batteries nor underground caverns. The system uses ambient air as its working fluid. During off-peak hours, surplus electricity drives a three-stage centrifugal compressor that raises purified air to about 7 MPa. The heat of compression is captured and stored as hot water at up to 195°C. The air is then cooled in stages and liquefied at around minus 194°C, before being held in insulated cryogenic tanks at close to atmospheric pressure. When demand peaks, the liquid air is pressurised, heated and returned to a gaseous state, using both the stored compression heat and the cold storage media. The expanding gas drives turbines connected to generators. The cold released during vaporisation is retained for later charging cycles, forming a closed loop that stores off-peak power for peak use. Liquid air is about 750 times denser than ambient air and can be stored safely at atmospheric pressure. According to the developer, this addresses the relatively low energy density and weaker safety performance of some traditional storage options. Because the working medium is air, the plant produces no carbon dioxide or other pollutant emissions during operation. The equipment has a long service life and is not tied to any particular geography, allowing stable operation in extreme environments such as the Gobi Desert and high plateaus. The facility is designed to supply electricity continuously for 10 hours. CGDG estimates it can absorb about 600 MWh of surplus renewable electricity a day and deliver roughly 180 GWh a year, equal to the consumption of about 30,000 homes. The plant’s rotating machinery can also provide inertial support to the grid. It sits in Qinghai’s Qaidam Basin, a region rich in renewable resources, where long-duration storage could shift surplus solar and wind output to periods of higher demand. The plant was built by state-owned CGDG together with the Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). Construction began in July 2023. Hualu Engineering & Technology carried out the engineering design, and China National Chemical Engineering Third Construction took part in building the plant. The technology grew out of earlier CAS work that demonstrated liquid air storage at the 100 kW scale. To reach this scale, the joint team overcame bottlenecks in ultra-low-temperature cascade cold storage, developed an atmospheric-pressure low-temperature storage system, and solved the challenges of air storage and constant-pressure release. Domestically developed technologies include large centrifugal compressors, liquid expanders, cryogenic heat exchangers and integrated control systems. The project was selected for China’s national new-type energy storage demonstration programme and is listed among the National Energy Administration’s major first-of-a-kind energy technologies and equipment. Author: Bryan Groenendaal

artigo.texto: Insurance shortfalls, financial losses crippling St Bess business recovery Loading article... WESTERN BUREAU: Crippling financial losses, inadequate insurance coverage and mounting borrowing costs are threatening the survival of several businesses across St Elizabeth, leaving some operators contemplating permanent closure as they continue to reel from Hurricane Melissa’s devastating 2025 blow. Kadian Myers-Brown, president of the Black River chapter of the St Elizabeth Chamber of Commerce, and businessman Jason Henzell, chairman of the South Coast chapter of the Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association, believe that financial pressure continues to undermine recovery efforts. Myers-Brown said several long-standing, family-operated businesses in Black River remain shuttered because of the inability to finance repairs or replace equipment and stock destroyed during the hurricane, which struck as a Category 5 system just over a year ago. “Some persons are saying, ‘Hey, I’m just gonna give up.’ Some persons are saying that they are not going to reinvest ... not knowing what the plans truly are from the Government,” she told The Gleaner. Myers-Brown, an attorney-at-law, said some establishments had operated for generations without adequate financial reserves or insurance protection, leaving their owners particularly vulnerable to the hurricane’s devastating impact. “Some of them were like mom-and-pop stores operating for almost a century,” she said. A survey commissioned by the St Elizabeth Homecoming Foundation revealed that 46 per cent of Black River businesses suffered devastating or total destruction, with average rebuilding costs estimated at $17 million. Only 1.4 per cent had insurance coverage. It also found that 28 per cent of businesses reported income losses ranging from 70 to 100 per cent, with full recovery projected to take approximately 26 months. Among the establishments yet to recover are the popular Sunrise Bakery, several furniture stores, variety shops, barbershops, and farm supply businesses. Myers-Brown said supermarkets, pharmacies, hardware stores and medical offices were among businesses that had reopened, largely through the determination of their operators. Meanwhile, Henzell, who is also CEO of Jakes Hotel and chairman of the Treasure Beach Foundation, said tourism operators were receiving insurance settlements much lower than anticipated, creating additional financial difficulties. “If I were to take a survey of what people have told me in terms of the settlement that they got, it was probably two-thirds of what they were expecting. You know, it’s probably 65 per cent of what they were hoping for,” he said. Henzell further explained that lengthy delays in processing claims had forced some operators to borrow money. “If you have to go and borrow money now, because of the delay, remember you have to add that interest cost,” he said. He warned that dissatisfaction with insurance settlements was prompting some business owners without outstanding bank loans to reconsider renewing their policies, potentially leaving them exposed to future disasters. Henzell also stressed the importance of understanding insurance conditions, deductibles and underinsurance, suggesting educational workshops to help tourism operators make better financial decisions. “You could have the best hotel operationally, but you had the wrong mix of insurance,” he said, in highlighting the need for sound financial decisions. However, despite the setbacks, Henzell said all accommodation properties in Treasure Beach have reopened, noting that the recent Food, Rum and Reggae Festival generated strong occupancy across southwest St Elizabeth, extending into Junction. However, Myers-Brown said uncertainty surrounding the Government’s proposed Black River urban centre continued to discourage reinvestment, particularly among coastal operators, who are worried about what protection will be put in place to combat future hurricanes and storm surges. “It would not make sense to regain or restore business as per usual, not knowing what the effects of another storm will be like,” she said. “People are suffering. Businesses are suffering. Businesses want to really regain some sort of restoration at their peak level.” albert.ferguson@gleanerjm.com

artigo.texto: Maxell Begins Mass Production of All-Solid-State Battery Backup Modules for Industrial Equipment Power Supply Module Incorporating All-Solid-State Battery Helps Reduce Maintenance Workload and Improve Equipment Maintainability TOKYO–(BUSINESS WIRE)–Maxell, Ltd. (TOKYO: 6810) will begin mass production of its “All-Solid-State Battery Backup Module” incorporating the ceramic packaged all-solid-state battery, PSB401010H, and will start sales in Japan for industrial equipment applications in early November. Maxell has been conducting field tests*1 of power supply modules incorporating its all-solid-state batteries in manufacturing equipment at customers’ factories since 2024, with the aim of reducing the workload associated with battery replacement at production sites. The tests confirmed stable backup performance under actual manufacturing conditions, and customers highly valued the modules for their ability to improve equipment maintainability. Based on these results, Maxell developed four models of the All-Solid-State Battery Backup Module. The module is available with output voltages corresponding to those of ER batteries (3.6 V) and CR batteries (3.0 V), which are widely used as backup power sources. Two battery capacity options are available for each voltage type, offering a lineup of four models that can be selected according to the application. The all-solid-state battery incorporated into the module has an expected service life of more than 10 years*2. As a result, the module is expected to reduce the labor associated with primary battery replacement and the risk of downtime caused by unexpected battery depletion. In addition, the module can operate at temperatures of up to 85°C. Maxell will exhibit the module at Maintenance Munich 2026 (October 14-15, 2026; MOC – Event Center Messe München, Germany) and at other exhibitions in Japan.
