artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Winning Data Center Bids Starts with the Investment Tax Credit Contractors can win more data center bids by planning for the Investment Tax Credit early and helping owners capture more value. Picture two proposals for a data center bid. The pricing is similar. The timelines are similar. One covers the construction scope. The other shows how the project can be structured not just on a blueprint but on a tax return to unlock additional financial value. For an owner weighing the full economics of a data center investment, the difference can be compelling. For years, apart from the largest industry players, few other contractors could submit bids at that scale, much less win them. They couldn't compete with the giants on labor availability, balance sheet strength, or track record. Today, that landscape is changing. AI demand and an unprecedented wave of data center developments are stretching even the largest players. More firms are getting a chance to compete. The question for contractors is how to stand out once they are at the table. One of the most overlooked advantages is the availability of tax incentives, particularly the federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC). In projects that include eligible energy property, the ITC can materially improve project economics. In an industry where margins are tight, and bids are often won by fractions of a percentage point, that matters. Where the Value Comes From Power now sits at the center of every data center project. Developers are under pressure to meet rising energy demand while keeping long-term costs under control. As a result, more projects are investing in on-site solar, battery storage, microgrids, and other systems built for resilience. These assets may qualify for federal incentives, including the ITC. One of us spent years inside the IRS helping shape how the agency administered the ITC. The detail that surprises many contractors is that the credit is not simply a fixed rate applied at the end of a project. It is designed to stack, and its value can change substantially based on decisions made throughout development and construction. Where materials are sourced, how labor is structured, whether prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements are satisfied, and how compliance is documented can all affect the size of the credit. Many of those decisions sit with the contractor. Why Timing Matters When contractors hear the word "tax" or "credit," many assume it is a matter for the owner's finance team or tax advisors to figure out long after construction is completed. That assumption leaves value on the table. Here's the thing most advisors don't tell you: by the time construction is finished, the best opportunities have usually passed. If sourcing is locked, labor plans are set, and the schedule was built without compliance in mind, the opportunity to maximize the ITC may be sharply reduced. Contractors who plan for the credit from the start can flag sourcing and labor choices that affect eligibility and size. They can build prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements into the budget and set up documentation early, so the record will stand up to review. In doing so, the value they can deliver to a client can climb from 6% to as much as 60%. How the ITC Can Help Contractors Win a Bid Submitting a bid with an ITC strategy takes less tax expertise than many contractors expect. Contractors do not need to become tax experts. They need enough working knowledge to spot opportunities, ask good questions, and invite the right specialists at the right time. That is a realistic goal for a mid-sized firm, and it starts with the first planning conversation. Many of your competitors can build. Fewer can show an owner how to capture more value from the same project by aligning construction planning with the economics of eligible energy investments. For contractors looking to break into or move up in the data center sector, the Investment Tax Credit may be one of the smartest ways to win.

artigo.texto: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport. Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? artigo.texto: Camila Valadão questiona licenciamento e impactos socioambientais A deputada estadual Camila Valadão (PSOL) apresentou uma indicação ao Governo do Estado, sob gestão de Ricardo Ferraço (MDB) solicitando a realização de consulta e audiência pública sobre a instalação de um data center voltado à inteligência artificial em Baixo Guandu, no Noroeste do Espírito Santo. A parlamentar protocolou um requerimento de informações sobre o licenciamento ambiental e os possíveis impactos socioambientais do empreendimento, além de questionar a participação da população e a disponibilidade de recursos hídricos. O empreendimento integra o Projeto Rubi, apresentado pela empresa capixaba Line Solution, e prevê investimento estimado em R$ 7,4 bilhões. Além do centro de processamento de dados, com capacidade inicial anunciada de 100 megawatts (MW), o complexo inclui condomínios logístico e industrial. A área total prevista é de aproximadamente 11 milhões de metros quadrados. A iniciativa da deputada ocorre em meio à falta de informações públicas sobre a origem da água que será utilizada pelo complexo e os procedimentos necessários para autorizar sua captação. Em resposta ao Século Diário, a Agência Nacional de Águas e Saneamento Básico (ANA) informou que não possui registro de pedidos de outorga de direito de uso de recursos hídricos destinados especificamente a data centers. O órgão esclareceu, entretanto, que a competência para autorizar a utilização de águas subterrâneas é dos estados. Na indicação encaminhada à Secretaria de Estado do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos (Seama), Camila solicita a realização de consulta pública, na modalidade de reunião participativa, e audiência pública para apresentação do empreendimento e dos estudos ambientais. A parlamentar também pede ampla divulgação das atividades para assegurar a participação dos moradores de Baixo Guandu. “Não podemos permitir que um projeto desse tamanho seja discutido apenas entre empresas e governo, sem ouvir quem vive no território. Estamos falando de um empreendimento que pode transformar a realidade de Baixo Guandu, com impactos sobre a água, o meio ambiente e a vida da população. É fundamental que as pessoas tenham acesso aos estudos, possam fazer perguntas e participar das decisões sobre o futuro da cidade”, afirma. O requerimento de informações foi encaminhado à Seama e ao Instituto Estadual de Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos (Iema). Entre os questionamentos estão a existência de estudos de impacto ambiental e outros documentos apresentados pelos responsáveis pelo projeto, além da disponibilização dos materiais para consulta pública. A disponibilidade hídrica é uma das principais questões levantadas sobre o empreendimento. Em reportagem publicada anteriormente pelo Século Diário, o prefeito de Baixo Guandu, Lastênio Cardoso (MDB), afirmou que a água necessária ao funcionamento do data center viria de uma represa no Rio Doce. Ele não soube informar se os estudos ambientais já haviam sido apresentados e direcionou as perguntas sobre essa etapa ao empresário Mário Rodrigues, fundador e CEO da Line Solution. Procurado novamente por Século Diário, Mário Rodrigues ficou de retornar à reportagem para prestar explicações sobre o projeto, mas não encaminhou informações até o fechamento da edição. Questionada agora sobre a existência de autorizações para o uso de água por empreendimentos desse tipo, a ANA respondeu: “Até o momento a Agência Nacional de Águas e Saneamento Básico não tem registro de pedidos de outorga de direito de uso de recursos hídricos para a finalidade específica de data centers”. O órgão acrescentou que, caso o Projeto Rubi utilize águas subterrâneas, os pedidos de outorga devem ser apresentados à Agência Estadual de Recursos Hídricos (Agerh), uma vez que esse tipo de recurso é de domínio estadual, conforme a Constituição Federal. A distinção é importante porque a competência para autorizar a captação depende do manancial escolhido. O Rio Doce é um curso d’água de domínio da União, enquanto rios e demais corpos hídricos estaduais estão sujeitos à competência dos órgãos estaduais, por isso a definição da fonte de abastecimento é fundamental para identificar os procedimentos de autorização aplicáveis ao empreendimento. Em resposta ao Século Diário, a Agerh informou que não havia recebido pedidos de outorga de direito de uso de recursos hídricos ou de autorização da empresa responsável pelo Projeto Rubi e afirmou que, por essa razão, não dispunha de informações sobre eventual previsão de captação em mananciais da região para atender às necessidades do empreendimento. A preocupação com a água também foi levantada pelo coordenador do Observatório Capixaba da Água e do Meio Ambiente, Merci Fardin. Ao comentar o projeto em reportagem anterior, ele defendeu que os impactos sejam analisados de maneira conjunta, considerando os demais empreendimentos previstos para a região. Segundo o ambientalista, a instalação de novas estruturas industriais e logísticas pode ampliar a pressão sobre os recursos naturais e a infraestrutura local. Por isso, a avaliação não deve se restringir à disponibilidade de água nas proximidades do terreno destinado ao data center. A Line Solution informou à midia capixaba que pretende utilizar um sistema fechado de resfriamento, com reutilização contínua da água e reposição mensal estimada em volume equivalente ao consumo de três casas populares. A empresa também divulgou a previsão de criação de até 550 empregos, sendo 500 durante as obras e 50 na operação, além de arrecadação anual de R$ 50 milhões a R$ 60 milhões em Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS). As projeções são da própria companhia e ainda dependem da implantação do complexo. Para além dos números anunciados, a definição da demanda hídrica efetiva, da fonte de abastecimento e das condições de disponibilidade dos recursos naturais permanece necessária para avaliar os efeitos do empreendimento sobre o território. artigo.texto: MIDDLETOWN, Calif. – The Middletown Area Town Hall, or MATH, will discuss data center protections and energy policy when it meets this week. MATH will meet from 6:30 to 8 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12, in the Middletown Community Meeting Room/Library at 21256 Washington St., Middletown. The meeting is open to the public. Viewers can participate via PEG TV at www.youtube.com/LakeCountyPegTV or on Zoom. Among MATH’s key items for the Tuesday meeting is the discussion of a proposed letter to the Board of Supervisors requesting consideration of adoption of a comprehensive Lake County Energy Policy. The letter also asks the supervisors to approve a resolution “to temporarily prevent new permits or land-use approvals for data centers, energy exploration, and similar developments from moving forward until appropriate energy policies and protections are fully established.” Once that resolution is in place, the letter said MATH has a “near future goal” of establishing a permanent zoning prohibition on data centers and all other similar developments within the MATH jurisdiction, which includes Anderson Springs, Callayomi Valley, Cobb, Cobb Mountain, Guenoc Valley, Hidden Valley Lake, Jerusalem Grade, Loch Lomond and Middletown. “We recognize the permanent zoning prohibition may be a lengthier process for approval and adopting the temporary resolution will provide the immediate needed protections for our community,” the letter notes. There also will be a report from District 1 Supervisor Helen Owen, an update from the advisory group to the Building and Planning Department, and an action item regarding discussion and a recommendation regarding personnel at Middletown High School. MATH – established by resolution of the Lake County Board of Supervisors on Dec. 12, 2006 – is a municipal advisory council serving the residents of Anderson Springs, Cobb, Coyote Valley (including Hidden Valley Lake), Long Valley and Middletown. For more information email mathtownhall@gmail.com. Email Elizabeth Larson at elarson@lakeconews.com. Follow her on Twitter, @ERLarson, and on Bluesky, @erlarson.bsky.social. artigo.texto: Foto da manchete: ilustração-Divulgação Por Jurandir Antonio – Voz: Enéas Jacobina Texto do áudio O governador Otaviano Pivetta está participando da 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas, a COP 31, em Antália, na Turquia, com uma agenda voltada à abertura de oportunidades econômicas para Mato Grosso por meio da comercialização internacional de créditos de carbono e outros ativos ambientais. A missão acontece em um momento que o Governo do Estado busca estruturar instrumentos jurídicos e financeiros para transformar resultados de redução do desmatamento em receitas destinadas à conservação ambiental e à implementação de políticas de desenvolvimento sustentável. A COP 31 segue até 20 de novembro, reunindo representantes governamentais, instituições financeiras, empresas e organizações internacionais para discutir medidas relacionadas às mudanças climáticas, ao mercado de carbono e ao financiamento da preservação ambiental. Em Mato Grosso, uma das principais medidas relacionadas ao projeto é a proposta de criação da Companhia Mato-grossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. O projeto de lei foi encaminhado pelo governador à Assembleia Legislativa e prevê a constituição de uma sociedade de economia mista destinada à estruturação, gestão e comercialização de créditos de carbono, créditos de biodiversidade e outros ativos ambientais gerados no território estadual. O Estado possui áreas dos biomas Amazônia, Cerrado e Pantanal, que apresentam características ambientais diferentes e exigem estratégias específicas de conservação. A programação da delegação também contempla discussões sobre riscos climáticos, prevenção e combate a incêndios florestais, economia florestal e estratégias para enfrentar crimes ambientais. Outro aspecto importante da conferência será a discussão sobre mecanismos capazes de ampliar o financiamento climático destinado a regiões que concentram grandes áreas de vegetação nativa. Pivetta permanecerá fora de Mato Grosso até 18 de novembro, de acordo com a programação divulgada pelo Governo do Estado. Sapicuá Rádio Agência, da redação em Cuiabá, Enéas Jacobina

artigo.texto: Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O desenvolvimento de novos projetos de data centers no Brasil mostra que a tendência é que os investidores busquem instalar seus empreendimentos em locais próximos às infraestruturas de energia, para garantir maior segurança no fornecimento de energia elétrica. Em entrevista ao estúdio eixos, durante a EVEx Lisboa 2026, a sócia do Neves, De Rosso e Fonseca Advogados (NDF), Rossana Fonseca, conta que, por mais resiliente que o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) seja, ele está sujeito a interrupções no suprimento. Confira na íntegra. “Hoje a tendência é que os contratos firmados entre os data centers e as empresas de suprimento de energia elétrica estabeleçam multas, porque espera-se que o fornecimento dessa energia seja realizado de forma perene, sem interrupção”. Mas ao mesmo tempo, quando você observa o funcionamento do ONS [Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico], você percebe que é praticamente impossível que um fornecimento, por mais resiliente que ele seja, ocorra sem que haja um mínimo que seja de queda… Isso obviamente empurra os investidores a ter um cuidado maior na busca da localidade de instalação desses data centers”, comentou. A advogada destaca que o Redata traz estímulos ao desenvolvimento de data centers no Brasil, mas ainda há gargalos importantes no licenciamento estadual desses empreendimentos Ela cita que falta linearidade entre os estados no processo de licenciamento – alguns, segundo ela, exigem licença de empreendimentos pequenos que deveriam ser dispensados pelos princípios da Lei Geral do Licenciamento Ambiental. “A gente vê que não há uma linearidade entre os estados para concessão dessas licenças. Para você ter ideia, existem estados, por exemplo, que estão exigindo licenças de pequenos empreendimentos, de pequenos data centers, com consumo não muito grande e que, nesses casos, a ideia é que não fosse necessária licença para esses empreendimentos”, disse. Principais assuntos tratados: - Redata estimula data centers, mas ainda há gargalos no licenciamento estadual. - Falta linearidade entre os estados, e alguns exigem licença de empreendimentos pequenos que deveriam ser dispensados. - Tendência é que investidores busquem localizar data centers perto de subestações. - Litígios climáticos já surgem nos EUA, e o Redata tenta blindar projetos; - Insegurança jurídica vem do Judiciário, do legislador e do regulador, e o Redata busca previsibilidade mínima. - Na mobilidade elétrica, Portugal tem gestão unificada e serviço público, enquanto o Brasil adota lógica comercial com liberdade de preço. artigo.texto: The 442 MWh Smareg 13 battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Vöhringen, Bavaria, Germany, is advancing through a partnership between ju:niz Energy and Envision Energy. Also known as Vöhringen II, the project will add large-scale electricity storage capacity to ju:niz Energy’s German portfolio and support grid flexibility as renewable energy generation expands. Announced on November 9, 2026, Smareg 13 will provide 442 MWh of energy storage capacity. The project will use Envision Energy’s Gen 8 battery storage platform. Additionally, it is designed for four-hour storage and will feature grid-forming capabilities to support grid stability. However, the announcement did not disclose its power output in MW, investment value or expected completion date. ju:niz Energy will oversee project development, financing and delivery. It will also manage the facility’s long-term operation. Meanwhile, Envision Energy will supply the battery storage technology and support project delivery. Smareg 13 is the third project under the companies’ partnership. Together, their portfolio will reach nearly 600 MWh. However, this figure represents the combined capacity of their projects, not Smareg 13 alone. Smareg 13 BESS: Project Scope and Technical Specifications The Smareg 13 BESS project will be built next to the existing Smareg 12 battery storage facility in Vöhringen. Additionally, this location will expand ju:niz Energy’s storage presence in the area. It will also strengthen the company’s collaboration with Envision Energy. However, Smareg 12 is already operational, while Smareg 13 remains a separate project under development. The installation will use Envision’s Gen 8 battery energy storage platform. It combines battery technology with grid-forming capabilities. Additionally, these controls can help stabilise grid voltage and frequency. However, their performance will depend on the system configuration and the requirements of the connected network. The four-hour storage design means the facility is intended to discharge energy over a longer period than a typical two-hour battery installation. However, the exact discharge rate, usable energy, efficiency and operating parameters for the project have not been disclosed yet. The Smareg 13 BESS project also features a low-noise design to address site acoustic requirements. Additionally, this is important for battery installations near existing developments and noise-sensitive areas. Cooling systems and other equipment can affect noise levels. However, specific noise limits and performance figures remain undisclosed. Development Status and Delivery Outlook Smareg 13 BESS project is currently at an advanced stage of development. Construction has also not started. The project’s commissioning date and cost have also not been disclosed yet. The project builds on a partnership involving two earlier battery storage developments. However, Envision stated that those projects had not yet completed delivery when Smareg 13 was announced. Consequently, the new development expands the companies’ project pipeline, while further delivery milestones remain to be confirmed. Contribution to Germany’s Energy Infrastructure Battery energy storage systems help balance electricity supply and demand. They charge when power is available and discharge when the grid needs additional electricity. Additionally, they support Germany’s growing use of wind and solar energy. These renewable sources vary with weather conditions and time of day. Smareg 13 aims to provide additional flexibility and grid-balancing capacity in Bavaria. However, its contribution will depend on construction completion, grid connection and operational performance. Furthermore, the project will support the wider expansion of grid-scale storage infrastructure. This is essential for managing changing electricity generation patterns and maintaining a reliable power supply. Other countries in Europe are also working to increase their battery storage portfolio. Some such as the UK are even repurposing former coal site for storage projects as it being done at the Fiddler’s Ferry BESS site in Warrington, England. For ju:niz Energy, the development adds to a business model covering project development, financing, construction and long-term operation. For Envision Energy, it extends the company’s battery technology deployment in Germany through a growing relationship with a local storage developer. However, the companies have not yet disclosed the full project schedule, financing structure or commercial operating arrangements. It’s in the advanced stage of development Primary purpose: Electricity storage, grid flexibility and renewable energy integration Smareg 13 BESS Project Principal Companies ju:niz Energy GmbH : Responsible for developing, financing and delivering Smareg 13, and for operating the battery storage system over the long term. Envision Energy : Supplier of the Gen 8 battery storage platform and technology and project delivery partner. SMAREG 13 GmbH & Co. artigo.texto: Calibrant Energy has closed a $145 million debt financing facility led by Investec to support solar and battery storage projects across multiple U.S. electricity markets, including a 120 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery energy storage system serving a hyperscale data center customer in PJM. Announced November 10, 2026, the financing combines the recapitalization of operating assets with funding for new construction as the company expands its energy infrastructure portfolio. Citi, Liberty Bank and Siemens Financial Services also participated in the facility. Calibrant said construction mobilization has begun for the 120 MWh battery project, although it has not identified the data center customer, project location, battery supplier or expected completion date. The transaction comes as data center developers face increasing difficulty securing electricity and timely grid connections. Calibrant is positioning battery storage as a way for large electricity users to manage their demand more flexibly, potentially reducing the infrastructure requirements associated with connecting new facilities. $145M financing supports existing and new energy assets The Investec-led facility covers solar and battery storage projects across several U.S. power markets. Its structure serves two purposes: refinancing or recapitalizing operating assets and providing capital for new construction. This makes the transaction broader than a single-project construction loan. Calibrant is using the financing to support an established portfolio while advancing additional infrastructure for large commercial and industrial electricity users. The company has not disclosed how the $145 million is divided between operating assets and new developments. It has also not identified the individual projects included in the financing, provided the loan’s maturity or interest rate, or disclosed how much capital will support the 120 MWh data center installation. Calibrant develops, finances, owns and operates distributed energy infrastructure, including solar generation and battery storage. Its turnkey model allows customers to obtain energy infrastructure without funding the full upfront construction cost themselves. Backed by Macquarie Asset Management, Calibrant reported more than 2.2 gigawatts (GW) of power capacity and 5.9 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage across projects in operation, under construction or covered by exclusive development agreements. The company also disclosed that its portfolio includes additional battery storage sites associated with the same hyperscale data center customer involved in the 120 MWh project. However, it has not provided their locations, capacities or individual development schedules. 120 MWh battery project targets PJM data center power constraints The largest specifically identified battery installation within the financing portfolio is a 120 MWh system serving an undisclosed hyperscale data center customer in the PJM electricity market. Calibrant said site mobilization has begun, marking a move from project financing toward construction. The company has not released the system’s power rating in megawatts, so its discharge duration cannot yet be established. That distinction is important when evaluating the project’s ability to support a data center. A battery’s MW rating determines how much electricity it can deliver at a given moment, while its MWh capacity measures the amount of energy it can store and discharge. For example, a 120 MWh battery rated at 30 MW could theoretically deliver its full rated output for four hours. However, Calibrant has not confirmed that configuration, and the actual discharge duration will depend on the project’s undisclosed power rating and operating conditions. The company says its engineered storage systems allow energy-intensive customers to control when and how they draw electricity from the grid. By charging batteries during selected periods and discharging them when demand rises, data centers can potentially reduce peak grid demand and offer utilities a more flexible load. Calibrant argues that this approach can support faster interconnection timelines and reduce the need for costly grid infrastructure upgrades that might otherwise affect other electricity customers. However, the announcement does not identify which specific grid upgrades the 120 MWh project could avoid, the utility responsible for its interconnection or the operating restrictions attached to the customer’s electricity supply. The extent to which the battery can accelerate the data center’s connection will depend on those arrangements. Previous projects demonstrate Calibrant’s data center strategy The PJM installation builds on Calibrant’s earlier partnerships with data center operators seeking alternatives to lengthy utility infrastructure upgrades. In October 2025, Calibrant and Aligned Data Centers announced plans for a 31 MW/62 MWh battery system at Aligned’s Hillsboro campus in Oregon. The companies designed the installation to help the data center obtain grid power and scale its operations years earlier than conventional utility upgrades would otherwise allow. The project involves coordination with a regional utility to use battery storage as a flexibility resource. Rather than treating the data center as an inflexible electricity consumer, the arrangement allows its power demand to respond to grid requirements. Calibrant also partnered with Iron Mountain in February 2026 to deploy a 23 MWh battery system at an Iron Mountain data center in New Jersey. The installation is designed to integrate with an existing 7.2 MW rooftop solar facility. These projects demonstrate two applications of Calibrant’s model: using battery storage to facilitate data center grid access and combining storage with existing on-site renewable generation. artigo.texto: BYD mira Rolls-Royce com sedã elétrico de mais de 1.000 km de autonomia Apresentado em Abu Dhabi, o Yangwang Altior tem 5,60 metros, um motor por roda e bancos traseiros inspirados na primeira classe O grupo BYD foi a Abu Dhabi mostrar até onde pretende levar sua marca de ultraluxo. Apresentado no sábado (7), o Yangwang Altior é um sedã 100% elétrico de 5,60 metros que mira o território do Rolls-Royce Ghost e do Mercedes-Maybach Classe S. Carros que ficam a milhas de distância do Brasil. O Altior tem quatro motores, portas traseiras que abrem para trás e autonomia anunciada superior a 1.000 km no ciclo chinês CLTC. Mas o melhor lugar para entender o carro é no banco de trás, disse em reserva à coluna Wolfgang Josef Egger, chefe de design da BYD global. O sedã de ultra luxo tem quatro lugares na configuração apresentada, 3,50 metros de entre-eixos, o que significa um super espaço para as pernas. Atrás, os dois assentos reclinam, têm massagem e elevam os apoios para as pernas. Ao acionar o modo de relaxamento, as persianas se fecham e a luz da cabine baixa. O passageiro ainda pode rebater o banco dianteiro com um toque para abrir espaço. Se precisar voltar ao trabalho, há uma tela retrátil de 21,4 polegadas no teto para videoconferências. O som Dynaudio na ficha do automóvel tem 39 alto-falantes e o porta-malas leva 532 litros. Jade, seda e um motor por roda A dianteira quase vertical e as portas de abertura oposta remetem à escola britânica do luxo. O Rolls-Royce é assim. A assinatura chinesa aparece nos detalhes. A Yangwang diz ter buscado inspiração num ding, antigo recipiente cerimonial de bronze que também dá origem a Dingyao, nome do carro na China. Na cabine, que estava fechada para acesso, deu para ver o telão de ponta a ponta do painel, há jade amarelo de hetian polido à mão nas saídas de ar, bordado de seda de Suzhou, couro semi-anilina e tapetes de lã. É no acabamento que a marca procura dar ao sedã uma identidade própria diante dos europeus. Irretocável. A base técnica é a plataforma e⁴, com um motor elétrico por roda e controle independente de torque. Segundo a fabricante, o sistema ajusta a força em cada roda mais de 100 vezes por segundo. É daí que vem a capacidade de girar sobre o próprio eixo, uma manobra curiosa em um carro desse tamanho. A marca também anuncia flutuação de emergência como no SUV U8. No dia a dia, o recurso que mais interessa a quem vai atrás é a suspensão ativa DiSus, que lê o piso à frente e ajusta a resposta em tempo real para reduzir as oscilações da carroceria. É mordomia total. A bateria Blade de segunda geração responde pelo alcance divulgado no ciclo combinado CLTC, padrão de homologação chinês. O Altior também é compatível com o sistema de recarga rápida Flash Charging, cujos tempos para este modelo ainda serão divulgados. A Yangwang não tratou dos valores muito menos dos dados técnicos mas anunciou duas versões: a Executive e a Bespoke. A série limitada Shanhe Dingyun inaugura a linha personalizável com carroceria em tons de marrom e dourado que será exibida no próximo salão de Xangai entre 23 de abril e 2 de maio de 2027 no National Exhibition and Convention Center (NECC). E no Brasil? Como esta coluna antecipou, a Yangwang prepara sua chegada ao Brasil entre o final do primeiro e começo do segundo semestre de 2027, com o SUV U8 e o esportivo U9 entre os primeiros modelos previstos. "O Altior segue sem estreia comercial no país", disse, em Abu Dhabi, Tyler Li, presidente da montadora no país.

artigo.texto: Industrial Manufacturing Data Center Ballot Measures Pass by Wide Margins in Dozens of Communities In last week's elections, voters in small and rural communities adopted dozens of local proposals to pause, limit or ban construction of data centers. Released Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Written by John Egan for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary In last week's elections, voters in small and rural communities adopted dozens of local proposals to pause, limit or ban construction of data centers. Voters Turn Against Data Centers in Local Elections On November 3, voters in 40 local jurisdictions across 10 states turned decisively against data centers, voting to either pause, impede or ban them by 3-to-1 or 4-to-1 margins, according to data tracked by the ballot-tracking website Ballotpedia. The local results are best read as strong, place-specific NIMBY ("Not in My Backyard") resistance in communities where the issue was salient enough to reach the ballot, typically in smaller and rural communities. In a comparatively small handful of local communities, voters backed data center bans, moratoria, size limits or extra review requirements. But there were no state-wide or national data center measures on the November 3 ballot. Ohio alone had 21 data center measures, all of which went against data centers. In addition, seven Illinois communities also voted against data center measures. Small or rural communities in California, Florida, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey and Wisconsin also voted against data center-related measures on Election Day, Ballotpedia said. Earlier this year, the vote-tracking website said voters opposed data center measures in six small communities in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Michigan and California. Later this year, voters will decide the fate of data center initiatives in three small communities in Arkansas and North Dakota, Ballotpedia said. Only one of those local measures passed: In Harwood, North Dakota, voters rejected a proposal that would require additional review before the city could approve of future industrial developments, including data centers. Although data center measures appeared on ballots for federal, state and local offices, the results do not appear to signal a generalized, national turn against the data centers many see as key to dominating 21st century economic and national security strength. In an NBC voter exit poll, voters said four issues--government corruption, cost of living, the war in Iran and immigration enforcement--were the most important issues for them. Approximately 56% said artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. By the Numbers - 41: Number of initiatives relating to data centers that went before the voters in small and rural communities in 10 states November 3. Voters in nearly all cases opposed data centers. - 6: Number of local initiatives in four states opposing or limiting data centers that were voted on before November 3. - 3: Number of voter initiatives relating to data centers in Arkansas and North Dakota that will be voted on in December. Data Centers Likely to Continue Moving Forward The scope and scale of U.S. data center construction plans is unprecedented. For more on that, see September 22, 2026, article - As Data Center Construction Plans Soar, U.S. Electric Utilities Race to Serve Once-in-a-Lifetime Load Growth. Despite votes against data centers in small and rural communities in a number of states, voters surveyed in a national exit poll from NBC, and a national pre-Election Day poll from Fox News, agreed that other issues, among them government corruption, high prices, the war in Iran and immigration enforcement, were far more important to voters across the country. That said, Big Tech companies and data center developers will have to work with a very different Congress and a number of new governors. On a national level, Democrats flipped at least seven seats in the U.S. Senate and at least 41 in the House of Representatives, with about two dozen races still undecided. But both houses will have Democratic majorities when the next congressional term begins in January. Although a few newly elected senators strongly oppose data centers, they will be the most junior members in that chamber when they take their oath of office in two months. Junior members of the U.S. Senate typically do not have the ability to push their measures through that body absent broad support from their party, or from the other party. Election Day also brought a new crop of Democratic governors to office, and some of them opposed data centers. Voters elected new governors in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, states where the previous executives had been enthusiastic supporters of data centers. Those three states accounted for about 173 gigawatts (GW) of data center capacity, roughly 39% of the data center pipeline, according to an analysis by Industrial Info Resources. That said, the outlook for data center construction is not black and white. For example, of the 173 GW of planned data center capacity in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, 14.2 GW already is under construction. And no state, aside from New York, has instituted a pause on data center construction. Will the newly elected governors of those three states follow through on their campaign promises to oppose data center construction? If so, executive orders won't be forthcoming until next January at the earliest. Legislation will take even longer. In either case, litigation may commence. In several states, voters cast their ballots for candidates vying to be members of the state public utility commission, which regulate utilities. Early indications are that several data center skeptics were elected. artigo.texto: BYD faz acordo com a TIM para conexão da frota e da fábrica no Brasil Com parceria, diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades A TIM fechou um contrato com a BYD para fornecer internet a toda a frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil, além do seu polo industrial. Com a parceria, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades onde a operadora oferece cobertura. A previsão é de que cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa contem com essa conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. Assim, a BYD busca avançar no desenvolvimento de novas funcionalidades que envolvam serviços conectados. Com o crescimento de serviços como inteligência artificial e uso de funções como mapas e streaming a bordo, um carro já tem consumo de dados quase equiparável a de um plano básico pós-pago, tipo 'controle'. Do lado da TIM, o negócio representa uma expansão no setor automotivo, onde já oferece conexão para cerca de 630 mil veículos. A tele italiana possui uma parceria com a antiga FCA (Fiat Chrysler Automóveis) – hoje parte do grupo Stellantis – para fornecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em veículos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram no Brasil. O contrato entre a TIM e a BYD envolve também a implantação de infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da montadora em Camaçari, na Bahia. Essa é a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina, com 4,6 milhões de m². O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, garantindo uma rede preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e as demandas tecnológicas do complexo.

artigo.texto: Governo planeja investir R$ 46,3 milhões em plataforma de gerenciamento de dados em data centers O Ministério das Comunicações informou nesta segunda-feira (9) que o governo federal planeja investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma de gerenciamento e distribuição de dados entre mini data centers no Brasil. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados, distribuindo automaticamente os recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Na prática, o Executivo espera que a tecnologia reduza gastos com energia e custos operacionais, acelere o acesso às informações e aumente a proteção de dados estratégicos. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), e o projeto será executado pelo Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD). O prazo de execução é de 36 meses, a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Filho, afirmou que o projeto possibilitará maior autonomia e soberania no tratamento de dados no País. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirmou em nota.

artigo.texto: Newswise — O3-type layered oxides are attractive SIB cathodes because they combine high theoretical capacity with high initial sodium content and flexible TM chemistry. At high voltages (≥4.0 V), deep sodium extraction weakens electrostatic screening between adjacent TM–O slabs, promoting slab gliding, O–P phase transitions, and redox-coupled distortion of TMO6 octahedra. These structural changes can accelerate lattice degradation and compromise electrochemical reversibility. Electrochemically inactive dopants can reinforce the framework, but they may also dilute the redox-active components and reduce reversible capacity. Moreover, their selection has remained largely empirical, often guided by average ionic radius, oxidation state, or elemental composition. Such averaged descriptors cannot fully account for the distribution of ionic field strengths among constituent TM cations, which is associated with local bonding heterogeneity, strain accumulation, and nonuniform phase evolution. A quantitative descriptor that connects dopant chemistry with ionic field strength heterogeneity is therefore essential for designing structurally reversible, high-voltage O3-type cathodes. The study, published (DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c11691) online on October 20, 2026, in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, comes from Nankai University, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, the China Spallation Neutron Source Science Center, the Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the Haihe Laboratory of Sustainable Chemical Transformations. The team combined synthesis, structural analysis, electrochemical testing, and computation to test the design rule for O3-type SIB cathodes. The work systematically investigates how ionic field strength disparity influences local TM–O coordination, phase evolution, lattice-strain accumulation, and electrochemical stability under high-voltage operation. The study compares a low-η cathode (η = 0.34) with a high-η analogue (η = 0.395). Both adopt the same O3-type framework, but the low-η material follows a more reversible O3–P3–O3 path structural evolution, and avoids the additional high-voltage phase transitions seen in the high-η sample. In situ X-ray diffraction reveals smaller changes in lattice parameters for the low-η cathode, indicating improved structural stability during deep desodiation. Differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) shows no detectable O₂ evolution within the investigated voltage window and substantially suppressed CO₂ generation, suggesting mitigated oxygen-related degradation and interfacial side reactions. Furthermore, synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy and atomic-resolution strain mapping reveal reduced local coordination disorder, improved structural reversibility, and suppressed heterogeneous strain accumulation. These improvements are consistent with an ionic field strength compensation mechanism, in which inactive cations with intermediate field strengths mitigate disparities among redox-active cations, promoting more homogeneous TM–O bonding and coordinated structural evolution during cycling. Notably, the low-η cathode exhibits a much smaller increase in η during desodiation (7.35%) than the high-η counterpart (17.72%), further supporting the importance of maintaining a stable ionic field strength distribution. The descriptor also enables composition-guided dopant screening, as demonstrated by two additional cathode chemistries with improved electrochemical performance. A control pair with comparable average ionic radii and TM valence states but different η values further confirms the significance of ionic field strength disparity beyond conventional averaged descriptors. The authors said η turns dopant selection from an empirical search into a quantitative design task. They said the descriptor captures local chemical-field disparities that average composition, radius, or valence cannot resolve, and that lowering it helps synchronize TM–O bond changes and phase evolution during deep desodiation. They added that low η does not require maximal compositional complexity and that simpler cation combinations may avoid capacity and processing penalties. They also said the framework should be extended cautiously to oxygen-redox cathodes, where TM migration and lattice-oxygen loss add separate failure modes. The approach could accelerate cathode development for stationary storage and high-voltage SIBs by narrowing dopant candidates before costly cell testing. Because η is calculated from formal valence, ionic radius, and cation fraction, it can be adapted to other multicomponent O3-type layered oxides. The results also suggest that low disparity, rather than high entropy alone, should guide composition design; excessive inactive ions can reduce reversible capacity and increase synthesis risk. Before commercial use, the rule needs validation across more compositions, including oxygen-redox-active cathodes, and under practical full-cell conditions. By connecting cation-level chemical descriptors with macroscopic electrochemical performance, this work provides a quantitative foundation for the design of more durable sodium-ion battery cathodes. ### References DOI Original Source URL https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c11691 Funding information The Acknowledgments list the Ministry of Science and Technology of China (2025YFE0100200); National Natural Science Foundation of China (22479080, 92372203, 92372001); Tianjin Natural Science Foundation Project (24JCJQJC00220, 24ZXZSSS00310); Haihe Laboratory of Sustainable Chemical Transformations (25HHWCSS00013); Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities of Nankai University (63253167, 63261001); and the “111 Center” (B25010). artigo.texto: Energy Investment LLC and CORNEX New Energy have entered into a strategic cooperation agreement to develop a 1 GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Romania, supporting the country’s efforts to strengthen energy storage infrastructure and integrate renewable energy into its electricity network. The agreement follows an announcement made in June 2026 during The smarter E Europe exhibition, held in Munich from June 23 to 25. CORNEX highlighted the partnership in its official communication regarding its participation in the event, referring to a 1 GWh agreement with Energy Investment for a project in Romania. Under the arrangement, Energy Investment LLC will be responsible for the complete development and execution of the project, while CORNEX New Energy will supply the battery energy storage technology. The cooperation agreement represents a development partnership and does not indicate that the proposed storage capacity is already operational. According to information published by Energy Investment on LinkedIn on June 26, 2026, the company will oversee the project’s development and implementation. Romanian publication Profit.ro also reported on June 29 that CORNEX would provide the storage technology. Marius Ion, Founder and CEO of Energy Investment LLC, stated that energy storage would play an important role in Romania’s energy transition by enabling renewable electricity to be used when required by the power system. He highlighted that the partnership with CORNEX would provide access to the technology needed to advance the proposed 1 GWh project. The company indicated that the first projects could reach commissioning in 2027. However, the timeline remains dependent on several development stages, including permitting, grid connection, regulatory authorizations, financing and equipment procurement. The proposed project is expected to support Romania’s renewable energy integration by providing storage capabilities to improve electricity system flexibility. The partnership also reflects growing cooperation between international technology suppliers and project developers as European markets expand their battery storage infrastructure. artigo.texto: Seu navegador não suporta esse video. Oposição terá, no mínimo, 54 senadores, caminha para maioria robusta na Câmara e elege governadores em estados importantes e simbólicos. O mercado financeiro focado em tecnologia não tem vivido seus melhores dias recentemente e o índice Nasdaq chegou a registrar sua maior queda diária desde abril de 2025 na última quinta-feira (5). A queda foi de 5,5% e resultou na redução de US$ 2,5 trilhões (R$ 13,4 trilhões em conversão direta) do valor de mercado das principais empresas do setor, influenciadas pelas midterms dos Estados Unidos. O motivo para esse derretimento abrupto tem relação com as recentes eleições de meio de mandato, as midterms norte-americanas. Na última rodada, a expressiva vitória do Partido Democrata contra o Partido Republicano no pleito acendeu o temor de que a expansão da inteligência artificial sofra mais regulações nas mãos dos democratas. A Nvidia, empresa mais poderosa do planeta e absoluta na venda de chips para servidores, viu suas ações caírem 9%. Com a rival direta, a AMD, a queda foi ainda mais chamativa e bateu nos 17%. O índice de semicondutores da Filadélfia (SOX) também registrou uma queda notória de 12%, o nível mais baixo dos últimos seis meses. O clima pesado não está restrito somente aos Estados Unidos e chega a outros países em um efeito cascata. Bolsas asiáticas, como a japonesa Nikkei e a sul-coreana Kospi, operaram em forte queda. O índice VIX, chamado de “termômetro do medo” em Wall Street, registrou seu maior salto desde 2024 e aumentou a apreensão dos acionistas. - 🪧Índice VIX (Termômetro do medo): essa é uma métrica de Wall Street que mede a expectativa de volatilidade do mercado para os próximos 30 dias. Quando o índice dispara, significa que há insegurança por parte de investidores e possibilidade de quedas na bolsa. IA pode esbarrar em decisões políticas Analistas do mercado financeiro mostram que o receio de acionistas e investidores é que os democratas façam força contra a construção de novos data centers em solo americano. Um dos motivos é o fato desses centros de dados exigirem grandes volumes de água para resfriar os servidores, além dos gastos em energia e o barulho. Uma estimativa do UBS aponta que quase 30% da capacidade adicional de data centers esperada para 2028 nos Estados Unidos tem risco de sofrer paralisações. Como o mercado de IA se expandiu rapidamente nos últimos anos, isso se tornou um empecilho para investidores da categoria, que demandam novas instalações para o treinamento dos modelos de IA. Gigantes responsáveis por essas tecnologias, como a Amazon e Alphabet (dona do Google) viram quedas de 2,2%. No caso da Microsoft, o recuo foi de 3,6%. Aliás, a companhia de Redmond já teria começado a apertar a supervisão de projetos terceirizados de data centers. Por falar em IA e problemas financeiros, o caso de infidelidade do CEO da Nvidia pode trazer grandes consequências à empresa e ao mercado global. Não esqueça de continuar ligado no TecMundo para acompanhar outros artigos como esse e não perder as principais informações da indústria de tecnologia. Com informações de Reuters.

artigo.texto: Prefeitura abre licitação de R$ 7 milhões para manter data center da Capital Empresa vencedora ficará responsável pelo suporte por 2 anos A Prefeitura de Campo Grande lançou licitação para contratar uma empresa especializada em manter o funcionamento e a "alta disponibilidade" do data center da Capital. De acordo com o aviso de licitação publicado nesta segunda-feira (9), o Executivo pode investir até R$ 7 milhões. RESUMO Nossa ferramenta de IA resume a notícia para você! A Prefeitura de Campo Grande abriu licitação para contratar empresa que mantenha o funcionamento e a alta disponibilidade do data center da Capital, com investimento de até R$ 7 milhões. O contrato prevê estrutura em contêiner, operação ininterrupta, manutenção preventiva, preditiva e corretiva, peças, insumos e suporte técnico por dois anos. Segundo a Agetec, o data center, no Horto Florestal, já existe, e a lei impede aditivos. As propostas vão até 25 de novembro de 2026, às 7h44. O edital prevê que a estrutura que dará suporte ao data center será um contêiner. A empresa vencedora deverá entregar a estrutura, com operação ininterrupta, manutenção integral preventiva, preditiva e corretiva, fornecer peças, insumos e suporte técnico para garantir a estabilidade e a segurança por dois anos. Ao Campo Grande News, o diretor-presidente da Agetec (Agência Municipal de Tecnologia da Informação e Inovação de Campo Grande), Leandro Basmage, explicou que já há um data center, localizado na região do Horto Florestal, e que a licitação é referente ao serviço que garante o funcionamento. Segundo ele, a licitação foi lançada porque a legislação não permite aditivos e renovação. O certame será coordenado pela Secretaria Especial de Licitações e Contratos. As empresas interessadas têm até as 7h44 do dia 25 de novembro de 2026 para enviar suas propostas. A sessão de disputa de preços será aberta logo em seguida, às 7h45 do mesmo dia, pelo site compras.campogrande.ms.gov.br. Receba as principais notícias do Estado pelo Whats. artigo.texto: A 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), iniciada na segunda-feira (9), em Antália, na Turquia, colocou a execução dos compromissos internacionais como fiel das negociações entre os países. Até o dia 20, governos, instituições financeiras, empresas e organizações internacionais discutem mecanismos para transformar as metas do Acordo de Paris em investimentos, políticas públicas e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Para o agronegócio, a agenda inclui financiamento de sistemas produtivos resilientes, recuperação de terras degradadas, redução das emissões de metano e instrumentos econômicos relacionados à conservação ambiental. “Além de enviar sinais, a COP31 precisa acelerar as soluções”, afirmou Simon Stiell, secretário-executivo da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (UNFCCC), durante a abertura oficial. Em seu discurso, Stiell cobrou medidas para ampliar o financiamento da adaptação climática, facilitar o acesso dos países aos recursos já comprometidos e acelerar a redução das emissões. A conferência ocorre em um momento no qual os governos precisam detalhar como executar seus planos nacionais, incluindo políticas de energia, uso da terra, indústria e infraestrutura. Um dos pontos apresentados pela presidência turca é a segurança alimentar, incluída entre os dez temas prioritários da Agenda de Ação da COP31. O programa contempla a relação entre disponibilidade de água, produção agrícola e mudanças climáticas, além do financiamento para mulheres agricultoras, participação de jovens e desenvolvimento de sistemas produtivos capazes de enfrentar eventos extremos. A proposta é coordenar iniciativas governamentais e privadas, embora os compromissos anunciados nessa agenda não tenham automaticamente o mesmo caráter das decisões negociadas entre os países. A conferência é presidida por Murat Kurum, ministro do Meio Ambiente, Urbanização e Mudança Climática da Turquia, enquanto Chris Bowen, ministro australiano de Mudança Climática e Energia, conduz as negociações formais. O arranjo entre os dois países foi definido durante a COP30, realizada em Belém, no Pará, em 2025. Na abertura, Kurum apresentou uma iniciativa denominada Climate Implementation Bridge, concebida para conectar necessidades locais de financiamento e tecnologia à capacidade de instituições e governos de executar projetos. A estrutura e os resultados desse mecanismo ainda dependem dos desdobramentos da conferência. Para o Brasil, que passou a presidência da COP à Turquia, uma das frentes é ampliar o financiamento de atividades agropecuárias relacionadas à recuperação de áreas degradadas e à redução de emissões. No primeiro dia, a programação do Pavilhão Brasil incluiu um debate organizado com a participação do Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária, do Imaflora e de organizações internacionais sobre recuperação de terras agrícolas, segurança alimentar e mitigação de metano. A atividade integra os trabalhos da iniciativa RAIZ, voltada ao investimento em agricultura resiliente e à meta de degradação líquida zero de terras. A discussão prossegue em 11 de novembro, quando representantes da Organização das Nações Unidas para a Alimentação e a Agricultura (FAO), do Ministério da Agricultura e da coalizão internacional Food and Land Use Coalition participam de um encontro sobre investimentos na restauração produtiva de terras e em sistemas agroalimentares resilientes. Dois dias depois, em 13 de novembro, o tema retorna à programação brasileira em um painel com participação do Conselho Empresarial Mundial para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável (WBCSD), do Ministério da Agricultura e da consultoria Boston Consulting Group (BCG), dedicado à mobilização de capital internacional para a recuperação produtiva de áreas degradadas. A presença dessas iniciativas na programação coloca em discussão um dos desafios da transição agrícola: a disponibilidade de financiamento para práticas que exigem investimento antes de gerar retorno econômico. Recuperação de pastagens, melhoria do manejo do solo e adoção de sistemas integrados dependem de recursos, assistência técnica e acompanhamento dos resultados. O financiamento também aparece entre as prioridades das negociações internacionais. Stiell defendeu a implementação do compromisso de triplicar os recursos destinados à adaptação climática, estabelecido na conferência anterior. A questão envolve a capacidade dos países em desenvolvimento de financiar obras de infraestrutura, sistemas de produção, gestão de recursos hídricos e medidas de proteção contra secas e inundações. O acesso aos recursos, as condições de financiamento e os mecanismos de acompanhamento permanecem entre os assuntos que dependem de decisões dos governos. Mercado de carbono entra nas discussões Outra frente da participação brasileira é a implantação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), criado para estabelecer um mercado regulado de carbono no país. O Ministério da Fazenda informou que uma das ações na COP31 será debater os avanços da regulamentação e da cooperação internacional nessa área. A programação inclui a participação da secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis, em debates sobre mensuração, relato e verificação de emissões, contabilidade de carbono e integração entre os sistemas nacionais. O Brasil preside a Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono, lançada durante a COP30, com China e União Europeia na copresidência. artigo.texto: Solidion Technology Reaffirms Commitment to Address Growing Energy Storage Needs of AI Data Centers Solidion’s patented anode technology and PEAK UPS design target the space, lifespan and cost demands of AI-scale infrastructure. DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI) (“Solidion Technology” or “the Company”), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion’s approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company’s strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion’s portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion, said, AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage, “Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs.” Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market Solidion Technology Reaffirms Commitment to Address Growing Energy Storage Needs of AI Data Centers, source

artigo.texto: ‘We are all in’: Honda solid-state battery plans are advanced and could blow past BYD, Chery and more Dom works as CarsGuide's News Editor after starting his career at the Sydney Morning Herald's Drive section before moving into News Corp's automotive coverage. Read full bio CarsGuide puts every effort into ensuring the accuracy of the information it publishes. Double-check the details that matter to you before buying. Learn more about how we fact check. Key takeaways: - Honda is well advanced in its plans to produce solid-state batteries at scale - Honda Australia boss said solid-state batteries have cost, weight, performance, charging times benefits - The CEO said it was just a matter of reducing the time needed to make the cells so it can be scaled for mass-production A new electric car arms race is coming to a head, with multiple car and battery makers claiming solid-state cells are just around the corner. Honda Australia boss Jay Joseph told CarsGuide the benefits of the new electric car power-plant are off the charts. “Solid-state absolutely is a game-changer,” said Joseph. “Cost, weight, performance, charging times. It is a hard reset in the capability of battery electric vehicles (BEVs), and we are all in on that. “Dr Chris Brooks, who’s the chief scientist over in the lab that’s doing [solid-state development] absolutely believes this is a game-changer. You can get twice the energy density in the same way, or you can get the same energy density in half the weight at a dramatically reduced cost,” he said. Solid-state battery production problems Many carmakers have been claiming solid-state batteries are imminent for years, but all have blown past their claimed deadline. Joseph said there are two elements to this: one is the battery chemistry and the other is scaling production. Honda appears to have the chemistry sorted, with the company well advanced in the manufacturing stage. Subscribe to our newsletter Stay up to date with the CarsGuide weekly newsletter By subscribing you agree to our Privacy Policy. “The way batteries are developed, you develop the chemistry, you figure out what works, you do all the testing on that, and then you start figuring out how to manufacture it,” he said. “We’re fairly advanced in that production proof of concept. “It’s just getting the time out of the process so that we can scale it out.” Joseph explained the structure of solid-state batteries is more brittle and the testing environment for automotive is the toughest outside of military-specification, which is part of the difficulty getting the cells to market. Honda won’t waste solid-state benefits Joseph cautioned against carmakers wasting the benefits of the futuristic cells by making bigger and heavier electric cars to house them. He said the batteries could be used to make EVs lighter and deliver the same driving range as current vehicles. Lighter electric cars would be more efficient, drive better, be safer and create less wear and tear on roads and consumable parts such as brakes. Honda currently has one electric vehicle on sale in Australia, the compact Super One. It has a small battery that delivers a claimed range of 202km, but if it has a solid-state battery in the future it could have a driving range of more than 400km with the same sized power-source. Honda is building a new factory in the US state of Ohio to build large hybrid SUVs before switching to EVs. Honda’s solid-state proof of concept solid-state production line is also in Ohio, which points to potential future US-built large electric SUVs. Chery hot on Honda’s heels Chery has confirmed its Exlantix sub-brand - called Exeed in China - is headed to Australia in 2027. Exeed is the "crown jewel" in Chery’s stable and will be the first to debut the company’s solid-state battery tech in 2027. The first Exeed vehicle in China to score the new battery is claimed to have an electric driving range of up to 1500km. Chery Australia Chief Operating Officer Lucas Harris said “we won’t be left wanting” for solid-state battery-powered cars Down Under. When and what form those vehicles will be is still a mystery. artigo.texto: MINNEAPOLIMEDIA NEWS | Minneapolis Advances Data Center Restrictions as Residents Challenge Energy Demand, Water Use and the Future of Downtown Development With a temporary moratorium approaching expiration, the City Council faces a November 12 vote on regulations that would limit where data centers can operate and how much space their computing equipment can occupy. MINNEAPOLIS, MN (November 10, 2026). Minneapolis is moving toward its first specific zoning regulations for data centers as city officials confront growing public opposition to facilities that consume substantial electricity and water while offering developers another potential use for vacant commercial buildings. A City Council committee advanced proposed regulations Monday, November 9, setting up a full council vote scheduled for Thursday, November 12. The proposal would permit data centers in existing buildings within two downtown zoning districts while limiting the space devoted to servers and related computing equipment to 150,000 square feet. The debate comes as Minneapolis approaches the November 21 expiration of a six-month moratorium on new data centers. If city officials fail to adopt new regulations or extend the moratorium, additional facilities could continue to qualify for permits under existing zoning rules. The decision has implications for neighborhoods, electricity customers, water resources, commercial property owners and the city's long-term development strategy. Eight Existing Facilities, Limited Specific Regulation Minneapolis already has eight data centers. Yet the city's zoning code does not explicitly establish a separate regulatory category for them. Under existing rules, data centers can generally be permitted in 10 of the city's 15 primary zoning districts without specific limits on their size. That arrangement has become increasingly controversial as demand for computing capacity grows alongside artificial intelligence and cloud-based services. Data centers house servers, networking equipment and supporting infrastructure. Their operations require continuous electricity and systems capable of controlling equipment temperatures. The scale of those requirements varies substantially by facility, making it important to distinguish a smaller urban installation from a massive industrial computing campus. Minneapolis officials are attempting to establish standards before additional development proposals advance. A Proposal Focused on Downtown Buildings The ordinance recommended Monday would restrict data centers to certain existing buildings in two downtown zoning districts. It would also impose a 150,000-square-foot limit on white space, the area occupied by computing equipment and servers. That distinction matters because a building's total square footage can include offices, corridors, mechanical equipment and other areas not used directly for computing. Limiting white space is one way to regulate the scale of an operation through land-use authority. The proposal would narrow the range of locations where data centers could be developed, rather than permitting them broadly across the city. Supporters of tighter restrictions argue that facilities should not be allowed to expand without meaningful examination of their effects on surrounding neighborhoods and public infrastructure. Others contend that data centers could help restore activity and property value to underused downtown commercial buildings. Public Opposition Has Grown The proposal follows months of public debate. Approximately 50 people testified during an October Planning Commission hearing, while more than 1,600 public comments have been submitted concerning data center regulations. Reporting indicates that the overwhelming majority of those comments opposed additional data centers. Some residents have called for a complete ban. A council committee previously deadlocked 6–6 on such a proposal, demonstrating that elected officials remain divided over how restrictive the city's approach should be. The debate has intensified following opposition to a proposed data center at the former Minnesota Star Tribune printing facility. For opponents, the central concern is whether the economic benefits of new development justify the demands placed on public resources. Water and Electricity Are Central Questions Data centers can require substantial electricity to power servers and supporting systems. Some also consume significant water for cooling, depending on the technology used. Minneapolis planning officials have argued that the city's existing water infrastructure can accommodate facilities of the scale contemplated under the proposed ordinance. The city has the capacity to draw approximately 100 million gallons of water per day from the Mississippi River and currently uses roughly 55 million gallons daily, according to figures cited during the debate. Those numbers describe system capacity, not the water consumption of any particular proposed facility. One existing data center associated with Sleep Number has reportedly averaged approximately 3 million gallons of water per month. That example illustrates why residents want project-specific information rather than general assurances about capacity. Questions also remain about electricity demand, infrastructure upgrades and whether increased consumption could affect costs borne by other customers. Those effects depend on utility regulation, project design and the financial arrangements governing new infrastructure. The Limits of City Authority Minnesota municipalities can regulate aspects of data center development through zoning, including location, physical size and certain noise impacts. However, state law limits municipal authority over matters such as electrical megawatt capacity, air emissions and heating and cooling systems. That division of responsibility complicates the debate.
