artigo.texto: GOOCHLAND COUNTY, Va. — Hundreds of Goochland and Henrico County residents packed Goochland High School Tuesday evening as concerns grow over the possibility of additional hyperscale data center development near the Goochland-Henrico border. The crowd filled the auditorium, with some attendees standing near the entrance as nearly 30 people took the podium during public comment. “Put a stop to this immediately,” one speaker told county leaders. “The livelihood and safety of so many people are at stake.” One project in particular drew attention Tuesday night. Google is considering purchasing roughly 1,000 acres in West Creek Business Park, where the technology company could build a 1,200-megawatt data center campus. Google is currently conducting due diligence on the property and has not committed to purchasing the land or submitted a site plan to Goochland County. The proposed site is north of Patterson Avenue near Route 288 and sits within Goochland County’s recently approved Technology Overlay District. That designation has become a major concern for some residents because data centers within the district can be developed by right, meaning an individual project would not have to go through a separate public hearing and approval process. The potential Google campus is one of several large data center proposals to surface in eastern Goochland County. A 900-megawatt data center proposed near Henrico County’s Tuckahoe area is already moving through Goochland’s public approval process. Three additional proposed developments totaling roughly 2,000 megawatts have also surfaced nearby, including the potential Google project. Those additional sites fall within the Technology Overlay District. Residents who spoke Tuesday raised concerns about transparency surrounding the projects, as well as their possible effects on the environment, public health and local infrastructure. One speaker urged county leaders to require more information from developers before allowing projects to move forward, including a health impact assessment, environmental impact analysis, air quality analysis, decommissioning plan and monitoring plan. Others said they worry residents could lose their opportunity to influence projects once developers move further into the planning process. “We’re asking you to make sure progress doesn’t come at the expense of the people who call Goochland home,” another speaker said. The debate is also drawing residents from neighboring Henrico County. Opponents of the proposed development say more than 28,000 Henrico residents and 10 schools are within 2.5 miles of the potential Google site. Google’s interest in Goochland became public after the county announced the company was evaluating the West Creek property. According to the county, discussions surrounding the site date back to early 2024, when the Virginia Economic Development Partnership contacted Goochland about showing potential sites to a data center user. A July 14 State Corporation Commission filing also referenced a potential 1,200-megawatt data center campus in eastern Goochland without identifying the company behind it. Google later confirmed its interest in the West Creek site. For now, the project remains only a possibility. Google has not purchased the property or submitted plans to the county. But residents who packed Tuesday’s meeting said they want answers about the potential impacts of large-scale data center development before projects are allowed to move forward. artigo.texto: Fort Worth residents overwhelmingly supported pausing data center development and urged city officials to use a temporary suspension to carefully develop strict but sound regulations during a public hearing about the city’s plan to adopt a moratorium. Fort Worth City Council held the first of two public hearings required to adopt the moratorium on data center development, hearing testimony from about two dozen speakers Nov. 10. Before meeting for the hearing, council members received a recommended list of data center regulations from the advisory committee created this summer to help shape Fort Worth’s relationship with the booming industry. “Fort Worth has a unique opportunity to take the bull by the horns and make real progress that is for the community,” speaker Esmeralda Zuniga said during the hearing. “The moratorium should be passed.” Tuesday’s hearing was the next step in a state-mandated process regulating how cities may launch a moratorium to pause development on specific types of properties. Council members voted unanimously in August to initiate the process of a moratorium, but they must host two public hearings and take two separate votes before the moratorium can begin. Under the timeline required by law, Fort Worth’s data center moratorium would go into effect Feb. 23, if approved by three-fourths of the council. It would end May 24 unless the council extended it for another 90 days. During that period, Texas lawmakers convene in the 90th Legislature, considering statewide regulations to the booming data center industry Gov. Greg Abbott welcomed to the state last year. Abbott has since directed state agencies to halt permitting on data centers and audit all projects seeking to connect to the state’s electric grid. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, an Austin-area Democrat, defeated Abbott in the midterm election after criticizing his handling of the industry throughout her campaign and calling for a statewide moratorium on data centers to last at least until the Legislature meets in January. Last month, Hinojosa vowed to issue a ban on data center approvals until the Legislature passes laws “to protect Texans.” Other priorities from her campaign include stopping data center developers from using nondisclosure agreements that make it hard to track their projects, requiring data center operators to hire union workers and protecting water supplies. It’s unclear how a statewide pause would impact the moratorium Fort Worth already has in process. Several speakers spoke of the Nov. 3 midterm results, which saw Tarrant County and Texas flip blue after decades of GOP leadership. The election results showed how Fort Worth and Texas voters feel about data centers, said Julie Waters, the founder of Texans United Against Data Centers. “Texas is not for sale. Fort Worth is not for sale,” Waters said. “Pass this moratorium and make it loud and clear to every data center developer that they cannot steal our land and water just because they donated to your campaign.” All but one speaker supported the moratorium. Fort Worth resident David Martinez opposed the plan, speaking in favor of artificial intelligence and its potential for technological innovation. Once in effect, Fort Worth’s moratorium would last 90 days, legally barring new data centers from being built and halting city decision-making on requests from developers for zoning changes and building permits to accommodate data centers. Construction would continue on data center projects that had already been approved and permitted, such as the $10 billion project led by energy conglomerate Black Mountain in southeast Fort Worth. Meanwhile, bill filing opened Monday for the Legislature, and proposals so far include banning tax incentives for data centers and requiring operators to share more information about their water usage. State Rep. Salman Bhojani, a Euless Democrat, filed a bill that would require data center developers to register their projects with affected local governments and disclose their water and electricity usage, as well as submit assessments of their impact on such resources. Incoming Republican Rep. Armin Mizani, the former Keller mayor elected last week to a Texas House seat representing northeast Tarrant County, filed a bill that would require city approval for data centers to be built within a municipality’s boundaries and county approval to build one within an unincorporated area. At a panel on data centers hosted by the Fort Worth Report last month, Tarrant County commissioner Matt Krause and Fort Worth City Council member Elizabeth Beck said they hope the Legislature expands authority for local governments to regulate where data centers may be built as the industry continues to grow. They also agreed on a desire to see lawmakers adopt regulations on the state’s water supply, air quality, energy use and state sales taxes in relation to data centers. During the panel, Krause said he plans to introduce a resolution at this month’s commissioners court meeting that would end tax abatements for data centers in Tarrant County. A vote on that resolution is expected Nov. 17. Cecilia Lenzen is a government accountability reporter for the Fort Worth Report. Contact her at cecilia.lenzen@fortworthreport.org. artigo.texto: NTPC Green Energy Limited (NGEL) has invited online bids for the supply of battery containers and Grid-Forming Power Conversion Systems (PCS) for its 10 GW/40 GWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) programme. The last date for submission of bids is December 8, 2026. The tender is being issued free of cost. Brief Scope of Work Under the scope of work, NGEL has specified that the bidder must supply lithium-ion (LFP)-based containerised battery systems integrated with Grid-Forming Power Conversion Systems (PCS). The total BESS capacity covered under the tender is 40.580 GWh, which will be developed across three blocks in different phases. Bidders are permitted to quote for any one, multiple or all blocks across the specified phases. Under Phase 1, the required capacities are 4.98 GWh, 6.600 GWh and 5.840 GWh. Phase 2 covers a capacity of 4.560 GWh, while Phase 3 comprises capacities of 5.800 GWh, 6.800 GWh and 6.000 GWh. The projects will be executed in phases, with the selected bidder responsible for supervising the erection, installation and commissioning of the systems at the respective project sites, up to the PCS output terminals. The bidder will also be responsible for servicing and maintaining the systems for 15 years from the commissioning date of each project under a Long-Term Service Agreement (LTSA).

artigo.texto: AUBURNDALE, Fla. — Roughly 500 people packed an Auburndale meeting Tuesday night to hear more about a proposed data center, with hundreds more watching online, as questions about water use, electricity, and the project's impact on the community took center stage. The proposed Auburndale Technology Center would convert two existing warehouse buildings along Pace Road into a data storage and computing facility. Texas-based Hillwood Development Company says the project is designed to be a smaller alternative to large, hyperscale data centers and to address concerns that have emerged around similar developments. Watch report from Chad Mills: But for many people who came to the meeting, the assurances were not enough. “My concerns are the water usage, the electric usage, what they’re going to be doing with the water once they use it — whether it’s going to affect the environment,” said Teresa Necaise Waggle, who lives in Lake Alfred. Robert Morris, also of Lake Alfred, said he is concerned about whether the facility could put additional strain on the electric grid. “We have a new neighborhood, and our power goes out all the time, so it flickers and it’s gone out quite a few times without even rain or anything, so that’s kind of concerning,” Morris said. Why the project doesn't need another City Commission vote One of the central questions surrounding the project is how it can move forward without another vote from the Auburndale City Commission. The answer goes back to 2023. The property was annexed into Auburndale in December 2022. In December 2023, commissioners approved a change to the property's future land-use designation and rezoned it as an Industrial Planned Unit Development. The original proposal for the property included research and development buildings, an e-commerce and logistics building, and other commercial buildings. The Planning Commission voted 3-2 in October 2023 to recommend denying that initial proposal. They cited concerns about logistics, building size, and traffic. The plan was subsequently revised. Distribution as the primary use was prohibited in two of the buildings, while research and development, light manufacturing, health technology, and information sciences were among the uses allowed. The city says the 2023 zoning approval allows the property to now be used as a data center. The city approved the zoning before Hillwood acquired the property and proposed a data center and before data centers became a lightning rod issue across Florida and the country. City Manager Jeffrey Brown said the public had an opportunity to attend and comment during the 2023 approval process. He also said the city does not need another Commission vote for the current proposal. However, that does not mean the project has cleared every regulatory hurdle. City staff received an application on Nov. 4 for the interior retrofit of the two buildings. The city attorney emphasized during the workshop that the project is still going through the permitting process, with additional work required by agencies outside the City Commission. Water use and cooling remain major concerns Hillwood estimates the facility will use approximately 4,665 gallons of water per day for both buildings. The company says it will use a closed-loop cooling system that recirculates water rather than continuously drawing in new water to cool the computer systems. Hillwood argues the projected use is lower than the amount anticipated for the warehouse development previously planned for the property. The city's presentation cited an earlier estimate of approximately 9,500 gallons of potable water per day for the entire site, with a maximum permitted amount of 42,975 gallons per day under the previous development idea. But the water questions go beyond the developer's daily-use estimate. The Southwest Florida Water Management District told Tampa Bay 28 that an Environmental Resource Permit would not be required if the data center uses the existing buildings and the developer makes no other site changes. However, the district said any existing Water Use Permit would need to be modified to reflect data center operations. Those modifications would require approval from the district's Governing Board. Hillwood's senior vice president, Charles Korrell, said the project was designed to reduce its environmental footprint. “This project was designed to minimize environmental impact, use less water, and have less impact than the existing industrial use,” Korrell said. Power demand and noise also draw scrutiny Electricity is another major issue. Hillwood says the first phase of the project will require approximately 350 megawatts of electricity. At full development, the facility could require as much as 700 megawatts. Tampa Electric Company is expected to supply the power. The developer says it will pay all costs associated with generating and delivering electricity to the facility, consistent with relatively new protections in state law. Noise was also discussed. “Noise at the property line will be less than the truck distribution facility and at a level consistent with a quiet conversation,” Korrell with Hillwood said. The promise drew some laughter from the room. Developer points to jobs and economic impact Hillwood is also arguing that the project could bring significant economic benefits to Auburndale and Polk County. The company projects approximately 300 permanent jobs and as many as 1,300 construction jobs at peak activity. It also projects billions of dollars in economic and tax benefits over 15 years. Some people who attended the meeting said they see potential in that argument. Tony Acosta, who lives just outside Auburndale, said he believes the project could be a better model than some other data center proposals in Polk County. “I think in comparison to the other data centers that, you know, have been proposed around the county and around the state, I think this is probably one of the better models that they have,” Acosta

artigo.texto: O Acre deu mais um passo no processo de certificação internacional de seus créditos de carbono. Nesta terça-feira, 10, em Antalya, na Turquia, a governadora Mailza Assis, que ali participa da 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), reuniu-se com a direção da ART Trees, entidade responsável por registrar e validar projetos de carbono considerados de alta integridade ambiental., para discutir o andamento da auditoria necessária ao reconhecimento dos créditos de carbono jurisdicionais do estado. A reunião é um desdobramento das articulações realizadas em junho, durante a Semana de Ação Climática de Londres, quando Mailza se encontrou com Mary Grady, presidente da ART. Desta vez, participaram a presidente do Instituto de Mudanças Climáticas e Regulação de Serviços Ambientais (IMC), Neide de Lima; o consultor internacional de mercados de carbono, Victor Hugo Rondon; o chefe de gabinete Madson Cameli e a diretora associada da ART, Lúcia Madrid. O objetivo foi atualizar o andamento da auditoria e alinhar os procedimentos necessários para avançar na certificação. O reconhecimento internacional permitirá ao Acre, caso todas as exigências sejam cumpridas, registrar créditos de carbono jurisdicionais e abrir caminho para futuras negociações no mercado internacional. Durante o encontro, Mailza agradeceu a disponibilidade da representante do ART e reforçou o compromisso do governo em concluir o processo. “Estamos colocando um grande esforço, por meio do IMC, para concluir esse processo, que será muito importante para o desenvolvimento do Acre”, afirmou a governadora. Segundo Neide Lima, a auditoria é realizada por uma empresa independente, seguindo os critérios técnicos e metodológicos estabelecidos pelo padrão internacional ART Trees, que estabelece critérios internacionais para a contabilização, verificação e registro de reduções de emissões provenientes do desmatamento e da degradação florestal em escala jurisdicional, como estados e países. “Precisamos cumprir integralmente os requisitos previstos no padrão internacional para concluir satisfatoriamente essa etapa”, frisou. Atualmente, o Acre está na oitava das 11 etapas previstas no processo de certificação. Entre os procedimentos ainda necessários estão a conclusão das verificações técnicas e a submissão dos resultados à instância deliberativa da ART. Uma nova etapa está prevista para o primeiro trimestre de 2027, quando auditores deverão visitar comunidades acreanas para realizar verificações relacionadas à certificação. Para Neide, além do rigor técnico, o processo tem uma dimensão social importante, pois os recursos que poderão ser obtidos com a futura comercialização dos créditos deverão contribuir para o desenvolvimento nas comunidades. “Ainda precisamos da aprovação e da submissão ao conselho deliberativo da ART Trees, para que possamos ter os créditos de carbono jurisdicionais disponíveis para negociação”, destacou. Conservação da floresta e geração de oportunidades Victor Hugo Rondon ressaltou que o trabalho busca assegurar o cumprimento de todas as exigências internacionais, considerando também as prioridades sociais e ambientais estabelecidas pelo governo acreano. Segundo o consultor, a estratégia orientada pela governadora integra as políticas de conservação ambiental, valorização das comunidades, participação da sociedade civil e desenvolvimento econômico. A Companhia de Desenvolvimento de Serviços Ambientais (CDSA) também deverá participar das próximas etapas, especialmente das estratégias relacionadas à futura negociação dos créditos certificados. A expectativa do governo é que a certificação abra oportunidades para captar investimentos destinados à agricultura familiar, ao extrativismo sustentável, aos povos indígenas e às comunidades tradicionais, além de fortalecer iniciativas de prevenção ao desmatamento e proteção da floresta. A certificação envolve uma avaliação independente para verificar se os resultados ambientais apresentados atendem aos requisitos estabelecidos. Cada crédito de carbono corresponde a uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e) cuja emissão foi reduzida ou removida, conforme as regras aplicáveis. O IMC continua realizando agendas estratégicas durante a COP31 em defesa da valorização das comunidades. A agenda se desenvolve paralelamente à participação do Acre na COP31, onde o Estado apresenta projetos de desenvolvimento sustentável e busca ampliar o diálogo com governos, investidores e instituições internacionais.

artigo.texto: Amazônia Solar Business chega à 3ª edição com o armazenamento de energia no centro do debate Com inscrições gratuitas, encontro realizado pela Amerenováveis e pelo Sebrae Amazonas acontece no dia 12 de novembro no Clube da OAB Amazonas; No dia seguinte, a presidente da Absolar, Bárbara Rubim, conduz no SebraeLab o Amazônia Solar Business Vip, imersão em armazenamento de energia para 50 participantes Manaus recebe nesta quinta (12) a 3ª edição do Amazônia Solar Business, encontro que reúne empresas, especialistas, instituições e poder público em torno do mercado de energias renováveis na região. Com realização conjunta da Associação Amazonense de Energias Renováveis (Amerenováveis) e do Serviço Brasileiro de Apoio às Micro e Pequenas Empresas no Amazonas (Sebrae Amazonas) e apoio do Polo Sebrae de Energias Renováveis, o evento acontece das 9h às 19h no Clube da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil, Seccional Amazonas (OAB Amazonas), localizado na Avenida Efigênio Salles, bairro Parque 10 de Novembro. A participação é gratuita e as inscrições podem ser feitas pelo link na bio do perfil da Amerenováveis no Instagram (@amerenovaveis). A organização espera 200 participantes, o dobro do público da edição anterior, que reuniu cerca de 100 pessoas. O encontro é voltado a empresários e empreendedores do setor, engenheiros, instaladores, especialistas e representantes de instituições e do poder público. Durante o evento, será sorteada uma bicicleta elétrica Ideal Mutz Banco Estendido, de 500W, oferecida pela patrocinadora Mutz Energia Solar & Mobilidade Elétrica. Com o tema “A Nova Era da Liberdade Energética”, a edição de 2026 vai além da geração solar fotovoltaica. A programação, cujos palestrantes ainda serão anunciados, começa com uma abertura institucional sobre as diretrizes macroeconômicas para o estado e segue com a palestra “O Capital da Transição e o Financiamento da Nova Infraestrutura Energética”. Ao longo do dia, cinco painéis tratam de atualizações regulatórias e reforma tributária, do cenário energético no Amazonas e na Região Norte, da complementaridade entre gás, biomassa, hidrelétricas e solar, de autonomia energética com armazenamento em baterias (os chamados BESS, sigla em inglês para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias), sistemas híbridos e geração off-grid, e de mobilidade elétrica. O encerramento fica com a palestra “BESS: Regulação, Novas Tecnologias e Perspectivas para o Mercado”. Segundo a presidente da Amerenováveis e diretora estadual da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) no Amazonas, Helane Souza, a escolha dos temas parte de uma particularidade do estado: o atendimento a localidades isoladas, que ainda dependem em grande parte do diesel. Ela cita como exemplo o leilão de 2025 para suprimento dos sistemas isolados, que contratou mais de 50 megawatts (MW) em projetos no Amazonas e no Pará com soluções híbridas que combinam diesel, energia solar e baterias. “A edição de 2026 busca discutir não apenas como o setor cresceu, mas qual será o próximo estágio desse crescimento e quais tecnologias, políticas e modelos de negócio serão necessários para sustentá-lo”, afirma. Sebrae aposta na cadeia local Para o Sebrae Amazonas, realizar o evento é uma forma de fortalecer os pequenos negócios do setor, aproximando integradores, empreendedores e empresários locais de grandes empresas e especialistas do segmento. “O setor de energias renováveis no Amazonas apresenta perspectivas positivas de crescimento, impulsionado pelo avanço tecnológico, pela crescente demanda por fontes limpas de energia e pelo fortalecimento da cadeia produtiva local”, avalia Noíra Auzier, gestora do Projeto de Petróleo, Gás e Energia do Sebrae Amazonas. A gestora reconhece que o caminho tem obstáculos, entre eles a qualificação profissional, a logística regional e o acesso a investimentos. Em contrapartida, o segmento abre espaço para novos negócios, geração de emprego e renda e ganho de competitividade para as empresas amazonenses. Esta é a segunda edição do Amazônia Solar Business realizada em parceria entre o Sebrae e a associação. “Por meio de parcerias estratégicas e eventos como este, buscamos contribuir para um ambiente cada vez mais competitivo, sustentável e preparado para acompanhar o crescimento do mercado, gerando impactos positivos para as empresas, os profissionais e a economia do Amazonas”, salienta. Amazônia Solar Business Vip Na sexta (13), é a vez do SebraeLab Amazonas, na Avenida Leonardo Malcher, Centro, receber o Amazônia Solar Business Vip, encontro exclusivo para 50 participantes com a presidente da Absolar, Bárbara Rubim, e a equipe da Solfácil. Também realizado pela Amerenováveis e pelo Sebrae Amazonas, o encontro tem vagas sorteadas entre os inscritos no evento do dia 12. Advogada especialista em regulação do setor elétrico, Bárbara é diretora de Energia da Federação das Indústrias do Estado de São Paulo (Fiesp) e vice-presidente Jurídica e de Relações Institucionais da Solfácil, além de sócia da Bright Strategies, consultoria de estruturação de projetos renováveis. Nos últimos cinco anos, participou do desenvolvimento de mais de 780 MW em projetos e capacitou mais de 8.300 profissionais. Para ela, a regulamentação do armazenamento avançou, com regras de autorização tanto para sistemas autônomos quanto para os associados à geração, mas ainda precisa consolidar as condições de operação, contratação e remuneração dos serviços. No caso amazonense, vê espaço concreto para a tecnologia, com uma ressalva. “Nos sistemas isolados, a combinação de solar e baterias pode reduzir o consumo de diesel e a exposição às dificuldades de transporte de combustível. No Amazonas, a capacidade de sustentar a operação localmente é determinante para que o benefício previsto se concretize”, pontua. artigo.texto: Groups ask DEQ to reject application for public water supply to serve data center project Quantica wants well to facilitate ‘hyperscale data center,’ hides ‘true scope’ of project, groups allege A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images) Approving a water supply well to serve the Quantica Big Sky Campus would “hide the true scope” of a data center project that could be the largest in Montana history, a group of watchdog and conservation organizations allege in a letter to a state agency. But a Department of Environmental Quality spokesperson said the agency is still reviewing public comment about the well application — such as the one from the groups — and additional environmental review could be warranted. Quantica Big Sky Campus is a 5,100-acre data center development located 30 miles north of Billings, according to a May news release from Quantica Infrastructure. Quantica said the site, near Broadview, is designed to support “multiple data center buildings,” with the first expected to be operational in 2029. Big Sky Digital Infrastructure, of Quantica, and consultant Tetra Tech submitted an application to the Department of Environmental Quality for testing a public water supply well. The DEQ describes the project as a proposed well that would provide water during construction and, later, drinking water for the campus. In a news release and application, Quantica said the campus is expected to use as much as 150,000 gallons of water per day to support workforce needs and construction activities during the construction phase, and water use would “decline significantly” to 20,000 gallons a day during operations. The DEQ describes the site construction footprint for the well as roughly 100 feet by 100 feet and said the maximum footprint needed to house “the necessary water treatment” would be “similar to a small shed.” The DEQ also said the well may be used to “provide cooling water” to the data center’s cooling system. In an initial decision, the DEQ found the project qualified for a “categorical exclusion,” or an exemption from closer environmental scrutiny in the Montana Environmental Policy Act. The groups ask the DEQ to withdraw that decision. In an extensive letter, the 13 organizations represented by Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center said the application is asking the DEQ to review the project in “piecemeal fashion,” and in doing so, disregarding the effects of the “massive” undertaking. The groups also allege the DEQ’s ambiguous permitting process interferes with the constitutionally protected right to know and right to participate. “DEQ and Quantica must release additional information about the proposed data center and any associated electricity generation assets — including a reported 1,785-megawatt gas plant — to ensure that the public can meaningfully participate in a public comment process,” the groups said. They call on the DEQ to reject the application as flawed and incomplete, deny Quantica’s request to expedite the application, and conduct a full environmental impact statement, or complete review, including greenhouse gas emissions. “Documents submitted to DEQ prove that the well exists solely to facilitate a much larger undertaking, including a hyperscale data center,” said a letter from the groups. “Quantica asks DEQ to hide the true scope of this project from the public by seeking review of the application in isolation.” They said DEQ records show Quantica is pursuing permits for 585 megawatts of gas-fired engines and 1,200 megawatts of gas-fired turbines, which “exceeds the combined capacity of every gas plant now operating in Montana.” They also said much more details are needed from Quantica or the DEQ about the proposed cooling system, such as how much water needs to be added periodically, any chemicals added, and what happens when the system is flushed. The organizations submitting the letter are the following: Butte Watchdogs for Social and Environmental Justice, Citizens for Clean Energy, Families for a Livable Climate, Honor the Earth, Montana Conservation Voters, Montana Environmental Information Center, Montana Health and Climate, Montana Public Interest Research Group, Northern Plains Resource Council, Park County Environmental Council, Sierra Club Montana Chapter, Upper Missouri Waterkeeper and 350 Montana. On Oct. 21, DEQ announced it had extended the public comment period for the water supply well through Nov. 6. Monday, a spokesperson for the DEQ said the agency will begin reviewing comments, and an environmental impact statement is possible. “DEQ will consider the public comments and supporting information and determine whether additional environmental review is warranted,” said DEQ spokesperson Madison McGeffers. A spokesperson for Quantica did not comment Monday on the letter from the groups, but the company earlier said it is focused on responsible development that “pays its own way for power, creates good jobs and invests in local communities.” In a statement in August, Big Sky Digital Infrastructure general counsel Damon Obie said he grew up on a ranch in Montana and doesn’t take water for granted. “We designed the Big Sky Campus to use minimal water and to source it deep underground, away from the wells our neighbors rely on,” Obie said. “Protecting Montana’s water is a responsibility we take seriously.” In the letter, the groups present a lengthy review of the project and call for more information about it. They allege the DEQ is providing contradictory information about the project — for example, describing just “one public water supply well” in one document that would exempt the project from a full environmental review while not acknowledging a second well referenced in the application. “Granting Quantica’s application would authorize the first water-supply infrastructure for what may become one of the largest industrial developments in Montana’s history,” the groups said. artigo.texto: New battery claims 2000km of driving range: Lithium-air to smash solid-state batteries and would revolutionise 2026 Zeekr 7X, Tesla Model Y, Geely EX5 Dom works as CarsGuide's News Editor after starting his career at the Sydney Morning Herald's Drive section before moving into News Corp's automotive coverage. Read full bio CarsGuide puts every effort into ensuring the accuracy of the information it publishes. Double-check the details that matter to you before buying. Learn more about how we fact check. Key takeaways: - CATL — the world's largest EV battery maker — is working on a new type of battery dubbed lithium-air - Lithium-air batteries are claimed to be 14 times more energy dense that standard batteries - They are claimed to be capable of pushing driving range past 2000km on a single charge Battery makers have only scratched the surface with what is possible from electric car cells, but an all-new type of battery could be the holy grail of energy sources. Dubbed lithium-air batteries, this new type of cells could deliver a driving range of more than 2000km and energy density of five times more than the game-changing solid-state batteries. This new technology is still in its infancy but CATL — the world’s largest electric car battery maker - has been working behind the scenes and has reportedly claimed lithium-air batteries are CATL's future strategic direction. How lithium-air batteries work Conventional lithium-ion batteries are a closed system with lithium-ion moving between the positive and negative electrodes when charging and discharging. Lithium-air batteries are open and use oxygen from the air to react with lithium. This creates a chemical reaction that creates energy. This reaction is claimed to be reversible, with ‘charging’ used to break the lithium and oxygen molecules apart, with the oxygen released back into the air. This means they are a lot lighter than regular batteries because they use oxygen gathered from an external source rather than an element contained in the closed environment. This leads to a higher energy density per cell and fantastical theoretical driving range claims. On paper this means they can hold up to 3500Wh per kg, which is 14 times more than standard Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) batteries and more than five times more potent than even the densest solid-state battery targets. Subscribe to our newsletter Stay up to date with the CarsGuide weekly newsletter By subscribing you agree to our Privacy Policy. When will lithium-air batteries become a reality There are several hurdles the cells face according to Chinese reports. These include the size of the prototype cells that make them unsuitable for vehicles. Air isn’t just made up of oxygen and can cause side reactions. They aren’t as efficient as current batteries, with lots of energy lost as heat during charging. For now these cells are only theoretical, with no production versions to speak of. That puts them at least a decade away. Solid-state batteries started to make noise at the start of this decade, but still have not become a reality. So don’t expect these lithium-air cells to magically appear overnight, but one can dream of an EV with 2000km of range and with little need for many unsustainable raw materials. artigo.texto: European real asset investment platform MetaWealth signed the purchase agreement on November 4th for the third project in its Romanian battery energy storage (BESS) program, a standalone 50 MW / 100 MWh system located in Dolj County. Total investment in the new project is estimated at approximately €20 million. Together with the Dumbrava and Sânpaul projects, the portfolio reaches 148 MW / 300 MWh, with all three projects due to start commercial operation in 2027. The new project comes less than three months after MetaWealth secured a €19 million financing package for Dumbrava, the program’s first project in August. The package includes a seven-year senior credit facility of approximately €10 million from CEC Bank. The Dumbrava project, already under construction, is scheduled to reach commercial operation in Q2 2027. At Sânpaul, construction starts in Q1 2027, with commercial operation planned for Q3 2027. With the Dolj project, the program reaches Oltenia, after Moldavia and Transylvania. The Dolj project is ready to build, as the land has been secured, the technical grid connection approval has been issued and the building permit has been obtained, the company said in a statement. The site is close to a grid node, which reduces connection costs and risks. Construction is scheduled to start in Q2 2027, with commercial operation expected in Q3 2027. MetaWealth’s model is based on acquiring projects that already hold the necessary permits and can move straight into construction. The three projects will come online in a critical year for the energy system. Unit 1 of the Cernavodă nuclear power plant, which supplies around 10% of the country’s electricity generation, is due to be taken offline in 2027 for a 32-month refurbishment, according to Nuclearelectrica. The adequacy study prepared for Transelectrica shows that, under the reference scenario, the adequacy standard required of the system could not be met in 2027, with most critical situations occurring in winter, at times of peak demand. Storage facilities absorb electricity when generation exceeds demand, for example at midday, when solar output is high, and release it during peak hours. At the beginning of October, Romania’s installed storage capacity was about 2.31 GWh. For 2027, the same adequacy study estimates a need for approximately 6000 MWh of battery storage. “In August, our 100 MWh Dumbrava project reached financial close with CEC Bank. Less than three months later, we have three projects in three regions of the country, all scheduled to reach commercial operation in 2027,” said Michael Topolinski, Founder & CEO of MetaWealth. “Investor demand for bonds financing our battery storage projects has been very strong. For 2028, our goal is to achieve commercial operation for an additional 500 MWh. We are building a platform designed to grow over the long term, in an energy system that needs storage capacity.” At Dumbrava, Parapet Group is working on site. Equipment deliveries are under way: the main transformer, the power conversion systems (PCS) and the medium-voltage (MV) skids are already at the Port of Constanța, and the batteries are due to arrive there between 20th of November and 4th of December. In parallel, MetaWealth has launched a divestment process for the Dumbrava project which will run up to the project’s Commercial Operation Date in Q2 2027. To date, six offers have been received and over a dozen interested parties are in the process, including large renewable energy funds, European energy companies and internationally listed investors. The divestment is part of the program’s model: the first three projects are developed through to commercial operation and sold to realise the development margin, while subsequent projects will remain in MetaWealth’s portfolio for energy arbitrage and long-term trading.

artigo.texto: BOISE, Idaho — The Boise City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to approve a six-month moratorium on mega data centers within city limits, following a proposal from Mayor Lauren McLean. WATCH: Boise approves 6-month pause on large data centers The moratorium temporarily stops new large data centers over 100,000 square feet or that require more than 200 megawatts of power. City staff said the 100,000-square-foot threshold comes from the scale it evaluated as having the potential for detrimental impacts on neighbors and the surrounding environment. Sydney Hair fought back tears at the podium Tuesday night, telling Boise City Council members she's worried about what the growth of artificial intelligence and the data centers that support it could mean for her future. "AI has been pretty devastating for my generation because it's been almost impossible to find a job," she said. READ MORE | Why now? Boise mayor explains push to pause mega data centers before any are proposed Hair graduated with a creative writing degree in 2022. She said she's struggled to find work in her field and has instead found jobs centered around training AI. "I don't like the future that we are headed towards with what AI currently is right now and what data centers currently are right now," Hair said. Hair was far from the only person asking the city to slow down. Every person who testified Tuesday spoke in favor of the moratorium, raising concerns about water, power, land and the environment. "Who cares what profit could be gained if it devastates water and power resources we need to survive? We cannot eat or drink data," Alyssa Banner said. Some residents wanted the city to go further, calling for an outright ban. But city staff member Hannah Brass Greer said the six-month pause will give the city time to figure out what it can legally regulate. "Is it a land use that we can outright ban? I don't think we can do that right now, so the moratorium gives us the time to look into that," Brass Greer said. Council member Jimmy Hallyburton said Idaho's private property rights can make some restrictions difficult, and he doesn't expect data centers to disappear completely. "We're adding to the use of those data centers every single day. You use them when you're using your phone, you're using them when you're posting social media," Hallyburton said. "There is a need for data centers and there will continue to be a need, and that's why it's so important that we have to figure out a way to do them right." The moratorium will go into effect immediately. This story was initially reported by a journalist and has been, in part, converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. artigo.texto: Moura lança na Fenatran nova bateria para máquinas agrícolas Companhia reforça sua atuação em soluções de energia para o agronegócio com a Moura M100HA Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de sua linha pesada desenvolvida para atender às exigências elétricas cada vez mais complexas de máquinas agrícolas. Segundo levantamento da Companhia Nacional de Abastecimento (Conab), a safra brasileira de grãos 2026/27 poderá alcançar 367,1 milhões de toneladas, alta de 1,4% sobre o ciclo anterior. A área prevista de plantio chega a 85,4 milhões de hectares, expansão de 2,3%. Ao mesmo tempo, a Anfavea registra queda de 15,8% nas vendas de máquinas agrícolas de janeiro a agosto de 2026. Com a renovação mais lenta, preservar a disponibilidade dos equipamentos ganha peso na gestão da safra. A indisponibilidade de uma máquina pode exigir socorro, reparos e reprogramação de atividades, além de afetar o ritmo de outros equipamentos envolvidos no plantio ou na colheita. Ao apresentar a M100HA, a Moura reforça sua atuação em soluções de energia para o agronegócio, com suporte de sua rede nacional de pós-venda e destinação ambientalmente adequada das baterias ao fim da vida útil. "No campo, a produtividade não depende apenas da capacidade da máquina, mas de ela estar disponível quando o clima permite operar. Uma falha na partida pode interromper uma frente de trabalho inteira. Por isso, a escolha da bateria deve considerar o motor, as condições de uso e a instalação elétrica", afirma Felipe Godoy, Diretor de Negócios Corporativos e Novos Mercados da Rede Moura. Além do esforço exigido na partida de motores a diesel, tratores e colheitadeiras incorporam atualmente computadores de bordo, GPS, telemetria, sensores e iluminação auxiliar. Esses recursos exigem conexões elétricas confiáveis. Com o motor ligado, o sistema de geração assume o fornecimento de energia. À bateria cabe garantir a corrente de partida e as funções previstas no projeto. A M100HA é uma bateria chumbo-ácido de 12 volts e 100 ampères-hora, com corrente de partida a frio de 930 ampères. Um de seus diferenciais é o posicionamento dos terminais, adequado aos chicotes originais de determinadas máquinas agrícolas. Quando a aplicação é compatível, a configuração dispensa extensões, emendas e esforços indevidos nos cabos, fatores que podem comprometer conexões sob vibração. A estrutura interna também contempla proteção e sustentação das placas, além de ligas de chumbo e separadores de alta retenção, recursos voltados à resistência mecânica e à durabilidade. Esses elementos são relevantes para máquinas submetidas à trepidação e ao uso intensivo no campo. A escolha exige observar as especificações do equipamento e não dispensa manutenção preventiva.

artigo.texto: After spending three months developing recommendations on how Fort Worth can best regulate data centers, the Data Center & Infrastructure Commission unveiled its findings to city leaders Tuesday. The 11-member commission developed 19 recommendations across water and natural resources, land use, economic impact and electricity — all of which are detailed in a 156-page report. The committee’s findings, some of which build on existing ordinances, were presented to city council members by Michael Slattery, environmental director at Texas Christian University and director of its Institute for Environmental Studies, who was tapped by the city to lead the advisory group. In a meeting following the presentation, council members also held the city’s first public hearing on Fort Worth’s adoption of the 90-day moratorium, as required by state law. The committee was formed after zoning commissioners in July voted down proposed regulations on zoning requirements for data centers, recommending Fort Worth staffers create stricter ordinances. That vote prompted city officials to make three votes related to data centers on Aug. 11, including the inception of the advisory group and the moratorium process. Slattery prefaced his presentation to council members by saying data center development is the most contested land-use issue in Fort Worth, adding the commission’s goal was to produce an evaluation of data center development based on fact, not advocacy. “Skepticism is healthy and it’s exactly why getting the science right in this commission absolutely mattered,” Slattery said. The report was developed by the advisory group’s 11 members. The formation of the group was approved by the city in early August and consists of representatives with backgrounds in economic development, data centers and related infrastructure, natural resource management and environmental advocacy. The commission and its findings are intended to guide city staffers on how best to regulate data center development amid a nationwide boom in the tech hubs and opposition from communities. The recommendations include a potential regulation for the city to require a “zero-water” solution, echoing what Fort Worth officials proposed earlier this year. Under this regulation, data centers would need to equip a nonevaporative, closed-loop technology supplemented with limited adiabatic cooling — the process of cooling ambient air through controlled evaporation. Commissioners also recommended making water usage publicly available, as well as protecting local water supplies through utility and service reviews. On proposed electricity regulation, the group’s members recommend Fort Worth require a technical fact sheet from developers and include verifiable commitments that would relieve strain on the electric grid. The recommendation related to land use that Slattery spoke to most was the committee’s proposal to protect homes with zoning standards that can be measured. That involves requiring a minimum 350-foot setback between homes and a data center and establishing a framework to enforce noise limits. Setbacks between properties should increase if data centers and their infrastructure’s height increase, Slattery said. Council member Jeanette Martinez said she would like to see larger setbacks between homes and data centers. “I foresee that people will probably make that request,” on increased separations between properties, Martinez said. Asked by council member Chris Nettles how the decision on the proposed setback was made, Slattery explained that the committee analyzed distances between properties in other cities, adding that most residents would like to see data centers located as far away as possible. “We have to find something that is realistic, that is enforceable. I absolutely hear what you say,” Slattery said. In a briefing with reporters following the presentation, Slattery said the biggest disagreements among the commission’s members came on the decision to recommend a 350-foot setback. It was critical for recommendations from the group’s members to be science- and research-backed, Slattery added. The land-use proposals also call on the city to include thermal impacts and community feedback on data centers in Fort Worth’s 2050 comprehensive plan, the document that details the city’s vision and long-term planning. The recommendations covering the report’s four sectors were developed to tailor what city officials have authority over. The document details that major power decisions are made by power distributors and state officials. Council member Elizabeth Beck asked why land-use recommendations did not detail zones in which data centers can be developed. The committee decided to not make recommendations on how data centers should be zoned so the city could put in place regulations that would be protective of residents without restricting the data center industry, Slattery said. “I don’t want that to sound like advocacy. … The data center developers that I spoke with wanted certainty and they wanted predictability. And they said, ‘Whatever you folks come up with, we will work with,’” Slattery said. The commission’s report comes as lawmakers prepare to deliberate various facets of data center operations and development in the upcoming 90th legislative session. Fort Worth officials went back-and-forth on creating and implementing data center regulations earlier this year, stating local control could be affected by directives from Gov. Greg Abbott — while he serves the remainder of his term — and laws that come out of the Texas Capitol in 2027. During her campaign run, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa said she would continue a statewide data center moratorium until legislators meet in January, adding she would pass “real protections” for communities, The Texas Tribune reported. A day after bill filing opened, the Legislature’s agenda was filled with hundreds of bills, including proposals on regulating data centers. State Rep. Salman Bhojani, D-Eule

artigo.texto: Nove organizações, incluindo Greenpeace, fazem atos e abaixo-assinado para exigir a suspensão de projetos até que o país tenha estudos de impacto e regras rigorosas. Atividades aconteceram em Fortaleza, Belém e Pindamonhangaba, onde há projetos em andamento. Confira as fotos de todas as atividades aqui São Paulo, 9 de novembro de 2026 – Nove organizações da sociedade civil lançaram a mobilização nacional “Parem os mega data centers! O Brasil não é colônia das Big Techs”. A iniciativa pede que nenhum projeto de centro de dados de hiperescala avance no país enquanto não houver estudos de impacto, licenciamento ambiental completo e uma lei que garanta participação das comunidades atingidas. O lançamento aconteceu em 6 de novembro com atos em Fortaleza (CE), Belém (PA) e Pindamonhangaba (SP), onde há projetos desse tipo, e integra o Dia de Ação Global contra mega data centers, que mobilizou mais de 100 organizações de diferentes países nos dias 6 e 7 de novembro. Assinam o texto: Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil. As organizações pedem ainda o fim das isenções fiscais concedidas ao setor pelo Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em setembro, com previsão de regulamentação pelo Governo Federal ainda neste ano. Na avaliação delas, o país oferece benefícios fiscais, energia e água a essas empresas antes de ter análise dos riscos, planejamento territorial, regras socioambientais e contrapartidas sobre à soberania digital. “Acabamos de testemunhar a interferência dos bilionários da tecnologia no nosso processo eleitoral. Se, por um lado, precisamos regulamentar essas plataformas, por outro, precisamos impedi-las de construir suas casas de máquinas — os data centers — no nosso território da forma como têm feito, transferindo para a nossa população os seus custos socioambientais, sem ganho nenhum pro país”. Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil. “É um absurdo um data center na Amazônia. O Pará já lidera o número de mortes por causa do calor extremo. Nós repudiamos esse projeto.” João Paulo Guimarães, ativista do Amazônia Sem Data Center. “A principal questão para nós está na falta de transparência e total ausência de participação social. Em 2026, é inaceitável um empreendimento desse porte e com grande impacto ambiental, sem que haja um rigoroso licenciamento ambiental”. Mariana Ceres, ativista da Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba. “A ação é fundamental para que as vozes dos territórios cheguem ao mundo e denunciem a ofensiva das big techs contra os bens comuns do Sul Global. Não podemos gerar insegurança energética num país que ainda enfrenta pobreza energética: queremos água e energia para o povo, não para as big techs!” Andréa Camurça, coordenadora de Incidência Política do Instituto Terramar/CE. “Aqui no Rio de Janeiro, estamos acompanhando a chegada de um megaempreendimento que vai afetar a vida de toda a população da cidade, mas que, em momento algum, ouviu o que tínhamos a dizer. Por isso, junto com o Decodifica e o Coding Rights, estamos enfrentando a falta de transparência e exigindo mais estudos de impacto”. Polinho Mota, diretor do Data_labe. Ações no Dia de Ação Global sobre Data Centers As mobilizações no Brasil começaram no dia 6 pela manhã, em Belém. A campanha Amazônia Sem Data Center esteve na comunidade Residencial Miramar Shalon, para uma roda de conversa com os moradores que podem ser impactados pelo projeto BEL1, da Elea Data Centers e Axia Energia. No Ceará, onde o data center do TikTok está em fase avançada de construção, ativistas se reuniram com a população na orla da Praia de Iracema, em Fortaleza, em atividade organizada pelo Instituto Terramar e pelo Greenpeace Brasil. Um caminhão de LED percorreu as ruas da cidade com informações sobre os impactos no aumento da conta de luz e na poluição sonora, além do documentário “Inteligência Natural”, produzido pela Coding Rights, sobre o empreendimento que está sendo construído pelas empresas Omnia e Casa dos Ventos em território indígena Anacé, em Caucaia, na região metropolitana. Já em Pindamonhangaba, a ação foi organizada pelas Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba. Moradores da região se reuniram em uma praça de grande circulação para alertar a população sobre o projeto Riverhook Village 18, planejado para a cidade. O que são data centers Os mega data centers, ou centros de dados de hiperescala, são complexos industriais voltados sobretudo ao treinamento de modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA) por grandes empresas de tecnologia, as Big Techs. Funcionam sem pausa, ocupam grandes áreas e consomem grandes volumes de energia e água para refrigeração. Nas cidades que recebem esses projetos, a preocupação dos moradores vai do barulho contínuo das máquinas à pressão sobre o abastecimento de água e a conta de luz. Petição: https://datacentersnao.org.br/ Sobre o Greenpeace Brasil O Greenpeace Brasil é uma organização ativista ambiental sem fins lucrativos, que atua desde 1992 na defesa do meio ambiente. Ao lado de todas as pessoas que buscam um mundo mais verde, justo e pacífico, a organização atua há mais de 30 anos na defesa do meio ambiente, denunciando e confrontando governos, empresas e projetos que incentivam a destruição das florestas. artigo.texto: Winnebago County begins preparations for potential data centers with community feedback ROCKFORD, Ill. (Rockford News First) - Winnebago County leaders believe now is the time to start planning for a data center, despite none currently being in the works. The preparation started with a Zoning Board of Appeals meeting Tuesday night, where residents were able to share their opinions and what they’d like the potential project to look like. “I don’t think that there’s any reason a data center has to exist in a way that harms anybody’s health, and there’s a lot of people who are very worried about that, and I think that we can assure them that we wouldn’t let that happen,” Winnebago County board member Paul Arena said. Noticing Winnebago County had not yet created any regulations surrounding data centers, Arena brought the conversation to the forefront. “With all the interest that exists among the public about a data center, we thought rather than wait until something is proposed and then having to play catch-up, we would be up front and establish some parameters,” Arena said. Community members were invited to speak their minds on the topic at the meeting. “Environmentally it’s horrendous. What it’ll do to our land, our water, the animals that exist here with the various habitats right there, that’s a no-brainer,” Winnebago County resident and attendee Kim Lowman Vollmer said. However, some of them believe it may already be too late to stop a potential data center. “I suspect that this is lip service and not really a serious attempt to write a regulation with teeth,” fellow Winnebago County resident and attendee Alyson Broman Conn said. For Arena, he said the meeting’s intentions were to assure residents and inform them and developers down the line how a data center would operate in Winnebago County. “The point of this is to kind of dispel that, right? Let people feel comfortable with what’s going on, let them be heard, let them understand,” Arena said. Arena also wants his constituents to know if a data center begins to come to fruition, their voices will be a part of the decision. “If the majority of the community in the end doesn’t want any data center at all under a special use permit, we can consider as a board whether or not we allow anything to happen at all,” Arena said. At this time, Arena adds there are no data centers in the works for Winnebago County and if a developer were to come forward, there is less than a dozen places where one could potentially be built. The Zoning Board of Appeals approved a motion to continue the data centers hearing, with their next meeting scheduled for February 10 of next year. Copyright 2026 Rockford News First. artigo.texto: Solução flexível de armazenamento de energia amplia oportunidades para integradores solares foto DAH SOLAR smart pcs Lançamento da DAH Solar permite adicionar baterias a sistemas fotovoltaicos existentes e atender clientes que buscam backup sem instalar painéis solares O avanço do armazenamento de energia abre novas oportunidades para integradores fotovoltaicos, que podem ampliar seu portfólio e atender clientes com diferentes necessidades. Nesse cenário, a DAH Solar apresenta o Smart PCS, equipamento que permite incorporar baterias a sistemas fotovoltaicos já instalados e criar soluções de backup para imóveis sem geração solar própria. O potencial de mercado é expressivo. O Brasil já reúne mais de 4,65 milhões de sistemas fotovoltaicos de geração distribuída, que somam mais de 53 GW de potência instalada, segundo dados divulgados pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL). Com potência nominal de 2 kW e versões monofásicas de 127V e 220V, o Smart PCS utiliza arquitetura de acoplamento em corrente alternada (AC-coupled). Conectado ao quadro elétrico da instalação, o equipamento permite adicionar armazenamento sem necessariamente substituir o inversor fotovoltaico existente, dependendo das condições técnicas, seja ele tradicional ou baseado em microinversores. Mais possibilidades para o integrador A flexibilidade de aplicação é um dos principais diferenciais do Smart PCS. Além de modernizar sistemas on-grid, o equipamento pode atender residências, apartamentos e estabelecimentos comerciais que não possuem painéis solares, mas precisam manter equipamentos prioritários em funcionamento durante interrupções no fornecimento de energia. Nessa configuração, a bateria pode ser carregada pela rede elétrica e utilizada para alimentar as cargas definidas no projeto durante um apagão, por exemplo. A solução amplia o público potencial dos integradores, que podem oferecer armazenamento e backup mesmo quando a instalação de um sistema fotovoltaico não é viável ou não faz parte dos planos do cliente. Outro diferencial é o protocolo de comunicação aberto, que permite avaliar a integração com baterias de diferentes fabricantes, dependendo dos requisitos elétricos e de comunicação de cada modelo. O sistema permite conectar até 16 baterias em paralelo por PCS, ampliando a capacidade de armazenamento conforme as necessidades do projeto, desde que mantida a potência de 2 kW por equipamento. Além do backup, o Smart PCS permite aplicações de time shifting, com carregamento das baterias em períodos de menor tarifa e utilização da energia armazenada nos horários mais caros, quando as condições tarifárias favorecem essa estratégia. Em configurações específicas, o equipamento também pode contribuir para a formação de uma rede elétrica local (grid forming), viabilizando aplicações em locais sem conexão convencional à rede, como embarcações e regiões ribeirinhas, desde que utilizados os componentes compatíveis e o dimensionamento adequado. “Com o Smart PCS, queremos ampliar as possibilidades de aplicação do armazenamento de energia. O integrador pode atender tanto quem deseja adicionar baterias a um sistema fotovoltaico existente quanto quem precisa de backup, mas não possui painéis solares. Essa flexibilidade permite desenvolver soluções de acordo com as necessidades de cada cliente”, afirma Leonardo Rodrigues, Head Latam de vendas da DAH Solar. Da geração ao armazenamento O Smart PCS integra a estratégia da DAH Solar de ampliar sua atuação em diferentes etapas da cadeia energética. A fabricante chinesa possui um portfólio que inclui módulos fotovoltaicos, inversores, microinversores, baterias de lítio e soluções BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) para aplicações comerciais, industriais e de maior porte. A proposta é oferecer um conjunto integrado de tecnologias, com suporte e pós-venda centralizados para os produtos da marca. Para integradores e distribuidores, a combinação de soluções permite explorar novas configurações de projetos e ampliar o relacionamento com clientes já atendidos, desde a geração fotovoltaica até o armazenamento e o fornecimento de energia de backup. Sobre a DAH Solar Fundada em 2009, a DAH Solar é uma das principais fabricantes chinesas especializadas em desenvolvimento de tecnologia e fabricação de módulos fotovoltaicos, com atuação também na construção e operação de usinas de energia solar. Sua unidade industrial em Hefei possui capacidade anual de produção de 10 GW em módulos e 5,5 GW em células fotovoltaicas, certificadas por órgãos nacionais e internacionais, como CQC, Líder, ISO 9001, ISO 14001, OHSAS 18001, TÜV, CE, CEC, Inmetro e FIDE. Presente em mais de 100 países e estabelecida no Brasil desde 2017, a empresa segue expandindo sua presença global com foco em inovação, eficiência e su stentabilidade. artigo.texto: Moura lança na Fenatran nova bateria para máquinas agrícolas Companhia reforça sua atuação em soluções de energia para o agronegócio com a Moura M100HA Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de sua linha pesada desenvolvida para atender às exigências elétricas cada vez mais complexas de máquinas agrícolas. Segundo levantamento da Companhia Nacional de Abastecimento (Conab), a safra brasileira de grãos 2026/27 poderá alcançar 367,1 milhões de toneladas, alta de 1,4% sobre o ciclo anterior. A área prevista de plantio chega a 85,4 milhões de hectares, expansão de 2,3%. Ao mesmo tempo, a Anfavea registra queda de 15,8% nas vendas de máquinas agrícolas de janeiro a agosto de 2026. Com a renovação mais lenta, preservar a disponibilidade dos equipamentos ganha peso na gestão da safra. A indisponibilidade de uma máquina pode exigir socorro, reparos e reprogramação de atividades, além de afetar o ritmo de outros equipamentos envolvidos no plantio ou na colheita. Ao apresentar a M100HA, a Moura reforça sua atuação em soluções de energia para o agronegócio, com suporte de sua rede nacional de pós-venda e destinação ambientalmente adequada das baterias ao fim da vida útil. "No campo, a produtividade não depende apenas da capacidade da máquina, mas de ela estar disponível quando o clima permite operar. Uma falha na partida pode interromper uma frente de trabalho inteira. Por isso, a escolha da bateria deve considerar o motor, as condições de uso e a instalação elétrica", afirma Felipe Godoy, Diretor de Negócios Corporativos e Novos Mercados da Rede Moura. Além do esforço exigido na partida de motores a diesel, tratores e colheitadeiras incorporam atualmente computadores de bordo, GPS, telemetria, sensores e iluminação auxiliar. Esses recursos exigem conexões elétricas confiáveis. Com o motor ligado, o sistema de geração assume o fornecimento de energia. À bateria cabe garantir a corrente de partida e as funções previstas no projeto. A M100HA é uma bateria chumbo-ácido de 12 volts e 100 ampères-hora, com corrente de partida a frio de 930 ampères. Um de seus diferenciais é o posicionamento dos terminais, adequado aos chicotes originais de determinadas máquinas agrícolas. Quando a aplicação é compatível, a configuração dispensa extensões, emendas e esforços indevidos nos cabos, fatores que podem comprometer conexões sob vibração. A estrutura interna também contempla proteção e sustentação das placas, além de ligas de chumbo e separadores de alta retenção, recursos voltados à resistência mecânica e à durabilidade. Esses elementos são relevantes para máquinas submetidas à trepidação e ao uso intensivo no campo. A escolha exige observar as especificações do equipamento e não dispensa manutenção preventiva.

artigo.texto: 10 de novembro de 2026, às 13:26 A Infineon Technologies elevou sua meta de vendas ligadas a inteligência artificial (IA) para o novo ano fiscal, sinalizando que espera demanda forte por semicondutores e continuidade do ritmo de expansão de data centers. A fabricante alemã de chips informou nesta terça-feira, 10, que a receita de data centers no ano fiscal até setembro de 2027 deve ficar próxima de 4 bilhões de euros, acima da orientação anterior de aproximadamente 2,5 bilhões de euros. A revisão para cima indica que a Infineon vê a demanda por IA permanecendo robusta mesmo após temores de parte do mercado de que a vitória dos democratas com maioria nas duas casas do Congresso dos EUA poderia afetar o ciclo de construção de data centers. Assim como outras empresas que fornecem chips para alimentar data centers, a Infineon tem sido beneficiada por compromissos de investimentos de centenas de bilhões de dólares feitos por grandes grupos de tecnologia para infraestrutura de IA. Suas ações acumulam alta de mais de 45% em 12 meses. A empresa destacou que a IA vem se tornando uma fonte relevante de receita e reduzindo a dependência do setor automotivo, que pressionou resultados nos últimos anos enquanto montadoras consumiam estoques de chips formados no auge da pandemia. O CEO Jochen Hanebeck disse esperar aumento significativo de receita e rentabilidade em 2027, citando como motores principais: semicondutores para fontes de energia de data centers, expansão e modernização da infraestrutura energética, eletromobilidade e veículos definidos por software. Para o ano fiscal de 2027, a Infineon projeta receita de cerca de 20 bilhões de euros, acima dos 16,35 bilhões de euros reportados em 2026. No trimestre encerrado em setembro, a receita subiu 19% em relação ao ano anterior, para 4,71 bilhões de euros, em linha com as previsões. O lucro líquido avançou para 532 milhões de euros, de 231 milhões um ano antes. Analistas, porém, esperavam lucro líquido maior (678 milhões de euros), segundo a Vara Research. artigo.texto: PRESS RELEASE Data Center Power Demand Is Set to Surge, Raising New Climate Challenges: BloombergNEF - A new report from BloombergNEF, commissioned by Bloomberg Philanthropies indicates that data center electricity demand is set to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 7% of global electricity demand. - The rush for “speed to power” is pushing some developers toward on-site gas. BNEF has tracked 181GW of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, with more than 90% in the US. - Policies can help limit near-term emissions impacts, but the appropriate approach varies by market. Faster grid connections, financial commitments, flexible connections, special zones and clean-power procurement are among the approaches reviewed, while continued power-system decarbonization remains vital. New York, November 11, 2026 – Data center power demand is set to surge as developers seek to bring new computing capacity online quickly. BloombergNEF (BNEF) expects data center electricity demand to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 7% of global electricity consumption, according to a new report commissioned by Bloomberg Philanthropies. Powering the Data Center Boom: How Grid Policy Can Deliver Clean Power Faster finds that grid constraints in the US and Europe are delaying new connections for large loads, while the financial rewards for energizing quickly are driving some developers to build on-site gas-fired power as they await a grid connection. BNEF has tracked 181GW of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of which is in the US. The announced pipeline varies widely in maturity and timing and should be viewed as an indication of potential scale rather than a forecast of what will ultimately be built. If all announced on-site gas plants proposed for US data centers were built and operated at the assumptions used by BNEF, they would emit about 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent a year. That would be 152MtCO2e more than if the associated data center capacity were supplied by average US grid electricity, an amount equivalent to 10% of US power-sector emissions in 2025. Although many of these projects are intended to supply power while data centers await a grid connection, BNEF finds that once they are online, the economics could encourage them to continue generating energy, creating a longer-term fossil-fuel lock-in risk beyond the annual emissions. In developed markets such as the US and Europe, ensuring new data centers are grid-connected is the more sustainable option, making faster grid connections important to limiting near-term emissions impacts and fossil-fuel lock-in risk. Continuing to decarbonize the power system in parallel also remains vital.The report reviews policies across 17 markets that aim to accelerate the grid connection process. The policy landscape is still emerging and while many efforts should reduce waiting times for connections, there is currently limited empirical evidence to demonstrate which will be most effective. Mark Daly, Head of Data Centers and Emerging Tech at BloombergNEF said, “The extraordinary economics around AI are making speed to power one of the most important priorities for defining constraints on data center developers. The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand.” In emerging markets, the challenges of mitigating the climate impact of data centers differs. BNEF finds that, where power systems remain heavily reliant on coal, grid-connected data centers can be even worse than those powered by on-site gas. This highlights how much more central it is in these markets to enable more clean generation alongside sources of new power demand. The four emerging markets examined in the report are: - Brazil: BNEF expects almost all incremental generation needed to meet data center demand through 2035 to come from renewables. Large consumers buy directly with renewable generators, and new data center demand could absorb some renewable generation that is currently curtailed, although transmission remains a constraint. - India: Data center electricity demand is expected to rise from 11TWh in 2025 to 91TWh in 2035. Existing coal plants supply much of the additional electricity in the near term under BNEF’s Economic Transition Scenario, but data centers can procure clean power through bilateral and captive projects, and companies are already backing new solar and wind capacity. - Indonesia: Coal and gas supplied 82% of state utility PLN’s on-grid power in 2025. Current rules do not allow data centers to contract directly with independent renewable generators, limiting their ability to link corporate demand clearly to new clean-power capacity. - Malaysia: Data center electricity demand is set to rise from 7TWh in 2025 to 45TWh by 2035. Additional demand is expected to increase the use of existing coal and gas plants in the near term, while continued demand growth is likely to result in new gas capacity and coal life extensions over the longer term. Data centers can contract with third-party renewable generators and are already supporting new solar projects, although network charges can affect the economics of these contracts. The report finds that policies to accelerate grid connections can help limit the near-term emissions impact and fossil-fuel lock-in risk in developed markets, but the challenge differs across markets. Continued power-system decarbonization and frameworks that allow data centers to support additional clean power will also be important as data center electricity demand grows. BloombergNEF clients can find the full report on bnef.com and at this link. O deputado Danilo Forte (PP/CE) promete apresentar nesta terça-feira (10/11) o parecer ao PL 3.716/2026, que muda o rateio dos custos da contratação de baterias, em meio à pressão de associações de geração e armazenamento para aprovar a proposta antes dos leilões de dezembro. A previsão do relator foi antecipada pelo eixos PRO. De autoria de Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), o projeto altera a lei nº 15.269/2025 e retira dos geradores a obrigação de custear sozinhos a contratação, submetendo as baterias à regra geral da reserva de capacidade, o que inclui os consumidores na divisão da conta. A urgência foi aprovada pela Câmara em 13 de outubro. Forte foi designado relator de plenário em 28 de outubro. A apresentação do parecer é o próximo passo para a análise do mérito pelos deputados. Pressão das associações Em carta enviada a seis ministérios em 4 de novembro, Abeeólica, Abihv, Abrage, Abragel, Absae, Absolar e Apine pedem apoio à tramitação e aprovação do projeto antes dos leilões de armazenamento marcados para o início de dezembro. O documento foi dirigido à Casa Civil, Minas e Energia, Planejamento, Desenvolvimento, Fazenda e Secretaria de Relações Institucionais. As entidades argumentam que a reserva de capacidade beneficia o conjunto dos usuários do sistema elétrico e que não há justificativa para aplicar às baterias um regime de custeio diferente das demais tecnologias. Também sustentam que concentrar a cobrança nos geradores não impede o repasse aos consumidores, porque o encargo tende a ser incorporado aos preços da energia. A preocupação é que a indefinição sobre quem paga aumente os riscos e os custos da contratação. Na carta, as associações também alertam para possíveis impactos sobre a implantação dos projetos e os investimentos da cadeia de equipamentos, engenharia e serviços. Os leilões estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Desafios pela frente Um interlocutor das associações avalia que a mudança tem condições de passar com relativa facilidade pela Câmara. O receio é que o relator acrescente outros temas ao parecer, os chamados jabutis. Entre eles, está o critério de adicionalidade, que vincula o atendimento de uma nova demanda de energia à implantação de novos projetos de geração. À eixos, Forte afirmou que pretende incluir a exigência no PL 490/2026, dos data centers verdes, de Duda Ramos (Podemos/RR), que também relata. Um jantar previsto para esta semana com representantes de algumas das entidades, Jardim e Forte foi adiado por causa da COP31, que ocorre entre hoje e 20 de novembro na Turquia. A expectativa é que o encontro ocorra após a votação do PL na Câmara. A passagem do texto pelo Senado é considerada outro desafio para concluir a mudança da legislação antes dos leilões, uma vez que há uma avaliação de que o projeto de lei encontrará maior resistência entre os senadores. Paralelamente ao projeto, a Aneel prepara as regras de rateio sob a legislação vigente. A diretora substituta Ludimila Lima disse à eixos que o edital foi desenhado para absorver eventuais mudanças na lei, além da resolução sobre a divisão dos custos que está em discussão na agência.

artigo.texto: Ohio Chamber study: Data centers added more than $9B to state economy in 2025 COLUMBUS, Ohio (WSYX) — Ohio’s growing data center industry added more than $9 billion to the state’s economy last year, according to a new study commissioned by the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. The study found that data centers and the construction needed to build them supported nearly 70,000 jobs in Ohio last year. About 14,000 people work directly in the data center industry, with average pay and benefits of about $148,000 a year, the report said. Looking ahead, the study estimated that planned construction and equipment spending through 2030 could support more than 257,000 jobs for a year. The report also examined the fiscal impact of incentives and investment tied to the industry. It said the state gave up more than $1.5 billion in tax revenue, but that the investment has generated a $2.7 billion fiscal surplus.
